items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that everyone may slaughter, and their slaughter is valid, except for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, who might ruin their slaughter. If others watch them, their slaughter is valid.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהכל שוחטין ושחיטתן כשרה, חוץ מחרש שוטה וקטן, ואם אחרים רואים אותם שחיטתן כשרה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that everyone may slaughter and their slaughter is valid, except for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, who might ruin their slaughter, but if others watch them, their slaughter is valid.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת וקובעת שהכל שוחטין ושחיטתן כשרה, למעט חרש שוטה וקטן, ואם אחרים רואים אותם שחיטתן כשרה.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על לשון המשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's phrase 'everyone slaughters' implies ab initio, while 'their slaughter is valid' implies post facto, creating a contradiction.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: 'הכל שוחטין' משמע לכתחילה, ואילו 'ושחיטתן כשרה' משמע דיעבד, וזו סתירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction in the Mishnah's phrasing: 'everyone slaughters' implies לכתחילה (the ideal standard), while 'their slaughter is valid' implies בדיעבד (after the fact).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הסתירה בין 'הכל שוחטין' שמשמע לכתחילה לבין 'ושחיטתן כשרה' שמשמע דיעבד.

items.text: Rav Acha's objection from substitution
items.text_en: Rav Acha's objection from substitution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava objects to Rav Ashi: does 'everyone' always mean ab initio? The verse about substitution says 'he shall not substitute', so substitution is forbidden ab initio, yet the Mishnah uses 'everyone substitutes'.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's objection to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava objects to Rav Ashi: if 'everyone' always means לכתחילה (the ideal standard), then the Mishnah's 'everyone substitutes' would imply substitution is permitted לכתחילה, but the verse explicitly forbids it.

items.text: Gemara's answer: substitution is post facto
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: substitution is post facto
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that regarding substitution, the Mishnah means post facto: one is not permitted to substitute, but if he did, it is substituted and he receives lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that regarding substitution, the Mishnah means post facto: one is not permitted to substitute, but if he did, it is substituted and he receives lashes.

items.text: קושייה נוספת ממשנת ערכין
items.text_en: Objection from vows and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a further objection from the Mishnah 'everyone makes valuations and is valued, vows and is vowed', which cannot be ab initio because the Torah discourages vowing. It cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir says it is better not to vow at all, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is better to vow and pay, but even Rabbi Yehuda only permits when one says 'this is...'.
items.desc: רב אחא מקשה ממשנת ערכין: 'הכל מעריכין' – האם גם שם לכתחילה? הרי נאמר 'וכי תחדל לנדור לא יהיה בך חטא'. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על מחלוקת רבי מאיר ורבי יהודה בנדרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah 'everyone makes valuations and is valued, vows and is vowed', asking whether this too is meant לכתחילה (the ideal standard), given the verse discouraging vowing.
sub.desc: רב אחא מקשה ממשנת ערכין: 'הכל מעריכין' – האם גם שם לכתחילה? הרי נאמר 'וכי תחדל לנדור לא יהיה בך חטא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Meir says it is better not to vow at all, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is better to vow and pay, but even Rabbi Yehuda only permits when one says 'this is...'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על מחלוקת רבי מאיר ורבי יהודה בנדרים, ומסיימת שאפילו רבי יהודה מתיר רק באומר 'הרי זו'.

items.text: Gemara's initial challenge: is 'הכל' always ab initio?
items.text_en: Gemara's initial challenge: is 'הכל' always ab initio?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's use of 'הכל' (everyone) implies permissibility ab initio, citing other cases like sukkah and tzitzit where 'הכל' is used ab initio. It then distinguishes between 'הכל' that is ab initio and 'הכל' that is ex post facto, suggesting the Mishnah's 'הכל' might be ex post facto.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that if one says 'I pledge' (a vow), the animal is not subject to the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's use of 'הכל' (everyone) always implies permissibility לכתחילה (ab initio), citing examples like sukkah and tzitzit where 'הכל' is used ab initio.
The Gemara objects that the example of 'הכל סומכין' (everyone may lean) must be ab initio, as the verse commands leaning, so the Mishnah's 'הכל' cannot be purely ex post facto.
The Gemara resolves that there are two types of 'הכל' — one ab initio and one ex post facto — and the Mishnah's 'הכל' might be ex post facto, so the challenge is not decisive.

items.text: Second challenge: the Mishnah's double language
items.text_en: Second challenge: the Mishnah's double language
items.desc_en: A voice objects that the Mishnah's phrase 'שחיטתן כשרה' (their slaughter is valid) indicates ex post facto, implying that 'הכל' in the first clause must be ab initio; otherwise, why mention both?

sub.desc_en: The objector argues that the Mishnah's phrase 'שחיטתן כשרה' (their slaughter is valid) indicates בדיעבד (after the fact), proving that 'הכל' in the first clause must be לכתחילה (the ideal standard), otherwise why mention both?

items.text: פירוש רבה בר עולא למשנה
items.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's resolution: the Mishnah's true meaning
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla explains that the Mishnah actually teaches that everyone may slaughter ab initio, even a tamei person for chullin that are treated with the purity of kodashim. He details the procedure to avoid contact and notes exceptions for deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor.
items.desc: רבה בר עולא מפרש שהמשנה מתירה לטמא לשחוט לכתחילה בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, תוך שימוש בסכין ארוכה כדי לא לגעת בבשר. במוקדשים אסור לכתחילה, אך אם שחט וטוען שלא נגע – שחיטתו כשרה. חרש שוטה וקטן פסולים אף בדיעבד מחשש שהייה, דרסה והחלדה.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla resolves the difficulty by reinterpreting the Mishnah: 'Everyone may slaughter' means even a tamei person may slaughter chullin treated with the purity of kodashim, since such chullin are considered like kodashim.
sub.desc: רבה בר עולא מפרש שהמשנה מתירה לטמא לשחוט לכתחילה בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, משום שהם כקודש.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla describes the procedure: the tamei person brings a long knife and slaughters without touching the meat, to avoid transmitting impurity.
sub.desc: מסביר כיצד הטמא שוחט בלי לגעת בבשר: מביא סכין ארוכה.

sub.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's exception for kodashim
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla adds that for actual kodashim, a tamei person should not slaughter ab initio, but if he did and claims he did not touch the meat, his slaughter is valid after the fact.
sub.desc: מבחין בין מוקדשים, שאסור לכתחילה אך בדיעבד כשר אם טוען ברי שלא נגע.

sub.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's exception for deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla excludes deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor from slaughtering even for ordinary chullin, even after the fact, because they may cause disqualifying delays, pressing, or slipping.
sub.desc: מוציא חרש שוטה וקטן, שאפילו בחולין גרידא שחיטתם פסולה בדיעבד מחשש שהייה, דרסה והחלדה.

items.text: קושיה על פירוש רבה בר עולא
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's final clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrase 'וכולן ששחטו' (and all of them who slaughtered), analyzing whether it refers to the deaf-mute, the tamei in chullin, or the tamei in kodashim, concluding that for kodashim the condition 'ברי לי' suffices.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על פירוש רבה בר עולא: הביטוי 'וכולן ששחטו' – לאיזה מקרה הוא מתייחס? לא לחרש שוטה וקטן (שהרי לא שוחטים כלל), לא לטמא בחולין (שמותר לכתחילה), ולא לטמא במוקדשים (שבבריא לי סגי). המסקנה: מדובר בטמא במוקדשים כשאינו לפנינו לשאול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to which case the Mishnah's phrase 'וכולן ששחטו' (and all of them who slaughtered) refers, considering the deaf-mute, the tamei in chullin, and the tamei in kodashim, and concludes that for kodashim the condition 'ברי לי' suffices.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: לאיזה מקרה מתייחס 'וכולן ששחטו'? לא לחרש שוטה וקטן (שהרי עליהם עומד, והיה צריך לומר 'ואם שחטו'), ולא לטמא בחולין (שמותר לכתחילה).

items.text: מקור הדין לטמא במוקדשים
items.text_en: Source for tamei in kodashim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the law of a tamei person slaughtering kodashim is derived from another source (a baraita listing all unfit individuals). It debates which source is primary and which is secondary.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם דין טמא במוקדשים נלמד מהמשנה כאן או ממשנה בזבחים. התשובה: כאן הוא העיקר, ושם נשנה אגב שאר פסולין; או להיפך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the law of a tamei person slaughtering kodashim is derived from the present Mishnah, and cites a baraita listing all unfit individuals including טמאים (impure persons) in kodashim.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם דין טמא במוקדשים נלמד מהמשנה כאן או ממקור אחר, ומביאה את המשנה בזבחים כראיה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah is the primary source, and the baraita merely includes the case of a tamei person in kodashim incidentally alongside other unfit individuals.
sub.desc: תירוץ ראשון: המשנה כאן היא העיקר, ובזבחים נשנה אגב שאר פסולין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the baraita is the primary source since it deals with kodashim, and the Mishnah includes the case of a tamei person in kodashim incidentally alongside the case of a tamei person in chullin.
sub.desc: תירוץ ראשון: המשנה כאן היא העיקר, ובזבחים נשנה אגב שאר פסולין.

items.text: בירור סוג הטומאה של הטמא
items.text_en: Question about the type of impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of impurity the tamei person contracted, suggesting it might be from a corpse, citing the verse 'בחלל חרב'.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה לברר באיזו טומאה מדובר: האם בטומאת מת? ומביאה פסוק 'בחלל חרב' להקשות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of impurity the tamei person contracted, suggesting it might be from a corpse, citing the verse 'בחלל חרב'.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת באיזו טומאה מדובר, ומציעה טומאת מת תוך הבאת הפסוק 'בחלל חרב'.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על טומאת הסכין והבשר
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a knife can become impure from a corpse and then transmit impurity to the meat, suggesting instead that the meat was impure from a creeping animal, or that the slaughter was done with a reed.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם אדם טמא מת נוגע בסכין, הסכין נעשית אב הטומאה ומטמאת את הבשר. התשובה הראשונה היא שהאדם טמא בשרץ, והשנייה ששחט בקרומית של קנה שאינה מקבלת טומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a knife can become impure from a corpse and then transmit impurity to the meat, suggesting instead that the meat was impure from a creeping animal, or that the slaughter was done with a reed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם אדם טמא מת נוגע בסכין, הסכין נעשית אב הטומאה ומטמאת את הבשר.

items.text: פירוש אביי למשנה: כותי וישראל עומד על גביו
items.text_en: Abaye's interpretation of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the Mishnah permits slaughter by a Cuthean only when an Israelite is supervising, but if the Israelite leaves and returns, the slaughter is invalid. He adds that if the Cuthean slaughtered, the Israelite cuts a piece of meat and gives it to him; if eaten, the slaughter is permitted, otherwise not. Excluded are deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors, whose slaughter is invalid even after the fact.
items.desc: אביי מפרש שהמשנה מתירה לכתחילה שחיטת כותי רק כשישראל עומד על גביו, אבל ביוצא ונכנס אסור לכתחילה. אם שחט בלא השגחה, בודקים על ידי נתינת כזית בשר לכותי – אם אכלו מותר, ואם לאו אסור. חוץ מחרש שוטה וקטן ששחיטתם פסולה אף בדיעבד.

sub.desc_en: Abaye introduces his interpretation of the Mishnah: the Mishnah permits slaughter by a Cuthean only when an Israelite is supervising, but if the Israelite leaves and returns, the Cuthean may not slaughter לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
sub.desc: אביי פותח בפירוש המשנה: הכול שוחטין ואפילו כותי, אך לכתחילה רק כשישראל עומד על גביו, לא ביוצא ונכנס.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds the בדיעבד (after the fact) rule: if the Cuthean slaughtered, the Israelite cuts a piece of meat and gives it to him; if the Cuthean eats it, the slaughter is permitted, otherwise it is forbidden.
sub.desc: אביי ממשיך: בדיעבד, אם שחט בלא השגחה, בודקים על ידי נתינת כזית בשר לכותי – אם אכלו מותר, ואם לאו אסור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye excludes deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors, whose slaughter is invalid even בדיעבד (after the fact), due to concerns of שהייה (pausing), דריסה (pressing), or החלדה (covering the knife).
sub.desc: אביי מסיים: חוץ מחרש שוטה וקטן ששחיטתם פסולה אף בדיעבד, שמא ישהו, ידרסו, או יחלידו.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על פירוש אביי: 'וכולן ששחטו'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Abaye's version
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'and all who slaughtered' in the Mishnah: if it refers to deaf-mutes etc., it should say 'if they slaughtered'; if to a Cuthean, then Abaye said that with supervision he may slaughter even initially, so the case of 'if he slaughtered' is irrelevant.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על פירוש אביי: הביטוי 'וכולן ששחטו' – אם הכוונה לחרש שוטה וקטן, היה צריך לומר 'ואם שחטו'; ואם הכוונה לכותי, הרי אמרת שכשישראל עומד על גביו שוחט לכתחילה, וקשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: 'And all who slaughtered' — what does it refer to? If it refers to deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, then the phrase 'if they slaughtered' would be needed!
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הביטוי 'וכולן ששחטו' – אם הכוונה לחרש שוטה וקטן, היה צריך לומר 'ואם שחטו'.

items.text: דחיית רבא: יוצא ונכנס מותר לכתחילה
items.text_en: Rava's initial challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye's ruling that a Cuthean may not slaughter initially when the Israelite leaves and returns, citing a Mishnah where leaving and returning is permitted. The Gemara distinguishes: the cited Mishnah uses 'one who leaves' (מניח) for an after-the-fact case, but Rava brings a different source that permits leaving and returning even initially.
items.desc: רבא מקשה על אביי: מדוע יוצא ונכנס אסור לכתחילה? הרי ממשנה בעבודה זרה משמע שמותר לכתחילה. הגמרא דוחה את הראיה הראשונה (מניח נכרי בחנות) כי שם מדובר בדיעבד, אך מביאה ראיה ממשנה אחרת (שומר יוצא ונכנס) שמותר לכתחילה.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye's ruling that a Cuthean may not slaughter לכתחילה (the ideal standard) when the Israelite leaves and returns, citing a Mishnah where leaving and returning is permitted.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה על אביי: מדוע יוצא ונכנס אסור לכתחילה? הרי משנה במסכת עבודה זרה מתירה יוצא ונכנס.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes the cited Mishnah as a בדיעבד (after the fact) case, then brings an alternative source that permits leaving and returning even לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה ממשנה אחרת בעבודה זרה ששומר יוצא ונכנס מותר לכתחילה.

items.text: פירוש רבא למשנה: יוצא ונכנס מותר לכתחילה
items.text_en: Rava's revised interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: a Cuthean may slaughter initially even when the Israelite leaves and enters; only if the Israelite finds him already slaughtered must he test by giving a piece of meat. The Gemara again questions the phrase 'and all who slaughtered', and Rava's version also faces a contradiction since he permits initial slaughter even when leaving and entering.
items.desc: רבא מפרש שהמשנה מתירה לכתחילה שחיטת כותי כשישראל יוצא ונכנס, ורק אם בא ומצאו ששחט בלא השגחה כלל – בודקים בנתינת כזית בשר. הגמרא מקשה שוב על הביטוי 'וכולן ששחטו' – אם הכוונה לכותי, הרי יוצא ונכנס מותר לכתחילה, וקשה.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: a Cuthean may slaughter לכתחילה (the ideal standard) even when the Israelite leaves and enters; only if the Israelite finds him already slaughtered must he test by giving a piece of meat.
sub.desc: רבא מפרש את המשנה: כותי שוחט לכתחילה כשישראל יוצא ונכנס, ואם בא ומצאו ששחט – בודקים בנתינת כזית בשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrase 'and all who slaughtered' (וְכוּלָּן שֶׁשָּׁחֲטוּ) in Rava's version, arguing that if it refers to the deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor, the Mishnah should have used 'and if they slaughtered' (וְאִם שָׁחֲטוּ) instead.
sub.desc: רבא מוסיף שהחרגת חירש שוטה וקטן נשארת, ושחיטתם פסולה אפילו בדיעבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the phrase refers to a Cuthean, Rava's version permits him to slaughter even when the Israelite leaves and enters, contradicting the need for a test.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הכוונה לכותי, הרי יוצא ונכנס מותר לכתחילה, וקשה.

items.text: פירוש רב אשי: ישראל משומד
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah refers to a Jewish apostate who eats neveilot for appetite, citing Rava's principle about such an apostate.
items.desc: רב אשי מפרש שהמשנה עוסקת בישראל משומד האוכל נבילות לתיאבון, ושחיטתו כשרה בדיעבד כשישראל יוצא ונכנס, כדברי רבא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains the baraita: 'Everyone slaughters, even an apostate Israelite. Apostate for what? To eat neveilot for appetite.'
sub.desc: רב אשי מיישב את סתירת המשנה בכך שעוסקת בישראל משומד האוכל נבילות לתיאבון, ושחיטתו כשרה בדיעבד כשישראל יוצא ונכנס, כדברי רבא.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who checks the knife and gives it to a slaughterer may eat from the slaughter; if he did not check, he must check afterward; if the knife is found to be good, the meat is permitted, otherwise forbidden. It then lists exceptions: a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor, whose slaughter is invalid even after the fact due to concerns of pausing, pressing, or inserting the knife.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for checking the knife before slaughter and the exceptions for a deaf-mute, an imbecile, and a minor.

items.text: Gemara's question on 'וכולן ששחטו'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on 'וכולן ששחטו'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom the phrase 'וכולן ששחטו' (and all of them who slaughtered) refers. It rejects the possibility that it refers to the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, as the Mishnah already states their slaughter is invalid; it would need to say 'ואם שחטו' (if they slaughtered). It then suggests it refers to a Jewish apostate, but raises difficulties: if the knife was checked, it is permitted initially; if not checked, why not check it now? And if the knife is not present, what do others seeing him help? Perhaps he slaughters with a defective knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom the phrase 'וכולן ששחטו' (and all of them who slaughtered) refers.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that it refers to the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, because the Mishnah already states their slaughter is invalid and would need to say 'ואם שחטו' (if they slaughtered).
The Gemara suggests the phrase refers to a Jewish apostate, but raises difficulties: if the knife was checked, it is permitted initially; if not checked, why not check it now?
The Gemara objects: if the knife is present, check it now; if not, what do others seeing him help? Perhaps he slaughters with a defective knife.

items.text: Ravina's first version: 'הכל מומחין שוחטין'
items.text_en: Ravina's first version: 'הכל מומחין שוחטין'
items.desc_en: Ravina explains the Mishnah differently: 'הכל שוחטין' means 'all experts may slaughter', even if they are not established (מוחזקין). The Mishnah then clarifies: if one knows the laws of slaughter, he may slaughter initially; if not, he may not slaughter initially, but if he did, we examine him; if he knows the laws, his slaughter is permitted, otherwise forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Ravina introduces a new version of the Mishnah: 'הכל מומחין שוחטין' (all experts may slaughter), meaning experts even if not established (מוחזקין).

Ravina explains the distinction: one known to know the laws of slaughter may slaughter לכתחילה (ab initio); one not known is examined after the fact, and his slaughter is permitted only if he demonstrates knowledge.

items.text: Gemara's question on Ravina's version
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Ravina's version
items.desc_en: The Gemara again asks about 'וכולן ששחטו' in Ravina's version. It rejects that it refers to the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor. It then suggests it refers to those who are not experts (שאין מומחין), but objects: examining them should suffice! The Gemara answers: the case is where the examiner is not present to examine him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the phrase 'וכולן ששחטו' (and all of them who slaughtered) refers to in Ravina's version, rejecting that it refers to the deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor because the Mishnah would then need to say 'ואם שחטו' (and if they slaughtered).

The Gemara suggests that 'וכולן' refers to those who are not experts (שאין מומחין), but objects that examining them should suffice, and answers that the case is where the examiner is not present to examine him.

items.text: Ravina's second version: 'הכל מוחזקין שוחטין'
items.text_en: Ravina's second version: 'הכל מוחזקין שוחטין'
items.desc_en: An alternative version: Ravina said the Mishnah means 'all who are established (מוחזקין) may slaughter', even if not experts. The Mishnah clarifies: if they slaughtered before us two or three times without fainting, they may slaughter initially; if not, they may not, lest they faint. If they slaughtered and said 'I am certain I did not faint', the slaughter is valid.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version: Ravina said the Mishnah means 'all who are established (מוחזקין) may slaughter', even if not experts.
Ravina clarifies: if they slaughtered before us two or three times without fainting, they may slaughter initially; if not, they may not, lest they faint.
If they slaughtered and said 'I am certain I did not faint', the slaughter is valid.
The Gemara questions the clause 'And any of them who slaughtered' — if it refers to deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor, the phrasing should be 'And if they slaughtered'.

items.text: Gemara's question on the second version
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the second version
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about 'וכולן ששחטו' in the second version: it refers to those who are not established (שאין מוחזקין), but you said that claiming 'I am certain' suffices! The answer: the case is where the person is not present to be asked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the clause refers to those who are not established (שאין מוחזקין), but you said that claiming 'I am certain' suffices, why is supervision needed?
The answer: the case is where the person is not present before us so that we can ask him whether he fainted.

items.text: Discussion of Amoraim's positions on the difficulty of 'וכולן'
items.text_en: Discussion of Amoraim's positions on the difficulty of 'וכולן'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Ravina, Rabbah bar Ulla, Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi each did not adopt certain positions due to the difficulty of the phrase 'וכולן'. It explains that all did not hold like Rabbah bar Ulla because of a dispute about whether the primary context is here or in tractate Kodashim. All did not hold like Ravina because of assumptions about the majority being experts or concerns about fainting. Rava did not hold like Abaye due to his own difficulty; Abaye did not hold like Rava because of a distinction about contact with a corpse. Rav Ashi did not hold like both because he considered Samaritans as true converts. Abaye did not hold like Rav Ashi because he did not accept Rava's reasoning. The Gemara then asks why Rava did not hold like his own teaching, and answers that he was speaking according to Abaye's reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that Ravina, Rabbah bar Ulla, Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi each did not adopt certain positions due to the difficulty of the phrase 'וכולן'.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for Rabbah bar Ulla
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for Rabbah bar Ulla
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that all did not hold like Rabbah bar Ulla because of a dispute about whether the primary context is here or in tractate Kodashim, and because חולין (non-sacred meat) prepared with the purity of sacred meat is not considered like sacred meat.

The Gemara explains that all did not hold like Ravina because, according to one version, the majority of people near slaughter are experts, and according to another version, we are not concerned about fainting.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for Rava and Abaye
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for Rava and Abaye
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava did not hold like Abaye due to his own difficulty, and Abaye did not hold like Rava because of a distinction about contact with a corpse.
The Gemara explains that Rav Ashi did not hold like both because he considered Samaritans as true converts.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation for Abaye regarding Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation for Abaye regarding Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Abaye did not hold like Rav Ashi because he did not accept Rava's reasoning.
The Gemara asks why Rava did not hold like his own teaching.
The Gemara answers that Rava was speaking according to Abaye's reasoning, but he himself did not hold that view.

items.text: Baraita on Samaritan slaughter
items.text_en: Baraita on Samaritan slaughter
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: the slaughter of a Samaritan is permitted. This applies when an Israelite stands over him; but if one finds him having already slaughtered, he cuts an olive-sized piece and gives it to him; if he ate it, the slaughter is permitted, otherwise forbidden. Similarly, if one finds a knife in his hand...

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that Samaritan slaughter is permitted, with the condition that an Israelite stands over him; if found already slaughtered, a test piece is given.
The baraita adds a parallel case: if one finds a knife in the Samaritan's hand, the same rule applies.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The case of the bird decoy
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The case of the bird decoy
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where a bird decoy is used; if the decoy eats from the slaughtered bird, the slaughter is permitted, otherwise it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a bird decoy: if the decoy eats from the slaughtered bird, the slaughter is permitted; otherwise it is forbidden.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's interpretations of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's interpretations of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava derive different rulings from the Mishnah: Abaye infers that only if the Israelite stands over the decoy is it valid, while Rava infers that even if the decoy comes and goes, it is valid. They resolve the apparent contradictions by reinterpreting the terms.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Abaye infers from the Mishnah's first clause and Rava infers from its last clause.
Abaye infers from the first clause that only if the Israelite stands over the decoy is the slaughter valid, but if he comes and goes, it is not.
Rava infers from the last clause that even if the decoy comes and goes, the slaughter is valid.
The Gemara objects that the last clause contradicts Abaye, and Abaye answers that even a decoy that comes and goes is called 'came and found it'.
The Gemara objects that the first clause contradicts Rava, and Rava answers that even a decoy that comes and goes is considered as if standing over it.

items.text: Question about finding a bird decoy in hand
items.text_en: Question about finding a bird decoy in hand
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions a similar case: if one finds a bird decoy in someone's hand, why is it permitted? Perhaps it is the same bird that was slaughtered properly. Rav Menasheh and Rav Mesharshiya explain that the decoy is placed under the wing and the bird is handled, ensuring it is not the same one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: in a similar case where one finds a bird decoy in hand, why is it permitted? Perhaps it is the same bird that was slaughtered properly.
Rav Menasheh answers that the decoy is placed under the wing, ensuring it is not the same bird.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the decoy was given a distinguishing mark inside it, so it could still be the same bird.
Rav Mesharshiya answers that the decoy is handled and rubbed, so any mark would be erased, ensuring it is not the same bird.

items.text: Addressing the concern about Kutim's belief in bird slaughter
items.text_en: Addressing the concern about Kutim's belief in bird slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the possibility that Kutim do not believe in the Torah's requirement for bird slaughter. It counters by noting that other slaughter details (like shehiyah, derasah) are not written explicitly, yet Kutim are trusted because they have established a tradition. Similarly, here they are trusted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the objection that perhaps the Kutim do not believe in the Torah's requirement for bird slaughter.

The Gemara counters by noting that other slaughter details like שהייה (pausing), דרסה (pressing), חלדה (covering), הגרמה (slipping), and עיקור (displacing) are not written explicitly in the Torah either.
The Gemara resolves that just as Kutim are trusted for those details because they have established a tradition (אחזוקי), here too they are trusted for bird slaughter.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about Kutim's reliability
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about Kutim's reliability
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute regarding Kutim's matzah: the first Tanna permits it, Rabbi Elazar forbids it, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says they are meticulous. The Gemara analyzes the differences between them, focusing on whether the commandment is written or whether they have established a tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute about Kutim's reliability regarding a commandment that is not written but which they have adopted.
The baraita states that matzah of a Kuti is permitted and one fulfills his obligation with it on Passover.
Rabbi Elazar forbids it because Kutim are not expert in the fine details of commandments like Israel.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that for any commandment Kutim have adopted, they are more meticulous than Israel.
The Gemara questions why the first Tanna's ruling is not obvious, and explains it teaches that Kutim are expert in guarding matzah.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar holds Kutim are not expert in guarding matzah.
The Gemara asks whether Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's statement is identical to the first Tanna's.
The Gemara explains the difference: for a written commandment they have not adopted, the first Tanna permits it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires adoption.
The Gemara objects that if the difference is about adoption, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel should have said 'if they adopted' rather than 'any commandment they adopted'.
The Gemara resolves that the actual dispute is about an unwritten commandment they have adopted: the first Tanna rejects it, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel accepts it because they are meticulous.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a Jewish apostate's slaughter
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a Jewish apostate's slaughter
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a Jewish apostate who eats non-kosher meat for appetite may be given a checked knife, and his slaughter is permitted. The Gemara questions why checking is necessary, and the rabbis cite a supporting baraita about the chametz of sinners.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that a Jewish apostate who eats non-kosher meat for appetite may be given a checked knife, and his slaughter is permitted.
Rava explains the reasoning: since the apostate has both permitted and forbidden food available, he will not abandon the permitted to eat the forbidden.
The Gemara objects: if so, even without checking the knife, the apostate would not bother to slaughter improperly.
The rabbis cite a supporting baraita to Rava about the chametz of sinners after Passover, which parallels the case.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bread baked by non-Jews after Passover is permitted immediately because they exchange their dough.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that bread baked by non-Jews after Passover is permitted immediately because they exchange their dough.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that chametz after Passover is a biblical prohibition, and the reasoning 'because they exchange' implies people do not leave permitted food for forbidden. It then considers Rabbi Shimon, who holds it is rabbinic, and argues that even according to Rabbi Shimon, the Mishnah states 'because they exchange' as a certainty, so the principle applies a fortiori to biblical prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna the Mishnah follows, suggesting it is Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects that it might be Rabbi Shimon, who holds chametz after Passover is only rabbinic, and leniency applies only to rabbinic laws, not biblical ones.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi Shimon, the Mishnah states 'because they exchange' as a certainty, so the principle applies a fortiori to biblical prohibitions.

items.text: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah about slaughter
items.text_en: Supporting evidence from the Mishnah about slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that everyone may slaughter, including a Cuthean, an uncircumcised person, and an apostate Israelite. It clarifies that the uncircumcised person is an apostate to circumcision, and this supports the principle that an apostate to one thing is not an apostate to the entire Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a supporting baraita that everyone may slaughter, including a uncircumcised Jew, and explains that this refers to one who is a apostate regarding circumcision, implying that an apostate for one matter is not an apostate for the entire Torah.

items.text: Analysis of the apostate in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Analysis of the apostate in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the case of the apostate Israelite in the Mishnah, concluding that it must refer to an apostate to that specific matter (idolatry), as per Rava's principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the latter clause of the baraita, 'even a apostate Israelite', and asks what type of apostate this refers to.
The Gemara answers that it must refer to an apostate for a different matter, not the same one, in accordance with Rava's principle.

items.text: Rejection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rejection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the previous explanation, arguing that an apostate to that specific matter (idolatry) would consider it permitted. Instead, it explains that the Mishnah refers to an apostate to idolatry, and cites Rav Anan quoting Shmuel that such an apostate's slaughter is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this, explaining that an apostate for the same matter is not considered an apostate for the entire Torah because he treats the forbidden act as permitted.
The Gemara concludes that the apostate in the baraita is one who is an apostate for idolatry, citing Rav Anan in the name of Shmuel that such a person's slaughter is permitted to eat.
Rav Anan quotes Shmuel that an Israelite apostate to idolatry (עבודה זרה) is permitted to eat from his slaughter.

items.text: Proof from Jehoshaphat and Ahab
items.text_en: Proof from Jehoshaphat and Ahab
items.desc_en: Rav Anan quoting Shmuel brings a proof from Jehoshaphat king of Judah, who benefited from Ahab's feast, as it is written: 'And Ahab slaughtered for him sheep and cattle in abundance.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan cites Shmuel's ruling that an apostate for idolatry's slaughter is permitted, citing the precedent of Jehoshaphat partaking of Ahab's feast.

items.text: Challenges and defenses of the proof
items.text_en: Challenges and defenses of the proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises several challenges: perhaps Ahab only slaughtered but Jehoshaphat did not eat; perhaps the enticement was only through words; perhaps Jehoshaphat only drank but did not eat; perhaps Obadiah slaughtered; perhaps the seven thousand prophets slaughtered; perhaps Ahab's men were righteous; perhaps Jehoshaphat's men were not righteous. Each challenge is answered, ultimately supporting the proof.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps Ahab only slaughtered but Jehoshaphat did not eat, and that the enticement was only through words, not actions.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing verses showing that enticement can involve eating and drinking, though it distinguishes the case of Job's enticement as different.
The Gemara challenges that perhaps Jehoshaphat only drank but did not eat, and the Gemara responds that if drinking is permitted for an idolater, eating should also be permitted.
The Gemara objects that drinking was permitted because gentile wine had not yet been forbidden, but eating might still be forbidden if the idolater is considered a total apostate.

The Gemara offers two alternative answers: either it is not the way of a king to drink without eating, or the verse 'וַיִּזְבַּח … וַיְסִיתֵהוּ' indicates that the enticement was through the slaughter itself.
The Gemara challenges that perhaps Obadiah slaughtered, and answers that the verse says 'לָרוֹב' (in great quantity), which Obadiah could not have supplied.
The Gemara challenges that perhaps the seven thousand prophets slaughtered, and answers that they were hiding from Jezebel.

The Gemara challenges that perhaps Ahab's men were righteous, and answers with the verse 'מֹשֵׁל מַקְשִׁיב עַל דְּבַר שֶׁקֶר כׇּל מְשָׁרְתָיו רְשָׁעִים' (a ruler who listens to falsehood, all his servants are wicked).
The Gemara challenges that perhaps Jehoshaphat's men were not righteous, and answers that from the same verse, one who listens to truth has righteous servants.
The Gemara raises a final challenge: perhaps Ahab and his men ate the slaughter of Ahab's men, and Jehoshaphat and his men ate the slaughter of Jehoshaphat's men, leaving the proof unresolved.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Who may slaughter?
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Who may slaughter?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anyone may slaughter, including a Cuthean, an uncircumcised man, or even a Jewish meshummad. The Gemara begins questioning the definition of meshummad.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anyone may slaughter, including a Cuthean, an uncircumcised man, or even a Jewish meshummad.
The Gemara asks what the case of the uncircumcised man is, and suggests that if his brothers died from circumcision, he is a full-fledged Jew.
The Gemara concludes that the uncircumcised man is a meshummad with regard to circumcision, i.e., he refuses to be circumcised.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Defining meshummad
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Defining meshummad
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is a meshummad only one who rejects a single commandment (like circumcision), or one who rejects idolatry entirely? It cites a baraita distinguishing partial vs. total apostasy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the latter clause of the baraita: the case of a Jewish transgressor must be a meshummad (apostate) for idolatry, supporting Rav Anan.
The Gemara rejects that interpretation, citing the principle that a meshummad (apostate) for idolatry is considered a meshummad (apostate) for the entire Torah.
The Gemara reinterprets the transgressor in the latter clause as one who is a meshummad (apostate) for that specific matter (eating unslaughtered carcasses), in accordance with Rava's opinion.
A baraita is cited that derives from the verse 'מִכֶּם' (from you) that offerings are not accepted from a meshummad (apostate), except for certain categories, raising an objection to Rav Anan.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita: it first excludes a meshummad (apostate) but then says offerings are accepted from Jewish transgressors.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the baraita
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: the first clause excludes a total apostate (meshummad to the whole Torah), while the middle clause excludes one apostate to a single matter (like idolatry or Sabbath desecration in public).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the first clause refers to a total apostate (meshummad to the entire Torah), while the middle clause refers to an apostate to a single matter.

The Gemara challenges the resolution by analyzing the last clause: if the apostate there is a total apostate, it duplicates the first clause; if an apostate to one matter, it contradicts the middle clause.

The Gemara concludes that the last clause refers to an apostate for idolatry or public Sabbath desecration, proving that such an apostate is considered a total apostate, which refutes the opinion of רב ענן (Rav Anan).

items.text: Final conclusion: Meshummad to idolatry = total apostate
items.text_en: Final conclusion: Meshummad to idolatry = total apostate
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a meshummad to idolatry is considered an apostate to the entire Torah, and thus excluded from korbanot. This resolves the earlier objection.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the halakha excluding a meshummad from korbanot is derived from the verse there (regarding sin offerings), not from the verse cited here.

items.text: Opening statement: Meshummad excluded from 'am ha'aretz'
items.text_en: Opening statement: Meshummad excluded from 'am ha'aretz'
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the phrase 'me'am ha'aretz' to exclude a meshummad (apostate) from the category of am ha'aretz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the phrase 'me'am ha'aretz' to exclude a meshummad (apostate) from the category of am ha'aretz.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei's ruling and Rav Hamnuna's distinction
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei's ruling and Rav Hamnuna's distinction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei cites Rabbi Shimon that one who does not repent from his knowledge does not bring a sin-offering. Rav Hamnuna explains the difference between this view and the previous one: a meshummad for eating chelev who brings a sacrifice for blood.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei citing Rabbi Shimon
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei cites Rabbi Shimon that one who does not repent from his knowledge does not bring a sin-offering for his inadvertent transgression.
The gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two positions (the previous anonymous view and Rabbi Shimon's view).
Rav Hamnuna answers that the difference is a meshummad (apostate) for eating chelev who brings a sacrifice for blood.

items.text: Need for both cases: sin-offering and burnt-offering
items.text_en: Need for both cases: sin-offering and burnt-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (sin-offering and burnt-offering) are necessary: each has a unique aspect that would otherwise lead to a mistaken leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both cases (sin-offering and burnt-offering) are necessary, each teaching a unique aspect that prevents a mistaken leniency.

items.text: Discussion of 'behemah' as a derogatory term
items.text_en: Discussion of 'behemah' as a derogatory term
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether 'behemah' always indicates inferiority, citing a verse where it is praiseworthy, and distinguishes between cases where 'behemah' stands alone versus paired with 'adam'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the term 'בהמה' (beast) always implies inferiority.

The Gemara objects by citing a verse where 'בהמה' is used in a praiseworthy context, and cites Rav Yehuda and Rav's interpretation that it refers to people who are clever in knowledge but humble themselves like beasts.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: there the term is paired with 'אדם' (man), but here 'בהמה' stands alone, indicating inferiority.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic 'niklaf' is provided to aid memory of the following discussion.

sub.desc_en: The mnemonic 'niklaf' is introduced to aid memory of the following discussion.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's ban on Samaritan slaughter and Rabbi Zeira's question
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's ban on Samaritan slaughter and Rabbi Zeira's question
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan reports in a chain that Rabban Gamliel and his court voted to forbid Samaritan slaughter. Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether this applies only when no Jew supervises; Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi rebukes him for asking an obvious question.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanan's report via Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanan's report via Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan reports in a chain that Rabban Gamliel and his court voted to forbid Samaritan slaughter.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether the ban applies only when no Jew supervises the Samaritan.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi rebukes Rabbi Zeira for asking an obvious question, implying the ban applies even with a Jew present.

items.text: Did Rabbi Yochanan accept the ban?
items.text_en: Did Rabbi Yochanan accept the ban?
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Assi ate from Samaritan slaughter. Rabbi Zeira wonders if they were unaware of the ban or rejected it. He concludes they must have known and rejected it, reasoning that God would not cause righteous people to sin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yochanan accepted the ban on Samaritan slaughter or not, based on Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's report that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Assi ate from it.
Rabbi Zeira resolves that they must have heard the ban and rejected it, reasoning that God would not cause righteous people to sin.

items.text: Conclusion that Rabbi Meir's decree was accepted
items.text_en: Conclusion that Rabbi Meir's decree was accepted
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Meir's decree had not been accepted, the earlier contradiction could have been resolved by distinguishing between when a Jew is present and when not. Since this distinction was not made, it proves the decree was accepted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if Rabbi Meir's decree had not been accepted, the earlier contradiction could have been resolved by distinguishing between when a Jew is present and when not; since this distinction was not made, it proves the decree was accepted.

items.text: Reason for the decree and the story of the dove
items.text_en: Reason for the decree and the story of the dove
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Sages decreed against Samaritans, citing a story where Rabbi Meir sent Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to bring wine from Samaritans, and an old man warned him with a verse. Rabbi Shimon reported to Rabbi Meir, who then decreed. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains they found a dove idol on Mount Gerizim, and Rabbi Meir, concerned for the minority, decreed due to the majority. Rabban Gamliel and his court agreed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages decreed against Samaritans.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the old man
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar and the old man
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story where Rabbi Meir sent Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar to bring wine from Samaritans, and an old man warned him with a verse, leading Rabbi Meir to decree against them.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Samaritans were found worshipping a dove idol on Mount Gerizim, and Rabbi Meir, concerned for the minority, decreed due to the majority, with Rabban Gamliel and his court agreeing.

items.text: פשוטו של מקרא: 'ושמת סכין בלועך'
items.text_en: Interpretation of the verse used in the story
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the plain meaning of the verse cited by the old man, applying it to a student sitting before his teacher: if the student knows the teacher can respond, he should engage; if not, he should be silent and leave.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'ושמת סכין בלועך' על תלמיד היושב לפני רבו, ומסבירה כיצד על התלמיד לנהוג לפי יכולתו של הרב להשיב על שאלותיו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara digresses to explain the plain meaning of the verse cited in the story, interpreting it as referring to a student sitting before his teacher, with conditions for when to speak and when to withdraw.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על פשוטו של הפסוק 'ושמת סכין בלועך' במה הכתוב מדבר, ומביאה את דברי רבי חייא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya teaches that the verse applies to a student sitting before his teacher.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת על פשוטו של הפסוק 'ושמת סכין בלועך' במה הכתוב מדבר, ומביאה את דברי רבי חייא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse: if the student knows the teacher can respond, he should engage; if not, he should be silent and leave.
sub.desc: הברייתא מפרטת: אם התלמיד יודע שרבו יודע להחזיר לו טעם – ישאל, ואם לאו – יבין את אשר לפניו וישים סכין בלועו, ואם בעל נפש הוא – יפרוש ממנו.

items.text: הפיכת הכותים לגויים גמורים
items.text_en: Another story: Rabbi Avahu and the Samaritans declared complete gentiles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak ben Yosef was sent by Rabbi Avahu to bring wine from Samaritans, but an old man said there are no Torah observers there. Rabbi Yitzchak reported to Rabbi Avahu, who told Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, and they declared the Samaritans complete gentiles. The Gemara questions why this was necessary if a decree already existed, and explains that the earlier decree was not accepted, but Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi's decree was accepted. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchac explains that 'complete gentiles' means they are considered gentiles for the laws of nullifying and granting domain.
items.desc: הגמרא מספרת כיצד רבי אמי ורבי אסי גזרו על הכותים והפכו אותם לגויים גמורים, ומסבירה שמדובר בביטול רשות ונתינת רשות בשבת.

items.text: דיני ביטול רשות ונתינת רשות
items.text_en: Baraita on a Jewish apostate and domain laws
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that a Jewish apostate who publicly keeps Shabbat can nullify and grant domain, but one who does not keep Shabbat cannot. The Gemara explains that a Jew can grant or nullify domain, while a gentile must rent. The method of acquisition is described.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרטת את ההבדל בין ישראל משומד השומר שבת לבין זה שאינו שומר, ואת דיני ביטול רשות ונתינת רשות לגבי גוי.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules that a Jewish apostate who publicly keeps Shabbat can nullify and grant domain, while one who does not keep Shabbat cannot.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בהבחנה בין ישראל המשומר שבת, שיכול לבטל רשות, לבין מי שאינו שומר שבת, שאינו יכול.

sub.desc_en: The baraita explains the general rule: a Jew can grant or nullify domain, while a gentile must rent.
sub.desc: הברייתא מבארת את הטעם: ישראל יכול לבטל רשות, אבל גוי צריך לשכור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes the method of acquisition: the owner says 'my domain is acquired by you' or 'my domain is nullified for you,' and the recipient acquires without formal acquisition.
sub.desc: הברייתא מדגימה כיצד מבטלים רשות: באמירת 'רשותי קנויה לך' או 'רשותי מבוטלת לך', וקונה בלא צורך בקניין.

items.text: תערובת דמאי וחשש תקלה לצדיקים
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Asi about demai mixture
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Asi were served eggs cooked in wine. Rabbi Zeira did not eat, questioning the mixture of demai. Rabbi Asi ate, saying he did not think about it. Rabbi Zeira then argued that if even the animals of the righteous are not caused to stumble, surely the righteous themselves are not. He then found a mishnah stating that one who buys wine for mixtures is liable for demai, but the mixtures themselves are permitted because they are a mixture, implying no decree on demai mixtures.
items.desc: הגמרא מספרת על רבי זירא ורב אסי שאכלו ביצים מבושלות ביין, ורבי זירא חשש לתערובת דמאי, ולאחר מכן מצא ברייתא המתירה תערובת דמאי, ומסיק שלא גזרו על תערובת דמאי.

sub.desc_en: The gemara recounts that Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Asi visited an inn and were served eggs cooked in wine; Rabbi Zeira did not eat, but Rabbi Asi did.
sub.desc: מסופר שרבי זירא ורב אסי התארחו בפונדק, הוגשו להם ביצים שבושלו ביין, רבי זירא נמנע מלאכול ורב אסי אכל, וכשנשאל רב אסי אם אינו חושש לתערובת דמאי השיב שלא עלה על דעתו.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Asi why he is not concerned about the mixture of demai (doubtfully tithed produce), and Rabbi Asi replies that he did not think about it.
sub.desc: מסופר שרבי זירא ורב אסי התארחו בפונדק, הוגשו להם ביצים שבושלו ביין, רבי זירא נמנע מלאכול ורב אסי אכל, וכשנשאל רב אסי אם אינו חושש לתערובת דמאי השיב שלא עלה על דעתו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects that if the Sages decreed against demai mixtures, it is impossible that Rabbi Asi would eat forbidden food, arguing from the principle that the righteous are not caused to stumble.
sub.desc: רבי זירא מהרהר: האם ייתכן שגזרו על תערובת דמאי, ורב אסי אכל איסור? הרי אם אין הקב"ה מביא תקלה על ידי בהמות צדיקים, קל וחומר שלא יביא תקלה על ידי צדיקים עצמם.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's finding of a mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira finds a mishnah stating that one who buys wine for mixtures is liable for demai, but the mixtures themselves are permitted because they are a mixture, proving that no decree was made on demai mixtures.
sub.desc: רבי זירא יצא, בדק ומצא ברייתא הקובעת שתערובת דמאי מותרת, ולכן לא גזרו על תערובת דמאי, ומכאן שרב אסי לא אכל איסור.

items.text: Debate on whether the Sages decreed on demai mixtures
items.text_en: Debate on whether the Sages decreed on demai mixtures
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the conclusion from the mishnah with a baraita about a woman baking with her neighbor's dough, where she is not concerned for demai unless told to use her own. The Gemara distinguishes because when told to use her own, it is like mixing by hand. Rafram adds that leaven and spices are for flavor, which is not nullified. Another challenge about exchanging is answered by Rabbi Yehuda's explanation that a mother-in-law wants to fix her daughter's marriage and is embarrassed before her son-in-law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the earlier conclusion by citing a baraita that a woman baking with her neighbor's dough is not concerned for demai mixtures.
The baraita adds that if she is told to use her own dough, she must be concerned for demai.
The Gemara distinguishes that when told to use her own, it is like mixing by hand, which is a direct action.
Rafram adds that leaven and spices are for flavor, which is not nullified in a mixture.
The Gemara objects with a mishnah about a mother-in-law exchanging goods, implying concern for substitution.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the mother-in-law wants to fix her daughter's marriage and is embarrassed before her son-in-law, so she does not exchange.

items.text: Opening question: Must we suspect exchange?
items.text_en: Opening question: Must we suspect exchange?
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens by questioning whether we must suspect exchange (halipha) when giving items to a storekeeper, citing a mishna that a storekeeper suspected of exchanging must tithe both what he gives and takes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we never suspect exchange, citing a mishna that one who gives to a storekeeper suspected of exchanging must tithe both what he gives and takes.

items.text: Objection: Why not suspect exchange with a friend's wife?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not suspect exchange with a friend's wife?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not suspect exchange when a friend's wife grinds with an am ha'aretz? A baraita says she may grind when unclean but not when clean, implying no suspicion of exchange.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not suspect exchange when a friend's wife grinds with an am ha'aretz? It cites a baraita that permits grinding when she is טמאה (ritually impure) but forbids when she is טהורה (pure), implying no suspicion of exchange.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Elazar's stricter view
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elazar's stricter view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elazar adds: even when unclean she should not grind, because her friend gives her and eats, implying exchange suspicion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon bar Elazar adds that even when the woman is טמאה (ritually impure) she should not grind with her friend, because the friend might give her food to eat, creating suspicion of exchange.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: Storekeeper case is different
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: Storekeeper case is different
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the storekeeper case is different because she explicitly says 'Torah from my threshing floor I eat', implying no theft, so exchange is not suspected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the storekeeper is suspected of outright theft, would she not certainly be suspected of exchanging?
Rabbi Yosef answers: there too she is afraid and says 'I eat Torah from my threshing floor,' so exchange is not suspected.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's testimony about Beit She'an
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's testimony about Beit She'an
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz testified before Rabbi Meir that Rabbi Meir ate a leaf of vegetables in Beit She'an, and Rabbi Meir permitted the entire city based on that precedent.

sub.text: Testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz
sub.text_en: Testimony of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz testified before Rabbi Meir that Rabbi Meir ate a leaf of vegetables in Beit She'an, and Rabbi Meir permitted the entire city based on that precedent.

items.text: Family objection: Why permit where ancestors forbade?
items.text_en: Family objection: Why permit where ancestors forbade?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir's brothers and father's house objected: why permit a place where your ancestors forbade? They argued that the precedent of Asa and Jehoshaphat burning idolatry shows one must follow ancestral prohibitions.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir's brothers and father's house
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's brothers and father's house
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir's family objects: why permit a place where your ancestors forbade, implying ancestral prohibition is binding.

Rabbi Meir cites the verse about Hezekiah destroying the copper serpent, arguing that even Asa and Jehoshaphat, who burned all idolatry, did not destroy it, showing ancestral practice is not always binding.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's scriptural defense: Asa and Jehoshaphat did not burn all
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's scriptural defense: Asa and Jehoshaphat did not burn all
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir responds by citing the verse about the copper serpent that Moses made, which Israel burned later. He argues: could Asa and Jehoshaphat have failed to burn it? No, they burned all idolatry, so ancestral practice is not absolute.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir cites the verse about King Hezekiah destroying the copper serpent, arguing that since Asa and Jehoshaphat burned all idolatry, ancestral practice is not absolute.

items.text: The principle of not uprooting a Torah scholar's ruling
items.text_en: The principle of not uprooting a Torah scholar's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a place was left for the scholar to distinguish himself, and derives from this that a Torah scholar's halachic statement is not to be moved or abandoned. Three versions of the phrase are given, each supported by a biblical or mishnaic source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Sages left a place for the scholar to distinguish himself, and Rabbi Yosei applies this to himself.
The Gemara derives from this that a Torah scholar's halachic statement is not to be moved, with three versions of the verb given.

The Gemara supports each version of the verb with a biblical or mishnaic source: 'מזיחין' from the verse about the breastplate, 'מזניחין' from the verse about God not forsaking, and 'מזחיחין' from the mishna about haughty hearts increasing disputes.

items.text: The status of Beit She'an and cities not conquered by the returnees from Babylon
items.text_en: The status of Beit She'an and cities not conquered by the returnees from Babylon
items.desc_en: Judah son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi objects to the assumption that Beit She'an is not part of Eretz Yisrael, citing a verse that Menashe did not drive out its inhabitants. The Gemara resolves this by citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's tradition that many cities were conquered by those who returned from Egypt but not by those who returned from Babylon, and the first sanctification was only for its time, not for the future, leaving them for the poor in the Sabbatical year.

sub.text: Judah son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's objection
sub.text_en: Judah son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's objection
sub.desc_en: Judah son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi objects to the assumption that Beit She'an is not part of Eretz Yisrael, citing the verse that Menashe did not drive out its inhabitants.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's tradition
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's tradition
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim's tradition that many cities were conquered by those who returned from Egypt but not by those who returned from Babylon.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the halachic status
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the halachic status
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first sanctification was only for its time, not for the future, leaving these cities for the poor in the Sabbatical year.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's consumption of vegetables and the principle of righteous people
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's consumption of vegetables and the principle of righteous people
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about Rabbi Meir eating vegetables from Beit She'an, which might be exempt from tithes. Rabbi Zeira answers that he ate from a bundle, and the Mishnah states that bundled vegetables become obligated. The Gemara then questions whether it might have been unintentional, but argues that if God does not bring a stumbling block through the animals of the righteous, certainly not through the righteous themselves. Further objections about tithing from a different place or eating from one side while looking at another are dismissed by noting the greatness of the witness.

sub.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question to Rabbi Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira how Rabbi Meir could eat vegetables from Beit She'an, which might be exempt from tithes.
Rabbi Zeira answers that Rabbi Meir ate from a bundle, and the Mishnah states that bundled vegetables become obligated in tithes.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Meir ate unintentionally, without knowing the vegetables were obligated.
The Gemara rejects the objection by arguing that if God does not cause a stumbling block through the animals of the righteous, certainly not through the righteous themselves.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Meir tithed from a different place, which is invalid.
The Gemara rejects the objection by stating that associates (חֲבֵרִים) are not suspected of tithing from a non-adjacent source.
The Gemara objects that perhaps Rabbi Meir looked at one side of the bundle and ate from another, which might avoid the obligation.
Rabbi Zeira dismisses the objection by pointing to the greatness of the witness (Rabbi Meir) who testifies about the practice.

items.text: The story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the river Ginai
items.text_en: The story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and the river Ginai
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts the story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair going to redeem captives. He commands the Ginai River to split for him, which it does after initially refusing. The river also splits for a man carrying wheat for Passover and for an Arab traveler, to avoid a bad reputation. Rav Yosef marvels at the three miracles, comparing them to the single miracle at the Red Sea with Moses and six hundred thousand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is meant by 'the animals of the righteous' and introduces the story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair was going to redeem captives and encountered the Ginai River.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair commands the Ginai River to split its waters so he can cross.
The Ginai River objects, arguing that it is certainly fulfilling its Creator's will while Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's success is uncertain.

sub.text: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's threat and the river's compliance
sub.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's threat and the river's compliance
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair threatens to decree that no water ever pass through the river, and the river splits for him.

sub.text: Second miracle for the man with wheat
sub.text_en: Second miracle for the man with wheat
sub.desc_en: The river also splits for a man carrying wheat for Passover, at Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's request, because the man is engaged in a מצוה (commandment).

sub.text: Third miracle for the Arab traveler
sub.text_en: Third miracle for the Arab traveler
sub.desc_en: The river splits a third time for an Arab traveler accompanying them, to avoid a bad reputation for the Jewish people.
Rav Yosef marvels that Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair is greater than Moses and six hundred thousand, because at the Red Sea there was only one miracle, while here there were three.
The Gemara objects that perhaps here too it was only one miracle, and Rav Yosef's statement is clarified to mean that Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair is comparable to Moses and six hundred thousand.

items.text: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refuses to eat untithed grain
items.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refuses to eat untithed grain
items.desc_en: The story continues: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair arrives at an inn, and they place barley before his donkey, but it does not eat, indicating that the barley was not properly tithed.

sub.desc_en: The narrative recounts that Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair arrived at an inn, and they placed barley before his donkey, but it refused to eat.

items.text: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's refusal to eat untithed food and the Gemara's discussion on demai
items.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's refusal to eat untithed food and the Gemara's discussion on demai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refuses to eat untithed food, leading him to suspect it was not tithed. After tithing, the donkey eats. The Gemara questions whether the donkey was obligated in tithes, citing a mishnah that exempts certain purchases from demai. Rabbi Yochanan clarifies that the exemption applies only if originally bought for animal use, but if bought for human consumption and then redirected to animal, tithing is required.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey refuses to eat untithed food, and after tithing it eats, prompting his exclamation about feeding טבלים (untithed produce) to an animal going to do its Creator's will.
The Gemara questions whether the donkey was obligated in tithes, citing a mishnah that exempts purchases for animal use from דמאי (doubtfully tithed produce).
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the exemption applies only if originally bought for animal use, but if bought for human consumption and then redirected to animal, tithing is required.
A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling: one who buys produce for human consumption and then decides to give it to an animal must tithe before feeding it.

items.text: Rabbi invites Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair to eat, but he declines due to a vow
items.text_en: Rabbi invites Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair to eat, but he declines due to a vow
items.desc_en: Rabbi goes out to greet Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair and invites him to eat. Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair initially agrees, causing Rabbi's face to brighten. However, Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair then explains that he is not under a vow, but rather that some Israelites are generous and some are not, citing a verse. He says he is currently busy with a mitzvah and will come later.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi hears that Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair is coming, goes out to greet him, and invites him to eat; Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair initially agrees, causing Rabbi's face to brighten.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair objects that he is not under a vow, but explains that some Israelites are generous and some are not, citing a verse, and notes that Rabbi is both willing and able.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair resolves that he is currently busy with a mitzvah and will come to Rabbi later.

items.text: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair sees white mules and refuses to enter, leading to a miracle
items.text_en: Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair sees white mules and refuses to enter, leading to a miracle
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair returns, he sees white mules at Rabbi's entrance and declares that the Angel of Death is in Rabbi's house, so he will not eat there. Rabbi explains he sells them, but Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair cites the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind. Rabbi offers to abandon them, but Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair notes the loss, then rejects killing them due to bal tashchit. A mountain rises between them, and Rabbi weeps, citing Rabbi Chama bar Chanina that the righteous are greater in death than in life, as seen with Elisha's bones reviving a dead man.

sub.desc_en: When Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair returns, he encounters white mules at Rabbi's entrance and declares that the Angel of Death is in Rabbi's house, so he will not eat there.
Rabbi goes out to meet him and explains that he sells the mules, implying they are not a permanent fixture.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair objects by citing the prohibition of placing a stumbling block before the blind, implying that selling the mules would cause others to stumble.

Rabbi offers to abandon the mules, but Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair notes the loss; Rabbi then suggests uprooting them, but is told there is צער בעלי חיים (suffering of living creatures); finally Rabbi suggests killing them, but is told there is a prohibition of בל תשחית (do not destroy).
A mountain rises between them, and Rabbi weeps, citing Rabbi Chama bar Chanina that the righteous are greater in death than in life, as seen with Elisha's bones reviving a dead man.

items.text: Discussion on Elisha's revival of the dead man
items.text_en: Discussion on Elisha's revival of the dead man
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye if the revival was merely to fulfill Elisha's blessing for a double portion of Elijah's spirit. Abaye rejects this, citing a baraita that the man stood on his feet but did not go home, implying he was fully revived. Rabbi Yochanan explains that Elisha's merit revived him because he healed Naaman's leprosy, which is considered like death.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether the revival of the dead man was merely to fulfill Elisha's blessing for a double portion of Elijah's spirit.
Abaye rejects the suggestion, citing a baraita that the man stood on his feet but did not go home, implying full revival.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Elisha's merit revived him because he healed Naaman's leprosy, which is considered like death.

items.text: Explanation of the name 'yemim' for mules
items.text_en: Explanation of the name 'yemim' for mules
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that mules are called 'yemim' because their terror is cast upon creatures. Rabbi Chanina notes he never saw a white mule wound heal, but the Gemara clarifies that the reference is to white mules with white legs, which are fatal.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that mules are called 'yemim' because their terror is cast upon creatures.
Rabbi Chanina testifies that no one ever asked him about a white mule wound and survived, supporting the terror of mules.
The Gemara objects that we see white mules that do survive.
The Gemara suggests that the statement means 'and it healed' rather than 'and it lived', but then objects that we see such wounds do heal.
The Gemara resolves that the reference is specifically to white mules with white legs, which are fatal.

items.text: The power of sorcery and divine providence
items.text_en: The power of sorcery and divine providence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets 'There is none else besides Him' to exclude even sorcery. A woman tries to take dust from under his feet for sorcery, but he tells her it won't work. The Gemara questions this, citing Rabbi Yochanan that sorcery can affect the heavenly retinue, but answers that Rabbi Chanina's merit protected him. Rabbi Chanina then states that no one injures a finger below unless decreed from above, citing a verse. Rabbi Elazar adds that the blood of a wound atones like a burnt offering, and Rava specifies this applies to the right thumb, a second wound, and when going to perform a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets the verse 'There is none else besides Him' to exclude even the power of sorcery.
A woman tries to take dust from under Rabbi Chanina's feet for sorcery, but he tells her it will not succeed because of the verse.
The Gemara objects by citing Rabbi Yochanan that sorcery is called 'כשפים' because it weakens the heavenly retinue, implying it has power.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina is different because his merit is so great that sorcery cannot affect him.
Rabbi Chanina states that no one injures a finger below unless it is decreed from above, citing a verse.
Rabbi Elazar adds that the blood from such a wound atones like the blood of a burnt offering.
Rava specifies that this atonement applies only to a wound on the right thumb, a second wound, and when one is going to perform a מצוה (commandment).

items.text: Concluding praise of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's piety
items.text_en: Concluding praise of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's piety
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a statement about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair: he never broke bread over a loaf that was not his own, and from the time he reached maturity, he never benefited from his father's meal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a statement about Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair: he never broke bread over a loaf that was not his own, and from the time he reached maturity, he never benefited from his father's meal.

items.text: Opening statement by Rabbi Zeira quoting Shmuel
items.text_en: Opening statement by Rabbi Zeira quoting Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Shmuel that if one heated a knife and slaughtered with it, the slaughter is valid because the sharpening precedes the heating. The Gemara notes that the sides of the knife are not an issue because the slaughtering area is wide.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Shmuel that if one heated a knife and slaughtered with it, the slaughter is valid because the sharpening precedes the heating.
The Gemara objects that the sides of the knife might burn the flesh, and answers that the slaughtering area is wide enough to avoid contact.

items.text: Inquiry about a heated spit and its halakhic classification
items.text_en: Inquiry about a heated spit and its halakhic classification
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether one who heated a spit and struck with it is judged as a boil (shchin) or a burn (michva). The practical difference is that boils and burns do not combine for impurity. The Gemara describes the scenario where half a gris of a boil already existed and the spit added another half gris, and questions whether the blow or the heat comes first.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who heated a spit and struck with it is judged as a boil (שחין) or a burn (מכוה).
The Gemara cites a baraita that boils and burns do not combine for impurity, establishing the practical difference.
The Gemara cites another baraita defining a boil as from non-fire sources and a burn as from fire sources.
The Gemara cites a third baraita that if one precedes the other, the later cancels the earlier.
The Gemara describes the scenario: half a gris of a boil existed, then the heated spit added another half gris.
The Gemara questions whether the blow or the heat comes first, determining if they combine or not.

items.text: Attempted proofs from earlier statements
items.text_en: Attempted proofs from earlier statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that the blow comes first from Rabbi Zeira's statement about a knife, but is rejected because a knife's sharpening is different. Another attempt from the case of a spit is also rejected because the spit was sharpened.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that the blow comes first from Rabbi Zeira's statement about a knife, citing that sharpening precedes heating.
The Gemara rejects the proof, arguing that sharpening (חידוד) is different from the blow in the case of a spit.
The Gemara attempts another proof from the case of a spit, where the ruling that it is judged as a burn from fire implies the blow comes first.
The Gemara rejects this proof as well, explaining that the spit was also sharpened, making it analogous to the knife case.

items.text: Discussion of a knife used for idolatry
items.text_en: Discussion of a knife used for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that a knife used for idolatry is permitted for slaughter (since it damages) but forbidden for cutting meat (since it improves). Rava adds exceptions: slaughter is forbidden in a dangerous case, and cutting is permitted for meat designated for a sacrifice. The Gemara objects that one should also be concerned about forbidden fat residue.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha's ruling that a knife used for idolatry is permitted for slaughter (since it damages) but forbidden for cutting meat (since it improves).
Rava adds exceptions: slaughter is forbidden in a dangerous case, and cutting is permitted for meat designated for a sacrifice.
The Gemara objects that one should also be concerned about forbidden fat residue on the knife.

items.text: דין סכין חדשה וישנה לעבודה זרה
items.text_en: Opening discussion: Knife used for idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling about a new knife used for idolatry, arguing that even according to Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva, such knives are merely accessories to idolatry and are not forbidden until they are actually used. Two answers are proposed: either the knife had a handle designated for idolatry, or it was an old knife that was rebuilt with fire.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות שמדובר בסכין חדשה, שכן כלי שרת של עבודה זרה אינם אסורים עד שיעבדו. מוצעים שני תירוצים: שחתך ענף לעבודה זרה בסכין, או שמדובר בסכין ישנה שליבן באור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a new knife used for idolatry is forbidden, arguing that even according to Rabbi Yishmael or Rabbi Akiva, accessories to idolatry are not forbidden until they are actually used.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בדחיית האפשרות שמדובר בסכין חדשה.

sub.desc_en: The first answer proposes that the knife had a handle designated for idolatry, which makes it forbidden even before use.
