sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: סכין חדשה אינה אסורה עד שתשמש לעבודה זרה.

sub.desc_en: The second answer proposes that it was an old knife that was rebuilt with fire, which is considered an act of worship.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: סכין חדשה אינה אסורה עד שתשמש לעבודה זרה.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ורבה בר בר חנה בשחיטה בסכין של גויים
items.text_en: Dispute about slaughtering with a gentile's knife
items.desc_en: Rav and Rabbah bar bar Chanah disagree on how to treat meat slaughtered with a gentile's knife: Rav says to peel the area, Rabbah bar bar Chanah says to rinse it. The Gemara initially suggests they argue about whether the slaughtering area is cold or hot, but then offers two alternative explanations: one assumes it is hot (so peeling is necessary, rinsing is sufficient because the signs are busy expelling blood), and another assumes it is cold (so rinsing is fine, but peeling is needed due to the pressure of the knife causing absorption).
items.desc: רב אומר שצריך לקלוף את מקום השחיטה, ורבה בר בר חנה אומר שדי בהדחה. הגמרא מציעה שני תירוצים למחלוקת: האם בית השחיטה רותח או צונן, ובהתאם לכך הטעמים משתנים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a dispute: Rav says one must peel the meat slaughtered with a gentile's knife, while Rabbah bar bar Chanah says rinsing suffices.
sub.desc: הצגת מחלוקת בין רב לרבה בר בר חנה בדין השוחט בסכין של גויים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the dispute hinges on whether the slaughtering area is cold or hot.
sub.desc: הצגת מחלוקת בין רב לרבה בר בר חנה בדין השוחט בסכין של גויים.

sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection and first alternative explanation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the initial suggestion and explains that both agree it is hot: peeling is ideal, but rinsing suffices because the trachea and esophagus are busy expelling blood and do not absorb.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההצעה ומסבירה שלכולי עלמא בית השחיטה רותח, והטעם לשיטת רבה בר בר חנה הוא שהסימנים טרודים בהוצאת דם ואינם בולעים.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version holds that both agree it is cold: rinsing is fine, but peeling is required because the pressure of the knife causes absorption.
sub.desc: גרסה חלופית: לכולי עלמא בית השחיטה צונן, והטעם לשיטת רב הוא שבגלל לחץ הסכין הבשר בולע.

items.text: דין סכין ששחט בה טריפה
items.text_en: Dispute about a treif knife
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina disagree about how to kasher a treif knife: one says with hot water, the other says with cold water. The halakha is that even cold water suffices, and if there is a Persian whetstone to sharpen it, no water is needed. The Gemara then questions the one who requires hot water, arguing that the knife absorbs both forbidden and permitted substances, but the absorption occurs only when the knife is hot, which happens at the end of slaughter when the meat is permitted.
items.desc: מחלוקת בין רב אחא ורבינא: אחד אומר צריך להגעיל בחמין, ואחד אומר די בצונן. ההלכה כמיקל בצונן, ואם יש בליתא דפרסא לקנח אין צריך. הגמרא מקשה על השיטה המחמירה ומתרצת שהסכין בולעת רק בסוף שחיטה שאז ההיתר כבר מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces a dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina about how to kasher a treif knife, stating the halakha that cold water suffices and a Persian whetstone eliminates the need for water.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רב אחא ורבינא לגבי הכשרת סכין ששחט בה טריפה, וקובע את ההלכה כמיקל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the opinion requiring hot water, arguing that the knife absorbs both forbidden and permitted substances, including אבר מן החי (a limb from a living animal).
sub.desc: מקשה על השיטה המחמירה: אם הטעם משום בליעת איסור, הרי גם בהיתר בולע איסור אבר מן החי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the knife absorbs only when hot, which occurs at the end of slaughter when the meat is permitted, so the absorption of forbidden substances is not a concern.
sub.desc: מקשה על השיטה המחמירה: אם הטעם משום בליעת איסור, הרי גם בהיתר בולע איסור אבר מן החי.

items.text: צורך בשלושה סכינים לטבח
items.text_en: Requirement for three knives for a butcher
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav states that a butcher needs three knives: one for slaughtering, one for cutting meat, and one for cutting fats. The Gemara questions why one knife cannot be used for both meat and fats sequentially, and explains that there is a decree lest one cut fats first and then meat. The Gemara then asks why the knives won't be confused, and answers that since the butcher is required to have two distinct knives, there is a recognizable distinction.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב אומר שהטבח צריך שלושה סכינים: אחד לשחיטה, אחד לחתוך בשר, ואחד לחתוך חלב. הגמרא דנה באפשרות להשתמש בסכין אחד ומסבירה שהגזירה היא שמא יחתוך חלב ואחר כך בשר, וההפרדה מונעת טעות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav states that a butcher requires three knives: one for slaughtering, one for cutting meat, and one for cutting fats.
The Gemara questions why one knife cannot suffice for both meat and fats if used sequentially.
The Gemara explains that there is a decree lest one mistakenly cut fats first and then meat.
The Gemara objects that even with two knives, the butcher might confuse them.
The Gemara resolves that since the butcher is required to have two distinct knives, there is a recognizable distinction between them.

items.text: צורך בשני כלי מים לטבח
items.text_en: Requirement for two water vessels for a butcher
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav further states that a butcher needs two water vessels: one for rinsing meat and one for rinsing fats. The Gemara questions why one vessel cannot be used sequentially, and explains the same decree and reasoning as with the knives.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב אומר שהטבח צריך שני כלי מים: אחד להדחת בשר ואחד להדחת חלב. הגמרא דנה באפשרות להשתמש בכלי אחד ומסבירה שגזירה שמא ידיח חלב ואחר כך בשר, וההפרדה מונעת טעות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav rules that a butcher needs two water vessels: one for rinsing meat and one for rinsing fats.
The Gemara questions why one vessel cannot be used sequentially, first for meat then for fats.
The Gemara explains the decree is a precaution lest one mistakenly rinse fats first and then meat.
The Gemara objects that even with two vessels, the butcher might still confuse them.
The Gemara resolves that since the butcher is required to have two vessels, he will have a recognizable distinction and not confuse them.

items.text: איסור הנחת כפלי על גבי בשר
items.text_en: Prohibition against placing fat on meat
items.desc_en: Ameimar in the name of Rav Pappa rules that one should not place fat on top of meat, because the fat melts and is absorbed by the meat. The Gemara questions why this would not also apply when the fat is placed on the side, and answers that the skin separates from below.
items.desc: אמימר בשם רב פפא אוסר לסחוף כפלי על גבי בשר שמא יזוב החלב ויבלע בבשר. הגמרא מקשה שגם כשהכפלי מונחים כרגיל יש חשש, ומתרצת שהקרום מפסיק מלמטה.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar in the name of Rav Pappa rules that one should not place fat on top of meat, because the fat melts and is absorbed by the meat.
sub.desc: אמימר בשם רב פפא אוסר להניח כפלי על גבי בשר מחשש שהחלב יימס וייבלע בבשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the same concern would not apply when the fat is placed on the side of the meat.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שגם בהנחה רגילה (תריצי) החלב עלול להימס ולהיבלע בבשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that when the fat is on the side, the skin separates from below, preventing absorption.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שגם בהנחה רגילה (תריצי) החלב עלול להימס ולהיבלע בבשר.

items.text: Clarification of the previous sugya's question about the hide
items.text_en: Clarification of the previous sugya's question about the hide
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is also a hide on the upper part of the neck, and answers that the butcher's hand crushes it due to constant handling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is also a hide on the upper part of the neck.
The Gemara answers that the butcher's hand crushes it due to constant handling.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement on what a Torah scholar must learn
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement on what a Torah scholar must learn
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that a Torah scholar must learn three things: writing, slaughter, and circumcision. Rav Chananya bar Shelemaya adds the knot of tefillin, the blessing of grooms, and tzitzit. The Gemara explains that the latter are common.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that a Torah scholar must learn three things: writing, slaughter, and circumcision.

sub.text: Rav Chananya bar Shelemaya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chananya bar Shelemaya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya bar Shelemaya adds three more items in the name of Rav: the knot of tefillin, the blessing of grooms, and tzitzit.
The Gemara explains that the additional items are common, so they are not included in the original list.

items.text: The butcher must know the laws of slaughter
items.text_en: The butcher must know the laws of slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that a butcher who does not know the laws of slaughter is forbidden to eat from his slaughter. The Gemara questions why this is necessary since the laws are taught in the Mishnah, and explains that it applies even if he slaughtered properly a few times, because without full knowledge he might err.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel stating that a butcher who does not know the laws of slaughter is forbidden to eat from his slaughter, listing the five disqualifying defects: שהייה (pausing), דרסה (pressing), חלדה (covering), הגרמה (slanting), and עיקור (tearing).
The Gemara asks why Shmuel's statement is necessary, since all these laws are already taught in the Mishnah.

The Gemara explains that the statement is needed even for a butcher who has slaughtered properly several times, because without full knowledge (גמיר) he might err by pausing or pressing without realizing it.

items.text: The butcher must check the simanim after slaughter
items.text_en: The butcher must check the simanim after slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the butcher must check the simanim after slaughter. Rav Yosef cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon says 'if he paused for the time of bikkur,' and suggests it means checking the simanim. Abaye corrects him, citing Rabbi Yochanan that it means the time for a wise person to examine, and then clarifies it means the time for a wise butcher to examine.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that the butcher must check the simanim (trachea and esophagus) after slaughter.
Rav Yosef cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Shimon says 'if he paused for the time of bikkur,' suggesting it refers to checking the simanim.
Rav Yosef infers that 'bikkur' means checking the simanim.
Abaye rejects Rav Yosef's inference, citing Rabbi Yochanan that 'bikkur' means the time for a wise person to examine.
The Gemara objects that if 'bikkur' means a wise person's examination, the measure is undefined.
Abaye clarifies that 'bikkur' means the time for a wise butcher to examine, providing a defined measure.

items.text: Dispute about the status of an animal if the butcher did not check
items.text_en: Dispute about the status of an animal if the butcher did not check
items.desc_en: If the butcher did not check, Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus says it is a terefah and forbidden to eat. A baraita teaches it is a nevelah and imparts impurity. The Gemara explains they disagree based on Rav Huna's principle: a live animal is in a presumption of prohibition until it is known how it was slaughtered; after slaughter it is in a presumption of permission until it is known how it became terefah. One opinion holds the presumption of prohibition applies, the other does not extend it to impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the status of an animal is if the butcher did not check the simanim after slaughter.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus in the name of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus rules that the animal is a טריפה (terefah) and forbidden to eat.
A baraita teaches that the animal is a נבלה (nevelah) and imparts ritual impurity through carrying.
The Gemara asks what principle underlies the dispute between the two opinions.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is based on Rav Huna's principle: a live animal is in a presumption of prohibition until slaughter, and after slaughter it is in a presumption of permission until known to be a terefah.

The Gemara resolves the dispute: one opinion holds the animal is in a presumption of prohibition (so it is a terefah), while the other holds the presumption of prohibition applies but not the presumption of impurity (so it is a nevelah but does not impart impurity).

items.text: Rav Huna's principle and the case of a wolf that removed the intestines
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle and the case of a wolf that removed the intestines
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on Rav Huna's statement that after slaughter the animal is in a presumption of permission even if a defect arises. Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna about a case where a wolf took the intestines and returned them perforated: do we suspect the wolf perforated them in a place that would make it a terefah? Rav Huna answers we do not suspect that.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's principle
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna's principle
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Huna's principle that after slaughter the animal is in a presumption of permission even if a defect arises.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna about a case where a wolf took the intestines and returned them perforated: do we suspect the wolf perforated them in a place that would make it a terefah?
Rav Huna answers that we do not suspect the wolf perforated them in a place that would make it a terefah.

items.text: Objection from a bird pecking at a fig and a mouse at melons
items.text_en: Objection from a bird pecking at a fig and a mouse at melons
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a case where one sees a bird pecking at a fig or a mouse at melons, implying that we do suspect the animal might have been damaged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a case where one sees a bird pecking at a fig or a mouse at melons, implying that we do suspect the animal might have been damaged.

items.text: Opening statement: concern for a possible puncture
items.text_en: Opening statement: concern for a possible puncture
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that perhaps the knife punctured the animal in a place of a hole, implying a potential issue.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that perhaps the knife punctured the animal in a place of a hole, implying a potential issue.

items.text: Rava's challenge: comparing danger and prohibition
items.text_en: Rava's challenge: comparing danger and prohibition
items.desc_en: An interlocutor distinguishes between danger and prohibition, but Rava argues that both should be treated stringently when in doubt.

sub.desc_en: The interlocutor objects to Rava's comparison, arguing that danger (סכנה) is fundamentally different from prohibition (איסור) and thus treated more stringently.
Rava rejects the distinction, asserting that both ספק סכנה (doubtful danger) and ספק איסור (doubtful prohibition) are treated לכתחילה (stringently).

items.text: Abaye's objection: evidence from tumah and uncovered water
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: evidence from tumah and uncovered water
items.desc_en: Abaye objects by citing a case where doubt about tumah in the public domain is lenient, while doubt about uncovered water is stringent, showing a difference.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the distinction between prohibition and danger is not absolute, citing the case where doubt about טומאה (ritual impurity) in the public domain is lenient while doubt about uncovered water is stringent.

items.text: Answer: halakha derived from sotah
items.text_en: Answer: halakha derived from sotah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leniency for tumah in the public domain is a halakhic tradition derived from sotah, which applies only in a private domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leniency for טומאה (ritual impurity) in the public domain is a halakhic tradition derived from סוטה (the suspected adulteress), which applies only in a private domain.

items.text: Rav Shimi's objection: weasel and terumah loaves
items.text_en: Rav Shimi's objection: weasel and terumah loaves
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi raises a case where a weasel with a dead creeping animal in its mouth walks over terumah loaves, and the doubt is resolved leniently, unlike uncovered water.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi raises a case where a weasel with a dead creeping animal in its mouth walks over terumah loaves, and the doubt is resolved leniently, unlike uncovered water.

items.text: Answer: the principle of da'at l'hishe'el
items.text_en: Answer: the principle of da'at l'hishe'el
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leniency applies only to an object that has the capacity to be interrogated, derived from sotah, unlike uncovered water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the leniency for uncovered water applies only to an object that has the capacity to be interrogated (דבר שיש בו דעת לישאל), derived from the case of the sotah (סוטה).

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a baraita about a flask left uncovered and found covered, which is deemed impure. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains the reasoning behind this ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi brings a baraita about a flask left uncovered and found covered, which is deemed impure, as a proof for the principle that uncovered water is forbidden.
The baraita continues with the case of a flask left covered and found uncovered, which is ruled unfit if a weasel or snake could drink from it, or if dew fell into it at night.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks for the reasoning behind the baraita's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah about uncovered liquids
items.text_en: Gemara's inference from the Mishnah about uncovered liquids
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's distinction between finding a vessel covered or uncovered that if it is found as it was left, there is no concern. This leads to the conclusion that the danger of uncovered liquids is more stringent than mere prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining the Mishnah's reasoning: creeping things typically uncover vessels, not cover them.
The Gemara offers an alternative inference: if the vessel is found exactly as left, there is no טומאה (impurity) or פסול (invalidity).
The Gemara concludes that the danger of uncovered liquids is more stringent than mere prohibition, as even ספק (doubt) renders them forbidden.

items.text: Baraita on the time and distance for uncovered liquids
items.text_en: Baraita on the time and distance for uncovered liquids
items.desc_en: A baraita lists three liquids forbidden due to exposure and defines the time they must be left uncovered to be forbidden: enough time for a reptile to come from a nearby place and drink. Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda defines the nearby place as from under the ear of the vessel. The Gemara clarifies that the reptile drinks and returns to its hole.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three liquids forbidden due to exposure and defines the forbidden time as that required for a reptile to come from a nearby place and drink.
Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda defines the 'nearby place' as from under the ear of the vessel.
The Gemara objects: if the reptile drinks, it would be seen by the person, contradicting the assumption of secrecy.
The Gemara resolves: the reptile drinks and then returns to its hole, so it is not seen.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about a found nick in the knife
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda about a found nick in the knife
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chisda dispute the status of an animal slaughtered with a knife later found to be nicked. Rav Huna rules it invalid, suspecting the nick occurred on the skin. Rav Chisda rules it valid, suspecting it occurred on a bone.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about an animal slaughtered with a knife later found to be nicked.
Rav Huna rules the slaughter invalid, suspecting the nick occurred on the skin.
Rav Chisda rules the slaughter valid, suspecting the nick occurred on a bone.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Chisda's reasoning: a bone definitely nicks, but skin only possibly nicks. Since we have a definite slaughter (the animal is before us), a doubt (about the skin) cannot override a certainty.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Chisda's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rav Chisda's reasoning: a bone definitely nicks, but skin only possibly nicks, so a doubt cannot override a certainty.

items.text: Rava's attempted support from the case of immersion with an interposition
items.text_en: Rava's attempted support from the case of immersion with an interposition
items.desc_en: Rava attempts to support Rav Huna from a case where one immersed and later found an interposing substance: even if he dealt with that substance all day, the immersion is invalid unless he can say he is certain it was not there before. The Gemara deflects by distinguishing: there we can say the person never immersed (standing him on his presumptive impurity), but here the animal is slaughtered before us. The Gemara further distinguishes: the knife has a defect, but the animal does not.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita about immersion with an interposition to support Rav Huna's position that a found defect retroactively invalidates the slaughter.
The Gemara deflects by noting that in the immersion case, one can stand the person on his presumptive impurity and say he never immersed, unlike here where the animal is before us.
Rava objects that one could similarly stand the animal on its presumptive status and say it was never slaughtered, but the animal is slaughtered before us.
The Gemara rejects the objection by noting that in the immersion case, a defect (the interposition) was found, creating a presumption of invalidity.
The Gemara resolves the discussion by distinguishing that the knife has a defect (found to be nicked), but the animal itself has no defect, so the cases are not analogous.

items.text: Baraita about a slipped gullet and the principle of doubt in slaughter
items.text_en: Baraita about a slipped gullet and the principle of doubt in slaughter
items.desc_en: A baraita presents cases of slaughter where the gullet was cut and the windpipe was found slipped. If the order is unknown, the slaughter is invalid. The Gemara clarifies that this principle of 'any doubt in slaughter is invalid' applies to cases of possible delay or pressing, not to the knife-nick case.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents two clear cases: cutting the gullet after the windpipe slipped is valid, but cutting the gullet after the windpipe slipped is invalid.
The baraita adds a case of doubt about the order of slipping and slaughter, and rules that any doubt in slaughter is invalid.
The Gemara asks: what does the principle 'any doubt in slaughter is invalid' come to include? Does it include this type of doubt?
The Gemara answers: no, it comes to include cases of possible delay (שהייה) or possible pressing (דרסה), not the knife-nick case.

items.text: Distinction between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on knife defects
items.text_en: Distinction between Rav Huna and Rav Chisda on knife defects
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between a blemished animal and a nicked knife. It then rules that Rav Huna's view applies when the knife did not break a bone, and Rav Chisda's view applies when it did break a bone, clarifying that the defect must be in the neck bone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what distinguishes the case of a blemished animal from a nicked knife, and answers that in the animal the defect arose in the animal itself, while here the knife was defective but the animal was not.
The Gemara rules that Rav Huna's view applies when the knife did not break a bone, and Rav Chisda's view applies when it did break a bone, clarifying that the defect must be in the neck bone.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on thirteen animals
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on thirteen animals
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef ruled that up to thirteen animals were treif, and the Gemara debates whether he followed Rav Huna (invalidating the first animal) or Rav Chisda (invalidating all but the first). An alternative explanation suggests he always followed Rav Huna, as the defect could have been in a later neck bone.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that Rav Yosef ruled up to thirteen animals as טריפה (ritually unfit), and questions whether he followed Rav Huna (invalidating even the first) or Rav Chisda (invalidating all but the first).
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Rav Yosef always followed Rav Huna, because the defect could have been in a later neck bone (מפרקת), not necessarily the first.

items.text: Rav Kahana's requirement to check between each animal
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's requirement to check between each animal
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava tells Rav Ashi that Rav Kahana required checking the knife between each animal. The Gemara questions why a Sage's inspection is not needed, and answers that a single witness is trusted for prohibitions, and showing the knife to a Sage is only for his honor.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava reports to Rav Ashi that Rav Kahana required checking the knife between each animal, and explains the reasoning in terms of Rav Huna and Rav Chisda's positions.
The Gemara questions why, if the knife must be checked between each animal, a Sage's inspection is not also required.
The Gemara answers that a single witness is trusted for prohibitions, so a Sage's inspection is not needed.
The Gemara objects that if a single witness suffices, then even initially no Sage's inspection should be required.
The Gemara resolves by citing Rabbi Yochanan that showing the knife to a Sage was only instituted for the Sage's honor, not as a halachic requirement.

items.text: Source for the principle of establishing a matter on its presumptive status
items.text_en: Source for the principle of establishing a matter on its presumptive status
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rabbinic principle that we establish a matter on its presumptive status. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse from the laws of leprosy in houses, arguing that the priest's inspection assumes the house remains unchanged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rabbinic principle that we establish a matter on its presumptive status.

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of Rabbi Yonatan cites a verse from the laws of leprous houses, arguing that the priest's inspection assumes the house remains unchanged, thus deriving the principle of establishing a matter on its presumptive status.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's challenge and the response
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's challenge and the response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov challenges the proof, suggesting the priest might exit through the back. Abaye responds with two refutations: exiting backwards is not considered exiting, and the back of the door has no window. Rava counters with examples from the High Priest on Yom Kippur and the law of a dark house, distinguishing between established and unestablished presumptions.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects to the proof from the priest's exit, suggesting the priest might exit backwards and thus still see the plague.
Abaye responds with two refutations: first, exiting backwards is not considered a valid exit.
Abaye's second refutation: the back of the door has no window, and one cannot open a window in a dark house to see the plague.
Rava counters Abaye's first point by citing the High Priest on Yom Kippur, who exits backwards and that is still called a valid exit.
Rava resolves the second point by distinguishing between an unestablished presumption (where one cannot open a window) and an established presumption (where one can).

items.text: Baraita contradicting Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.text_en: Baraita contradicting Rav Acha bar Yaakov
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that contradicts Rav Acha bar Yaakov's interpretation, explaining the precise location of the priest when inspecting the house. It derives that the priest must stand by the lintel, and that any form of isolation is valid. The Gemara notes that Rav Acha bar Yaakov's view is rejected.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that contradicts Rav Acha bar Yaakov, deriving from the verse that the priest must go to the door, not to his own house.
The baraita further derives that the priest must stand by the lintel, not under it, based on the phrase 'from the house'.
The baraita concludes that any form of isolation is valid, even if the priest went to his own house or stood inside the house.
The Gemara notes that Rav Acha bar Yaakov's view is rejected by the baraita.

items.text: Illustration of an observable majority
items.text_en: Illustration of an observable majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives an example of a majority that is directly observable: a row of men standing and saying that a certain person is standing as he was. This sets up the distinction between an observable majority and one that is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives an example of an observable majority: a row of men standing and saying that a certain person is standing as he was.

items.text: The question: source for non-observable majority
items.text_en: The question: source for non-observable majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rabbinic principle to follow the majority, citing the verse 'after the majority to incline'. It clarifies that the question is not about an observable majority (like nine stores or a Sanhedrin), but about a non-observable majority, such as the status of a minor male or female.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rabbinic principle to follow the majority, citing the verse 'after the majority to incline'.
The Gemara clarifies that an observable majority, such as nine stores or a Sanhedrin, is not the subject of the question.
The Gemara specifies that the question is about a non-observable majority, such as the status of a minor male or female, and asks for its source.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the head of the burnt-offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's derivation from the head of the burnt-offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar proposes deriving the principle from the head of the burnt-offering: the Torah says 'and he shall cut it into its pieces', implying that the head is cut into pieces but not the pieces into smaller pieces, yet we do not worry that the brain membrane might have been pierced, because we follow the majority. The Gemara challenges this: perhaps the priest splits the head and checks, and the verse's limitation applies only when cutting completely, not when merely splitting.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar proposes deriving the principle of following the majority from the head of the burnt-offering, where the Torah's limitation on cutting pieces does not lead to concern about the brain membrane being pierced, because we follow the majority.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the priest splits the head and checks, and the verse's limitation applies only when cutting completely, not when merely splitting.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's derivation from the prohibition of breaking a bone in the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's derivation from the prohibition of breaking a bone in the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina derives the principle from the Paschal lamb: the Torah says 'do not break a bone in it', yet we do not worry that the brain membrane might have been pierced, because we follow the majority. The Gemara challenges: perhaps one places a coal on the bone and burns it, and checks, as a baraita states that one who cuts through sinews or burns bones is not liable for breaking a bone.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina derives the principle of following the majority (זיל בתר רובא) from the Paschal lamb: the Torah forbids breaking a bone in it, yet we do not worry that the brain membrane might have been pierced, because we follow the majority.
The Gemara objects: perhaps one places a coal on the bone and burns it, and checks, as a baraita states that one who cuts through sinews or burns bones is not liable for breaking a bone.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's derivation from the tail of the burnt-offering
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's derivation from the tail of the burnt-offering
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the principle from the tail of the burnt-offering: the Torah requires 'its fat, the tail, whole', yet we do not worry that the spinal cord might have been severed, because we follow the majority. The Gemara challenges: perhaps one opens it and checks, and the requirement of 'whole' applies only when cutting it completely, not when merely splitting.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the principle of following the majority from the tail of the burnt-offering: the Torah requires 'its fat, the tail, whole', yet we do not worry that the spinal cord might have been severed, because we follow the majority.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the spinal cord is severed from below, but the verse specifies 'opposite the loin' (the place where the kidneys counsel), so the cut is made there, not at the spine.
The Gemara rejects the proof: perhaps one opens the tail and checks the spinal cord, and the requirement of 'whole' applies only when cutting it completely, not when merely splitting it.

items.text: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi's derivation from the heifer whose neck is broken
items.text_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi's derivation from the heifer whose neck is broken
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi derives the principle from the heifer whose neck is broken: the Torah requires it to be 'the heifer that is broken' – when it is whole, yet we do not worry that it might be a tereifah, because we follow the majority. The Gemara notes that one might ask why it matters, but the school of Rabbi Yannai says that atonement is written regarding it, like sacrifices.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi derives the principle of following the majority from the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה ערופה), arguing that since the Torah requires it to be whole yet we do not worry it might be a טריפה (ritually unfit animal), we must rely on the majority.

The Gemara raises an objection: why would it matter if the heifer were a טריפה, since it is not a sacrifice? The school of Rabbi Yannai answers that atonement (כפרה) is written regarding it, like sacrifices.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila's derivation from the red heifer
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila's derivation from the red heifer
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila derives the principle from the red heifer: the Torah says 'slaughter... and burn', just as its slaughter is when it is whole, so too its burning is when it is whole, yet we do not worry that it might be a tereifah, because we follow the majority. The Gemara notes that one might ask why it matters, but the Torah calls it a 'sin-offering'.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Sheila derives the principle of following the majority from the red heifer: the Torah requires slaughter and burning when whole, yet we do not suspect it might be a tereifah, because we follow the majority.
The Gemara raises an objection: why does it matter if the red heifer is a tereifah, since it is burned and not eaten?
The Gemara answers: the Torah calls it a 'sin-offering' (חטאת), implying it has the sanctity of a sacrifice, so its fitness matters.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from the scapegoat (begun)
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's derivation from the scapegoat (begun)
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov begins to derive the principle from the scapegoat: the Torah requires 'take the two goats' that they be equal, yet we do not worry... The daf cuts off here.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov begins to derive the principle of following the majority from the scapegoat, noting that the Torah requires the two goats to be equal, yet we do not worry about possible disqualifications.

items.text: First proof from Yom Kippur lottery
items.text_en: First proof from Yom Kippur lottery
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the lottery for the two goats on Yom Kippur follows the majority, as we assume the goat for Azazel is not a tereifah. It rejects the possibility of checking because the goat is broken into pieces before reaching the halfway point.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: perhaps one of the two Yom Kippur goats is a tereifah (טריפה), and answers that we follow the majority (רוב).
The Gemara objects: what difference does it make, since the lottery for Azazel requires an animal fit for God, and a tereifah is unfit.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of checking the goat, citing a baraita that the goat is broken into pieces before reaching the halfway point.

items.text: Rav Mari's proof from striking parents
items.text_en: Rav Mari's proof from striking parents
items.desc_en: Rav Mari proves the principle from the case of one who strikes his father or mother, where we assume the victim is indeed the parent, following the majority of marital relations. The Gemara objects that perhaps both parents were imprisoned, but the principle of no guardian for forbidden relations applies.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari proves the principle of following the majority from the case of one who strikes his father or mother, where the Torah commands execution despite the possibility that the victim is not the parent, because we follow the majority of marital relations.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the case involves parents who were imprisoned together, so the majority of marital relations does not apply.

The Gemara answers that even if imprisoned, the principle of 'אין אפוטרופוס לעריות' (there is no guardian for forbidden relations) applies, meaning we assume the worst-case scenario for sexual prohibitions, so the objection is neutralized.

items.text: Rav Kahana's proof from murder
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's proof from murder
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana proves the principle from the case of a murderer, where we assume the victim was not a tereifah. The Gemara rejects checking because it would degrade the body, and even if we consider the loss of a soul, we still worry about a possible perforation at the sword's location.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana proves the principle of following the majority (רוב) from the case of a murderer, where the Torah commands execution despite the possibility that the victim was a טריפה (dying person).
The Gemara objects that one could check the victim's body, but rejects this because it would degrade the body (נוול).

The Gemara further objects that even if one argues that the loss of a soul justifies degrading the body, we still worry about a possible perforation at the sword's location, so checking would be inconclusive.

items.text: Ravina's proof from conspiring witnesses
items.text_en: Ravina's proof from conspiring witnesses
items.desc_en: Ravina proves the principle from conspiring witnesses, where we assume the accused was not a tereifah. The Gemara rejects checking because Rabbi's baraita states that if the witnesses killed the accused, they are not executed, implying no prior examination.

sub.desc_en: Ravina proposes a proof from conspiring witnesses (עדים זוממין), arguing that the Torah's command to execute them assumes the accused was not a טריפה (ritually defective), relying on the principle of רוב (majority).
The Gemara objects that one might say we examine the accused, but cites Rabbi's baraita that if the witnesses killed the accused, they are not executed, implying no prior examination occurred.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from shechita itself
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from shechita itself
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves the principle from shechita itself, where we assume the slaughter is not at a perforated spot, following the majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi opens by stating that the principle of following the majority is derived from shechita itself, where the Torah commands to slaughter and eat.
The gemara raises a concern: should we not worry that the slaughter might be performed at a perforated spot, rendering the animal a טריפה (ritually unfit)?
Rav Ashi resolves the concern by invoking the principle of רוב (majority): we follow the majority, assuming the slaughter is not at a perforated spot.

items.text: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated this teaching before Rav Kahana (or Rav Shimi), who challenged that the principle applies only where checking is impossible, but where possible, we check. The Gemara counters that if so, Rabbi Meir, who worries about minorities, would never eat meat, which is absurd.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that he stated this teaching before Rav Kahana (or Rav Shimi), who challenged that the principle applies only where checking is impossible, but where possible, we check.
The Gemara counters that if the principle were limited to cases where checking is impossible, Rabbi Meir, who worries about minorities, would never eat meat, which is absurd.

items.text: Transition from previous discussion
items.text_en: Transition from previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about Passover and other sacrifices, stating that where possible one is stringent, where not possible one is lenient, and applies this to the current context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that regarding Passover and sacrifices, where possible one is stringent, where not possible one is lenient, and applies this principle to the current context.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and the challenge from the principle of רוב
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and the challenge from the principle of רוב
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says that if one saw a person slaughter, only if he watched from beginning to end is the meat permitted. The Gemara questions this: if the slaughterer is known to be expert, why require watching? If known to be inexpert, it's obvious. If uncertain, why not rely on the majority that people near slaughter are experts? The Gemara brings a supporting baraita about finding a slaughtered chicken in the market, which relies on that majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman says in the name of Rav: if one saw a person slaughter from beginning to end, the meat is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.
The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances? If the slaughterer is known to be expert, why require watching? If known to be inexpert, it is obvious.
If the onlooker does not know whether the slaughterer is expert, why not rely on the majority that people near slaughter are experts?
The Gemara cites a baraita: if one finds a slaughtered chicken in the market or his agent finds one slaughtered, its presumptive status is that it was slaughtered properly.
The Gemara argues: the baraita shows we rely on the majority that people near slaughter are experts; here too we should rely on that majority.

items.text: Resolution: case of partial observation
items.text_en: Resolution: case of partial observation
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where the slaughterer is known to be inexpert, but he properly slaughtered one siman in front of us. One might think the other siman was also done properly, but Rav teaches that we suspect the other siman might have involved a pause or pressing, so only full observation suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the case is where the slaughterer is known to be inexpert, but he properly slaughtered one סימן (shechita organ) in front of us. One might think the other סימן was also done properly, but Rav teaches that we suspect the other סימן might have involved a pause or pressing, so only full observation suffices.

items.text: Rav Dimi's inquiry about a messenger and the distinction between slaughter and terumah
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's inquiry about a messenger and the distinction between slaughter and terumah
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi asks Rav Nachman: if one tells his messenger to slaughter and finds the animal slaughtered, may he rely on it? Rav Nachman says yes. But if he tells him to separate terumah and finds it separated, he says no. The Gemara challenges the inconsistency. Rav Nachman explains that there is no presumption that a messenger fulfills his mission; in slaughter, we rely on the majority that people near slaughter are experts, so perhaps another person slaughtered it. In terumah, if another person separated it, it would be invalid because one cannot separate terumah without the owner's knowledge.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi asks Rav Nachman about the presumption of slaughter versus terumah when a messenger finds the animal slaughtered or produce separated.
The Gemara objects that Rav Nachman's two rulings are inconsistent: if a messenger is presumed to act, both should be valid; if not, neither should be.

Rav Nachman resolves the inconsistency: there is no presumption that a messenger fulfills his mission; in slaughter, we rely on the majority that people near slaughter are experts (רוב מצויין אצל שחיטה מומחין הן), but in terumah, another person's separation would be invalid because one cannot separate תרומה (priestly portion) without the owner's knowledge.

items.text: Debate between Tannaim about relying on רוב for found slaughtered animals
items.text_en: Debate between Tannaim about relying on רוב for found slaughtered animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the principle of relying on the majority might be a dispute between Tannaim. A baraita records a disagreement: Rabbi Yehuda prohibits found slaughtered goats or chickens, while Rabbi Chanina ben Yosi HaGelili permits. Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies when found in a garbage heap, Rabbi Chanina's when found in a house. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that all agree on the majority principle; the dispute is about whether a person is likely to throw a carcass into a garbage heap inside the house. The Gemara then clarifies the apparent contradiction in Rabbi's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the principle of relying on the majority (רוב מצויין אצל שחיטה מומחין הן) is a dispute between Tannaim.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda prohibits and Rabbi Chanina ben Yosi HaGelili permits found slaughtered animals, with Rabbi reconciling them by location.
The Gemara infers that the Tannaim dispute the principle of relying on the majority for slaughtered animals.

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rejects the inference, explaining that all agree on the majority principle; the dispute is about whether a person is likely to throw a carcass into a garbage heap inside the house.
The Gemara questions what 'garbage heap' means in Rabbi's statement, concluding it must be a garbage heap inside the house.
The Gemara questions what 'house' means in Rabbi's statement, concluding it must also refer to a garbage heap inside the house, and notes a contradiction in Rabbi's own rulings.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Yehuda's position on the ash-heap
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Yehuda's position on the ash-heap
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies only to a public ash-heap, where even Rabbi Chanina ben Yosei HaGlili agrees; the dispute is limited to a private ash-heap.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the apparent dispute by clarifying that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies only to a public ash-heap (אשפה שבשוק), where even Rabbi Chanina ben Yosei HaGlili agrees; the dispute is limited to a private ash-heap (אשפה שבבית).

items.text: Reason for excluding deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor
items.text_en: Reason for excluding deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says 'lest they ruin their slaughter,' implying a concern for future action, not past. Rava deduces that one may not initially give them non-sacred animals to slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'lest they ruin their slaughter' (שֶׁמָּא יְקַלְקְלוּ) rather than 'lest they have ruined' (שֶׁמָּא קִלְקְלוּ), implying a concern about future action.
Rava infers from the Mishnah's wording that one may not give non-sacred animals (חולין) to a deaf-mute, an imbecile, or a minor לכתחילה (as an initial action) for slaughter.
Rava deduces from the future tense that one may not give non-sacred animals to these individuals to slaughter לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Validity of slaughter with others watching and the source for no intent required
items.text_en: Validity of slaughter with others watching and the source for no intent required
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if others watch them, their slaughter is valid. The Gemara asks who holds that intent is not required for slaughter. Rava identifies it as Rabbi Natan, who validates slaughter even if a knife thrown into a wall kills the animal, and rules accordingly.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when others watch them, their slaughter is valid.
The Gemara asks which tanna holds that intent is not required for slaughter.
Rava identifies the tanna as Rabbi Natan.
Oshaya Ze'ira teaches a baraita: if one threw a knife into a wall and it slaughtered an animal, Rabbi Natan validates and the Sages invalidate.
Oshaya Ze'ira rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Natan.
The Gemara objects that we require moving the knife back and forth.
The Gemara answers that the knife went and came back in its proper manner.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry about a minor's intent
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's inquiry about a minor's intent
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks whether a minor has valid intent (מחשבה) for halakhic purposes. Rabbi Ami objects, noting that the Mishnah already states minors have action (מעשה) but no intent, citing a baraita about hollowed nuts used by children.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asks whether a minor has halakhically effective intent (מחשבה).
Rabbi Ami objects that the Mishnah already resolves the dilemma: minors have action (מעשה) but no intent (מחשבה).
The Gemara cites a baraita about hollowed nuts to support that minors have effective action but not thought.

items.text: Gemara's question about a minor's intent
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a minor's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's question is not about mere intent (מחשבה) but about intent recognizable through action (מחשבתו ניכרת מתוך מעשיו).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement that deaf-mutes, imbeciles, and minors have no valid intent (מחשבה).
The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's question is not about mere intent (מחשבה) but about intent recognizable through action (מחשבתו ניכרת מתוך מעשיו).

items.text: Example of recognizable intent
items.text_en: Example of recognizable intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides an example: if an olah was standing in the south and one brought it to the north and slaughtered it, is this considered intent for the olah or merely happenstance?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether bringing an olah from the south to the north and slaughtering it constitutes recognizable intent for the olah or is merely coincidental.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's precedent from tractate Makshirin
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's precedent from tractate Makshirin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about produce on a roof and dew, where Rabbi Yochanan ruled that if one turned the produce, it is considered intent. This shows that intent can be inferred from action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah from tractate Makshirin about produce on a roof and dew, establishing that intent can be inferred from action.
The mishnah adds that deaf-mute, insane, and minor children have action but no intent, reinforcing the distinction.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that if one turned the produce, the action reveals intent, making the produce susceptible to טומאה (ritual impurity).

items.text: Clarification of the question: biblical or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Clarification of the question: biblical or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan's question was whether the minor's action is valid on a biblical or rabbinic level.

sub.desc_en: Gemara's question: is the requirement biblical or rabbinic?

items.text: Alternative version of the question
items.text_en: Alternative version of the question
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents a different version: Rabbi Yochanan asked whether a minor has valid action (מעשה) or not. Rabbi Ammi objects, citing the mishnah that they have action but no intent. The Gemara resolves that the question is about biblical vs. rabbinic status, concluding that they have action even biblically, but no intent even rabbinically, except for intent recognizable through action which is rabbinic.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents a different version of the sugya: Rabbi Yochanan asked whether a minor has valid action (מעשה) or not.
Rabbi Ammi objects, arguing that just as the mishnah explicitly states that minors have no intent (מחשבה), it also explicitly states that they have action (מעשה), so why ask about action?

The Gemara resolves that the question was about biblical vs. rabbinic status: they have action even biblically (מדאורייתא), but no intent even rabbinically (מדרבנן), except for intent recognizable through action (מחשבתו ניכרת מתוך מעשיו), which is only rabbinic.

items.text: Source for disqualification of one preoccupied with sacred offerings
items.text_en: Source for disqualification of one preoccupied with sacred offerings
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav Huna for the source that one who is preoccupied with sacred offerings is disqualified. Rav Huna cites verses: 'and he shall slaughter the bull' indicates slaughter must be for the sake of the bull, and 'for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it' means sacrifice with intent.

sub.desc_en: Samuel asks Rav Huna: whence that one engaged with sacrifices is invalid? From the verse 'and he slaughtered the son of the ox' — that slaughter be for the son of the ox.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'וְשָׁחַט אֶת בֶּן הַבָּקָר' (and he shall slaughter the bull) to teach that slaughter must be for the sake of the bull.
Shmuel objects that the cited verse only establishes the requirement but not that it is indispensable (מעכב), and asks for the source that it invalidates the offering.
Rav Huna cites the verse 'לִרְצוֹנְכֶם תִּזְבָּחֻהוּ' (for your acceptance you shall sacrifice it) to teach that the sacrifice must be performed with conscious intent, and lack thereof disqualifies.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on an idolater's slaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on an idolater's slaughter
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that an idolater's slaughter is a neveilah and conveys impurity through carrying. The Gemara debates whether this implies no prohibition of benefit, and whether it follows Rabbi Eliezer or not. Rabbi Ammi offers a different version: an idolater's slaughter is neveilah, but a heretic's slaughter is for idolatry.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that an idolater's slaughter is a neveilah (carcass) and conveys impurity through carrying.
The Gemara infers from the mishnah's wording that the slaughter is a neveilah (carcass) but not prohibited for benefit.
The Gemara asks which Tanna is the author of this mishnah.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers that the mishnah does not follow Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that an idolater's default intent is for idolatry.
Rabbi Ammi offers a different version of the mishnah: an idolater's slaughter is a neveilah, but a heretic's slaughter is for idolatry.
The Gemara cites a baraita of the Sages that supports Rabbi Ammi's version, listing the halachic status of a heretic's slaughter, bread, wine, books, and produce.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters on Shabbat or Yom Kippur, though liable for capital punishment, produces a valid slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters on Shabbat or Yom Kippur, though liable for capital punishment, produces a valid slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's initial identification of Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial identification of Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a teaching that the meat is forbidden for consumption that day, and the colleagues attribute this to Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Abba identifies this as Rabbi Yehuda of Hanukah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda forbids feeding an animal a carcass that was not prepared before Shabbat, analogizing that here too the animal was not prepared from before Shabbat.

sub.text: Rav Huna citing Chiyya bar Rav in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Huna citing Chiyya bar Rav in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a teaching that meat slaughtered on Shabbat is forbidden for consumption that day.
The colleagues attribute this ruling to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks which Rabbi Yehuda is meant.

Rabbi Abba identifies this as Rabbi Yehuda of Hanukah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda forbids feeding an animal a carcass not prepared before Shabbat, analogizing that here too the animal was not prepared from before Shabbat.

items.text: Abaye's objection to the analogy
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to the analogy
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the comparison: in the baraita, the carcass was originally prepared for humans but now for dogs, whereas here the animal was originally prepared for humans and remains so. He argues that a live animal is not considered prepared for eating but for raising.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are not analogous: there the neveila was prepared for humans and now for dogs, but here the animal was alive and not designated for eating at all, only for breeding.

items.text: Response to Abaye: the principle of retroactive clarification
items.text_en: Response to Abaye: the principle of retroactive clarification
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how, according to Rabbi Yehuda, one can slaughter an animal on Yom Tov. The answer is that the animal stands both for eating and for raising; once slaughtered, it becomes clear that it was always designated for eating. This invokes the concept of bererah (retroactive clarification).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how, according to Rabbi Yehuda, one can slaughter an animal on Yom Tov at all, since it stands for both eating and breeding.
Abaye answers that once slaughtered, it is clarified retroactively (ברירה) that it was designated for eating; if not slaughtered, it is clarified that it was for breeding.

items.text: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda rejects bererah
items.text_en: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda rejects bererah
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda does not accept the principle of bererah, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda and others forbid a buyer of wine from Cutheans to rely on retroactive designation of tithes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda does not accept the principle of בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation), and asks from where we know this, suggesting it is from a baraita.

The baraita cites a case where a buyer of wine from Cutheans may retroactively designate tithes according to Rabbi Meir, but Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it, demonstrating their rejection of בְּרֵירָה.

items.text: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's reasoning for Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Gemara's citation of the Mishnah's reasoning for Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara recalls the Mishnah where Rabbi Meir is challenged about the possibility of the wine skin bursting, and he responds that the concern is only after the fact.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalls the Mishnah's reasoning for Rabbi Meir, where he responds to the objection about the wine skin bursting by saying the concern is only after the fact.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's condition in the baraita of Ayyo
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rabbi Yehuda's condition in the baraita of Ayyo
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the baraita of Ayyo where Rabbi Yehuda rules that one cannot stipulate two conditions simultaneously, and then questions why the case of east and west is different from the case of here and there, with Rabbi Yochanan resolving that the sage has already arrived.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the baraita of Ayyo as a source for Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's rule that one cannot stipulate two conditions simultaneously, only a single direction for the eiruv.
The Gemara questions why the case of 'here and there' is invalid due to lack of ברירה (retroactive selection), while east and west should also lack ברירה.
Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the sage has already arrived, making the stipulation effective retroactively.

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer: Rabbi Yehuda's view on utensils
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: Rabbi Yehuda's view on utensils
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Yehuda's position here is like his view on utensils, where broken pieces are only permitted if they serve a function similar to their original use, implying that if the function was not prepared from yesterday, it is forbidden; similarly, the animal was not prepared for slaughter from yesterday.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef introduces the view of Rabbi Yehuda on utensils, citing a Mishnah about broken vessels being movable on Shabbat only if they serve a function similar to their original use.

The Gemara infers from Rabbi Yehuda's position that since the specific function was not prepared from yesterday, the broken pieces are forbidden; similarly, the animal was not prepared for slaughter from yesterday, so it is forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's objection: Distinction between utensils and food
items.text_en: Abaye's objection: Distinction between utensils and food
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are not comparable: utensils become a new entity (noled), while food remains food even when broken, and Rabbi Yehuda permits such food.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the cases are not comparable: utensils become a new entity (נולד), while food remains food even when broken, and Rabbi Yehuda permits such food.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's view on squeezed fruits
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Yehuda's view on squeezed fruits
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits liquid that comes out of fruits for food, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says Rabbi Yehuda concedes regarding baskets of olives and grapes, implying that since they are designated for squeezing, one is aware; similarly, since the animal is designated for slaughter, one is aware.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between liquid that comes out of fruits for food (permitted) and for drink (forbidden).
Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel reports that Rabbi Yehuda concedes to the Sages regarding baskets of olives and grapes, where the liquid is forbidden.

The Gemara infers that since the baskets are designated for squeezing, one is aware and intends the liquid; similarly, since the animal is designated for slaughter, one is aware and intends the blood.

items.text: Rav's disagreement: Rabbi Yehuda disputed even in baskets of olives and grapes
items.text_en: Rav's disagreement: Rabbi Yehuda disputed even in baskets of olives and grapes
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav holds Rabbi Yehuda disputed even in the case of baskets of olives and grapes, so the previous proof does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav holds Rabbi Yehuda disputed even in the case of baskets of olives and grapes, undermining the previous proof.

items.text: Rav Sheishet's answer: Rabbi Yehuda's view on lamps
items.text_en: Rav Sheishet's answer: Rabbi Yehuda's view on lamps
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi explains that Rabbi Yehuda's position is like his view on lamps, where a new lamp may be moved but an old one may not due to disuse; the Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda applies this to muktzeh due to prohibition, and cites a mishnah where he does.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi answers that Rabbi Yehuda's position on the lamp is like his view on lamps: a new lamp may be moved but an old one may not, due to disuse (מיאוס).
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on lamps applies only to מוקצה מחמת מיאוס (disgust-based muktzeh) and not to מוקצה מחמת איסור (prohibition-based muktzeh).
The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda indeed applies מוקצה מחמת איסור (prohibition-based muktzeh), showing that his view extends to that category as well.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that metal lamps may be moved on Shabbat, except for one lit on that Shabbat. The Gemara begins to analyze this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that metal lamps may be moved on Shabbat, except for one lit on that Shabbat.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case is unique because the lamp is moved by hand, implying a distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case is unique because the lamp is moved by hand, implying a distinction.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution and Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution and Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda's view on cooking on Shabbat, citing the Tosefta where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar dispute whether food cooked on Shabbat may be eaten.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by identifying the Mishnah as following Rabbi Yehuda's view on cooking on Shabbat, citing the Tosefta where Rabbi Meir permits eating food cooked on Shabbat by an unintentional cook.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that food cooked unintentionally on Shabbat may be eaten after Shabbat, but if done intentionally it is permanently forbidden.
Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar adds that food cooked unintentionally may be eaten by others but not by the cook, and if intentional it is permanently forbidden for everyone.

items.text: Attempt to apply Rabbi Meir's view and rejection
items.text_en: Attempt to apply Rabbi Meir's view and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers interpreting the Mishnah as referring to an intentional act and following Rabbi Meir, but rejects this because the Mishnah compares to Yom Kippur, where both intentional and unintentional acts are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests interpreting the Mishnah as referring to an intentional act (מזיד) and following Rabbi Meir's view.
The Gemara rejects this because the Mishnah compares to Yom Kippur (יום הכיפורים), where both intentional and unintentional acts are forbidden, so the Mishnah cannot be limited to intentional acts.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the Mishnah's phrase
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase 'even though he is liable for his life' refers to an intentional act, but the ruling applies to an unintentional act, making the slaughter valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can be explained as referring to an unintentional act according to Rabbi Yehuda, given that the Mishnah explicitly says 'even though he is liable for his life'.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah means: even though in an intentional case he is liable for his life, here in an unintentional case his slaughter is valid.

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar's view
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar, but rejects this because he distinguishes between the person and others, while the Mishnah states 'his slaughter is valid' without distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah could follow Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar, who says that food cooked on Shabbat is never eaten.
The Gemara rejects this because Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar distinguishes between the person and others, while the Mishnah states 'his slaughter is valid' without distinction.

items.text: Rav's silence and the contradiction in his rulings
items.text_en: Rav's silence and the contradiction in his rulings
items.desc_en: A Tanna recited before Rav that one who cooks on Shabbat unintentionally may eat, but Rav remained silent. The Gemara questions why, noting that Rav taught his students like Rabbi Meir but lectured publicly like Rabbi Yehuda, and explains that the Tanna recited in his lecture hall where the audience listens to the lecturer, not the Tanna.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna recited before Rav that one who cooks on Shabbat unintentionally may eat, and Rav remained silent.
The Gemara questions why Rav remained silent, suggesting it might be because he holds like Rabbi Yehuda, but objects that one does not silence a Tanna who recites like Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rav Chanan bar Ami
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rav Chanan bar Ami
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects further, citing Rav Chanan bar Ami that Rav taught his students like Rabbi Meir but lectured publicly like Rabbi Yehuda due to the unlearned.
The Gemara resolves that the Tanna recited in Rav's lecture hall, where the audience listens to the lecturer (אמורא), not the Tanna, so Rav remained silent to avoid public confusion.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Tanna actually recited a case of slaughter on Shabbat, and Rav responded that Rabbi Meir only permits cooking because it is fit for eating, but slaughter is not. The Gemara notes a contradiction with a previous statement by Rav, and concludes that Rabbi Meir permits it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reports that a Tanna recited before Rav a case of slaughter on Shabbat, with the rule that if done unintentionally it may be eaten, but if intentional it may not.
Rav challenges the Tanna, saying that Rabbi Meir only permits cooking because it is fit for eating, but slaughter is not fit for eating, so Rabbi Meir would not permit it.

The Gemara objects that the Mishnah itself deals with slaughter, and Rav Huna reported that Chiyya bar Rav said in Rav's name that the meat is forbidden for eating that day, and the colleagues understood it as Rabbi Yehuda's view, implying that Rabbi Meir permits it.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir permits it, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Clarifying Rabbi Yehuda's position on slaughtering for a sick person
items.text_en: Clarifying Rabbi Yehuda's position on slaughtering for a sick person
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's prohibition by suggesting a case where the sick person was ill before Shabbat but recovered. This reframes the debate about whether the slaughter is permitted for the healthy person.

items.text: Rav's distinction between slaughtering and cooking for a sick person
items.text_en: Rav's distinction between slaughtering and cooking for a sick person
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Adda or Rav Yitzchak bar Adda quotes Rav: slaughtering for a sick person on Shabbat is forbidden for a healthy person, but cooking is permitted. The reason is that the meat is fit for eating raw, while the cooked dish is not.

items.text: Rav Pappa's reversal of the cases
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's reversal of the cases
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa notes that sometimes slaughtering is permitted (when the sick person was ill before Shabbat) and cooking is forbidden (when one cut a gourd for him). This shows the ruling depends on the specific circumstances.

items.text: Rav Dimi's ruling on slaughtering and cooking for a sick person
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's ruling on slaughtering and cooking for a sick person
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi from Nehardea rules: slaughtering for a sick person on Shabbat is permitted for a healthy person by means of a gentile (אומצא), because slaughter is essential for the meat; cooking is forbidden due to a decree lest one increase the amount for the healthy person.

items.text: Mishnah: Valid and invalid slaughtering implements
items.text_en: Mishnah: Valid and invalid slaughtering implements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that slaughtering with a hand sickle, flint, or reed is valid. It then lists the general rule: everyone may slaughter, at any time, with any implement except a harvest sickle, saw, teeth, or fingernail, because they cause choking.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah and resolution via attached vs. detached
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah and resolution via attached vs. detached
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses the term 'one who slaughters' (implying after the fact) for flint and reed, and cites a baraita permitting them initially. Rav Kahana resolves: the Mishnah refers to attached implements, the baraita to detached ones. Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya dispute attached slaughtering, but even Rabbi Chiya permits only after the fact.

items.text: Rejecting the resolution and reinterpreting the dispute
items.text_en: Rejecting the resolution and reinterpreting the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the attribution of the baraita to Rabbi Chiya, as it permits initially. It then reinterprets: the dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya is about after-the-fact validity, but Rabbi Chiya actually permits initially. The baraita's language 'to inform you of Rabbi's stringency' supports this.

items.text: Final resolution: Mishnah is Rabbi, and distinction between originally attached and later attached
items.text_en: Final resolution: Mishnah is Rabbi, and distinction between originally attached and later attached
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah is Rabbi's view, and Rabbi's own statements are reconciled by distinguishing between something originally attached and something detached and later reattached. A baraita supports this: slaughtering with a detached knife or a protruding rock is valid, but with a naturally growing reed is invalid.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction regarding attached vs. detached
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction regarding attached vs. detached
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two sources and concludes that there is a distinction between an object that was originally attached and one that was detached and then reattached.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between two sources by distinguishing between an object that was originally attached and one that was detached and then reattached.

items.text: Two resolutions for the contradiction about slaughtering with a detached handle
items.text_en: Two resolutions for the contradiction about slaughtering with a detached handle
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction between a ruling that slaughter with a detached handle (מוכני) is valid and a baraita that says it is invalid. Two answers are given: one distinguishes between a clay handle and a water handle, and the other distinguishes between primary force and secondary force.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between a ruling that slaughter with a detached handle (מוכני) is valid and a baraita that says it is invalid.
The first answer resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a clay handle (סרנא דפחרא) and a water handle (סרנא דמיא).
The second answer resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between primary force (כוח ראשון) and secondary force (כוח שני).

items.text: Rav Pappa's case of killing by water force
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's case of killing by water force
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa illustrates the distinction between primary and secondary force: one who ties another and pours a bucket of water on him, causing death, is liable because the water is considered his arrows (primary force), but with secondary force it is merely indirect causation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa illustrates the distinction between primary and secondary force: one who ties another and pours a bucket of water on him, causing death, is liable because the water is considered his arrows (primary force), but with secondary force it is merely indirect causation.

items.text: Proof that slaughter is performed on a detached object
items.text_en: Proof that slaughter is performed on a detached object
items.desc_en: Rav, sitting behind Rabbi Chiya, hears Rabbi state that slaughter must be on a detached object, citing the verse about Abraham taking the knife. Rav asks what Rabbi means, and Rabbi Chiya explains that Rabbi is referring to the letter vav written on the knife, while the verse itself merely teaches Abraham's alacrity.

sub.desc_en: The narrative sets the scene: Rav sits behind Rabbi Chiya, who is before Rabbi, and Rabbi states that slaughter must be performed on a detached object, citing the verse 'וַיִּקַּח אֶת הַמַּאֲכֶלֶת לִשְׁחֹט' (and he took the knife to slaughter).
Rav asks Rabbi Chiya what Rabbi means by his statement.
Rabbi Chiya explains that Rabbi is referring to the letter vav written on the knife (in the Torah scroll), not the verse itself.
Rav objects: but Rabbi cited the verse itself, not just the letter vav.
Rabbi Chiya resolves that the verse itself merely teaches Abraham's alacrity, not the law of slaughter on a detached object.

items.text: Rava's ruling on detached and reattached for idolatry
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on detached and reattached for idolatry
items.desc_en: Rava states that an object detached and then reattached is considered detached for the laws of idolatry, as one who bows to his own house renders it forbidden, and if it were considered attached, the verse 'their gods on the mountains' would not apply.
