The baraita then begins a derivation from the verse 'torim' meaning large ones.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule of mutual exclusion between turtledoves and pigeons regarding kosher age, and that the onset of yellowing disqualifies both.
The baraita elaborates the Mishnah's rule: large turtledoves are kosher, small ones invalid; small pigeons are kosher, large ones invalid, confirming the mutual exclusion.
A second baraita begins a derivation from the verse 'תּוֹרִים' (turtledoves) that it means large ones, not small ones, introducing a possible logical inference.

items.text: Derivation of age limits for turtle doves and young pigeons
items.text_en: Derivation of age limits for turtle doves and young pigeons
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a logical argument (kal vachomer) to determine the age limits for turtle doves and young pigeons. It concludes that the verses explicitly restrict turtle doves to adults and young pigeons to young ones, overriding the logical inference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if young pigeons, which are invalid as adults, are valid as young, then turtle doves, which are valid as adults, should certainly be valid as young.
The Gemara answers that the verse explicitly restricts turtle doves to adults and young pigeons to young ones, overriding the logical inference.

items.text: Rava's explanation of the biblical hint
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of the biblical hint
items.desc_en: Rava explains the scriptural hint: the verse could have written 'from the sons of turtle doves or from the dove' but instead wrote 'turtle doves' and 'young pigeons' to indicate the specific ages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the scriptural basis for this derivation?
Rava answers that the verse could have written 'from the young of turtle doves or from the pigeon,' but instead wrote 'turtle doves' and 'young pigeons,' indicating distinct age requirements.

items.text: Alternative interpretation and resolution
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the verse might allow both ages for turtle doves, but concludes by analogy to young pigeons that only adults are valid for turtle doves.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the verse only restricts young pigeons to young ones, but turtle doves could be brought either as adults or young.
The Gemara answers that turtle doves must be analogous to young pigeons: just as young pigeons are only young, so too turtle doves are only adults.

items.text: Baraita on the disqualification of beginning of yellowing
items.text_en: Baraita on the disqualification of beginning of yellowing
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that not all turtle doves or young pigeons are valid; the verses exclude those at the beginning of yellowing (a transitional stage). It specifies when turtle doves become valid (when they turn golden) and when young pigeons become invalid (when they turn yellow).

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that not all turtle doves and young pigeons are valid, excluding those at the beginning of yellowing (תחילת הציהוב).
The baraita specifies: turtle doves become valid when their feathers turn golden, and young pigeons become invalid when their feathers turn yellow.

items.text: Yaakov Korcha's definition for young pigeons
items.text_en: Yaakov Korcha's definition for young pigeons
items.desc_en: Yaakov Korcha teaches that young pigeons are valid from the time they can 'swallow' (a sign of maturity). He cites a verse and Abaye explains the timing: when one pulls a wing from it and blood comes.

sub.desc_en: Yaakov Korcha teaches that young pigeons are valid from the time they can 'swallow' (i.e., feed themselves).
Yaakov Korcha cites the verse 'its chicks swallow blood' (איוב לט:ל) to support his interpretation of 'swallowing' as a sign of maturity.
The Gemara asks: when does this swallowing ability begin?
Abaye answers: from the time one can pluck a wing feather from it and blood comes.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question about a vow and Rava's resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question about a vow and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if someone vows to bring an offering from turtle doves or young pigeons and brings one at the beginning of yellowing, is it valid (a doubt) or a distinct entity (invalid)? Rava brings a proof from the baraita that calls it 'excluded', implying it is a distinct entity, not a doubt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if one vows to bring an offering from turtle doves or young pigeons and brings one at the beginning of yellowing, is it a ספק (doubtful case) that can be resolved, or a distinct species that cannot?

Rava answers by citing the baraita that excludes the beginning of yellowing as invalid, arguing that if it were merely a doubt, the verse would not need to exclude it, so it must be a distinct species.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous discussion: birds are disqualified by bestiality and idolatry
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous discussion: birds are disqualified by bestiality and idolatry
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the verse was necessary: one might have thought that since birds are not disqualified by blemishes (as taught: תמות וזכרות is only for animals, not birds), they would also not be disqualified by bestiality or idolatry. The verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse was necessary to exclude animals that were used for bestiality (נרבע) or idolatry (נעבד) from being offered as sacrifices.

The Gemara raises a possible objection: since the verse says 'כי משחתם בהם מום בם' (for their corruption is in them, a blemish in them), and the school of Rabbi Yishmael taught that the term 'השחתה' (corruption) always refers to sexual immorality or idolatry, one might think that only animals blemished by these are disqualified.

The Gemara resolves that since birds are not disqualified by blemishes (as Mar taught: 'תמות וזכרות' applies only to animals, not birds), one might think they would also not be disqualified by bestiality or idolatry; therefore the verse teaches that they are indeed disqualified.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question about a פלגס as a vow offering
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question about a פלגס as a vow offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if one vows to bring an animal from the ram or lamb category, and brings a פלגס (an animal in its second year, intermediate between a lamb and a ram), what is the law? The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan, who says a פלגס is a distinct species (בריה), the question does not arise, because the Mishnah teaches that if one offers it, he brings the libations of a ram but it does not fulfill his vow.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks: if one vows to bring an animal from the ram or lamb category and brings a פלגס (an animal in its second year, intermediate between a lamb and a ram), what is the law?

sub.text: Gemara's clarification regarding Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's clarification regarding Rabbi Yochanan's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Yochanan, who considers a פלגס a distinct species (בריה), the question does not arise, because the Mishnah teaches that if one offers it, he brings the libations of a ram but it does not fulfill his vow.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the verse 'or to a ram' (ויקרא ז:יב) includes the פלגס, confirming its distinct status.

items.text: The question according to Bar Peda's view
items.text_en: The question according to Bar Peda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the question is relevant only according to Bar Peda, who holds a different view about the status of a פלגס. The discussion continues on the next daf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the question is only relevant according to Bar Peda's view, and the discussion continues on the next daf.

items.text: Query about a vow for a wild creature as a thanksgiving offering
items.text_en: Query about a vow for a wild creature as a thanksgiving offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who vows to bring a thanksgiving offering from a wild creature (beriyah) is obligated to bring it, or whether the vow is ineffective because the Torah specifies domesticated animals. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one who vows to bring a thanksgiving offering from a wild creature (beriyah) is obligated to bring it, or whether the vow is ineffective because the Torah specifies domesticated animals.
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku), suggesting the animal might be brought as a freewill offering.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's query about leavened starter in a vow for thanksgiving loaves
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's query about leavened starter in a vow for thanksgiving loaves
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about one who vows to bring loaves of thanksgiving from either leavened or unleavened bread and brings se'or (leavened starter). The Gemara analyzes the status of se'or according to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, and whether it can fulfill the vow. The discussion concludes with a teiku regarding whether the person fulfills his vow.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about one who vows to bring thanksgiving loaves from leavened or unleavened bread and brings sourdough (si'ur), questioning its validity.
The Gemara objects that the status of sourdough depends on the tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding its classification.
The Gemara refines the question to the case of Rabbi Yehuda's sourdough for Rabbi Yehuda, asking whether it is a doubt from which one can discharge the vow or a distinct entity that cannot.

The Gemara objects based on Rav Huna's ruling that one who vows thanksgiving loaves must bring both the offering and its loaves, but here the vower does not know whether to bring leavened or unleavened bread.
The Gemara answers that the case is where one vows a loaf to exempt another's thanksgiving offering, but the same ignorance problem persists.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where one did not say 'to exempt,' and the question of whether one discharges the vow remains unresolved (teiku).
The Gemara resolves: it is not necessary to consider that case; rather, the case is where he said 'I take upon myself a loaf to exempt so-and-so's thanksgiving offering.'
The Gemara concludes with a teiku (undecided): ultimately, since the person does not know whether he vowed for leavened or unleavened, does he fulfill his vow or not? The question stands unresolved.

items.text: Mishnah: Contrasting valid methods for the red heifer and the heifer whose neck is broken
items.text_en: Mishnah: Contrasting valid methods for the red heifer and the heifer whose neck is broken
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that what is valid for the red heifer (parah) is invalid for the heifer whose neck is broken (eglah), and vice versa.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the principle that what is valid for the red heifer (parah) is invalid for the heifer whose neck is broken (eglah), and vice versa.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita and attempted kal vachomer for the red heifer
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita and attempted kal vachomer for the red heifer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that specifies the red heifer is valid by slaughter and invalid by decapitation, while the heifer whose neck is broken is valid by decapitation and invalid by slaughter. It then attempts a kal vachomer to argue that the red heifer should also be valid by decapitation, but the argument is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the rules: the red heifer (פרה) is valid by slaughter (שחיטה) and invalid by decapitation (עריפה), while the heifer whose neck is broken (עגלה) is valid by decapitation and invalid by slaughter, concluding that what is valid for one is invalid for the other.

The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if the heifer, which is not valid by slaughter, is valid by decapitation, then the red heifer, which is valid by slaughter, should certainly be valid by decapitation.

items.text: Opening statement: עגלה ערופה requires עריפה, not שחיטה
items.text_en: Opening statement: עגלה ערופה requires עריפה, not שחיטה
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the verse says 'ושחט' and 'חוקה', implying that only שחיטה is subject to the rule of חוקה, not עריפה. This sets up the initial point about the calf.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by citing the verse 'ושחט' and 'חוקה', inferring that the rule of חוקה applies only to שחיטה, not to עריפה.

items.text: Challenge: Is a קל וחומר never applied where חוקה is written?
items.text_en: Challenge: Is a קל וחומר never applied where חוקה is written?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the principle by citing Yom Kippur, where חוקה is written yet a קל וחומר is used and then rejected by a verse. This shows that a קל וחומר would have been applied without the limiting verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) is never applied where a חוקה is written, citing the case of Yom Kippur where a קל וחומר is rejected by the verse 'ועשהו חטאת'.
The Gemara cites a baraita about Yom Kippur, showing that the verse 'ועשהו חטאת' teaches that the גורל (lot) makes the goat a sin-offering, not the divine name.
The baraita presents a hypothetical קל וחומר: if the divine name sanctifies where the lot did not, it should all the more so sanctify where the lot did.
The baraita rejects the קל וחומר with the verse 'ועשהו חטאת', teaching that the lot alone designates the sin-offering, not the divine name.
The Gemara concludes that only because the verse explicitly limits it, the קל וחומר is rejected; but without that verse, we would indeed apply the קל וחומר.

items.text: Resolution: The verse 'זאת' limits עגלה ערופה to עריפה
items.text_en: Resolution: The verse 'זאת' limits עגלה ערופה to עריפה
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the word 'זאת' in the context of עגלה ערופה excludes other methods. It then proposes a קל וחומר that the calf should be valid through שחיטה, but the verse 'וערפו' teaches that only עריפה is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the word 'זאת' (this) in the context of the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer) limits the method to עריפה (neck-breaking), excluding other methods.
The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that the heifer should be valid through שחיטה (slaughter) based on the red heifer.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'וערפו העגלה' (and they shall break the heifer's neck) teaches that only עריפה (neck-breaking) is valid, not שחיטה (slaughter).

items.text: Mishnah and baraita: Priests and Levites have opposite disqualifications
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita: Priests and Levites have opposite disqualifications
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that what is valid for priests is invalid for Levites and vice versa. The Gemara cites a baraita explaining that priests are disqualified by blemishes but not age, while Levites are disqualified by age but not blemishes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general principle: what is valid for priests is invalid for Levites, and vice versa.
The baraita explains the Mishnah: priests are disqualified by blemishes but not by age, while Levites are disqualified by age but not by blemishes.

items.text: Source for Levites: 'זאת אשר ללוים' excludes blemishes
items.text_en: Source for Levites: 'זאת אשר ללוים' excludes blemishes
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'זאת אשר ללוים' that only age disqualifies Levites, not blemishes, rejecting a קל וחומר from priests. Similarly, it derives that priests are not disqualified by age, using the phrase 'אשר ללוים' to exclude priests.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the rule that priests and Levites differ regarding blemishes and age.
The baraita cites the verse 'זאת אשר ללוים' to teach that only age disqualifies Levites, not blemishes, rejecting a קל וחומר from priests.
The baraita further derives that priests are not disqualified by age, using the phrase 'אשר ללוים' to exclude priests from the disqualification of age.

items.text: Limitation: These rules apply only when service is by shoulder
items.text_en: Limitation: These rules apply only when service is by shoulder
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that these disqualifications apply only in the wilderness, not in Shiloh or the Temple, as the verse 'לעבד עבדת עבדה ועבדת משא' indicates the context of carrying on the shoulder.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether these age restrictions apply also in Shiloh and the eternal Temple, and a baraita (תנו רבנן) cites the verse 'לעבד עבדת עבדה ועבדת משא' to limit them to the time when service was carried on the shoulder (the Tabernacle in the wilderness).

items.text: Reconciling verses on Levite age: 25 for study, 30 for service
items.text_en: Reconciling verses on Levite age: 25 for study, 30 for service
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction between verses stating Levites serve from age 25 and from age 30: the earlier age is for study, the later for actual service. This leads to a principle about students, with a dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two verses: one says Levites serve from age 25, another from age 30, and declares both must be reconciled.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: age 25 is for study, age 30 is for actual service.
The Gemara derives a principle: a student who does not see a good sign in his studies within five years will never see one.
Rabbi Yosei argues that the period is three years, citing the verse about Daniel and his companions being trained for three years.
The Sages object that the case of the Chaldean language is different because it is easy to learn.
Rabbi Yosei rebuts that the laws of the service are difficult, so the analogy to the Levites' study period is valid.

items.text: Baraita summarizing priest and Levite eligibility
items.text_en: Baraita summarizing priest and Levite eligibility
items.desc_en: A baraita summarizes: a priest is valid from puberty to old age, disqualified only by blemishes; a Levite is valid from 30 to 50, disqualified by age. This applies only in the Tabernacle, not in Shiloh or the Temple, where only voice disqualifies. Rabbi Yosei asks for the verse.

sub.desc_en: A baraita (תנו רבנן) summarizes: a priest is valid for service from the onset of two pubic hairs until old age, with blemishes disqualifying; a Levite is valid from thirty to fifty, with age disqualifying; this applies only to the Tabernacle in the wilderness, but in Shiloh and the eternal Temple they are disqualified only by voice; Rabbi Yosei asks for the scriptural source.
Rabbi Yosei asks for the scriptural source for the rule that Levites are disqualified by voice in Shiloh and the Temple.
The baraita limits the age disqualification to the Tabernacle in the wilderness; in Shiloh and the Temple, only voice disqualifies.
Rabbi Yosei asks for the scriptural source for this distinction.

items.text: Definition of 'zaken' (elder) for disqualification from service
items.text_en: Definition of 'zaken' (elder) for disqualification from service
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about the Levites ceasing service at age fifty and asks: until what age is one considered 'zaken' (old) for disqualification? Rabbi Il'a quoting Rabbi Chanina answers: until his hands tremble.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a verse about Levites ceasing service at age fifty.
The Gemara asks: until what age is one considered 'zaken' (old) for disqualification from service?
Rabbi Il'a in the name of Rabbi Chanina answers: until his hands tremble.

items.text: Definition of 'child' for impurity after immersion
items.text_en: Definition of 'child' for impurity after immersion
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a ba'al keri (one who had a seminal emission) who immersed but did not urinate: when he later urinates, he becomes impure. Rabbi Yose distinguishes between a sick/old person (impure) and a child/healthy person (pure). The Gemara asks: until what age is one considered a child? Rabbi Il'a quoting Rabbi Chanina answers: one who can stand on one foot and remove and put on his shoe. A story about Rabbi Chanina himself illustrates this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a ba'al keri (one who had a seminal emission) who immersed but did not urinate: when he later urinates, he becomes impure; Rabbi Yose distinguishes between a sick/old person (impure) and a child/healthy person (pure).
The Gemara asks: until what age is one considered a child for this halacha?
Rabbi Il'a quoting Rabbi Chanina answers: one who can stand on one foot and remove and put on his shoe.

A story is told about Rabbi Chanina himself, who at eighty years old could stand on one foot and remove and put on his shoe, attributing his vigor to the warm oil his mother anointed him with in childhood.

items.text: Age qualifications for priestly service and leading prayer
items.text_en: Age qualifications for priestly service and leading prayer
items.desc_en: A baraita states: when one's beard is full, he is fit to be a shaliach tzibbur (prayer leader) and to lift his hands (priestly blessing). For Temple service, he is fit from bringing two pubic hairs. Rabbi says: I say until he is twenty. Rav Chisda explains Rabbi's reasoning from a verse about Levites serving from age twenty, but the other opinion distinguishes because the verse says 'lenatze'ach' (to oversee). The Gemara addresses the objection that the verse is about Levites, not priests, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that in 24 places priests are called Levites.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states the age qualifications: a full beard qualifies one to be a prayer leader and perform the priestly blessing, while Temple service requires two pubic hairs; Rabbi says one must be twenty.
Rav Chisda explains Rabbi's reasoning from the verse about Levites serving from age twenty, and notes that the other opinion distinguishes because the verse says 'לנצח' (to oversee).
The Gemara objects that the verse is about Levites, not priests, and resolves it by citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that in 24 places priests are called Levites.

items.text: Dispute about the minimum age for priestly service
items.text_en: Dispute about the minimum age for priestly service
items.desc_en: Another baraita cites Rabbi Elazar: a minor is invalid for service even if unblemished, and is fit only from bringing two pubic hairs, but the priests do not allow him to serve until age twenty. The Gemara presents two interpretations: one says this is Rabbi's opinion (who invalidates even rabbinically), another says Rabbi does have rabbinic invalidation, and this baraita is the Rabbis' opinion, meaning only initially he may not serve, but if he served it is valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Elazar: a minor is invalid for service even if unblemished, and is fit only from bringing two pubic hairs, but the priests do not allow him to serve until age twenty.
One interpretation says this baraita reflects Rabbi's opinion, who invalidates even rabbinically.
Another interpretation says Rabbi does have rabbinic invalidation, and this baraita is the Rabbis' opinion, meaning only initially he may not serve, but if he served it is valid.

items.text: Mishnah: Contrasting impurity rules for earthenware and other vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Contrasting impurity rules for earthenware and other vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: what is pure in an earthenware vessel is impure in all other vessels, and what is pure in all other vessels is impure in an earthenware vessel. The Gemara cites a baraita explaining: the airspace of an earthenware vessel conveys impurity, but its outer side is pure; for all other vessels, the airspace is pure but their outer side conveys impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the contrasting impurity rules: what is pure in an earthenware vessel is impure in all other vessels, and vice versa.

The Gemara cites a baraita that explains the Mishnah: the airspace of an earthenware vessel conveys impurity but its outer side is pure, while for all other vessels the airspace is pure but their outer side conveys impurity.

items.text: Source for impurity of earthenware vessel's airspace
items.text_en: Source for impurity of earthenware vessel's airspace
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the source for this? A baraita derives from the verse 'tokho' (its interior) that impurity is conveyed even without contact. Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos argues by analogy: just as 'tokho' said for conveying impurity applies even without contact, so 'tokho' said for becoming impure applies even without contact. The Gemara then asks: from where do we derive that for conveying impurity? Rabbi Yonatan answers: the Torah testified about an earthenware vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters derived? It cites a baraita that derives from the verse 'תּוֹכוֹ' (its interior) that impurity is conveyed even without contact.
The baraita raises an objection: perhaps the verse means only if there is contact, not without contact.
Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtulmos answers by analogy: just as 'תּוֹכוֹ' said for conveying impurity applies even without contact, so 'תּוֹכוֹ' said for becoming impure applies even without contact.
The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that for conveying impurity (the first 'תּוֹכוֹ') it applies even without contact?
Rabbi Yonatan answers: the Torah testified about an earthenware vessel (that its airspace conveys impurity even without contact).

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even a mustard seed's worth of impurity can render a vessel impure, setting the stage for the Gemara's discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that even a mustard seed's worth of impurity can render a vessel impure.

items.text: Kal vachomer for earthenware vessel impurity from its outer surface
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for earthenware vessel impurity from its outer surface
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava proposes a kal vachomer that earthenware vessels should become impure from their outer surface, since other vessels do. The Gemara refutes this by citing a verse that limits impurity to when the vessel is open, implying that a sealed vessel is pure.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Ahava's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Ahava proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that an earthenware vessel should become impure from its outer surface, since other vessels do.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by citing a verse that limits impurity to when the vessel is open, implying that a sealed vessel is pure.

items.text: Kal vachomer for all vessels becoming impure from their airspace
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for all vessels becoming impure from their airspace
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that all vessels should become impure from their airspace, using a kal vachomer from earthenware vessels. This is refuted by a verse that says 'its interior' (תּוֹכוֹ), implying only earthenware vessels are impure from their airspace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) that all vessels should become impure from their airspace, based on earthenware vessels which become impure from their airspace even though they do not become impure from their outer surface.
The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by citing the verse 'תּוֹכוֹ' (its interior), which implies that only earthenware vessels are impure from their airspace, not other vessels.

items.text: Derivation of four instances of 'tocho'
items.text_en: Derivation of four instances of 'tocho'
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the word 'tocho' appears four times in the Torah, and each is used for a different derivation: one for the basic law, one for a gezerah shavah, one to exclude other vessels, and one to exclude the inner space of a vessel (even a vessel that is washed).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: But we have already expounded those instances of 'תוכו' (its interior) for other purposes, so how can one be used here?
The Gemara answers that four instances of 'תוכו' (its interior) are written in the Torah, providing sufficient material for multiple expositions.

The Gemara assigns each of the four instances: one for the basic law, one for a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy), one for 'its interior and not the interior of another', and one for 'its interior and not the interior of its interior', even for a vessel that is merely rinsed.

items.text: Kal vachomer that all vessels are not impure from their outer surface
items.text_en: Kal vachomer that all vessels are not impure from their outer surface
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that all vessels should not become impure from their outer surface, using a kal vachomer from earthenware vessels. This is refuted by a verse that implies all vessels (except earthenware) become impure from their outer surface regardless of sealing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that all other vessels should not become impure from their outer side, but only from their interior and by direct contact, since an earthenware vessel does not become impure from its outer side.
The Gemara refutes this by citing the verse 'וכל כלי פתוח' (Numbers 19:15), which implies that all other vessels become impure from their outer side regardless of whether they are sealed or not.

items.text: Mishnah: Pure in wooden vessels, impure in metal vessels
items.text_en: Mishnah: Pure in wooden vessels, impure in metal vessels
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that what is pure in wooden vessels may be impure in metal vessels, and vice versa, introducing the topic of unfinished vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that what is pure for wooden vessels is impure for metal vessels, and vice versa.
The Mishnah completes the statement by adding the reverse case: what is pure in metal vessels may be impure in wooden vessels.

items.text: Gemara: Unfinished wooden and metal vessels
items.text_en: Gemara: Unfinished wooden and metal vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa explaining that unfinished wooden vessels (golmei klei etz) are impure, while their flat forms are pure; for metal vessels, the opposite is true. It then defines what constitutes an unfinished wooden vessel and discusses a case where a vessel lacks a final smoothing step.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the general rule: unfinished wooden vessels are impure and flat ones pure, while for metal vessels the opposite holds.
The baraita defines unfinished wooden vessels as those needing smoothing, setting gems, planing, etc., or lacking a base, rim, or handle; lacking hollowing renders it pure.

The Gemara objects that lacking hollowing is obviously pure, and clarifies the case is where one hollowed a קְפִיזָא (three-log measure) in a vessel meant to hold a קַב (six log), so it is still incomplete.
The baraita begins to define unfinished metal vessels, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Impurity of vessels lacking certain parts
items.text_en: Impurity of vessels lacking certain parts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vessels lacking a base, rim, or ear are pure, but lacking a cover is impure. The Gemara questions the distinction, with Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Nachman offering different reasons. The discussion extends to bone vessels and their impurity status, supported by a baraita from Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that vessels lacking a base, rim, or ear are pure, but lacking a cover is impure.
The Gemara asks why there is a distinction between lacking a base/rim/ear and lacking a cover.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that these vessels are made for honor, so lacking a cover renders them unfit for use.
Rav Nachman answers that the vessels are expensive, so lacking a cover diminishes their value and renders them impure.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two opinions.
The Gemara answers that the difference lies in bone vessels, and cites Rav Nachman's view that bone vessels are like metal vessels in impurity.
The Gemara questions whether bone vessels indeed receive impurity.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael derives from a verse that vessels made from animal horns and hooves are susceptible to impurity, excluding birds.

items.text: משנה: שקדים מרים ומתוקים
items.text_en: Mishnah: Liability for bitter and sweet almonds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one liable for bitter almonds is exempt for sweet ones, and vice versa, establishing a distinction based on type.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהחייב במעשר בשקדים מרים פטור במתוקים, ולהפך, תלוי בגודלם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one liable for bitter almonds is exempt for sweet ones, and vice versa, establishing a distinction based on type.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת: החייב במעשרות בשקדים מרים פטור במתוקים, ולהפך.

items.text: גמרא: מחלוקות בשקדים
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute on almond liability
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita distinguishing liability based on size for bitter and sweet almonds. Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei reports a dispute: some say both are exempt, others say both are liable. Rabbi Il'a notes that Rabbi Chanina ruled in Tzippori like the one who says both are exempt. Rabbi Yochanan explains that even large bitter almonds can be sweetened by fire, thus they are liable.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרטת את דיני השקדים, ומחלוקת בין רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי (משם אביו) לבין אחרים אם כולם פטורים או כולם חייבים. רבי חנינא בציפורי פסק כדברי האומר שכולם פטורים. רבי יוחנן מסביר שהגדולים ראויים למתיקה באור.

sub.desc_en: The baraita establishes the baseline rule: small bitter almonds are liable, large ones exempt; for sweet almonds, large are liable, small exempt.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את הדין הבסיסי בשקדים: מרים קטנים חייבים וגדולים פטורים, מתוקים גדולים חייבים וקטנים פטורים.

sub.text: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי משם אביו
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei reports a dispute in his father's name: some say both types are exempt, others say both are liable.
sub.desc: רבי ישמעאל ברבי יוסי אומר משם אביו שכל השקדים פטורים, ויש אומרים שכל השקדים חייבים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Il'a reports that Rabbi Chanina ruled in Tzippori in accordance with the opinion that both types are exempt.
sub.desc: רבי אילעא מוסר שרבי חנינא בציפורי פסק כדברי האומר שכולם פטורים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that even large bitter almonds are liable because they can be sweetened by fire.
sub.desc: רבי אילעא מוסר שרבי חנינא בציפורי פסק כדברי האומר שכולם פטורים.

items.text: משנה: דיני תמד
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of temed (wine lees)
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that temed before fermentation cannot be bought with maaser money and invalidates a mikveh; after fermentation, it can be bought with maaser money and does not invalidate a mikveh.
items.desc: המשנה מבחינה בין תמד שלא החמיץ, שאינו נקנה בכסף מעשר ופוסל את המקווה, לבין תמד שהחמיץ, שדינו הפוך.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law of temed (wine lees): before fermentation it cannot be bought with maaser money and invalidates a mikveh; after fermentation it can be bought with maaser money and does not invalidate a mikveh.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת דיני תמד: לפני שהחמיץ אינו נקנה בכסף מעשר ופוסל את המקווה; לאחר שהחמיץ להפך.

items.text: משנה: אחין שותפין בקלבון ומעשר בהמה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Partners and exemptions
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that brothers who are partners are exempt from the half-shekel when liable for animal tithe, and vice versa.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאחין שותפין פטורים ממעשר בהמה כשחייבים בקלבון, ולהפך.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that brothers who are partners are exempt from the half-shekel when liable for animal tithe, and vice versa.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת: אחים שותפים, כשחייבים בקלבון פטורים ממעשר בהמה, ולהפך.

items.text: גמרא: זיהוי בעל המשנה בתמד
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the authority of the temed Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions which authority the Mishnah follows, noting a baraita where the Sages exempt and Rabbi Yehuda obligates one who adds water to temed and finds the original measure. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuah explains that the Mishnah cannot align with either view fully.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי הוא התנא של משנת התמד, ומבררת שאינה לא כרבי יהודה ולא כרבנן, ומביאה ברייתא המבחינה ביניהם. רב נחמן בשם רבה בר אבוה מנסה ליישב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which authority the Mishnah follows, noting it cannot be Rabbi Yehuda or the Sages.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי הוא התנא של משנת התמד, ומבררת שאינה לא כרבי יהודה ולא כרבנן.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where the Sages exempt and Rabbi Yehuda obligates one who adds water to temed and finds the original measure.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי הוא התנא של משנת התמד, ומבררת שאינה לא כרבי יהודה ולא כרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the problem: if the Mishnah follows the Sages, it should apply even after fermentation; if Rabbi Yehuda, even before fermentation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם המשנה כרבנן, קשה מדין החמיץ; ואם כרבי יהודה, קשה מדין לא החמיץ.

sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuah
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabba bar Avuah begins to explain the Mishnah's position, though the text cuts off.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם המשנה כרבנן, קשה מדין החמיץ; ואם כרבי יהודה, קשה מדין לא החמיץ.

items.text: מחלוקת בהחמצת תמד
items.text_en: Opening dispute: fermentation as the point of disagreement
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah's dispute is specifically about temed that has fermented, and that Rabbi Yehuda holds this view. Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina agrees that the dispute is only when it has fermented.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה לחכמים האם תמד שהחמיץ נחשב יין, ומצטטת את רבי יוסי בר חנינא המסביר שהמחלוקת היא דווקא כשהחמיץ.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the Mishnah's dispute is specifically about temed that has fermented.
Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina agrees that the dispute is only when the temed has fermented.

items.text: דין תמד שנלקח בכסף מעשר
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on temed bought with ma'aser money
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Rabbah bar Avuha that if temed was bought with second-tithe money and later fermented, it retroactively acquires the status of wine (and thus the tithe is valid). The reason is that fermentation reveals it was always a fruit product.
items.desc: רב נחמן בשם רבה בר אבוה קובע שתמד שנלקח בכסף מעשר ולבסוף החמיץ – קנה מעשר, משום שלמפרע מתברר שהיה פרי.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that temed bought with second-tithe money, if it later fermented, retroactively acquires the status of wine, because the fermentation reveals it was always a fruit product.

items.text: דחיית האפשרות שהתמד יחמיץ מאליו
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah and Rabbah's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah: why does it specify 'if it fermented'? Perhaps if left longer it would have fermented. Rabbah answers that the case is where a sample was left in a cup and did not ferment, proving it would not have fermented.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה שמשתמע ממנה שרק אם החמיץ, ולא אם לא החמיץ, ומתרצת בשם רבה שמדובר כששייר ממנו בכוס ולא החמיץ, כך שאין ספק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah: why does it specify 'if it fermented'? Perhaps if left longer it would have fermented.
Rabbah answers that the case is where a sample was left in a cup and did not ferment, proving it would not have fermented.

items.text: שיטת רבי יוחנן בן נורי במראה תערובות
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: Rava suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that appearance determines halakhic status. The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a mikveh where appearance is key, and argues that here too we follow appearance, so the temed is considered water.
items.desc: רבא מתרץ שהמשנה היא כרבי יוחנן בן נורי, הסובר שהולכים אחר המראה. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה נחלקו חכמים ורבי יוחנן בן נורי בתערובת יין או חלב במים, ומסיקה שגם כאן הולכים אחר המראה, והתמד נחשב מים.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by asserting that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a mikveh (מקוה) where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri rules that appearance determines the halakhic status of the water.
The Gemara concludes that just as Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri follows appearance (חזותא), here too the temed (תמד) is considered water because its taste and appearance are like water.

items.text: דעת רבי אלעזר ומחלוקת בהפרשה ממקום אחר
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's position and its implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that this view of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disagrees with Rabbi Elazar, who says all agree that one may not separate terumah from temed unless it has fermented. Rabbi Elazar holds that without fermentation there is a dispute, and Rabbi Yehuda only requires separation from the same batch, not from elsewhere, to avoid separating from the obligated for the exempt.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דעת רבי אלעזר הסובר שאין מפרישים על תמד ממקום אחר אלא אם החמיץ, ומבארת שהוא סובר שבתמד שלא החמיץ המחלוקת היא רק בתוך המין עצמו, אבל לא ממקום אחר, מחשש להפרשה מחיוב על פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the previous view of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri disagrees with Rabbi Elazar, who holds that all agree one may not separate תרומה (priestly portion) from temed unless it has fermented.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar holds that without fermentation there is a dispute, and Rabbi Yehuda only requires separation from the same batch (מִינֵּיהּ וּבֵיהּ), not from elsewhere, to avoid separating from the obligated for the exempt or vice versa.

items.text: תחילת ברייתא על תמד שלא החמיץ
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraisa on temed
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraisa that discusses the status of temed before it has fermented, setting up further analysis.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה להביא ברייתא העוסקת בדיני תמד לפני שהחמיץ, ומפסיקה באמצע.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa begins by introducing the topic of temed (wine lees) before it has fermented.

items.text: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah about immersing a dough
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on the Mishnah about immersing a dough
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's ruling about not immersing a dough after it has soured applies only when the water was initially pure and then became impure, but not if the water was impure from the start. Rav Geviha from Bei Ketil challenges this before Rav Ashi, arguing that the same logic should apply to water that was pure and then became impure, but the Gemara resolves that the case is different because the water is stirred.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one may immerse a dough in water, but once it has soured, one may not immerse it.
Rava limits the Mishnah: the rule applies only when the dough was initially pure and then became impure, but if it was impure from the start, immersion is ineffective.
Rav Geviha objects: if the reason is that water is heavier and the dough floats, then the same logic should apply to initially pure dough that later became impure.
The Gemara resolves: in both cases the water is stirred (בלבולי), so the dough is effectively immersed.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Sale and fine for a minor girl
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Sale and fine for a minor girl
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wherever there is a sale (of a minor daughter by her father), there is no fine (for seduction), and vice versa. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav identifies this as the view of Rabbi Meir, but the Sages hold that there is a fine even in a case where there is a sale. A baraita is cited detailing the ages for sale and fine according to Rabbi Meir and the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: wherever there is sale (of a minor daughter) there is no fine (for seduction), and vice versa.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say there is a fine in a place of sale.
A baraita details Rabbi Meir's position: from birth until two pubic hairs – sale but no fine; from two hairs until Bagrut – fine but no sale.
The Sages say: from three years and one day until Bagrut, she has a fine.
The Gemara clarifies: the Sages mean that she also has a fine in a place of sale, not that she has no sale.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Refusal and halitzah
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Refusal and halitzah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wherever there is refusal (mi'un), there is no halitzah, and vice versa. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav attributes this to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say there is refusal in a place of halitzah. A baraita is cited about the age until which a girl can perform refusal.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: wherever there is refusal (mi'un) there is no halitzah, and vice versa.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav attributes the Mishnah to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say there is refusal in a place of halitzah.
A baraita details: Rabbi Meir says a minor girl may refuse until she brings two pubic hairs; Rabbi Yehuda says until the black (hair) exceeds the white.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Shofar blowing and Havdalah on Yom Tov adjacent to Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Shofar blowing and Havdalah on Yom Tov adjacent to Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that wherever there is shofar blowing (on Yom Tov), there is no Havdalah, and vice versa. It details the practice when Yom Tov falls on Friday or Saturday night. The Gemara discusses how to blow the shofar (Rav Yehuda vs. Rav Asi), where to insert the Havdalah blessing (Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman say at the end, Rav Sheishet says also at the beginning), and Rabbi Dosa's version of the blessing. Rabbi Zeira adds a case for Yom Tov in the middle of the week.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: wherever there is shofar blowing there is no havdalah, and vice versa.
The Mishnah gives examples: on Yom Tov that falls on Friday, they blow the shofar but do not recite havdalah; on Saturday night, they recite havdalah but do not blow.
The Mishnah explains the havdalah formula: 'Who distinguishes between sacred and sacred'; Rabbi Dosa says 'between strict sacred and lenient sacred'.
The Gemara asks: how does one blow the shofar (on Yom Tov that falls on Friday)?
Rav Yehuda answers: one blows a tekiah and then a teruah within the same tekiah.
Rav Asi answers: one blows a tekiah and a teruah in a single breath.
Rav Asi established a practice in Hutzal according to his ruling.
A baraita is cited as an objection: on Yom Tov that falls on Friday, they blow but do not sound a teruah — does this mean no teruah at all?
The Gemara resolves: Rav Yehuda explains that 'no teruah' means not an independent teruah, but within the tekiah; Rav Asi explains it means not in two breaths, but in one breath.
The Gemara asks: where does one recite the havdalah (on Saturday night)?
Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman answer: in the concluding blessing (of the Amidah).
Rav Sheshet says: also in the opening blessing (of the Amidah).
The Gemara rules: the halacha is not in accordance with Rav Sheshet.
The Gemara rules: the halacha is not in accordance with Rabbi Dosa's formula.
Rabbi Zeira adds a digression: on Yom Tov that falls in the middle of Shabbat, one recites a longer havdalah formula listing all distinctions, because he is enumerating the order of distinctions.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the required number of simanim to cut for valid slaughter: one in fowl and two in beast, and that the majority of each is equivalent to the whole. Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the veins. It also rules on cases of partial cuts.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: one siman (סימן) in fowl and two in beast suffice for valid slaughter, and the majority of each is equivalent to the whole.
Rabbi Yehuda adds the requirement to cut the veins (ורידין) for valid slaughter.
The Mishnah rules that cutting half of one siman in fowl or one and a half in beast invalidates the slaughter.
The Mishnah concludes that cutting the majority of one siman in fowl or the majority of two in beast renders the slaughter valid.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's opening phrase 'השוחט' implies only after the fact, not initially. It questions whether two cuts in a beast are not allowed initially, and offers two resolutions: either the restriction applies to one cut in fowl, or to the ruling that a majority is like the whole.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's wording 'השוחט' that the ruling applies only after the fact, not לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara questions whether cutting two סימנים (shechita organs) in a beast is indeed not permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard).
The Gemara offers the first resolution: the restriction applies to cutting one סימן (shechita organ) in a bird.
The Gemara offers the second resolution: the restriction applies to the ruling that a majority of one סימן (shechita organ) is like the whole.
A mnemonic note indicating that the following discussion is organized by the letters ק, מ, ש.

items.text: Rav Kahana's derivation from 'וְשָׁחַט'
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's derivation from 'וְשָׁחַט'
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives that slaughter must be from the neck by interpreting 'וְשָׁחַט' as 'where one bends (שח) the neck'. He supports the meaning of 'חיטוי' as bending from verses. The Gemara rejects alternative locations (tail, ear) and questions why not cut until the blood vessels. It concludes that the source is tradition (גמרא), and the verse only teaches not to sever the head entirely (גיסטרא).

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives that slaughter must be from the neck by interpreting 'וְשָׁחַט' as 'from the place where it bends (שח), purify it (חטהו)', and supports the meaning of 'חיטוי' as purification from verses.
The Gemara objects that slaughter could be from the tail or ear, and the Gemara rejects the tail because it is perpetually bent, and the ear because it does not spill blood of the soul.

The Gemara objects that one could cut from the ear until the blood of the soul, and further questions the source for the disqualifications of shechita; it concludes that the requirement of slaughter from the neck is learned through tradition (גמרא).
The Gemara resolves that the verse comes only to teach that one should not sever the head completely, rendering it a broken animal (גיסטרא).

items.text: Rav Yemar's derivation from 'וְזָבַחְתָּ'
items.text_en: Rav Yemar's derivation from 'וְזָבַחְתָּ'
items.desc_en: Rav Yemar derives the same law from 'וְזָבַחְתָּ', interpreting it as 'where blood flows (זב) from the breaking (חתוי)'. He supports 'חתוי' as breaking from a verse. The Gemara rejects the nose and heart, and again concludes that the source is tradition, and the verse only teaches not to make it a גיסטרא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yemar derives that shechita is from the neck by interpreting 'וְזָבַחְתָּ' as 'from the place where blood flows (זב) from breaking (חתוי)'.
Rav Yemar supports that 'חתוי' means breaking by citing the verse 'אַל תִּירָא וְאַל תֵּחָת' (do not fear nor be broken).
The Gemara objects that one might think the nose is the place, but rejects it because blood flows from the nose spontaneously without breaking.
The Gemara objects that one might think the heart is the place, but it is rejected implicitly.
The Gemara asks: from where are the laws of shehiyah, derasah, chaladah, hagramah, and ikkur derived?
The Gemara answers that these laws are derived from tradition (גְּמָרָא).
The Gemara concludes that the law of shechita from the neck is also from tradition.
The Gemara explains that the verse comes only to teach not to make the animal a גיסטרא (a broken vessel, i.e., not to sever the head completely before finishing the shechita).

items.text: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from 'וְשָׁחַט' read as 'וְסָחַט' (squeeze), meaning from where one squeezes (סח) the neck. The Gemara rejects the tongue and the possibility of cutting until the blood, concluding again that the source is tradition and the verse only teaches not to make it a גיסטרא.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches a homiletic reading of 'וְשָׁחַט' as 'וְסָחַט' (squeeze), deriving that slaughter is performed from the place where one squeezes (סח) the neck.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the place of squeezing is the tongue, not the neck.
The Gemara rejects the tongue because it lacks the lifeblood (דם הנפש), then raises the possibility of cutting until the blood.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of deriving the location from the verse, noting that other laws of slaughter (שהייה, דרסה, etc.) are from tradition (גמרא), so the location is also from tradition.
The Gemara concludes that the verse comes only to teach that one should not make the animal a גיסטרא (a broken vessel, i.e., cut through the entire neck).

items.text: Rabbi Chiyya's derivation from the arrangement of the limbs
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya's derivation from the arrangement of the limbs
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya derives that slaughter is from the neck from the verse about arranging the limbs, where the head is listed separately, implying it was already severed from the neck. The Gemara clarifies the derivation and addresses a textual inconsistency, concluding that the verse teaches that the head and fat precede other limbs.

sub.desc_en: The tanna introduces Rabbi Chiyya's derivation that slaughter is from the neck, citing the verse about arranging the limbs.
Rabbi Chiyya explains that the separate mention of the head and fat in the verse teaches that the head was already partially severed from the neck, implying slaughter is from the neck.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Chiyya's statement that the head was already severed that slaughter is from the neck.
The Gemara questions the textual inconsistency in the baraita, which opens with one verse and concludes with another, and resolves that the derivation comes from the first verse.
The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to teach that the head and fat precede all other limbs when arranged on the altar.

items.text: Derivation of bird slaughter from the verse 'Zot Torat habehema veha'of'
items.text_en: Derivation of bird slaughter from the verse 'Zot Torat habehema veha'of'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the purpose of the extra 'peder' (fat) mentioned in the Torah, explaining it is needed for a baraita about covering the fat. It then cites a Tanna who derives from the verse that just as an animal requires shechita, so does a bird, but rejects the possibility that it requires a majority of two simanim like an animal, using the word 'zot' to limit it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah wrote the first mention of 'peder' (fat), and answers that it is needed for a baraita describing how to cover the fat as an honor.
A Tanna cites the verse 'Zot Torat habehema veha'of' and notes the differences in impurity laws between animal and bird.
The Gemara resolves that the verse teaches that just as an animal requires shechita, so does a bird, but the word 'zot' limits it to one siman (organ) rather than two.

items.text: דרשת רבי אליעזר על הצוואר
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's derivation: bird slaughter from the neck
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the verse equates animal and bird to teach that just as a bird is kosher from the neck, so too an animal is kosher from the neck. He rejects the possibility that the animal requires 'mimul oreph' (from the back of the neck) like a bird, citing the verse about melikah that specifies the bird's head is from the back of the neck, not another's.
items.desc: רבי אליעזר דורש את הפסוק להשוואת בהמה לעוף לעניין הכשר מהצוואר, ודוחה אפשרות של 'ממול עורף' לעוף.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse that just as a bird is kosher from the neck, so too an animal is kosher from the neck.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר דורש את הפסוק להשוואת בהמה לעוף לעניין הכשר מהצוואר.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that perhaps the animal requires slaughter from the back of the neck (ממול עורף) like a bird, and Rabbi Eliezer rejects this by citing the verse about melikah that specifies the bird's head is from the back of the neck, not another's.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדברי ר' אליעזר, ודוחה את האפשרות שדין עוף חל על בהמה לגבי ממול עורף.

items.text: שימושה של 'זאת' לרבי אליעזר
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's use of 'zot'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the word 'zot'. It explains that without 'zot', one might think that just as a bird requires only one siman, so too an animal requires only one siman; therefore the Torah wrote 'zot' to teach otherwise.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה עושה רבי אליעזר בפסוק 'זאת', ומתרצת שהוא בא למעט שחיטה בסימן אחד לבהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer does with the word 'zot' (this), since he did not use it in the previous derivation.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה דורש רבי אליעזר מהמילה 'זאת' בפסוק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without 'zot', one might have thought that just as a bird requires only one siman (organ), so too an animal requires only one siman; therefore the Torah wrote 'zot' to teach otherwise.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה דורש רבי אליעזר מהמילה 'זאת' בפסוק.

items.text: דרשת בר קפרא על סימן אחד לעוף
items.text_en: Bar Kappara's teaching: bird between animal and fish
items.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that the verse 'Zot Torat habehema veha'of' placed the bird between animal and fish: it cannot require two simanim because it is already compared to fish, and it cannot be exempt entirely because it is compared to animal; therefore its kosher method is with one siman.
items.desc: בר קפרא דורש את הפסוק להטלת עוף בין בהמה לדגים, המחייבתו בסימן אחד.

sub.desc_en: Bar Kappara teaches that the verse places the bird between animal and fish, so its kosher method requires one siman.
sub.desc: בר קפרא דורש את הפסוק להטלת עוף בין בהמה לדגים, המחייבתו בסימן אחד.

items.text: מקור אי-שחיטת דגים
items.text_en: Source that fish do not require shechita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know fish do not require shechita. It considers a proof from the verse about gathering fish, but rejects it because the same language is used for quail, which do require shechita. It concludes that the difference is that for fish, gathering is written in place of shechita for other creatures, while for quail it is not.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת מניין שדגים אינם טעונים שחיטה, ומתרצת מפסוקי אסיפה תוך דחיית קושיה משליו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that fish do not require shechita, and suggests a proof from the verse that distinguishes gathering fish from slaughtering animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מניין שדגים אינם טעונים שחיטה, ומציעה הוכחה מפסוקי אסיפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same gathering language is used for quail, which do require shechita, undermining the proof.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה משליו שגם נאמר בהם אסיפה, ומתרצת שהאסיפה שם אינה במקום שחיטה של אחרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that for fish, gathering is written in place of shechita for other creatures, while for quail it is not, so the proof stands.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה משליו שגם נאמר בהם אסיפה, ומתרצת שהאסיפה שם אינה במקום שחיטה של אחרים.

items.text: דרשת עובר גלילאה על בריאת העוף
items.text_en: Ober Galila'a's drasha and the creation of birds
items.desc_en: Ober Galila'a teaches that animals created from dry land require two simanim, fish from water require none, and birds from 'rekak' (mud) require one. Rav Shmuel Kappotka'a adds that birds have scales on their legs like fish. The Gemara then discusses a contradiction in verses about whether birds were created from water or earth, and resolves it with the answer that they were created from 'rekak'. When students are puzzled, the teacher explains that he dismissed his opponent with a weak answer, but the true answer is that birds were created from water, and they were brought to Adam to be named.
items.desc: עובר גלילאה דורש את בריאת העוף מהרקק, ורב שמואל קפוטקאה מוסיף ראיה מקשקשת. הגמרא מביאה קושיה מפסוקים סותרים ותירוץ על בריאת העוף מהמים.

sub.desc_en: Ober Galila'a teaches that animals created from dry land require two simanim, fish from water require none, and birds from 'rekak' (mud) require one.
sub.desc: עובר גלילאה דורש שבריאת העוף מהרקק מחייבת הכשר בסימן אחד, בניגוד לבהמה (שני סימנים) ודגים (ללא כלום).

sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel Kappotka'a adds that birds have scales on their legs like fish, supporting the idea that birds are intermediate between fish and land animals.
sub.desc: עובר גלילאה דורש שבריאת העוף מהרקק מחייבת הכשר בסימן אחד, בניגוד לבהמה (שני סימנים) ודגים (ללא כלום).

sub.desc_en: Students ask about a contradiction in verses: one verse says birds were created from water, another says from earth.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מפסוקים סותרים: האחד מורה שעוף נברא מהמים, והשני מהאדמה.

sub.desc_en: Ober Galila'a answers that birds were created from 'rekak' (mud), resolving the contradiction.
sub.desc: עובר גלילאה מתרץ שהעוף נברא מהרקק, ולאחר שתלמידיו תמהים על דחייתו, הוא מגלה שזו הייתה דחייה בקש, ובאמת העוף נברא מהמים, והפסוק השני מתייחס לקריאת השמות.

sub.desc_en: The teacher explains that he dismissed his opponent with a weak answer, but the true answer is that birds were created from water, and they were brought to Adam to be named.
sub.desc: עובר גלילאה מתרץ שהעוף נברא מהרקק, ולאחר שתלמידיו תמהים על דחייתו, הוא מגלה שזו הייתה דחייה בקש, ובאמת העוף נברא מהמים, והפסוק השני מתייחס לקריאת השמות.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Ober Galila'a said the weak answer to the heretic and the true answer to his students, because of the verse 'וַיִּצֶר' (and He formed).

items.text: מחלוקת על שחיטת עוף מהתורה
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's opinion: no biblical shechita for birds
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Pinchas states that there is no shechita for birds from the Torah, only 'shficha' (pouring). The Gemara objects that the same could be said for a chaya (wild animal), but it is compared to disqualified sacrifices. For birds, it is compared to animals via the verse 'Zot Torat habehema veha'of', but the verse 'veshafach et damo' is written. The Gemara asks why we apply this to birds and not to chaya, and answers that it is because the verse 'veshafach' is written in the context of birds.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי יצחק בן פנחס טוען שאין שחיטה לעוף מהתורה אלא שפיכה. הגמרא מקשה מחיה ומתרצת בהיקשים.

sub.text: רב יהודה משם רבי יצחק בן פנחס
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rabbi Yitzchak ben Pinchas
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Pinchas that there is no biblical requirement of shechita for birds, only a pouring of blood (שפיכה).
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי יצחק בן פנחס קובע שאין שחיטה לעוף מן התורה, אלא די בשפיכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if birds require only pouring, the same could apply to a חיה (wild animal), but the Torah compares a חיה to disqualified sacrifices, requiring shechita.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, גם חיה תיפטר משחיטה? ומתרצת שחיה הוקשה לפסולי המוקדשין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that birds are compared to animals via the verse 'זאת תורת הבהמה והעוף', yet the verse 'ושפך את דמו' is written specifically for birds, indicating a different rule.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם כן, גם חיה תיפטר משחיטה? ומתרצת שחיה הוקשה לפסולי המוקדשין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse 'ושפך' is applied specifically to birds rather than to a חיה.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע דוחים את הפסוק 'ושפך' לעוף ולא לחיה? ומתרצת: מסתבר שדוחים למה שסליק מיניה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that it is logical to apply the pouring requirement to birds because the verse 'ושפך' appears in the context of birds (the subject of the passage).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע דוחים את הפסוק 'ושפך' לעוף ולא לחיה? ומתרצת: מסתבר שדוחים למה שסליק מיניה.

items.text: סימן וקושיות מברייתות
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about covering blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: one who slaughters and the animal becomes a neveila, or one who stabs or tears, is exempt from covering the blood. If there is no biblical shechita for birds, then stabbing would be its slaughter and should require covering. The Gemara deflects: the baraita refers to a chaya, not a bird. Another baraita: one who slaughters and needs the blood must cover it; how? By stabbing or tearing it.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה סימן ומקשה מברייתות על השוחט ונתנבלה ועל השוחט וצריך לדם, ומתרצת שהן בחיה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one who slaughters and the animal becomes a neveila, or one who stabs or tears, is exempt from covering the blood.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא האומרת שהשוחט ונתנבלה פטור מכיסוי, ומכאן שאם שחיטת עוף אינה מן התורה, הרי ניחורו הוא שחיטתו והיה חייב בכיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if there is no biblical shechita for birds, then stabbing would be its slaughter and should require covering the blood.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא האומרת שהשוחט ונתנבלה פטור מכיסוי, ומכאן שאם שחיטת עוף אינה מן התורה, הרי ניחורו הוא שחיטתו והיה חייב בכיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects: the baraita refers to a chaya, not a bird.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא האומרת שהשוחט ונתנבלה פטור מכיסוי, ומכאן שאם שחיטת עוף אינה מן התורה, הרי ניחורו הוא שחיטתו והיה חייב בכיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: one who slaughters and needs the blood must cover it; how? By stabbing or tearing it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא נוספת האומרת שהשוחט וצריך לדם חייב לכסות, ומכאן שאם שחיטת עוף אינה מן התורה, הרי ניחורו הוא שחיטתו והיה חייב בכיסוי.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא הראשונה
items.text_en: Clarifying the earlier Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about a bird refers to needing its blood for sprinkling (like a chatas) or for a non-sacred purpose. It concludes it refers to a non-domesticated animal (chayah) needing its blood for a non-sacred purpose.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם המשנה עוסקת בעוף, שצריך את דמיו ליניקה? ודוחה: לא, מדובר בחיה שצריך את דמיו ללכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling about a bird refers to needing its blood for sprinkling (like a chatas) or for a non-sacred purpose.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם המשנה עוסקת בעוף, שצריך את דמיו ליניקה? ודוחה: לא, מדובר בחיה שצריך את דמיו ללכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that it refers to a non-domesticated animal (chayah) needing its blood for a non-sacred purpose.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם המשנה עוסקת בעוף, שצריך את דמיו ליניקה? ודוחה: לא, מדובר בחיה שצריך את דמיו ללכה.

items.text: ברייתא על מליקה בסכין
items.text_en: Challenge from melikah with a knife
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa: if one performed melikah with a knife, it conveys impurity of garments at the gullet. If there is no Torah-level shechitah for birds, even if breaking the spine makes it a tereifah, the knife should still purify it from neveilah status. This challenges the view that bird slaughter is not Torah-based.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא: המולק בסכין מטמא בגדים בבית הבליעה, ומקשה: אם אין שחיטה לעוף מן התורה, הרי גם אם שבר את השדרה והמפרקת נעשתה טריפה, מה מועיל הסכין לטהרה מנבלה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa: if one performed melikah with a knife, it conveys impurity of garments at the gullet, challenging the view that bird slaughter is not Torah-based.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא: המולק בסכין מטמא בגדים בבית הבליעה, ומקשה: אם אין שחיטה לעוף מן התורה, הרי שבירת השדרה עושה אותו טרפה, ומה מועיל הסכין לטהרו מנבלה?

items.text: ברייתא של רבי אלעזר הקפר ומחלוקת רבי
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's derivation and Rabbi's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the previous challenge aligns with a specific Tanna: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, who derives from a verse that birds have no Torah-level shechitah, only rabbinic. Then it asks who disagrees with him, and answers: Rabbi, who holds that Moses was commanded about the esophagus and trachea, and about a majority of one siman in birds and two in animals.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא של רבי אלעזר הקפר המלמדת שעוף אין לו שחיטה מן התורה אלא מדברי סופרים, ואת מחלוקת רבי האומר שנצטווה משה על הוושט והקנה, על רוב אחד בעוף ועל רוב שנים בבהמה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous challenge aligns with a specific Tanna, namely Rabbi Elazar HaKappar, and introduces his baraita.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה את הברייתא של רבי אלעזר הקפר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar derives from a verse that birds have no Torah-level shechitah, only rabbinic, by comparing deer and ibex to disqualified consecrated animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה את הברייתא של רבי אלעזר הקפר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna disagrees with Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's position that birds have no Torah-level shechitah.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי חולק על רבי אלעזר הקפר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rabbi is the one who disagrees, as he holds that Moses was commanded about the esophagus and trachea, and about a majority of one siman in birds and two in animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מי חולק על רבי אלעזר הקפר.

items.text: Dispute over 'one siman' in birds
items.text_en: Dispute over 'one siman' in birds
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and Rav Adda bar Ahavah argue about the meaning of 'one siman' in birds: Rav Nachman says either the esophagus or the trachea, while Rav Adda bar Ahavah says specifically the esophagus and not the trachea. Each supports his view with a reading of the word 'echad'.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about the meaning of 'one siman' in birds.
Rav Nachman states that 'one siman' means either the esophagus or the trachea.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah argues that 'one siman' refers specifically to the esophagus and not the trachea.
Rav Nachman supports his view by interpreting 'echad' as 'any one'.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah supports his view by interpreting 'echad' as 'unique' (the esophagus alone).

items.text: Siman for the following challenges
items.text_en: Siman for the following challenges
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is given for the upcoming series of challenges: 'Shachat, chatsa'in, gargeres, pegimah, dechattas ha'of.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic (סימן) listing the topics of the upcoming challenges: 'Shachat, chatsa'in, gargeres, pegimah, dechattas ha'of.'

items.text: תיובתא ראשונה: ברייתא על שמיטת גרגרת
items.text_en: Challenge from a case of a slipped trachea
items.desc_en: A baraisa is brought: if one slaughtered the esophagus and then the trachea slipped, it is valid; if the trachea slipped first and then he slaughtered the esophagus, it is invalid. The Gemara notes that the baraisa does not mention slaughtering the trachea, implying that only the esophagus is required for birds. The Gemara deflects: the trachea is prone to slipping, so it is not mentioned.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על שחט את הוושט ואחר כך נשמטה הגרגרת – כשרה, ומקשה: הרי לא נזכרה שחיטת גרגרת בעוף, מה שסותר את רב אדא בר אהבה. הגמרא דוחה: גרגרת עבידא לאישתמוטי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Adda bar Ahava by citing a baraisa that lists cases involving the esophagus but never mentions slaughtering the trachea, implying that only the esophagus is required for birds.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא על רב אדא בר אהבה, שכן הברייתא מזכירה רק שחיטת הוושט ולא את הגרגרת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the challenge by explaining that the trachea is prone to slipping, so the baraisa does not mention slaughtering it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהברייתא לא הזכירה גרגרת משום שדרכה להשמט, ולכן אינה צריכה שחיטה נפרדת.

items.text: תיובתא שנייה: ברייתא על שני חצאי סימנים
items.text_en: Challenge from two half-simanim
items.desc_en: Another baraisa: if one slaughtered two half-simanim in a bird, it is invalid; Rabbi Yehudah says one must slaughter the esophagus and the veins because the esophagus is near the veins. This implies that both simanim are needed, challenging Rav Adda bar Ahavah.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא: שחט שני חצאי סימנים בעוף – פסולה, ורבי יהודה אומר בעוף עד שישחוט את הוושט ואת הוורידין. מכאן ששחיטת סימן אחד בעוף כשרה, בניגוד לרב אדא בר אהבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa: if one slaughtered two half-simanim in a bird, it is invalid, and needless to say in an animal.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא: שחט שני חצאי סימנים בעוף – פסולה; רבי יהודה אומר: בעוף צריך לשחוט את הוושט ואת הורידין.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehudah adds that in a bird one must slaughter the esophagus and the veins because the esophagus is near the veins.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא: שחט שני חצאי סימנים בעוף – פסולה; רבי יהודה אומר: בעוף צריך לשחוט את הוושט ואת הורידין.

items.text: Challenge from half a trachea with waiting
items.text_en: Challenge from half a trachea with waiting
items.desc_en: A baraisa: if one slaughtered half the trachea, waited, and completed the slaughter, it is valid. The Gemara initially assumes this is about a bird and that 'completed' means completing the trachea, but deflects: it is about an animal, and 'completed' means completing the entire slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraisa about slaughtering half a trachea, waiting, and completing the slaughter, which is valid.
The Gemara initially assumes the case is about a bird and that 'completed' means completing the trachea.
The Gemara deflects: the case is about an animal, and 'completed' means completing the entire slaughter.

items.text: Challenge from a damaged trachea with addition
items.text_en: Challenge from a damaged trachea with addition
items.desc_en: Another baraisa: if half the trachea was damaged and one added any amount and completed it, the slaughter is valid. The Gemara initially assumes this is about a bird and 'completed' means completing the trachea, but deflects: it is about an animal, and 'completed' means completing the esophagus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraisa: if half the trachea was damaged and one added any amount and completed it, the slaughter is valid, and challenges that this implies it is about a bird where completing the trachea suffices.
The Gemara deflects: it is about an animal, and 'completed' means completing the esophagus, not the trachea.

items.text: תיובתא חמישית: מליקת חטאת העוף
items.text_en: Conclusive challenge from the procedure of bird chatas
items.desc_en: A baraisa describes how to perform melikah for a bird chatas: cut the spine and neck without most flesh until reaching the esophagus or trachea, then cut one siman with most flesh. For an olah, two simanim. This proves that one siman suffices, and it can be either the esophagus or the trachea, refuting Rav Adda bar Ahavah. The Gemara deflects weakly: perhaps the case is different because the spine and neck are present.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על מליקת חטאת העוף, שבה חותך סימן אחד ורוב בשר עמו, ומכאן ששחיטת סימן אחד בעוף כשרה – תיובתא לרב אדא בר אהבה. הגמרא דוחה: שאני התם דאיכא שדרה ומפרקת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita describing the procedure for pinching a bird sin offering, showing that one siman (either the esophagus or trachea) suffices, which conclusively refutes Rav Adda bar Ahava's position.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על מליקת חטאת העוף: חותך שדרה ומפרקת עד שמגיע לוושט או לקנה, ואז חותך סימן אחד. ומקשה: זו תיובתא לרב אדא בר אהבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara weakly deflects the refutation by suggesting that the case of pinching is different because the spine and neck bone are present, so the ruling may not apply to ordinary slaughter.

items.text: מעשה באווזא בבית רבא
items.text_en: Practical dilemma about a goose
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story: a goose in Rava's house came with its neck dripping blood. Rava asks what to do, implying a practical question about slaughter.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה באווזא בבית רבא, ורבא שואל כיצד לעשות, מה שמרמז על המשך הדיון.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the halakha is and cites an incident of a goose in Rava's house with blood on its neck, prompting Rava's question about what to do.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה מעשה: אווזא בבית רבא, בא כי ממסמס קועיה דמא, ורבא שואל: היכי נעביד?

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על בדיקת הוושט
items.text_en: The dilemma of checking the windpipe before slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if one finds a needle in the windpipe after slaughter, should one have checked it beforehand? But checking from outside is impossible, as Rabbah said. Rav Yosef suggests checking the windpipe, slaughtering it, then turning the animal to check the esophagus. Rava praises him, implying that 'one' means either one or the other.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על הצורך בבדיקת הוושט לפני השחיטה, ומציעה חלופות. רב יוסף מציע פתרון לבדוק את הקנה ולשחוט אותו, ואז להפוך את הוושט ולבדוק אותו. רבא משבח את רב יוסף על חוכמתו בטריפות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: if one finds a needle in the windpipe after slaughter, should one check it beforehand? But checking from outside is impossible, as Rabbah said.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם בדיקת הוושט צריכה להיעשות מבפנים, כיצד ניתן לבדוק לפני השחיטה; ומציעה אפשרות של שחיטה ואז בדיקה, אך דוחה זאת מחשש שמא שוחט במקום נקב, ולכן בודקים מבחוץ אך רבא קבע שאין לו בדיקה מבחוץ.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests checking the windpipe, slaughtering it, then turning the animal to check the esophagus; Rava praises him, implying that 'one' means either one or the other.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מציע: בודקים את הקנה, שוחטים אותו ומכשירים אותו, ואז הופכים את הוושט ובודקים אותו.

items.text: דברי רב חסדא על רבי יהודה
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion limited to fowl
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yehuda's requirement to cut the jugular veins applies only to fowl, which is roasted whole, but not to an animal, which is cut into pieces.
items.desc: רב חסדא מסביר שרבי יהודה דורש שחיטת הוורידים רק בעוף, כי צולה אותו שלם, אבל בבהמה לא צריך.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that shechita requires cutting the jugular veins.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה קובע שהשחיטה כשרה עד שישחוט, כלומר רק בשעת שחיטה יש צורך לחתוך את הוורידין, לא אחר כך.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that Rabbi Yehuda's requirement applies only to fowl, which is roasted whole, but not to an animal, which is cut into pieces.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה קובע שהשחיטה כשרה עד שישחוט, כלומר רק בשעת שחיטה יש צורך לחתוך את הוורידין, לא אחר כך.

items.text: בירור טעמו של רבי יהודה
items.text_en: The reason for Rabbi Yehuda's requirement: blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's reason is due to blood, citing a mishnah where he requires cutting the veins. It reinterprets 'until he cuts' as 'until he pierces during slaughter.' A baraisa confirms that the veins must be pierced during slaughter, and the Sages argue that since the purpose is to let out blood, timing doesn't matter. Rabbi Yehuda holds that during slaughter the blood is flowing, but later it congeals.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת האם טעמו של רבי יהודה הוא משום דם, ומביאה ברייתא שבה חכמים מקשים עליו. הגמרא מסבירה שרבי יהודה סובר שצריך לנקוב את הוורידים בשעת שחיטה, כי אז הדם חם ויוצא, ולא לאחר מכן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's requirement to cut until slaughter is due to blood.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם טעמו של רבי יהודה הוא משום דם.
