sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the veins, not just blood flow.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם טעמו של רבי יהודה הוא משום דם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets 'until he cuts' as 'until he pierces the veins during slaughter.'
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת ש'עד שישחוט' פירושו 'עד שינקוב בשעת שחיטה', כלומר רבי יהודה דורש לנקוב את הוורידין דווקא בשעת שחיטה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that veins must be pierced during slaughter according to Rabbi Yehuda.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא נוספת התומכת בפירוש: 'וורידין בשחיטה, דברי רבי יהודה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the baraita means the veins must be pierced during slaughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא נוספת התומכת בפירוש: 'וורידין בשחיטה, דברי רבי יהודה'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited where the Sages argue to Rabbi Yehuda that since the veins' purpose is to let out blood, timing is irrelevant.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה חכמים מקשים על רבי יהודה: 'מה לי בשחיטה, מה לי שלא בשחיטה?' ומכאן שרבי יהודה סובר שצריך בשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Sages' argument that Rabbi Yehuda indeed holds that the veins must be pierced during slaughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה חכמים מקשים על רבי יהודה: 'מה לי בשחיטה, מה לי שלא בשחיטה?' ומכאן שרבי יהודה סובר שצריך בשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that during slaughter the blood flows, but later it congeals, so timing matters.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שחכמים התכוונו: 'מה לי לנקבן בשעת שחיטה, מה לי לנקבן שלא בשעת שחיטה?' ורבי יהודה סובר שבשעת שחיטה הדם חם ויוצא, שלא בשעת שחיטה הדם קר ואינו יוצא.

items.text: בעיית רבי ירמיה ותשובת רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's question about delays and pressing on the veins
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether, according to Rabbi Yehuda, if one paused or pressed on the veins during slaughter, the animal is invalid. An elder answers in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one may pierce them with a thorn and they are valid.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה שואל על דין שהייה ודרסה בוורידים לרבי יהודה. זקן אחד משיב בשם רבי יוחנן שניתן לנקוב אותם בקוץ והם כשרים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether, according to Rabbi Yehuda, if one paused (שהה) or pressed (דרס) on the veins during slaughter, the animal is invalid.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה שואל מה דין שהייה ודרסה בוורידים לשיטת רבי יהודה.

sub.text_en: Elder in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: An elder answers in the name of Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Yochanan, that one may pierce the veins with a thorn and they are valid, implying no invalidation from delay or pressing.
sub.desc: זקן משיב בשם רבי יוחנן שניתן לנקוב את הוורידים בקוץ והם כשרים, וממילא שהייה ודרסה אינן פוסלות.

items.text: ברייתא כתמיכה לרב חסדא
items.text_en: Baraisa supporting Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: A baraisa supports Rav Chisda: if one slaughtered two half-simanim in a fowl it is invalid, and Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the windpipe and veins in a fowl.
items.desc: ברייתא תומכת בדברי רב חסדא: בעוף ששחט שני חצאי סימנים פסול, ורבי יהודה אומר שבעוף צריך לשחוט גם את הוושט וגם את הוורידים.

sub.desc_en: A baraisa supports Rav Chisda: if one slaughtered two half-simanim in a fowl it is invalid.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת ברב חסדא: בעוף ששחט שני חצאי סימנין – פסול, ומפורש שרבי יהודה מחייב גם וורידין בעוף.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the windpipe and veins in a fowl.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת ברב חסדא: בעוף ששחט שני חצאי סימנין – פסול, ומפורש שרבי יהודה מחייב גם וורידין בעוף.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ורב כהנא על חצי שיעור
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Kahana: half-cut as majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rav says half-cut is considered a majority (based on 'do not leave a majority'), while Rav Kahana says it is not (based on 'slaughter a majority'). The mishnah states that cutting half of one siman in a fowl is invalid; if half is considered a majority, why is it invalid? The Gemara answers that it is a rabbinic decree lest one come to cut only half.
items.desc: רב ורב כהנא נחלקו אם חצי על חצי נחשב כרוב. הגמרא מביאה סימן ומקשה ממשנה על שיטת רב, ומתרצת שהפסול הוא מדרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records the dispute: Rav says half-cut is considered a majority (כרוב), while Rav Kahana says it is not.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין חצי אחד בעוף וחצי בבהמה ששחיטתו פסולה.

sub.desc_en: Rav derives his position from the divine instruction 'do not leave a majority' (לא תשייר רובא), implying that half is considered a majority.
sub.desc: כל אחד מהחכמים מביא ראיה מדרשת הפסוקים למחלוקתם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana derives his position from the divine instruction 'slaughter a majority' (שחוט רובא), implying that half is not a majority.
sub.desc: כל אחד מהחכמים מביא ראיה מדרשת הפסוקים למחלוקתם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: the mishnah rules that cutting half of one siman in a fowl is invalid; if half is considered a majority, why is it invalid?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה ממשנה שלכאורה סותרת את שיטת רב שחצי נחשב כרוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the invalidation is a rabbinic decree (מדרבנן), lest one come to cut only half (פלגא) and not a full majority.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה ממשנה שלכאורה סותרת את שיטת רב שחצי נחשב כרוב.

items.text: ראיה נוספת של רב קטינא
items.text_en: Proof from a case of splitting a carcass
items.desc_en: Rav Katina brings a proof: if one splits a carcass into two equal parts, both are impure because exact division is impossible. But if exact division were possible, they would be pure, yet each would contain a majority. Rav Pappa answers that two majorities cannot exist in one item.
items.desc: רב קטינא מביא ראיה ממשנה על חצאי שיעור, ורב פפא דוחה את הראיה בטענה שאי אפשר שיהיו שני רובין באותו דבר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Katina brings a proof from a case of splitting a carcass into two equal parts, where both are impure because exact division is impossible.
sub.desc: רב קטינא מביא ראיה ממשנה על חצאי שיעור, המוכיחה שאם אפשר לצמצם הרי הם טהורים, ומכאן שחצי על חצי אינו כרוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions: if exact division were possible, why would both halves be pure? Each would contain a majority (רוב).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם אפשר לצמצם, מדוע החצאים טהורים? הרי בכל חצי יש רוב של הטומאה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa answers that two majorities (רוב) cannot exist in one item, so the halves cannot both be considered a majority.
sub.desc: רב פפא דוחה את הראיה: אי אפשר שיהיו שני רובין באותו דבר, ולכן אין מכאן ראיה לחצי על חצי.

items.text: תחילת דיון על חצי גרגרת
items.text_en: Beginning of a new case: half a ring and pausing
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new inquiry: if one slaughtered half a ring (of the trachea) and paused...
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה לדון במקרה של שחיטת חצי גרגרת ושהייה בה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new case: one who slaughtered half a ring (of the trachea) and paused.
sub.desc: תחילת הבאת ברייתא: שחט חצי גרגרת ושהה בה – פותחת סוגיה על שיעורי שהייה.

items.text: Question on half-and-half as majority
items.text_en: Question on half-and-half as majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if half-and-half is considered a majority, then a bird with half the trachea cut would be invalid (טריפה). It then suggests the mishnah might refer to a bird, not an animal, and analyzes both possibilities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: if half-and-half is considered a majority (רוב), then a bird with half the trachea cut would be invalid (טריפה), contradicting the mishnah's ruling.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah might refer to a bird, not an animal, and analyzes both possibilities: if half-and-half is a majority, the bird's majority is achieved; if not, nothing is done.

items.text: Proof from a defective reed
items.text_en: Proof from a defective reed
items.desc_en: A baraisa is cited: if half the reed (trachea) was defective and one added any amount, the slaughter is valid. If half-and-half were a majority, it would be invalid. Rava distinguishes: for treifot, we require a visible majority (רוב הנראה לעינים).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if half the trachea was defective and one added any amount and completed the slaughter, the slaughter is valid, implying that half-and-half is not considered a majority.
The Gemara objects: if half-and-half were considered a majority, the animal would be a treifa (ritually unfit), contradicting the baraita's ruling.
Rava distinguishes: for treifot (ritual unfitness), we require a visible majority (רוב הנראה לעינים), so the baraita's case does not prove the general rule.

items.text: Abaye's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that if treifot require a visible majority, then shechitah, which requires a majority for validity, should certainly require a visible majority.

sub.desc_en: Abaye argues by a קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if treifot require a visible majority, then shechitah, which requires a majority for validity, should certainly require a visible majority.

items.text: Resolution: dispute applies to Pesach
items.text_en: Resolution: dispute applies to Pesach
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that everyone agrees half-and-half is not a majority for shechitah. The dispute between Rav and Rav Kahana about half-and-half being like a majority was stated regarding Pesach, where half the people are pure and half impure. Rav's reasoning is that an individual is deferred, but the community is not deferred.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees half-and-half is not like a majority for shechitah, and the dispute between Rav and Rav Kahana was stated regarding Pesach.
The Gemara cites the case of half-pure and half-impure Israelites for Pesach, where Rav and Rav Kahana dispute whether half-and-half is like a majority.
Rav explains his position: an individual is deferred from bringing the Pesach offering when impure, but the community is not deferred, based on the verse 'איש איש כי יהיה טמא לנפש'.

items.text: Majority of one in a bird: need for two teachings
items.text_en: Majority of one in a bird: need for two teachings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the principle 'the majority of one is like the whole' is taught twice (in chullin and kodashim) and explains why both are necessary: for chullin, one might think a half suffices since blood is not needed; for kodashim, one might think the entire organ is required since blood is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the rule 'the majority of one in a bird' is already taught once, stating that the majority of one is like the whole.
An editorial note provides a mnemonic sign (הכ״ש פש״ח) for the following discussion.

Rav Hoshaya explains that the rule is taught once for חולין (non-sacred) and once for קדשים (sacred), and both are necessary: for חולין, one might think a half suffices since blood is not needed, but for קדשים, one might think the entire organ is required since blood is needed.
Rav Hoshaya concludes that if only the sacred case were taught, one might think for חולין a half suffices, so the second teaching informs us that a majority is required even for חולין.

items.text: Identifying which mishnah is chullin and which is kodashim
items.text_en: Identifying which mishnah is chullin and which is kodashim
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana, Rav Shimi bar Ashi, and Rav Pappa each offer proofs to identify the first clause (רישא) as referring to chullin and the latter clause (סיפא) as kodashim, based on terminology like 'shochet' vs. 'molek' and the requirement of two simanim for a burnt offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which clause of the mishna refers to non-sacred slaughter and which to sacrificial slaughter.

Rav Kahana argues that the first clause is about non-sacred slaughter because it uses the term 'השוחט' (the one who slaughters) rather than 'המולק' (the one who pinches the nape) which would be required for sacrificial birds.

The Gemara objects that if the latter clause is about sacrificial slaughter, it should say 'מליקתו כשרה' (his pinching is valid) instead of 'שחיטתו כשרה' (his slaughter is valid), but then resolves that the term 'שחיטתו' is used because the tanna concluded with mention of animal slaughter.

Rav Shimi bar Ashi provides additional evidence that the first clause is about non-sacred slaughter because it mentions 'אחד בעוף (one siman in a bird), but a bird burnt offering requires two simanim.

The Gemara explains that the latter clause can still refer to sacrificial slaughter: 'רוב אחד means the majority of each and every one, and the tanna did not teach 'רוב two because the sin offering suffices with one siman.
Rav Pappa proves the first clause is about non-sacred slaughter because Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the veins, and the Rabbis disagree; if it were sacrificial, the blood is needed anyway.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the prohibition of slaughtering two animals
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the prohibition of slaughtering two animals
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves the latter clause is kodashim from the mishnah's statement that slaughtering two heads at once is valid only after the fact (דיעבד), not initially (לכתחילה), because of a verse prohibiting one person slaughtering two sacrifices. In chullin, it would be permitted even initially.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that the latter clause of the mishna refers to sacrificial animals, citing the mishna's language that slaughtering two heads at once is valid only after the fact (דיעבד), not initially (לכתחילה).

Rav Ashi explains that if the mishna refers to sacrificial animals, the prohibition against slaughtering two animals initially (לכתחילה) is derived from Rav Yosef's teaching on the verse 'תִּזְבַּח' and 'תִּזְבָּחֻהוּ'.

Rav Kahana notes that the verse is written as 'תִּזְבָּחֵהוּ' (singular), reinforcing the prohibition; but if the mishna referred to non-sacred animals (חולין), slaughtering two heads at once would be permitted even initially (לכתחילה).

items.text: Reish Lakish's support and the reason for the two teachings
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's support and the reason for the two teachings
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish agrees that the first clause is chullin and the latter kodashim. He explains why the mishnah taught both 'the majority of one is like the whole' and 'a majority of one in a bird and a majority of two in an animal': to teach that if the blood was not sprinkled, the offering is not invalid, contrary to a possible inference.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish agrees that the first clause is about non-sacred animals and the latter about sacrificial animals, and asks why the mishnah taught both principles.
Reish Lakish explains that the second teaching was necessary to counter a possible inference from the Yom Kippur service that if the blood was not sprinkled the offering would be invalid.
The Gemara questions the hypothetical scenario presented by Reish Lakish.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about 'most of one in fowl and most of two in animal' is not to exclude a biblical disqualification, but to reject even a rabbinic concern. The phrase 'why do I need to sharpen?' is answered: it is a mitzvah to sharpen the knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah's statement is taken literally, it would imply that the High Priest's service on Yom Kippur could be performed by another, contradicting a baraita that all Yom Kippur service must be done by him alone.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's phrase 'most of one in fowl and most of two in animal' is meant to exclude even a rabbinic disqualification, and the question 'why do I need to sharpen?' is answered: it is a mitzvah to sharpen the knife.

items.text: Dispute on the definition of shechitah
items.text_en: Dispute on the definition of shechitah
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Levi Saba states that shechitah is only at the end, while Rabbi Yochanan says shechitah exists from beginning to end.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish citing Levi Saba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish citing Levi Saba
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish in the name of Levi Saba states that shechitah (שחיטה) is only at the end.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that shechitah (שחיטה) exists from beginning to end.

items.text: Rava's clarification of the dispute
items.text_en: Rava's clarification of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rava states that all agree that if a gentile slaughtered one siman and a Jew the other, it is invalid. Similarly, in bird olah, if one siman was done below and one above, it is invalid. The dispute is only about slaughtering one siman outside the Temple and one inside: according to Rabbi Yochanan one is liable, according to Resh Lakish not.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that all agree that if a gentile slaughtered one siman and a Jew the other, the animal is invalid because a treifa act was performed by a gentile.
Rava adds a parallel case: in a bird olah, if one siman was pinched below and one above, it is invalid because a chatat bird act was performed below.

Rava concludes that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is only about slaughtering one siman outside the Temple and one inside: Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable, Resh Lakish holds not.

items.text: Rabbah bar Shimi's correction
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Shimi's correction
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shimi reports that Rav Yosef said the dispute is actually about slaughtering a minority of the simanim outside and completing them inside, not about whole simanim.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Shimi reports that Rav Yosef actually said the dispute is about slaughtering a minority of the simanim outside and completing them inside, not about whole simanim.
Rabbah bar Shimi concludes that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish applies only when a minority of the simanim is slaughtered outside and completed inside.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the Parah Adumah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection from the Parah Adumah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises an objection from the laws of the red heifer: if shechitah exists from beginning to end, then a disqualification during shechitah should differentiate between before and after, but the Mishnah does not make such a distinction. Rava answers that when shechitah is invalidated, it is revealed retroactively that it was never shechitah at all.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira raises an objection from the Mishnah of the red heifer (פרה אדומה), which distinguishes between disqualification during shechitah and during sprinkling regarding impurity of garments, implying that shechitah is not considered a continuous act from beginning to end.

Rabbi Zeira argues that if shechitah exists from beginning to end, the Mishnah should have distinguished between before and after the disqualification during shechitah, just as it does for sprinkling.
Rava answers that when shechitah is invalidated, it is revealed retroactively (מגליא מילתא למפרע) that it was never shechitah at all, so no distinction between before and after applies.

items.text: Rava's further challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.text_en: Rava's further challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the view that shechitah is only at the end: in the red heifer, if two people slaughter, the first should not transmit impurity and the second should. Rav Yosef responds that two people slaughtering one animal is prohibited by the verse 'tizbach' (you shall slaughter) – not two slaughtering one offering. Rav Kahana adds that the verse is written 'tizbachehu' (you shall slaughter it).

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the view that shechitah is only at the end: in the red heifer, if two people slaughter, the first should not transmit impurity and the second should.
Rav Yosef responds that two people slaughtering one animal is prohibited by the verse 'תִּזְבַּח' (you shall slaughter) – not two slaughtering one offering.
Rav Kahana adds that the verse is written 'תִּזְבָּחֵהוּ' (you shall slaughter it), reinforcing the prohibition.

items.text: Abaye's citation of a tradition
items.text_en: Abaye's citation of a tradition
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that a statement was made about this: Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that this is the view of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Abaye notes that a statement was made about this: Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that this is the view of Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: דין שחיטה בשני סודרים
items.text_en: Gemara's initial discussion on slaughter by two people
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier discussion about two people slaughtering one animal is according to the Sages, but for Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon, the case would be one person slaughtering with two cloths, where the first cloth does not become impure but the second does. The Gemara notes that the discussion is about the disqualification of the red heifer, not its preparation.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בדעת חכמים ורבי אלעזר ברבי שמעון לגבי שחיטה בשני סודרים, ומסבירה שהדיון הוא בפסול פרה, לא בהכשרה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara clarifies that the earlier discussion about two people slaughtering one animal is according to the Sages.
The gemara shifts to Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's view, presenting a case of one person slaughtering with two cloths where the first cloth does not become impure but the second does.
The gemara resolves that the discussion is about the disqualification of the red heifer (פרה), not its preparation (הכשרה).

items.text: קושיית רב אידי בר אבין על פסח
items.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin's objection and Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin raises an objection from a Mishnah about one who slaughters a Passover offering on a festival day: if done for its own sake, he is exempt; if not for its own sake, he is liable. The Gemara infers that if done without specification, he is exempt, implying that a Passover offering requires a special act of designation (עקירה). Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda resolves that the case involves owners who are impure from a corpse, who are deferred to the second Passover, so the unspecified slaughter is assumed to be for its own sake and requires designation, but otherwise not.
items.desc: רב אידי בר אבין מקשה ממשנה בפסחים, והגמרא דנה בטעם הפטור בסתמא, ומסיקה שפסח בשאר ימות השנה צריך עקירה. רבי חייא בר גמדא מתרץ שהעוסקים טמאי מתים הם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin raises an objection from a Mishnah about one who slaughters a Passover offering on a festival day: if done for its own sake, he is exempt; if not for its own sake, he is liable.
The Gemara infers that if done without specification, he is exempt, implying that a Passover offering requires a special act of designation (עקירה).

The Gemara questions why he is exempt, since a Passover offering slaughtered at other times of the year is a peace-offering, and concludes that a Passover offering at other times requires a special act of designation (עקירה).

Rabbi Chiya bar Gamda resolves that the case involves owners who are impure from a corpse, who are deferred to the second Passover, so the unspecified slaughter is assumed to be for its own sake and requires designation, but otherwise not.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of slaughter from beginning to end
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of slaughter from beginning to end
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers two possibilities: if slaughter is valid from beginning to end, then the animal becomes invalid from the start of slaughter; but if slaughter is only valid at the end, then once a small amount is cut, the animal is removed from Passover status, and the rest is slaughtered as a peace offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma: if slaughter is valid from beginning to end, the animal becomes invalid from the start; but if slaughter is only valid at the end, once a small cut is made, the animal is removed from Passover status.
Abaye objects: even if the animal is removed from the Passover offering status, is it also removed from the monetary value of the Passover offering?

The Gemara cites a baraita that if one slaughtered two or most of two simanim and the animal is still convulsing, it is considered alive for all purposes, implying that the animal's value is not yet removed.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that one who slaughters in two or three places, the slaughter is valid.
Shmuel objects that we require a continuous slaughter (שחיטה מפורעת), and here it is lacking.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish supports Shmuel's view, citing a verse that slaughter must be continuous (שחיטה מפורעת).
Rabbi Elazar objects from a mishnah where two people hold a knife and slaughter together, which seems to lack continuous slaughter.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the mishnah refers to one knife and two people, so the slaughter is still continuous.
Rabbi Abba objects that if it is one knife, the mishnah's concern about them trampling each other would be irrelevant, but if two knives, the concern makes sense.
Rabbi Avin answers that the mishnah should be read as 'אין חוששין' (we are not concerned) about them trampling, implying two knives.

items.text: Abaye's question and the requirement of standing and evaluation
items.text_en: Abaye's question and the requirement of standing and evaluation
items.desc_en: Abaye asks: even if the animal is removed from Passover status, is it removed from the monetary value of the Passover offering? The Gemara then raises the issue of requiring standing and evaluation (העמדה והערכה), citing a Mishnah that if one slaughtered two or the majority of two limbs and the animal is still convulsing, it is considered alive for all purposes.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks: even if the animal is removed from Passover status, is it removed from the monetary value of the Passover offering?

The Gemara raises the requirement of standing and evaluation (העמדה והערכה) and cites a Mishnah that if one slaughtered two or the majority of two limbs and the animal is still convulsing, it is considered alive for all purposes.

items.text: דין שחיטה בשני מקומות
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav and Resh Lakish on continuous slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav that slaughter in two or three places is valid, but Shmuel objects that we require continuous slaughter (שחיטה מפורעת) and this is lacking. Resh Lakish agrees, citing a verse from Jeremiah about a 'slaughtered arrow' to support the requirement of continuous slaughter.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב אומר ששוחט בשניים או שלושה מקומות שחיטתו כשרה, אך שמואל ורבי שמעון בן לקיש דורשים שחיטה מפורעת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that slaughter performed in two or three places is valid.
Shmuel objects that we require continuous slaughter (שחיטה מפורעת) and this is lacking.
Resh Lakish agrees with Shmuel, citing a verse from Jeremiah about a 'slaughtered arrow' to support the requirement of continuous slaughter.

items.text: קושיית רבי אלעזר על שחיטה בשני אוחזים
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's objection and resolution about two people holding one knife
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects from a Mishnah that two people holding a knife and slaughtering, even one above and one below, is valid, which seems to contradict the requirement of continuous slaughter. Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that the Mishnah refers to one knife and two people. Rabbi Abba questions this, noting that the Mishnah says 'we do not worry that they will trample each other,' which would be more appropriate for two knives. Rabbi Avin then teaches that the correct text is 'we do not worry.'
items.desc: רבי אלעזר מקשה ממשנה ששניים אוחזים בסכין ושוחטים, והגמרא דנה בתירוצים של רבי ירמיה ורבי אבא ורבי אבין, ומסיקה שהמשנה עוסקת בסכין אחד ושני בני אדם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar objects from a Mishnah that two people holding one knife and slaughtering, even one above and one below, is valid, which seems to contradict the requirement of continuous slaughter (שחיטה מפורעת).
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that the Mishnah refers to one knife and two people, so the slaughter is continuous through the single knife.

Rabbi Abba objects that if the Mishnah refers to one knife, the phrase 'we do not worry that they will trample each other' (אין חוששין שמא יטרפו זה על זה) would be inappropriate; it would fit only if there were two knives and two people, where one might rely on the other to cut the majority.

Rabbi Abba further argues that with one knife, the concern should be about trampling (ידרוסו), not about trampling (יטרפו), so the Mishnah's wording is inconsistent with Rabbi Yirmeya's interpretation.
Rabbi Avin teaches that the correct text of the Mishnah is 'אין חוששין' (we do not worry), without specifying the concern, thereby resolving the textual inconsistency.

items.text: Rabbi Avin's objection and resolution regarding interrupted shechita
items.text_en: Rabbi Avin's objection and resolution regarding interrupted shechita
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin raises an objection from a mishna where the esophagus and trachea are cut at different heights, which seems to lack a continuous shechita. He resolves it by explaining that the shechita was performed in a quill-like manner (straight line).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that the two simanim (trachea and esophagus) might press upon each other during shechita.
Rabbi Avin objects from a mishna that permits shechita even when the esophagus and trachea are cut at different heights, which seems to lack continuous shechita.
Rabbi Avin resolves the objection by explaining that the shechita was performed in a straight line like a quill (קולמוס), so the cuts align vertically.

items.text: מעשה בתורא דאישחט בשני מקומות
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's lesson from a case of multiple cuts
items.desc_en: A story is told of an ox slaughtered in two or three places; Rabbi Zeira comments that this teaches the mishna about two knives and two people.
items.desc: מסופר על שור שנשחט בשני מקומות, ורב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא לקח מהשפירי. רבי זירא אמר לו שלימדנו משנתנו בשני סכינים ושני בני אדם.

sub.text: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta
sub.desc_en: A story is told about an ox slaughtered in two or three places, and Rabbi Zeira learns from Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's action that the mishna's rule applies even with two knives and two people.
Rabbi Zeira says to him: You have taught us our mishna about two knives and two people (that multiple simultaneous cuts are valid).

items.text: דין החלדת הסכין בין סימן לסימן
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on inserting the knife between simanim and under the skin
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if one inserted the knife between siman and siman and cut, it is invalid; under the skin it is valid. The Gemara explains that this teaches a novel case: cutting from above downward is valid, unlike the mishna which only discussed from below upward.
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר רב: החלדת הסכין בין סימן לסימן פוסלת, תחת העור כשרה. הגמרא מבררת מה חידש, ומסבירה שהחידוש הוא במקרה מלמעלה למטה, שאף על פי שנעשה כדרך שחיטה, עדיין פסול.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that inserting the knife between the simanim and cutting invalidates the slaughter, but inserting it under the skin is valid.
The Gemara asks what novel point Rav is teaching, citing the mishna where Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Akiva already discuss a similar case of inserting the knife under the second siman.

The Gemara explains that without Rav's statement one might have thought the mishna only invalidates cutting from below upward, but Rav teaches that even cutting from above downward is invalid when the knife is inserted between the simanim.

items.text: Be Rav's uncertainty about under the skin and other cases
items.text_en: Be Rav's uncertainty about under the skin and other cases
items.desc_en: Be Rav says they do not know the ruling for under the skin. The Gemara then raises further inquiries about under a patch or under matted wool, concluding with teiku.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that the school of Rav (בֵּי רַב) says they do not know the ruling for slaughter performed under the hide.
A dilemma is raised: according to the school of Rav (בֵּי רַב), what is the ruling if one concealed the knife under a patch or under matted wool?
The Gemara concludes that these dilemmas stand unresolved (תֵּיקוּ).

items.text: Rav Pappa's inquiry about inserting the knife in a minority of simanim
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's inquiry about inserting the knife in a minority of simanim
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about inserting the knife in a minority of the simanim, and the Gemara leaves it unresolved with teiku.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks about inserting the knife into a minority of the simanim, and this too remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: משנת השוחט שני ראשים כאחד
items.text_en: Mishna: Slaughtering two heads at once and other cases
items.desc_en: The mishna rules that slaughtering two heads at once is valid, as is two people holding one knife. If one severed the head in one stroke it is invalid, but if there is a full neck-length on the knife it is valid. The same applies for two heads with one neck-length. These rules apply only if the knife was moved in one direction, but if moved back and forth, any amount suffices.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת: השוחט שני ראשים כאחד – שחיטתו כשרה. שנים אוחזים בסכין ושוחטים – כשרה. המתיז את הראש בבת אחת – פסולה, אלא אם יש בסכין מלוא צוואר. אם הוליך והביא – כשרה בכל גודל.

sub.desc_en: The mishna opens with a series of rulings: slaughtering two heads at once is valid, two people holding one knife is valid, severing the head in one stroke is invalid unless the knife has a full neck-length, and moving the knife back and forth makes any amount sufficient.

items.text: גמרא על מקור דין הולכה והבאה
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the requirement of drawing from verses
items.desc_en: Shmuel derives from the verse 'a sharpened arrow is their tongue' that shechita requires drawing. The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from 'veshachat' that it means drawing, citing 'zahav shachut' and the arrow verse. The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to counter the possibility that 'zahav shachut' refers to gold drawn into thread.
items.desc: שמואל דורש מהפסוק 'חץ שחוט לשונם' שהשחיטה היא משיכה. תנא דבי רבי ישמעאל דורש 'ושחט' – ומשך, ומביא ראיה מ'זהב שחוט' ומ'חץ שחוט'. הגמרא מבררת את הצורך בשני הפסוקים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where are these matters (the requirement of drawing in shechita) derived?
Shmuel answers that the verse 'a sharpened arrow is their tongue' (Jeremiah 9:7) implies drawing, as a sharpened arrow is drawn back.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the word 'וְשָׁחַט' (and he shall slaughter) means drawing, citing 'זָהָב שָׁחוּט' (beaten gold) and the arrow verse as support.
The Gemara explains that the second verse is needed to counter the possibility that 'זָהָב שָׁחוּט' refers to gold drawn into thread, so the arrow verse clarifies that it means drawing.

items.text: מעשה רבא בבדיקת גירא
items.text_en: Rava's test with an arrow and concern for chalada
items.desc_en: Rava tested an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa and slaughtered a bird with it as it flew. The Gemara questions whether this might involve chalada (insertion under the siman), but notes that we saw otherwise.
items.desc: רבא בדק חץ לרבי יונה בר תחליפא, ושחט בו עוף תוך כדי תעופה. הגמרא שואלת שמא עשה חלדה, ועונה שראו שלא.

sub.text: Story about Rava and Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa
sub.text_en: Story about Rava and Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Rava testing an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa and slaughtering a bird with it while it flew, and the Gemara questions whether this might involve haladah (insertion under the skin).
The Gemara questions whether this might involve חלדה (insertion under the siman).
The Gemara dismisses the concern, noting that we saw otherwise (that no chalada occurred).

items.text: קושיית כיסוי הדם בגידפי דמיפרמי
items.text_en: Covering blood from a detached head
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the blood from a detached head can be covered, given the requirement for earth below and above. It resolves that the earth is prepared in advance for the entire piece.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על גידפי דמיפרמי שצריכים כיסוי, ומתרצת שמזמינים עפר לכל הפיתקא. מובאת ברייתא של רבי זירא בשם רב שצריך עפר למטה ולמעלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the blood from a detached head (גִּידְפֵי דְּמִיפַּרְמִי) can be covered, given Rabbi Zeira's requirement for earth below and above.
sub.desc: הצגת המקרה של גידפי דמיפרמי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the earth is prepared in advance for the entire piece (דְּמַזְמֵין לֵיהּ לְעָפָר דְּכוּלַּהּ פִּתְקָא).

items.text: שיעור מלא צוואר וחוץ לצוואר
items.text_en: The required length of the knife for cutting two heads
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that the knife must have a length of a full neck plus beyond the neck. The Gemara questions whether this means two full necks or a full neck plus a little. A baraita resolves that it means a full neck beyond two necks, proving the latter interpretation.
items.desc: רבי זירא אומר שצריך מלא צוואר וחוץ לצוואר. הגמרא מסתפקת אם הכוונה כמלא צוואר אחד או משהו. מובאת ברייתא המוכיחה שמדובר במלא צוואר חוץ לשני צווארין, ומסיקה שמלא צוואר וחוץ לצוואר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that when one slaughters and severs two heads simultaneously, the knife must have a length of a full neck plus beyond the neck.
sub.desc: רבי זירא אומר שצריך מלא צוואר וחוץ לצוואר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: does 'a full neck plus beyond the neck' mean two full necks, or a full neck plus a little extra?
sub.desc: הגמרא מסתפקת אם הכוונה כמלא צוואר אחד או משהו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if one slaughters two heads at once, a knife with a full neck-length suffices, and clarifies that this means a full neck beyond two necks, resolving the question.
sub.desc: הבאת ברייתא המוכיחה שמדובר במלא צוואר חוץ לשני צווארין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes definitively that the phrase means a full neck beyond the neck (i.e., a full neck plus a little extra).
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שמלא צוואר וחוץ לצוואר פירושו כמלא צוואר אחד.

items.text: דין איזמל שאין לו קרניים ומחט
items.text_en: The knife without a back and the needle
items.desc_en: Rav Menashe explains that the Mishnah's case of a knife without a back refers to a scalpel without a back. Rav Acha asks about a needle, and Rav Menashe distinguishes between a regular needle and a cobbler's needle, concluding that the Mishnah's 'any amount' refers to a scalpel, not a needle.
items.desc: רב מנשה מפרש שהמשנה מדברת באיזמל שאין לו קרניים. רב אחא בריה דרב אויא שואל על מחט, ורב מנשה משיב שמחט בוצע. נדחית האפשרות שמדובר במחט דאושכפי, ומסיקים שהמשנה באה להשמיע שאין לגזור איזמל שאין לו קרניים אטו איזמל שיש לו קרניים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashe explains that the Mishnah's case of a knife without a back refers specifically to a scalpel (איזמל) that has no back.
sub.desc: רב מנשה מפרש שהמשנה מדברת באיזמל שאין לו קרניים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Menashe about the status of a needle in this context.
sub.desc: רב אחא שואל על דין מחט.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashe answers that a regular needle merely tears (does not cut properly), so it is invalid.
sub.desc: רב מנשה משיב שמחט בוצע ואינה כשרה לשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks about a cobbler's needle, which is thicker and might cut.
sub.desc: רב אחא שואל על דין מחט של אושכפי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Menashe initially suggests that the Mishnah's phrase 'even any amount' refers to a cobbler's needle.
sub.desc: רב מנשה משיב שמחט בוצע ואינה כשרה לשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this, noting that the Mishnah explicitly mentions a scalpel (איזמל) in the earlier clause, so 'any amount' cannot refer to a needle.
sub.desc: רב מנשה משיב שמחט בוצע ואינה כשרה לשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is explaining itself: 'any amount' refers to the scalpel (איזמל), not to a needle.
sub.desc: רב מנשה משיב שמחט בוצע ואינה כשרה לשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides logical support: if a cobbler's needle were permitted, why would the Mishnah need to mention a scalpel at all?
sub.desc: רב אחא שואל על דין מחט של אושכפי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the scalpel is needed to teach that a scalpel without a back is permitted, lest one decree that it is forbidden due to a scalpel with a back.
sub.desc: רב אחא שואל על דין מחט של אושכפי.

items.text: Mishnah: Knife fell and slaughtered
items.text_en: Mishnah: Knife fell and slaughtered
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a knife fell and slaughtered, even if it slaughtered normally, it is invalid, based on the verse 'you shall slaughter and eat'—only what you slaughter you may eat. The Gemara infers that if one threw the knife, it is valid, even without intent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a knife fell and slaughtered, even if it slaughtered normally, it is invalid, based on the verse 'you shall slaughter and eat'—only what you slaughter you may eat.
The Gemara infers that if one threw the knife, it is valid, even without intent.

items.text: The Tanna who does not require intent for slaughter
items.text_en: The Tanna who does not require intent for slaughter
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Nathan, who validates slaughter even without intent. The Gemara explains why both cases (throwing a knife and others slaughtering) are necessary to teach, as each has a unique leniency that might not apply to the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that slaughter does not require intent.
Rava identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Nathan, citing a baraita where Rabbi Nathan validates slaughter even without intent, and rules in accordance with him.
The Gemara objects that Rava already stated this ruling elsewhere, questioning why it is repeated here.
The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary, as each has a unique leniency that might not apply to the other, so both are taught.

items.text: דין נידה שנאנסה וטבלה וצורך כוונה בטבילה
items.text_en: Intent for immersion: the case of a raped niddah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Yochanan debate whether a niddah who was forced to immerse is pure for her husband. Rava questions Rav Nachman about the logic, and Rav Nachman argues that immersion for chullin does not require intent, citing a mishnah about a wave that purifies without intent. The Gemara questions whether that case involves a person waiting for the wave.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת בין רב לרבי יוחנן בנידה שנאנסה וטבלה. רבא מקשה על רב, ורב נחמן מתרץ שטבילת חולין אינה צריכה כוונה, ומוכיח מגל שנתלש. הגמרא דוחה את הראיה שמא מדובר ביושב ומצפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules that a niddah who was raped and immersed is pure for her husband but forbidden to eat תרומה (priestly portion), while Rabbi Yochanan rules she is not even pure for her husband.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רב לרבי יוחנן בנידה שנאנסה וטבלה.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Rav Nachman: according to Rav, who permits the niddah to her husband (an עון כרת (punishment of karet) offense), why is she still forbidden to eat תרומה (a lesser מיתה (death) penalty)?
sub.desc: רבא מקשה על רב: אם התרת איסור כרת, קל וחומר שאיסור מיתה מותר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman answers that her husband is חולין (non-sacred), and immersion for חולין does not require כוונה (intent), citing a mishnah where a wave that detaches and falls on a person purifies without the person's intent.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מתרץ שטבילת חולין אינה צריכה כוונה, ומוכיח מגל שנתלש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the mishnah about the wave deals with a person sitting and waiting for the wave, who does have intent, so it does not prove that intent is unnecessary.
sub.desc: דוחה את הראיה שמא מדובר ביושב ומצפה, שיש כוונה.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution about intention for vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution about intention for vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares vessels to a person, requiring intention for immersion. It then considers whether to decree against using 'heads' (ראשין) due to 'caps' (כיפין), and concludes that no such decree is made.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether vessels require intention for immersion, drawing an analogy to a person who requires intention.
The Gemara objects: if one is sitting and watching, what is there to say? (i.e., intention is already present).
The Gemara resolves that one might have thought to decree against using 'heads' (ראשין) due to 'caps' (כיפין), but the mishnah teaches that no such decree is made.

items.text: ראיה מאין מטבילים בכיפין
items.text_en: Proof that immersion is not done in caps
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that one immerses in 'heads' but not in 'caps', because immersion cannot be performed in the air.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שאין מטבילים בכיפין, ומסיקה שאין גוזרים גזירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that one immerses in 'heads' but not in 'caps', proving that immersion cannot be performed in the air.

items.text: מקור לחולין שאינם צריכים כוונה
items.text_en: Source that non-sacred food does not require intention
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about fruits that fell into a water channel: if one with impure hands took them without intending to wash the fruits, the hands become pure and the fruits are not susceptible to impurity. This shows that for non-sacred food, intention is not required.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה על פירות שנפלו למים, המוכיחה שחולין אינם צריכים כוונה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about fruits that fell into a water channel: if one with impure hands took them without intending to wash the fruits, the hands become pure and the fruits are not susceptible to impurity, proving that non-sacred food does not require intention.

items.text: קושיית רבא לרב נחמן ותירוצה
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution regarding immersion for non-sacred food
items.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman from a baraita: one who immersed for non-sacred food and was designated for non-sacred food is forbidden for tithes. Rav Nachman explains that even if designated, it is forbidden for tithes. Another baraita states that one who immersed without designation is as if not immersed at all, but this is explained to mean only for tithes, not for non-sacred food. A supporting baraita is found.
items.desc: רבא מקשה על רב נחמן מברייתא על טבילה לחולין, ורב נחמן מתרץ שהברייתא עוסקת בטבילה למעשר, ומביא ראיה מברייתא מפורשת.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman from a baraita: one who immersed for non-sacred food and was designated for non-sacred food is forbidden for tithes, implying that without designation it would be permitted.
Rav Nachman explains that the baraita means even if designated for non-sacred food, it is forbidden for tithes.
Rava objects with another baraita: one who immersed without designation is as if he did not immerse at all, implying no effect at all.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita means as if not immersed for tithes but immersed for non-sacred food, and a supporting baraita confirms: one who immersed without designation is permitted for non-sacred food and forbidden for tithes.

items.text: קושיית אביי לרב יוסף ותירוץ בשם רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rabbi Yochanan and the defense via Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether this is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan. Rav Yosef responds that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef, who derives from the verse 'וְכוּבַּס שֵׁנִית' that a second washing requires intention, just as the first does. However, the verse 'וְטָהֵר' teaches that the priest's intention is not required for purification.
items.desc: אביי מקשה על רבי יוחנן מברייתא, ורב יוסף מתרץ שרבי יוחנן סובר כרבי יונתן בן יוסף, הדורש 'וכבס שנית' להקיש טבילה שנייה לראשונה שצריכה דעת.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether the previous baraita constitutes a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan's position that intention is required for immersion in חולין (non-sacred food).
Rav Yosef responds that Rabbi Yochanan follows Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef, who derives from the verse 'וְכוּבַּס שֵׁנִית' that a second washing requires intention, just as the first does.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef
sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's full derivation: the second washing is compared to the first regarding intention, but the verse 'וְטָהֵר' teaches that the priest's intention is not required for purification.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's objection and resolution regarding Rabbi Yochanan's position
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects: Did Rabbi Yochanan really say that? He holds that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah, and we have a Mishnah where a knife fell and slaughtered, which is invalid, implying that if one threw it, it is valid even without intention. Rava explains that this is Rabbi Natan's view, and even Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef would agree regarding slaughter, since the Torah explicitly disqualifies 'עסוק' in sacred matters, implying that non-sacred does not require intention.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects to the attribution of the view to Rabbi Yochanan, noting that Rabbi Yochanan rules that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi cites a Mishnah where a knife fell and slaughtered, which is invalid, implying that if one threw it, it is valid even without intention.
Rava explains that the Mishnah's lenient position is Rabbi Natan's view, not the anonymous Mishnah that Rabbi Yochanan follows.

Rava resolves that even Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef would agree regarding slaughter, since the Torah explicitly disqualifies 'עסוק' (preoccupation) in sacred matters, implying that non-sacred slaughter does not require intention.

items.text: Rabbis' distinction and Rava's refutation
items.text_en: Rabbis' distinction and Rava's refutation
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that while intention is not required for the act of slaughter (זביחה), it is required for the cutting (חתיכה). Rava refutes this: if the verse says 'וְזָבַחְתָּ' and not 'וְחָתַכְתָּ', then either intention is required for both or for neither.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis concede that intention is not required for the act of slaughter (זביחה) but insist it is required for the cutting (חתיכה).
Rava refutes the Rabbis: since the verse says 'וְזָבַחְתָּ' (you shall slaughter) and not 'וְחָתַכְתָּ' (you shall cut), either intention is required for both slaughter and cutting, or for neither.

items.text: דיון בנידה שנאנסה וטבלה
items.text_en: Discussion of a niddah who was forced to immerse and related cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a niddah who was forced to immerse: if a friend forced her, the friend's intention is valid. A Mishnah about a deaf, insane, or blind woman who can eat terumah if supervised is cited. Rav Pappa explains the cases for Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis. Rava concludes that if one slaughtered a cow and another animal with it, according to all opinions it is invalid.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה של נידה שנאנסה וטבלה, ומביאה דעות שונות: רב פפא ורבא מפרשים את המחלוקת בין רבי נתן לרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case of a niddah who was forced to immerse, and immediately rejects the possibility that a friend forced her, since the friend's intention is valid.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a deaf, insane, or blind woman who can eat תרומה (priestly portion) if supervised by competent women, supporting the principle that intention can be supplied by another.

Rav Pappa explains the case: according to Rabbi Natan, she fell from a bridge (unintentional), and according to the Rabbis, she went down to cool off (intentional for cooling but not for purification).
Rava concludes that if one slaughtered a cow and another animal with it, according to all opinions the slaughter is invalid.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about a cow and another animal slaughtered together
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about a cow and another animal slaughtered together
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Natan and the Rabbis regarding a case where a cow (for a chatat) and another animal (chullin) are slaughtered together. Rabbi Natan rules the cow is invalid and the other animal valid, while the Rabbis rule the opposite.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: if a cow (for a chatat) and another animal (chullin) are slaughtered together, Rabbi Natan rules the cow invalid and the other valid, while the Rabbis rule the opposite.

The Mishnah states the rulings for when another animal was slaughtered alongside the consecrated animal: according to Rabbi Natan, the cow is invalid; according to the Sages, the cow is valid and the non-consecrated animal is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's clarification: Why the case of another animal was necessary
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification: Why the case of another animal was necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to mention the case of another animal (chullin) with the cow, and explains that without it, one might think only two cows together are invalid, but a chullin animal might be permitted. The Gemara teaches that it is also invalid according to Rabbi Natan.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needed to teach the case of another animal (chullin) with the cow, since it seems obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case was necessary for Rabbi Natan, to counter a possible inference that only two cows together are invalid, but a chullin animal might be permitted.
The Gemara asks: this ruling is obvious! Why was it necessary to state the case where another animal was slaughtered together with the consecrated one?

The Gemara answers: the ruling was needed by Rabbi Natan, because one might have thought that the verse 'ונשחט אותה' (and he shall slaughter it) excludes slaughtering it together with its fellow only when both are of the same consecrated type, but here the other animal is unconsecrated, so it might be allowed; the Mishnah teaches us otherwise.

items.text: דין חתך דלעת עם השחיטה
items.text_en: Clarification: Cutting the gullet with it vs. being cut
items.desc_en: The Mishnah distinguishes between actively cutting the gullet (dal'at) with the animal (invalid for all) and the gullet being cut on its own (valid for all).
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה דין נוסף: אם חתך דלעת יחד עם השחיטה, הכל מודים שהיא פסולה; אם נחתכה הדלעת מאליה, הכל מודים שהיא כשרה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one actively cut the gullet (dal'at) together with the animal, all agree it is invalid; if the gullet was cut on its own, all agree it is valid.

The Mishnah distinguishes between two cases: if one cut the animal's throat together with its fellow, the animal is invalid according to all opinions; if the throat was cut together with its fellow after the fact, it is valid according to all opinions.

items.text: משנת שהייה בשחיטה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Interruptions during shechita
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of interruption during slaughter (e.g., knife falls, tools fall, sharpening knife, friend slaughters) and states that if the pause is as long as the time for shechita, the animal is invalid. Rabbi Shimon says the measure is the time for inspection (bikur).
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאם נפלה הסכין והגביהה, או נפלו כליו והגביהן, או השחיז את הסכין ועף, ובא חברו ושחט – אם שהה כדי שחיטה, השחיטה פסולה. רבי שמעון אומר: אם שהה כדי ביקור.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of interruption during slaughter and states that if the pause is as long as the time for shechita, the animal is invalid.
Rabbi Shimon says the measure is the time for inspection (bikur).

The Mishnah rules: if a knife fell and the slaughterer picked it up, or his tools fell and he picked them up, or he sharpened the knife and flew off, and his friend came and slaughtered — if there was an interruption of the time it takes to slaughter, the animal is invalid. Rabbi Shimon says: if he paused the time it takes to inspect the knife.

items.text: Gemara: Defining 'kdei shechita' and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara: Defining 'kdei shechita' and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'kdei shechita' means. Rav says it is the time to slaughter another animal. Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask if it is animal for animal and fowl for fowl, or even animal for fowl. Rav initially does not know, but later it is reported that Rav says animal for animal and fowl for fowl, while Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say even animal for fowl. Rabbi Chananya says it is the time to bring another animal and slaughter, but this is questioned as giving a measure. Rav Pappa says the difference is whether the animal is standing to be slaughtered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the measure of 'kdei shechita' (the time for slaughter) is.
Rav defines 'kdei shechita' as the time to slaughter another animal.

sub.text: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.text_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav whether the measure is animal for animal and fowl for fowl, or even animal for fowl.
Rav responds that he was not in a cheerful mood to ask his teacher about this.
It is reported that Rav says animal for animal and fowl for fowl, while Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan say even animal for fowl.
Rabbi Chananya defines it as the time to bring another animal and slaughter, but the Gemara objects that this gives an undefined measure.
Rav Pappa explains that the difference between the opinions is whether the animal is standing to be slaughtered.

items.text: Alternative definition: Time to lift and lay down the animal
items.text_en: Alternative definition: Time to lift and lay down the animal
items.desc_en: In the West, they say in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina that 'kdei shechita' is the time to lift the animal, lay it down, and slaughter it, with a distinction between small and large animals.

sub.text: Western tradition in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Western tradition in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Western tradition defines 'kdei shechita' as the time to lift the animal, lay it down, and slaughter it, with a distinction between small and large animals.

sub.text: Teaching from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.text_en: Teaching from the West in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina
sub.desc_en: The Sages in the West teach in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina: the measure is the time it takes to lift the animal, lay it down, and slaughter it — a small animal for a small animal and a large animal for a large animal.

items.text: בעיות שהייה נוספות: סכין רעה, צירוף שהיות, ושהייה במיעוט סימנים
items.text_en: Rava's ruling and further questions on shehiya
items.desc_en: Rava rules that if one slaughters with a bad knife, even if it takes all day, it is valid. Rava then asks whether multiple pauses (shehiyot) combine to invalidate. The Gemara notes that his own ruling implies they do not, but that case is different. Rav Huna bar Rav Natan asks about a pause during slaughter of only a minority of the simanim, and the question remains unresolved (teiku).
items.desc: רבא פוסק שהשוחט בסכין רעה אפילו כל היום – כשרה. רבא בעי אם שהיות מצטרפות, והגמרא דוחה את הפשיטה מדבריו. רב הונא בריה דרב נתן בעי דין שהייה במיעוט סימנים, ומסיים בתיקו.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that if one slaughters with a bad knife, even if it takes all day, it is valid.
Rava asks whether multiple pauses (שהיות) combine to invalidate the slaughter.
The Gemara objects that Rava's own ruling (that a bad knife is valid all day) implies that pauses do not combine.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the case of a bad knife involves no actual pause (שהייה).

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's question
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan's question
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Natan asks about a pause during slaughter of only a minority of the simanim (סימנים).
The question remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: פירוש 'כדי ביקור' של רבי שמעון
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's measure: 'kdei bikur' defined
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Shimon's measure: 'kdei bikur' is the time for a wise person to inspect. Initially thought to be the inspection of a sage, which is too variable, it is clarified as the inspection of a skilled butcher.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת את שיטת רבי שמעון: רבי יוחנן אומר 'כדי ביקורו של חכם', והגמרא מקשה שזה שיעור משתנה, ומתרצת: כדי ביקור טבח חכם.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon's opinion that the measure of delay is 'kdei bikur' (the time for inspection).
The Gemara asks what 'kdei bikur' means.
Rabbi Yochanan answers: the time for a sage to inspect.
The Gemara objects that this makes the measure variable and undefined.
The Gemara resolves: it means the inspection time of a skilled butcher, a fixed standard.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of improper slaughter and the dispute between Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of improper slaughter and the dispute between Rabbi Yeshevav and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of improper slaughter (e.g., cutting the esophagus after severing the trachea, waiting until death, inserting the knife under the second siman). Rabbi Yeshevav rules it is a neveila, while Rabbi Akiva says it is a treifa. Rabbi Yeshevav states a general principle: if the animal is invalidated by the act of slaughter itself, it is a neveila; if the slaughter was proper but another factor caused invalidation, it is a treifa. Rabbi Akiva agrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of improper slaughter and presents the dispute: Rabbi Yeshevav rules it is a neveila, Rabbi Akiva says it is a treifa.
Rabbi Yeshevav states a general principle distinguishing neveila from treifa, and Rabbi Akiva agrees.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction with another Mishnah on treifot
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction with another Mishnah on treifot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva agreed with Rabbi Yeshevav, and then raises a contradiction from a Mishnah listing treifot in animals, implying a different classification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara quotes the Mishnah: 'Slaughtered the esophagus... and Rabbi Akiva conceded to him'.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from the Mishnah listing treifot in animals, which implies a different classification from Rabbi Yeshevav's principle.

items.text: Rava's initial resolution of the contradiction
items.text_en: Rava's initial resolution of the contradiction
items.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita by distinguishing the order: if one slaughtered and then cut, the animal is invalidated by slaughter; if one cut and then slaughtered, it is as if another factor caused the invalidation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of a perforated esophagus and a severed windpipe.

Rava resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the order: if one slaughtered and then cut, the animal is invalidated by slaughter; if one cut and then slaughtered, it is as if another factor caused the invalidation.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Huna's objection and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Huna's objection and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna cites a baraita that states if one cut the gullet and then slaughtered the windpipe, it is a neveilah, contradicting Rava. Rava deflects by saying the baraita means the slaughter of the windpipe occurred first, but Rav Acha bar Huna points out two flaws: it is the same as the first case, and the baraita says 'afterwards'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Huna objects to Rava by citing a baraita that rules if one cut the gullet and then severed the windpipe, or severed the windpipe and then cut the gullet, the animal is a neveilah (carcass).
Rava deflects by claiming the baraita means the slaughter of the gullet had already occurred initially (i.e., the windpipe severance came after valid slaughter).

Rav Acha bar Huna points out two flaws in Rava's deflection: the baraita's case is identical to the first case, and the baraita explicitly says 'afterwards' (וְאַחַר כָּךְ), indicating the severance came after the slaughter.

items.text: תירוץ רבא השני
items.text_en: Rava's revised answer: the Mishnah lists forbidden cases, some neveilot
items.desc_en: Rava now explains that the Mishnah teaches cases of forbidden animals, some of which are neveilot and some tereifot. The Gemara questions why certain cases (like those of Chizkiyah and Rabbi Elazar) are not included, and answers that the Mishnah only lists neveilot that do not convey impurity while alive.
items.desc: רבא מתרץ שהברייתא מונה איסורים, חלקם נבלות וחלקם טריפות, ולכן אין סתירה.

sub.desc_en: Rava revises his answer: the Mishnah lists forbidden cases, some of which are neveilot and some tereifot.

The Gemara objects: why does the Mishnah not include the cases of Chizkiyah (who ruled that an animal made into a 'gistra' is a neveila) and Rabbi Elazar (who ruled that an animal whose thigh and cavity were removed is a neveila)?
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah only lists neveilot that do not convey impurity while alive, but neveilot that convey impurity while alive are not listed.

items.text: תירוץ ריש לקיש
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the slaughter was at the site of the cut or not: if at the site, it is invalidated by slaughter; if not, it is as if another factor caused the invalidation.
items.desc: ריש לקיש מתרץ את הסתירה על ידי הבחנה בין שחיטה במקום חתך לבין שחיטה שלא במקום חתך.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish resolves the contradiction by distinguishing whether the slaughter was performed at the site of the cut or not: if at the site, the animal is invalidated by the slaughter itself; if not, it is as if another factor caused the invalidation.

items.text: Challenge to Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish from his own statement that slaughtering the windpipe and then puncturing the lung renders the animal kosher, implying the cut is like a basket. Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by distinguishing before and after his retraction, noting the Mishnah remained in place.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Resh Lakish by citing his own statement that slaughtering the windpipe and then puncturing the lung renders the animal kosher, implying the cut is like a basket, and argues the same logic should apply here.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after Resh Lakish's retraction, noting the Mishnah remained in place.

items.text: דיון נוסף: ריאה ובני מעיים
items.text_en: Rava's limitation of Resh Lakish's ruling and Rabbi Zeira's objection
items.desc_en: Rava limits Resh Lakish's ruling to the lung because its life depends on the windpipe, but not for other intestines. Rabbi Zeira objects that once signs of tereifah appear, it should be the same. Rabbi Zeira then retracts and asks about a puncture between simanim, comparing it to Ilfa's question about a fetus extending its hand between simanim.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בהבחנת רבא בין ריאה לבני מעיים, ומביאה את התקפת רבי זירא וחזרתו, ואת בעיית אילפא.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Resh Lakish's ruling
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Resh Lakish's ruling
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Resh Lakish's original ruling that if one slaughtered the windpipe and then the lung was punctured, the animal is kosher.
Rava limits Resh Lakish's ruling to the lung because its life depends on the windpipe, but not for other intestines.
Rabbi Zeira objects that once signs of tereifah appear, it should be the same for all organs.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's retraction and new question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's retraction and new question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira retracts his objection and asks about a puncture between simanim, whether the first siman combines with the second to purify from neveila status.
The Gemara notes that this is the same as Ilfa's question about a fetus extending its hand between simanim.

items.text: בעיית הצטרפות סימנים לטהרה מידי נבלה
items.text_en: Question about combining signs for taharah from neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the first sign of slaughter combines with the second to purify the animal from the status of neveilah, but clarifies that the question only applies to taharah, not to the prohibition of eating.
items.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק: האם סימן ראשון מצטרף לסימן שני לטהרה מידי נבלה? ומבהירה שהספק הוא רק לטהרה, אבל לאכילה אסורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the first sign of slaughter combines with the second to purify the animal from the status of neveilah, but clarifies that the question only applies to taharah, not to the prohibition of eating.

items.text: דחיית דברי רבי זירא
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav's challenge to Ravina
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav suggests to Ravina that perhaps Rava never retracted his original position, and that Rabbi Zeira was only speaking according to Rava's reasoning but did not hold that view himself.
items.desc: רב אחא בר רב אומר לרבינא שאולי רבי זירא לא חזר בו, אלא אמר לדברי רבא ולא סבירא ליה.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav to Ravina
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav to Ravina
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav objects to Ravina's interpretation, suggesting that Rabbi Zeira never retracted and was only speaking hypothetically to Rava's position.

items.text: דין זימון על בני מעיים לישראל ולגוי
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's proof from Reish Lakish about zimmun
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's statement that a Jew may include fetuses in a zimmun but a gentile may not, because for Jews the matter depends on valid slaughter, while for gentiles it depends on death, making the fetus like a limb from a living animal.
items.desc: רב אחא בר יעקב אומר משמע מרבי שמעון בן לקיש שמזמנים ישראל על בני מעיים, אבל אין מזמנים גוי על בני מעיים, כי ישראל תלוי בשחיטה וגוי בנחירה, והרי זה כאבר מן החי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov cites a statement from Reish Lakish about the difference between Jews and Gentiles regarding the status of meat from a live animal, supporting the principle that the question of combining signs applies only to taharah.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov explains the rationale: for Jews the matter depends on valid slaughter (שחיטה), so the fetus is permitted, but for gentiles it depends on death, so the fetus is like a limb from a living animal (אבר מן החי).

items.text: הרהור רב פפא על דברי רב אחא
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's reflection on Rav Acha bar Yaakov's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa recounts that he was sitting before Rav Acha bar Yaakov and wanted to ask if there is anything permitted to a Jew but forbidden to a gentile, but refrained because Rav Acha bar Yaakov had already given a reason.
items.desc: רב פפא מספר שישב לפני רב אחא בר יעקב וביקש לשאול: האם יש דבר שמותר לישראל ואסור לגוי? אך לא שאל כי רב אחא כבר נתן טעם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa recounts that he sat before Rav Acha bar Yaakov and considered challenging his statement, but refrained because he realized Rav Acha bar Yaakov had already provided a reason.

items.text: ברייתא ומעשה המסייעים לרב אידי בר אבין
items.text_en: Baraita contradicting Rav Acha bar Yaakov, supporting Rav Idi bar Avin
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who wishes to eat from an animal before its death may cut a kezayit of meat from the slaughter area, salt it, rinse it, wait for the animal to die, and eat it, and this is permitted to both Jew and gentile. This supports Rav Idi bar Avin's similar ruling in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan.
items.desc: תניא שלא כרב אחא בר יעקב: מותר לגוי ולישראל לאכול מבהמה קודם שתצא נפשה, בתנאי שיחתוך כזית בשר מבית השחיטה וימלח וידיח. וכן מסייע לרב אידי בר אבין שאמר בשם רב יצחק בר אשיאן.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that one who wishes to eat from an animal before its death may cut a kezayit of meat from the slaughter area, salt it, rinse it, wait for the animal to die, and eat it, and this is permitted to both Jew and gentile, contradicting Rav Acha bar Yaakov.

sub.text: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.text_en: Rav Idi bar Avin citing Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin cites Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan's similar ruling that one who seeks to recuperate may cut a kezayit of meat from the slaughter area, salt it, rinse it, wait for the animal to die, and eat it, and this is permitted to both Jew and gentile, supporting the baraita.

items.text: משנת השוחט שלא יצא דם
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaughter without blood flow and hand impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters an animal and no blood emerges, the meat is kosher and may be eaten with unclean hands because the blood did not make it susceptible to impurity. Rabbi Shimon argues that the act of slaughter itself makes it susceptible.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת: השוחט בהמה חיה ועוף ולא יצא מהם דם – כשרים, ונאכלים בידים מסואבות, כי לא הוכשרו בדם. רבי שמעון אומר: הוכשרו בשחיטה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that slaughter without blood flow yields kosher meat that may be eaten with unclean hands, since the blood did not render it susceptible to impurity.
Rabbi Shimon argues that the act of slaughter itself renders the meat susceptible to impurity, even without blood.

items.text: גמרא על המשנה: דין חולין וקדשים
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah and proof that it deals with non-sacred meat
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why blood would make the meat susceptible if hands are only second-degree impurity and cannot impart third-degree to non-sacred food. It proves the Mishnah deals with non-sacred meat because it mentions wild animals (not in sacrifices), and if it were sacred, lack of blood would not render it invalid, and blood of sacrifices does not make food susceptible. Additionally, sacred meat is made susceptible by the sanctity itself.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע אם יצא דם אין נאכלים בידים מסואבות? הרי ידים שניות ואין שני עושה שלישי בחולין. ומבררת שהמשנה עוסקת בחולין, לא בקדשים, ומביאה ראיות מרבי יוחנן שדם קדשים אינו מכשיר, ומקשה על חיבת הקודש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why blood would make the meat susceptible to impurity, since hands are only second-degree impurity and cannot impart third-degree to non-sacred food.
The Gemara proves the Mishnah deals with non-sacred meat because it mentions wild animals (not in sacrifices), and if it were sacred, lack of blood would not render it invalid.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's proof that blood of sacrifices does not make food susceptible, based on the verse 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים' (you shall pour it on the ground like water).
The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah dealt with sacred meat, the sanctity itself would make it susceptible, so the lack of blood would not prevent susceptibility.

items.text: תירוץ רב נחמן: בחולין שלקחן בכסף מעשר
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution: dealing with second tithe money animals
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuah explains that the Mishnah deals with non-sacred animals purchased with second tithe money, and not according to Rabbi Meir's view.
items.desc: רב נחמן אמר בשם רבה בר אבוה: כאן עוסקים בחולין שלקחן בכסף מעשר, ושלא כרבי מאיר, כפי ששנינו.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha resolves the difficulty by explaining that the Mishnah deals with חולין (non-sacred food) purchased with מעשר שני (second-tithe) money, and not according to Rabbi Meir's opinion.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything requiring immersion by rabbinic decree defiles kodashim, disqualifies terumah, but is permitted for chullin and ma'aser according to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages prohibit it for ma'aser.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שכל הטעון ביאת מים מדברי סופרים מטמא את הקודש, פוסל את התרומה, ומותר בחולין ובמעשר, דברי רבי מאיר. חכמים אוסרים במעשר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that anything requiring immersion by rabbinic decree defiles kodashim, disqualifies terumah, but is permitted for chullin and ma'aser according to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages prohibit it for ma'aser.
sub.desc: משנת הפתיחה: כל הטעון ביאת מים מדברי סופרים מטמא את הקודש, פוסל את התרומה, ומותר בחולין ובמעשר, דברי רבי מאיר; חכמים אוסרים במעשר.

items.text: קושיית רב שימי בר אשי
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi challenges the Mishnah, suggesting that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Meir regarding eating ma'aser, not regarding touching ma'aser or eating chullin. He supports this by noting that the Mishnah discusses eating with soiled hands, implying the Sages permit it.
items.desc: רב שימי בר אשי מקשה: שמא חכמים חלקו על רבי מאיר רק באכילת מעשר, אך לא בנגיעת מעשר ובאכילת חולין? הגמרא דוחה זאת מתוך הברייתא העוסקת בנגיעה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi challenges the Mishnah, suggesting that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Meir regarding eating ma'aser, not regarding touching ma'aser or eating chullin.
sub.desc: רב שימי בר אשי מקשה: שמא חכמים חלקו על רבי מאיר רק באכילת מעשר, אך לא בנגיעת מעשר ובאכילת חולין?

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi supports his challenge by noting that the Mishnah discusses eating with soiled hands, implying the Sages permit it.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: הרי הברייתא עוסקת בנגיעה, שהרי נאמר 'נאכלין בידים מסואבות' ומדובר כשחברו מאכילו.

items.text: תירוץ רב פפא: ידיים תחילות
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah deals with hands that are first-degree impurity, and follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir, who holds that hands can be first-degree for chullin and second-degree for terumah. The Gemara clarifies the statement.
items.desc: רב פפא מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת בידיים תחילות לחולין, והיא כרבי שמעון בן אלעזר בשם רבי מאיר. הברייתא מפרשת שידיים תחילות לחולין ושניות לתרומה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves the difficulty by stating that the Mishnah deals with hands that are first-degree impurity, and follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Meir, who holds that hands can be first-degree for chullin and second-degree for terumah.
sub.desc: רב פפא מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת בידיים תחילות לחולין, והברייתא מפרשת שידיים תחילות לחולין ושניות לתרומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement means hands are first-degree even for chullin, and second-degree only for terumah, not for chullin.

items.text: בירור מקור ידיים תחילות
items.text_en: Source for first-degree hands
