items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether first-degree hands exist, and cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva says hands that enter a leprous house become first-degree, while the Sages say second-degree. The dispute is whether the rabbis decreed hands like the body or like ordinary hands.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם יש ידיים תחילות? ומביאה ברייתא על הכנסת ידיים לבית המנוגע, שם נחלקו רבי עקיבא וחכמים. הגמרא מבארת שהמחלוקת היא בגזירה אטו גופו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether first-degree hands (ידיים תחילות) exist at all.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם יש מושג של ידיים תחילות.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Akiva rules that hands entering a leprous house become first-degree (תחילות), while the Sages say second-degree (שניות).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם יש מושג של ידיים תחילות.

sub.desc_en: The Sages dispute Rabbi Akiva, holding that the hands become only second-degree (שניות).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם יש מושג של ידיים תחילות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the dispute is not about the law of partial entry, but about whether the rabbis decreed hands like the body (first-degree) or like ordinary hands (second-degree).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת שהמחלוקת היא בגזירה אטו גופו, האם גזרו על ידיים כגופו או לא.

items.text: דחיית אוקימתא כרבי עקיבא
items.text_en: Attempt to align with Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers explaining the Mishnah according to Rabbi Akiva, but rejects it because Rabbi Akiva's first-degree hands apply only to terumah and kodashim, not chullin. Even if they were second-degree, Rabbi Akiva holds that a second-degree can make a third-degree in chullin, but that applies only to Torah impurity, not rabbinic.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע לא מוקמים את המשנה כרבי עקיבא, ודוחה: רבי עקיבא אמר ידיים תחילות רק לתרומה וקודשים, אך לחולין הן שניות. גם אם הן שניות, רבי עקיבא סובר ששני עושה שלישי בחולין, אך זה דווקא בטומאה דאורייתא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes explaining the Mishnah according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that hands can be first-degree (תחילות).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע לא מוקמת המשנה כרבי עקיבא הסובר שידיים תחילות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this, noting that Rabbi Akiva's ruling about first-degree hands applies only to תרומה (terumah) and קדשים (kodashim), which are stringent, but for חולין (chullin) the hands would be second-degree (שניות).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע לא מוקמת המשנה כרבי עקיבא הסובר שידיים תחילות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara counters that even if the hands are second-degree, Rabbi Akiva holds that a second-degree can make a third-degree in חולין (chullin).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: גם אם ידיים שניות, הרי רבי עקיבא סובר ששני עושה שלישי בחולין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Akiva taught that a second-degree food can make a third-degree in חולין (chullin), based on the verse 'יִטְמָא' (it shall become impure).
The Gemara rejects this, explaining that Rabbi Akiva's principle applies only to טומאה דאורייתא (Torah-level impurity), not to the rabbinic impurity of hands involved here.
sub.desc: דוחה: דברי רבי עקיבא נאמרו בטומאה דאורייתא, אבל כאן מדובר בטומאה דרבנן.

items.text: תירוץ רבי אלעזר בשם רבי הושעיא
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya explains that the Mishnah deals with chullin prepared with the purity of kodashim, and not according to Rabbi Yehoshua. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to chullin prepared with the purity of terumah, not kodashim, as Rabbi Yehoshua holds there is no third-degree in chullin prepared with kodashim purity.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר בשם רבי הושעיא מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, ודלא כרבי יהושע. מובאת ברייתא על מחלוקת רבי אליעזר ורבי יהושע בדרגות טומאה, ומבואר שרבי יהושע סובר שאין שלישי בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar citing Rabbi Hoshaya introduces the explanation that the Mishnah deals with chullin prepared with the purity of kodashim, and not according to Rabbi Yehoshua.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר בשם רבי הושעיא מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, ודלא כרבי יהושע.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited presenting the positions of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the impurity levels of foods.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר בשם רבי הושעיא מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, ודלא כרבי יהושע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah actually deals with chullin prepared with the purity of terumah, not kodashim.
sub.desc: מבואר שהברייתא עוסקת בחולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua holds there is no third-degree impurity in chullin prepared with kodashim purity, so the Mishnah must be about chullin prepared with terumah purity.
sub.desc: מבואר שרבי יהושע סובר שאין שלישי בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש.

items.text: קושיה נוספת
items.text_en: Unfinished question
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new question but the text is cut off.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת קושיה נוספת: 'ולוקמה' – ומבקשת להעמיד את המשנה באוקימתא אחרת, אך הקטע נקטע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new question but the text is cut off, leaving the argument incomplete.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת קושיה נוספת, מבקשת להעמיד את המשנה באוקימתא אחרת, אך הקטע נקטע.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על המשנה
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question: hullin prepared with terumah purity or kodashim?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's case of meat becoming a third degree refers to hullin prepared with the purity of terumah or of kodashim. It rejects terumah because the Mishnah mentions 'meat', which does not exist in terumah, and rejects kodashim because wild game is not found in kodashim, though meat could be confused with meat but not with fruit.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה העוסקת בבשר בחולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה, ושואלת אם הכוונה לתרומה או לקודשים, תוך דחיית האפשרויות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's case of meat becoming a third degree refers to hullin prepared with the purity of terumah or of kodashim, and rejects terumah because meat does not exist in terumah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה: אם עסקינן בתרומה, והרי אין בשר בתרומה, שהרי תרומה היא פירות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects kodashim because wild game is not found in kodashim, though meat could be confused with meat but not with fruit.
sub.desc: הגמרא פונה לאפשרות שהמשנה עוסקת בקדשים, ודוחה אותה משום שחיה אינה בקדשים, וממילא אין מקום להשוות בשר לפירות.

items.text: Ulla's resolution and identification of the disputants
items.text_en: Ulla's resolution and identification of the disputants
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that the colleagues say the Mishnah refers to hullin prepared with the purity of kodashim and not according to Rabbi Yehoshua. Ulla himself argues it is Rabbi Yehoshua, who spoke in a 'need not say' manner: not only hullin prepared with kodashim purity, which is stringent and has a third degree, but even hullin prepared with terumah purity has a third degree. The colleagues are identified as Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan, who asks what Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debated.

sub.text: Ulla's report of the colleagues' position
sub.text_en: Ulla's report of the colleagues' position
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that the colleagues say the Mishnah refers to hullin prepared with the purity of kodashim and not according to Rabbi Yehoshua.

Ulla argues that the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehoshua, who spoke in a 'need not say' manner: not only hullin prepared with kodashim purity, which is stringent and has a third degree, but even hullin prepared with terumah purity has a third degree.
The gemara identifies the colleagues as Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan, who asks what Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debated.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's argument: eater is more severe than food
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's argument: eater is more severe than food
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that we find an eater more severe than the food: the carcass of a clean bird outside does not impart impurity, but one who eats it imparts impurity to garments at the point of swallowing. Therefore, why should we not make the eater like the food (i.e., the eater becomes a third degree like the food he eats)?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that the eater is more severe than the food, citing the case of a clean bird's carcass which does not impart impurity but the eater does, and asks why the eater should not be treated like the food.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's counter-argument: food is more severe than eater
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's counter-argument: food is more severe than eater
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua rejects the analogy from the clean bird carcass because it is a novelty. Instead, he argues that food is more severe than the eater: food imparts impurity in the volume of an egg, while the eater requires eating half a loaf. Therefore, why should we make the eater like the food?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua rejects Rabbi Eliezer's analogy from the clean bird carcass because it is a novelty (חידוש) and thus not a valid basis for a general rule.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that food is more severe than the eater: food imparts impurity in the volume of an egg, while the eater requires eating half a loaf.
Rabbi Yehoshua asks rhetorically: if food is more severe, why should we make the eater like the food?

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's rebuttal: impurity from measures not learned, and second-degree issue
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's rebuttal: impurity from measures not learned, and second-degree issue
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer responds that impurity is not derived from measures, and furthermore, according to your view that a first degree makes a second, you say well, but what is a second degree doing to a second?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer rejects Rabbi Yehoshua's argument by asserting that impurity is not derived from measures (שיעורין), and then challenges: according to your view that a first-degree food makes a second, what does a second-degree food make a second?

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's answer: second makes second through liquids, and Rabbi Eliezer's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's answer: second makes second through liquids, and Rabbi Eliezer's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua answers that we find that a second degree makes a second through liquids. Rabbi Eliezer objects that liquids themselves are a first degree, as taught: anything that disqualifies terumah renders liquids a first degree, except for a tevul yom.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua answers Rabbi Eliezer's objection by citing a principle: we find that a second-degree impurity makes a second degree through liquids.
Rabbi Eliezer objects that liquids themselves are a first-degree impurity, as taught in a baraita: anything that disqualifies terumah renders liquids a first degree, except for a tevul yom.

items.text: קושיית רבי אליעזר על שלישי שני ותשובת רבי יהושע
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's final question and Rabbi Yehoshua's limitation to terumah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer further asks: what is a third degree doing to a second? Rabbi Yehoshua responds that he only said this regarding terumah, whose purity... (the text breaks off).
items.desc: רבי אליעזר מקשה על רבי יהושע: שלישי שני למה? ורבי יהושע משיב שאמר זאת רק בתרומה שטהרתה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks: why does a third-degree food render a second-degree food impure?
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מקשה על רבי יהושע: מדוע שלישי נקרא שני, מה טעם הדבר?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua responds that he only stated this rule regarding תרומה (terumah), whose purity standards are higher.
sub.desc: רבי יהושע משיב שלא אמר דבריו אלא לגבי תרומה שטהרתה, ולא לגבי קודש.

items.text: Opening statement: Rabbi Yannai's ruling
items.text_en: Opening statement: Rabbi Yannai's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Rabbi Yannai via Rabbi Asi: one who eats a third-degree of unconsecrated produce prepared in purity of consecrated food becomes a second-degree for consecrated food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yannai's ruling via a chain of transmission: one who eats a third-degree of unconsecrated produce prepared in purity of consecrated food becomes a second-degree for consecrated food.

items.text: קושיית רבי זירא ותירוץ
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects from a baraita that a third-degree is second for consecrated food but not second for terumah, implying only for purity of terumah, not consecrated food. Rabbi Asi deflects, saying the baraita is not exhaustive, and the amoraim differ on Rabbi Yochanan's intent.
items.desc: רבי זירא מקשה על רבי אסי מברייתא האומרת ששלישי נעשה שני לקודש רק בחולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה, ולא על טהרת הקודש. רבי אסי מתרץ שהברייתא לא מיבעיא קאמר, ויש מחלוקת אמוראים בדבר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira objects to Rabbi Asi from a baraita that a third-degree food makes the eater second only for consecrated food, not for terumah, implying the rule applies only to חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה (non-sacred food prepared with the purity of terumah), not to חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש (non-sacred food prepared with the purity of consecrated food).
sub.desc: רבי זירא מקשה על רבי אסי מברייתא האומרת ששלישי נעשה שני לקודש רק בחולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה, ולא על טהרת הקודש.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi deflects the objection by claiming the baraita is not exhaustive — it merely states the more obvious case (חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה) but does not exclude the other.
sub.desc: רבי אסי מתרץ שהברייתא לא מיבעיא קאמר, כלומר היא באה לומר שאין זה פשוט אלא חידוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that the amoraim (Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Asi) disagree about Rabbi Yochanan's intent, so the baraita's wording is not decisive.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שהברייתא מפורשת שאינה מתירה אלא בתרומה, ומתרצת שיש מחלוקת אמוראים בדבר, והברייתא נאמרה אליבא דרבי יוחנן.

items.text: אמרת עולא ופירושה
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling and its novelty
items.desc_en: Ulla states: one who eats a third-degree of unconsecrated produce prepared in purity of terumah becomes disqualified from eating terumah. The Gemara questions what he adds to the baraita, and Ulla explains that without his statement one might think the baraita only denies second-degree status but allows third-degree, so he clarifies that it disqualifies the body.
items.desc: עולא אומר שהאוכל שלישי של חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה נפסל גופו מלאכול בתרומה. הגמרא שואלת מה חידש, ומסבירה שבלי דבריו היינו טועים שהשלישי אינו פוסל כלל.

sub.desc_en: עולא (Ulla) rules that one who eats a third-degree impure unconsecrated food prepared in purity of תרומה (teruma) becomes disqualified from eating תרומה (teruma).
sub.desc: עולא קובע שהאוכל שלישי של חולין שנעשו על טהרת תרומה נפסל גופו מלאכול בתרומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions what עולא (Ulla) adds, citing the baraita that already implies third-degree impurity disqualifies from תרומה (teruma).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה חידש עולא, הרי כבר שנינו ששלישי פוסל בתרומה?

sub.desc_en: עולא (Ulla) explains that without his statement one might misinterpret the baraita as denying both second- and third-degree impurity, so he clarifies that third-degree impurity indeed disqualifies the body.

items.text: קושיית רב המנונא לעולא
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah of Nazid HaDem'a
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects to Ulla from the Mishnah: a third-degree of unconsecrated produce is eaten in Nazid HaDem'a, implying it does not disqualify the eater. Ulla responds by setting aside that case, as Nazid HaDem'a is different.
items.desc: רב המנונא מקשה על עולא מברייתא האומרת ששלישי נאכל בנזיד הדמע, ומשמע שאינו פוסל את הגוף. עולא דוחה את הקושיה ואומר להניח לנזיד הדמע.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna objects to Ulla from the Mishnah of Nazid HaDem'a, which states that a third-degree of unconsecrated produce is eaten in Nazid HaDem'a, implying it does not disqualify the eater.
sub.desc: רב המנונא מקשה על עולא מברייתא האומרת ששלישי נאכל בנזיד הדמע, ומשמע שאינו פוסל את הגוף.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rejects the objection by setting aside the case of Nazid HaDem'a, arguing that it is different and does not apply to the general rule.
sub.desc: עולא דוחה את הקושיה ואומר להניח לנזיד הדמע, כלומר שהברייתא אינה עוסקת בדין פיסול הגוף.

items.text: הנחת היסוד: דליכא כזית בכדי אכילת פרס
items.text_en: Opening condition: no olive's bulk within the time of eating a half-loaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara sets the context: the previous discussion assumed there is no olive's bulk of food within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf (כדי אכילת פרס).
items.desc: הקטע מציג את התנאי הבסיסי לדיון: שאין כזית בכדי אכילת פרס, כלומר שהאוכל לא אכל כשיעור המצטרף לטומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara sets the context that the previous discussion assumed there is no olive's bulk of food within the time it takes to eat a half-loaf (כדי אכילת פרס).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה שאין כזית בכדי אכילת פרס.

items.text: ברייתא דרבי יונתן וצורך הכפילות עם דעולא
items.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's ruling on third-degree terumah and its necessity alongside Ulla's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan says in the name of Rabbi: one who eats third-degree terumah itself is forbidden to eat but permitted to touch. The Gemara explains that both Ulla's earlier statement and Rabbi Yonatan's are necessary: without both, one might mistakenly think that terumah itself is forbidden even in contact, or that hullin prepared with terumah purity is permitted even in eating.
items.desc: רבי יונתן בשם רבי אומר שהאוכל שלישי של תרומה עצמה אסור באכילה אך מותר בנגיעה. הגמרא מסבירה מדוע יש צורך גם בדין דעולא וגם בדין זה, כדי למנוע טעות שבתרומה נגיעה אסורה או שבחולין אכילה מותרת.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan reports in the name of Rabbi: one who eats a third-degree food of תרומה (priestly portion) itself is forbidden to eat but permitted to touch.
The Gemara explains that both Ulla's and Rabbi Yonatan's statements are necessary: without both, one might mistakenly extend the leniency or stringency to the wrong domain.

items.text: דין רב יצחק בר שמואל: שלישי בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש
items.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta's statement about third-degree hullin prepared with sanctuary purity
items.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta states before Rav Nachman: one who eats third-degree hullin prepared with sanctuary purity is pure to eat sanctuary food, because only holy food from holy food can produce a fourth degree in the sanctuary.
items.desc: רב יצחק בר שמואל אומר בשם רב נחמן שהאוכל שלישי של חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש טהור לאכול בקודש, כי אין דבר שעושה רביעי בקודש אלא קודש מקודש בלבד.

sub.text: רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta citing a tradition
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta, sitting before Rav Nachman, states that one who eats a third-degree food of חולין (non-sacred food) prepared in purity of קודש (sacred food) is pure to eat קודש, because only קודש from קודש creates a fourth degree.
sub.desc: רב יצחק בר שמואל בר מרתא יושב לפני רב נחמן ואומר: האוכל שלישי של חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש – טהור לאכול בקודש, כי אין דבר שעושה רביעי בקודש אלא קודש מקודש בלבד.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's objection from a baraita about third-degree hullin prepared with terumah purity
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's objection from a baraita about third-degree hullin prepared with terumah purity
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama raises an objection: a baraita states that third-degree hullin prepared with terumah purity is second for the sanctuary but not second for terumah. He asks: why? It is not holy food from holy food!

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects: a third-degree food is second to קודש and not second to תרומה, in the context of חולין prepared in purity of תרומה — why? It is not קודש from קודש.

items.text: Rav Nachman's answer: terumah's purity is impurity for the sanctuary, with proof from a mishna
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's answer: terumah's purity is impurity for the sanctuary, with proof from a mishna
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds: set aside terumah, for its purity is impurity for the sanctuary. He proves this from a mishna: the clothes of an am ha'aretz are a midras for perushim, the clothes of perushim are a midras for terumah eaters, and the clothes of terumah eaters are a midras for the sanctuary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman responds to the objection by setting aside terumah, explaining that its purity is considered impurity for the sanctuary.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's proof from a mishna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's proof from a mishna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a mishna showing a hierarchy of midras impurity: clothes of an am ha'aretz are a midras for perushim, clothes of perushim for terumah eaters, and clothes of terumah eaters for the sanctuary, proving that terumah's purity is treated as impurity for the sanctuary.

items.text: Rava's objection: midrasot are different
items.text_en: Rava's objection: midrasot are different
items.desc_en: Rava objects: you speak of midrasot? Midrasot are different (and cannot be used as a proof for other types of impurity).

sub.desc_en: Rava objects: you speak of midras-impurities? Midras-impurities are different (and do not prove the general rule).

items.text: דין פירות בטומאת אישה נידה
items.text_en: Initial statement about produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the concern about a wife sitting on them applies only to vessels, not to produce, and notes that Rabbi Yitzchak said the same about produce.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה האם האיסור לשבת על פירות שנגעה בהם אישה נידה חל גם על פירות, ומביאה את דעת רבי יצחק שגם בפירות אמרו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the concern about a wife sitting on them applies only to vessels, not to produce, and notes that Rabbi Yitzchak said the same about produce.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את דעת רבי יצחק שגם בפירות אמרו את האיסור לשבת עליהם.

items.text: קושיית רבי ירמיה מדיפתי ותירוץ
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's objection and answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti objects: if we say 'her purification is impurity' regarding produce, then terumah should render kodshim impure. The Gemara answers that this is a case of impurity through contact, where trust regarding kodshim extends to terumah.
items.desc: רבי ירמיה מקשה מברייתא על האמירה בפירות, ומתרץ רבי יוחנן שהטומאה מדובר בטומאה בחיבורין, ששם נאמן על הקודש ולכן נאמן גם על תרומה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya from Difti objects: if we say 'her purification is impurity' regarding produce, then terumah should render kodshim impure, citing a baraita that a person trusted for kodshim is not trusted for terumah.
sub.desc: רבי ירמיה מקשה מברייתא: אם אמר 'הפרשתי לתוכה רביעית קודש' נאמן, ואילו לדעת האומר שטוהרתה טומאה היא אצל הקודש, תרומה תטמא קודש?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that this is a case of טומאה בחיבורין (impurity through contact), where trust regarding kodshim extends to terumah.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מתרץ: הקושיה עוסקת בטומאה בחיבורין, ששם נאמן על הקודש ולכן נאמן גם על תרומה.

items.text: קושיית רב הונא בר נתן
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Natan's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan objects with a baraita about the degrees of impurity in chullin prepared on the purity of kodshim, challenging the previous distinction.
items.desc: רב הונא בר נתן מקשה מברייתא על דיני טומאת חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש, ומעלה שאלה לגבי דרגות הטומאה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Natan objects by citing a baraita that details the impurity levels of chullin prepared on the purity of kodshim, challenging the previous distinction.
sub.desc: רב הונא בר נתן מקשה מברייתא על דין חולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש.

items.text: מחלוקת תנאים בחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on chullin prepared on purity of kodshim
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by presenting a tannaitic dispute: one opinion holds such chullin are like ordinary chullin, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok says they are like terumah, and Rabbi Shimon says they are rendered susceptible by slaughter, with Rav Asi clarifying that Rabbi Shimon means slaughter renders susceptible, not blood.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת תנאים: תנא קמא סובר שחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש הרי הם כחולין, רבי אלעזר בר רבי צדוק אומר הרי הם כתרומה, ורבי שמעון אומר שהוכשרו בשחיטה. רב אסי מוסיף שרבי שמעון אומר ששחיטתו מכשרת ולא דם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a tannaitic dispute, stating that the anonymous first Tanna holds that chullin prepared on the purity of kodshim are treated as ordinary chullin.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שהמחלוקת היא בין תנאים, ומצטטת את השיטה הראשונה שהחולין שנעשו על טהרת הקודש הרי הם כחולין.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok holds that such chullin are like תרומה (priestly portion), capable of imparting second-degree טומאה (impurity) and disqualifying first-degree items.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר בר רבי צדוק מביא את שיטתו שהחולין הללו הרי הם כתרומה, ומפרט דיני טומאה ופסול.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position with Rav Asi's clarification
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon holds that slaughter renders the meat susceptible to טומאה (impurity), and Rav Asi clarifies that Rabbi Shimon means the act of slaughter itself renders susceptible, not the blood.
sub.desc: רבי שמעון מביא את שיטתו שהשחיטה מכשירה את החולין, ורב אסי מוסיף בשמו שהשחיטה מכשרת ולא הדם.

items.text: בירור דעת רבי שמעון: שחיטה מכשרת ולא דם
items.text_en: Attempt to support Rav Asi's interpretation
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from Rabbi Shimon's statement 'rendered susceptible by slaughter' that it means slaughter and not blood, but concludes it could mean even slaughter, and a further citation shows Rabbi Shimon meant slaughter as well, not exclusively.
items.desc: הגמרא מנסה להוכיח מדברי רבי שמעון שהכשר הוא בשחיטה ולא בדם, ומסיקה שהכוונה 'אף בשחיטה' ולא רק בדם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon's statement 'rendered susceptible by slaughter' supports Rav Asi's interpretation that slaughter alone, not blood, renders susceptible.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם ניתן להוכיח מדברי רבי שמעון שהכשר הוא בשחיטה ולא בדם?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the proof, explaining that Rabbi Shimon's phrase 'by slaughter' could mean even slaughter, not exclusively slaughter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם ניתן להוכיח מדברי רבי שמעון שהכשר הוא בשחיטה ולא בדם?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a further citation where Rabbi Shimon explicitly says 'Does blood alone render susceptible? Even slaughter renders susceptible,' confirming that slaughter is included but not exclusive.

items.text: דיון בדם המת ודם שחיטה
items.text_en: Further attempts to prove blood of slaughter renders susceptible
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings two more baraitot: one about blood of a corpse and one about blood of a plague, each time initially inferring that blood of slaughter renders susceptible, but each time rejecting the inference and explaining the necessity of the specific case.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שדם המת אינו מכשיר, ומנסה להסיק שדם שחיטה מכשיר, אך דוחה שהכוונה לדם חללים. לאחר מכן מביאה ברייתא על דם מגפתו, ומסיקה שדם שחיטה אינו מכשיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says blood of a corpse does not render susceptible, and infers that blood of slaughter does render susceptible.
The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the baraita only teaches that blood of חללים (those killed by others) renders susceptible, but blood of slaughter may not.
The Gemara brings another baraita where Rabbi Shimon says blood of a plague does not render susceptible, and again infers that blood of slaughter does.

The Gemara rejects again, explaining that the baraita only teaches about blood of חללים, and the specific case of plague blood was needed to counter a possible distinction between killing the whole animal versus half.

items.text: לימוד מפסוקים: דם חללים מכשיר, דם שחיטה לא
items.text_en: Distinction between blood of slain and blood of slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why blood of slain (חללים) renders susceptible, citing a verse, and addresses the counter-argument from the verse about pouring blood like water, which is interpreted as permitting benefit from blood of disqualified consecrated animals.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת שדם חללים מכשיר מפסוק 'ודם חללים ישתה', ודוחה את הלימוד מפסוק 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים' שמיועד להיתר הנאה מפסולי המוקדשים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why blood of slain (חללים) renders susceptible, and answers with a verse.
sub.desc: הגמרא עונה: ומה שנא דם חללים מכשיר? שכתוב: 'ודם חללים ישתה'. דם שחיטה גם כתוב: 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים'! ההוא למישרי דמן דפסולי המוקדשין בהנאה הוא דאתא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a verse about pouring blood like water could also apply to blood of slaughter, and resolves that it permits benefit from blood of disqualified consecrated animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהפסוק 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים' בא להתיר דם פסולי המוקדשים בהנאה, ולא ללמד על הכשרת דם שחיטה.

items.text: Rejection of the assumption that blood requires burial
items.text_en: Rejection of the assumption that blood requires burial
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the notion that since blood of a firstborn is forbidden for shearing and labor, it should require burial. The verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the assumption that since the blood of a firstborn is forbidden for shearing and labor, it should require burial, and the verse teaches otherwise.

items.text: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Derivation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the verse 'and drinks the blood of the slain' excludes gushing blood, which does not render seeds susceptible.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the verse 'and drinks the blood of the slain' excludes gushing blood (דם קילוח), which does not render seeds susceptible to ritual impurity.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Sages taught: One who slaughters and splashes blood on a gourd – Rabbi says it is susceptible, Rabbi Chiyya says it is suspended.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi rules that blood splashed on a gourd renders it susceptible to impurity, while Rabbi Chiyya rules that it is suspended (undecided).

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's proposal to rely on Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's proposal to rely on Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya suggests relying on Rabbi Shimon's view that slaughter renders susceptible, not blood.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya proposes that since Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya disagree, we should rely on Rabbi Shimon's view that slaughter renders susceptible, not blood.

items.text: Rav Papa's explanation of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Papa's explanation of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that all agree if blood is present throughout, it renders susceptible. They dispute when blood is wiped away between simanim: Rabbi holds slaughter is continuous, Rabbi Chiyya holds it is only at the end, and 'suspended' means pending the end of slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa opens by stating that all agree when blood is present throughout slaughter, it renders susceptible; the dispute is only when blood is wiped away between the simanim.

sub.text: Rav Papa's explanation of Rabbi's position
sub.text_en: Rav Papa's explanation of Rabbi's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that Rabbi holds slaughter is continuous from start to end, so the blood is considered slaughter blood.

sub.text: Rav Papa's explanation of Rabbi Chiyya's position
sub.text_en: Rav Papa's explanation of Rabbi Chiyya's position
sub.desc_en: Rav Papa explains that Rabbi Chiyya holds slaughter is only at the end, so the wiped blood is wound blood, and 'suspended' means pending the end of slaughter.

items.text: Objection to relying on Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Objection to relying on Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Shimon says it does not render susceptible, but Rabbi Chiyya says it does! The answer: In the case of wiped blood, both agree it does not render susceptible, so Rabbi is a single opinion against two.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: How can we rely on Rabbi Shimon's opinion that blood does not render susceptible, when Rabbi Chiyya holds that it does render susceptible?
The Gemara answers: In the case of wiped blood, both Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Chiyya agree it does not render susceptible, so Rabbi is a single opinion against two and we follow the majority.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says 'suspended' always means doubt. Rabbi Chiyya is uncertain whether slaughter is continuous or only at the end, so 'suspended' means neither eat nor burn. The reliance on Rabbi Shimon is only for burning: both agree not to burn, so Rabbi is a single opinion against two.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that 'suspended' always means permanent doubt; Rabbi Chiyya is uncertain whether slaughter is defined from beginning to end or only at the end, so 'suspended' means neither eat nor burn.
The Gemara asks: According to this explanation, what is the meaning of relying on Rabbi Shimon, since Rabbi Shimon says it does not render susceptible and Rabbi Chiyya is uncertain?
The Gemara answers that regarding burning, both Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Chiyya agree not to burn, so they are aligned.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi is a single opinion against two, and the rule for such cases is: one may neither eat nor burn.

items.text: Resh Lakish's question about meal-offering vessels
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's question about meal-offering vessels
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks whether a dry vessel for meal-offerings counts days of impurity as first and second. Rabbi Elazar answers from a verse, but Resh Lakish already knows that. The real question is whether sanctity is like a liquid. Rabbi Elazar explains from an extra verse.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks whether a dry vessel for meal-offerings counts first and second degrees of impurity, or whether the sanctity only disqualifies the item itself.
Rabbi Elazar answers by citing a verse that only food that comes into contact with water is rendered susceptible to impurity, implying that sanctity alone does not count degrees.
The Gemara objects that Resh Lakish already knows the halakha about food that comes into contact with water, and clarifies that his real dilemma is whether sanctity is like a liquid.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar's proof comes from the extraneous wording of the verse, showing that the extra phrase teaches that only water, not sanctity, counts degrees of impurity.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the two verses about susceptibility (הכשר) for impurity from a corpse and a creeping thing are both needed, and explains that each teaches a unique case: corpse impurity requires susceptibility because it does not impart impurity in the size of a lentil, while a creeping thing does not require susceptibility because it does not impart seven-day impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the two verses about susceptibility (הכשר) for impurity from a corpse and a creeping thing are both needed, and answers that each teaches a unique case.

The Gemara explains that both verses are necessary: corpse impurity requires susceptibility because it does not impart impurity in the size of a lentil, while a creeping thing does not require susceptibility because it does not impart seven-day impurity.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection from Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects based on Rabbi Shimon's statement that meat is rendered susceptible by slaughter (הוכשרו בשחיטה) even to count as first or second degree of impurity. The Gemara questions how slaughter can make it susceptible since it is not a food that came into contact with water. Abaye answers that the Sages treated it like susceptibility by water rabbinically.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects by citing Rabbi Shimon's statement that slaughter makes meat susceptible, questioning how this can be since the meat is not a food that came into contact with water.
Abaye answers that the Sages treated slaughter as a rabbinic susceptibility (הכשר) equivalent to water.
Abaye answers that the Sages treated slaughter like susceptibility by water rabbinically.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's supporting proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's supporting proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira brings a proof from the dispute between Shammai and Hillel about one who harvests grapes for the winepress: Shammai says it is susceptible, Hillel says not, and Hillel was silent. The Gemara questions how it can be susceptible without water contact, and Abaye again answers that the Sages treated it as rabbinic susceptibility.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites a dispute between Shammai and Hillel about grapes picked for the winepress, where Shammai says they are susceptible and Hillel says not, and Abaye again explains it as a rabbinic enactment.
The Gemara questions how the grapes can be susceptible without contact with water.
Abaye answers that the Sages treated it as rabbinic susceptibility (הכשר מים מדרבנן).

items.text: Rav Yosef's challenge and clarification
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's challenge and clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Abaye's answer, noting that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's question about חיבת הקודש was not about whether it makes meat susceptible for impurity (to be burned) but for the purpose of burning it, not for counting degrees of impurity. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's question was about burning, not about susceptibility.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that Abaye's answer about חיבת הקודש (sanctity's affection) making meat susceptible for impurity applies equally to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's question, but Abaye's response was inconsistent.

Abaye clarifies that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's question was not about making the meat susceptible for impurity (to be burned) but about burning it directly, so the answer of חיבת הקודש (sanctity's affection) applies differently.

items.text: Source for biblical חיבת הקודש
items.text_en: Source for biblical חיבת הקודש
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source for חיבת הקודש being from the Torah. It considers the verse 'And the flesh that touches any unclean' and questions how the flesh became susceptible. It rejects blood of sacrifices (since it does not make susceptible) and liquids of the slaughterhouse (which are pure and do not make susceptible), concluding that it must be through חיבת הקודש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of חיבת הקודש (the sanctity's capacity to render susceptible to impurity), noting that the verse 'And the flesh that touches any unclean' implies the flesh was already susceptible, and questions what made it susceptible.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that the flesh was made susceptible by blood of sacrifices, citing Rabbi Yochanan's teaching that blood which is not poured like water (i.e., sacrificial blood) does not render susceptible to impurity.

The Gemara rejects the possibility that the flesh was made susceptible by liquids of the slaughterhouse, citing Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina that these liquids are pure and do not render susceptible, and concludes that it must be through חיבת הקודש (the sanctity's capacity).

items.text: Alternative explanation and final proof
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and final proof
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative explanation based on Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: a cow of peace-offerings that was passed through a stream and still had moisture when slaughtered. It then brings a proof from the end of the verse 'and the flesh' which includes wood and incense, which are not edible but are made susceptible by חיבת הקודש, concluding that here too חיבת הקודש makes them susceptible.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the proof from the verse might be rejected, suggesting instead the case is like that of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: a cow of peace-offerings passed through a stream with moisture still on it when slaughtered.

The Gemara resolves by citing the end of the verse 'וְהַבָּשָׂר' (and the flesh), which includes wood and incense — inedible items made susceptible by חיבת הקודש (the sanctity's affection) — concluding that here too חיבת הקודש makes them susceptible.

items.text: Unresolved question about sanctity's attachment
items.text_en: Unresolved question about sanctity's attachment
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a teiku (undecided) question: does the attachment of sanctity (חיבת הקודש) render the animal fit to be counted as first or second for impurity purposes, or is it irrelevant?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו): does the attachment of sanctity (חיבת הקודש) affect the animal's status for impurity counting, or is it irrelevant?

items.text: Mishnah: Signs of life in a goses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Signs of life in a goses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute about the required signs of life for a dangerously ill animal (מסוכנת). Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires both hand and leg movement; Rabbi Eliezer says a kick (זינוק) suffices; Rabbi Shimon adds a case of finding blood on walls; and the Sages require either hand or leg movement or tail wagging. The Mishnah concludes with the rule that for a small animal, stretching out a leg without retracting is a sign of death, and these signs apply only to a presumed goses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute about signs of life for a dangerously ill animal (מסוכנת), listing the positions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Shimon, and the Sages.
The Mishnah adds the rule that for a small animal, stretching out a leg without retracting is a sign of death, and these signs apply only to a presumed goses.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Why is a goses permitted?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Why is a goses permitted?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we know that a goses is permitted? It suggests that the verse 'This is the animal you may eat' implies only a living animal is permitted, and a goses might not be considered alive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where we know that a goses (dying animal) is permitted for consumption, given the verse 'This is the animal you may eat' implies only a living animal is permitted.

items.text: First answer: From the prohibition of neveilah
items.text_en: First answer: From the prohibition of neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: from the fact that the Torah prohibits neveilah (carcass), it implies that a goses is permitted, because if a goses were forbidden while alive, it would be redundant to forbid it after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that from the prohibition of neveilah (carcass) we infer that a goses (dying animal) is permitted, because if it were forbidden while alive, the prohibition after death would be redundant.

items.text: Objection and counter: Neveilah and goses might be identical
items.text_en: Objection and counter: Neveilah and goses might be identical
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps neveilah and goses are the same, with a goses being forbidden by a positive commandment and after death by a negative commandment. The Gemara rejects this by citing the verse that calls it neveilah only after death.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps neveilah (neveilah) and goses (goses) are the same entity.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing the verse that calls it neveilah only after death, not while alive.

The Gemara raises a counter-objection: perhaps neveilah and goses are identical, with a goses being forbidden by a positive commandment (עשה) while alive, and after death by a negative commandment (לאו).

items.text: Second answer: From the prohibition of treifah
items.text_en: Second answer: From the prohibition of treifah
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a second answer: from the prohibition of treifah (torn animal), it implies that a goses is permitted, because if a goses were forbidden, a treifah would be even more obvious. The Gemara then considers and rejects the possibility that goses, treifah, and neveilah are all distinct prohibitions, ultimately concluding that the derivation from treifah is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a second answer: from the prohibition of טריפה (a torn animal), it implies that a goses (dying animal) is permitted, because if a goses were forbidden, a treifah would be even more obvious.

The objection suggests that goses and treifah might be the same prohibition, and then questions why the Torah would separately write the prohibition of נבלה (carrion) if goses already carried a לאו and עשה.

The Gemara rejects the objection by considering the possibility that goses, treifah, and neveilah are all distinct prohibitions, each adding a separate לאו or עשה, but concludes that the derivation from treifah alone is insufficient.

items.text: Final derivation: From the verse about chelev
items.text_en: Final derivation: From the verse about chelev
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a definitive derivation from the verse about chelev (fat) of neveilah and treifah, citing the principle that the Torah teaches that the prohibition of neveilah and treifah can apply to the prohibition of chelev, implying that a goses is not included in these prohibitions and is therefore permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with a definitive derivation from the verse about chelev (fat) of neveilah and treifah, citing the principle that the Torah teaches that the prohibition of neveilah and treifah can apply to the prohibition of chelev, implying that a goses is not included in these prohibitions and is therefore permitted.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference from the verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if terefah were identical to mesukkenet, the Torah would have written 'fat of a terefah' instead of 'fat of a neveilah'; since it wrote 'neveilah', terefah is not mesukkenet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if טריפה (a terefah) were identical to מסוכנת (a dying animal), the Torah would have written 'fat of a terefah' instead of 'fat of a neveilah', and then infers that the prohibition of terefah would apply even after death.
The Gemara concludes that since the Torah wrote 'neveilah', it follows that טריפה (terefah) is not the same as מסוכנת (a dying animal).

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's objection
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's objection
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges the inference, suggesting that 'neveilah' might refer to a case where the animal was killed by a gistra (a type of wound) without prior mesukkenet, but the Gemara counters that some mesukkenet always precedes the fatal wound.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges the inference, suggesting that 'neveilah' might refer to a case where the animal was killed by a gistra without prior mesukkenet, but the Gemara counters that some mesukkenet always precedes the fatal wound.

items.text: Alternative proof from the repetition of 'chelev'
items.text_en: Alternative proof from the repetition of 'chelev'
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another proof: if terefah were mesukkenet, the verse would say 'chelev neveilah u-terefah'; the extra 'chelev' indicates a case where fat is not distinct from flesh, which is mesukkenet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative proof: the repetition of 'chelev' in the verse indicates a case where fat is not distinct from flesh, which is the mesukkenet (dying animal).

items.text: Proof from Ezekiel's verse
items.text_en: Proof from Ezekiel's verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ezekiel's statement distinguishing neveilah and terefah, and explains the verse's details: not eating meat of a kus kus (a doubtful case) and not eating from an animal about which a sage ruled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Ezekiel's verse as an alternative proof that a טריפה (torn animal) is not the same as a מסוכנת (dying animal), and explains the verse's details: not eating meat of a כוס כוס (a doubtful case) and not eating from an animal about which a sage ruled.
Rabbi Natan interprets the verse as referring to not eating from an animal whose priestly gifts (מתנות) had not been separated.

items.text: Implication of Ezekiel's greatness
items.text_en: Implication of Ezekiel's greatness
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if mesukkenet were forbidden, Ezekiel's statement would not demonstrate his piety; therefore mesukkenet must be permitted, proving it is distinct from terefah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if mesukkenet were permitted, Ezekiel's statement would demonstrate his piety; if forbidden, it would not.

items.text: Definitions of mesukkenet
items.text_en: Definitions of mesukkenet
items.desc_en: Rav Yehudah citing Rav defines mesukkenet as an animal that cannot stand; Rav Chanina bar Shelemya adds even if it eats vegetables; Rami bar Yechezkel adds even if it eats beams. Two versions of the tradition are given.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of a מסוכנת (animal in danger of imminent death), and Rav Yehudah citing Rav answers that it is any animal that cannot stand when stood up.

sub.text: Rav Chanina bar Shelemya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanina bar Shelemya in the name of Rav adds that even if the animal eats pieces of wood, it is still considered a מסוכנת if it cannot stand.
Rami bar Yechezkel says that even if the animal eats beams, it is still considered a מסוכנת if it cannot stand.
The Gemara notes that in סורא (Sura) they taught the tradition in one way, and in פומבדיתא (Pumbedita) they taught it in another way, with the same definitions but different phrasing.

items.text: Shmuel's inquiry about Rav's opinion
items.text_en: Shmuel's inquiry about Rav's opinion
items.desc_en: Shmuel asks Rav's students what Rav said about mesukkenet, and they report Rav's definition.

sub.desc_en: The narrator reports that שמואל (Shmuel) found the students of רב (Rav) and asked them what Rav said about a מסוכנת (animal in danger of imminent death).
Rav's students respond that Rav said the following (the definition of a מסוכנת is about to be quoted).

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: הגדרת פירכוס
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and initial definition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes signs of פרכוס: lowing, excreting, and ear-twitching. The Gemara cites a statement that these are needed to distinguish from a dead animal's actions.
items.desc: המקור מתאר סימני פירכוס בבהמה: גועה, מטילה רעי ומכשכשת באזנה, וקובע שכל שאינה עושה דברים שהמתה עושה – הרי זה פירכוס.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists three signs of פרכוס (convulsion): lowing, excreting, and ear-twitching.
An anonymous statement explains that these signs are needed to distinguish from actions a dead animal might perform.

items.text: פירוש דברי המתה על ידי רב ענן
items.text_en: Clarification of 'things a dead animal does'
items.desc_en: Rav Anan explains from Shmuel that bending and extending a limb is a sign of life, while extending and then bending is not. The Gemara notes this teaches a nuance beyond the Mishnah.
items.desc: רב ענן מבאר בשם שמואל מה הם 'דברים שהמתה עושה': יד כפופה ופשטתה – דבר שהמתה עושה; פשוטה וכפפתה – דבר שאין המתה עושה. הגמרא מקשה מברייתא ומתרצת שהחידוש הוא במקרה של פשוטה וכפפתה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what are the specific movements that a dead animal makes.
Rav Anan reports from Shmuel that bending a straight foreleg is a sign of life, while straightening a bent foreleg is a sign of death.
The Gemara asks what novel point Shmuel is teaching, given the Mishnah already addresses this.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that extending a foreleg without returning it is a sign of death, but returning it indicates life.
The Gemara explains that without Shmuel, one might think only the sequence of bending-straightening-bending is valid, but Shmuel teaches that straightening-bending is also valid.

items.text: קושיית רבי יוסי על דברי רבי מאיר ותירוץ
items.text_en: Contradiction between sources on lowing and excreting
items.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei disputing whether lowing or excreting constitute פרכוס. The Gemara resolves the contradictions by distinguishing between loud and soft lowing, and between streaming and spurting excretion.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יוסי אומר בשם רבי מאיר שגועה בשעת שחיטה אינה פירכוס, ורבי אלעזר ברבי יוסי מוסיף שאפילו הטילה רעי וכשכשה בזנבה אינה פירכוס. הגמרא מקשה סתירות בין המקורות ומתרצת: גועה – תלוי בעובי הקול; רעי – תלוי בשותתת או במתרזת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei rule that lowing or excreting are not פרכוס (convulsions), contradicting Rav's earlier statement.
The Gemara resolves the contradictions: lowing is a convulsion only when the voice is rich, and excreting is a convulsion only when expelled with force, not in a trickle.

items.text: Rav Chisda: פרכוס at the end of slaughter
items.text_en: Rav Chisda: פרכוס at the end of slaughter
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that פרכוס must occur at the end of slaughter, meaning in the middle (to exclude the beginning). He proves this from the Mishnah about a small animal that stretched its leg and did not retract it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the required פרכוס (convulsion) must occur at the end of slaughter, meaning in the middle of slaughter, to exclude the beginning.
Rav Chisda proves his position from the Mishnah about a small animal that stretched its leg and did not retract it, inferring that the case must be in the middle of slaughter.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the Mishnah refers to the very end of slaughter, and the lack of movement indicates the soul was already removed.

sub.desc_en: Rava responds to Rav Chisda's proof by insisting that the Mishnah's case of an animal that stretches its leg without retracting it refers to the end of slaughter, and the lack of movement proves the soul was already removed beforehand.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: פרכוס at the beginning
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: פרכוס at the beginning
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that פרכוס must be at the beginning of slaughter, proving it from the Mishnah about blood spurting on walls, which only makes sense if the animal convulses at the start.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the required convulsion (פרכוס) must occur at the beginning of slaughter.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves his position from the Mishnah about blood spurting on walls, arguing that if convulsion were required at the end, one would worry the spurt occurred at the beginning.

items.text: Discussion on the strength of spurting
items.text_en: Discussion on the strength of spurting
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether spurting is a stronger sign, citing a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis. It concludes that the Rabbis require פרכוס, and spurting alone is insufficient.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that spurting (זינוק) might be different because it is a stronger sign of life.

The Gemara questions whether spurting is indeed stronger, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says spurting is sufficient, which is lenient compared to Rabban Gamliel but stringent compared to the Sages.
Ravina reports that Samma bar Chilka raised a difficulty: is spurting really stronger than the Sages' position, given that the Sages require פרכוס (convulsion) in the hand or foot?
The Gemara analyzes which position the Sages are responding to: if to Rabban Gamliel, the wording should have been 'once it convulses' (כיון שפירכסה).
The Gemara concludes that the Sages are clearly responding to Rabbi Eliezer, and if spurting were stronger, why would the Sages use the term 'עד' (until) implying a limit?

items.text: דברי רבא: פירכוס בסוף שחיטה וראיה מברייתא
items.text_en: Rava's final position and proof
items.desc_en: Rava reiterates that פרכוס is at the end of slaughter, citing a baraita about an ox that convulses at the end.
items.desc: רבא חוזר על דעתו שפירכוס הוא בסוף שחיטה, ומביא ראיה מברייתא שפותחת במילה 'שור' (המשך הדף).

sub.desc_en: Rava states his position that the convulsion (פִּירְכּוּס) which renders the animal kosher occurs at the end of slaughter.
Rava introduces a baraita as the source for his position, beginning to cite it.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Exclusions from the law of a newborn animal
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Exclusions from the law of a newborn animal
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists exclusions from the requirement that a newborn animal be under its mother for seven days: kil'ayim (crossbreed), nidmeh (resembling another species), yotzei dofen (born by Caesarean section), mechusar zeman (born prematurely), and yatom (orphaned).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists five exclusions from the requirement that a newborn animal be under its mother for seven days: kil'ayim (crossbreed), nidmeh (resembling another species), yotzei dofen (born by Caesarean section), mechusar zeman (born prematurely), and yatom (orphaned).

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the orphaned animal exclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the orphaned animal exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what constitutes a yatom (orphaned animal). It rejects the possibility that the mother died after birth, as the animal would then live normally. It concludes that the orphan is one whose mother died before birth, and the exclusion is derived from the phrase "ki yivaled" (when it is born). The Gemara then explains that the exclusion is necessary only if we require life at the end of birth; otherwise, it would be redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes an orphaned animal, rejecting the possibility that the mother died after birth.
The Gemara suggests the orphan is one whose mother died before birth, but notes this is already excluded by the phrase 'ki yivaled'.
The Gemara concludes that the orphan is one whose mother died at the end of birth, and the exclusion is necessary only if we require life at the conclusion of birth.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a small animal that extended its foreleg
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a small animal that extended its foreleg
items.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows the baraita: a small animal that extended its foreleg and did not retract it is invalid for slaughter. The baraita distinguishes between foreleg and hindleg, and between small and large animals. For a bird, even minimal movement like fluttering a wing or wagging its tail is considered a sign of life (pirkus).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that the halakha follows the baraita: a small animal that extended its foreleg and did not retract it is invalid.
The baraita distinguishes between foreleg and hindleg: movement of the foreleg alone is not a sign of life, but hindleg movement is valid.
The baraita distinguishes between small and large animals: for a large animal, any leg movement is valid.
The baraita adds that for a bird, even minimal movement like fluttering a wing or wagging its tail is considered a sign of life (pirkus).

items.text: Gemara's question: Why repeat the baraita?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why repeat the baraita?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rava needed to state the halakha, since the baraita's rulings are already known from the Mishnah. It answers that the case of a bird was necessary, as it was not taught in the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rava's statement adds, since the Mishnah already teaches the rules for small and large animals, and answers that the rule about a bird was necessary because it was not taught in the Mishnah.
The Gemara explains that Rava's statement was necessary only for the case of a bird, which is not explicitly taught in the mishnah.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי אליעזר ורבי יוסי בשחיטה לנכרי
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaughtering for a gentile – dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that slaughtering for a gentile is valid, but Rabbi Eliezer invalidates it, arguing that a gentile's unspecified intent is for idolatry. Rabbi Yosei counters with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if in sacred matters intent invalidates only when the one performing the act intends, then in non-sacred matters, the intent of the one for whom it is slaughtered should not invalidate.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת: השוחט לנכרי – שחיטתו כשרה, ורבי אליעזר פוסל. רבי אליעזר טוען שסתם מחשבת נכרי לעבודה זרה, ורבי יוסי מקל וחומר: במקום שהמחשבה פוסלת במוקדשין – הכל הולך אחר העובד, ובחולין שאין מחשבה פוסלת – הכל הולך אחר השוחט.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters for a gentile has a kosher shechita, but Rabbi Eliezer invalidates it because he holds that a gentile's default intention is for idolatry.

Rabbi Yosei argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) that if in sacred matters, where intention can invalidate, everything follows the one who performs the act, then in non-sacred matters, where intention does not invalidate, surely everything should follow the slaughterer, not the gentile's intention.

Rabbi Yosei counters with a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if in sacred matters intent invalidates only when the performer intends, then in non-sacred matters the intent of the one for whom it is slaughtered should not invalidate.

items.text: בירור מחלוקת התנאים בעניין מחשבת נכרי
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that these Tannaim hold the view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei, who said that owners can render a sacrifice piggul (invalid through intent). The first Tanna holds that only if we heard the gentile explicitly intend idolatry does it invalidate; Rabbi Eliezer holds that unspecified intent is for idolatry; Rabbi Yosei holds that even if we heard the gentile intend, the one slaughtering is not considered the worshipper. An alternative version says they dispute when we heard the intent: the first Tanna distinguishes between inside and outside the Temple.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את שיטות התנאים: תנא קמא סובר שסתם מחשבת נכרי אינה לעבודה זרה, רבי אליעזר סובר שסתם מחשבת נכרי לעבודה זרה, ורבי יוסי סובר שאפילו כששמעינן דחשיב – זה מחשב וזה עובד לא אמרינן. יש גרסה אחרת שהמחלוקת היא דווקא כששמעינן דחשיב, ובחוץ לא אמרינן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that these Tannaim (in the Mishnah) hold the view of Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei, who taught that owners can render a sacrifice piggul (invalid through intent).
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Yosei explicitly states that owners can render a sacrifice piggul.
The Gemara explains that the first Tanna holds that only if we heard the gentile explicitly intend idolatry does it invalidate; unspecified intent is not considered for idolatry.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer holds that even without hearing explicit intent, unspecified intent of a gentile is assumed to be for idolatry.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei holds that even if we heard the gentile explicitly intend idolatry, the one slaughtering is not considered the worshipper, so the slaughter is valid.

An alternative version states that the dispute is specifically when we heard the gentile's intent: the first Tanna distinguishes between inside and outside the Temple, while Rabbi Eliezer applies the principle even outside.

items.text: סיום מחלוקת רבי אליעזר ורבי יוסי
items.text_en: Recap of earlier dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara recalls the earlier disagreement: Rabbi Eliezer holds we derive from outside to inside (חוץ מפנים), while Rabbi Yosei argues that even inside, we do not say 'this one intends and that one acts' (זה מחשב וזה עובד).
items.desc: הקטע מסיים את הדיון הקודם: רבי אליעזר סובר שלומדים חוץ מפנים, ורבי יוסי סובר שאפילו בפנים לא אומרים 'זה מחשב וזה עובד'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recalls the earlier dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds we derive from outside to inside (חוץ מפנים), while Rabbi Yosei argues that even inside, we do not say 'this one intends and that one acts' (זה מחשב וזה עובד).

items.text: מחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש בשחיטה לעבודה זרה
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on slaughter for idolatry
items.desc_en: A new dispute is presented: if one slaughters an animal intending to sprinkle its blood or burn its fat for idolatry, Rabbi Yochanan rules it is forbidden (פסולה), while Reish Lakish rules it is permitted (מותרת). Each explains his reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds we derive from one service to another (מעבודה לעבודה) and from outside to inside (חוץ מפנים); Reish Lakish rejects both derivations.
items.desc: נאמרה מחלוקת: השוחט בהמה לזרוק דמה לעבודה זרה ולהקטיר חלבה – רבי יוחנן פוסל, וריש לקיש מתיר. רבי יוחנן סובר שמחשבים מעבודה לעבודה ולומדים חוץ מפנים, וריש לקיש חולק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: if one slaughters an animal intending to sprinkle its blood or burn its fat for idolatry, Rabbi Yochanan rules it is forbidden (פסולה), while Reish Lakish rules it is permitted (מותרת).
Rabbi Yochanan explains his ruling: we derive from one service to another (מעבודה לעבודה) and from outside to inside (חוץ מפנים).
Reish Lakish explains his ruling: we do not derive from one service to another, and we do not derive from outside to inside.

items.text: מחלוקת נוספת וצורך בהצגת שתיהן
items.text_en: Supporting dispute and necessity of both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a related dispute: slaughtering for its own name but intending to sprinkle blood not for its own name. Rabbi Yochanan again rules forbidden, Reish Lakish permits. The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: from the first case one might think Reish Lakish only permits there because of the outside/inside issue, but in the second case (inside/inside) he might agree; from the second case one might think Rabbi Yochanan only forbids there, but in the first case he might agree. Thus both are needed.
items.desc: מובאת מחלוקת דומה בשחיטה לשמה לזרוק דמה שלא לשמה, ומסבירים מדוע יש צורך בשתי המחלוקות: כדי שלא נאמר שראש לקיש מודה במקרה אחד או שרבי יוחנן מודה במקרה אחר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a related dispute: slaughtering for its own name but intending to sprinkle blood not for its own name, with Rabbi Yochanan ruling forbidden and Reish Lakish permitting.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds that intention transfers from one service to another and learns from piggul (פיגול) intention, while Reish Lakish rejects both.

The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: from the first case one might think Reish Lakish only permits there due to the outside/inside issue, but in the second case (inside/inside) he might agree; from the second case one might think Rabbi Yochanan only forbids there, but in the first case he might agree.

items.text: קושיית רב ששת מברייתא של רבי יוסי
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection from Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet raises an objection based on Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer: in sacred matters where improper intent (מחשבה) disqualifies, everything follows the one performing the service; in non-sacred matters where intent does not disqualify, shouldn't everything follow the slaughterer? The Gemara clarifies that the kal vachomer refers to intent from one service to another (מעבודה לעבודה), not to idolatry itself.
items.desc: רב ששת מקשה מברייתא של רבי יוסי: מקל וחומר ממוקדשים לחולין, שבחולין אין מחשבה פוסלת מעבודה לעבודה, ולכן הכל הולך אחר השוחט. הגמרא מבררת את משמעות הברייתא ומסיקה שהיא עוסקת במחשבה מעבודה לעבודה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet raises an objection by citing Rabbi Yosei's kal vachomer: in sacred matters where improper intent disqualifies, everything follows the one performing the service; in non-sacred matters where intent does not disqualify, shouldn't everything follow the slaughterer?
The Gemara asks: what does 'intent does not disqualify in non-sacred matters' mean? If it means no disqualification at all, how can one find a case of slaughter for idolatry that is forbidden?

The Gemara clarifies: it is obvious that the kal vachomer refers to intent from one service to another (מעבודה לעבודה), and this is what Rabbi Yosei says: in sacred matters where intent disqualifies from one service to another, everything follows the one performing the service; in non-sacred matters where intent does not disqualify from one service to another but only within the same service, shouldn't everything follow the slaughterer?

items.text: תירוץ הקושיה על רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Resolution: Reish Lakish retracted, Rabbi Yochanan answers for himself
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the kal vachomer poses a difficulty for both: 'inside' (פנים) is difficult for Reish Lakish, 'outside' (חוץ) for Rabbi Yochanan. It resolves that Reish Lakish's earlier view was before he heard from Rabbi Yochanan; after hearing, he retracted. For Rabbi Yochanan, he himself raises and answers the objection, explaining that the kal vachomer applies only to the four primary services (ארבע עבודות), not to all cases.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הברייתא קשה על ריש לקיש בעניין 'פנים' ועל רבי יוחנן בעניין 'חוץ'. מתורצת הקושיה על ריש לקיש בכך שחזר בו, ועל רבי יוחנן מתורצת על ידי רב ששת עצמו: הברייתא עוסקת בארבע עבודות, והכל הולך אחר העובד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the kal vachomer poses a difficulty for both: 'inside' (פנים) is difficult for Reish Lakish, 'outside' (חוץ) for Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara resolves that Reish Lakish's earlier view was before he heard from Rabbi Yochanan; after hearing, he retracted, so 'inside' is not difficult for him.
For Rabbi Yochanan, he himself raises and answers the objection, explaining that the kal vachomer applies only to the four primary services (ארבע עבודות), not to all cases.

items.text: קושיית רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Opening argument from Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that since thought does not disqualify in חולין except in two acts, it is logical that the entire status follows the slaughterer.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן טוען שמקום שאין מחשבה פוסלת בחולין אלא בשתי עבודות, אינו דין שיהיה הכל הולך אחר השוחט.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that since thought does not disqualify in חולין (non-sacred meat) except in two acts, it is logical that the entire status follows the slaughterer.

items.text: Supporting baraita
items.text_en: Supporting baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: one who slaughters for idolatry renders the animal זבחי מתים, but if he slaughtered first and then intended, the case in Caesarea was left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yochanan: one who slaughters for idolatry renders the animal זבחי מתים, but if he slaughtered first and then intended, the case in Caesarea was left unresolved.

items.text: Rav Chisda's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the lack of ruling was due to respect: no prohibition out of respect for the Sages, no permission out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that the lack of ruling was due to respect: no prohibition out of respect for the Sages, no permission out of respect for Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: דחיית טעם השתיקה – הוכיח סופו על תחילתו
items.text_en: Two challenges to Rav Chisda
items.desc_en: Two alternative explanations are proposed: perhaps the Sages only ruled leniently because they didn't hear the intent, but here where intent is known, הוכיח סופו על תחילתו applies; or Rabbi Eliezer only ruled stringently for a gentile, but for a Jew the principle does not apply.
items.desc: דחייה: שמא רבנן לא אמרו שם אלא משום שלא שמענו שחשב, אבל כאן ששמענו – הוכיח סופו על תחילתו. אי נמי, רבי אליעזר לא אמר שם אלא גבי נכרי שסתם מחשבתו לעבודה זרה, אבל ישראל לא אמרינן הוכיח סופו על תחילתו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Chisda's explanation by proposing that the Sages' leniency only applied because they did not hear the intent, but here where intent is known, the principle of הוכיח סופו על תחילתו (the end proves the beginning) applies.
An alternative explanation is offered: Rabbi Eliezer's stringency only applied to a gentile, whose default intent is for idolatry, but for a Jew the principle of הוכיח סופו על תחילתו is not applied.

items.text: טעם חדש של רב שיזבי – כבוד רשב
items.text_en: Rav Sheizvi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi says the permission was out of respect for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, and asks which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is meant.
items.desc: רב שיזבי אומר: לא אמרו בה היתר משום כבודו דרבן שמעון בן גמליאל, ושואלים: הי רבן שמעון בן גמליאל?

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi proposes that the permission was out of respect for Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The Gemara asks which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is meant.

items.text: דחיית רשב
items.text_en: First suggestion: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of Gittin
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the reference is to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from Gittin, who applies הוכיח סופו על תחילתו in a case of a man who says 'write a get' and then falls. The Gemara rejects this because there the man explicitly said 'write', unlike the slaughter case.
items.desc: מנסים לומר שמדובר ברשב

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the reference is to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from Gittin, citing the Mishnah about a healthy man who says 'write a get' and then falls from a roof, where Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies הוכיח סופו על תחילתו (the end proves the beginning).

The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah in Gittin, explaining that it was missing a clause and actually teaches the principle of הוכיח סופו על תחילתו (the end proves the beginning) as a general rule, with the story as an illustration.

The Gemara rejects this suggestion, arguing that the case in Gittin is different because the man explicitly said 'write' (כתבו), indicating his initial intent, unlike the slaughter case where no such explicit statement was made.

items.text: רשב
items.text_en: Second suggestion: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel of gifts
items.desc_en: Ravina identifies the reference as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from a case of writing property to others, where he applies הוכיח סופו על תחילתו regarding slaves and terumah. The Gemara explains the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
items.desc: רבינא אומר: הכוונה לרשב

sub.desc_en: Ravina identifies the reference as Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel from a baraita about writing property to others, where slaves eat תרומה (priestly portion) if the recipient refuses.
The Gemara asks whether the Tanna Kamma holds that the recipient acquires even if he stands and protests.
Rabbah (or Rabbi Yochanan) clarifies that all agree: if he protests initially he does not acquire; if he is silent and later protests he does acquire.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is when the recipient was silent and later protested; Tanna Kamma holds silence effects acquisition and the protest is a retraction.

Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies the principle of הוכיח סופו על תחילתו (the end proves the beginning), reasoning that initial silence was because the recipient thought the property had not yet come into his possession.

items.text: הלכה כרבי יוסי ומעשה בטייעי
items.text_en: Practical rulings and closing discussion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says the halakha follows Rabbi Yosi. A case of Arab merchants giving animals to Jewish butchers is ruled accordingly. Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi about a similar case with Rabbi Eliezer's view, and Rav Ashi distinguishes based on the butcher's ability to refuse.
items.desc: רב יהודה אמר שמואל: הלכה כרבי יוסי. מעשה בטייעי שנתנו אילים לטבחי ישראל ואמרו דמא ותרבא לדידן, משכא ובישרא לדידכו. רב טובי בר רב מתנה שאל את רב יוסף, ופסק כרבי יוסי. רב אחא בריה דרב אויא שאל את רב אשי לגבי רבי אליעזר, וענה: אם הוא איש אלים – אסור, ואם לא – אמר לו 'רישיך והר'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yosi.
A case of Arab merchants giving rams to Jewish butchers with a condition about blood and fat is brought before Rav Yosef, who rules according to Rabbi Yosi.

sub.text: Rav Acha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks Rav Ashi about a similar case according to Rabbi Eliezer's view.
Rav Ashi distinguishes based on whether the butcher can refuse the payment: if the butcher is strong enough to refuse, it is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.

items.text: משנת השוחט לשם הרים וגבעות
items.text_en: Mishnah: slaughter for natural features
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who slaughters for the sake of mountains, hills, seas, rivers, or deserts renders the slaughter invalid.
items.desc: משנה: השוחט לשם הרים, גבעות, ימים, נהרות, מדברות – שחיטתו פסולה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that slaughtering for the sake of mountains, hills, seas, rivers, or deserts renders the slaughter invalid.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: שחיטה לשם עבודה זרה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two people hold a knife and slaughter, one for an invalid intent and one for a valid intent, the slaughter is invalid.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת ששניים האוחזים בסכין ושוחטים, אחד לשם אחד מכל אלו (עבודה זרה) ואחד לשם דבר כשר – שחיטתו פסולה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two people hold a knife and slaughter, one for a forbidden intent and one for a valid intent, the slaughter is invalid.

The Gemara questions the Mishnah's implication that the slaughter is merely invalid (פסולה) but not considered זִבְחֵי מֵתִים (offerings to the dead), citing a baraita that lists such intents as rendering the animal זִבְחֵי מֵתִים.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between slaughtering for the mountain itself and slaughtering for the angel of the mountain (גדא דהר), proving his point from the parallel case of Michael the great prince.

Rav Huna rules that if a friend's animal was lying before an idol, slaughtering one siman (סימן, organ) renders it forbidden, supported by Rabbi Yochanan's principle that bowing to another's animal does not forbid it but performing an act (like slaughter) does.

Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna: if slaughtering one siman forbids the animal, then slaughtering a sin-offering on Shabbat outside the Temple for idolatry should not be liable for slaughtering outside (since it is already forbidden), contradicting the baraita that says one is liable for three sin-offerings.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's implication
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's implication
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'invalid' but not 'offerings to the dead', and raises a contradiction from a baraita that lists various idolatrous intentions which render the animal an offering to the dead.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah says 'invalid' but not 'offerings to the dead', implying a distinction, and raises a contradiction from a baraita listing various idolatrous intentions that render the animal an offering to the dead.

items.text: Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who says 'for the mountain' (invalid but not an offering to the dead) and one who says 'for the spirit of the mountain' (an offering to the dead). He supports this from the parallel with Michael the great prince.
