sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who says 'for the mountain' (invalid but not an offering to the dead) and one who says 'for the spirit of the mountain' (an offering to the dead), supporting this from the parallel with Michael the great prince.

items.text: דין רב הונא: בהמת חברה הרבוצה לפני עבודה זרה
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on an animal before idolatry
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a friend's animal was crouching before an idol, once one cuts one siman (sign of slaughter), the animal becomes forbidden. He bases this on Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that prostrating to another's animal does not forbid it, but performing an act upon it does.
items.desc: רב הונא אומר: אם בהמת חברו הייתה רבוצה לפני עבודה זרה, כיון ששחט בה סימן אחד – אסרה. הוא סובר כעולא בשם רבי יוחנן, שאף על פי שהשתחווה לבהמת חברו לא אסרה, עשייה (שחיטה) אוסרת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a friend's animal was crouching before an idol, once one cuts one siman (sign of slaughter), the animal becomes forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Huna follows Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan (רבי יוחנן) that prostrating to another's animal does not forbid it, but performing an act upon it does.

items.text: קושיית רב נחמן על רב הונא
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's objection to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna from a baraita about one who slaughters a sin-offering on Shabbat outside the Temple for idolatry: he is liable for three sin-offerings. If, as Rav Huna says, cutting one siman already forbids the animal, then the slaughter outside should not incur liability.
items.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על רב הונא מברייתא: השוחט חטאת בשבת בחוץ לעבודה זרה חייב שלוש חטאות. אם סימן אחד אוסר, מדוע יתחייב על שחיטת חוץ?

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Rav Huna's position by citing a baraita: one who slaughters a sin-offering (חטאת) on Shabbat (שבת) outside the Temple for idolatry (עבודה זרה) is liable for three sin-offerings; if cutting one siman (סימן, shechita organ) forbids the animal, as Rav Huna says, then the act of slaughtering outside should not incur liability.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על 'מחתך בעפר'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's initial explanation of Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a bird sin-offering, where all parts of the slaughter come together, so the act is considered complete.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על דין 'מחתך בעפר', ורב פפא מתרץ שמדובר בחטאת העוף שבה כל החתיכות באות יחד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rav Huna's ruling seems to describe merely cutting in the dirt, not valid slaughter.
Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a bird sin-offering (חטאת העוף), where all the slaughter organs come together, so the act is considered complete.

items.text: בירור שיטת רב הונא ועולא
items.text_en: Questioning Rav Huna's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's ruling aligns with Ulla's view, and notes that Ulla only spoke of a minimal act.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת על מי סמך רב הונא את דבריו, ומסיקה שעולא אמר 'מעשה כל דהו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Huna's ruling aligns with Ulla's view, and notes that Ulla only spoke of a minimal act.

items.text: תירוץ נוסף וקושיה עליו
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the case is where one says 'I will complete the slaughter,' but objects that this would apply to any offering, not just a sin-offering.
items.desc: הגמרא מציעה תירוץ אחר: האומר 'בגמר זביחה הוא עובדה', אך מקשה: אם כן, למה דווקא חטאת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative: the case is where one says 'I will complete the slaughter,' meaning the act is performed at the final stage of slaughter.
The Gemara objects: if so, why specifically mention a sin-offering (חטאת)? The same reasoning would apply to any offering (זבח).

items.text: תירוץ מר זוטרא משם רב פפא
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's resolution with a defective reed
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa explains that the case involves a half-broken reed knife, where one adds a minimal amount and completes the slaughter, so all parts come together.
items.desc: מר זוטרא בשם רב פפא מתרץ שמדובר בחצי קנה פגום שהוסיף עליו כל שהוא וגמרו, כך שהכל בא יחד.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a half-broken reed knife (חצי קנה פגום), where one adds a minimal amount and completes the slaughter, so all parts come together (דכולהו בהדי הדדי קאתיין).

items.text: Rav Pappa's first observation on the refutation
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's first observation on the refutation
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa notes that without Rav Huna's mention of 'one sign,' the sin-offering would not be a refutation, and explains that 'act' refers to a major act.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa observes that without Rav Huna's mention of 'one sign,' the sin-offering would not be a refutation, and explains that 'act' refers to a major act.

items.text: Rav Pappa's second observation and its clarification
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's second observation and its clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa notes that without Rav Huna's mention of 'another's animal,' the sin-offering would not be a refutation, because one cannot prohibit another's property. The Gemara clarifies that this is obvious, but the teaching is needed lest one think that since the animal is acquired for atonement, it is like one's own.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that without Rav Huna's mention of 'another's animal,' the sin-offering would not be a refutation, because one cannot prohibit another's property.
The Gemara objects that Rav Pappa's observation is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the teaching is needed lest one think that since the animal is acquired for atonement (כפרה), it is considered like one's own, so the statement teaches otherwise.

items.text: אמוראים: אין אדם אוסר דבר שאין שלו
items.text_en: General principle stated by Rav Nachman and others
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak state that a person cannot prohibit something that is not his own.
items.desc: רב נחמן, רב עמרם ורב יצחק אומרים שאין אדם יכול לאסור דבר שאינו שלו.

sub.text: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak state the general principle that a person cannot prohibit something that is not his own.

items.text: קושיה מברייתא על השוחט חטאת בשבת
items.text_en: Supporting challenge from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a challenge from a baraita about one who slaughters a sin-offering on Shabbat outside for idolatry, which is liable for three sin-offerings, and it is established as a bird sin-offering with a half-broken reed, implying the principle holds.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא על השוחט חטאת בשבת בחוץ לעבודה זרה, ומוקמת בחטאת העוף ובחצי קנה פגום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about one who slaughters a sin-offering on Shabbat outside for idolatry, who is liable for three sin-offerings, and it is established as a bird sin-offering with a half-broken reed, implying the principle holds.
The Gemara explains that the baraita's case is specifically a bird sin-offering where all the slaughter actions come together, supporting the principle that a minimal addition completes the act.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על דין חטאת העוף
items.text_en: Challenge from bird sin-offering
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier assumption that a person cannot prohibit another's property: if so, why is a bird sin-offering singled out? Even a animal sin-offering should be considered as belonging to the owner for atonement.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם אדם אינו אוסר דבר שאינו שלו, מדוע חטאת העוף נאסרת במחשבת פיגול? הרי חטאת בהמה גם היא נקנית לכפרה ונחשבת כשלו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that a person cannot prohibit another's property: if so, why is a bird sin-offering singled out? Even an animal sin-offering should be considered as belonging to the owner for atonement.

items.text: ברייתא על שותפות בשחיטה
items.text_en: First resolution: joint ownership
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about two people holding a knife and slaughtering with different intentions, where the slaughter is invalid. It explains that this case involves joint ownership of the animal.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על שניים האוחזים בסכין ושוחטים, אחד לשם עבודה זרה ואחד לשם דבר כשר, והשחיטה פסולה. הגמרא מתרצת שמדובר בשותפות בקרבן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: two people holding a knife and slaughtering, one for an invalid intent and one for a valid intent, the slaughter is invalid.
The Gemara answers that the case involves a partner who has a share in the animal.

items.text: Second resolution: joint ownership in other cases
items.text_en: Second resolution: joint ownership in other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita about one who renders wine unfit for libation, and explains that this too involves joint ownership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites another baraita: one who renders terumah impure, mixes it with chullin, or pours wine for idolatry — if unintentional, exempt; if intentional, liable.
The Gemara answers that here too the case involves a partner who has a share in the item.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about a gentile's libation
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about a gentile's libation
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a tannaitic dispute: if a gentile pours wine of an Israelite not before an idol, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava permit it, arguing that libation is only before an idol and the owner can say 'you cannot forbid my wine against my will.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a Tannaic dispute: a gentile who pours an Israelite's wine for idolatry not in its presence — the first opinion prohibits it, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava permit it for two reasons: one, libation is only done in the presence of idolatry; two, the owner can say 'you cannot forbid my wine against my will.'
The Tanna Kamma forbids the wine, while Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava permit it.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava
sub.desc_en: They give two reasons: libation is only before an idol, and the owner can say 'you cannot forbid my wine against my will.'

items.text: דברי רב נחמן ורב עמרם ורב יצחק
items.text_en: Distinction between gentile and Israelite
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak state that even according to the one who says a person can prohibit another's property, this applies only to a gentile; an Israelite intends only to cause distress.
items.desc: רב נחמן, רב עמרם ורב יצחק אומרים שאפילו למי שאומר שאדם אוסר דבר שאינו שלו, זה דווקא בגוי, אבל ישראל מתכוון לצער את חבירו ולא לאסור.

sub.text: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman, Rav Amram, and Rav Yitzchak rule that even according to the opinion that a person can prohibit another's property, this applies only to a gentile, but an Israelite intends to cause distress.

items.text: ברייתא על ישראל מומר
items.text_en: Resolution with an apostate Israelite
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the earlier baraitot: the case of two holding a knife involves an apostate Israelite, and the case of rendering wine unfit also involves an apostate Israelite.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה שוב את הברייתא על שניים האוחזים בסכין, ומתרצת שמדובר בישראל מומר. וכן לגבי המטמא והמדמע והמנסך, גם שם מדובר בישראל מומר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing the mishna about two people holding a knife and slaughtering, where one slaughters for an improper intent and the slaughter is invalid, implying that a Jew can render another's animal forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the case involves an apostate Israelite, who does intend to worship idols and thus renders the animal forbidden.
The Gemara brings another mishna about one who renders another's food impure, mixes teruma, or pours wine as a libation, where intentional action incurs liability, as further evidence.
The Gemara answers that here too the case involves an apostate Israelite, who renders the item forbidden.

items.text: שאלת רב אחא בריה דרבא לרב אשי
items.text_en: Definition of an apostate
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about an apostate who was warned and accepted the warning. Rav Ashi responds that such a person has permitted himself to be killed, and there is no greater apostate than this.
items.desc: רב אחא בריה דרבא שואל את רב אשי: אם התרו בו וקיבל עליו התראה, מה הדין? רב אשי עונה: הרי התיר עצמו למיתה, ואין לך מומר גדול מזה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about the status of a Jew who was forewarned and accepted the forewarning before slaughtering another's animal for idolatry.
Rav Ashi responds that such a person has permitted himself to death, and there is no greater apostate than this, so he renders the animal forbidden.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה על דיני שחיטה
items.text_en: Mishnah: places where slaughter is prohibited
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists places where one may not slaughter: into seas, rivers, or vessels, but one may slaughter into a pit of water, and on a ship onto vessels. One may not slaughter into a pit at all, but may make a pit in his house for blood to collect, though not in the market due to suspicion of idolatry.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בדיני שחיטה: אין שוחטין לתוך ימים, נהרות או כלים, אבל שוחט לתוך עוגה של מים. בספינה על גבי כלים. אין שוחטין לגומא כלל, אבל עושה גומא בביתו כדי שייכנס הדם לתוכה, ובשוק לא יעשה כן.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah begins: one may not slaughter into seas, rivers, or vessels, but may slaughter into a bowl of water; on a ship, on top of vessels; one may not slaughter into a pit at all, but may make a pit in one's house for the blood to flow into; in the marketplace one should not do so, lest...

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: איסור שחיטה לעבודה זרה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not slaughter into a pit or into water, nor into a vessel, but one may slaughter into a trough of water. In a market, one may not do so at all, because it imitates the practices of heretics.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאין שוחטים לתוך ימים, נהרות, גומא או עוגה של מים, מחשש לחיקוי דרכי המינים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not slaughter into a pit or into water, nor into a vessel, but one may slaughter into a trough of water; in a market, one may not do so at all, because it imitates the practices of heretics.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על איסור שחיטה לתוך מים
items.text_en: Gemara's question on water and pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why slaughtering into the sea is prohibited (due to suspicion of offering to the sea deity) but into a water trough is permitted, and answers that the trough must be of murky water, avoiding the same suspicion.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מה ההבדל בין ים לעוגת מים? ומתרצת שהאיסור הוא במים עכורים, כהסברו של רבא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why slaughtering into a sea is prohibited (due to suspicion of idolatry) and why a trough of water is also prohibited (due to suspicion of a water deity).
Rava answers that the Mishnah's permission for a trough of water refers only to muddy water, not clear water.

items.text: דיון באיסור שחיטה לגומא
items.text_en: Clarification of the pit prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's statement that one may not slaughter into a pit at all, but the Mishnah later permits it in a market? Abaye explains the first clause refers to a pit in the market. Rava objects that the later clause explicitly mentions the market, implying the first does not. Rava then reinterprets: the Mishnah means one may not slaughter into a pit at all, but if one wants to clean his courtyard, he may slaughter outside the pit so blood trickles into it, but not in the market, to avoid imitating heretics.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במשנה האוסרת שחיטה לגומא. אביי ורבא חולקים בפירוש: אביי מפרש שמדובר בגומא שבשוק, ורבא מסביר שהאיסור הוא עקרוני, אך מותר לשחוט מחוץ לגומא והדם שותת לתוכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's blanket prohibition of slaughtering into a pit, given that the Mishnah later permits it in a market.
Abaye explains that the first clause refers to a pit located in the market.
Rava objects that the later clause explicitly mentions the market, implying the first clause does not.

Rava reinterprets the Mishnah: one may not slaughter into a pit at all, but if one wants to clean his courtyard, he may slaughter outside the pit so blood trickles into it, but not in the market, to avoid imitating heretics.

items.text: ברייתא כרבא
items.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rava
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava's interpretation: one traveling on a ship may extend his hand outside and slaughter, with blood trickling down the ship's side, but may not slaughter into a pit at all. It also repeats the rule about cleaning a courtyard and adds that if one does so in the market, the animal requires inspection, because of the prohibition against following their statutes.
items.desc: מובאת ברייתא התומכת בדברי רבא, המפרטת דיני שחיטה בספינה ובחצר, ומדגישה את האיסור לעשות כן בשוק משום חוקות הגויים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rava's interpretation, describing a case of one traveling on a ship who slaughters outside the ship, with blood dripping down, and the rule that one may not slaughter into a pit at all; it adds that in the market one may not do so because of the verse 'and in their statutes you shall not walk', and if one does so, the meat requires inspection.
The baraita repeats the rule about cleaning a courtyard and adds that if one does so in the market, the animal requires inspection, because of the prohibition against following their statutes.

items.text: משנה: שחיטה לשם קרבנות
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: slaughter for specific offerings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists offerings for which slaughtering invalidates the animal (e.g., burnt offering, peace offerings, etc.), with Rabbi Shimon deeming it valid. It then discusses a case where two hold a knife and slaughter, one for an invalid intent and one for a valid intent. Finally, it lists offerings for which slaughtering is valid (e.g., sin offering, guilt offering, etc.) and gives a rule: anything that is vowed or donated is invalid when slaughtered for its name; what is not vowed or donated is valid.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת אילו קרבנות פוסלים את השחיטה כשנשחטים לשמם (עולה, זבחים, אשם תלוי, פסח, תודה) ואילו כשרים (חטאת, אשם ודאי, בכור, מעשר, תמורה), וקובעת כלל: כל הנידר ונידב אסור, ושאינו נידר ונידב כשר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists offerings for which slaughtering in their name renders the slaughter invalid (with Rabbi Shimon permitting), and those for which it is valid, concluding with a general rule: anything that is vowed or donated is forbidden when slaughtered in its name; anything not vowed or donated is valid.
The Mishnah records Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion that such slaughter is valid.
The Mishnah presents a case where two people hold a knife and slaughter, one with invalid intent and one with valid intent, ruling the slaughter invalid.
The Mishnah lists offerings (sin offering, definite guilt offering, firstborn, tithe, substitute) for which slaughtering with intent for their name is valid.
The Mishnah gives a general rule: anything that is vowed or donated is invalid when slaughtered for its name; what is not vowed or donated is valid when slaughtered for its name.

items.text: Gemara on guilt offering and Passover
items.text_en: Gemara on guilt offering and Passover
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a guilt offering (which is not normally vowed) appears in the list. Rabbi Yochanan identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Elazar, who holds one can donate a guilt offering daily. It then questions Passover, which has a fixed time, and Rabbi Oshaya answers that Passover is different because its designation can be made all year.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a guilt offering (אשם תלוי) appears in the Mishnah's list, since it is not normally a vowed or donated offering.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi Elazar, who holds that one can donate a guilt offering (אשם תלוי) daily.
The Gemara questions how Passover (פסח) appears in the list, since it has a fixed time and is not a voluntary donation.
Rabbi Oshaya answers that Passover is different because its designation (הפרשה) can be made all year, making it similar to a donated offering.

items.text: Distinction between unblemished and blemished animals
items.text_en: Distinction between unblemished and blemished animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai limits the Mishnah's rule to unblemished animals, but for blemished animals it is obvious they are not for an offering. Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, saying even blemished animals might be suspected if the blemish is not obvious.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yannai says that the Mishnah's rule about slaughtering for a Passover offering applies only to unblemished animals, but for blemished animals it is obvious that the slaughter is not for Passover.
Rabbi Yochanan says that even blemished animals are included, because sometimes a blemish may be overlooked and not known.

items.text: Clarification of sin offering and guilt offering
items.text_en: Clarification of sin offering and guilt offering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that the Mishnah's ruling on sin offering applies only when one is not obligated to bring a sin offering; if obligated, he might be slaughtering for his own sin offering. Rabbi Abahu adds that this applies when he explicitly says 'for my sin offering.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says that the Mishnah's ruling that slaughtering for a sin-offering is valid applies only when one is not obligated to bring a sin-offering; if obligated, one might be doing it for his own sin-offering.
The Gemara asks: But he did not say 'for my sin-offering'?
Rabbi Avahu answers that the case is where he explicitly says 'for my sin-offering'.

items.text: Clarification of temurah
items.text_en: Clarification of temurah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar limits the Mishnah's ruling on temurah to when one has no animal at home; if he does, he might be declaring it a temurah. Rabbi Abahu adds that this applies when he says 'for the temurah of my offering.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says that the Mishnah's ruling that slaughtering for a substitute (תמורה) is valid applies only when one has no other offering in his house; if he does, one might be declaring it a substitute.
The Gemara asks: But he did not say 'for the substitute of my offering'?
Rabbi Avahu answers that the case is where he explicitly says 'for the substitute of my offering'.
Rabbi Abahu resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah's ruling applies specifically when the slaughterer says 'for the temurah of my offering.'

items.text: Expansion of the rule: additional cases
items.text_en: Expansion of the rule: additional cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the rule 'this is the principle' includes, and answers it includes the burnt offering of a nazirite, which might be thought not to be a vow. It also includes the burnt offering of a woman after childbirth. Rabbi Elazar adds that this applies only when he has no wife; if he has a wife, he might be slaughtering for her offering. Rabbi Abahu adds that this applies when he says 'for my wife's burnt offering.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what additional cases the rule 'this is the principle' comes to include.
The Gemara answers that it includes the burnt offering of a nazirite, which might have been thought not to be a vow but rather a private matter.
The Gemara adds that the rule also includes the burnt offering of a woman after childbirth, which is not a vowed or donated offering.
Rabbi Elazar objects that the ruling applies only when he has no wife; if he has a wife, he might be slaughtering for her offering.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that the mishnah does not say 'for my wife's burnt offering.'
Rabbi Abahu resolves that the mishnah deals with a case where he explicitly says 'for my wife's burnt offering.'

items.text: Final question: is this obvious?
items.text_en: Final question: is this obvious?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the last point is obvious, implying a discussion of whether the clarification is necessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Elazar's ruling is obvious, implying a discussion of whether the clarification is necessary.

items.text: סיום הפרק הקודם
items.text_en: Concluding remark on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous discussion about a calf found dead in its mother's womb, suggesting that if it had been born alive there would have been noise, but here it was stillborn.
items.desc: הגמרא מסיימת דיון קודם בעניין לידה, ומחדשת שאפשר לומר הפילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case of a calf found dead in the womb is a stillbirth, not a live birth that died, because if it had been born alive there would have been noise.

items.text: הדרן לפרק השוחט
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah of 'The Slaughterer' (השוחט) which lists the terefot.
items.desc: הגמרא חוזרת לפרק 'השוחט' ומתחילה משנה חדשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara signals a return to the Mishnah of 'The Slaughterer' (השוחט) which lists the terefot.

items.text: משנת הטריפות
items.text_en: Mishnah: The Terefot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the conditions that render an animal a terefah: perforation of the esophagus, severance of the trachea, etc. It includes opinions of Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda, and concludes with the general rule: anything that cannot live is a terefah.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת את סוגי הטריפות בבהמה: נקב בוושט, פסוקת הגרגרת, נקב בקרום המוח, נקב בלב, שבר בשדרה, נטילת הכבד, נקב בריאה, בקיבה, במרה, בדקין, בקרקבן, ובכיס השתן. כמו כן נפילה מהגג, שבר בצלעות, ודריסת טורף. רבי יהודה מבדיל בין דקה לגסה, וניתן כלל: כל שאין כמוה חיה – טריפה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by listing the initial conditions that render an animal a terefah (טְרֵפָה), including perforation of the esophagus, severance of the trachea, and other fatal injuries.

sub.text: Mishnah continues with Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.text_en: Mishnah continues with Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehuda
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah continues with additional terefot (טְרֵפוֹת) and records the positions of Rabbi Shimon regarding the lung and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the size of a perforation in the stomach.

The Mishnah lists further terefot (טְרֵפוֹת) including falls and predator attacks, records Rabbi Yehuda's distinctions for different animals, and concludes with the general principle that any animal that cannot survive is a terefah (טְרֵפָה).

items.text: דרשת ריש לקיש: רמז לטריפה שאינה חיה
items.text_en: Gemara: Biblical source for a terefah that cannot live
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks for a biblical hint that a terefah cannot live. He cites the verse 'And this is the animal that you shall eat' to derive that only a living animal may be eaten, implying a terefah is not considered alive.
items.desc: ריש לקיש שואל מהיכן רמז שטריפה אינה חיה. הוא דורש מהפסוק 'וזאת החיה אשר תאכלו' – חיה אכול, שאינה חיה לא תאכל, ומכאן שטריפה אינה חיה.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks for a biblical hint that a terefah (טריפה) cannot live, noting that the Mishnah's rule implies it but the source is unclear.

The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'וְזֹאת הַחַיָּה אֲשֶׁר תֹּאכְלוּ' (and this is the animal that you shall eat), deriving that only a living animal may be eaten, implying a terefah (טריפה) is not considered alive.

items.text: שיטת האומר טריפה חיה
items.text_en: Alternative view: Terefah is alive
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers the opinion that a terefah is considered alive. For that view, the verse 'This is the animal' is interpreted to exclude only non-kosher species, not terefot.
items.desc: למי שסובר שטריפה חיה, הדרשה שונה: 'זאת החיה' – זאת אכול, חיה אחרת לא תאכל, ומכאן שטריפה חיה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the view that a terefah is alive, from where does he derive the exclusion of terefot from the verse?
The alternative view derives from the verse 'זֹאת הַחַיָּה' (this is the animal) that only non-kosher species are excluded, implying that a terefah is alive.

items.text: Reconciling the verses
items.text_en: Reconciling the verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains how the first opinion uses the word 'this' for another teaching (that God showed Moses each species). For the one who holds terefah is alive, the source is a different baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school listing eighteen terefot given to Moses at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the one who holds that a terefah is alive, what does he do with the word 'זֹאת' (this) in the verse?
The Gemara answers: he needs it for the teaching of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, that God showed Moses each species and said 'this eat, and this do not eat'.
The Gemara objects: but the other opinion (who holds terefah is not alive) also needs the word 'זֹאת' for that same teaching!

The Gemara resolves: indeed, that is the case; rather, the one who holds terefah is alive derives it from another baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, which lists eighteen terefot given to Moses at Sinai.

items.text: Challenge: Are there only eighteen?
items.text_en: Challenge: Are there only eighteen?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that there are more than eighteen terefot, citing the acronym בסג״ר and the seven laws (שבע שמעתתא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that there are more than eighteen terefot, citing the acronym בסג״ר and the seven laws (שבע שמעתתא).

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על תני דבי רבי ישמעאל
items.text_en: First challenge: animal whose legs are cut above the knee
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Tanna of Bei Rabbi Yishmael, who says there are only 18 tereifot, accounts for the case of an animal whose legs are cut from the knee upward, which is a tereifah. It answers that he holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says the animal can heal and live.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על התנא דבי רבי ישמעאל, שמונה שמונה עשרה טריפות, שהרי יש טריפה נוספת: בהמה שנחתכו רגליה מן הארכובה ולמעלה. ומתרצת שסובר כרבי שמעון בן אלעזר שיכולה ליכוות ולחיות.

sub.desc_en: The gemara questions how the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael, who lists only 18 treifot, accounts for the case of an animal whose legs are cut from the knee joint upward, which is also treifah.
The gemara answers that the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who holds that such an animal can survive by leaning on its stumps.

items.text: דחיית התירוץ הראשון
items.text_en: Refinement: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds it is kosher
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even if the animal can heal, the Tanna of Bei Rabbi Yishmael holds that a tereifah can live, so this would still be a tereifah. It resolves that the Tanna actually holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who explicitly says it is kosher.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את התירוץ, שכן התנא דבי רבי ישמעאל סובר שטריפה חיה, ואילו רבי שמעון בן אלעזר אמר 'כשרה היא', כלומר אינה טריפה כלל. לכן התירוץ אינו עולה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that even if the animal can survive, the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that a treifah can live, so Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's leniency would not help.

The gemara resolves that the Tanna of the school of Rabbi Yishmael actually follows Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's other statement that such an animal is completely kosher (כשרה), not merely capable of surviving.

items.text: קושיית חסרון בשדרה
items.text_en: Second challenge: deficiency in the spine
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises another omission: the case of a deficiency in the spine, which is a tereifah according to a mishnah and the statement of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel. This is not in the list of 18.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על התנא דבי רבי ישמעאל מחסרון בשדרה, ששנינו במשנה שהוא טריפה, ואינו נמנה ברשימתו. ומביאה את דברי רב יהודה בשם שמואל שכן הדין לטריפה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks about the case of a deficiency in the spine, which the Mishnah (with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel) and Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rule is treifah, yet it is not listed among the 18.

items.text: תירוץ: המסס ובית הכוסות נחשבו כאחת
items.text_en: Resolution: count the spleen and the peritoneum as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Tanna counts the spleen (hemes) and the peritoneum (beit hakosot) as one category, thereby freeing up one slot to include the spine deficiency.
items.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמסס ובית הכוסות, שנחשבו בשתי טריפות, נחשבו ברשימת התנא דבי רבי ישמעאל כאחת, ובכך הוציא אחת והכניס אחת.

sub.desc_en: The gemara answers that the Tanna counted 'hemesess' (the membrane) and 'beit hakosot' (the stomachs) as two separate items in his list, but they are actually one category, so he can remove one and add the missing case of spinal deficiency.

items.text: קושיית גלודה ותירוץ כרבי מאיר
items.text_en: Third challenge: skinless animal (geludah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case of an animal whose skin is removed (geludah), which is not in the list. It answers that the Tanna holds like Rabbi Meir, who deems it kosher.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מגלודה, ומתרצת שהתנא דבי רבי ישמעאל סובר כרבי מאיר שמכשיר גלודה, ולכן אינה טריפה ברשימתו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks about the case of an animal whose skin is peeled off (גלודה), which is not listed, and answers that the Tanna follows Rabbi Meir who considers it kosher.

items.text: קושיית חרותא ומרה
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: perforated gall bladder (charuta) vs. missing gall bladder (marah)
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the case of a perforated gall bladder (charuta). It answers that the Tanna who lists the missing gall bladder (marah) is Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda; the Tanna of Bei Rabbi Yishmael excludes marah and includes charuta instead.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מחרותא, ומתרצת שהתנא דבי רבי ישמעאל מוציא מרה (שנשנית על ידי רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה) ומכניס חרותא במקומה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks about the case of 'charuta' (a perforated gall bladder), and answers that the Tanna who lists 'marah' (the gall bladder) is Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda, so he can remove 'marah' and add 'charuta' instead.

items.text: קושיית שבע שמעתתא ותירוץ
items.text_en: Fifth challenge: seven additional tereifot from amoraim
items.desc_en: The Gemara lists seven tereifot from various amoraim (Rav Matna, Rachish bar Pappa, Rav Avira, Rabbah bar bar Chanah, Rabbah bar Rav Sheila) that are not in the list. It resolves that the Tanna counts the perforations as one category, thereby including these seven.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה משבע הלכות טריפה ששנויות בגמרא, ומתרצת שנקבי תמניא הוו, חשבינהו בחד, אפיק שבע ועייל שבע.

items.text: קושיית פסוקי ותירוץ
items.text_en: Final objection: counting issues and Rav Avira's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Tanna counts the perforations as one, then the list would have only 17, and also Rav Avira's statement about a punctured spleen is itself a perforation, so it should already be included.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם כן, גם הפסוקים (הנקבים) היו שניים, וחשבינהו בחד, ובצר להו חדא. ועוד, דרב עוירא משמיה דרבא נמי נקובה היא.

sub.desc_en: The gemara objects that if so, the categories of 'psukei' (severed organs) are also two, and counting them as one reduces the count by one, and moreover, Rav Avira's ruling about a punctured spleen is itself a perforation, so it is already included.

items.text: Rejection of the two additional cases
items.text_en: Rejection of the two additional cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the two cases previously excluded should not be excluded, implying they are included in the eight categories.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the two previously excluded cases should not be excluded, implying they are included in the eight categories.

items.text: Ulla's statement: Eight categories of treifot
items.text_en: Ulla's statement: Eight categories of treifot
items.desc_en: Ulla states that eight categories of treifot were told to Moses at Sinai: perforated, split, removed, missing, torn, mauled, fallen, and broken. This excludes the case of a wound from a weasel mentioned by Rav Pappa.

sub.desc_en: Ulla states that eight categories of treifot were told to Moses at Sinai: perforated, split, removed, missing, torn, mauled, fallen, and broken.
The gemara notes that this list excludes the case of a wound from a weasel mentioned by Rav Pappa.

items.text: Chiyya bar Rava: Eight subcategories of perforation
items.text_en: Chiyya bar Rava: Eight subcategories of perforation
items.desc_en: Chiyya bar Rava states that there are eight subcategories of treifot within the category of perforation. If one counts nine, it includes the gall bladder according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, who rules that a perforated gall bladder renders the animal treif. A mnemonic is provided.

sub.desc_en: Chiyya bar Rava states that there are eight subcategories of treifot within the category of perforation, and if one counts nine, it includes the gall bladder according to Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.
A baraita is cited: if the abomasum or intestines are perforated it is a tereifa, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that even a perforated gallbladder is a tereifa.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for the following statements: halakhot, friend, olive-bulk, gallbladder, and gizzard.

items.text: Halakha like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Halakha like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda regarding the gall bladder.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda regarding the gall bladder.

items.text: Proof from Job and the miracle argument
items.text_en: Proof from Job and the miracle argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's colleagues challenged him from Job 30:11, but he responded that one does not cite miracles as proof, as Job survived a miracle.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef asks in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: what did Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's colleagues 'remind' him? The verse 'He pours his gall upon the earth' and Job still lives. He answered: we do not mention miracles, for if not for that verse 'He splits my kidneys and does not spare', would he live? But a miracle is different, as it says 'Only guard his soul'. Here too a miracle is different.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda responds that one does not cite miracles as proof, because Job's survival was a miracle, as the verse 'only his life he spared' indicates.

items.text: Halakha like the one who says a kezayit
items.text_en: Halakha like the one who says a kezayit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows the one who says a kezayit (of liver remaining suffices). The Gemara questions this from another statement of Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows an unattributed mishnah, which implies that any remaining liver suffices, even less than a kezayit. The Gemara resolves that these are different amora'im interpreting Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the binding law (הלכה) follows the opinion requiring a kezayit (olive-sized portion) of liver to remain.
The Gemara objects: Did Rabbi Yochanan really say that? He elsewhere ruled that the law follows an unattributed mishnah, which implies that any remaining liver suffices, even less than a kezayit.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: these are different amora'im (Talmudic sages) transmitting conflicting traditions in Rabbi Yochanan's name.

items.text: Two rulings: Gall bladder sealed by liver and gizzard with intact membrane
items.text_en: Two rulings: Gall bladder sealed by liver and gizzard with intact membrane
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan that if the gall bladder was perforated but the liver seals it, the animal is kosher. Similarly, if the gizzard was perforated but its membrane remains intact, it is kosher.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if the gall bladder was perforated but the liver seals it, the animal is kosher.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef further reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that if the gizzard was perforated but its membrane remains intact, the animal is kosher.

items.text: Perforation of the membrane alone and the esophagus
items.text_en: Perforation of the membrane alone and the esophagus
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if the membrane was perforated but the gizzard remains intact, what is the ruling? Rav Nachman says that if one is perforated without the other, it is kosher. Rava adds that the esophagus has two layers: an outer red and inner white; if one is perforated without the other, it is kosher. If they are reversed, it is treif.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the pouch was perforated but the gizzard remains, what? Hear from Rav Nachman: if one was perforated without the other — kosher. Rava says: the esophagus has two skins, outer red and inner white; if one was perforated without the other — kosher. Why mention outer red and inner white? Because if they are swapped — treif.
Rav Nachman rules that if one of the two (membrane or gizzard) is perforated without the other, the animal is kosher.
Rava adds that the esophagus (וושט) has two layers—an outer red and inner white—and if one is perforated without the other, it is kosher.
Rava explains why he specified the colors: if the layers are reversed (outer white, inner red), the animal is treif.

items.text: Perforations not aligned in esophagus vs. gizzard
items.text_en: Perforations not aligned in esophagus vs. gizzard
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if both layers are perforated but not opposite each other, what is the ruling? Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa says: in the esophagus it is kosher, in the gizzard it is invalid. Rav Ashi objects, arguing the opposite due to the esophagus's movement. Rav Acha bar Yosef tells Rav Ashi that Mar Zutra's tradition actually supports his view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if both were perforated but not opposite each other, what? Mar Zutra says in the name of Rav Papa: in the esophagus — kosher, in the gizzard — invalid. Rav Ashi objects: on the contrary, the esophagus where food passes and expands, it swallows and stretches, sometimes they touch each other; the gizzard sits and rests, as it stands! Rav Acha bar Yosef tells Rav Ashi: we say in the name of Mar Zutra, who says in the name of Rav Papa like you.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa rules: in the esophagus it is kosher (כשר), in the gizzard it is invalid (פסול).

Rav Ashi objects, arguing the opposite: the esophagus, which expands and contracts during eating, may cause the perforations to align, so it should be invalid; the gizzard, which is stationary, should be kosher.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Yosef to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef tells Rav Ashi that the tradition from Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa actually supports Rav Ashi's view (i.e., the opposite of what was initially reported).

items.text: Rabbah's rulings on the esophagus
items.text_en: Rabbah's rulings on the esophagus
items.desc_en: Rabbah states that a membrane that forms over a wound in the esophagus is not considered a valid membrane. He also says that the esophagus cannot be inspected from the outside, only from the inside. The Gemara asks what practical difference this makes.

sub.desc_en: Rabba says: a membrane that rises from a wound in the esophagus is not a [true] membrane. Rabba says: the esophagus has no external inspection, only internal. What is the practical difference?
Rabbah rules that the esophagus (וושט) cannot be inspected from the outside (מבחוץ) for perforations, but only from the inside (בפנים).
The Gemara asks what practical difference (למאי נפקא מינה) these rulings make, implying that the halachic implications need clarification.

items.text: Case of a doubtful drusah
items.text_en: Case of a doubtful drusah
items.desc_en: A case of a doubtful drusah came before Rabbah. He initially examined the esophagus from the outside, but Abaye objected that the esophagus can only be examined from the inside. Rabbah then turned it over and found two drops of blood, declaring the animal a tereifah. The Gemara explains that Rabbah only did this to sharpen Abaye's understanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a doubtful drusah (predator attack).
Abaye objects that Rabbah himself taught that the esophagus can only be examined from the inside.
Rabbah turns the esophagus over, finds two drops of blood, and declares the animal a tereifah.
The Gemara explains that Rabbah only did this to sharpen Abaye's understanding.

items.text: Ulla's ruling on a thorn in the esophagus
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling on a thorn in the esophagus
items.desc_en: Ulla states that if a thorn lodged in the esophagus, we do not worry that it healed (and caused a tereifah). This is a standalone ruling.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules that if a thorn lodged in the esophagus, we do not suspect that it healed (and caused a tereifah).

items.text: Mnemonic sign
items.text_en: Mnemonic sign
items.desc_en: A mnemonic sign is provided: 'Darash ḥatikhot be-sakin teme'ah' (He cut pieces with a contaminated knife). This is a memory aid for the following discussions.

sub.desc_en: A mnemonic sign is provided: 'Darash ḥatikhot be-sakin teme'ah' (He cut pieces with a contaminated knife), serving as a memory aid for the following discussions.

items.text: Distinguishing Ulla's ruling from other cases
items.text_en: Distinguishing Ulla's ruling from other cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Ulla's ruling: why is a thorn different from a doubtful drusah? Ulla holds we do not worry about doubtful drusah. The Gemara then compares to cases of two pieces (one forbidden fat, one permitted), a defective knife, and doubtful impurity in a private domain. It concludes that the law of doubtful impurity is a tradition from Sotah, not comparable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Ulla's ruling about a thorn is different from the case of a doubtful drusah (a predator's attack).
The Gemara answers that Ulla holds we do not worry about a doubtful drusah.
The Gemara asks why Ulla's case is different from the case of two pieces, one of forbidden fat (חלב) and one of permitted fat (שומן).
The Gemara answers that there, the prohibition was established (a חזקה of prohibition exists).
The Gemara asks why Ulla's case is different from the case of one who slaughters with a knife and it is found to be defective.
The Gemara answers that there, a defect was born in the knife (a ריעותא was discovered).
The Gemara asks why Ulla's case is different from doubtful impurity in a private domain, where the doubt is ruled impure.
The Gemara objects: according to your reasoning, why not compare it to doubtful impurity in a public domain, where the doubt is ruled pure?
The Gemara resolves that the laws of doubtful impurity are a tradition learned from the Sotah (סוטה) case, and are not comparable to the present case.

items.text: Clarification of Ulla's statement: 'yashev' vs. 'nimtse'
items.text_en: Clarification of Ulla's statement: 'yashev' vs. 'nimtse'
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi stated that Ulla said 'nimtse' (found), implying that if a thorn merely sat, we worry. Rav Kahana corrected him: Ulla said 'yashev' (sat), and 'nimtse' was unnecessary because all wild animals eat thorns.

sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi sitting before Rav Kahana mistakenly states that Ulla said 'נִמְצֵאת' (found), implying that if a thorn merely sat, we worry.
Rav Kahana corrects him: Ulla said 'יָשַׁב' (sat), and 'נִמְצֵאת' was unnecessary because all wild animals eat thorns.

items.text: Dispute about the esophageal collar (turbaẓ ha-veshet)
items.text_en: Dispute about the esophageal collar (turbaẓ ha-veshet)
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the required amount for slaughter in the esophageal collar: Rav says any amount (since it is a place of slaughter), Shmuel says the majority (since it is not a place of slaughter). The Gemara then defines the collar: according to one version, it is the part that expands when cut; according to another, it is the part that stays in place. The actual esophagus is the part that contracts. Yona said it is the 'mavla'ata' (the swallowing part), and Rav Avya gave its size as less than a barley grain but larger than a wheat grain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav holds the esophageal collar requires any amount (משהו) for valid slaughter, Shmuel holds it requires the majority (רובו), and explains their reasoning.
The Gemara asks for the definition of the esophageal collar (תורבץ הוושט).

sub.text: Mari bar Mar Ukva citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Mari bar Mar Ukva citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Mari bar Mar Ukva reports in Shmuel's name: the part that expands when cut is the collar, the part that stays in place is the esophagus itself.
Rav Pappi objects that the master (Shmuel) did not say that, and identifies the correct source as Rav Beivai bar Abaye.

sub.text: Corrected definition from Rav Beivai bar Abaye
sub.text_en: Corrected definition from Rav Beivai bar Abaye
sub.desc_en: The corrected definition: the part that stays in place when cut is the collar, and the part that contracts is the esophagus itself.
Yona reports in Zeira's name that the collar is called 'mavla'ata' (the swallowing part).
Rav Avya gives the size of the collar: less than a barley grain but larger than a wheat grain.

items.text: Case of an ox slaughtered in the collar and esophagus
items.text_en: Case of an ox slaughtered in the collar and esophagus
items.desc_en: An ox belonging to the sons of Rav Ukva had slaughter begun in the collar and completed in the esophagus. Rava declared it a tereifah by applying both Rav's and Shmuel's stringencies. The matter later came before Rabbi Abba, who ruled the ox is permitted according to both Rav and Shmuel, and ordered the son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama to pay for the ox.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case of an ox belonging to the sons of Rav Ukva, where slaughter began in the collar (תורבץ הוושט) and was completed in the esophagus.
Rava declares that he applies both Rav's and Shmuel's stringencies to the case and rules the ox a tereifah.
The matter later comes before Rabbi Abba, who rules the ox is permitted according to both Rav and Shmuel, and orders the son of Rav Yosef bar Ḥama to pay for the ox.

items.text: Mar bar Ravina's objection to Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Mar bar Ravina's objection to Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina raises an objection against Rava's ruling, citing the principle that one may follow either Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel, but not the leniencies of both. He implies Rava's combination of stringencies was improper.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina objects to Rava's ruling, citing the principle that one may follow either Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel, but combining the leniencies of both makes one a wicked person (רשע).

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah's ruling on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah's ruling on Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah that allows one to follow either Beit Shammai or Beit Hillel in their stringencies and leniencies, and resolves it by distinguishing between before and after the Bat Kol, or by attributing it to Rabbi Yehoshua who disregards the Bat Kol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's contradiction: it first states the law follows Beit Hillel, then allows one to follow Beit Shammai's stringencies and leniencies.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the Bat Kol (heavenly voice) that declared Beit Hillel's view authoritative.
Alternatively, even after the Bat Kol, the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehoshua who disregards the Bat Kol.

items.text: Rav Tavut's statement and Rav's ruling on the veshet
items.text_en: Rav Tavut's statement and Rav's ruling on the veshet
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous resolution is still difficult, and Rav Tavut cites Rav's ruling that the veshet has a fixed measure, implying that the תורבץ הוושט is not a valid place for shechita, yet the Mishnah permits it with a minimal amount.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous resolution is still difficult.

Rav Tavut cites Rav's ruling that the וושט (esophagus) has a fixed measure, implying that the תורבץ הוושט (esophageal extension) is not a valid place for shechita, yet the Mishnah permits it with a minimal amount.

items.text: Defining the upper and lower limits of the veshet
items.text_en: Defining the upper and lower limits of the veshet
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman defines the upper limit as the hand's grip and the lower limit as the point where hair begins to grow. The Gemara questions this based on a statement by Ravina about a handbreadth near the crop, and resolves it by distinguishing between a cow and other animals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: up to where (above) is the limit of the veshet?
Rav Nachman defines the upper limit as the hand's grip (the point where the hand grasps the veshet).
The Gemara asks: down to where (below) is the limit of the veshet?

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuha's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha defines the lower limit as the point where hair begins to grow.

sub.text: Gemara's objection based on Ravina's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection based on Ravina's statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Ravina said in the name of Geniva citing Rav that a handbreadth in the veshet near the crop is considered the inner crop, implying the veshet extends further down than the hair point.
The Gemara rejects the objection: if that were the case, one would be slaughtering in the crop itself, which is invalid.
The Gemara resolves: read the statement as 'a handbreadth in the crop near the veshet is the inner crop', not in the veshet itself.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves: Rav's statement about the handbreadth applies to a cow, which has more hair (so the hair point is lower).

items.text: The law of a removed or loosened esophagus
items.text_en: The law of a removed or loosened esophagus
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that if the entire תורבץ הוושט is removed from the jaw, the animal is kosher, supported by a Tanna. Rav Pappa objects due to the roots of the simanim, and the Gemara distinguishes between cases of complete removal and loosening, and between folding and separation.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that if the entire תורבץ הוושט (esophagus flange) is removed from the jaw, the animal is kosher, and a supporting baraita adds that if the lower jaw itself is removed, the animal is also kosher.
Rav Pappa objects: when the entire esophagus is removed, the roots of the סימנים (shechita organs) are also removed, which should render the animal a neveila.
The Gemara asks: according to Rav Pappa, the baraita that says removal of the lower jaw is kosher is also problematic, since the roots of the simanim would be removed.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita about the lower jaw is not a problem for Rav Pappa because it refers to a case where the jaw was merely folded over the simanim (איגום איגומי) rather than completely removed (עקור עקורי); but for Shmuel's ruling about the esophagus, the difficulty remains.
The Gemara emends Shmuel's ruling: do not say 'the entire esophagus flange,' but rather 'most of it' (רובו), so that the roots of the simanim remain attached.
Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Shmuel's own ruling that if most of the simanim are loosened (נדלדלו), the animal is treif, contradicting the emended version.

sub.text: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi's distinction
sub.text_en: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi's distinction
sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha brei d'Rav Idi resolves the contradiction: the case of loosening (נדלדלו) refers to folding (איקפל איקפולי) where the siman is bent but still attached, whereas the case of removal (ניטל) refers to complete separation (אפרוק אפרוקי), which is more severe.

items.text: The measure of a broken gullet
items.text_en: The measure of a broken gullet
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to discuss the law of a broken gullet (פסוקת הגרגרת), citing a Tanna that its measure is the majority, and Rav begins to define how much that majority is.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna states that the measure of a broken gullet (פסוקת הגרגרת) is its majority (רובה).
The Gemara asks how much that majority (רובה) is.
Rav begins to define the measure of the majority, but the text cuts off here.

items.text: The dispute between Rav and Rabba bar bar Chana on the criterion for a kosher trachea
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav and Rabba bar bar Chana on the criterion for a kosher trachea
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a severed trachea came before Rav, who examined it by the majority of its thickness (רוב עוביה). Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged him, saying he should have used the majority of the cavity (רוב חללה). Rav then sent it to Rabba bar bar Chana, who examined it by the majority of the cavity and declared it kosher, and then bought meat from the animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: whether the criterion for a kosher trachea is the majority of its thickness (רוב עוביה) or the majority of its cavity (רוב חללה).

The Gemara recounts the case: a severed trachea came before Rav, who examined it by the majority of its thickness; Rav Kahana and Rav Assi challenged him, so Rav sent it to Rabba bar bar Chana, who examined it by the majority of the cavity, declared it kosher, and bought meat from the animal.

items.text: Question on Rabba bar bar Chana's action: contradicting a colleague's ruling
items.text_en: Question on Rabba bar bar Chana's action: contradicting a colleague's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabba bar bar Chana could permit what Rav had examined, citing a baraita that a sage who declares something impure or forbidden cannot be overruled by a colleague. The Gemara answers that Rav did not actually forbid it definitively, so Rabba bar bar Chana was not contradicting him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabba bar bar Chana could rule after Rav, given the principle that a sage who declares something forbidden cannot be overridden by a colleague.
The Gemara cites a baraita that a sage who declares something impure or forbidden cannot be overridden by a colleague.
The Gemara answers that this case is different because Rav did not definitively forbid the animal.

items.text: Question on Rabba bar bar Chana eating from the animal he permitted
items.text_en: Question on Rabba bar bar Chana eating from the animal he permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabba bar bar Chana could eat from the animal after he had ruled on it, citing the verse where Ezekiel says he never ate from an animal on which a sage had ruled. The Gemara explains that this refers to a case where the sage relied on his own reasoning, but Rabba bar bar Chana relied on tradition (אגמריה סמך).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabba bar bar Chana could eat from the animal after a sage had ruled on it, citing the verse where Ezekiel says he never ate meat from an animal about which a sage ruled.

The Gemara interprets the verse: 'my soul was not defiled' means no improper thoughts, 'neveila and treifa I did not eat' means no meat from a 'kos kos' animal, and 'pigul meat' means no meat from an animal about which a sage ruled; Rabbi Natan adds it means no meat from an animal whose priestly gifts were not separated.
The Gemara resolves that the prohibition applies only when the sage relied on his own reasoning, but Rabba bar bar Chana relied on tradition (אגמריה סמך), so it was permitted for him to eat.

items.text: Distinction between reasoning and tradition
items.text_en: Distinction between reasoning and tradition
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the prohibition against eating from an animal one ruled on applies only when the ruling is based on personal reasoning (סברא), but Rabba bar bar Chana relied on a tradition (אגמריה), so it was permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse applies only to matters dependent on reasoning, but Rabba bar bar Chana relied on the tradition (גמרא) he received.

items.text: Concern of suspicion (חשדא) and the distinction regarding purchase
items.text_en: Concern of suspicion (חשדא) and the distinction regarding purchase
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern of suspicion: even if it is halakhically permitted, one should avoid the appearance of impropriety. It answers that this concern applies only when the item is sold based on the sage's reputation, but here the meat was sold by weight (מתקלא מוכח), so there is no suspicion. The Gemara supports this with a story about Rabba and the daughter of Rav Chisda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern of suspicion (חשדא) based on a baraita that teaches one should distance from impropriety.
The Gemara answers that the concern applies only when sold by reputation, but here the meat was sold by weight (מתקלא מוכח), and supports this with a story about Rabba and the daughter of Rav Chisda.

items.text: Distinction between firstborn and treifa regarding suspicion
items.text_en: Distinction between firstborn and treifa regarding suspicion
items.desc_en: Rabba explains to Bat Rav Chisda that a firstborn (בכור) is sold based on its reputation, so a sage should not buy from it, but a treifa is sold by weight, so there is no suspicion. He dismisses the concern of a superior butcher, as he always buys from the best butcher.

sub.desc_en: Rabba explains that the concern of suspicion applies to a firstborn (בכור) sold by reputation, but a treifa is sold by weight, so there is no suspicion.
Rabba dismisses the concern of a superior butcher, stating he always buys from the best butcher.

items.text: Rav Chisda's definitions of a Torah scholar and the reward for self-reliance
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's definitions of a Torah scholar and the reward for self-reliance
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda defines a Torah scholar as one who examines a treifa for himself, and applies the verse 'he who hates gifts will live' to such a person. Mar Zutra adds that one who reads, reviews, examines a treifa for himself, and serves Torah scholars is blessed. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Zeira exemplify different attitudes toward gifts from the Nasi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda defines a Torah scholar as one who examines a treifa for himself.
Rav Chisda applies the verse 'he who hates gifts will live' to one who examines a treifa for himself.
Mar Zutra adds that one who reads, reviews, examines a treifa for himself, and serves Torah scholars is blessed.
Rav Zevid explains that such a person inherits both this world and the World to Come.
Rabbi Elazar refuses gifts and invitations from the Nasi's house, citing the verse about hating gifts.
Rabbi Zeira refuses gifts but accepts invitations from the Nasi's house.

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier statement about the trachea being honored is merely figurative, not halachic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the earlier statement about the trachea being honored is merely figurative, not halachic.

items.text: Combining perforations in the trachea
items.text_en: Combining perforations in the trachea
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says that perforations in the wing of the trachea combine to constitute a majority. Rav Yirmeya objects based on a baraita about skull perforations, but the Gemara deflects by citing Rav's own statement that perforations with loss combine for an issar, without loss for a majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that perforations in the wing of the trachea combine to constitute a majority (רוב).

Rav Yirmeya objects from a baraita about skull perforations: since the measure is a מלא מקדח (full drill-hole), perforations combine only for that measure; similarly here, since the measure is an איסר (issar coin), they should combine only for an issar, not for a majority.

The Gemara deflects Rav Yirmeya's objection by citing Rav's own statement (via Rabbi Chelbo and Rav Chama bar Gurya) that perforations with loss (חסרון) combine for an issar, but those without loss combine for a majority (רוב).

items.text: Strip removed from the trachea
items.text_en: Strip removed from the trachea
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana says that a strip removed from the trachea combines for an issar. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani asks about a perforation in the wing, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers with the same principle.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana said Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a strip removed from it joins to an issar.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about the law regarding a perforation in the wing of the trachea.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answers by citing the general principle: perforations with missing tissue combine to an issar, while those without missing tissue combine to a majority (רוב).

items.text: Perforation in a bird's trachea
items.text_en: Perforation in a bird's trachea
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a bird. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani explains that Rabbi Elazar said to fold the wing and place it over the trachea; if it covers most of the trachea, it is treifa. Rav Pappa gives a mnemonic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the law regarding a perforation in a bird's trachea?
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani reports that Rabbi Elazar said: fold the wing and place it over the trachea; if it covers most of the trachea, the bird is treifa; otherwise, it is kosher.
Rav Pappa provides a mnemonic: the wing is like a sieve (נפיא) that covers the trachea.

items.text: Trachea crushed like a door or split
items.text_en: Trachea crushed like a door or split
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman says a crushed trachea is treifa if an issar enters its width. Rav says if split, even one ring above and below remains, it is kosher. Rabbi Yochanan objects to Rav's wording, saying even a little above and below suffices. He praises the Babylonians for their explanation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a trachea crushed like a door is a treifa (טריפה) if an issar coin can enter its width.
Rav rules that if the trachea is split, even if only one ring remains above and one below, the animal is kosher (כשרה).
Rabbi Yochanan objects to Rav's wording, questioning the need to specify a full ring, and suggests that even a minimal amount above and below suffices.
Rabbi Yochanan corrects Rav's statement, ruling that even a minimal amount above and below suffices for the animal to be kosher.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's praise of the Babylonians
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's praise of the Babylonians
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan praises the Babylonian scholars for explaining the matter with this reasoning, after hearing that Rabbi Yonatan had taught the same correction.

items.text: Boundaries of the neck for slaughter
items.text_en: Boundaries of the neck for slaughter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef teaches that the entire neck is valid for slaughter, from the large ring to the lower lung wings. Rava clarifies that the lower wing is actually the upper one, meaning the part that extends when the animal stretches its neck, provided it is not forced.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman: if it is flattened like a door, the measure is that an issar can enter its width.
Rava clarifies that the 'lower wing' is actually the upper one, meaning the part that extends when the animal stretches its neck, provided it is not forced.

items.text: Forced slaughter and perforation below the chest
items.text_en: Forced slaughter and perforation below the chest
items.desc_en: Rav Chanina asks about an animal that forces itself; the question remains unresolved. Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish conclude that if the simanim were forced and then slaughtered, it is invalid. A perforation of the trachea below the chest is judged like a lung.

sub.desc_en: Rav: if it is cracked, even if only one ring remains above and one below — kosher.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's conclusion
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's conclusion
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish conclude that if the simanim were forced and then slaughtered, it is invalid; a perforation of the trachea below the chest is judged like a lung.

items.text: Definition of the chest
items.text_en: Definition of the chest
items.desc_en: The Sages define the chest as the part facing the ground, from below the neck to above the stomach, and describe how to cut it for the priestly gift.

sub.desc_en: They said before Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yonatan thus; he said to them: do the Babylonian colleagues know to explain this reasoning?

items.text: Perforation of the brain membrane and related laws
items.text_en: Perforation of the brain membrane and related laws
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel debate whether the outer membrane alone suffices for treifa, or only if both are perforated. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani gives a mnemonic. Rabba bar bar Chana says it is recognizable in the eggs. Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi says the brain is judged as brain until it begins to extend, then as spinal cord, and Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani describes the start of extension.

sub.desc_en: Introduces the case of a perforated brain membrane as a treifa condition.
Rav and Shmuel both rule that perforation of the outer membrane alone renders the animal a treifa, even if the inner membrane is intact.
An opposing view holds that the animal is treifa only if both membranes are perforated.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani provides a mnemonic: the outer membrane is like the animal's skin that holds the brain, implying it alone suffices for treifa.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the corresponding membrane in eggs is recognizable, supporting the distinction between outer and inner membranes.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi states in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi citing Bar Kappara that the brain is judged as brain as long as it is within the skull cavity.
Once the brain begins to extend into the spinal column, it is judged by the laws of the spinal cord.
The gemara asks from where the extension of the brain begins.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi described the start of the extension as being like two [threads].

items.text: Opening Mishnah: The poles on the pot
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: The poles on the pot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that beans placed on the rim of a pot have an uncertain status: those inside are considered inside, those outside are considered outside, and the beans themselves are uncertain, but the prevailing assumption is that they are considered inside.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for beans placed on the rim of a pot: those inside are considered inside, those outside outside, and the beans themselves are uncertain but the prevailing assumption is that they are considered inside.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's test on a bird
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's test on a bird
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya examined a bird and found two bean-like structures on the opening of the pot (the heart), confirming the Mishnah's analogy.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya examined a bird and found two bean-like structures on the opening of the heart, confirming the Mishnah's analogy.

items.text: The heart's chamber: large or small?
items.text_en: The heart's chamber: large or small?
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether the heart's chamber (chalal) refers to a small or large cavity. Abaye challenges the question, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says 'until it is perforated into the sinuses' and Rav's statement that it means the large sinus. The Gemara then distinguishes between the two cases: there it is 'into the sinuses' (all of them), here it is 'into its chamber' – so what difference does it make?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks whether the heart's chamber (חלל) refers to a small cavity or a large one.
Abaye challenges the question, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says 'until it is perforated into the sinuses' and Rav's interpretation that it means the large sinus.
The Gemara distinguishes the cases: there it says 'into the sinuses' (all of them), here it says 'into its chamber' – so the question of large vs. small chamber remains unresolved.

items.text: The cane of the heart: Rav and Shmuel dispute
items.text_en: The cane of the heart: Rav and Shmuel dispute
items.desc_en: Rav says the cane of the heart (kaneh halev) is treif with any perforation, while Shmuel says only with a majority. The Gemara then identifies the cane as the fat on the sides of the lungs, correcting an initial misunderstanding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav rules that a perforation of the cane of the heart (קנה הלב) renders the animal treif even with the slightest hole, while Shmuel requires a majority.
The Gemara asks: What exactly is the cane of the heart?
Rabbah bar Yitzchak in the name of Rav identifies it as the fat on the sides (דפנות).
The Gemara objects: Can one really say 'sides' (דפנות) without further specification?
The Gemara corrects: Rather, it is the fat on the sides of the lungs (דופני ריאה).

items.text: Three canes: dispute and rejection
items.text_en: Three canes: dispute and rejection
items.desc_en: Ameimar in the name of Rav Nachman states there are three canes: one to the heart, one to the lungs, one to the liver. The lung's cane is like the lung, the liver's like the liver, and the heart's is disputed. Mar bar Chiya reverses the rulings. Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef reports Rav's statement to Shmuel, who dismisses Rav's knowledge of treifot.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar reports Rav Nachman's statement that there are three canes (to heart, lungs, liver), with the lung's cane like the lung, the liver's like the liver, and the heart's disputed.
Mar bar Chiya reverses the rulings: the lung's cane is like the liver, the liver's like the lung, and the heart's remains disputed.
Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef reports Rav's statement to Shmuel, who dismisses Rav as knowing nothing about טריפות (treifot).

items.text: The spinal cord: breakage and majority
items.text_en: The spinal cord: breakage and majority
items.desc_en: The Tannaim dispute: Rabbi says the spinal cord is treif if most of its thread is broken, Rabbi Yaakov says even if perforated. Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Yaakov, but Rav Huna says the halakha is not like Rabbi Yaakov. The Gemara then debates whether 'most' means most of the skin or most of the marrow, concluding with a practical test by Rav Nathan bar Avin.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute: Rabbi rules that the spinal cord (חוט השדרה) is treif if most of its thread is broken, while Rabbi Yaakov rules even if it is merely perforated.
Rabbi ruled in practice like Rabbi Yaakov, but Rav Huna declares that the הלכה (binding law) is not like Rabbi Yaakov.
The Gemara asks: what constitutes 'most' (רוב) — most of the outer skin (עור) or most of the inner marrow (מוח)?
The Gemara notes that according to the opinion requiring most of the marrow, most of the skin is certainly included, but the reverse is not necessarily true.
A supporting statement: Nivli reports that Rav Huna explicitly ruled that 'most' means most of the skin, and the marrow is irrelevant.

sub.text: Practical test (Rav Nathan bar Avin before Rav)
sub.text_en: Practical test (Rav Nathan bar Avin before Rav)
sub.desc_en: Rav Nathan bar Avin, sitting before Rav, tested both the skin and the marrow, and Rav confirmed that if most of the skin remains intact, the marrow is irrelevant.

items.text: Crushed and dissolved spinal cord
items.text_en: Crushed and dissolved spinal cord
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a crushed (nitmarech) or dissolved (nitmasmes) spinal cord is invalid. The Gemara defines these terms and discusses a case of 'nitmazmez' (shaken), concluding that it is kosher unless dissolved, despite a contradictory baraita and a story about Levi.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that a crushed (נתמרך) or dissolved (נתמסמס) spinal cord is invalid, and defines the terms: crushing is when it pours like a pitcher, dissolving is when it cannot stand upright.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether the dissolving definition applies if the cord cannot stand only because of its weight (i.e., it is heavy but not truly dissolved).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).
Bei Rav rules that a dissolved cord (נתמסמס) is invalid, but a shaken one (נתמזמז) is kosher.
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar rules that an animal whose brain was shaken (נתמזמז) is a טריפה (non-kosher), contradicting Bei Rav's leniency.
The Gemara rejects the objection, asserting that the baraita actually referred to a dissolved (נתמסמס) brain, not a shaken one.
The Gemara objects further from a story where Levi saw a man whose head was struck and declared that his shaken brain (נתמזמז) would not survive, implying that shaking is fatal.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that Levi's statement meant the man would be infertile (אינו מוליד), not that he would die, so shaking does not render the animal a טריפה.

items.text: Extent of the spinal cord
