sub.desc_en: The stam explains that Ravina rejects Rav Acha bar Yaakov's version and teaches Amemar's statement in a different formulation: eggs of a doubtful tereifah are left to see if the hen lays again.
Rav Ashi objects to Amemar from the Mishnah that the egg of a tereifah is forbidden because it grew in prohibition.
Amemar answers that the Mishnah refers to the first egg, and when Rav Ashi objects that the text says 'גָּדְלָה' (grew) rather than 'גָּמְרָה' (completed), Amemar emends the text to read 'גָּמְרָה'.

items.text: Alternative explanation of the dispute and final ruling
items.text_en: Alternative explanation of the dispute and final ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: the dispute is about a tereifah that became pregnant and then was tereifah, based on whether the fetus is considered a limb of the mother. The Gemara again explains why the dispute is about the altar. It concludes that they agree the first egg is forbidden because it is part of the mother's body. The halakhah is stated for a male (12 months) and female (until she gives birth).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the baraita regarding the offspring of a tereifah, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about sacrificing it on the altar.

The Gemara explains that the dispute is about a case where the mother became pregnant and then was tereifah, with Rabbi Eliezer holding that the fetus is like the mother's thigh and Rabbi Yehoshua holding it is not.
The Gemara objects that if so, they should have disputed whether it is permitted to an ordinary person rather than about the altar.
The Gemara answers that the dispute is about the altar to show the power of Rabbi Yehoshua's lenient opinion, as it is preferable to emphasize leniency.
The Gemara concludes that they agree the first egg of a tereifah is forbidden because it is part of the mother's body.
The Gemara states the halakhah: for a male animal of uncertain tereifah status, it is prohibited for twelve months; for a female, until she gives birth.

items.text: Rav Huna's principle and Rav Pappa's inference
items.text_en: Rav Huna's principle and Rav Pappa's inference
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that any creature without a bone does not survive twelve months. Rav Pappa infers from this that Shmuel's ruling about a gourd that became wormy in its stalk is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna states that any creature without a bone does not survive twelve months.
Rav Pappa infers from Rav Huna's principle that Shmuel's ruling about a gourd that became wormy in its stalk is forbidden.

items.text: Dates stored in a jar and the lifespan of a gnat
items.text_en: Dates stored in a jar and the lifespan of a gnat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses dates stored in a jar that become permissible after twelve months. Rav states that a gnat does not live a year, and a bee does not live a year. Rav Pappa questions this based on folk sayings, and Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the sayings refer to years of their own kind.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a ruling that dates stored in a jar are permitted after twelve months.
Rav states that a gnat does not live a year and a bee does not live a year.
Rav Pappa questions Rav's statement by citing a folk saying that a gnat lived seven years.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the folk sayings refer to years of the gnat's own kind, not human years.

items.text: Animal with extra or missing limbs
items.text_en: Animal with extra or missing limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about an animal with five or three legs being considered blemished. Rav Huna adds that if the extra or missing limb is a leg, the animal is also a tereifah, because any extra limb is considered as if it were removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that an animal with five or three legs is considered blemished.
Rav Huna rules that the Mishnah's leniency applies only to missing or extra forelegs, but missing or extra hind legs render the animal a tereifah.
Rav Huna explains the rationale: any extra limb is considered as if it were removed, thus the animal lacks a proper leg and is a tereifah.

items.text: Animal with two spleens
items.text_en: Animal with two spleens
items.desc_en: A case is brought of an animal with two spleens, and Ravina declared it a tereifah based on Rav Huna's principle. However, if the two spleens are attached to each other, the animal is kosher.

sub.desc_en: A case is introduced of an animal that had two spleens, brought before Ravina.
Ravina declared the animal a tereifah based on Rav Huna's principle that any extra limb is considered as if removed.
The gemara adds a qualification: if the two spleens are attached to each other, the animal is kosher.

items.text: Two cases of a protrusion from the rumen to the abomasum
items.text_en: Two cases of a protrusion from the rumen to the abomasum
items.desc_en: Two cases are presented: one where a protrusion goes from the rumen (בית הכוסות) to the abomasum (הובלילא), and another where it goes from the rumen to the stomach (כרסא). In the first case, Rav Ashi thought to declare it a tereifah, but Rav Huna Mar bar Chiyya told him that all wild animals have this. In the second case, Mar bar Rav Ashi thought to permit it, but Rav Oshaya objected, saying that not all cases are the same.

sub.desc_en: A case is presented of a protrusion from the rumen (בית הכוסות) to the abomasum (הובלילא), and Rav Ashi considered declaring the animal a tereifah.
Rav Huna Mar bar Chiyya told Rav Ashi that all wild animals have this protrusion, so it is not a tereifah.
A second case is presented of a protrusion from the rumen (בית הכוסות) to the stomach (כרסא), and Mar bar Rav Ashi considered permitting it.
Rav Oshaya objected, arguing that not all cases are the same, and the ruling in the first case does not apply here.

items.text: Testimony of Nathan bar Sheila about two intestines
items.text_en: Testimony of Nathan bar Sheila about two intestines
items.desc_en: Nathan bar Sheila testified before Rabbi about two intestines emerging from an animal together, which is a tereifah, but in a bird it is kosher. This applies only if they emerge from two places; if from one place and they taper to a finger's breadth, it is kosher. Rav Ami and Rav Asi dispute whether the intestines must rejoin and intertwine, or even if they do not. The Gemara explains the phrase 'up to a finger's breadth' according to each opinion.

sub.desc_en: Nathan bar Sheila testified before Rabbi about two intestines emerging together from an animal (a tereifah) and from a bird (kosher), with the condition that if they emerge from one place and taper to a finger's breadth, it is kosher.
The Gemara notes that Rav Ami and Rav Asi dispute the meaning of the testimony: one says the intestines must rejoin and intertwine, and the other says even if they do not.

The Gemara resolves the phrase 'up to a finger's breadth' according to each opinion: for the one requiring rejoining, it refers to the tapering; for the other, it means the intestines are measured from below.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael on feathers
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael on feathers
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says that if the feather (נוצה) is removed, the bird is invalid (as a tereifah). Rabbi Yochanan says that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael said the same thing. Rava objects, arguing that Rabbi Yehuda's statement about treifah is specific to that context, while Rabbi Yishmael's statement about feathers joining (for the purpose of covering the blood) is different.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda rules that if the feather (נוצה) is removed, the bird is invalid as a tereifah.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael said the same thing, citing Rabbi Yishmael's ruling that the feather joins (for covering blood).

Rava objects that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on tereifah is specific to that context (where the feather provides no protection), while Rabbi Yishmael's ruling about feathers joining is for covering blood, and in the context of tereifah the feather does not protect.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on animals that ingested harmful substances
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on animals that ingested harmful substances
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists conditions that do not render an animal a tereifah, such as blood congestion, smoke inhalation, etc. However, if it ate poison or was bitten by a snake, it is prohibited due to danger. The Gemara brings a baraita that includes additional substances like asafoetida (חלתית), and a contradiction arises. The Gemara resolves the contradictions by distinguishing between leaves and pills, and between animal poison and human poison. It also identifies the identity of תיע.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists conditions that do not render an animal a tereifah, and those that render it forbidden due to danger.
Shmuel rules that if an animal was fed asafoetida (חלתית), it is a tereifah because it perforates its intestines.
Rav Sheizvi cites a baraita that lists asafoetida (חלתית) among permissible substances, contradicting Shmuel's ruling, and also notes a contradiction regarding the poison (סם המוות).

The Gemara resolves the contradictions: the baraita refers to asafoetida leaves, while Shmuel refers to pills; the poison that is permitted is animal poison, while the forbidden one is human poison, and the poison of an animal is the same as הרדופני (oleander).
The Gemara asks what the substance 'תיע' (tia) mentioned in the baraita is.
Rav Yehuda begins to answer the question about the identity of 'תיע'.

items.text: Medical warnings about eating asafetida
items.text_en: Medical warnings about eating asafetida
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda warns that eating three shekels of asafetida on an empty stomach will strip one's skin. Rabbi Avahu recounts his own experience of eating one shekel and needing to soak in water to avoid skin loss, citing the verse 'Wisdom preserves the life of its possessor.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of asafetida (חילתית).
Rav Yehuda warns that eating three shekels of asafetida on an empty stomach will strip one's skin.
Rabbi Avahu recounts his own experience of eating one shekel of asafetida and needing to soak in water to avoid skin loss, citing the verse 'Wisdom preserves the life of its possessor.'

items.text: Warning about eating specific foods in summer
items.text_en: Warning about eating specific foods in summer
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef warns that eating sixteen eggs, four nuts, seven flying insects, and drinking a quarter-log of honey during the summer solstice on an empty stomach will uproot one's heart.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef warns that eating sixteen eggs, four nuts, seven flying insects, and drinking a quarter-log of honey during the summer solstice on an empty stomach will uproot one's heart.

items.text: Story of a deer and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Story of a deer and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: A deer with severed hind legs came to the house of the Exilarch. Rav examined the sciatic nerve and declared it kosher. He intended to eat it with rennet, but Shmuel warned about potential perforation. Rav suggested placing it in the oven to test itself, but it fell apart. Shmuel quoted 'No harm befalls the righteous' about Rav, and Rav quoted 'All secrets are revealed to you' about Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: A deer with severed hind legs came to the Exilarch's house; Rav examined the sciatic nerve and declared it kosher.
Rav intended to eat the deer with rennet, but Shmuel questioned whether he was concerned about potential perforation.
Rav suggested placing the deer in the oven to test itself, but it fell apart into pieces.

sub.text: Shmuel and Rav's exchange of verses
sub.text_en: Shmuel and Rav's exchange of verses
sub.desc_en: Shmuel quoted 'No harm befalls the righteous' about Rav, and Rav quoted 'All secrets are revealed to you' about Shmuel.

items.text: Mishnah: Signs of kosher animals, birds, locusts, and fish
items.text_en: Mishnah: Signs of kosher animals, birds, locusts, and fish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that signs for kosher mammals are from the Torah, but for birds they were given by the Sages: any bird that is a predator is impure; one with an extra toe, a crop, and a gizzard that can be peeled is pure. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok says a bird that spreads its feet is impure. For locusts, signs include four legs, four wings, jumping legs, and wings covering most of the body; Rabbi Yose adds that its name must be 'grasshopper.' For fish, signs are fins and scales; Rabbi Yehuda says two scales and one fin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that signs for kosher mammals are from the Torah, but for birds they were given by the Sages: any bird that is a predator is impure; one with an extra toe, a crop, and a gizzard that can be peeled is pure.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok adds that a bird that spreads its feet is impure.
The Mishnah lists signs for kosher locusts: four legs, four wings, jumping legs, and wings covering most of the body.
Rabbi Yose adds that the locust's name must be 'grasshopper.'
The Mishnah states signs for kosher fish: fins and scales; Rabbi Yehuda specifies two scales and one fin, and defines scales as fixed to the fish and fins as those with which it swims.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the signs of a kosher mammal
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the signs of a kosher mammal
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: any animal that chews its cud and has no upper teeth is pure. The Gemara objects with the camel, which chews cud but is impure, but notes the camel has incisors. It further objects with a young camel, the hyrax, and the hare, which have upper teeth yet are impure. The Gemara then reinterprets: any animal without upper teeth certainly chews cud and has split hooves and is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing the signs of a kosher mammal: any animal that chews its cud certainly has no upper teeth and is pure.
The Gemara objects: the camel chews its cud and has no upper teeth, yet it is impure; the Gemara answers that the camel has incisors.
The Gemara objects further: a young camel has no incisors yet is impure, and the hyrax and hare have upper teeth yet are impure.
The Gemara questions whether upper teeth are even mentioned in the Torah as a sign.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that any animal without upper teeth certainly chews its cud and has split hooves and is pure.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking the mouth when hooves are cut
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking the mouth when hooves are cut
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules: if one finds an animal with cut hooves, check its mouth; if no upper teeth, it is pure, provided one can distinguish a camel (which has incisors) or a young camel. The Gemara objects that there might be another species similar to a young camel, but the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the Torah singled out the camel with 'hu' to indicate no other cud-chewing impure animal exists.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not check the hooves (rather than the mouth)?

The Gemara answers: the case is where the hooves are cut off, and cites Rav Chisda's ruling that one checks the mouth; if no upper teeth, it is pure, provided one can distinguish a camel or a young camel.
The Gemara objects: just as there is a young camel, there might be another species similar to a young camel.
The Gemara rejects the objection: it cannot enter the mind that there is another such species.

sub.text: Supporting baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the Torah singled out the camel with the word 'hu' to indicate that no other cud-chewing impure animal exists.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking hooves when the mouth is damaged
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking hooves when the mouth is damaged
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules: if one finds an animal with a damaged mouth, check its hooves; if they are split, it is pure, provided one can distinguish a pig. The Gemara objects about a species similar to a pig, but the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the Torah singled out the pig with 'hu' to indicate no other split-hoofed impure animal exists.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules: if one finds an animal with a damaged mouth, check its hooves; if split, it is pure, provided one can distinguish a pig.
The Gemara objects: even if one can distinguish a pig, there might be another species similar to a pig.
The Gemara rejects the objection, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the Torah singled out the pig with 'hu' to indicate no other split-hoofed impure animal exists.

items.text: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking the flesh when both mouth and hooves are damaged
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's ruling: checking the flesh when both mouth and hooves are damaged
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules: if both mouth and hooves are damaged, check the flesh; if it grows in a crisscross pattern, it is pure, provided one can distinguish the arvad (a type of animal). The Gemara asks about a similar species, but it is established that none exists. Abaye or Rav Chisda says to check the wings of the tail.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that if one finds an animal in the desert with damaged mouth and hooves, one checks the flesh for a crisscross pattern to determine purity, provided one can distinguish the arvad (a type of animal).
The Gemara questions whether there might be another species similar to the arvad that could cause confusion.
The Gemara answers that it is established tradition that no such similar species exists.
The Gemara asks where on the animal one should check for the crisscross pattern.
Abaye, or alternatively Rav Chisda, answers that one checks the wings of the tail.

items.text: Introduction to signs of a chaya (undomesticated animal)
items.text_en: Introduction to signs of a chaya (undomesticated animal)
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins discussing the signs of a chaya, questioning whether it is included in the category of behemah for signs, and Rabbi Zeira begins to address this.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma opens by stating that the signs of a chaya (undomesticated animal) are taught in a baraita.
The Gemara questions whether a chaya is included in the category of behemah (domesticated animal) for the purpose of these signs.
Rabbi Zeira begins to address the question, though his full response is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Dosa's statement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Dosa's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the signs of a chaya whose fat is permitted are having horns and hooves. Rabbi Dosa adds that if it has horns, you need not check for hooves, but if it has hooves, you must check for horns, and the keresh is permitted even with only one horn.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule: the signs of a חיה (non-domesticated kosher animal) whose חלב (forbidden fat) is permitted are having horns and hooves.

Rabbi Dosa adds that horns are the primary sign: if it has horns, hooves are not needed, but if it has hooves, horns must be checked; the קרש (keresh, a type of deer) is permitted even with only one horn.

items.text: Gemara's refinement of the horn criteria
items.text_en: Gemara's refinement of the horn criteria
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the general rule is sufficient, noting that a goat has horns and hooves but its fat is forbidden. It refines the criteria: horns must be layered (כרוכות), then grooved (חרוקות), then split (מפוצלות), and finally hollow (חדורות). The conclusion is that if the horn is split, no further check is needed; if not, it must have all the other features and the grooves must be absorbed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the general rule by pointing to a goat (עֵז), which has horns and hooves but its fat is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the horns must be layered (כְּרוּכוֹת).
The Gemara objects that an ox (שׁוֹר) has layered horns yet its fat is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the horns must also be grooved (חֲרוּקוֹת).
The Gemara objects that a goat has grooved horns yet its fat is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that the horns must be split (מְפוּצָּלוֹת).
The Gemara objects that a deer (צְבִי) has unsplit horns yet its fat is permitted.
The Gemara answers that the horns must be hollow (חֲדוּרוֹת).
The Gemara concludes that if the horn is split, no further check is needed; if not, it must have all the other features and the grooves must be absorbed.

items.text: The case of the goat with a karkuz and the ruling
items.text_en: The case of the goat with a karkuz and the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a specific case of a goat with a karkuz (a type of horn) in the house of the Exilarch, from which a basket of fat was extracted. Rav Achai forbade it, while Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu ate it, citing a verse. A ruling was sent from the academy that the halakha follows Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu, but caution is advised regarding Rav Achai, who is a great scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a goat with a karkuz (a type of horn) in the Exilarch's house, from which a basket of fat was extracted.
Rav Achai forbade eating the fat from this goat.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu's ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu ate from the fat, citing the verse 'From the fruit of a man's mouth his belly is satisfied' (Proverbs 18:20).
The academy sent a ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Avahu, but they cautioned to be careful regarding Rav Achai, who is a great scholar (מאיר עיני גולה).

items.text: Description of the keresh and the lion of Bei Ila'i
items.text_en: Description of the keresh and the lion of Bei Ila'i
items.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the keresh, citing Rav Yehuda that the keresh is the mountain goat of Bei Ila'i, and the lion of Bei Ila'i is its tiger. Rav Kahana and Rav Yosef describe the immense size of the lion and the goat, with distances between its ears and the thickness of its hide.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara returns to the keresh, restating that it is permitted even with only one horn.
Rav Yehuda identifies the keresh as the mountain goat of Bei Ila'i and the lion of Bei Ila'i as its tiger.
Rav Kahana describes the immense size of the lion of Bei Ila'i, stating that the distance between its ears is nine cubits.
Rav Yosef adds that the hide of the mountain goat of Bei Ila'i is sixteen cubits thick.

items.text: The emperor's questions about God and the lion
items.text_en: The emperor's questions about God and the lion
items.desc_en: The emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya about God being compared to a lion, and requests to see the lion of Bei Ila'i. Rabbi Yehoshua prays, and the lion is uprooted from its place. Its roars cause destruction, and the emperor begs for it to be returned. The emperor then asks to see God, and Rabbi Yehoshua explains he cannot.

sub.desc_en: The emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya why God is compared to a lion, since a cavalryman can kill a lion.
Rabbi Yehoshua explains that God is compared to the lion of Bei Ila'i, not an ordinary lion.
The emperor asks to see the lion; Rabbi Yehoshua says he cannot see it.
The emperor insists he wants to see it; Rabbi Yehoshua prays and the lion is uprooted from its place.
When the lion is 400 parasangs away, it roars, causing miscarriages and the collapse of the wall of Rome.
When the lion is 300 parasangs away, it roars again, causing teeth to fall out and the emperor to fall from his throne.
The emperor begs Rabbi Yehoshua to pray that the lion return to its place.
Rabbi Yehoshua prays and the lion returns to its place.
The emperor asks to see God; Rabbi Yehoshua says he cannot see Him.
The emperor insists he wants to see God.

items.text: Story of the emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya about seeing the sun and feeding God
items.text_en: Story of the emperor and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya about seeing the sun and feeding God
items.desc_en: The emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua to look at the sun, and when he cannot, Rabbi Yehoshua argues that if one cannot look at a servant of God, how much less can one see the Shechinah. Then the emperor asks to feed God, and Rabbi Yehoshua tells him to go to the riverbank and try to feed a large fish, but the fish is swept away by wind and drowned by rain, showing the impossibility.

sub.desc_en: The emperor positions Rabbi Yehoshua facing the sun and asks him to look; Rabbi Yehoshua cannot, and argues that if one cannot look at the sun, a servant of God, one certainly cannot see the Shechinah (Divine Presence).

The emperor asks Rabbi Yehoshua to feed bread to God; Rabbi Yehoshua tells him to go to the riverbank and try to feed a large fish, but the fish is swept away by wind and drowned by rain, showing the impossibility.

items.text: Story of the emperor's daughter and the carpenter God
items.text_en: Story of the emperor's daughter and the carpenter God
items.desc_en: The emperor's daughter mocks that God is a carpenter, and asks Rabbi Yehoshua to have God make her a spindle. Rabbi Yehoshua prays, and she is afflicted with leprosy. She is placed in the Roman market where lepers receive spindles, and she sits there unraveling spindles. Later, Rabbi Yehoshua passes by and comments on the spindle, leading to a retort from her.

sub.desc_en: The emperor's daughter mocks that God is a carpenter and asks Rabbi Yehoshua to have God make her a spindle.
Rabbi Yehoshua agrees, prays for her, and she is afflicted with leprosy.
She is placed in the Roman market where lepers receive spindles, so that people will see her and pray for her.
Rabbi Yehoshua passes by, comments on the spindle, and she retorts; he responds that God gives but does not take back.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching on ox and donkey characteristics
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching on ox and donkey characteristics
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that an ox has a large head and large tail, while a donkey has the opposite; this distinction is relevant for buying and selling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches that an ox has a large head and large tail, while a donkey has the opposite, and this distinction is relevant for buying and selling.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching on the ox of Adam: single horn and precedence of horns
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching on the ox of Adam: single horn and precedence of horns
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches that Adam's first offering had a single horn on its forehead, as derived from the verse 'מקרין מפריס', which is read as 'מקרן' (singular). He also teaches that its horns preceded its hooves, as the verse lists 'מקרין' before 'מפריס'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda teaches that Adam's first offering had a single horn on its forehead, citing the verse 'מקרין מפריס', and the gemara notes that 'מקרין' implies two horns.
Rav Nachman resolves the difficulty by explaining that the verse is read as 'מקרן' (singular), indicating a single horn.
Rav Yehuda further teaches that the horns of Adam's offering preceded its hooves, as the verse lists 'מקרין' before 'מפריס'.

items.text: Support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: all creation was created fully formed
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: all creation was created fully formed
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rav Yehuda's teaching supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who said that all creation was created in its full stature, with its full knowledge, and with its full desire, as derived from the verse 'ויכלו השמים והארץ וכל צבאם' read as 'צביונם'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Yehuda's teaching as support for Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's statement that all creation was created fully formed, with full knowledge and full desire, derived from the verse 'ויכלו' read as 'צביונם'.

items.text: Derasha of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa: the grasses' kal vachomer and the angel's praise
items.text_en: Derasha of Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa: the grasses' kal vachomer and the angel's praise
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa teaches that the verse 'יהי כבוד ה' לעולם' was said by the angel Sar HaOlam. When God commanded 'למינהו' for trees, the grasses reasoned: if God wants order, why did He command it for trees? And if trees, which do not naturally grow mixed, were commanded 'למינהו', how much more so should we grasses grow in our own species. Immediately each grass grew in its own species, and Sar HaOlam praised God.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa teaches that the verse 'יהי כבוד ה' לעולם' was said by the angel Sar HaOlam when God commanded 'למינהו' for trees, and the grasses drew an a fortiori inference.

The grasses reason: if God wanted mixing, why command 'למינהו' for trees? And if trees, which do not naturally mix, were commanded 'למינהו', how much more so should we grasses grow in our own species.
Immediately each grass grew in its own species, and Sar HaOlam praised God with the verse 'יהי כבוד ה' לעולם'.

items.text: Ravina's question about grafting two grasses
items.text_en: Ravina's question about grafting two grasses
items.desc_en: Ravina asks a question about grafting two grasses together, which is left unresolved.

sub.desc_en: Ravina raises a question about the status of grafting two species of grass together, which is left unresolved.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's view
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's opinion: since the phrase 'to their kinds' is not written regarding certain items, is one exempt, or because they agreed with their hands, is it considered as if 'to their kinds' is written? The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question about Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa's view: since the phrase 'to their kinds' is not written regarding certain items, is one exempt, or because they agreed with their hands, is it considered as if 'to their kinds' is written?

items.text: The moon's complaint and diminishment
items.text_en: The moon's complaint and diminishment
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi notes a contradiction between verses about the great lights. The moon complains to God that two kings cannot share one crown. God tells the moon to diminish itself. Despite the moon's protests, God offers compensations: ruling by day and night, Israel counting days and years by it, and righteous people being called 'small'. God then commands a sin-offering for Himself for diminishing the moon, as Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains regarding the goat of the New Moon.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi raises a contradiction between two verses about the great lights, and the moon complains to God that two kings cannot share one crown, so God tells the moon to diminish itself.

The moon objects that it is unfair to diminish itself after making a valid argument, and God offers various compensations, including ruling by day and night, Israel counting days and years by it, and righteous people being named after it as 'small'.

sub.text: God's atonement and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's teaching
sub.text_en: God's atonement and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's teaching
sub.desc_en: Seeing the moon was not appeased, God commands a sin-offering for Himself for diminishing the moon, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains that the goat-offering of the New Moon is an atonement for God's act.
The moon protests that since its argument was valid, it should not be punished by diminishment.
God offers the moon rule by day and night, but the moon rejects this as useless like a lamp in daylight.
God offers that Israel will count days and years by the moon, but the moon counters that days are also counted by the sun through seasons.
God offers that righteous people will be called by the moon's name 'small', citing examples like Jacob the small, Samuel the small, and David the small.
Seeing the moon still not appeased, God commands a sin-offering for Himself for diminishing the moon, which Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains is the goat of the New Moon.

items.text: Creation of vegetation and the power of prayer
items.text_en: Creation of vegetation and the power of prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi notes a contradiction between verses about vegetation emerging on the third day and not yet being in the field on the sixth day. This teaches that the plants stood at the ground's opening until Adam prayed for rain, showing that God desires the prayers of the righteous. Rabbi Nachman bar Pappa's personal experience confirms this teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi raises a contradiction between the verse that vegetation emerged on the third day and the verse that no shrub was yet in the field on the sixth day, and resolves that the plants stood at the ground's opening until Adam prayed for rain.

sub.text: Rabbi Nachman bar Pappa's personal story
sub.text_en: Rabbi Nachman bar Pappa's personal story
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Nachman bar Pappa confirms Rabbi Asi's teaching through his own experience: he planted seeds in his garden, they did not grow until he prayed, and rain came.

items.text: The shasuah as a unique creature
items.text_en: The shasuah as a unique creature
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan bar Rava states that the shasuah is a unique creature with two backs and two spines. He questions whether Moses was a hunter or a taxidermist, concluding that this provides a refutation to those who deny the Torah's divine origin. Rav Chisda instructs Rav Tachlifa bar Avina to write 'hunter and taxidermist' in his aggadah and explain it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanan bar Rava states that the shasuah is a unique creature with two backs and two spines.

sub.text: Rabbi Chanan bar Rava's rhetorical question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chanan bar Rava's rhetorical question
sub.desc_en: He rhetorically asks whether Moses was a hunter or a taxidermist, implying that Moses could not have known of such a creature without divine revelation.
He concludes that this provides a refutation to those who deny the Torah's divine origin.
Rav Chisda instructs Rav Tachlifa bar Avina to write 'hunter and taxidermist' in his aggadah and explain it.

items.text: The five lords of the Philistines and the Avvim
items.text_en: The five lords of the Philistines and the Avvim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the verse lists five lords of the Philistines but then mentions six names. Rabbi Yonatan explains that 'Avvim' refers to their satraps, which are five. Rav Chisda instructs Rav Tachlifa to write 'satraps' and explain. This disagrees with Rav, who says the Avvim came from Teman. A baraisa supports Rav, explaining the name 'Avvim' in three ways, and Rav Yosef adds that each has sixteen rows of teeth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: the verse lists five lords of the Philistines but then enumerates six names.
Rabbi Yonatan resolves the contradiction by explaining that the sixth name, 'Avvim', refers to their satraps, which are five.
Rav Chisda instructs Rav Tachlifa to write 'satraps' in his aggadic notebook and explain it.
The Gemara notes that this disagrees with Rav, who says the Avvim came from Teman, implying they are a separate people, not satraps.
A baraisa supports Rav, explaining the name 'Avvim' in three ways: they distorted their place, they desired many gods, or they caused a twisting sensation in viewers.
Rav Yosef adds that each of the Avvim has sixteen rows of teeth.

items.text: Seemingly superfluous verses as essential Torah
items.text_en: Seemingly superfluous verses as essential Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish states that many verses that seem fit for burning are actually essential parts of the Torah. He questions the purpose of the verse about the Avvim dwelling in villages up to Gaza. The Gemara explains that it teaches about God's plan: the Caphtorim would come from the Avvim (the Philistines), and Israel would come from the Caphtorim. Similarly, the verse about Heshbon teaches that Sihon would come from Moab, and Israel from Sihon, as Rav Pappa says that Ammon and Moab were purified through Sihon.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish opens by stating that many verses that seem fit for burning like heretical books are actually essential parts of the Torah.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish questions the purpose of the verse about the Avvim dwelling in villages up to Gaza.
The Gemara explains that the verse teaches about God's plan: the Caphtorim (Philistines) would come from the Avvim, and Israel would come from the Caphtorim, based on Avimelech's oath to Abraham.
The Gemara provides a parallel example: the verse about Heshbon teaches that Sihon would come from Moab, and Israel from Sihon, explaining the prohibition against attacking Moab.
Rav Pappa states that Ammon and Moab were purified through Sihon, meaning their land became permitted to Israel after Sihon conquered it.

items.text: The mountains of Israel and the cities of refuge
items.text_en: The mountains of Israel and the cities of refuge
items.desc_en: A baraisa teaches that the Sidonians called Hermon 'Siryon', and that each nation built a great city named after the mountains of Israel, showing the nations' love for the land. Similarly, the verse about transferring the people to cities teaches that one should not call exile upon one's brothers.

sub.desc_en: The baraisa teaches that the Sidonians called Hermon 'Siryon', and that every nation built a great city named after the mountains of Israel, showing the nations' love for the land.
The Gemara brings a parallel teaching from the verse about transferring the people to cities, demonstrating that one should not call exile upon one's brothers.

items.text: Beginning of bird signs discussion
items.text_en: Beginning of bird signs discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether bird signs were not stated, citing a baraisa that begins with the eagle, indicating that the topic of bird signs is about to be discussed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the signs of birds were not stated, and cites a baraita that contradicts this.

items.text: Mishnah and Abaye's comment
items.text_en: Mishnah and Abaye's comment
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the signs of a kosher bird: an extra toe, a crop, a gizzard that can be peeled, and not being a predator. Abaye notes that these signs are not from the Torah but from the Scribes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four signs of a kosher bird (extra toe, crop, peelable gizzard, non-predator) and states that any bird matching the eagle's lack of signs is טמא (impure), while any matching the dove's possession of all four is טהור (pure).
Abaye comments that the detailed identification of these signs is not from the Torah itself but from the Scribes (דברי סופרים).

items.text: Rabbi Chiya's teaching: one sign suffices
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya's teaching: one sign suffices
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches that a bird with even one sign is kosher, because it does not resemble the eagle, which has no signs. The Gemara infers that if a bird has one sign, it may be eaten.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches that a bird with even one sign is kosher, because it does not resemble the eagle.
The Gemara infers that since the eagle lacks all signs and is forbidden, any bird with even one sign is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question: learn from doves?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: learn from doves?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not learn from doves, which require all four signs, that all birds need all four signs?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we should not learn from doves, which require all four signs, that all birds require all four signs.

items.text: First answer: other unclean birds
items.text_en: First answer: other unclean birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: if so, why did the Torah list other unclean birds? That would be superfluous if all birds needed four signs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that if all birds required four signs, the Torah's listing of other unclean birds would be superfluous.

items.text: Second question: learn from both?
items.text_en: Second question: learn from both?
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes: learn from both the eagle and doves, that three signs are forbidden, and certainly two or one?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes to learn from both the eagle and doves that three signs render a bird forbidden, and certainly two or one sign would also be forbidden.

items.text: Second answer: raven superfluous
items.text_en: Second answer: raven superfluous
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers: if so, why did the Torah specify the raven? Now that a bird with three signs is not eaten, one with two signs certainly should not be eaten, making the raven unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the raven is superfluous because if a bird with three signs is not eaten, one with two signs certainly should not be eaten.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why list the eagle if we can learn from the raven?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why list the eagle if we can learn from the raven?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah lists the eagle (nesher) if we could learn from the raven that any bird with two simanim is forbidden; it then argues that if so, the vulture and osprey would be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah lists the eagle (nesher) if we could learn from the raven that any bird with two simanim is forbidden; it then argues that if so, the vulture and osprey would be superfluous.

items.text: Alternative derivation from vulture and osprey
items.text_en: Alternative derivation from vulture and osprey
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers learning from the vulture and osprey that a bird with one siman is forbidden, but then argues that this would make the eagle superfluous; it concludes that the eagle teaches that only a bird with no simanim is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not learn from the vulture and osprey that any bird with one siman is forbidden, which would make the eagle superfluous.
The Gemara resolves that the eagle, which has no simanim, is the only forbidden bird with one siman; any bird with one siman is permitted.

items.text: Defense: Vulture and osprey are two verses that come as one
items.text_en: Defense: Vulture and osprey are two verses that come as one
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without the eagle, one might have learned from the vulture and osprey, but they are two verses that come as one and thus cannot teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that without the eagle, one might learn from the vulture and osprey, but they are two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) and thus cannot teach a general rule.

items.text: Tradition: Each bird has unique simanim
items.text_en: Tradition: Each bird has unique simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that the vulture and osprey each have a siman not found in the other, so they are not truly two verses that come as one; nevertheless, among the 24 non-kosher birds, it is impossible that one siman is not found in the others, making them two verses that come as one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that the vulture and osprey each have a unique siman (identifying sign) not found in the other.

The Gemara concludes that among the 24 non-kosher birds, it is impossible that one siman is not found in the others, making the vulture and osprey two verses that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד), which cannot teach a general rule.

items.text: Detailed tradition: 24 birds and 4 simanim
items.text_en: Detailed tradition: 24 birds and 4 simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates on the tradition: 24 non-kosher birds have 4 simanim; 20 have three each, the raven has two, the vulture and osprey each have one unique siman; the eagle teaches that only a bird with no simanim is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition that among the 24 forbidden birds, 20 have three simanim, the raven has two, and the vulture and osprey each have one unique siman, so the eagle teaches that only a bird with no simanim is forbidden.
The Gemara elaborates: three simanim are common to all, 20 birds have three each, the raven has two, and the vulture and osprey each have one unique siman.

The Gemara resolves: lest one think to learn from the vulture or osprey, the Torah wrote 'נשר' (eagle) to teach that only a bird with no simanim is forbidden, but one with a single siman is permitted.

items.text: Question: Why list doves (torin)?
items.text_en: Question: Why list doves (torin)?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah lists doves (torin) among kosher birds, and Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that they are for sacrifices; Rav Nachman adds further explanation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah lists doves (torin) if they are already permitted.
Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that doves are listed for the purpose of sacrifices (קרבן).
Rav Nachman begins to offer a further explanation regarding the listing of doves.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Expert vs. non-expert in bird signs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Expert vs. non-expert in bird signs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one is expert in the birds and their names, a bird with one kosher sign is pure; if not, one sign makes it impure, two signs make it pure, provided one recognizes the raven.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for bird purity based on expertise and number of kosher signs, with the condition of recognizing the raven.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rabbi Eliezer's dispute about the raven's species
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rabbi Eliezer's dispute about the raven's species
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's mention of only the raven, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer includes the zarzir (starling) and the white swallow (סנונית לבנה) as species of raven. The Sages object based on local practices, but Rabbi Eliezer insists they will be held accountable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's mention of only the raven, implying that other species should also be included.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Eliezer interprets 'עורב' (raven) to include the zarzir (starling) as a species of raven.
The Sages object to Rabbi Eliezer, noting that people of Kfar Temarta eat the zarzir because it has a crop, indicating it is a kosher bird.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that those who eat the zarzir will be held accountable, asserting his halachic position.
Rabbi Eliezer further interprets 'למינהו' to include the white swallow (סנונית לבנה) as a species of raven.
The Sages object again, citing that people of Upper Galilee eat the white swallow because its gizzard is peelable, indicating it is kosher.
Rabbi Eliezer reiterates that those who eat the white swallow will be held accountable, maintaining his position.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's phrase 'עורב' (raven) includes all species of raven, resolving the challenge.

items.text: Amemar's ruling and discussion with Rav Ashi
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling and discussion with Rav Ashi
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that a bird with one kosher sign is pure, provided it does not prey. Rav Ashi asks about Rav Nachman's view, and Amemar dismisses it. The Gemara notes that the peres and ozniyah are not found in settled areas.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar rules that a bird with one kosher sign is pure, provided it does not prey.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar about the opinion of Rav Nachman on this matter.

Ameimar says he has not heard of Rav Nachman's view, implying he does not accept it, and explains that the concern about the peres and ozniah (osprey and vulture) is irrelevant because they are not found in settled areas.
The Gemara explains that the concern about the peres and ozniyah does not apply because these birds are not found in settled areas.

items.text: Rav Yehuda: The white swallow is kosher for purification of a leper
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda: The white swallow is kosher for purification of a leper
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that the bird that scratches (מסרט) is kosher for the purification of a leper, and this is the white swallow (סנונית לבנה) about which Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages disputed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah states that the bird that scratches (the white swallow) is fit for the purification of a leper, and this is the same bird about which Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages disagreed.

items.text: Amemar and Mar Zutra's dispute about the white swallow's color
items.text_en: Amemar and Mar Zutra's dispute about the white swallow's color
items.desc_en: Amemar says all agree that a white-bellied swallow is permitted; the dispute is about a green-bellied one, with Rabbi Eliezer forbidding and the Rabbis permitting, and the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer. Mar Zutra reverses the positions, saying all agree the green-bellied is forbidden, and the dispute is about the white-bellied, with the halakha following the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Amemar states that all agree a white-bellied swallow is permitted; the dispute is about a green-bellied one, with Rabbi Eliezer forbidding and the Rabbis permitting, and the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Mar Zutra reverses the positions, saying all agree the green-bellied swallow is forbidden, and the dispute is about the white-bellied one, with the halakha following the Rabbis who permit it.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's consistency with the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute's consistency with the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the view that the dispute is about a white-bellied swallow, the Mishnah's phrase 'this is the white swallow' is consistent. According to the view that the dispute is about a green-bellied one, the phrase excludes a black-bellied swallow.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to the version where the dispute is over a white-bellied swallow, the phrase 'white swallow' fits, but according to the version where the dispute is over a green-bellied swallow, the phrase 'white swallow' excludes the house swallow (which is black).
The Gemara asks: according to the view that the dispute is about a green-bellied swallow, what does the Mishnah's phrase 'this is the white swallow' mean?
The Gemara answers: the phrase excludes a black-bellied swallow.

items.text: Rachbah's ruling on the tassil bird and its status
items.text_en: Rachbah's ruling on the tassil bird and its status
items.desc_en: Rachbah quotes Rabbi Yehuda that the tassil bird is invalid due to doves but valid due to pigeons, and the birds of Rachbah are valid due to doves and invalid due to pigeons. Rav Daniel bar Rav Katina raises an objection.

sub.desc_en: Rachbah quotes Rabbi Yehudah that the תסיל (a bird) is invalid due to doves but valid due to pigeons, and the אציפי and doves of Rachbah are valid due to doves and invalid due to pigeons.

sub.text: Rav Daniel bar Rav Kattina's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Daniel bar Rav Kattina's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Daniel bar Rav Kattina raises an objection beginning with 'all birds' (the text is cut off).

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists doves separately from other birds that disqualify purification water, and Rabbi Zeira explains the difference between sucking and regurgitating.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on certain birds and the objection
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on certain birds and the objection
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda declares certain birds (כּוּפְשָׁנֵי צוּצְיָינֵי) fit for the altar, but a baraita objects with a list of invalid hyssop types. Abaye and Rava resolve the contradiction by distinguishing name changes before the Torah and local naming conventions.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's rulings on other birds
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's rulings on other birds
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules on the permissibility of certain birds (כְּרָזֵי דְּבֵי חִילְפֵי, צְרָדָא, בַּרְדָּא, מַרְדָּא), with Ravina adding that lashes are given for one of them due to the prohibition of a creeping bird.

items.text: Rav Asi's list of eight doubtful birds and the test
items.text_en: Rav Asi's list of eight doubtful birds and the test
items.desc_en: Rav Asi lists eight birds of doubtful kosher status, explaining that their crops peel only with a knife, unlike kosher birds whose crops peel by hand. The Gemara contrasts this with a goose of Shmuel's household whose crop peeled after being softened in the sun.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Pappa on the marsh rooster
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Pappa on the marsh rooster
items.desc_en: Abaye identifies the marsh rooster as one of the eight doubtful birds (מַרְדּוּ). Rav Pappa distinguishes between the male (forbidden) and female (permitted) marsh rooster, with a sign from Ammonites. Marimar adds that the female is forbidden if seen eating by predation.

items.text: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Pappa on additional birds and signs
items.text_en: Rav, Shmuel, and Rav Pappa on additional birds and signs
items.desc_en: Rav rules on Shabur and Peruz anadarpatta with a sign from the wicked Peruz. Rav Huna rules on Bunya (permitted) and Parva (forbidden) with a sign from a Magus. Rav Pappa distinguishes between bowing and prostrating behavior in the bird Mardu, and Shmuel forbids a bird that drinks wine or mixes wine, with biblical signs.

items.text: Opening statement on the bat mazga bird
items.text_en: Opening statement on the bat mazga bird
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the bat mazga bird, which drinks wine, is permitted, and provides a mnemonic: 'The power of the son is greater than that of the father.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the bat mazga bird, which drinks wine, is permitted, and provides a mnemonic: 'The power of the son is greater than that of the father.'

items.text: Rav Yehuda's classification of birds by color and shape
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's classification of birds by color and shape
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that long-legged, long-necked, and red birds are permitted (mnemonic: murzema), while short-legged, red birds are forbidden (mnemonic: 'nanus pasul'), and long-legged, green birds are forbidden (mnemonic: 'yerukin pesulin').

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda lists permitted and forbidden birds: shkitana, long-legged red ones are permitted; short-legged red ones are forbidden; long-legged green ones are forbidden, each with a mnemonic.
Rav Yehuda rules that short-legged, red birds are forbidden, with the mnemonic 'nanus pasul'.
Rav Yehuda rules that long-legged, green birds are forbidden, with the mnemonic 'yerukin pesulin'.

items.text: זיהוי שלָךְ ודוכיפת
items.text_en: Etymology of shalakh and duchifat, and Rabbi Yochanan's exclamations
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that 'shalakh' is the bird that draws fish from the sea, and 'duchifat' has its crest doubled (hod kafut). A baraita confirms this, adding that the duchifat brought the shamir worm to the Temple. Rabbi Yochanan, upon seeing a shalakh, would recite a verse about God's judgments in the deep, and upon seeing an ant, a verse about God's righteousness.
items.desc: רב יהודה מזהה את השלָךְ כעוף השולה דגים, ואת הדוכיפת כעוף שהודו כפוי. מובאת אגדה על הדוכיפת שהביא שמיר לבית המקדש, ורבי יוחנן נוהג לומר פסוקים למראה השלָךְ והנמלה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies the shalakh as the bird that draws fish from the sea and the duchifat as the bird with its crest doubled.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מזהה את השלָךְ כעוף השולה דגים ואת הדוכיפת כעוף שהודו כפוי, ומביא ברייתא תומכת המזהה את הדוכיפת כמי שהביאה שמיר לבית המקדש.

sub.desc_en: A baraita confirms the identification of the duchifat and adds that it brought the shamir worm to the Temple.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מזהה את השלָךְ כעוף השולה דגים ואת הדוכיפת כעוף שהודו כפוי, ומביא ברייתא תומכת המזהה את הדוכיפת כמי שהביאה שמיר לבית המקדש.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's exclamation upon seeing a shalakh
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, upon seeing a shalakh, recites a verse about God's judgments in the deep.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן נוהג לומר פסוקים למראה השלָךְ והנמלה, מתוך תפיסה שכל בריה מלמדת על מידותיו של הקב"ה.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's exclamation upon seeing an ant
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, upon seeing an ant, recites a verse about God's righteousness.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן נוהג לומר פסוקים למראה השלָךְ והנמלה, מתוך תפיסה שכל בריה מלמדת על מידותיו של הקב"ה.

items.text: Amemar's ruling on lakni, batni, shaknai, and batnai
items.text_en: Amemar's ruling on lakni, batni, shaknai, and batnai
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that lakni and batni are permitted, while shaknai and batnai depend on local custom. The Gemara questions this, and Amemar resolves that the distinction is based on whether peres and oznia (vulture-like birds) are common in the area.

sub.desc_en: Ameimar rules that lakni and batni are permitted, while shaknai and batnai depend on local custom.
The Gemara questions whether the permissibility of a bird can depend on local custom.
The Gemara answers that the distinction is based on whether the place has peres and oznia birds, which are forbidden and could be confused with the permitted ones.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on kuei, kakoei, and kakoata
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on kuei, kakoei, and kakoata
items.desc_en: Abaye states that kuei and kakoei are forbidden, but kakoata is permitted. In the West, they would flog for eating kakoata, calling it tachvata.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that kuei and kakoei are forbidden, but kakoata is permitted, and in the West they flog for it and call it tachvata.
Abaye adds that in the West they flog for eating kakoata, calling it tachvata.

items.text: Baraitot on tinshemet among birds and creeping things
items.text_en: Baraitot on tinshemet among birds and creeping things
items.desc_en: Two baraitot teach that the word 'tinshemet' refers to a bird in the context of birds (using the hermeneutic principle of context), and to a creeping thing in the context of creeping things.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita teaches that the word 'tinshemet' in the context of birds refers to a bird, using the principle of context (דבר הלמד מעניינו).
A second baraita similarly teaches that 'tinshemet' in the context of creeping things refers to a creeping thing, applying the same hermeneutic principle.

items.text: Identifications of tinshemet, ka'at, racham, and the legend of the racham
items.text_en: Identifications of tinshemet, ka'at, racham, and the legend of the racham
items.desc_en: Abaye identifies the tinshemet among birds as kipof and among creeping things as kurpedai. Rav Yehuda identifies ka'at as kuk and racham as shrakrak. Rabbi Yochanan explains that racham is named for bringing mercy (rachamim) to the world. Rav Beivai bar Abaye adds that it sits on a branch and chirps, and it is tradition that if it sits on the ground and chirps, the Messiah will come. Rav Adda bar Shimi challenges this with a story of a bird that chirped and was killed, but Mar bar Rav Idai responds that bird was a demon.

sub.desc_en: Abaye identifies the tinshemet among birds as kipof and among creeping things as kurpedai.
Rav Yehuda identifies ka'at as kuk and racham as shrakrak.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that the racham is named because when it comes, mercy (רחמים) comes to the world.

Rav Beivai bar Abaye adds that the racham sits on a branch and chirps, and tradition holds that if it sits on the ground and chirps, the Messiah will come, citing the verse 'אשרקה להם ואקבצם' (I will whistle for them and gather them).
Rav Adda bar Shimi objects with a story of a bird that sat on the ground and chirped, and a clod of earth split its skull.
Mar bar Rav Idai resolves that the bird in the story was a demon, not a real racham.

items.text: זיהוי העורב ומיניו
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'orev' and its subspecies
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'orev' refers to the raven, 'et kol orev' includes the valley raven, and 'lemino' includes the raven with a pigeon-like head. The Gemara clarifies that 'orev' is the black raven, 'ha'emki' is the white raven, and 'orev hava berashei yonim' means its head resembles a pigeon's.
items.desc: ברייתא דורשת 'עורב' – עורב שחור, 'כל עורב' – עורב העמקי (לבן), ו'למינו' – עורב הבא בראשי יונים (ראשו דומה ליונה). רב פפא מבהיר שאין הכוונה לעוף הבא עם יונים אלא לדמיון הראש.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines 'עוֹרֵב' as the raven, 'אֶת כׇּל עוֹרֵב' includes the valley raven, and 'לְמִינוֹ' includes the raven with a pigeon-like head.
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק: 'עורב' – עורב סתם, 'כל עורב' – עורב העמקי, 'למינו' – עורב הבא בראשי יונים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the baraita's statement that 'עוֹרֵב' is the raven, asking if it is standing before us (i.e., stating the obvious).
sub.desc: מר מבהיר ש'עורב' הוא עורב שחור, ומסביר ש'עורב העמקי' הוא לבן, על פי היקש לפסוקים.

sub.desc_en: Mar clarifies that 'עוֹרֵב' refers specifically to the black raven, citing the verse 'שְׁחֹרוֹת כָּעוֹרֵב' (black as a raven).
sub.desc: מר מבהיר ש'עורב' הוא עורב שחור, ומסביר ש'עורב העמקי' הוא לבן, על פי היקש לפסוקים.

sub.desc_en: Mar explains that 'הָעִמְקִי' is the white raven, citing the verse 'וּמַרְאֵהוּ עָמֹק מִן הָעוֹר' (its appearance is deeper than skin), comparing it to the sun's depth relative to shadow.
sub.desc: מר מבהיר ש'עורב' הוא עורב שחור, ומסביר ש'עורב העמקי' הוא לבן, על פי היקש לפסוקים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa resolves that 'עוֹרֵב הַבָּא בְּרָאשֵׁי יוֹנִים' does not mean it comes with pigeon heads, but rather its head resembles a pigeon's.
sub.desc: רב פפא מבהיר ש'עורב הבא בראשי יונים' אינו עוף הבא עם יונים אלא ראשו דומה לשל יונה.

items.text: זיהוי הנץ, החסידה והאנפה
items.text_en: Identifications of netz, chasida, and anafah
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that 'netz' is the hawk, and 'leminehu' includes bar chirya, which Abaye identifies as shurinka. Rav Yehuda identifies 'chasida' as the white diyah, named for its kindness (chasidut) with its friends, and 'anafah' as the angry diyah, named for its adultery (menaefet) with its friends.
items.desc: ברייתא מזהה את הנץ כנץ ואת בר חיריא (שורינקא) כמינו. רב יהודה מזהה את החסידה כדיה לבנה (עושה חסד) ואת האנפה כדיה רגזנית (מנאפת).

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by identifying 'netz' as the hawk and adding 'leminehu' to include bar chirya.
sub.desc: ברייתא מזהה את הנץ כנץ ואת בר חיריא כמינו.

sub.desc_en: Abaye identifies bar chirya as shurinka (a type of bird).
sub.desc: ברייתא מזהה את הנץ כנץ ואת בר חיריא כמינו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies 'chasida' as the white diyah, named for its kindness (חסידות) with its friends.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מזהה את החסידה כדיה לבנה ומסביר את שמה בכך שהיא עושה חסד עם חברותיה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda identifies 'anafah' as the angry diyah, named for its adultery (מנאפת) with its friends.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מזהה את החסידה כדיה לבנה ומסביר את שמה בכך שהיא עושה חסד עם חברותיה.

items.text: מניין עשרים וארבעה עופות טמאים
items.text_en: Resolving the count of 24 forbidden birds
items.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda quotes Rav that there are 24 forbidden birds. He challenges this from the lists in Leviticus (20) and Deuteronomy (21). Rav Chisda answers by including the four instances of 'leminehu' etc., but Abaye notes that would make 26. Abaye then resolves that da'ah and ra'ah are the same bird.
items.desc: רב אומר שיש עשרים וארבעה עופות טמאים. רב חנן מקשה על המניין מהכתובים, ורב חסדא מתרץ באמצעות כפל 'למינה' ו'למינהו'. אביי מיישב את החשבון בכך שדאה וראה הם עוף אחד.

sub.text: רב חנן בר רב חסדא משם רב חסדא ורב חנן בר רבא משם רב
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda reports in the name of Rav that there are 24 forbidden birds.
sub.desc: רב חנן בר רב חסדא מוסר בשם רב חסדא ורב חנן בר רבא בשם רב: ישנם עשרים וארבעה עופות טמאים.

sub.text_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda's challenge to Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan bar Rav Chisda challenges Rav Chisda: counting the birds from Leviticus gives 20, from Deuteronomy 21, and even adding the da'ah (דָּאָה) unique to Leviticus yields only 22, not 24.
sub.desc: רב חנן בר רב חסדא מקשה על רב חסדא: מניין העשרים וארבעה? בפרשת ויקרא עשרים, במשנה תורה עשרים ואחד, ואם מוסיפים את הדאה – עשרים ושנים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the four instances of 'לְמִינָהּ' etc. in the Torah add four birds, bringing the total to 24.
sub.desc: רב חנן בר רב חסדא מקשה על רב חסדא: מניין העשרים וארבעה? בפרשת ויקרא עשרים, במשנה תורה עשרים ואחד, ואם מוסיפים את הדאה – עשרים ושנים.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that adding four to 22 would make 26, not 24.
sub.desc: רב חנן בר רב חסדא מקשה על רב חסדא: מניין העשרים וארבעה? בפרשת ויקרא עשרים, במשנה תורה עשרים ואחד, ואם מוסיפים את הדאה – עשרים ושנים.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves that da'ah (דָּאָה) and ra'ah (רָאָה) are the same bird, so the count from the verses is 21 (not 22), and adding the four 'לְמִינָהּ' instances yields 24.
sub.desc: רב חנן בר רב חסדא מקשה על רב חסדא: מניין העשרים וארבעה? בפרשת ויקרא עשרים, במשנה תורה עשרים ואחד, ואם מוסיפים את הדאה – עשרים ושנים.

items.text: Gemara's first inference: ra'ah and da'ah are the same
items.text_en: Gemara's first inference: ra'ah and da'ah are the same
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the Mishneh Torah (Deuteronomy) lists both 'ra'ah' and 'da'ah' while the first listing (Leviticus) only has 'da'ah', this shows they are the same species, otherwise the duplication would be superfluous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara argues that since the Mishneh Torah (Deuteronomy) lists both 'ra'ah' and 'da'ah' while the first listing (Leviticus) only has 'da'ah', this shows they are the same species, otherwise the duplication would be superfluous.

items.text: Abaye's extension: ayah and dayah are also the same
items.text_en: Abaye's extension: ayah and dayah are also the same
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that just as ra'ah and da'ah are one, so too ayah and dayah are one, based on the redundant mention of 'leminehah' for each in the Mishneh Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: but still, that would make twenty-five species, not twenty-four.
Abaye answers: just as ra'ah and da'ah are one, so too ayah and dayah are one, reducing the count to twenty-four.
Abaye proves his claim by noting that if ayah and dayah were distinct, the redundant 'leminehah' for each in Mishneh Torah would be unnecessary.

items.text: Rabbi's explanation for writing both ayah and dayah
items.text_en: Rabbi's explanation for writing both ayah and dayah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both names are written if they are the same, and answers with Rabbi's teaching: to prevent a disputant from claiming a different name, so both are written in the Mishneh Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: since ayah and dayah are the same, why did the Torah write both names?
A baraita of Rabbi explains: both names are written to prevent a disputant from claiming a different species, as in the Mishneh Torah they are listed together.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that birds are repeated because of the ra'ah, implying it is an addition. The Gemara resolves that in animals the repetition adds a species, but in birds it merely explains an existing one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that says the repetitions in animals and birds are for different reasons, implying ra'ah is a separate species.
The Gemara rejects the objection: in animals the repetition adds a species, but in birds it merely clarifies the identity of ra'ah.

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's etymology: ra'ah is ayah
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's etymology: ra'ah is ayah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu explains that ra'ah is the same as ayah, named for its sharp sight, as per a verse, and a tradition says it can see a carcass from Babylon to Israel.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu says that ra'ah is actually ayah, and explains the name ra'ah because it sees exceptionally far, citing a verse and a tradition about its vision.

items.text: Gemara's final deduction: da'ah, ra'ah, ayah, and dayah are all one
items.text_en: Gemara's final deduction: da'ah, ra'ah, ayah, and dayah are all one
items.desc_en: From Rabbi Avahu's statement that ra'ah is ayah, the Gemara infers that da'ah is not ra'ah, but then resolves the contradiction by concluding that da'ah, ra'ah, ayah, and dayah are all the same species, based on the Torah's wording.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that from Rabbi Avahu's statement that ra'ah is ayah, it follows that da'ah is not ra'ah, and questions why the Torah writes 'da'ah' in one place and not in the other.
The Gemara resolves that da'ah, ra'ah, and ayah are all the same species.
The Gemara further notes that from ra'ah being ayah, it follows that dayah is not ayah, and questions why the Torah writes 'לְמִינֵהוּ' on ayah in one place and on dayah in another.
The Gemara concludes that da'ah, ra'ah, dayah, and ayah are all one species.

items.text: Traditions about the number of bird species
items.text_en: Traditions about the number of bird species
items.desc_en: Isi ben Yehudah says there are 100 non-kosher birds in the east, all of the 'ayah' type. Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu adds that there are 700 fish species, 800 locust species, and kosher birds are countless, resolving the apparent contradiction with the 24 listed.

sub.desc_en: A baraita of Isi ben Yehuda states that there are one hundred unclean birds in the East, all of the ayah species.

sub.text: Baraita of Avimi son of Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Baraita of Avimi son of Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu teaches that there are 700 fish species and 800 locust species, and for clean birds there is no number, resolving the apparent contradiction with the twenty-four listed.
Avimi bar Rabbi Avahu continues that there are 800 locust species and kosher birds are countless.
The gemara objects that only 24 bird species are listed in the Torah, contradicting the claim that kosher birds are countless.
The gemara resolves the contradiction by clarifying that the statement refers to kosher birds (עופות טהורים) being countless, not all birds.

items.text: Rabbi's principle and Rav Huna's teaching
items.text_en: Rabbi's principle and Rav Huna's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbi explains that the Torah lists fewer kosher animals (since non-kosher are more numerous) and fewer non-kosher birds (since kosher birds are more numerous). Rav Huna in the name of Rabbi Meir adds that one should always teach concisely.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi explains that the Torah lists fewer kosher animals (since non-kosher are more numerous) and fewer non-kosher birds (since kosher birds are more numerous).

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna citing Rav citing Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Huna citing Rav citing Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi's teaching supports Rav Huna's principle in the name of Rabbi Meir that one should always teach concisely.

items.text: Reliability of tradition for kosher birds
items.text_en: Reliability of tradition for kosher birds
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak says a kosher bird can be eaten based on tradition, and a hunter is trusted if he says his teacher told him it is kosher. Rabbi Yochanan adds that he must be familiar with the birds and their names. Rabbi Zeira questions whether the teacher must be a scholar or a hunter, and concludes from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the teacher must be a hunter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak states that a kosher bird may be eaten based on tradition, and a hunter is trusted if he says his teacher transmitted it to him as kosher.
Rabbi Yochanan adds that the hunter must be familiar with the birds and their names.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether the teacher referred to by Rabbi Yochanan is a scholar or a hunter.
The Gemara resolves from Rabbi Yochanan's statement that the teacher must be a hunter, since only a hunter would be familiar with the birds themselves, not just their names.

items.text: Buying eggs from non-Jews
items.text_en: Buying eggs from non-Jews
items.desc_en: The rabbis teach that eggs can be bought from non-Jews without concern for carcasses or treifot. The Gemara questions if they might be from non-kosher birds, and Shmuel's father answers that it is when the seller specifies it is from a particular kosher bird. The Gemara explains why he doesn't just say 'from a kosher bird'—to prevent evasion.

sub.desc_en: The rabbis teach that eggs may be purchased from non-Jews anywhere without concern for נבלות (carcasses) or טרפות (treifot).
The Gemara questions whether the eggs might come from a non-kosher bird.
Avuh deShmuel answers that the ruling applies when the seller specifies it is from a particular kosher bird.
The Gemara asks why the seller cannot simply say 'from a kosher bird' instead of naming a specific species.
The Gemara explains that if the seller said only 'from a kosher bird,' he could later evade responsibility by claiming he meant a different kosher bird.

items.text: Question about checking signs and the beginning of a new topic
items.text_en: Question about checking signs and the beginning of a new topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not check the eggs by their signs, citing a baraita that egg signs are like fish signs. It then corrects itself regarding fish signs (which are explicitly given by the Torah) and begins to rephrase, but the segment ends mid-argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not check the eggs by their signs (simanim)?
A baraita is cited that the signs of eggs are like the signs of fish, but the Gemara corrects the text to say 'so are the signs of eggs' (not fish).

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on signs of eggs
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Baraita on signs of eggs
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing signs for kosher eggs: rounded shape with one pointed end, albumen outside and yolk inside indicate kosher; the opposite indicates non-kosher; mixed yolk and albumen indicates a reptile egg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing signs for kosher eggs: rounded shape with one pointed end, albumen outside and yolk inside indicate kosher; the opposite indicates non-kosher; mixed yolk and albumen indicates a reptile egg.

items.text: Gemara's question on buying eggs from non-Jews
items.text_en: Gemara's question on buying eggs from non-Jews
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether one can rely on these signs when buying eggs from non-Jews, citing a baraita that prohibits selling a terefah egg to a non-Jew unless it is scrambled in a bowl, and therefore one should not buy scrambled eggs from them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks that since the eggs are scrambled in a bowl, one cannot check the signs of the yolk and white, so how can one buy them from non-Jews?
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that prohibits buying scrambled eggs from non-Jews, since one cannot verify they are not from a טריפה (ritually unfit) bird.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's principle: signs are not Torah law
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's principle: signs are not Torah law
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira argues that these signs are not Torah-mandated (lo de'oraita), citing Rav Assi's list of eight doubtful cases where one cannot rely on egg signs, proving that signs are only rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asserts that the signs for identifying kosher eggs are not Torah law (לאו דאורייתא), but rather rabbinic.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's proof from Rav Assi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's proof from Rav Assi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira supports his claim by citing Rav Assi's list of eight doubtful cases, arguing that if signs were Torah law, one could resolve the doubt by checking the eggs of those animals.

items.text: Practical application of the signs
items.text_en: Practical application of the signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the practical halakha: certain signs (both ends round or pointed, yolk outside) indicate definite impurity; other signs (one round one pointed, albumen outside) allow reliance only if the seller identifies the bird; otherwise, one cannot rely due to similarity to ravens.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: For what practical halakha did the Tanna teach the signs of eggs?

The Gemara answers: The signs are for practical use — certain signs indicate definite impurity, while others allow reliance only if the seller identifies the bird, otherwise one cannot rely due to similarity to ravens.

items.text: Discussion on mixed yolk and albumen
items.text_en: Discussion on mixed yolk and albumen
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the case of mixed yolk and albumen: Rav Ukva bar Chama says it indicates a reptile egg that imparts impurity if it forms a lentil-sized embryo; Ravina objects that it might be a snake egg; Rava says one is liable for eating it as a sheretz. The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies impurity, as even a kosher bird's egg with a developed embryo would be prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's statement that mixed yolk and albumen indicate a reptile egg.
The Gemara asks what practical halachic purpose this identification serves.
Rav Ukva bar Chama answers that if the egg forms a lentil-sized embryo and is punctured, it imparts ritual impurity (טומאה).
Ravina objects that the egg might be from a snake, which is a different category of reptile.
Rava answers that one who eats the egg after it has formed an embryo is liable for violating the prohibition of eating a sheretz (creeping thing).
The Gemara questions why the baraita specifies impurity, since even a kosher bird's egg with an embryo would be prohibited.
The Gemara cites a baraita that extends the prohibition of eating a sheretz to any egg with an embryo, including kosher species.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah's inclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the Mishnah's inclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's inclusion of unhatched chicks whose eyes have not opened is a rabbinic decree, and the verse cited is merely a support.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah's inclusion of unhatched chicks whose eyes have not opened is a rabbinic decree, and the verse is merely a support (אסמכתא בעלמא).

items.text: Baraita on egg blood spots and debate
items.text_en: Baraita on egg blood spots and debate
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited regarding the permissibility of eggs with blood spots, distinguishing between the yolk and the white. Rabbi Yirmeya and Dostat's father offer different opinions, and Rav Geviha reports a version of the baraita that Abaye reconciled.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that egg blood spots (גיעולי ביצים) are permitted, and that a blood spot found on the egg is removed and the rest is eaten.
Rabbi Yirmeya qualifies that the blood spot is only permitted if found on the egg's connecting thread (קשר שלה).
Dostat's father teaches that the baraita's leniency applies only when the blood spot is on the white (חלבון), but if on the yolk (חלמון) the entire egg is forbidden.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Dostat's father's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Dostat's father's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains Dostat's father's reasoning: a yolk blood spot indicates the blood spread throughout the egg, rendering it entirely forbidden.
