Rav Geviha reports to Rav Ashi that a Tanna recited the baraita in reverse order before Abaye, and Abaye reconciled it for him.

items.text: Chizkiyah's scriptural derivation for a non-kosher bird's egg
items.text_en: Chizkiyah's scriptural derivation for a non-kosher bird's egg
items.desc_en: Chizkiyah derives from the verse 'and the daughter of the ostrich' that a non-kosher bird's egg is prohibited by Torah law, interpreting 'daughter' as the egg. He rejects the possibility that 'daughter' is the bird's name, citing another verse.

sub.desc_en: Chizkiyah asks for the scriptural source that a non-kosher bird's egg is prohibited by Torah law.
Chizkiyah interprets the phrase 'בת היענה' (daughter of the ostrich) as referring to the egg, since an ostrich does not have a literal daughter.
The Gemara objects that 'בת היענה' might simply be the bird's name, not a reference to the egg.
Chizkiyah rejects the objection by citing a verse where 'יענים' (ostriches) is used as a name, showing that 'בת היענה' must refer to the egg.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding 'daughters of the ostrich'
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding 'daughters of the ostrich'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing verses where 'daughters of the ostrich' clearly refers to the bird itself, not an egg. It resolves that the verse 'daughter of the ostrich' is written as two separate words, indicating a different meaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing multiple verses where 'בנות יענה' (daughters of the ostrich) clearly refers to the bird itself, not an egg, challenging the identification of 'בת היענה' as an egg.
The Gemara resolves that the verse writes 'בת היענה' as two separate words, indicating a different meaning — the egg — unlike the compound 'בנות יענה' which refers to the bird.

items.text: Final distinction based on scribal division
items.text_en: Final distinction based on scribal division
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the distinction lies in the scribal practice of dividing the phrase into two words in the verse 'daughter of the ostrich', unlike the other instances.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the distinction by noting that the scribe divides the phrase into two words in the verse 'בת היענה' (daughter of the ostrich), unlike other instances where 'בנות יענה' is written as one word.

items.text: Gemara's question about two words and two names
items.text_en: Gemara's question about two words and two names
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a verse split into two words by a scribe indicates two distinct names, using the example of 'את כדר לעמר'. It distinguishes between splitting into two words and splitting into two lines, concluding that here even splitting into two lines is done.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a verse split into two words by a scribe indicates two distinct names.
The Sages respond that the case of 'את כדר לעמר' is split into two words but not two lines, whereas here even splitting into two lines is done.

items.text: Tannaitic sources on bird signs
items.text_en: Tannaitic sources on bird signs
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Sages said 'every bird' (that has certain signs). A baraita is cited with opinions of Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok, and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar on how to determine if a bird is kosher or not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the Sages said 'every bird' (that has certain signs).
A baraita is cited with Rabban Gamliel's opinion that a bird that is a predator is definitely impure, while one with an extra toe, a crop, and a peelable gizzard is definitely pure.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Tzadok says one stretches a string and if the bird divides its legs two on each side it is impure, three on one side and one on the other it is pure.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says any bird that snatches food from the air is impure.

items.text: Abaye's clarification on 'kolte'
items.text_en: Abaye's clarification on 'kolte'
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a certain bird (ציפַּרְתָּא) also catches from the air. Abaye explains that the Sages meant 'kolte ve'ochel' (catches and eats), not just catches.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the bird ציפַּרְתָּא (a certain bird) also catches from the air, challenging the criterion of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.
Abaye explains that the Sages meant 'קוֹלֵט וְאוֹכֵל' (catches and eats), not merely catches, thereby resolving the objection.

items.text: Others' opinion and its support
items.text_en: Others' opinion and its support
items.desc_en: A baraita cites 'Acherim' who say that a bird that dwells with impure birds is impure, and with pure birds is pure. The Gemara asks whose opinion this is, suggesting it follows Rabbi Eliezer, who said that the zarzir (starling) goes with the raven because it is its species. Alternatively, even the Rabbis might agree, as they say 'dwells and resembles'.

sub.desc_en: Acherim state a baraita: a bird that dwells with impure birds is impure, and with pure birds is pure.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this baraita follows.
The Gemara suggests it follows Rabbi Eliezer, who said the zarzir (starling) goes with the raven because it is its species.
Alternatively, even the Rabbis might agree, as they say the criterion is 'dwells and resembles'.

items.text: Definition of 'rov' for locusts
items.text_en: Definition of 'rov' for locusts
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says that for locusts, any that has... etc. The Gemara asks what 'rov' (majority) means. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says: the majority of its length, and some say: the majority of its circumference. Rav Pappa concludes that we require both the majority of its length and the majority of its circumference.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'rov' (majority) means in the Mishnah's rule about locusts.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that 'rov' means the majority of its length.
An alternative tradition states that 'rov' means the majority of its circumference.
Rav Pappa rules that both the majority of its length and the majority of its circumference are required.

items.text: The case of the zachal
items.text_en: The case of the zachal
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches: If a locust does not have legs now but will grow them later, like the zachal, it is permitted. Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei adds a verse. Abaye identifies the zachal as the askera (a type of locust).

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma states that a locust which currently lacks legs but will grow them later, like the zachal, is permitted.
Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Yosei adds a verse (אֲשֶׁר לֹא כְרָעַיִם) to support that even without legs now, if they will grow later, it is permitted.
Abaye identifies the zachal as the askera (a type of locust).

items.text: Identifying the four types of locusts
items.text_en: Identifying the four types of locusts
items.desc_en: A baraita explains the four types of locusts mentioned in the Torah: arbeh is the govai, sal'am is the rashon, chargol is the nippul, and chagav is the nadyan. The four instances of 'lemino' come to include additional species. The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches about general principles and specific details.

sub.desc_en: A baraita identifies the four types of locusts mentioned in the Torah and explains that the four instances of 'lemino' come to include additional species.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches about general principles and specific details in the identification of locusts.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the fourth type of kosher locust: צִיפּוֹרֶת כְּרָמִים.

items.text: Derivation of simanim from the four species
items.text_en: Derivation of simanim from the four species
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives the simanim for kosher locusts from the Torah's four species: אַרְבֶּה, סָלְעָם, חַרְגֹּל, and חָגָב. Each species teaches a specific feature (e.g., גַּבַּחַת, זָנָב, רֹאשׁ אָרוֹךְ), and the common denominator of the first three yields the general rule: four legs, four wings, קַרְצוּלַּיִם, and wings covering most of the body.

items.text: Exclusion of צרצור and requirement of all simanim
items.text_en: Exclusion of צרצור and requirement of all simanim
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the צרצור (a type of locust) has all the physical simanim but is forbidden, because it is not called חָגָב. Conversely, a locust named חָגָב must also have all the simanim, derived from לְמִינֵהוּ.

items.text: Rav Achai's challenge to the derivation
items.text_en: Rav Achai's challenge to the derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Achai challenges the derivation: the three species (אַרְבֶּה, סָלְעָם, חַרְגֹּל) share the common trait of not having a long head, so the rule might be limited. He argues that if they are equal in four simanim, then חַרְגֹּל should also be redundant.

items.text: Counter-challenge and further difficulty
items.text_en: Counter-challenge and further difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara responds that one could similarly challenge: the three species lack a tail, so the derivation is flawed. Rav Achai's point is that the same problem applies to the long head.

items.text: Rav Achai's resolution: סָלְעָם teaches long head
items.text_en: Rav Achai's resolution: סָלְעָם teaches long head
items.desc_en: Rav Achai concludes that סָלְעָם is extraneous (יַתִּירָא) and is written to teach the siman of a long head. Without it, one could derive the rule from אַרְבֶּה and חַרְגֹּל, but the extra species is needed for the long head.

items.text: Dispute between the school of Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Dispute between the school of Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute is about between the school of Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael, and explains that they argue over the interpretation of the verse regarding a locust with a long head. The school of Rav holds that the verse is a general principle and a detail, while the school of Rabbi Yishmael holds it is a general principle, a detail, and a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute is about between the school of Rav and the school of Rabbi Yishmael, and explains that they argue over the interpretation of the verse regarding a locust with a long head.
The school of Rav holds that the verse is a general principle and a detail, so only what is explicitly listed and similar in two aspects is included.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael holds that the verse is a general principle, a detail, and a general principle, so only what is similar to the detail in one aspect is included.

items.text: Clarification of the general principles
items.text_en: Clarification of the general principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difference between the first general principle and the last general principle, explaining that the first general principle refers to having legs, while the last general principle requires all four signs. It then notes that the school of Rabbi Yishmael uses this type of general principles and details, and that this is a known method.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the first general principle (כלל) differs from the last general principle, since they appear contradictory.
The Gemara explains that the first general principle refers to having legs (כרעים), while the last general principle requires all four signs (סימנים) for kosher locusts.
The Gemara notes that the school of Rabbi Yishmael uses this type of general principles and details (כללי ופרטי), and that this method is derived from here.

items.text: Discussion of the locust signs
items.text_en: Discussion of the locust signs
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the statement that if a locust is called 'chagav', it might be thought to not need all the signs, but the verse says 'leminehu' to require all signs. It then asks why the verse mentions 'sal'am' if not to include a long head, and suggests it might include anything, but the verse teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Mar's statement that if a locust is called 'chagav', one might think it does not need all the signs, but the verse says 'leminehu' to require all signs.
The Gemara questions why a locust lacking all signs would even be considered, since the Torah explicitly lists 'arbeh' and 'chargol' as distinct species.
The Gemara explains that without the word 'sal'am', the argument would stand, but since it is written, it comes to include a long head, and the Gemara teaches that it does not include anything else.

items.text: Identification of locust species
items.text_en: Identification of locust species
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why in one place 'sal'am' is identified as 'rashon' and 'chargol' as 'nipul', while in another place the identifications are reversed. It answers that each teacher follows the terminology of his own locale.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the identifications of 'sal'am' and 'chargol' are reversed between two places in the Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that each teacher follows the terminology of his own locale.

items.text: Signs for kosher fish
items.text_en: Signs for kosher fish
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for fish, any that have fins and scales is kosher. The Gemara adds a baraita that if a fish currently lacks scales but will grow them later, it is permitted, and if it has scales but sheds them when leaving the water, it is also permitted, giving examples.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the general rule that any fish with fins and scales is kosher.
The baraita adds that a fish lacking scales now but will grow them later is permitted, and a fish that sheds scales when leaving the water is also permitted, giving examples.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Kosher fish must have fins and scales
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Kosher fish must have fins and scales
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any fish with scales also has fins, but some have fins without scales — those are unclean. The Gemara begins by questioning the necessity of writing both 'fins' and 'scales' in the Torah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists kosher fish and states the rule: any fish with scales has fins, but some have fins without scales—those are unclean.

The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote both 'fins' and 'scales' when only scales are decisive, and answers that without 'fins' one might mistakenly think 'scales' means fins, including unclean fish.
The Gemara asks further: since we now know 'scales' means a covering (as in the verse 'and he wore a coat of scales'), why not write only 'scales' and omit 'fins'?

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Yishmael answer that the Torah wrote both to 'magnify and glorify the Torah' (יגדיל תורה ויאדיר).

items.text: Rabbi Avahu's principle: Torah expands and glorifies
items.text_en: Rabbi Avahu's principle: Torah expands and glorifies
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and the school of Rabbi Ishmael teach that the Torah deliberately expands its language to glorify and magnify the commandments, not to restrict them.

sub.text: Rabbi Avahu and the School of Rabbi Ishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avahu and the School of Rabbi Ishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu and the School of Rabbi Ishmael resolve the question by citing the principle that the Torah expands its language to glorify and magnify the commandments, not to restrict them.

items.text: Tanna's teaching: Dual implication of 'eat what has' and 'do not eat what lacks'
items.text_en: Tanna's teaching: Dual implication of 'eat what has' and 'do not eat what lacks'
items.desc_en: The Tanna derives from the phrasing 'eat what has fins and scales' that one may eat fish with both, and from 'do not eat what lacks' that one may not eat fish lacking either. The redundancy teaches a positive and negative commandment simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna teaches that the Torah's phrasing 'eat what has fins and scales' and 'do not eat what lacks' creates both a positive and negative commandment, so that one who eats a non-kosher fish violates both a positive and a negative command.

items.text: Gemara's inference: 'From all that are in the water' includes vessels
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: 'From all that are in the water' includes vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that the general phrase 'from all that are in the water' (including vessels) would permit eating fish even without fins/scales, contradicting the specific prohibition. It resolves by noting that the specific phrase 'in the seas and in the streams' excludes vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah added the general phrase 'תֹּאכְלוּ מִכֹּל אֲשֶׁר בַּמָּיִם' (you may eat from all that are in the water), since one might have thought that just as the explicit permission (in the specific verse) only permits fish in vessels, so too the general permission only permits fish in vessels.

The Gemara answers that the general phrase comes to include pits, ditches, and caves (בּוֹרוֹת שִׁיחִין וּמְעָרוֹת) as sources of water from which one may drink without concern, teaching that the general phrase expands the permission beyond vessels.

items.text: Clarification: 'In the seas and in the streams' excludes vessels
items.text_en: Clarification: 'In the seas and in the streams' excludes vessels
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the specific phrase 'in the seas and in the streams' applies only to natural water bodies, excluding artificial vessels. Thus, fish in vessels may be eaten even without fins/scales, as the general rule permits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the phrase 'in the seas and in the streams' excludes vessels, so fish without fins or scales caught in vessels are permitted.

items.text: Objection: Vessels with fins/scales should also be prohibited?
items.text_en: Objection: Vessels with fins/scales should also be prohibited?
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: if vessels are included by the general rule, then even fish with fins/scales in vessels should be prohibited, contradicting the specific allowance. The Gemara resolves by noting that the specific phrase 'in the seas and in the streams' only applies to natural habitats, not vessels.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: if vessels are included by the general rule, then even fish with fins/scales in vessels should be prohibited, contradicting the specific allowance. The Gemara resolves by noting that the specific phrase 'in the seas and in the streams' only applies to natural habitats, not vessels.

items.text: General and specific rule: 'In the water' includes all, 'seas/streams' restricts
items.text_en: General and specific rule: 'In the water' includes all, 'seas/streams' restricts
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the hermeneutic principle of 'general and specific' (כלל ופרט). The general 'in the water' includes all water bodies, but the specific 'in the seas and in the streams' restricts to natural flowing waters, excluding standing waters like pits and cisterns.

sub.desc_en: Proposes applying the hermeneutic principle of 'general and specific' (כלל ופרט): the general phrase 'in the water' included all, then 'in the seas and in the streams' narrowed it, implying only natural flowing waters, not pits and channels.
Adds that the verse then returns with another general statement 'in the water', creating a case of general–specific–general.

Explains that these two general statements are adjacent, invoking the Western tradition that whenever two generalities are adjacent, they are not treated as a classic 'general–specific' sequence but rather as independent inclusions.

items.text: Resolution: 'In the water' repeated as a second general rule
items.text_en: Resolution: 'In the water' repeated as a second general rule
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Torah repeats 'in the water' as a second general rule after the specific list, applying the principle of 'two adjacent general rules' (שני כללות הסמוכים). This allows the general to include what the specific excludes, namely standing waters.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the repetition of 'in the water' constitutes a second general rule, applying the principle of two adjacent general rules (שני כללות הסמוכים) to include standing waters.

items.text: Ravina's explanation: Two adjacent general rules
items.text_en: Ravina's explanation: Two adjacent general rules
items.desc_en: Ravina explains the principle: when two general rules are adjacent, the second general rule includes what the first specific rule excluded. Here, 'in the water' (first general) excludes standing waters via 'seas/streams' (specific), but the repeated 'in the water' (second general) re-includes them.

sub.desc_en: Ravina resolves the exegetical difficulty by invoking the Western principle that when two general rules are adjacent, the second general rule re-includes what the specific rule excluded.

items.text: First derivation: כלל ופרט וכלל
items.text_en: First derivation: כלל ופרט וכלל
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל to the verse, deriving that only flowing waters (מים נובעים) are included, thereby forbidding חריצין ונעיצין and permitting בורות שיחין ומערות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes applying the hermeneutic principle of כלל ופרט וכלל (general-particular-general) to the verse's three occurrences of 'במים'.

The Gemara concludes that the principle limits inclusion to flowing waters (מים נובעים), thereby forbidding חריצין ונעיצין (ditches and trenches) and permitting בורות שיחין ומערות (cisterns, pits, and caves).

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the פרט
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the פרט
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative understanding of the פרט: water that grows on the ground, which would include even בורות שיחין ומערות and exclude only vessels. It then asks why the verse adds the word 'תֹּאכְלוּ' if this interpretation is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation of the פרט (detail): just as the detail is water that grows on the ground, so too all water that grows on the ground is included, which would include even בורות שיחין ומערות (pits, ditches, and caves) and exclude only vessels.
The Gemara objects: if this interpretation is correct, what purpose does the word 'תֹּאכְלוּ' (you may eat) serve, since it would be redundant?

items.text: Second derivation: ריבה ומיעט וריבה
items.text_en: Second derivation: ריבה ומיעט וריבה
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the repetition of 'בַּמָּיִם' indicates a principle of ריבה ומיעט, which includes everything except what is explicitly excluded, yielding the same result as the first derivation.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that the repetition of 'בַּמָּיִם' indicates a principle of ריבה ומיעט, which includes everything except what is explicitly excluded, yielding the same result as the first derivation.

items.text: Alternative interpretation of ריבה ומיעט
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of ריבה ומיעט
items.desc_en: The Gemara again suggests an alternative: that the ריבה includes בורות שיחין ומערות and the מיעט excludes vessels, but the same objection about 'תֹּאכְלוּ' is raised.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative interpretation of the ריבה ומיעט (inclusion and exclusion) pattern: the inclusion (ריבה) covers בורות שיחין ומערות (cisterns, pits, and caves) for prohibition, and the exclusion (מיעט) removes vessels from prohibition.
The Gemara objects: if so, what purpose does the verse 'תֹּאכְלוּ' (you may eat) serve, since it would be superfluous under this interpretation?

items.text: Resolution by Matityah bar Yehuda
items.text_en: Resolution by Matityah bar Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the objection by citing Matityah bar Yehuda, who explains that בורות שיחין ומערות are permitted because they are enclosed like vessels, while חריצין ונעיצין are forbidden because they are not enclosed.

sub.desc_en: Matityah bar Yehuda resolves the objection by explaining that בורות שיחין ומערות (cisterns, pits, and caves) are permitted because they are enclosed like vessels, while חריצין ונעיצין (trenches and ditches) are forbidden because they are not enclosed.

items.text: Dispute about 'סתום' and 'מפורש'
items.text_en: Dispute about 'סתום' and 'מפורש'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha and Ravina dispute the definitions of 'סתום' (enclosed) and 'מפורש' (exposed) in the context of water sources, with each providing a reason based on the permissibility of vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definitions of 'סתום' (enclosed) and 'מפורש' (exposed) in the context of water sources, noting that Rav Acha and Ravina dispute this.
One opinion holds that a water source with a vessel is 'מפורש' (exposed) and without is 'סתום' (enclosed), while the other reverses the definitions.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the first opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first opinion (yesh lo m'forash) reasons that from such a source vessels are permitted, so it is considered 'exposed'.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the second opinion
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the second opinion (ein lo m'forash) reasons that a source without a vessel is 'exposed' because otherwise one might mistakenly permit even vessels that have a source, so the verse teaches that even with a source one may not eat from vessels.

items.text: Practical halakha: straining beer
items.text_en: Practical halakha: straining beer
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one should not strain beer through a sieve at night due to concern that a creeping creature might crawl above the sieve and fall back into the cup, violating the prohibition of 'שֶׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל הָאָרֶץ'. The Gemara supports this with a baraita about בורות שיחין ומערות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one should not strain beer through a sieve at night, lest a creeping creature crawl above the sieve and fall back into the cup, violating the prohibition of 'שֶׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ עַל הָאָרֶץ'.
The Gemara objects: if so, even drinking from a vessel should be forbidden, lest a creature crawl on the vessel's wall and fall into it.
The Gemara answers: there, the vessel's wall is the creature's natural habitat (רביתיה), so it is not considered as if it is 'crawling on the earth'.

The Gemara cites a baraita that permits drinking from בורות שיחין ומערות (cisterns, pits, and caves) despite the same concern, because the wall is the creature's habitat, and applies the same reasoning to Rav Huna's case.

items.text: Support from Rav Chisda and Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Support from Rav Chisda and Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita supporting Rav Huna, and Shmuel begins a statement about a wormy cucumber, which is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda cites a baraita that supports Rav Huna's position: the verse 'כל השרץ השורץ על הארץ' includes filtered gnats, implying that unfiltered ones are permitted.
Shmuel begins a statement about a wormy cucumber, which is cut off at the section boundary.

items.text: Reconciling two baraitot on insects in produce
items.text_en: Reconciling two baraitot on insects in produce
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to reconcile two baraitot: one that permits insects in legumes and dates, and another that forbids those in the roots of olives and vines. It initially suggests they refer to different stages of growth, but ultimately distinguishes between fruit and the tree itself.

items.text: Unresolved queries about worms that leave the fruit
items.text_en: Unresolved queries about worms that leave the fruit
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef and Rav Ashi raise unresolved questions (teiku) about the status of a worm that leaves the fruit and dies, partially emerges, or is exposed to the air, as well as worms found on the surface of a date or moving between dates.

items.text: Debate about the permissibility of kukyanei (worms in dates)
items.text_en: Debate about the permissibility of kukyanei (worms in dates)
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet bar Rav Idi forbids kukyanei (worms found in dates) because they come from outside, while Rav Ashi objects that if so, they would be found in the rectum. An alternative version permits them, but Rav Ashi rejects that reasoning as well.

items.text: Halakhic ruling on kukyanei and worms in meat and fish
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling on kukyanei and worms in meat and fish
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that kukyanei are forbidden because worms enter from outside while the fruit is sleeping. Worms found in meat are forbidden, but those in fish are permitted.

items.text: Ravina's request to eat worms from fish and the objection
items.text_en: Ravina's request to eat worms from fish and the objection
items.desc_en: Ravina asks his mother to swallow worms from fish for him to eat, but Rav Mesharshiya objects based on a baraita about worms in animal carcasses. Ravina distinguishes: animal meat requires slaughter, but fish are permitted by mere gathering, so worms that grow in them are permitted.

items.text: Identifying creeping creatures and the Leviathan
items.text_en: Identifying creeping creatures and the Leviathan
items.desc_en: A baraita identifies the snake, the centipede, and other creatures based on biblical verses. Rabbi Yosei ben Dormaskit declares the Leviathan a kosher fish, citing verses about its scales and fins.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a birthing animal extends its fetus's limb and then retracts it, the limb is permitted. However, if the head emerges, it is considered born. It also distinguishes between cutting a fetus (permitted) and cutting from the mother's own organs (forbidden).
items.desc: המשנה קובעת דינים לגבי בהמה המקשה ללדת: עובר שהוציא ידו והחזירה מותר באכילה, אבל הוציא ראשו הרי הוא כילוד. כמו כן, חיתוך מעובר שבמעיה מותר, אבל חיתוך מהטחול והכליות אסור, והכלל: דבר שגופה אסור, שאינו גופה מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a limb extended and retracted by a fetus is permitted, but the head's emergence constitutes birth, and distinguishes between cutting the fetus (permitted) and cutting the mother's organs (forbidden).
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדיני בהמה המקשה ללדת וקובעת כללים לגבי מעובר וטחול וכליות.

items.text: אמירת רב על איסור אבר שיצא
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement and reason
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Rav that a limb that emerged is forbidden. The reason is derived from the verse 'flesh in the field, a carcass, do not eat' – once flesh exits its boundary, it becomes forbidden.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מוסיף שאבר עצמו אסור, ומסביר את הטעם מהפסוק 'ובשר בשדה טרפה לא תאכלו', כיון שיצא חוץ למחיצתו נאסר.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Rav that a limb that emerged from the womb is forbidden.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב פותח ואומר שהאבר עצמו אסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reason: the verse 'וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ' (flesh in the field, a carcass, do not eat) teaches that once flesh exits its boundary, it becomes forbidden.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את טעם האיסור מהפסוק 'ובשר בשדה טרפה לא תאכלו', כיון שיצא חוץ למחיצתו נאסר.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על רב ותירוץ ראשון
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling that the limb is permitted refers to the limb itself or the entire fetus. It concludes that it refers to the fetus, and the mention of retraction is for stylistic consistency with the latter clause.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב מהמשנה: האם המשנה מתירה את האבר שיצא? ודוחה שהמשנה מדברת בעובר כולו, לא באבר. ושואלת: אם בעובר, למה נקט 'והחזירו'? ומתרצת שזהו היקש לסיפא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling that the limb is permitted refers to the limb itself or to the entire fetus.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב מהמשנה: האם המשנה מתירה את האבר שיצא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to the fetus, and the mention of retraction is for stylistic consistency with the latter clause.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב מהמשנה: האם המשנה מתירה את האבר שיצא?

items.text: בירור חידוש הסיפא
items.text_en: Discussion on the head emerging
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what the Mishnah's latter clause teaches, suggesting it might be about birth. It cites a baraita about a firstborn for inheritance, and distinguishes between human and animal cases, noting that a human's face is significant while an animal has no 'vestibule'.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בסיפא: מה חידוש יש בהוצאת ראש? ומביאה ברייתא על בכור, ומסיקה שהחידוש הוא בבהמה, כי אדם ובהמה לא ילפי מהדדי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the latter clause of the Mishnah teaches us.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו החידוש בסיפא של המשנה, שהרי ברור שיציאת ראש נחשבת לידה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a firstborn for inheritance, distinguishing between a live and dead head emerging.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו החידוש בסיפא של המשנה, שהרי ברור שיציאת ראש נחשבת לידה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita discusses a human, not an animal, so it may not apply.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהחידוש הוא בבהמה, שכן הסיפא מלמדת שגם בבהמה יציאת ראש נחשבת לידה לעניין פטר רחם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that human and animal cases are not analogous because a human's face is significant and an animal has no 'vestibule' (פְּרוֹזְדוֹר).
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת מדוע לא ניתן ללמוד אדם מבהמה או בהמה מאדם, בשל ההבדלים ביניהם: לבהמה אין פרוזדור, ולאדם יש פרצוף פנים חשוב.

items.text: Further challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a placenta as a sign of birth, challenging the earlier distinction. It then argues that if the Mishnah's retraction is not literal, the entire Mishnah would be redundant, leading to a resolution that the Mishnah refers to the place of the cut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a placenta that partially emerged, which is forbidden to eat, as a sign of birth in a woman is also a sign of birth in an animal, challenging the earlier distinction that the Mishnah's retraction is not literal.
The Gemara argues that if the Mishnah's retraction in the first clause is literal, then the second clause is taught only because of the first clause, which is consistent.
The Gemara rejects the alternative: if neither clause is literal, the entire Mishnah would be redundant, which is impossible.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the Mishnah's ruling is only needed for the place of the cut, resolving the earlier difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: the Mishnah's permission is needed for the place of the cut (מְקוֹם חֲתָךְ) on the fetus.

items.text: ברייתא נוספת על דיני יד שיצאה
items.text_en: Final baraita and its implications
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited detailing cases where the limb is retracted before or after slaughter, and where it is cut. The Gemara's analysis continues, but the text breaks off.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא נוספת המפרטת דינים שונים: החזרת היד לאחר שחיטה, חיתוך היד לפני שחיטה, ודין טומאה וטהרה. הברייתא ממשיכה לדון במקרה של שחיטה ואחר כך חיתוך.

sub.desc_en: The baraita is cited as a supporting source, presenting a case where the limb was retracted before slaughter and the meat is permitted.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה דין בהמה המקשה לילד שהוציא עובר את ידו והחזירה לפני שחיטה, ולאחר מכן שחט את אמו – מותר באכילה; אך אם שחט את אמו ואחר כך החזירה – אסור.

sub.desc_en: The baraita continues with a contrasting case where slaughter occurs before retraction, rendering the limb forbidden.
sub.desc: הברייתא מציגה דין נוסף: שחט את אמו ואחר כך חתך את יד העובר – מעמד הדין נשאר פתוח בשל קטיעת הברייתא.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a third case where the limb was cut after being extended, distinguishing between the outside portion (impure and forbidden) and the inside portion (pure and permitted).
sub.desc: הברייתא ממשיכה במקרה שהוציא את ידו של העובר וחתכה לפני שחיטה: חלק היד שבחוץ טמא ואסור באכילה, ואילו חלק שבפנים טהור ומותר.

sub.desc_en: The baraita begins a fourth case (slaughter before cutting) but the text breaks off, leaving the conclusion unstated.
sub.desc: הברייתא מציגה דין נוסף: שחט את אמו ואחר כך חתך את יד העובר – מעמד הדין נשאר פתוח בשל קטיעת הברייתא.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: מחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding the status of meat that touched a neveilah versus a tereifah that was slaughtered.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת בין רבי מאיר לחכמים בדין הבשר היוצא מהעובר: רבי מאיר מחשיבו כמגע נבילה, וחכמים כמגע טריפה שחוטה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's position that meat that touched a neveilah (carcass) is treated as a neveilah.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר קובע שהבשר היוצא מהעובר נחשב כמגע נבילה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages counter that meat which touched a tereifah that was slaughtered is treated as a tereifah, not a neveilah.
sub.desc: חכמים חולקים על רבי מאיר וקובעים שהבשר היוצא מהעובר נחשב כמגע טריפה שחוטה.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על המשנה והבחנה בין אבר לעובר
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about a fetal limb that emerged and was reinserted refers to the limb itself or the fetus. It resolves that it refers to the place of the cut (מקום חתך).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה: האם הדין מתייחס לאבר או לעובר? היא מביאה ראיה מהרישא והסיפא, ומתרצת בעזרת רב נחמן בר יצחק שהדין נצרך רק למקום החתך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's first clause, which permits the fetus after the mother is slaughtered, refers to the limb that emerged or to the fetus itself.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקושיה על המשנה: הרישא קובעת שהוציא העובר ידו והחזירה, ואחר כך שחט את אמו – מותר באכילה; ושואלת: הלא על אבר נאמר, ומכאן דין היתר באבר שיצא וחזר?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the ruling applies to the fetus, the second clause (which forbids the fetus when the mother was slaughtered before the limb was reinserted) would be inexplicable.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves that both clauses refer only to the place of the cut (מקום חתך) on the limb, not to the limb itself or the fetus.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק מיישב: הדין לא נצרך אלא למקום החתך, כלומר במקום שנחתך האבר מהעובר, וכך גם בכאן הדין נצרך רק למקום החתך.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita brought by Avimi
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita brought by Avimi
items.desc_en: Avimi brings a baraita stating that if a hoof was reinserted, the fetus is permitted. The Gemara questions whether this refers to the hoof itself, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak again explains it refers to the place of the cut.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous explanation by citing a baraita that Avimi brought, which states that if a hoof was reinserted, one may eat, and asks whether this does not refer to eating the hoof itself.
The Gemara initially answers that the baraita means one may eat the fetus, but then objects that if so, why mention reinsertion, as even without reinsertion the fetus would be permitted.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the difficulty by explaining that the baraita refers only to the place of the cut, not to the hoof itself.

items.text: Interpretation of two verses
items.text_en: Interpretation of two verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the two verses cited in the baraita refer to the place of the cut and to a קלוט (a calf with hoof-like feet) in the cow's womb, according to Rabbi Shimon who permits it while inside the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita cites two verses, suggesting one might refer to a limb and the other to the place of the cut.
The Gemara answers that one verse refers to the place of the cut and the other to a קלוט (hoof-like calf) inside the cow, which Rabbi Shimon permits while still in the womb.

items.text: דברי עולא בשם רבי יוחנן: האבר עצמו מותר
items.text_en: Ulla's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits the limb itself. Rav Yehudah objects, citing Rav and Shmuel who forbid it. Rabbi Yochanan explains that all meat was included in the prohibition of 'meat in the field' (בשר בשדה), but the verse about a chatat that left its boundary and returned teaches that only that specific case is forbidden.
items.desc: עולא אומר בשם רבי יוחנן שהאבר עצמו מותר, ומסביר שהכל היו בכלל 'בשר בשדה טריפה' עד שפרט הכתוב בחטאת שיצתה מחיצתה, אבל כל מילי כיון דהדור – שרי.

sub.text_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan permits the limb itself.
sub.desc: עולא מביא בשם רבי יוחנן שהאבר שיצא חוץ למחיצתו וחזר – מותר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehudah objects, citing Rav and Shmuel who forbid the limb itself.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מקשה לעולא: הרי רב ושמואל שניהם אוסרים את האבר עצמו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that all meat was included in the prohibition of 'בשר בשדה' (meat in the field), but the verse about a chatat that left its boundary and returned teaches that only that specific case is forbidden, while anything that returns is permitted.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מקשה לעולא: הרי רב ושמואל שניהם אוסרים את האבר עצמו.

items.text: תיובתא על עולא מברייתא
items.text_en: Refutation of Ulla
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought that interprets 'בשר בשדה טרפה' to mean that just as a tereifah has no remedy, so too meat that left its boundary has no remedy. This is a conclusive refutation of Ulla.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על עולא מברייתא הדורשת 'בשר בשדה טריפה' – כשם שטריפה אין לה היתר, כך בשר שיצא מחיצתו אין לו היתר. ומסיקה: תיובתא דעולא.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that interprets the verse 'בשר בשדה טרפה לא תאכלו' (flesh in the field, a tereifah, do not eat) to teach that just as a tereifah has no remedy, so too meat that left its boundary has no remedy.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על עולא מברייתא הדורשת את הפסוק 'בשר בשדה טריפה', ומדגישה את הדמיון בין טריפה לבשר שיצא מחיצתו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains the analogy: just as a tereifah (טריפה) once rendered unfit has no remedy, so too meat that left its boundary has no remedy, thereby concluding that this is a conclusive refutation of Ulla.
sub.desc: רבא מבאר שהדמיון לטריפה מלמד שכשם שטריפה אין לה היתר לעולם, כך בשר שיצא מחיצתו אין לו היתר, ובכך מוכיח שהברייתא היא תיובתא על עולא.

items.text: בירור המקור למעשר שני וביכורים
items.text_en: Source for maaser sheni and bikurim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the source for the ruling that maaser sheni and bikurim that left their boundary and returned are permitted, citing the verse 'לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך'.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת היכן מצינו שמעשר שני וביכורים מותרים כשיצאו וחזרו, ומביאה את הפסוק 'לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך' – דווקא בשעריך אסור, אבל יצאו וחזרו מותרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the source is found for the claim that maaser sheni and bikurim that left their boundary and returned are permitted.
sub.desc: מר טוען שיש מקור במעשר שני ובכורים לכך שיצאו וחזרו מותרים, ומציין שיש לברר היכן מצינו זאת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing the verse 'לֹא תוּכַל לֶאֱכֹל בִּשְׁעָרֶיךָ' (Deuteronomy 12:17), inferring that only within the gates is forbidden, but if they left their boundary and returned, they are permitted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את הפסוק 'לא תוכל לאכול בשעריך' ומסיקה מדיוקו: דווקא בשעריך אסור, אבל יצאו וחזרו מותרים.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ורבי יוחנן: יש לידה לאברים
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan and subsequent inquiries
items.desc_en: In the West they teach that Rav says there is 'birth for limbs' (יש לידה לאברים) and Rabbi Yochanan says there is not. The Gemara explores the practical difference and raises two inquiries about a limb that was repeatedly extended and retracted, or cut off piecemeal, until the majority of the fetus emerged.
items.desc: במערבא שנינו: רב אמר יש לידה לאברים, ורבי יוחנן אמר אין לידה לאברים. הגמרא דנה בהבדל ביניהם ובשאלות על הוצאת יד והחזרה עד רובו, וחותמת בתא שמע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that in the West they teach the dispute: Rav holds יש לידה לאברים (there is 'birth' for limbs, i.e., each limb's emergence is halachically significant), while Rabbi Yochanan holds אין לידה לאברים (there is no 'birth' for limbs).
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את המחלוקת בין רב לרבי יוחנן בעניין יש לידה לאברים ומציגה את שיטותיהם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two positions, and answers that it concerns prohibiting a minority of a limb that remains inside the mother.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה ההבדל המעשי בין שיטת רב לשיטת רבי יוחנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the first inquiry: according to the opinion that there is no 'birth' for limbs, if a fetus repeatedly extended and retracted its limb until the majority of the fetus emerged, is the majority considered to have emerged, or does each retraction nullify the previous extension?
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה בעיה: לדברי האומר אין לידה לאברים, הוציא העובר את ידו והחזירה כמה פעמים עד רובו – האם נחשב שיצא רובו או לא?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the second inquiry: if the first inquiry is resolved that retraction nullifies the extension, what about a case where the limb was cut off each time it emerged, until the majority of the fetus emerged — is the majority considered to have emerged, or do we require the majority to emerge all at once?
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה בעיה נוספת: אם נניח שחזרת היד מבטלת את היציאה, מה הדין אם חתך את היד בכל פעם והוציא אחרת עד רובו – האם צריך רוב בבת אחת?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara transitions to resolve the inquiries by citing a supporting source, saying 'Come and hear'.
sub.desc: הגמרא פונה להביא ראיה מהברייתא להכריע את הספקות.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule: 'not part of her body' includes a calcified fetus in the womb
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's rule: 'not part of her body' includes a calcified fetus in the womb
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what cases are included in the Mishnah's phrase 'that is not part of her body.' It suggests it includes a case like one where the fetus's feet were extracted. The answer is that it actually refers to a calcified fetus in the womb, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who permits it while it is still inside the mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case the Mishnah's phrase 'that is not part of her body' comes to include, suggesting it might include a case where the fetus's feet were extracted.
The Gemara answers that the phrase actually comes to include a calcified fetus in the womb, in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who permits it while still inside the mother.

items.text: Rabbi Chananiah's inquiry: fetus's hand in the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Rabbi Chananiah's inquiry: fetus's hand in the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chananiah asks: if a fetus extended its hand into the Temple courtyard, does the courtyard's sanctity render it prohibited? Abaye resolves it: just as the question of sacrificial animals in Jerusalem is not raised because the fetus's partition is its mother, so too here, the mother is the fetus's partition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chananiah asks whether a fetus that extended its hand into the Temple courtyard is prohibited by the courtyard's sanctity, given that the mother serves as the fetus's partition.
Abaye resolves the inquiry by analogy: just as the question of sacrificial animals in Jerusalem is not raised because the mother is the fetus's partition, so too here the mother is the partition.

items.text: Ilfa's inquiry: status of a fetus between signs of slaughter
items.text_en: Ilfa's inquiry: status of a fetus between signs of slaughter
items.desc_en: Ilfa asks: if a fetus extended its hand between the two signs of ritual slaughter (simanim), is the first sign effective to purify it from the status of nevelah? Rava argues a kal vachomer: if the first sign allows it for eating, it should certainly purify it from nevelah.

sub.desc_en: Ilfa asks: if a fetus extended its hand between the two signs of ritual slaughter, what is the law?
The Gemara clarifies: does the first sign combine with the second to purify the fetus from the status of nevelah (carcass), or not?
Rava argues a kal vachomer (a fortiori): if the first sign is effective to permit the fetus for eating, it should certainly be effective to purify it from the status of nevelah.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry: concern for the offspring's mixture and the status of fetal fat
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry: concern for the offspring's mixture and the status of fetal fat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether we are concerned about the offspring's status when a permitted fetus (ben pekuah) mates. The Gemara refines the question: the case is when a ben pekuah mates with another ben pekuah. After determining that the offspring is mixed (the father's traits don't breed true), the question becomes whether a doubly prohibited fat (from both issur yotzei and issur chelev) is more stringent than a single prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether we are concerned about the offspring's status when a permitted fetus (בן פקועה) mates.
The Gemara refines the case: if the fetus mates with a normal animal, the question is trivial because even a regular בן פקועה would be problematic.
Rav Mesharshiya states that according to the opinion that we are concerned for the father's seed, a בן פקועה that mates with a normal animal produces an offspring with no remedy.

The Gemara specifies the case: the fetus mates with another בן פקועה, and asks whether the offspring inherits the father's limb (אבר מוליד אבר) and is permitted, or whether the seed is mixed and prohibited.
The Gemara retracts the first possibility, concluding that the seed is obviously mixed, otherwise a blind animal would always give birth to a blind offspring.

The Gemara reframes the question: since a normal animal comes from חלב ודם (fat and blood) and is permitted, is this case similar, or do we say that two prohibitions (איסור יוצא and איסור חלב) are considered but three are not?

items.text: Analyzing the dispute: Rabbi Meir vs Rabbi Yehuda on fetal fat, and the final question
items.text_en: Analyzing the dispute: Rabbi Meir vs Rabbi Yehuda on fetal fat, and the final question
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines which Tanna the previous question applies to: for Rabbi Meir, there is issur chelev but not issur yotzei; for Rabbi Yehuda, issur yotzei but not issur chelev. It cites a Mishnah about the gid hanasheh and fetal fat. The Gemara concludes that a double prohibition (issur yotzei and issur chelev) is not permitted. The final unresolved question is about 'sucking' the fat of such a fetus: is it like chelev from elsewhere which has a remedy of slaughter, or is it worse because it has no remedy? The question stands unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to which Tanna the previous question applies: for Rabbi Meir, there is issur chelev but not issur yotzei.
The Gemara considers the alternative: for Rabbi Yehuda, there is issur yotzei but not issur chelev.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the gid hanasheh (sciatic nerve) and fetal fat: Rabbi Meir prohibits both, Rabbi Yehuda permits both.
The Gemara concludes that a double prohibition (issur yotzei and issur chelev) is not permitted.
The Gemara asks: what about sucking the fat of such a fetus? Is it like chelev from elsewhere which has a remedy of slaughter, or is it worse because it has no remedy?
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Biblical derivation for the law of 'cutting from a fetus' and its limits
items.text_en: Biblical derivation for the law of 'cutting from a fetus' and its limits
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the source for the Mishnah's law that cutting from a fetus is permitted. It derives from the verse 'behemah...babehemah' to include the fetus. But if so, one could perform temurah with it? No, the Mishnah prohibits that. The verse 'otah' teaches that the mother must be whole. If so, why is a dove-shaped fetus prohibited? The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan that it is forbidden, implying the verse only permits a normally developed fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the biblical source of the Mishnah's law that cutting from a fetus is permitted.
The Gemara derives the law from the verse 'behemah...babehemah' (animal...in the animal) to include the fetus.
The Gemara objects that if the verse includes the fetus, one could perform temurah (exchange) with it, which is prohibited by the Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that the verse 'and every animal' is meant to include the fetus for the law of cutting, not for temurah.
The Gemara objects that if the verse includes the fetus, one could also cut from the spleen or kidneys, but the Mishnah prohibits that.
The Gemara answers that the verse 'otah' (her) teaches that the mother must be whole, not lacking organs like the spleen or kidneys.
The Gemara objects that if the verse permits cutting from the fetus, then finding a dove-shaped fetus should also be permitted.
The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that a dove-shaped fetus found in a slaughtered animal is forbidden to eat, implying the verse only permits a normally developed fetus.

items.text: Opening question on the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening question on the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling about a firstborn animal that was sold as limbs, asking why it is permitted if the majority was not yet born.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier ruling about a firstborn animal sold as limbs, asking why it is permitted if the majority was not yet born.

items.text: Objection from a fetus in a cow
items.text_en: Objection from a fetus in a cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection: if a fetus is found inside a slaughtered cow, why is it permitted? It cites Rabbi Yishmael's school who agree with Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai's interpretation of the verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if so, a cloven-hoofed fetus inside a cow should be forbidden, citing the school of Rabbi Yishmael who interprets the verse 'פַּרְסָה בַּבְּהֵמָה תֹּאכֵלוּ' (a hoof in the animal you may eat) like Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai.

items.text: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi explains that the earlier ruling about temurah not applying to limbs and fetuses follows Rabbi Shimon, who compares temurah to ma'aser.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi bar Ashi answers: the original reasoning stands, and the difficulty about 'אֵין מְמִירִין' (one may not exchange) is resolved by attributing it to Rabbi Shimon, who compares תמורה (exchange) to מעשר (tithe): just as tithe does not apply to limbs and fetuses, so too exchange does not apply to limbs and fetuses.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's proof from consecrated animals
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's proof from consecrated animals
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei argues that just as dedicating a limb makes the whole animal an olah, so too substituting a limb should make the whole animal a temurah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a supporting baraita: Rabbi Yosei argues that in consecrated animals, if one says 'this animal's leg is an עולה (burnt-offering),' the whole animal becomes an עולה, so similarly if one says 'this leg is in exchange for that,' the whole animal should be exchanged.

Rabbi Yosei argues by קל וחומר (a fortiori) from consecrated animals: just as dedicating a limb makes the whole animal an עולה (burnt offering), so too substituting a limb should make the whole animal a תמורה (substitute).

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei's proof applies to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, who hold that dedicating a limb does not make the whole animal holy, but only the limb's value is sold for olah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom Rabbi Yosei directed his proof, questioning whether Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, who reject the idea that dedicating a limb makes the whole animal holy, would accept it.

The Gemara cites a baraita in which Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda explicitly rule that dedicating a limb does not make the whole animal holy; the animal is sold for olah offerings, and only the limb's value is holy.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's opposing view
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's opposing view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon derive from the verse that dedicating a limb makes the whole animal holy.

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon's position
sub.desc_en: The baraita continues: Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say that from where do we know that saying 'this animal's leg is an עולה' makes the whole animal an עולה? The verse 'יִהְיֶה' (shall be) teaches to include all of it.

items.text: Gemara's conclusion and rejection
items.text_en: Gemara's conclusion and rejection
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosei's statement must be directed to Rabbi Shimon, but then rejects this, saying Rabbi Yosei was stating his own reasoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to whom Rabbi Yosei's statement is directed, and concludes it must be to Rabbi Shimon, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda would not hold that view.
The Gemara rejects the conclusion, stating that Rabbi Yosei was merely stating his own reasoning, not responding to anyone.

items.text: Mishnah: Firstborn animal in difficult labor
items.text_en: Mishnah: Firstborn animal in difficult labor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a firstborn animal is in difficult labor, one may cut off limbs and throw them to dogs; if the majority has emerged, it must be buried and the mother is exempt from the law of the firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: for a firstborn animal that is having difficulty giving birth, one may cut off limb by limb and throw it to the dogs; if most of the fetus emerged, it must be buried, and the mother is exempt from the law of the firstborn.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbah
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a case where a third of the fetus emerged and was sold to a non-Jew, then another third emerged. Rav Huna holds it is holy (retroactive sanctity), while Rabbah holds it is not holy (prospective sanctity).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbah regarding a case where a third of a fetus emerged and was sold to a non-Jew, then another third emerged: Rav Huna holds it is holy, Rabbah holds it is not holy.

Rav Huna explains his position: he holds that sanctity applies retroactively (למפרע קדוש), so once the majority emerged, it is revealed that the entire fetus was holy from the start, and the sale to the non-Jew was void.
Rabbah explains his position: he holds that sanctity applies only from now onward (מכאן ולהבא קדוש), so the sale to the non-Jew was valid and the fetus is not holy.

items.text: Supporting dispute: Birth through the side
items.text_en: Supporting dispute: Birth through the side
items.desc_en: A related dispute: if a third emerged through the side and two-thirds through the womb, Rav Huna says it is not holy (since the majority did not come through the womb), while Rabbah says it is holy (since the majority came through the womb).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a supporting dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbah regarding the sanctity of a firstborn that emerged partly through the side and partly through the womb.

Rav Huna rules that the animal is not holy, consistent with his view that sanctity applies retroactively (למפרע קדוש), and since the first third exited through the side, the majority never emerged through the womb.
Rabbah rules that the animal is holy, consistent with his view that sanctity applies from now onward (מכאן ולהבא קדוש), and since the majority (two-thirds) emerged through the womb, it is holy.

items.text: Need for both cases
items.text_en: Need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: to show that Rav Huna's leniency in one case does not imply agreement in the other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that both cases are necessary: in the first case Rav Huna rules leniently (not sanctified), but in the second case which is stringent (sanctified), one might think he would agree with Rabbah.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbah's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if Rabbah's statement was said regarding one case, it might not apply to another, necessitating the clarification that he agrees with Rav Huna in the latter case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbah's statement was said regarding one case, but in another case he agrees with Rav Huna, so both statements are necessary.

items.text: Mishnah analysis: Cutting and discarding limbs
items.text_en: Mishnah analysis: Cutting and discarding limbs
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may cut and discard limbs of a miscarrying animal, arguing that if the fetus is sanctified retroactively, the limbs should require burial. The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to cutting and discarding immediately, not cutting and setting aside, and the latter case would require burial like when most of the fetus emerged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that one may cut and discard limbs to dogs, arguing that if the fetus is sanctified retroactively, the limbs should require burial.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah refers to cutting and discarding immediately, not cutting and setting aside.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah should have distinguished between cutting and discarding versus cutting and setting aside, requiring burial in the latter case.

The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah indeed implies this distinction: cutting and discarding is permitted, but cutting and setting aside is treated like most of the fetus having emerged and requires burial.

items.text: Rava's inquiry: Following the majority in limbs
items.text_en: Rava's inquiry: Following the majority in limbs
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether we follow the majority of the fetus in determining sanctity when limbs emerge, or the majority of a limb. The Gemara clarifies the scenario: if half the fetus emerged within a majority of a limb, does the inner minority follow the limb's majority? It attempts to prove from the Mishnah that 'most of it' refers to half the fetus within a majority of a limb, but ultimately explains it as most of the fetus within a minority of a limb.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether, when limbs of a firstborn animal emerge during birth, we follow the majority of the limbs or the majority of the fetus in determining sanctity.
The Gemara clarifies the scenario: if most of the fetus emerged within a minority of a limb, does the outer minority follow the limb's majority or the fetus's majority?

sub.text: Gemara's rejection of the first scenario
sub.text_en: Gemara's rejection of the first scenario
sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects this scenario as obvious: we would not abandon the fetus's majority to follow the limb's majority.

sub.text: Gemara's second clarification of the scenario
sub.text_en: Gemara's second clarification of the scenario
sub.desc_en: The Gemara reframes the inquiry: if half the fetus emerged within a majority of a limb, does the inner minority follow the limb's majority?

sub.text: Gemara's attempted proof from the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Gemara's attempted proof from the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from the Mishnah's phrase 'most of it emerged' that it refers to half the fetus within a majority of a limb, rejecting the possibility that it means a literal majority.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's 'most of it' must refer to half the fetus within a majority of a limb.

The Gemara rejects this interpretation, explaining that the Mishnah refers to most of the fetus within a minority of a limb, teaching that we do not follow the limb's majority over the fetus's majority.

items.text: Rava's further inquiries: Wrapped or swallowed fetus
items.text_en: Rava's further inquiries: Wrapped or swallowed fetus
items.desc_en: Rava asks about cases where the fetus is wrapped in straw, his garment, or another placenta, or if a weasel swallowed and regurgitated it, or if two wombs are connected. The Gemara refines each scenario and concludes with 'teiku' (undecided) for the last case.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks about the status of a firstborn animal when the fetus emerges wrapped in straw or in his garment.
Rava asks about the case where the fetus is wrapped in its own placenta, but the Gemara refines this to a different placenta.
Rava asks about a case where the mother wrapped and held the fetus and brought it out, and the Gemara clarifies it refers to exiting feet-first.
Rava asks about a case where a weasel swallowed the fetus, then regurgitated it, and it emerged on its own.
Rava asks about a case where two wombs are connected and the fetus exits one and enters the other, and the Gemara concludes with 'teiku' (undecided).

items.text: Rav Acha's inquiry: Opened womb walls
items.text_en: Rav Acha's inquiry: Opened womb walls
items.desc_en: Rav Acha asks whether the airspace of the womb sanctifies the fetus or actual contact with the womb walls, when the walls are opened but the fetus is still inside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha asks whether the airspace of the womb sanctifies the fetus or actual contact with the womb walls, when the walls are opened but the fetus is still inside.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's inquiry: Displaced womb walls
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's inquiry: Displaced womb walls
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi asks about womb walls that are displaced and hanging around the fetus's neck, questioning whether they sanctify only in their place or even elsewhere.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi asks whether displaced womb walls that hang around the fetus's neck still sanctify the fetus outside their place, or only in their place.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry: Crushed womb walls
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's inquiry: Crushed womb walls
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about crushed womb walls. Rabbi Zeira relates it to an earlier inquiry by Rabbi Zeira from Rabbi Asi about the principle of 'standing majority' versus 'breach' when the fetus exits through a breach. The Gemara explains that the case of crushed walls was not previously asked.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks Rabbi Zeira about the status of a firstborn animal when the walls of the womb are crushed.

Rabbi Zeira responds that this touches on an earlier inquiry he had posed to Rabbi Asi about the principle of 'standing majority' (עומד מרובה) versus 'breach' (פרוץ) when the fetus exits through a breach.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Zeira's earlier inquiry only considered a case where there is some standing wall remaining, but the case of crushed walls was not previously asked.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a fetus dies in its mother's womb and the shepherd touches it, it is pure, whether the mother is a kosher or non-kosher animal. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili distinguishes: in a non-kosher animal it is impure, in a kosher animal it is pure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a dead fetus in its mother's womb, stating the Tanna Kamma's ruling that it is pure in both kosher and non-kosher animals, and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's dissenting view that it is impure in a non-kosher animal and pure in a kosher animal.

items.text: Gemara's first explanation for Tanna Kamma
items.text_en: Gemara's first explanation for Tanna Kamma
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the Tanna Kamma's reasoning using a kal vachomer argument: if the mother permits the fetus for consumption, she should also purify it from neveilah. The Gemara then derives the same ruling for a non-kosher animal from a scriptural juxtaposition of verses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Tanna Kamma (the first anonymous opinion in the Mishnah).
Rav Chisda answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if the mother permits the fetus for consumption, she should also purify it from the status of נבלה (neveilah).
The Gemara asks: we have found the source for a kosher animal, but from where do we derive the same ruling for a non-kosher animal?

The Gemara answers by citing a scriptural juxtaposition: the verse 'וכי ימות מן הבהמה' (when an animal dies) includes a non-kosher animal, and 'אשר היא לכם לאכלה' (which is for you to eat) refers to a kosher animal, teaching that a non-kosher animal's fetus is also pure.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's scriptural basis
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's scriptural basis
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak explains Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position: the verse 'every walker on its paws' teaches that animals that walk on paws (like non-kosher animals) are impure, implying their fetuses are impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning for his position?

Rabbi Yitzchak explains that Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives his position from the verse 'וכל הולך על כפיו' (every walker on its paws), which teaches that animals that walk on paws are impure, implying their fetuses are impure.

items.text: Challenges and resolution regarding Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's derivation
items.text_en: Challenges and resolution regarding Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises challenges: a cloven-hoofed animal in a cow's womb should be impure, and a cow in a camel's womb should be pure, but the verse 'and every walker' includes the latter. A cloven-hoofed animal in a cloven-hoofed mother would be impure, but Rav Chisda's kal vachomer overrides that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a cloven-hoofed animal in a cow's womb should be impure because it walks on its palms, but the verse limits impurity to palm-walkers within four-legged animals, and this is a four-legged animal within an eight-legged one.
The Gemara objects that a cow in a camel's womb should be pure, but the verse 'and every walker' includes it as impure.
The Gemara notes that a cloven-hoofed animal in a cloven-hoofed mother would be impure, but Rav Chisda's kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) overrides that and keeps it pure.

items.text: Rav Achadvoi's objection
items.text_en: Rav Achadvoi's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objects: a pig in a sow's womb should be impure since both walk on eight legs, but the kal vachomer would still apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami objects: a pig in a sow's womb should be impure since both walk on eight legs, but the kal vachomer would still apply.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative derivation
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives the impurity of a fetus in a non-kosher animal from a verse about neveilah, which implies that only a non-kosher animal's fetus is impure. The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation is still needed to exclude a different interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces an alternative derivation from a verse listing neveilah of a non-kosher animal.
The Gemara questions why the verse specifies non-kosher animal neveilah, since kosher animal neveilah also imparts impurity.
The Gemara answers that the verse refers to a fetus: in a non-kosher animal it is impure, in a kosher animal it is pure.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yitzchak's earlier derivation is needed, given Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative.
The Gemara resolves that without Rabbi Yitzchak's verse, one might have misapplied the verse to Rabbi Yehuda's view, so Rabbi Yitzchak's derivation teaches otherwise.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi Yonatan's discussion with Ben Azzai
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi Yonatan's discussion with Ben Azzai
items.desc_en: A baraita recounts Rabbi Yonatan's conversation with Ben Azzai about deriving the impurity of a kosher animal's carcass. Ben Azzai cites a verse, but Rabbi Yonatan argues it only applies to walkers on paws. Ben Azzai then asks what Rabbi Yishmael says, and Rabbi Yonatan cites a different verse to include all animals.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan opens by stating what has already been learned: that the carcass of a kosher animal and a non-kosher animal impart impurity, and the carcass of a non-kosher wild animal imparts impurity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yonatan's question to Ben Azzai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yonatan's question to Ben Azzai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yonatan asks Ben Azzai from where we derive that the carcass of a kosher wild animal imparts impurity, and Ben Azzai answers by citing the verse 'כָּל הוֹלֵךְ עַל כַּפָּיו' (every walker on its paws).
Rabbi Yonatan objects that the verse does not say 'every wild animal' but rather 'in every wild animal', meaning it only applies to walkers on paws within the category of wild animals.
Ben Azzai asks Rabbi Yonatan what Rabbi Yishmael says about this matter.

Rabbi Yonatan answers by citing the verse 'וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה' (when an animal dies) and explains that it teaches that a kosher wild animal is included in the category of kosher animal, and a non-kosher wild animal is included in the category of non-kosher animal.

items.text: Opening Tosefta: Behemah and Chayah interchangeability
items.text_en: Opening Tosefta: Behemah and Chayah interchangeability
items.desc_en: The Tosefta states that a non-kosher behemah is included in the category of non-kosher chayah, and a kosher behemah is included in kosher chayah. It adds a lament for ben Azzai who did not serve Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Tosefta states the interchangeability of behemah and chayah categories for kosher and non-kosher animals, and laments ben Azzai for not serving Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving the inclusions from verses
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving the inclusions from verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that chayah is included in behemah and vice versa, citing verses. It then specifies that kosher chayah is included in kosher behemah for signs, non-kosher chayah in non-kosher behemah for cross-breeding, and non-kosher behemah in non-kosher chayah for Rabbi's derivation about tum'at kodashim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that a chayah (wild animal) is included in the category of behemah (domestic animal), and answers by citing the verse listing both together.
The Gemara asks how we know that behemah is included in chayah, and answers by citing the verse that opens with 'chayah' and includes behemah.
The Gemara specifies that the inclusion of kosher chayah in kosher behemah is for the purpose of identifying signs of kashrut (סימנים).
The Gemara specifies that the inclusion of non-kosher chayah in non-kosher behemah is for the prohibition of cross-breeding (הרבעה).
The Gemara specifies that the inclusion of non-kosher behemah in non-kosher chayah is for the derivation of Rabbi (regarding tum'at kodashim).
A baraita is cited where Rabbi uses a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) from 'behemah teme'ah' to derive that the inclusion teaches about tum'at kodashim (ritual impurity of sacred offerings).

items.text: Gemara: Kosher behemah in kosher chayah for childbirth laws
items.text_en: Gemara: Kosher behemah in kosher chayah for childbirth laws
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that kosher behemah is included in kosher chayah for the laws of childbirth (yetzirah), citing a Mishnah of Rabbi Meir and the Sages. It then asks what the verse is for the Sages, and answers that the entire verse comes for Rabbi's derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a kosher behemah (domesticated animal) is included in a kosher chayah (non-domesticated animal) for the laws of childbirth (יצירה).

The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules that a woman who miscarries a non-human form must observe impurity days for a male or female, implying that kosher behemah is included in kosher chayah for childbirth laws.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Meir, stating that any offspring not in human form is not considered a viable birth (ולד).
The Gemara asks: according to the Sages (who reject the Mishnah's application), what purpose does the verse (that includes behemah in chayah) serve?
The Gemara answers that the entire verse comes only for Rabbi's derivation (regarding טומאת קודש, impurity of sacred items).

items.text: Mishnah: Woman whose fetus died and midwife touched it
items.text_en: Mishnah: Woman whose fetus died and midwife touched it
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a woman's fetus died in her womb and a midwife extended her hand and touched it, the midwife is impure with a seven-day impurity, but the woman remains pure until the fetus exits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the case of a woman whose fetus died in her womb and a midwife who touched it, ruling that the midwife is impure for seven days while the woman remains pure until the fetus exits.

items.text: Gemara: Principle of tumah belu'ah from the verse
items.text_en: Gemara: Principle of tumah belu'ah from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbah states that just as absorbed impurity does not impart impurity, so absorbed purity does not become impure. The Gemara derives tumah belu'ah from the verse about eating neveilah close to sunset, and addresses an objection about the animal not being fit for a ger, discussing the views of Rabbi Yochanan and bar Pada.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah states the principle that just as absorbed impurity (טומאה בלועה) does not impart impurity, so absorbed purity does not become impure.
The Gemara derives the principle of טומאה בלועה (absorbed impurity) from the verse about one who eats neveilah close to sunset, where the Torah declares him pure.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the case is different because the neveilah is not fit for a ger (convert) to eat, so it is not a standard case of impurity.
The Gemara notes that this objection is resolved according to Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that both severe and light impurity apply even for a dog, so the neveilah is fit for a dog.
The Gemara objects that according to Bar Pada, who distinguishes between severe impurity for a ger and light impurity for a dog, the neveilah is not fit for a ger, so the derivation fails.
The Gemara rejects the objection, arguing that even if the neveilah is not fit for a ger in his presence, it is fit for him when he is not present (i.e., after sunset), so the derivation stands.

items.text: Gemara: Deriving taharah belu'ah via kal vachomer
items.text_en: Gemara: Deriving taharah belu'ah via kal vachomer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of taharah belu'ah and derives it via a kal vachomer from a clay vessel sealed with a tight-fitting lid, which does not prevent impurity inside from escaping but does protect purity inside from becoming impure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the source for טומאה בלועה (absorbed impurity), but from where do we derive טהרה בלועה (absorbed purity)?
