The Gemara answers with a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a clay vessel sealed with a tight-fitting lid (צמיד פתיל), which does not protect the impurity inside from escaping (as it bursts upward), nevertheless protects the purity inside from becoming impure, then certainly absorbed purity is protected.

items.text: Initial a fortiori argument: from clay vessel to person
items.text_en: Initial a fortiori argument: from clay vessel to person
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר: if a clay vessel protects its absorbed impurity from spreading, it should certainly protect its absorbed purity from becoming impure. The argument is then applied to a person, who is more stringent than a clay vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a person protects absorbed impurity inside him from spreading impurity, all the more so should absorbed purity inside him be protected from becoming impure.

An objection is raised: clay vessels have the stringency that they do not become impure from their outer side, unlike a person who does become impure from his outer side, so the a fortiori argument may not apply.
The Gemara rejects the objection, pointing out that the argument concerns impurity absorbed from the inside (תוֹכוֹ), not from the outer side (גַּבּוֹ).
The Gemara counters that clay vessels are more stringent because they transmit impurity through their airspace (מאוירו), which a person does not.

items.text: Refutation and counter-argument
items.text_en: Refutation and counter-argument
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: a clay vessel is not susceptible to impurity from its outside, unlike a person. The Gemara counters that the discussion is about inside, not outside. Then a reverse argument is made: a clay vessel is more stringent because it imparts impurity through its airspace.

sub.desc_en: An objection is raised: a clay vessel is not susceptible to impurity from its outside, unlike a person, so the a fortiori argument is invalid.
The Gemara rejects the objection, clarifying that the discussion is about impurity from the inside, not the outside.
A counter-objection is raised: a clay vessel is more stringent because it imparts impurity through its airspace, so the a fortiori argument could still be challenged.

items.text: Extension from above to below
items.text_en: Extension from above to below
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the rule for absorbed impurity above (in the mouth), but from where do we derive it for below (in the digestive tract)? A קל וחומר is proposed: if above, where no digestion occurs, protects, then below, where digestion occurs, should certainly protect. The Gemara responds that digestion below is greater, but the argument stands.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found the rule for absorbed impurity above (in the mouth), but from where do we derive it for below (in the digestive tract)?
A קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) is proposed: if above, where no digestion occurs, protects, then below, where digestion occurs, should certainly protect.
The Gemara objects: does digestion below occur except by means of above (the mouth)?
The Gemara responds: even so, digestion below is greater (so the argument stands).

items.text: Extension from person to animal
items.text_en: Extension from person to animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have the rule for absorbed impurity in a person, but from where do we derive it for an animal? A קל וחומר is proposed: if a person, who is susceptible to impurity while alive, protects absorbed impurity, then an animal, which is not susceptible while alive, should certainly protect. An objection is raised: a person requires waiting in a leprous house, unlike an animal. The Gemara counters that an animal does not require waiting, but that applies only to vessels on its back; a person also does not require waiting for such vessels, as per a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have the rule for absorbed impurity in a person, but from where do we derive it for an animal?

The Gemara proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): if a person, who is susceptible to impurity while alive, protects absorbed impurity, then an animal, which is not susceptible while alive, should certainly protect.
An objection is raised: a person requires waiting in a leprous house, unlike an animal, which weakens the analogy.
The Gemara counters that the animal's exemption from waiting applies only to vessels on its back, and a person is also exempt for such vessels.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a person carrying vessels on his shoulder is immediately impure, but if wearing them, only after waiting a fixed time, showing the person-vessel distinction.

items.text: Rava's conclusion: both principles are explicit in mishnayot
items.text_en: Rava's conclusion: both principles are explicit in mishnayot
items.desc_en: Rava declares that both principles—absorbed impurity and absorbed purity—are already taught in mishnayot. He cites a mishnah about swallowing a contaminated ring (absorbed impurity) and another about swallowing a pure ring and entering a tent of a corpse (absorbed purity). The Gemara clarifies that Rava's novel case is when one swallows two rings, one impure and one pure, where the impure does not transmit impurity to the pure.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that both principles — טומאה בלועה (absorbed impurity) and טהרה בלועה (absorbed purity) — are already taught in mishnayot.
Rava cites the mishnah about swallowing a contaminated ring, which remains impure inside and does not transmit impurity, and upon regurgitation becomes impure and transmits impurity.
Rava cites the mishnah about swallowing a pure ring and entering a tent of the dead, where the ring remains pure even after regurgitation.

sub.text: Rava's novel case clarified by the Gemara
sub.text_en: Rava's novel case clarified by the Gemara
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rava's innovation is the case of swallowing two rings—one impure and one pure—where the impure does not transmit impurity to the pure.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על טומאת עובר בחיה
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a fetus, which is like two rings (connected to the mother), can transmit impurity to the mother, unlike a ring that does not.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי העובר והחיה דומים כשתי טבעות, והעובר מטמא את החיה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a fetus, which is like two rings (connected to the mother), can transmit impurity to the mother, unlike a ring that does not.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי העובר והחיה דומים כשתי טבעות, והעובר מטמא את החיה?

items.text: Rabbah and Rava's initial responses
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rava's initial responses
items.desc_en: Rabbah answers that a fetus is different because it will eventually exit, but Rava objects that a ring does not exit. Rava then attributes the true reason to the scholars of Pumbedita, specifically Rav Yosef.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the fetus is different because it is destined to exit.
Rava objects that a ring also has a destiny to exit (when removed), so the distinction fails.
Rava says that the Pumbeditans know the reason, and identifies Rav Yosef as the source.

items.text: Rav Yosef's explanation: impurity is rabbinic
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation: impurity is rabbinic
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a tradition from Shmuel that this impurity is not Torah law but rabbinic, applying even according to Rabbi Yishmael who holds a fetus is pure, as a decree.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that this impurity is not from the Torah but from the Scribes.
The Gemara clarifies that even according to Rabbi Yishmael, who holds the fetus is pure from the Torah, the Sages decreed impurity rabbinically.

items.text: טעם הגזירה: שמא יוציא ראשו
items.text_en: Reason for the decree and objection
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya explains the decree is lest the fetus extend its head outside the womb. The Gemara objects that the same should apply to the mother, but responds that the mother feels it, and the animal is preoccupied.
items.desc: רב הושעיא מסביר: גזירה שמא יוציא ולד ראשו חוץ לפרוזדור. הגמרא מקשה: אישה נמי? ומתרצת: אישה מרגשת בעצמה, אבל חיה טרודה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reason behind the rabbinic decree of impurity for a fetus in the womb.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה הטעם שגזרו טומאה על ולד שנולד דרך דופן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the same concern should apply to a human woman giving birth, yet the fetus inside her is not considered impure by rabbinic decree.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הטעם הוא חשש הוצאת ראש, הרי גם אישה יולדת עלולה להוציא ראש, ומדוע לא גזרו בה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that a woman feels the birth process and will prevent the fetus from extending its head, but an animal is preoccupied (טרידא) with labor and cannot prevent it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הטעם הוא חשש הוצאת ראש, הרי גם אישה יולדת עלולה להוציא ראש, ומדוע לא גזרו בה?

items.text: מחלוקת רבי ישמעאל ורבי עקיבא במקרא
items.text_en: Source of the dispute: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yishmael derives from 'upon the face of the field' to exclude a fetus in the womb, while Rabbi Akiva includes the cover and side of a grave.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את שיטות רבי ישמעאל ורבי עקיבא במקרא: רבי ישמעאל דורש 'על פני השדה' להוציא עובר במעי אשה, ורבי עקיבא מרבה גולל ודופק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute between Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva is.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהי שיטת רבי ישמעאל ומהי שיטת רבי עקיבא במקרא.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael who excludes a fetus in the womb from impurity, and Rabbi Akiva who includes the cover and side of a grave.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהי שיטת רבי ישמעאל ומהי שיטת רבי עקיבא במקרא.

items.text: דרשת רבי עקיבא ורבי ישמעאל בפסוק 'הנוגע במת בנפש'
items.text_en: Derivation for Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael's alternative
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya derives for Rabbi Akiva that a fetus is impure from 'the one who touches a dead person', while Rabbi Yishmael uses that verse for a quarter-log of blood from a corpse.
items.desc: רבי אושעיה מסביר שרבי עקיבא לומד טומאת עובר מהפסוק 'הנוגע במת בנפש', ורבי ישמעאל דורש פסוק זה לרביעית דם הבאה מן המת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Since Rabbi Yishmael learns the impurity of the גולל ודופק (tombstone and side-wall) from tradition, and Rabbi Akiva holds a fetus is impure from the Torah, what is Rabbi Akiva's scriptural source?
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהצגת מחלוקת: רבי ישמעאל גולל ודופק הלכתא גמירי לה, ורבי עקיבא דורש טומאת עובר מהפסוק.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya derives from the verse 'הנוגע במת בנפש' (one who touches a dead person with a soul) that a fetus in the womb is the dead thing with a human soul, thus impure.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהצגת מחלוקת: רבי ישמעאל גולל ודופק הלכתא גמירי לה, ורבי עקיבא דורש טומאת עובר מהפסוק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yishmael uses the same verse to teach that a quarter-log of blood from a corpse is impure, so Rabbi Akiva cannot derive the fetus's impurity from it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: ורבי ישמעאל, האי קרא מיבעי ליה לרביעית דם הבאה מן המת שמטמאה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva follows his own view that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses is impure in a tent, so he does not need the verse for the quarter-log and can use it for the fetus.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהצגת מחלוקת: רבי ישמעאל גולל ודופק הלכתא גמירי לה, ורבי עקיבא דורש טומאת עובר מהפסוק.

items.text: שיטת רבי עקיבא ברביעית דם משני מתים
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's consistent view on blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva holds that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses also imparts tent impurity, derived from the verse 'upon all the souls of the dead'.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה את שיטת רבי עקיבא הסובר שרביעית דם הבאה משני מתים מטמאה באהל, כפי שנלמד מהפסוק 'ועל כל נפשות מת לא יבוא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Akiva's view on fetal impurity is consistent with his position that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses imparts tent impurity, derived from the verse 'וְעַל כׇּל נַפְשֹׁת מֵת' (upon all the souls of the dead).
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהצגת שיטת רבי עקיבא הסובר שרביעית דם הבאה משני מתים מטמאה באהל.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דין בהמה המקשה לילד
items.text_en: Mishnah: Animal struggling to give birth
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of an animal struggling to give birth where the fetus extended its hand; if the hand is cut after slaughter, the meat is pure; if before, it is impure according to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages say it is like contact with a terefah slaughtered animal.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בהמה המקשה לילד והוציא עובר את ידו: אם חתכה ואחר כך שחט את האם – הבשר טהור; אם שחט ואחר כך חתכה – הבשר מגע נבלה לדברי רבי מאיר, וחכמים אומרים מגע טרפה שחוטה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of an animal struggling to give birth, where the fetus extended its hand; if the hand is cut after slaughter, the meat is pure; if before, it is impure according to Rabbi Meir.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין בהמה המקשה לילד: אם חתך את יד העובר ואחר כך שחט את האם – הבשר טהור; אם שחט ואחר כך חתך – הבשר מגע נבלה לדברי רבי מאיר.

sub.desc_en: The Sages state that the meat is like contact with a terefah (טריפה) that was slaughtered, meaning it is impure but not as severe as a neveila (נבלה).
sub.desc: חכמים חולקים על רבי מאיר וקובעים שהבשר הוא מגע טרפה שחוטה, ולא מגע נבלה.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Slaughter of a terefah purifies it, so slaughter of a live animal should purify a limb
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Slaughter of a terefah purifies it, so slaughter of a live animal should purify a limb
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a kal vachomer argument: just as slaughter purifies a terefah (which is forbidden to eat), so too should slaughter of a live animal purify a detached limb.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma presents a kal vachomer argument: just as slaughter purifies a terefah (a dying animal), so too should slaughter of a live animal purify a detached limb.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's objection: The limb is not part of the animal's body
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's objection: The limb is not part of the animal's body
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir rejects the kal vachomer, arguing that slaughter purifies the terefah because it is the animal's own body, but a detached limb is not part of the body.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir rejects the kal vachomer, arguing that slaughter purifies the terefah because it is the animal's own body, but a detached limb is not part of the body.

items.text: Gemara's question: Source for terefah's slaughter purifying it, and counterarguments
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Source for terefah's slaughter purifying it, and counterarguments
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where it is derived that slaughter purifies a terefah, and presents a series of arguments and counterarguments comparing a terefah to a non-kosher animal and to a newborn terefah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where it is derived that the slaughter of a טריפה (torn animal) purifies it from its carcass-impurity.
An objection is raised: just as a non-kosher animal (בהמה טמאה) is forbidden for eating and its slaughter does not purify it, so too a טריפה should not be purified by slaughter.

sub.text: First answer (distinction of a period of fitness)
sub.text_en: First answer (distinction of a period of fitness)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: the comparison fails because a non-kosher animal never had a period of fitness (שעת הכושר), whereas a טריפה did.

The Gemara counters: take away your argument — what about a טריפה born from the womb (נולדה טריפה מן הבטן), which never had a period of fitness; from where is it derived that its slaughter purifies it?

sub.text: Second answer (distinction of species having slaughter)
sub.text_en: Second answer (distinction of species having slaughter)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: the comparison to a non-kosher animal fails because a non-kosher animal's species has no valid slaughter at all, whereas a טריפה belongs to a species that does have slaughter (יש במינה שחיטה).

items.text: משנת בן שמונה חי
items.text_en: Mishnah: An eight-month fetus's slaughter does not purify
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that slaughter of a live eight-month fetus does not purify it, because its species (being non-viable) has no valid slaughter.
items.desc: המשנה מובאת: בן שמונה חי (עובר בן חודש שמיני) שחיטתו אינה מטהרתו, כי אין במינו שחיטה (הוא נחשב כנפל). זהו חיזוק לדברי חכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that slaughter of a live eight-month fetus does not purify it, because its species (being non-viable) has no valid slaughter.
sub.desc: מובאת משנה הקובעת שאין שחיטת בן שמונה מטהרתו, מפני שאינו נחשב מין שחיטה – חיזוק לעמדת חכמים.

items.text: גמרא – שאלת בית הסתרים
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why is the limb impure? It is hidden impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the limb from a live eight-month fetus is impure, arguing that it is hidden impurity (בית הסתרים) which does not transmit impurity, and suggests this follows Rabbi Meir's view.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מדוע שחיטת בן שמונה אינה מטהרת? הרי הטומאה היא טומאת בית הסתרים, שאינה מטמאה! ומציעה לומר שרבי מאיר לשיטתו, שהטומאה כן מטמאת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to state this, since the fetus's impurity is a טומאת בית הסתרים (concealed impurity) which normally does not transmit impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מדוע שחיטת בן שמונה אינה מטהרת, והלא טומאה זו היא טומאת בית הסתרים שאינה מטמאה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir's reasoning, who holds that concealed impurity can transmit impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מדוע שחיטת בן שמונה אינה מטהרת, והלא טומאה זו היא טומאת בית הסתרים שאינה מטמאה?

items.text: דיון במשנת שלש על שלש ופירושה
items.text_en: Supporting Mishnah: Rabbi Meir's view on impurity of a divided cloth
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules that a 3x3 handbreadth cloth that is split is pure from midras impurity but impure from contact with midras, and Rabbi Yosei objects, explaining the impurity is from contact with a zav.
items.desc: מובאת המשנה: שלש על שלש שנחלק – טהור ממדרס, ופירושה: לדעת רבי מאיר הטומאה נמשכת גם לאחר פירוק. רבי יוסי חולק. עולא מבחין בין חתיכה קטנה לחלק מבגד גדול. רבינא מוסיף: בגד אינו עומד להיחתך, אך עובר עומד להיחתך (ויש דין מיוחד).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir rules that a 3x3 handbreadth cloth that is split is pure from midras impurity but impure from contact with midras.
sub.desc: הבאת המשנה 'שלש על שלש שנחלק – טהור מן המדרס' כראיה לדיון.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei objects, explaining that the impurity is actually from contact with a zav, not from midras.

items.text: תירוץ עולא – שעת פרישה
items.text_en: Ulla's distinction: Only when the cloth is split, but when separated from a larger garment it receives impurity
items.desc_en: Ulla explains that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to a cloth that was split, but a 3x3 piece separated from a larger garment receives impurity from its source at the time of separation; similarly, the limb receives impurity from the animal at the time of separation.
items.desc: עולא מסביר: ההבדל הוא שבשעת פרישה, חתיכת בגד קטנה אינה מקבלת טומאה, אבל חתיכת עובר הנפרדת מהאם מקבלת טומאה. כאן מדובר באבר שנפרש מהגוף, ולכן מקבל טומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that Ulla said the Mishnah's ruling about a 3x3 cloth being pure from midras applies only when the cloth was split.
sub.desc: עולא מתרץ: לא שנו אלא שלושה על שלושה שנחלק.

sub.desc_en: Ulla explains that a 3x3 piece separated from a larger garment receives impurity from its source at the time of separation.
sub.desc: עולא מבהיר: ההבדל הוא שבשעת פרישה, חתיכת בגד קטנה אינה מקבלת טומאה, אבל חתיכת עובר הנפרדת מהאם מקבלת טומאה. כאן מדובר באבר שנפרש מהגוף, ולכן מקבל טומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies Ulla's principle to the case of the limb: at the time of its separation from the animal, it receives impurity from the animal.
sub.desc: עולא מבהיר: ההבדל הוא שבשעת פרישה, חתיכת בגד קטנה אינה מקבלת טומאה, אבל חתיכת עובר הנפרדת מהאם מקבלת טומאה. כאן מדובר באבר שנפרש מהגוף, ולכן מקבל טומאה.

items.text: סיום – דברי רבינא
items.text_en: Ravina's distinction: A garment is not destined to be cut, but a fetus is destined to be cut
items.desc_en: Ravina distinguishes between a garment, which is not intended to be cut into pieces, and a fetus, which is destined to be cut (i.e., the limb is considered separate from the start), so the limb does not receive impurity from the animal.
items.desc: רבינא מחדד: בגד אינו עשוי להיחתך, אבל עובר עשוי להיחתך (נולד או מנותק), ולכן יש לו דין מיוחד שמקבל טומאה בעת הפרישה.

sub.desc_en: Ravina offers a different explanation: a garment is not destined to be cut, but a fetus is destined to be cut (separated), so the principle of 'standing to be cut' applies and the Mishnah's ruling is needed.
sub.desc: רבינא מבחין בין בגד שאינו עומד להיחתך לעובר שעומד להיחתך, ובכך מיישב את הדין שנותן לעובר טומאה בזמן ההפרשה.

items.text: Gemara's initial analysis: comparing the fetus to a detached handle
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis: comparing the fetus to a detached handle
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the fetus is considered like a detached limb (כְּחָתוּךְ דָּמֵי), and compares this to Rabbi Meir's view in a Mishnah about long handles of vessels, where he rules that immersion up to the measured point suffices, while the Sages require full immersion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the fetus is considered like a detached limb (כְּחָתוּךְ דָּמֵי) and compares this to Rabbi Meir's view in a Mishnah about long handles of vessels.
The Sages require full immersion of the handle, contrasting with Rabbi Meir's lenient position.

items.text: Alternative explanation and resolution of the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and resolution of the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: even according to the Sages, the fetus is considered as if it were separated (חִבּוּרֵי אֳכָלִין כְּמַאן דְּמִפַּרְתִי דָּמֵי) and merely touching. It then resolves a discrepancy between Ulla and Ravina regarding the Mishnah's use of 'חֲתָכָהּ' in both the first and second clauses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: even according to the Sages, the fetus is considered as if it were separated (חִבּוּרֵי אֳכָלִין כְּמַאן דְּמִפַּרְתִי דָּמֵי) and merely touching.
The Gemara resolves a discrepancy between Ulla and Ravina regarding the Mishnah's use of 'חֲתָכָהּ' in both the first and second clauses.

items.text: The Sages' proof from a tereifah and the kal vachomer argument
items.text_en: The Sages' proof from a tereifah and the kal vachomer argument
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that a tereifah that was slaughtered is tamei in the case of consecrated animals, as per the father of Shmuel. They then draw a kal vachomer: just as slaughter purifies a tereifah from neveilah, so too should the slaughter of the mother purify the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Sages assert that a tereifah that was slaughtered conveys טומאה (ritual impurity) in consecrated animals, citing the father of Shmuel's ruling.
The Sages draw a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument): just as slaughter purifies a tereifah from neveilah status, so too should the mother's slaughter purify the fetus.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's objection and the Sages' response with the Mishnah of the fetus
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's objection and the Sages' response with the Mishnah of the fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir objects: if slaughter purifies the fetus from neveilah, it should also permit it for eating. The Sages respond that slaughter has more power over what is not part of the mother's body than over her own body, citing the Mishnah that a fetus cut from the womb is permitted for eating, while a limb from the mother is not.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir objects: if the mother's slaughter purifies the fetus from the status of neveilah (carcass), it should also permit it for eating.

The Sages respond that slaughter has more power over what is not part of the mother's body than over her own body, citing the Mishnah that a fetus cut from the womb is permitted for eating, while a limb from the mother is not.

items.text: Rava's correction of the Mishnah's text and the refined debate
items.text_en: Rava's correction of the Mishnah's text and the refined debate
items.desc_en: Rava (or some say Kedi) explains that the Mishnah is missing a line: Rabbi Meir said 'If so, permit it for eating!' and the Sages replied with the proof from a tereifah. Rabbi Meir then countered that a tereifah is its own body, while the fetus is not, and the Sages again cited the Mishnah about the fetus being permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's text actually means.
Rava (or some say Kedi) explains that the Mishnah is missing a line: Rabbi Meir said 'If so, permit it for eating!' and the Sages replied with the proof from a tereifah.
Rabbi Meir counters that a tereifah is its own body, while the fetus is not, so the analogy fails.
The Sages again cite the Mishnah about the fetus being permitted while the spleen and kidneys are forbidden, showing that the fetus has a special leniency.

items.text: A baraita with a different version of the debate including a detached limb
items.text_en: A baraita with a different version of the debate including a detached limb
items.desc_en: A baraita presents a version where Rabbi Meir argues that slaughter purifies a tereifah and its detached limb, so it should purify the fetus. The Sages respond with the same Mishnah about the fetus being permitted for eating, showing the greater power of slaughter over what is not part of the body.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that presents a version of the debate where Rabbi Meir asks whether the mother's slaughter purifies the limb from neveila status.
Rabbi Meir argues that if slaughter purifies the detached limb, it should also permit the fetus for eating, since the fetus is not part of the mother's body.

The Sages respond that slaughter has greater power over what is not part of the body, citing the Mishnah that a fetus cut from the womb is permitted for eating, while a limb from the mother's body is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on the scope of the disagreement
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on the scope of the disagreement
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish says the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies equally to fetuses and limbs. Rabbi Yochanan limits it to a limb of a fetus, but for a limb of the mother, all agree that slaughter makes it a neveilah. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: a limb of the mother can be reattached, but a fetus cannot.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies equally to fetuses and to limbs.
Rabbi Yochanan limits the dispute to a limb of a fetus, but for a limb of the mother, all agree that slaughter makes it a neveilah.
Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: a limb of the mother can be reattached, but a fetus cannot.

items.text: Objection from a baraita against Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita against Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir explicitly mentions a detached limb of a tereifah, implying the dispute applies to limbs as well, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Meir explicitly mentions a detached limb of a tereifah, implying the dispute applies to limbs as well, challenging Rabbi Yochanan's position.

items.text: Initial challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Initial challenge to Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Resh Lakish's position is consistent, but Rabbi Yochanan's view is difficult because he distinguishes between a limb from a fetus and a limb from an animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Resh Lakish's position is consistent because he treats a limb from a fetus and a limb from an animal identically.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yochanan's view is difficult because he distinguishes between a limb from a fetus and a limb from an animal.

items.text: Revised statement of the dispute
items.text_en: Revised statement of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara rephrases the dispute: Resh Lakish says the disagreement applies to both fetal and animal limbs, while Rabbi Yochanan says the disagreement is only about a fetal limb, but for an animal limb all agree slaughter does not cause neveilah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises the dispute: Resh Lakish says the disagreement applies to both fetal and animal limbs, while Rabbi Yochanan says the disagreement is only about a fetal limb, but for an animal limb all agree slaughter does not cause neveilah.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains that according to Rabbi Yochanan, a fetal limb is considered part of the mother's body, while an animal limb is not, hence the difference.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina explains Rabbi Yochanan's reasoning: a fetal limb is considered part of the mother's body (גופה), while an animal limb is not (לאו גופה), hence the difference in status.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's universal principle
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's universal principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that all agree death causes neveilah status, but slaughter does not cause neveilah status.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states a universal principle: all agree that death causes neveilah status (ניפּוּל), but slaughter does not cause neveilah status.

items.text: Gemara's question about the context
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the context
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case Rabbi Yochanan refers to, since if it is a fetal limb there is disagreement, and if it is an animal limb the Mishnah already teaches both death and slaughter cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case Rabbi Yochanan refers to, since if it is a fetal limb there is disagreement, and if it is an animal limb the Mishnah already teaches both death and slaughter cases.

items.text: Mishnah sources for death and slaughter
items.text_en: Mishnah sources for death and slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: for a dead animal, Rabbi Meir says the limb is tamei as an eiver min hachai but not as neveilah; for a slaughtered animal, Rabbi Meir says the blood makes the flesh susceptible, while Rabbi Shimon disagrees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah regarding a dead animal: Rabbi Meir rules that the limb is טמא (impure) as an איבר מן החי (limb from a living animal) but not as an איבר מן הנבלה (limb from a carcass).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah regarding a slaughtered animal: Rabbi Meir says the blood makes the flesh susceptible to טומאה (impurity), while Rabbi Shimon disagrees.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's statement about susceptibility might refer only to the flesh, not the limb, and a teaching is needed to include the limb despite its severe impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possible misinterpretation: from the Mishnah one might think 'הוכשרו' (they were made susceptible) refers only to the flesh, not the limb.

The Gemara objects that the term 'הוכשרו' (they were made susceptible) is plural, implying two distinct susceptibilities: one for flesh detached from the animal and one for flesh detached from the limb.

The Gemara resolves that the teaching is necessary because one might have thought that since the limb conveys severe impurity (טומאה חמורה) through its parent, it would not require הכשר (susceptibility), so the Mishnah teaches that it does.

items.text: Support from a baraisa and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Support from a baraisa and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says to hold Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's teaching, as Rabbah bar bar Chanah supports it with a baraisa about a detached limb being forbidden even after slaughter, citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef instructs to hold firmly to Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's teaching.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing a baraisa and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing a baraisa and Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef supports the teaching by citing that Rabbah bar bar Chanah aligns with it, bringing a baraisa about a detached limb being forbidden even after slaughter, and citing Rabbi Yochanan.

items.text: Opening statement: the principle of 'mitzvat perush'
items.text_en: Opening statement: the principle of 'mitzvat perush'
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous discussion concluded that there is only a requirement to separate (mitzvat perush) but no actual prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the previous discussion concluded that there is only a requirement to separate (מצות פרוש) but no actual prohibition.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta regarding eating a limb from a living animal
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta regarding eating a limb from a living animal
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rav Yehudah said Rav ruled that one who eats such a limb is lashed. A certain rabbi objects, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav that one is not lashed. Rav Huna asks whom to rely on, and Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between death (which causes neveilah status) and slaughter (which does not).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports that Rav Yehudah said Rav ruled that one who eats a limb from a living animal is lashed.
A certain rabbi objects, citing Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta in the name of Rav that one is not lashed.
Rav Huna asks whom to rely on given the conflicting reports from Rav.
Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between death (which causes neveilah status) and slaughter (which does not).

items.text: Rava's proof that death causes neveilah but slaughter does not
items.text_en: Rava's proof that death causes neveilah but slaughter does not
items.desc_en: Rava cites a verse about carcasses falling and conveying impurity, deducing that death causes neveilah but slaughter does not. Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects that the verse refers to creeping things, but Rava responds that it can be applied to animals. The Gemara notes that two instances of 'bemotam' are written, addressing another potential difficulty.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks for the source of the rabbinic principle that death causes neveilah (a carcass that conveys impurity) but slaughter does not, and derives it from the verse 'וכל אשר יפול עליו מהם במותם יטמא' (and anything on which any of them falls when dead shall become impure), arguing that the phrase 'במותם' (when they die) excludes slaughter.

Rav Adda bar Ahavah objects that the verse is written about creeping things (שרצים), not animals; Rava responds that if the verse is not needed for creeping things (which are not subject to slaughter), apply it to animals.

The Gemara notes that the verse is still needed to teach that only moist (fresh) carcasses convey impurity, not dry ones, but resolves that two instances of 'במותם' (when they die) are written in the Torah, one for each teaching.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah regarding a limb from a live or dead fetus
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbah regarding a limb from a live or dead fetus
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the dispute about whether slaughter causes neveilah applies only to a limb from a live fetus, but all agree that slaughter causes neveilah for a limb from a dead fetus. Rabbah argues that the dispute applies equally to both cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that the dispute (about whether slaughter causes neveila status) applies only to a limb from a live fetus, but for a limb from a dead fetus all agree slaughter causes neveila; Rabbah disagrees, saying the dispute applies to both cases.
Rabbah argues that the dispute applies equally to both a limb from a live fetus and a limb from a dead fetus.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about an eight-month-old live fetus
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about an eight-month-old live fetus
items.desc_en: A baraita states that an eight-month-old live fetus proves that even though its species is subject to slaughter, its own slaughter does not purify it. Rav Kahana explains that the fetus has slaughter through its mother, and the tanna of our Mishnah does not object to this point.

sub.desc_en: The gemara challenges the Mishnah's ruling about an eight-month-old live fetus by citing a baraita that says such a fetus's own slaughter does not purify it.
Rav Kahana explains that the fetus has slaughter through its mother, and the tanna of our Mishnah does not object to this point.

items.text: Source for a tereifah's slaughter purifying it
items.text_en: Source for a tereifah's slaughter purifying it
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the tanna who objects, the source that slaughter of a tereifah purifies it is derived from Rav Yehudah citing Rav, or from a baraita that interprets the verse 'When an animal dies' to exclude a tereifah that was slaughtered.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: for the Tanna who objects, from where does he derive that slaughter of a treifa purifies it? It answers from Rav Yehuda citing Rav, who derives from the verse 'וכי ימות מן הבהמה' that part of an animal conveys impurity and part does not, namely a treifa that was slaughtered.
The Gemara answers: he derives it from Rav Yehudah citing Rav, or alternatively from a baraita.
The baraita interprets the verse 'וְכִי יָמוּת מִן הַבְּהֵמָה' (When an animal dies) to exclude a tereifah that was slaughtered, showing that its slaughter purifies it.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's query about slaughtering a nine-month-old fetus inside the mother
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's query about slaughtering a nine-month-old fetus inside the mother
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether inserting one's hand into the mother's womb and slaughtering a live nine-month-old fetus is effective. He considers both Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' positions. Rav Chananya brings a proof from a case of a tereifah born from the womb, but Rava deflects by saying the baraita refers to a tereifah with five legs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether inserting one's hand into the mother's womb and slaughtering a live nine-month-old fetus is effective, and notes that the question applies to both Rabbi Meir's and the Sages' positions.

sub.text: Gemara's elaboration of the query regarding Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Gemara's elaboration of the query regarding Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Gemara elaborates that the query regarding Rabbi Meir is whether his requirement of slaughter for a live nine-month-old fetus applies only when it has emerged into the air of the world, but not while still inside the mother's womb.

sub.text: Gemara's alternative possibility regarding the Sages
sub.text_en: Gemara's alternative possibility regarding the Sages
sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises the alternative possibility that even according to the Sages, the Torah may have permitted four simanim (the shechita organs) for the fetus inside the womb.

Rav Chananya brings a proof from a baraita about a tereifah born from the womb, arguing that if slaughter inside the womb were effective, one could have inserted his hand and slaughtered it while it was still inside.

Rava deflects the proof by explaining that the baraita refers to a tereifah that was created with a defect from the womb, such as one with five legs, which never had a moment of fitness for slaughter.

items.text: Mishnah: Slaughtering an animal and finding a fetus
items.text_en: Mishnah: Slaughtering an animal and finding a fetus
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one slaughters an animal and finds an eight-month-old fetus (live or dead) or a nine-month-old dead fetus, one tears it and removes its blood. If a nine-month-old live fetus is found, it requires its own slaughter and is subject to the law of 'oto v'et bno' according to Rabbi Meir, while the Sages say its mother's slaughter purifies it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for an eight-month-old fetus (live or dead) or a nine-month-old dead fetus found in a slaughtered animal: one tears it and removes its blood.

The Mishnah presents Rabbi Meir's position: a live nine-month-old fetus requires its own slaughter and is subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition against slaughtering a parent and offspring on the same day).
The Mishnah concludes with the Sages' dissenting position: the mother's slaughter purifies the live nine-month-old fetus, so it does not require its own slaughter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri states that even a five-year-old fetus plowing in the field is purified by its mother's slaughter, but a live nine-month fetus requires its own slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri rules that even a five-year-old fetus plowing in the field is purified by its mother's slaughter, but a live nine-month fetus requires its own slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of Rabbi Elazar's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya initially says the Mishnah's leniency applies only to slaughter, excluding fat and sinew. After objections from a baraita about Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's dispute on the fat of a nine-month fetus, the Gemara revises the statement to apply only to eating, excluding bestiality and plowing.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya states that the Mishnah's leniency applies only to slaughter, excluding fat and sinew.
The Gemara objects that if the fat referred to is that of a fetus, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda already dispute its status, as cited in a baraita.
The Gemara rejects that interpretation and objects that even if the fat is from the sciatic nerve, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda still dispute its status.

sub.text: Revised statement of Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Revised statement of Rabbi Elazar quoting Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara revises Rabbi Elazar's statement to apply only to eating, excluding bestiality and plowing.

items.text: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on the blood of a fetus
items.text_en: Dispute between Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on the blood of a fetus
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that one who permits the fat of a fetus also permits its blood, while Rabbi Yochanan says even the permitter forbids its blood. Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita requiring removal of blood, and Rabbi Zeira explains it means no karet penalty. The Gemara clarifies that for Rabbi Yehuda, the blood of a fetus is like blood of exudation, but Rav Yosef resolves that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes based on whether the mother's blood would incur karet.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one who permits the fat of a fetus also permits its blood, and one who forbids its fat also forbids its blood.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, asserting that even the one who permits the fat forbids its blood.
Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita that requires tearing open the fetus and removing its blood, supporting his position.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the baraita only means there is no karet penalty for the blood, not that it is entirely permitted.
The Gemara asks: to which authority does Rabbi Zeira's explanation refer? It answers: to Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita is cited: blood of exudation (דַּם הַתַּמְצִית) is subject to a prohibition, but Rabbi Yehuda says it incurs karet.

Rav Yosef resolves before Rav Pappa that Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes based on the verse 'דָּם' and 'כׇל דָּם': wherever one is liable for the blood of the soul (דַּם הַנֶּפֶשׁ), he is also liable for blood of exudation; otherwise not.

items.text: Inquiry about redeeming a firstborn with a ben pekuah
items.text_en: Inquiry about redeeming a firstborn with a ben pekuah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a fetus found alive (ben pekuah) can be used to redeem a firstborn donkey. For Rabbi Meir, who requires its slaughter, it is a valid sheep. For the Rabbis, who say its mother's slaughter purifies it, the question is whether it is like meat in a basket or still called a sheep. Mar Zutra forbids, Rav Ashi permits, and they debate via a gezerah shavah from the Passover offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a ben pekuah (fetus found alive in its slaughtered mother) can be used to redeem a firstborn donkey, and clarifies that for Rabbi Meir, who requires its slaughter, it is a valid sheep.
The Gemara refines the question for the Rabbis, who hold that the mother's slaughter purifies the fetus, asking whether it is like meat in a basket or still called a sheep.
Mar Zutra forbids redeeming with a ben pekuah, while Rav Ashi permits it.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's objection to Mar Zutra
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection to Mar Zutra
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges Mar Zutra, asking if he derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שה' (sheep) used in the Passover offering.

The Gemara objects that if the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) were applied strictly, it would require the redeeming animal to be male, unblemished, and a year old, but the additional גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'תפדה' (redeem) expands the possibilities.
The Gemara further objects that if the expansion from 'תפדה' (redeem) includes everything, then the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from 'שה' (sheep) would be superfluous.

items.text: Dispute on impurity status of a ben pekuah
items.text_en: Dispute on impurity status of a ben pekuah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a ben pekuah can contract first and second degree impurity. Rabbi Yochanan says yes, Resh Lakish says no, comparing it to a nut rattling in its shell. They exchange objections: Resh Lakish cites a baraita about the meat being like a neveilah, and Rabbi Yochanan cites a case of crossing a river or entering a cemetery to argue it is a separate entity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a ben pekuah can contract first and second degree impurity.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that a ben pekuah can contract first and second degree impurity.
Resh Lakish rules that a ben pekuah cannot contract impurity, comparing it to a nut rattling in its shell.

sub.text: Resh Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Meir calls the meat 'מגע נבלה' (contact with a neveilah), implying it is a single entity with the mother.
The Sages in the same baraita call the meat 'מגע טריפה שחוטה' (contact with a slaughtered tereifah), offering a different impurity status.

sub.text: Resh Lakish's argument from the baraita
sub.text_en: Resh Lakish's argument from the baraita
sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish argues that his view (single entity) explains why the meat is rendered susceptible by the mother's blood, challenging Rabbi Yochanan to explain how it becomes susceptible.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's response to Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's response to Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan answers that the meat becomes susceptible through its own shechita, following Rabbi Shimon's opinion.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Resh Lakish
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Resh Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects by citing a baraita about a ben pekuah that crossed a river (becomes susceptible) or entered a cemetery (becomes impure), implying it is a separate entity.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan's argument from the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's argument from the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan argues that his view (two separate bodies) explains why susceptibility depends on external factors, while Resh Lakish's view (single entity) would mean it is already susceptible by the mother's blood.

items.text: Opening statement: the case of a dry slaughter
items.text_en: Opening statement: the case of a dry slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by referencing a case of slaughtering a dry (non-bleeding) animal, and notes that this does not follow Rabbi Shimon's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the case of a dry slaughter does not follow Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna: Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan identifies the Tanna who holds that crossing a river makes an animal susceptible to impurity, and visiting a cemetery makes it impure, as Rabbi Yose HaGelili. He then links Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view with Beit Shammai's view on when fish become susceptible to impurity, with the difference being a fish that is still convulsing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that crossing a river makes an animal susceptible to impurity and visiting a cemetery makes it impure.

Rabbi Yochanan identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yose HaGelili, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGelili holds that a live animal can contract food impurity and requires susceptibility, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan consistently holds that Rabbi Yose HaGelili and Beit Shammai said the same thing.

The Gemara elaborates: Rabbi Yose HaGelili's view is as stated, and Beit Shammai's view is from a Mishnah where Beit Shammai says fish become susceptible to impurity when caught, Beit Hillel says when they die, and Rabbi Akiva says when they can no longer live.
The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the opinions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the difference is a fish that is still convulsing after being caught.

items.text: Rav Chisda's query: signs of tereifah in fish
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's query: signs of tereifah in fish
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether signs of tereifah in fish affect their status as living creatures, considering the debate about whether a tereifah is considered alive. The query remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether fish that develop signs of טריפה (a fatal condition) are considered alive or dead, noting that the question applies to both sides of the debate about whether a טריפה is considered alive.

The Gemara elaborates on the query: even for those who say a טריפה is alive, perhaps fish have less vitality; and even for those who say a טריפה is not alive, perhaps fish are different because they have no שחיטה (ritual slaughter). The query remains unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on fat of a live fetus
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish on fat of a live fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish argue about the status of fat from a live nine-month-old fetus found inside a slaughtered animal. Rabbi Yochanan says its fat is like that of a domesticated animal (forbidden), while Reish Lakish says it is like that of a wild animal (permitted). They debate whether the cause is the air (of the womb) or the months (of gestation).

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan rules that the fat of a live nine-month-old fetus found inside a slaughtered animal is like the forbidden fat of a domesticated animal (בהמה), while Reish Lakish rules it is like the permitted fat of a wild animal (חיה).

The gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan attributes the status to the air of the womb (אוירא), which makes the fetus like a domesticated animal, while Reish Lakish attributes it to the completed months of gestation (חדשים), which make it like a wild animal.

An alternative version reframes the dispute: both agree that an incomplete-term fetus is nothing; they argue only about a live nine-month fetus removed from the womb by hand, where Rabbi Yochanan says months cause the status (forbidden) and Reish Lakish says both months and air cause it (permitted).

items.text: Scriptural challenge and response
items.text_en: Scriptural challenge and response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish from the verse about the fat and kidneys of the guilt-offering, which excludes a fetus. Reish Lakish responds that his view also derives from there. An alternative version has Reish Lakish challenging Rabbi Yochanan, who responds that the fetus is lacking time (not yet fully developed).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish by citing the verse about the fat and kidneys of the guilt-offering, which excludes a fetus (שליל), arguing that this supports his own view.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that for his own view the verse is needed to exclude the fetus, but for Reish Lakish's view the exclusion is unnecessary.
Reish Lakish responds that his own view also derives from this same verse.
An alternative version reverses the roles: Reish Lakish challenges Rabbi Yochanan with the same verse.
Reish Lakish argues that for his own view the verse excludes the fetus, but for Rabbi Yochanan's view the fetus should be offered as a sacrifice.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that the fetus is lacking time (not yet fully developed), so it is excluded from sacrifice.

items.text: Ruling on slaughtering a tereifah and finding a live fetus
items.text_en: Ruling on slaughtering a tereifah and finding a live fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ami and Rava discuss the case of slaughtering a tereifah and finding a live nine-month-old fetus. Rabbi Ami says that according to the one who forbids the fetus (as a tereifah), it is permitted, and vice versa. Rava argues that even the one who permits the fetus would permit it, because the Torah made it fit through four signs (simanim). Rav Chisda begins a related statement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami states that if one slaughters a טריפה (ritually unfit animal) and finds a live nine-month-old fetus, according to the one who forbids the fetus (Rabbi Meir), the fetus is permitted, and according to the one who permits it (the Rabbis), it is forbidden.
Rava argues that even according to the one who permits the fetus (the Rabbis), it is permitted, because the Torah made it fit through four סימנים (shechita organs).
Rav Chisda begins a related statement about one who slaughters a טריפה (ritually unfit animal) and finds a live nine-month-old fetus, but the statement is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a ben pekuah found alive requires shechita, is subject to the gifts of the foreleg, cheeks, and maw, and if it dies, it is pure from conveying impurity through carrying.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that a ben pekuah found alive requires shechita, is subject to the gifts of the foreleg, cheeks, and maw, and if it dies, it is pure from conveying impurity through carrying.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding Rava's question
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution regarding Rava's question
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the mishnah's consistency: requiring shechita aligns with Rabbi Meir, but purity from carrying aligns with the Rabbis. The Gemara notes a similar beraita by Rabbi Chiyya, and resolves that Rabbi Chiyya refers to a case where the fetus was already found dead. Rava then explains that the Torah permitted four simanim (signs) for the ben pekuah.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges the mishnah's inconsistency: requiring shechita aligns with Rabbi Meir, but purity from carrying aligns with the Rabbis.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya's beraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya's beraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that a similar beraita by Rabbi Chiyya presents the same inconsistency.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chiyya refers to a case where the fetus was already found dead, but Rava's own challenge remains.
Rava explains that his own challenge is not difficult, because the Torah permitted four simanim (signs) for the ben pekuah.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's encounter and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's encounter and the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Zeira ascended, he found Rav Asi sitting and teaching this halakha. Rabbi Zeira affirmed it and added that Rabbi Yochanan said the same, implying that Resh Lakish disagreed. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Zeira either delayed or drank and was silent about the disagreement.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira finds Rav Asi teaching the halakha and affirms it, adding that Rabbi Yochanan said the same.
The Gemara infers from Rabbi Zeira's silence that Resh Lakish disagreed with Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Zeira's silence was due to delay or drink, not disagreement.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's opinion and the distinction by Rav Kahana
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's opinion and the distinction by Rav Kahana
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri permits even more, but the Gemara questions how his view differs from the Tanna Kamma. Rav Kahana explains the difference: the case where the animal's hoof was split on the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's opinion that even more cases are permitted.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's opinion differs from the Tanna Kamma (first Tanna).
Rav Kahana explains the difference: the case where the animal's hoof was split on the ground (הפריס על גבי קרקע) distinguishes their positions.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's ruling on a ben pekuah mating with a regular animal
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's ruling on a ben pekuah mating with a regular animal
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya states that according to the one who is concerned for the father's lineage, if a ben pekuah mates with a regular animal, the offspring has no remedy (is forbidden).

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya rules that according to the opinion concerned with paternal lineage, if a ben pekuah mates with a regular animal, the offspring has no remedy.

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a kalu ben pekuah
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a kalu ben pekuah
items.desc_en: Abaye states that everyone agrees that a kalu (cloven-hoofed) ben pekuah is permitted, because such an unusual thing is remembered. An alternative version says a kalu ben kalu ben pekuah is permitted because two unusual things are remembered.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that everyone agrees a kalu (cloven-hoofed) ben pekuah is permitted because such an unusual thing is remembered.
An alternative version reports Abaye ruling that a kalu ben kalu ben pekuah is permitted because two unusual things are remembered.

items.text: Dispute between Ze'iri/Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan on the extent of permission
items.text_en: Dispute between Ze'iri/Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan on the extent of permission
items.desc_en: Ze'iri quoting Rabbi Chanina says the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who permits the ben pekuah's son and grandson forever. Rabbi Yochanan says the ben pekuah itself is permitted, but its son is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Ze'iri in the name of Rabbi Chanina rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who permits the ben pekuah's son and grandson forever.
Rabbi Yochanan objects, stating that the ben pekuah itself is permitted, but its offspring is forbidden.

items.text: Practical case before Rav Ashi and resolution
items.text_en: Practical case before Rav Ashi and resolution
items.desc_en: Adda bar Chavu had a ben pekuah that a wolf attacked; he came before Rav Ashi, who told him to slaughter it. Adda objected based on Ze'iri's ruling that Rabbi Shimon Shezuri permits even descendants. Rav Ashi replied that Rabbi Yochanan's statement was only according to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view. The Gemara then cites Ravin bar Chanina quoting Ulla quoting Rabbi Chanina that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri everywhere. Rav Ashi ultimately follows Rabbi Yonatan, who says the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri only in cases of danger (mesukan) and demai tithes.

sub.desc_en: Adda bar Chavu had a ben pekuah (an animal born from a slaughtered mother) that a wolf attacked; he came before Rav Ashi, who told him to slaughter it.
Adda objects that Ze'iri ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, who permits even descendants, and even Rabbi Yochanan only forbids the son but permits the animal itself.
Rav Ashi replies that Rabbi Yochanan's statement was only according to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view, not as a universal ruling.

sub.text: Adda bar Chavu's second objection (citing Ravin bar Chanina)
sub.text_en: Adda bar Chavu's second objection (citing Ravin bar Chanina)
sub.desc_en: Adda further objects citing Ravin bar Chanina quoting Ulla quoting Rabbi Chanina that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri everywhere.
Rav Ashi rules according to Rabbi Yonatan, who says the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon Shezuri only in cases of danger (mesukan) and demai tithes.
The Gemara cites a baraita about a person in danger (mesukan) who orders a get, where Rabbi Shimon ben Shezuri permits even the dangerously ill.
The Gemara cites a baraita about demai tithes that returned to their place, where Rabbi Shimon ben Shezuri permits even on a weekday to ask and eat on his word.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an animal's leg is cut below the knee joint (ארכובה), it is kosher; if above, it is a terefah. Similarly, if the צומת הגידין is removed, the animal is a terefah. If the bone is broken but most of the flesh remains, shechitah renders it kosher; otherwise, it does not.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שבהמה שנחתכו רגליה מהארכובה ולמטה כשרה, ולמעלה פסולה, וכן אם ניטל צומת הגידים. כמו כן, אם נשבר העצם ורוב הבשר קיים, השחיטה מטהרת אותו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rules for an animal whose leg is cut below or above the knee joint (ארכובה), and for a broken bone with most flesh remaining.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת דין בהמה שנחתכו רגליה מהארכובה ולמטה ולמעלה, וכן דין צומת הגידים ושבר עצם עם רוב בשר.

items.text: בירור מיקום הארכובה
items.text_en: Gemara's initial clarification of the knee
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya explains that 'below' means below the knee joint, and 'above' means above it. The knee in question is the one sold with the head. Ulla citing Rabbi Oshaya adds that in a camel, the corresponding point is recognizable.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רבי חייא מפרש ש'למטה' ו'למעלה' הם ביחס לארכובה הנמכרת עם הראש. עולא בשם רבי אושעיא מוסיף שסימנה בגמל ניכר.

sub.text: רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי חייא
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya defines 'below' as below the knee joint and 'above' as above it, specifying the knee sold with the head.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי חייא מבאר ש'למטה' ו'למעלה' במשנה נאמרו ביחס לארכובה הנמכרת עם הראש.

sub.desc_en: Ulla citing Rabbi Oshaya adds that in a camel, the corresponding point is recognizable.
sub.desc: עולא בשם רבי אושעיא מוסיף סימן היכר לארכובה זו: כנגדה בגמל ניכר.

items.text: קושיית עולא ותשובת רב יהודה
items.text_en: Ulla's challenge to Rav Yehuda and Rav Yehuda's response
items.desc_en: Ulla challenges Rav Yehuda: according to Ulla's view, the Mishnah's mention of 'and similarly if the צומת הגידין was removed' is consistent, but according to Rav Yehuda, what does it mean? Rav Yehuda initially answers that the Mishnah refers to two separate cases: the knee without the צומת הגידין, and the צומת הגידין without the knee. Ulla objects that the Mishnah says 'cut', not 'removed'. Rav Yehuda is silent. Later, he regrets not answering that 'below' means below the knee and 'above' means above the צומת הגידין, but then realizes the Mishnah says 'from the knee and above', which would not fit.
items.desc: עולא מקשה על רב יהודה: לשיטתו, מהי המשמעות של 'וכן שניטל צומת הגידין'? רב יהודה עונה שהכוונה לרכובה בלא צומת הגידים או צומת הגידים בלא רכובה. לאחר שתיקה, רב יהודה מהרהר שהיה יכול לתרץ אחרת, אך דוחה זאת.

sub.desc_en: Ulla challenges Rav Yehuda: according to Ulla's view the Mishnah's mention of 'and similarly if the צומת הגידין was removed' is consistent, but according to Rav Yehuda, what does it mean?
sub.desc: עולא מקשה על רב יהודה: לשיטתו, מהי המשמעות של הברייתא 'וכן שניטל צומת הגידין'?

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah refers to two separate cases: the knee without the צומת הגידין, and the צומת הגידין without the knee.
sub.desc: רב יהודה משיב: הכוונה לרכובה בלא צומת הגידים או צומת הגידים בלא רכובה. הגמרא מקשה עליו מברייתא האומרת 'נחתכו', והוא שותק.

sub.desc_en: Ulla objects that the Mishnah says 'cut', not 'removed', and Rav Yehuda is silent.
sub.desc: רב יהודה משיב: הכוונה לרכובה בלא צומת הגידים או צומת הגידים בלא רכובה. הגמרא מקשה עליו מברייתא האומרת 'נחתכו', והוא שותק.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda later regrets not answering that 'below' means below the knee and 'above' means above the צומת הגידין.
sub.desc: לאחר שיצא, רב יהודה מהרהר מדוע לא תירץ אחרת: 'למטה' הכוונה למטה מן הארכובה, ו'למעלה' הכוונה למעלה מצומת הגידין.

sub.text: דחיית הרהורו על ידי רב יהודה
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda then realizes that the Mishnah says 'from the knee and above', which would not fit his proposed answer.
sub.desc: רב יהודה דוחה את הרהורו הראשון: הרי יכול היה להקשות גם 'נחתכו' קתני? וגם כאן 'מן הארכובה ולמעלה' קתני, ולכן תירוצו הראשון נכון.

items.text: גרסת רב פפא
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's alternative version of the tradition
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa teaches a different version: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya said that 'below' means below both the knee and the צומת הגידין, and 'above' means above both. The Mishnah's 'and similarly if the צומת הגידין was removed' is a separate case. The knee itself is as per Ulla citing Rabbi Oshaya.
items.desc: רב פפא מוסר גרסה אחרת של דברי רב יהודה, המפרשת ש'למטה' ו'למעלה' הם ביחס לארכובה ולצומת הגידים, ומסכים עם עולא לגבי הארכובה עצמה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa introduces a different version of the tradition attributed to Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya.
sub.desc: רב פפא מציג גרסה חלופית לדברי רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי חייא.

sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's version of Rav Yehuda's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa's version states that 'below' means below both the knee and the צומת הגידין, and 'above' means above both, with the Mishnah's 'and similarly if the צומת הגידין was removed' as a separate case.
sub.desc: רב פפא מציג גרסה חלופית לדברי רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי חייא.

sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's clarification about the knee
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa concludes that the knee itself is defined as per Ulla citing Rabbi Oshaya.
sub.desc: רב פפא מציג גרסה חלופית לדברי רב יהודה בשם רב ורבי חייא.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על ההבדל בין חיתוך לשבירה
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Ashi's answer about terefot
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether there is a case where cutting below the knee would cause death while cutting above would allow the animal to live. Rav Ashi responds that one cannot compare terefot; each case is unique, as cutting in one place kills and in another does not.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: כיצד ייתכן שחיתוך הרגל במקום אחד הורג, ובמקום אחר לא? רב אשי עונה שאין לדמות טריפות זו לזו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether there is any case where cutting below the knee would cause death while cutting above would allow the animal to live.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: כיצד ייתכן שחיתוך במקום אחד הורג את הבהמה ובמקום אחר אינה הורגת, והלא שניהם חיתוך רגל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi responds that one cannot compare terefot (cases of fatal wounds); each case is unique, as cutting in one place kills and in another does not.
sub.desc: רב אשי עונה שאין לדמות טריפות זו לזו, שכן חיתוך ממקום אחד גורם מיתה וממקום אחר חיים.

items.text: מחלוקת במיקום צומת הגידים
items.text_en: Dispute over the location of the צומת הגידין
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the צומת הגידין? Rabbah citing Rav Ashi says: on the shank bone and outward. Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Ashi says: on the shank bone and inward. Rava the son of Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Asi says: above the ankle. A certain rabbi sitting before Rabbi Abba says it is the ankle itself, but Rabbi Abba rejects this, citing Rav Yehuda that it is where butchers cut, which aligns with Rava's view.
items.desc: רבא ורבה בר רב הונא ורבא בריה דרבה בר רב הונא חולקים במיקום צומת הגידים. רבי אבא דוחה דעה אחת וקובע כדעת רבא בריה דרבה בר רב הונא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of the צומת הגידין (the bundle of sinews).
sub.desc: רבא בשם רב אשי מציין את מיקום צומת הגידים מבחוץ לאגרמא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah citing Rav Ashi says the צומת הגידין is on the shank bone and outward.
sub.desc: רבא בשם רב אשי מציין את מיקום צומת הגידים מבחוץ לאגרמא.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Ashi says the צומת הגידין is on the shank bone and inward.

sub.text_en: Rava bar Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Asi
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Asi says the צומת הגידין is above the ankle.
sub.desc: רבא בשם רב אשי מציין את מיקום צומת הגידים מבחוץ לאגרמא.

sub.text: A certain rabbi before Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi before Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi sitting before Rabbi Abba says the צומת הגידין is the ankle itself.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba rejecting the previous view
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba rejecting the previous view
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba rejects that view, citing Rav Yehuda that the צומת הגידין is where butchers cut.
The Gemara concludes that this aligns with Rava bar Rabbah bar Rav Huna's statement citing Rav Asi.

items.text: הגדרת צומת הגידים ושיעורו
items.text_en: Definition and measurement of the צומת הגידין
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel defines the צומת הגידין as the place where the sinews are bound together, and from that point to where they spread out. Abaye gives measurements: four fingerbreadths in an ox. For a small animal, Abaye says: if the sinews are prominent, they are the צומת הגידין; if sunken, they are not. Hard sinews are the צומת הגידין; soft ones are not. Thick sinews are the צומת הגידין; thin ones are not. White sinews are the צומת הגידין; non-white ones are not.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם שמואל מגדיר את צומת הגידים כמקום שהגידים צומתים, ומפרט את שיעורו. אביי מוסיף סימנים: ארבעה בטדי בתורא, ובהמה דקה לפי ליטי/בליעי, אשוני/רכיכי, אלימי/קטיני, חוורי/לא חוורי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel defines the צומת הגידין as the place where the sinews are bound together, from that point to where they spread out.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם שמואל מגדיר את צומת הגידים כמקום שהגידים צמתים ומפרט את השיעור ממקום הצמיתה עד מקום ההתפשטות, ושמואל תומך בדבריו.

sub.desc_en: Abaye gives the measurement: four fingerbreadths in an ox.
sub.desc: אביי מוסיף סימנים ברורים לזיהוי צומת הגידים: ארבעה בטדי בתורא, ובהמה דקה לפי בליטי/בליעי, אשוני/רכיכי, אלימי/קטיני, חוורי/לא חוורי.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks: what is the measure for a small animal?
sub.desc: אביי מוסיף סימנים ברורים לזיהוי צומת הגידים: ארבעה בטדי בתורא, ובהמה דקה לפי בליטי/בליעי, אשוני/רכיכי, אלימי/קטיני, חוורי/לא חוורי.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers: if the sinews are prominent, they are the צומת הגידין; if sunken, they are not.
sub.desc: אביי מוסיף סימנים ברורים לזיהוי צומת הגידים: ארבעה בטדי בתורא, ובהמה דקה לפי בליטי/בליעי, אשוני/רכיכי, אלימי/קטיני, חוורי/לא חוורי.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds further criteria: hard sinews are the צומת הגידין, soft ones are not; thick sinews are, thin ones are not; white sinews are, non-white ones are not.

items.text: מחלוקת מר בר רב אשי ואמימר בשיעור הפסיקה בגידים
items.text_en: Dispute about the measure of severed sinews in animals
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi and Amemar present different views on whether the majority of sinews is determined by thickness (רוב בנין) or number (רוב מנין). Mar bar Rav Ashi rules leniently that if the thick sinew is severed, the majority of number remains, and if the thin ones are severed, the majority of thickness remains.
items.desc: מר בר רב אשי ואמימר נחלקו בדין גידים שנפסקו: אמימר מבחין בין גיד עבה לשני דקים, ומר בר רב אשי מקל בשניהם. הדיון מתמקד ברוב בנין ורוב מנין.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi states that if the sinews are severed (זיגי), even if they are not whitened (חוורי), the animal is a טריפה (ritually unfit).
sub.desc: מר בר רב אשי קובע שיש להתיר את הגידים הנפסקים כיוון שהם מזוגים (מחוברים), אף על פי שאינם מחוורים (לבנים).

sub.desc_en: Amemar in the name of Rav Zevid explains that there are three sinews: one thick and two thin; if the thick one is severed, the majority by thickness (רוב בנין) is gone, and if the thin ones are severed, the majority by number (רוב מנין) is gone, while Mar bar Rav Ashi rules leniently that the presence of the other sinews suffices.
sub.desc: אמימר בשם רב זביד חולק ומפרט: שלושה חוטים יש - אחד עבה ושניים דקים; אם נפסק העבה, הלך רוב הבניין; אם נפסקו הדקים, הלך רוב המניין.

items.text: דין עופות ומספר הגידים
items.text_en: Sixteen sinews in birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that birds have sixteen sinews, and if any one is severed, the bird is treifa. Mar bar Rav Ashi recounts a case where he found only fifteen, but upon examination discovered two that were joined.
items.desc: נאמר שבעופות יש שישה עשר גידים, ואם נפסק אחד מהם טריפה. מר בר רב אשי מעיד שמצא חמישה עשר, ואחד מהם היה כפול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that birds have sixteen sinews, and severing any one renders the bird a טריפה (ritually unfit).
sub.desc: קובע כלל שבעופות יש שישה עשר גידים, ואם נפסק אחד מהם הבהמה טריפה.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi recounts a case where he found only fifteen sinews, but upon examination discovered two that were joined together.
sub.desc: קובע כלל שבעופות יש שישה עשר גידים, ואם נפסק אחד מהם הבהמה טריפה.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ושמואל בצומת הגידים
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on צומת הגידים
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says that the requirement of 'רובו' for צומת הגידים means a majority of one sinew. Shmuel objects that since there are three, if one is severed, two remain. Ravnai cites Shmuel that even if only a thread's width remains, it is kosher. An alternative version interprets 'רובו' as a majority of each sinew, which supports Ravnai.
items.desc: רב מפרש 'רובו' כרוב אחד מהגידים, ושמואל חולק וסובר שצריך רוב כל אחד. מובאת דעת רבנאי בשם שמואל להקל גם במיעוט. יש גרסה שנייה המפרשת כרוב כל אחד ומסייעת לרבנאי.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the requirement of 'רובו' for צומת הגידים means a majority of one sinew.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מוסר בשם רב שצומת הגידין נפסל ברוב אחד מהגידים.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel objects that since there are three sinews, if one is severed, two remain, so the animal is kosher.
sub.desc: שמואל חולק על רב, וטוען שאם שלושה גידים הם, הרי שחסרון אחד מותיר שניים, ואין זה רוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that Shmuel requires two remaining sinews, contradicting Ravnai who cites Shmuel that even a thread's width suffices.
sub.desc: רבנאי מביא בשם שמואל הלכה מקילה שצומת הגידים כשרה גם אם נשאר בה כחוט הסרבל, בניגוד לשיטת רב.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version interprets 'רובו' as a majority of each sinew, which supports Ravnai's lenient position.
sub.desc: שמואל חולק על רב, וטוען שאם שלושה גידים הם, הרי שחסרון אחד מותיר שניים, ואין זה רוב.

items.text: דין עצם שנשברה ומחלוקת רב ושמואל
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on a broken bone
items.desc_en: Rav rules that for a broken bone above the knee, if most flesh remains, both the animal and the limb are permitted; if not, both are forbidden. Below the knee, the limb is forbidden but the animal is permitted. Shmuel rules that in both cases, if most flesh remains, both are permitted; if not, the limb is forbidden but the animal is permitted. Rav Nachman objects to Shmuel, and later a ruling is sent that the halakha follows Rav, then Shmuel, then Rav again, and the limb itself conveys impurity by carrying.
items.desc: רב מחלק בין מעל הארכובה ומתחתיה בדין רוב בשר, ושמואל מחמיר בשניהם. רב נחמן מקשה על שמואל, ונשלחות הלכות שונות מתם. לבסוף נפסק כרב, והאבר מטמא במשא.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that for a broken bone above the knee, if most flesh remains, both animal and limb are permitted; if not, both are forbidden. Below the knee, if most flesh remains, both are permitted; if not, the limb is forbidden but the animal is permitted.
sub.desc: פתיחת הסוגיה בהבאת המשנה העוסקת בעצם שנשברה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that whether the break is above or below the knee, if most flesh remains, both are permitted; if not, the limb is forbidden but the animal is permitted.
sub.desc: שמואל חולק על רב וקובע דין שווה בשני המקרים: האבר אסור והבהמה מותרת כשאין רוב בשר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects to Shmuel's ruling, arguing that people will mistakenly think a limb from which the animal lives can be discarded while the animal is permitted.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על שמואל: כיצד הבהמה מותרת כשהאבר מוטל באשפה?

sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna's response to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Huna points out that the same concern applies to Rav's ruling in the case below the knee.
sub.desc: רב אחא בר רב הונא משיב לרב נחמן שגם לשיטת רב קיימת אותה קושיה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman clarifies that his objection applies only to Shmuel's case above the knee, where the limb is vital to the animal's life.
sub.desc: רב אחא בר רב הונא משיב לרב נחמן שגם לשיטת רב קיימת אותה קושיה.

sub.desc_en: The academy sends conflicting rulings, ultimately deciding that the halakha follows Rav, and the limb itself conveys impurity by carrying.
sub.desc: שולחים מתם הלכה כרב, חוזרים ושולחים כשמואל, ולבסוף פוסקים כרב, ומוסיפים שהאבר מטמא במשא.

items.text: קושיית רב חסדא ותירוצי רבא ורבי זירא
items.text_en: Discussion on the impurity of a detached limb
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda raises an objection from a baraita about a treifa's slaughter purifying the fetus, but Rabba suggests citing a mishna. Rabbi Zeira reports that Shmuel retracted in favor of Rav.
items.desc: רב חסדא מקשה ממשנה על דין האבר, רבא דוחה את הקושיא ומציע להקשות ממשנה אחרת. רבי זירא מספר ששמואל חזר בו וקיבל את דעת רב.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda raises an objection from a baraita: if the slaughter of a treifa purifies the detached limb (a part of its body), it should also purify the fetus (not part of its body).
sub.desc: רב חסדא מקשה ממשנה על דין טומאת העובר: אם שחיטת טריפה מטהרת את האבר המדולדל שהוא גופה, שתטהר את העובר שאינו גופה?

sub.desc_en: Rabba suggests citing a mishna instead, which discusses whether slaughter of an animal renders its blood fit to receive טומאה (ritual impurity).
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את קושיית רב חסדא ומציע להקשות ממשנה אחרת על דין הכשר טומאה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects that the mishna can be dismissed, just as we dismiss it.
sub.desc: רב חסדא משיב שגם על משנה אחרת יש דחייה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Shmuel retracted his position in favor of Rav, resolving the dispute.
