sub.desc: רבי זירא מוסר ששמואל חזר בו מדבריו וקיבל דעת רב, לאחר שעלה לארץ ומצא את רב ירמיה לומד את הסוגיה.

items.text: דין עור ובשר החופים על העצם ומחלוקת בעור
items.text_en: Requirement of רוב עוביו and רוב הקיפו for skin and flesh covering a broken bone
items.desc_en: A baraita states that if skin and flesh cover most of a broken bone that protrudes, it is permitted. Rabbi Yochanan says this means a majority of the thickness (רוב עוביו) or a majority of the circumference (רוב הקיפו). Rav Pappa rules that both are required. Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan considers skin like flesh, but Rav Nachman questions whether skin combines with flesh. A case of a soft-skinned bird is distinguished.
items.desc: תנא: אם עור ובשר חופים את רוב העצם מותר. רבי יוחנן נחלקו בפירוש 'רובו' – רוב עוביו או רוב היקפו, ורב פפא פוסק שצריך שניהם. עולא ורב נחמן נחלקו אם עור מצטרף לבשר, ורבי יוחנן הכשיר במקרה מסוים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that if a bone breaks and protrudes, if skin and flesh cover most of it (רובו), the animal is permitted; otherwise, it is forbidden.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין עצם שנשברה ויצאה לחוץ, ותולה את ההיתר בכך שעור ובשר חופים את רובו.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks how much 'most of it' (רובו) means in this context.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין עצם שנשברה ויצאה לחוץ, ותולה את ההיתר בכך שעור ובשר חופים את רובו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yochanan gave two alternative definitions: a majority of the bone's thickness (רוב עוביו) or a majority of its circumference (רוב הקיפו).
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין עצם שנשברה ויצאה לחוץ, ותולה את ההיתר בכך שעור ובשר חופים את רובו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that both a majority of the thickness and a majority of the circumference are required.
sub.desc: רב פפא פוסק להחמיר שצריך גם רוב עוביו וגם רוב היקפו.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports that Rabbi Yochanan considers skin equivalent to flesh for the purpose of covering the bone.
sub.desc: עולא מביא בשם רבי יוחנן שעור נחשב כבשר לעניין הצטרפות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects that Ulla should have said skin combines with flesh (מצרף), since the baraita says 'skin and flesh' (עור ובשר).
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על עולא: מדוע לא אמרת 'עור מצטרף לבשר' שהרי הברייתא תני 'עור ובשר'?

sub.desc_en: Ulla rejects the objection, claiming that the baraita actually reads 'skin or flesh' (עור או בשר), not 'and'.
sub.desc: רב פפא פוסק להחמיר שצריך גם רוב עוביו וגם רוב היקפו.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Ulla reported Rabbi Yochanan as saying skin combines with flesh (מצטרף).
sub.desc: עולא מביא בשם רבי יוחנן שעור נחשב כבשר לעניין הצטרפות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects that Ulla should have said skin completes the flesh (משלים) to reach the strict requirement.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על עולא: מדוע לא אמרת 'עור מצטרף לבשר' שהרי הברייתא תני 'עור ובשר'?

sub.desc_en: Ulla cites a practical case: a soft-skinned bird (בר גוזלא) in Rabbi Yitzchak's house where skin combined with flesh, and Rabbi Yochanan ruled it permitted.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על עולא: מדוע לא אמרת 'עור מצטרף לבשר' שהרי הברייתא תני 'עור ובשר'?

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rejects the evidence, distinguishing that a soft-skinned bird (בר גוזלא) is different because its skin is tender.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מקשה על עולא: מדוע לא אמרת 'עור מצטרף לבשר' שהרי הברייתא תני 'עור ובשר'?

items.text: דין גידים רכים
items.text_en: Soft sinews that will harden
items.desc_en: Rabba rules that soft sinews that will eventually harden are not a concern, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle.
items.desc: רבא דן בגידים רכים שהגיעו לפניו, ומזכיר את דברי רבי יוחנן שגידים שסופן להקשות דינם שונה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of soft sinews brought before Rabba, who questions what concern there could be.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בשאלה על גידים רכים שבאו לפניו, מה יש לחשוש להם.

sub.desc_en: Rabba answers that there is no concern, citing Rabbi Yochanan's principle regarding sinews that will eventually harden.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בשאלה על גידים רכים שבאו לפניו, מה יש לחשוש להם.

items.text: דין עצם שבורה ובשר המכסה – מחלוקת רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav Pappa's silence
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions Rav's ruling that one may count on the animal for Passover, given that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds it is a Torah prohibition. Rav remains silent, and the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan retracted his opinion in favor of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.
items.desc: רב פפא מקשה על רבה מדברי ריש לקיש האוסר עצם שבורה שאין בשר מכסה רובה, ורבה שותק. הגמרא מסבירה שרבי יוחנן חזר בו והודה לריש לקיש, ולכן ההלכה כריש לקיש.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may count on the animal for Passover, and the Torah is concerned for Israel's money.
sub.desc: פתיחה המציגה את הדעה שמותר להימנות על גידים שסופן להקשות בפסח, משום שהתורה חסה על ממונם של ישראל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rabbah: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds it is a Torah prohibition, yet you say there is nothing to worry about?
sub.desc: רב פפא מקשה על רבה מדברי ריש לקיש האוסר להימנות על גידים שסופן להקשות, ומכאן שעצם שנשברה ויצאה לחוץ אסורה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah remains silent in response to Rav Pappa's question.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע רבה שתק? והלא רבא פסק שהלכה כריש לקיש רק בשלוש מחלוקות, וכאן לא נמנית זו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Why did Rabbah remain silent? Rava said the halacha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in those three cases.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע רבה שתק? והלא רבא פסק שהלכה כריש לקיש רק בשלוש מחלוקות, וכאן לא נמנית זו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that this case is different because Rabbi Yochanan retracted his opinion in favor of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, saying he teaches it as an individual opinion.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: כאן שאני, שרבי יוחנן חזר בו והודה לריש לקיש, ולכן ההלכה כריש לקיש.

items.text: מעשה בעצם שבורה שיצאה לחוץ
items.text_en: Case of a broken bone protruding
items.desc_en: A case is brought where a bone broke and a piece fell out. Abaye delayed the case for three festivals, and Rav Adda bar Matna advised going to Rava, who ruled that the law applies whether the bone fell out or remained.
items.desc: מסופר על בהמה שעצם שבורה יצאה לחוץ וחסר ממנה קורטית. אביי עיכב את התשובה, ורב אדא בר מתנא שלח את בעל הבהמה לרבא, שפסק שאין הבדל בין נפלה לעצם שעדיין במקומה, והתיר.

sub.desc_en: A case is brought where a bone broke and a piece fell out; the litigant came before Abaye, who delayed the case for three festivals.
sub.desc: פותח בסיפור מעשה על עצם שנשברה ויצאה לחוץ, וחסר ממנה קורטית, ואביי עיכב את תשובתו.

sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Matna's advice and Rava's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna advises going to Rava, who rules that the law applies whether the bone fell out or remained.
sub.desc: רב אדא בר מתנה מפנה את בעל הבהמה לרבא, ורבא פוסק שהבהמה מותרת בין אם העצם נפלה ובין אם היא במקומה.

items.text: Questions on various states of the bone
items.text_en: Questions on various states of the bone
items.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava about cases where the bone is crushed, pulverized, or disintegrated. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua defines a disintegrated bone as one that a doctor can cut.

sub.desc_en: Ravina asks Rava about the status of a bone that is crushed (מתקבץ), pulverized (מתרוסס), or disintegrated (מתמסמס).
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua defines a disintegrated bone (מתמסמס) as one that a doctor can cut with a scalpel.

items.text: Further inquiries: perforated, peeled, cracked, etc.
items.text_en: Further inquiries: perforated, peeled, cracked, etc.
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises additional questions about a bone that is perforated, peeled, cracked, or missing its lower third. Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that skin is like flesh, but this may refer to a specific case of a quill.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises multiple inquiries about a bone that is perforated, peeled, cracked, or missing its lower third.
Ulla cites Rabbi Yochanan that skin is like flesh, but the Gemara deflects that this may refer specifically to the skin of a quill.

items.text: Question on a ring-shaped hole
items.text_en: Question on a ring-shaped hole
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that they asked about a bone with a ring-shaped hole, and resolved it from Rav Yehuda citing Rav: scratching with a bone heals, but with metal it causes a wound. Rav Pappa adds that this applies to a quill bone.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that they asked about a bone with a ring-shaped hole (whether it is considered a wound).

sub.text: Resolution from Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Resolution from Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: They resolved the question from Rav Yehuda citing Rav: scratching with a bone heals, but with metal it causes a wound.
Rav Pappa adds that this ruling applies specifically to a quill bone (a type of bone).

items.text: משנת שליא בבהמה שחוטה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a placenta
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a placenta found inside a slaughtered animal may be eaten by a refined person, and it does not impart food or carcass impurity unless designated for food. A partially emerged placenta is forbidden. A firstborn animal's placenta is given to dogs, but in consecrated animals it is buried, with restrictions against Amorite practices.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת ששליא שנמצאת בבהמה שחוטה מותרת באכילה למי שאינו נמנע, ואינה מטמאה לא טומאת אוכלין ולא טומאת נבלות. אם חישב עליה לאכילה, מטמאה טומאת אוכלין. שליא שיצאה מקצתה אסורה באכילה, משום סימן ולד. במבכרת שהפילה שליא – מותר לזורקה לכלבים, ובמוקדשין תיקבר, ואין נוהגין בדרכי האמורי.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a placenta found inside a slaughtered animal may be eaten by a refined person and does not impart food or carcass impurity.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין שליה שנמצאת בבהמה שחוטה: מותרת באכילה למי שאינו נמאס, ואינה מטמאה לא טומאת אוכלין ולא טומאת נבלות; חישב עליה – מטמאה טומאת אוכלין.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that if one designated the placenta for food, it imparts food impurity but not carcass impurity.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין שליה שנמצאת בבהמה שחוטה: מותרת באכילה למי שאינו נמאס, ואינה מטמאה לא טומאת אוכלין ולא טומאת נבלות; חישב עליה – מטמאה טומאת אוכלין.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a placenta that partially emerged is forbidden to eat, as it is a sign of a fetus in both woman and animal.
sub.desc: המשנה מוסיפה ששליה שיצאה מקצתה אסורה באכילה, ומהווה סימן ולד.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a firstborn animal's placenta is given to dogs, but in consecrated animals it is buried.
sub.desc: המשנה מסיימת בדין בכור שהפיל שליה: מותר לזורקה לכלבים, ובמוקדשין תיקבר, ואין נוהגין בה מנהגי אמוריים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah concludes with restrictions against Amorite practices: not burying the placenta at a crossroads or hanging it on a tree.
sub.desc: המשנה מסיימת בדין בכור שהפיל שליה: מותר לזורקה לכלבים, ובמוקדשין תיקבר, ואין נוהגין בה מנהגי אמוריים.

items.text: מקור דין שליא – דרשה מהפסוק
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for the placenta's permissibility
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives from a verse that all in the animal may be eaten, including the placenta, but excludes a partially emerged placenta. It notes that the verse is merely a support, as a placenta never exists without a fetus.
items.desc: הגמרא דורשת את הפסוק 'כל בבהמה תאכלו' לרבות את השליא, ופסוק 'אותה' למעט שליא שיצאה מקצתה. הגמרא מקשה: הרי אין שליא בלא ולד, ולמה לי קרא? ומתרצת: קרא אסמכתא בעלמא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the Mishnah's ruling that a placenta found inside a slaughtered animal is permitted, and cites a baraita that derives it from the verse 'כֹּל בַּבְּהֵמָה תֹּאכֵלוּ' (every part in the animal you may eat), which includes the placenta.

The baraita raises the possibility that the verse might permit even a partially emerged placenta, but rejects this by citing the word 'אוֹתָהּ' (it), which excludes the placenta when it has partially emerged.

The Gemara concludes that since a placenta never exists without a fetus, the verse is merely an אסמכתא (supportive allusion) rather than a direct source, as the halacha is already known from the principle that the fetus is permitted.

items.text: שאלת עור חמור ששלקו – תחילת דיון
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nappacha's question on cooked donkey skin
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nappacha asks about the status of cooked donkey skin regarding impurity, noting that the Mishnah already addresses food impurity.
items.desc: רבי יצחק בר נפחא שואל על עור חמור ששלקו מה דינו לעניין טומאת אוכלין. הגמרא מתחילה לברר את השאלה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nappacha asks about the status of cooked donkey skin regarding impurity, noting that the Mishnah already addresses food impurity.

items.text: Impurity of the placenta and donkey skin
items.text_en: Impurity of the placenta and donkey skin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about placenta impurity refers to food impurity or carcass impurity. It cites a baraita about skin and placenta not being susceptible to food impurity unless prepared, and another about carcass impurity excluding skin and bones. Rabba bar Rav Hana clarifies that the latter applies only when they are made into pot herbs. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah deals with food impurity, and donkey skin is different because it is repulsive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about placenta impurity refers to food impurity or carcass impurity.
A baraita is cited stating that skin and placenta are not susceptible to food impurity unless the skin is boiled or the placenta is designated for food.
Another baraita is cited regarding carcass impurity, excluding skin, bones, sinews, horns, and hooves.
Rabba bar Rav Hana clarifies that the exclusion of skin and bones from carcass impurity applies only when they are made into pot herbs.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah deals with food impurity, and donkey skin is different because it is repulsive.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on placenta with fetus
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan on placenta with fetus
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says the Mishnah's concern about a second fetus applies only when no fetus accompanies the placenta, but if a fetus is present, there is no concern. Rabbi Yochanan argues that whether or not a fetus is present, we are concerned for another fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited regarding a placenta that emerged.
Rabbi Elazar states that the Mishnah's concern applies only when no fetus accompanies the placenta, but if a fetus is present, there is no concern for another fetus.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that whether or not a fetus is present, we are concerned for another fetus.

items.text: Reinterpretation of the dispute based on Rabbi Yirmeya's statement
items.text_en: Reinterpretation of the dispute based on Rabbi Yirmeya's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya notes that Rabbi Elazar's statement was made leniently. The Gemara reinterprets: Rabbi Elazar said the Mishnah applies only when the placenta is not attached to the fetus, but if attached, no concern. Rabbi Yochanan says we only have the case of placenta without fetus; if a fetus is present, attached or not, no concern. This aligns with Rabbi Yirmeya's leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: But Rabbi Yirmeya said that Rabbi Elazar stated his ruling leniently, contradicting the earlier understanding.

The Gemara resolves: If the statement was made, it was actually this: Rabbi Elazar said the Mishnah applies only when the placenta is not attached to the fetus, but if attached, no concern for another fetus.

Rabbi Yochanan says we only have the case of placenta without fetus; if a fetus is present, attached or not, no concern, and this aligns with Rabbi Yirmeya's statement that Rabbi Elazar ruled leniently.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Elazar's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Elazar's view
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar: if a woman miscarries a species of animal, bird, or beast with a placenta, if the placenta is attached, no concern for another fetus; if not attached, we impose the stringencies of two fetuses, because we suspect the fetus may have dissolved or the placenta may have belonged to another.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar's view: if a woman miscarries a species of animal, bird, or beast with a placenta, when the placenta is attached to the fetus there is no concern for another fetus; when not attached, we impose the stringencies of two fetuses, because we suspect the fetus may have dissolved or the placenta may have belonged to another.

items.text: Reason for the law of a firstborn that miscarries
items.text_en: Reason for the law of a firstborn that miscarries
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why a firstborn animal that miscarries requires burial: most animals give birth to something sanctified as a firstborn, a minority give birth to a non-sanctified 'dismembered' fetus. Since half are males and half females, the minority of dismembered cases combines with the female half, making males a minority. Therefore, the miscarried fetus is treated as a firstborn and buried.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a firstborn animal that miscarries requires burial.
Rav Ika breih d'Rav Ami answers that most animals give birth to something sanctified as a firstborn, while a minority give birth to a non-sanctified 'dismembered' fetus.

The Gemara explains that since half of births are males and half females, the minority of dismembered cases combines with the female half, making males a minority, so the miscarried fetus is treated as a firstborn.
The Gemara concludes that the miscarried fetus is buried because the majority of animals give birth to something sanctified as a firstborn.

items.text: Amorite practices and the exception for healing
items.text_en: Amorite practices and the exception for healing
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava state that anything with healing properties is not considered Amorite practice, but without healing it is. A baraita is cited about a tree that sheds its fruit: one paints it red and loads it with stones. This is permitted because it is a recognized remedy, not superstition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rava state the general principle that anything with healing properties is not prohibited as Amorite practice (דרכי האמורי), but anything without healing properties is prohibited.
A baraita is cited describing a practice for a tree that sheds its fruit: painting it red and loading it with stones, which is permitted because it is a recognized remedy, not superstition.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the condemned animal is marked with red paint: so that people see it and pray for mercy. Ravina attributes this practice to a specific Tanna. The section ends with the formal conclusion of the previous chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the condemned animal is marked with red paint, and answers that it is so people see it and pray for mercy.
A baraita is cited to support the practice: a person afflicted with impurity must announce it so that the public prays for him.
Ravina attributes the practice of hanging the red mark on a palm tree to a specific Tanna.
The Gemara formally concludes the previous chapter.

items.text: Mishnah: The law of אותו ואת בנו in various scenarios
items.text_en: Mishnah: The law of אותו ואת בנו in various scenarios
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day applies in all circumstances: in the Land of Israel and outside, with the Temple standing or not, for non-sacred and sacred animals. It then lists nine cases detailing the status of the first and second animals depending on whether they are חולין or קדשים, and whether the slaughter is inside or outside the Temple courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the prohibition of אותו ואת בנו (slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day) applies universally: in the Land of Israel and outside, with or without the Temple, for both non-sacred and sacred animals.
The Mishnah presents the first case: slaughtering both as חולין (non-sacred) outside the Temple courtyard — both are כשר (ritually fit), and the second animal incurs lashes.
The Mishnah presents the second case: slaughtering both as קדשים (sacred animals) outside the courtyard — the first incurs כרת (excision), both are פסול (invalid), and both receive lashes.

The Mishnah presents the third case: slaughtering both as חולין inside the courtyard — both are פסול, the second receives lashes; and slaughtering both as קדשים inside — the first is כשר and פטור (exempt), the second receives lashes and is פסול.
The Mishnah presents the fourth case: first חולין then קדשים outside — the first is כשר and פטור, the second receives lashes and is פסול.
The Mishnah presents the fifth case: first קדשים then חולין outside — the first incurs כרת and is פסול, the second is כשר, and both receive lashes.

The Mishnah presents the sixth case: first חולין then קדשים inside — both are פסול, the second receives lashes; and first קדשים then חולין inside — the first is כשר and פטור, the second receives lashes and is פסול.
The Mishnah presents the seventh case: first חולין outside then inside — the first is כשר and פטור, the second receives lashes and is פסול.
The Mishnah presents the eighth case: first קדשים outside then inside — the first incurs כרת, both receive lashes, and both are פסול.

The Mishnah presents the ninth case: first חולין inside then outside — the first is פסול and פטור, the second receives lashes and is כשר; and first קדשים inside then outside — the first is כשר and פטור, the second receives lashes and is פסול.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that אותו ואת בנו applies to consecrated animals
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that אותו ואת בנו applies to consecrated animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraitha that derives from the verse "שור או כשב או עז כי יולד" and the subsequent verse "ושור או שה אותו ואת בנו לא תשחטו ביום אחד" that the law applies to consecrated animals. It then considers and rejects alternative interpretations: that it applies only to consecrated animals, or only to non-sacred animals. Finally, it raises a challenge from the law of כלאים, citing a baraitha that the law applies to כלאים and כוי, and begins to address it with Rava's statement.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites the verses 'שור או כשב או עז כי יולד' and 'ושור או שה אותו ואת בנו לא תשחטו ביום אחד' to derive that the law of אותו ואת בנו applies to consecrated animals.
The Gemara objects: perhaps the law applies only to consecrated animals and not to non-sacred ones, since the word 'שור' interrupts the context.
The Gemara objects alternatively: perhaps the law applies only to non-sacred animals and not to consecrated ones, but the 'ו' in 'ושור' connects it to the previous context.

The Gemara raises a challenge: if the law is derived from consecrated animals, which do not apply to כלאים (hybrids), then perhaps אותו ואת בנו also does not apply to hybrids, but a baraita explicitly states it does.
The Gemara introduces an additional argument based on the word 'שה' and begins to cite Rava's statement.

items.text: Opening statement: The word "seh" excludes kil'ayim, and "or" includes it
items.text_en: Opening statement: The word "seh" excludes kil'ayim, and "or" includes it
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that the word "seh" (lamb) in the verse excludes kil'ayim (a hybrid animal), while the word "or" (or) comes to include kil'ayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara establishes a general principle: the word 'שֶׂה' (lamb) excludes kil'ayim (a hybrid), while the word 'אוֹ' (or) includes it.

items.text: Gemara's question: The word "or" is needed for division
items.text_en: Gemara's question: The word "or" is needed for division
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the word "or" to include kil'ayim, suggesting it is needed to teach that one is liable for slaughtering either a cow and its calf or a sheep and its lamb separately. The Gemara then cites a beraita that derives the division from the word "oto" rather than "or".

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the word 'אוֹ' (or) is needed to include kil'ayim, suggesting it is needed to teach that one is liable for slaughtering either a cow and its calf or a sheep and its lamb separately.
The Gemara answers that the division is derived from the word 'בְּנוֹ' (its offspring), not from 'אוֹ' (or).
The Gemara cites a baraita that derives the division from the word 'אוֹתוֹ' (it) rather than 'אוֹ' (or).

items.text: The dispute between Chananya and the Rabbis regarding the word "oto"
items.text_en: The dispute between Chananya and the Rabbis regarding the word "oto"
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that for the Rabbis, the word "oto" is superfluous and used for division, but for Chananya, who does not have a superfluous "oto", the division is derived from Rabbi Yonatan's principle that a verse can imply both together and separately unless specified otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: This works out well for the Rabbis, for whom the word 'אותו' (it) is superfluous, but for חנניה (Chananya), for whom 'אותו' is not superfluous, from where does he derive the division into separate prohibitions?
The Gemara answers: Chananya does not need a verse for division, because he holds like Rabbi Yonatan, who maintains that a verse can imply both together and separately unless specified otherwise.

A baraita is cited: From the verse 'איש אשר יקלל את אביו ואת אמו' (a man who curses his father and his mother), Rabbi Yoshiya derives that one is liable for cursing either parent alone, using the repetition in the verse.

Rabbi Yonatan says: The phrase 'father and mother' implies both together and each separately, unless the verse specifies 'together' (as in 'לא תחרוש בשור ובחמור יחדו' — you shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together).

items.text: Clarification of the dispute: Chananya and the Rabbis on the scope of the law
items.text_en: Clarification of the dispute: Chananya and the Rabbis on the scope of the law
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the positions of Chananya and the Rabbis: the Rabbis hold that the law of "oto v'et bno" applies only to females, while Chananya holds it applies to both males and females.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the positions of חנניה (Chananya) and the רבנן (Rabbis) are.
The baraita states the Rabbis' position: the law of אותו ואת בנו (it and its offspring) applies only to females, not to males.
The baraita states חנניה (Chananya)'s position: the law applies to both males and females.

items.text: The Rabbis' reasoning and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: The Rabbis' reasoning and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the Rabbis' reasoning through a beraita that uses a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument from the law of "em al habanim" (sending away the mother bird) to limit the law to females. The Gemara then addresses a potential objection and concludes with the derivation from the word "bno" (his son) to exclude males.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reasoning of the Rabbis who limit the prohibition to females.
The beraita presents a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument from the law of 'em al habanim' (sending away the mother bird) to conclude that the prohibition applies only to females.
An objection is raised: the kal vachomer is flawed because the law of 'em al habanim' does not apply to prepared birds, whereas the law of 'oto v'eto bno' does apply to prepared animals.
The beraita resolves the objection by citing the word 'oto' (it) to limit the prohibition to one parent, then returns to the kal vachomer to conclude it applies only to females.
The beraita offers an alternative derivation: the word 'bno' (its offspring) implies a parent whose offspring clings to it, excluding the male.
The Gemara clarifies the structure of the beraita: the phrase 'if it is your wish to say' introduces a refutation that the word 'oto' might imply a male, but the word 'bno' resolves this.

items.text: Hananiah's position on paternal lineage
items.text_en: Hananiah's position on paternal lineage
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Hananiah, the verse uses both 'אותו' (male) and 'בנו' (female), so the law applies to both males and females, indicating concern for paternal lineage.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Hananiah, the verse uses both 'אותו' (male) and 'בנו' (female), so the law applies to both males and females, indicating concern for paternal lineage.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and identification of Hananiah as the Sages
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and identification of Hananiah as the Sages
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya quotes Shmuel ruling like Hananiah, consistent with Shmuel's earlier statement that Rabbi Yehuda disregards paternal lineage but the Sages (identified as Hananiah) consider all mules as one species due to concern for paternal lineage.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Chiyya quoting Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya quoting Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chiyya quotes Shmuel ruling like Hananiah, and Shmuel's consistency is shown by citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda permits offspring of a horse even if the father is a donkey to mate with each other.
Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel explaining that the Mishnah reflects Rabbi Yehuda's view that paternal lineage is disregarded, while the Sages consider all mule species as one.
The Gemara identifies the Sages as Hananiah, who is concerned about paternal lineage, and thus all mules are considered one species.

items.text: Question: Is Rabbi Yehuda certain or uncertain about paternal lineage?
items.text_en: Question: Is Rabbi Yehuda certain or uncertain about paternal lineage?
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is Rabbi Yehuda certain that paternal lineage is disregarded, or is he uncertain? The practical difference is whether a hybrid offspring (פרי) is permitted with its mother.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: Is Rabbi Yehuda certain that paternal lineage is disregarded, or is he uncertain, with the practical difference being whether a hybrid offspring (פרי) is permitted with its mother.

items.text: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: First attempted proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's statement that offspring of a horse (even if father is a donkey) are permitted with each other, implying certainty. But the Gemara deflects: the case might be where both fathers are donkeys, and the concern is about the horse side mixing with the donkey side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's Mishnah that offspring of a horse, even if their father is a donkey, are permitted with each other, implying certainty that the father's seed is disregarded.
The Gemara deflects: the case might be where both fathers are donkeys, and the concern is about the horse side mixing with the donkey side, so the Mishnah teaches a novel ruling.

items.text: ראיה מברייתא: פרדה שאינה יודעת מינה
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from the baraita about a mule in heat
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to prove from Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a mule in heat may only be bred with its own kind, implying uncertainty about its mother's species. The Gemara deflects: the ruling is because we don't know its species, and even signs (like voice or ears) cannot help if the animal is mute or deaf.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה אוסר להרכיב על פרדה סוס או חמור אלא מינה, ומכאן שהיה מסתפק. אך דוחים: מדובר בפרדה שאין יודעים מין אמה, או באלמת וגידמת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a mule in heat may only be bred with its own kind, implying that the mother's species is unknown and thus the father's species is not determinative.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה אוסר להרכיב על פרדה סוס או חמור אלא מינה, ומכאן שהיה מסתפק בזרע האב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Yehuda is certain that the father's lineage is irrelevant, why not breed the mule with its mother's species? The answer is that we do not know the mother's species.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שבה רבי יהודה אוסר להרכיב על פרדה סוס או חמור אלא מינה, ומכאן שהיה מסתפק בזרע האב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies the baraita: Rabbi Yehuda means that one may not breed the mule with any horse or donkey because we simply do not know its species, not because the father's lineage is considered.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הברייתא אומרת 'אלא מינה', משמע שיודעים מינה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not determine the species by physical signs such as voice or ears?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הברייתא אומרת 'אלא מינה', משמע שיודעים מינה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye and Rav Pappa provide signs: a deep voice indicates a donkey-fathered mule, a high-pitched voice a horse-fathered one; large ears and a short tail indicate a donkey-fathered mule, small ears and a long tail a horse-fathered one.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הברייתא אומרת 'אלא מינה', משמע שיודעים מינה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the baraita deals with a mute and deaf mule, where these signs cannot be used.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי הברייתא אומרת 'אלא מינה', משמע שיודעים מינה.

items.text: הכרעה: רב הונא בר יהושע אומר שהכל מודים שפרי עם האם אסור
items.text_en: Resolution: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua states that everyone agrees a hybrid offspring with its mother is forbidden, implying Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain about paternal lineage. The Gemara concludes this is the correct resolution.
items.desc: רב הונא בר יהושע קובע שהכל מודים שפרי עם האם אסור, ומכאן שרבי יהודה מסתפק. הגמרא מסיקה: שמע מינה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua states that everyone agrees a hybrid offspring with its mother is forbidden, implying Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain about paternal lineage, and the Gemara concludes this is the correct resolution.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהי ההכרעה בשאלה שנשאלה.

items.text: מעשה רבי אבא: אין חוששים לזרע האב
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's practical instruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba instructs his attendant to bring mules that look alike, indicating he holds that paternal lineage is disregarded.
items.desc: רבי אבא מורה לשמשו להביא פרדות הדומות זו לזו בסימניהן, ומכאן שאינו חושש לזרע האב אלא רק לאם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba instructs his attendant to bring mules that look alike, demonstrating his position that paternal lineage is disregarded.
sub.desc: רבי אבא מורה לשמשו להביא פרדות הדומות זו לזו בסימניהן, ומכאן שאינו חושש לזרע האב אלא רק לאם.

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: סימנים דאורייתא
items.text_en: Opening statement: signs are Torah law
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a brief statement that the signs (of a kosher animal) are from the Torah, setting the stage for the discussion of hybrid animals.
items.desc: הקטע הפותח מציין שהסימנים הנדונים הם מהתורה, ומקדים את הדיון בכוי ובכלאיים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the signs of a kosher animal are from the Torah.

items.text: Baraita: Dispute on koy and kil'ayim
items.text_en: Baraita: Dispute on koy and kil'ayim
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the law of "it and its young" applies to kil'ayim and koy. Rabbi Eliezer says it applies to kil'ayim from a goat and ewe, but not to a koy. Rav Chisda defines the koy in dispute as the offspring of a ram and a doe.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the law of 'it and its son' applies to hybrids and the koy, with Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages disputing the koy's status, and Rav Chisda defines the koy as the offspring of a ram and a doe.
Rabbi Eliezer limits the law to kil'ayim from a goat and ewe, excluding koy.
Rav Chisda defines the disputed koy as the offspring of a ram and a doe.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: clarifying the case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: clarifying the case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the scenario: if it is a ram mating with a doe, the offspring is a doe, and all agree it is exempt from "it and its young" because the Torah said "seh" not "deer." If it is a deer mating with a ewe, the offspring is a ewe, and all agree it is liable because "seh" includes any offspring.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the case is a ram (תיש) mating with a doe (צבייה), the offspring is a doe, and Rav Chisda already ruled that all agree it is exempt from 'it and its young' because the Torah said 'seh' (שה) not 'deer' (צבי).

The Gemara answers: rather, the case is a deer (צבי) mating with a ewe (תיש), and the offspring is a ewe; Rav Chisda already ruled that all agree it is liable because the Torah said 'seh' (שה) and its offspring includes any offspring.

items.text: Resolution: the case of a granddaughter
items.text_en: Resolution: the case of a granddaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: the case is a ram mating with a doe, producing a daughter, and that daughter gives birth to a male. The Sages hold we consider the father's lineage, so "seh" includes even a partial sheep. Rabbi Eliezer holds we do not consider the father's lineage, and we do not say "seh" includes a partial sheep.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the case as a ram mating with a doe, producing a daughter, and that daughter giving birth to a male.
The Sages hold that we consider the father's lineage, so the term 'seh' includes even a partial sheep.

sub.text: Stam's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.text_en: Stam's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's position
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer holds that we do not consider the father's lineage, and we do not apply the rule that 'seh' includes a partial sheep.

items.text: קושיה ותירוץ: מדוע לא נחלקו בעיקר דין זרע האב
items.text_en: Question: why not dispute on the general principle?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not have them dispute on the general principle of considering the father's lineage (the dispute of Chananya and the Sages)? It answers: if they only disputed there, one might think the Sages agree here that we do not say "seh" includes a partial sheep, so the baraita teaches otherwise.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע לא נחלקו רבי אליעזר וחכמים בעיקר הדין של חוששין לזרע האב, ומתרצת שאם היו חולקים שם, היינו אומרים שגם חכמים מודים בכוי שאין אומרים 'שה ואפילו מקצת שה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why not have them dispute on the general principle of חוששין לזרע האב (considering the father's lineage), which is the dispute between Chananya and the Sages?
The Gemara answers: if they only disputed there, one might think the Sages agree here that we do not say 'שה ואפילו מקצת שה' (a sheep includes even a partial sheep), so the baraita teaches otherwise.

items.text: קושיה ממשנת כיסוי הדם: סתירה בדין כוי
items.text_en: Second baraita: covering the blood of a koy
items.desc_en: A baraita states: a koy may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and if slaughtered, its blood is not covered. The Gemara analyzes the case: if it is a ram mating with a doe, both sides would require covering (since it is a deer). If it is a deer mating with a ewe, the Sages would require covering, Rabbi Eliezer would not. The Gemara concludes: the Sages are uncertain whether we consider the father's lineage, while Rabbi Eliezer is certain.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה ממשנה האוסרת לשחוט כוי ביום טוב ואינה מחייבת כיסוי דמו, ומבררת באיזה כוי מדובר. לאחר דחיית אפשרויות, מסיקה שהמשנה כרבנן והם מסופקים אם חוששין לזרע האב, ואילו לרבי אליעזר פשיטא שאין חוששין.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that a koy may not be slaughtered on Yom Tov, and if slaughtered, its blood is not covered.
The Gemara asks: what case is this baraita dealing with? If it is a ram mating with a doe, both the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer would agree that covering is required, since it is a deer.
The Gemara objects: if it is a deer mating with a ewe, then for the Sages covering would be required, but for Rabbi Eliezer it would not.
The Gemara resolves: it is indeed a deer mating with a ewe, but the Sages are uncertain whether we consider the father's lineage, while Rabbi Eliezer is certain.

items.text: ברייתא שנייה: מחלוקת במתנות כהונה בכוי
items.text_en: Third baraita: priestly gifts for a koy
items.desc_en: A baraita states: the foreleg, jaw, and maw apply to a koy and kil'ayim. Rabbi Eliezer says kil'ayim from a goat and ewe is liable for gifts, but a koy is exempt. The Gemara analyzes: if it is a ram mating with a doe, Rabbi Eliezer's exemption is clear, but the Sages would require half the gifts. If it is a deer mating with a ewe, the Sages would require half, but Rabbi Eliezer would require all. The Gemara concludes: both are uncertain about considering the father's lineage, and they dispute about the principle of "seh" including a partial sheep.
items.desc: ברייתא נוספת עוסקת במתנות כהונה בכוי ובכלאיים. הגמרא מנתחת את המקרה ומגלה שגם רבי אליעזר מסתפק לגבי זרע האב, ולכן המחלוקת נותרת בעינה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that the priestly gifts of foreleg, jaw, and maw apply to a koy and kil'ayim, with Rabbi Eliezer exempting a koy but requiring gifts for kil'ayim from a goat and ewe.

The Gemara asks what case is being discussed, suggesting it might be a ram mating with a doe, which would explain Rabbi Eliezer's exemption since he does not apply the principle of 'seh' including a partial sheep.
The Gemara objects that even if the Sages apply 'seh' to a partial sheep, they should still require the other half of the gifts unless the owner brings proof that the father's lineage is considered.
The Gemara suggests the case is a deer mating with a ewe, where for the Sages 'obligated' means half the gifts, but for Rabbi Eliezer he should be obligated for all the gifts.
The Gemara resolves that both the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer are uncertain about considering the father's lineage, and their dispute is about the principle of 'seh' including a partial sheep.

items.text: Opening dispute on the meaning of 'seh'
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the meaning of 'seh'
items.desc_en: The Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer disagree whether the term 'seh' in the Torah includes a partial sheep (a hybrid) or only a full sheep.

sub.desc_en: The stam introduces the dispute: the Rabbis hold that 'seh' includes even a partial sheep, while Rabbi Eliezer holds that 'seh' excludes a partial sheep.

items.text: Rav Pappa's application to covering blood, gifts, and 'oto v'et bno'
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's application to covering blood, gifts, and 'oto v'et bno'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that the dispute applies to a deer that mates with a goat, and the uncertainty about whether we consider the father's seed determines the halakha for covering blood, priestly gifts, and the prohibition of slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by stating that the dispute about 'seh' applies only to a deer that mates with a goat, regarding covering blood and priestly gifts.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's explanation of the uncertainty
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's explanation of the uncertainty
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that both sides are uncertain whether we consider the father's seed, and they dispute only the interpretation of 'seh' including a partial 'seh'.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's transition to 'oto v'et bno'
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's transition to 'oto v'et bno'
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa shifts to the case of 'oto v'et bno' (slaughtering a parent and offspring on the same day), which applies both to a goat mating with a deer and a deer mating with a goat.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's analysis of the first subcase
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's analysis of the first subcase
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa analyzes the case of a goat mating with a deer: the Rabbis consider the father's seed and apply 'seh' even partially, forbidding it, while Rabbi Eliezer holds that even if we consider the father's seed, we do not apply 'seh' partially.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's analysis of the second subcase
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's analysis of the second subcase
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa analyzes the case of a deer mating with a goat regarding lashes: the Rabbis apply 'seh' partially and administer lashes, while Rabbi Eliezer holds there is a prohibition but no lashes due to uncertainty about the father's seed.

items.text: The nature of the koy
items.text_en: The nature of the koy
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman define the koy as an independent creature or a wild ram, and a baraita records a dispute among Tannaim whether it is a type of domesticated animal, a wild animal, or a distinct species.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda defines the koy as an independent creature whose status as a domesticated or wild animal was never resolved by the Sages.
Rav Nachman identifies the koy as a wild ram (אֵיל הַבָּר).

A baraita records a Tannaitic dispute: Tanna Kamma and Yesh Omrim identify the koy as a wild ram or a crossbreed, Rabbi Yosei calls it an unresolved independent creature, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel declares it a domesticated animal, citing that the house of Dushai raised herds of them.

items.text: The goats of Bala and their fitness for the altar
items.text_en: The goats of Bala and their fitness for the altar
items.desc_en: Rav Zera quotes Rav Safra quoting Rav Hamnuna that the goats of Bala are fit for the altar, based on Rabbi Yitzchak's list of ten animals. Rav Acha bar Yaakov and others challenge this, suggesting they might be a species of akko, te'o, or zemer, and Rav Chanan permits their fat.

sub.text: Rav Zera quoting Rav Safra quoting Rav Hamnuna
sub.text_en: Rav Zera quoting Rav Safra quoting Rav Hamnuna
sub.desc_en: Rav Zera reports in the name of Rav Safra and Rav Hamnuna that the goats of Bala are fit for the altar, based on Rabbi Yitzchak's statement that Scripture enumerated only ten species of animals and no more.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that the verse 'אַיָּל וּצְבִי' (deer and gazelle) is a פרט (specification) and 'כׇּל בְּהֵמָה' (every animal) is a כלל (generalization), so by the rule of כלל ופרט (general and specific) the generalization adds many more species beyond the ten.
The Gemara asks: if the generalization adds many species, why does Scripture list all those specific animals in the first place?

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika objects that perhaps the goats of Bala are a species of אקו (akko, a wild goat).

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rava and Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avya's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava and Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avya's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava (or alternatively Rav Acha brei d'Rav Avya) asks Rav Ashi whether the goats might be a species of תאו (te'o, wild ox) or זמר (zemer, a type of antelope).

sub.text: Rav Chanan's answer to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Chanan's answer to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chanan tells Rav Ashi that from the statement of Rav Hamnuna, their fat is permitted.

items.text: Further inquiry about the goats of Bala
items.text_en: Further inquiry about the goats of Bala
items.desc_en: Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya asks Rav Huna bar Chiyya about the goats of Bala, who distinguishes them from the wild ox (shor habar) and asserts all agree they are a type of goat. Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika and Ravina raise the possibility they are akko, te'o, or zemer, and Rav Nachman permits their fat.

sub.text: Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya's question
sub.text_en: Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya's question
sub.desc_en: Abba brei d'Rav Minyamin bar Chiyya asks Rav Huna bar Chiyya about the status of the goats of Bala (עיזי דבאלא) regarding the altar.
Rav Huna bar Chiyya answers that the dispute between Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis is only about the wild ox (שור הבר), but regarding the goats of Bala, all agree they are a type of goat.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika's objection
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rav Ika objects that perhaps the goats of Bala are a type of akko (אקו).
Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that perhaps the goats of Bala are a type of te'o (תאו) or zemer (זמר).
Rav Nachman tells Rav Ashi that from the statement of Rav Hanan, the fat of these animals is permitted.

items.text: Rabbi Oshaya's analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Oshaya's analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya states that the entire Mishnah (about slaughtering two animals) is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an invalid slaughter is not considered slaughter.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Oshaya states that the entire Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an invalid slaughter is not considered slaughter.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of slaughtering mother and calf
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of slaughtering mother and calf
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases: Chullin outside, Chullin inside, and Kodashim inside, detailing the status of the first and second animals regarding liability and validity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents three cases of slaughtering mother and calf: Chullin outside, Chullin inside, and Kodashim inside, detailing the status of the first and second animals regarding liability and validity.

items.text: Gemara's question on Chullin inside
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Chullin inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Shimon, an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter. Since the first animal was slaughtered outside, it is unfit, so why does the second animal incur lashes?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the second animal incurs lashes according to Rabbi Shimon, who holds that an unfit slaughter (שחיטה שאינה ראויה) is not considered slaughter, since the first animal was slaughtered outside and thus unfit.

items.text: Gemara's question on Kodashim inside
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Kodashim inside
items.desc_en: The Gemara extends the question to Kodashim inside: since slaughter of consecrated animals is not considered a fit slaughter until blood is sprinkled, why does the second animal incur lashes? The conclusion is that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for Kodashim inside: the first animal is fit and the slaughterer is exempt, while the second incurs lashes and is invalid.

The Gemara questions: since Rabbi Shimon holds that a slaughter which is not fit (שחיטה שאינה ראויה) is not considered slaughter, and slaughter of consecrated animals is not fit until blood is sprinkled, why does the second animal incur lashes and be invalid?
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah does not follow Rabbi Shimon's view.

items.text: Clarification: Kodashim slaughter is fit
items.text_en: Clarification: Kodashim slaughter is fit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that one might have thought Kodashim slaughter is fit because if the blood is sprinkled, the meat becomes permitted; thus the Mishnah teaches that it is not considered fit slaughter for the purpose of the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling about Kodashim slaughter is obvious, considering that if the blood is sprinkled, the meat becomes permitted, making it a fit slaughter.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah teaches that Kodashim slaughter is not considered fit slaughter for the purpose of the prohibition, countering a possible mistaken assumption.

items.text: Question about the prohibition of מחוסר זמן
items.text_en: Question about the prohibition of מחוסר זמן
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not include lashes for the prohibition of מחוסר זמן (an animal lacking the proper age), citing a baraita that derives this from the verse 'לא ירצה'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah does not also include lashes for the prohibition of מחוסר זמן (an animal lacking the proper age), citing a baraita that derives this from the verse 'לא ירצה'.
The baraita derives from the verse 'ושור ושה שרוע וקלוט' that all disqualifications of the bull and lamb, including מחוסר זמן, are subject to the prohibition of 'לא ירצה' and lashes.

items.text: Answer: Only counts prohibitions of 'Oto v'Et Bno'
items.text_en: Answer: Only counts prohibitions of 'Oto v'Et Bno'
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only counts the prohibitions related to 'Oto v'Et Bno', not other prohibitions. It then addresses an objection from the case of Kodashim outside, explaining that when there is no 'Oto v'Et Bno' prohibition, other prohibitions are counted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah only counts the prohibitions related to 'אותו ואת בנו' (itself and its offspring), not unrelated prohibitions.

The Gemara objects that in the case of קדשים בחוץ (sacrificial animals slaughtered outside the Temple courtyard), the Mishnah does count unrelated prohibitions, as it states both animals incur lashes.
The Gemara clarifies that the first animal's lashes in that case are due to the prohibition of שחוטי חוץ (slaughtering outside), not 'אותו ואת בנו' (itself and its offspring).

The Gemara resolves that wherever there is no 'אותו ואת בנו' (itself and its offspring) prohibition, the Mishnah lists unrelated prohibitions, but wherever there is such a prohibition, it does not list unrelated ones.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's alternative answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's alternative answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira suggests setting aside the case of מחוסר זמן, as the verse explicitly states the prohibition, implying a different reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira proposes to set aside the case of מחוסר זמן (an animal lacking the required age), because the verse explicitly states the prohibition, implying a different reasoning.

items.text: Gemara's initial derivation of a positive commandment
items.text_en: Gemara's initial derivation of a positive commandment
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse "from the eighth day onward it will be accepted" implies a positive commandment from a general rule, but this is challenged.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse is reassigned to a positive commandment, explaining that the phrase 'from the eighth day onward' implies exclusion of earlier days.
The Gemara answers that a negative inference from a positive statement constitutes a positive commandment.

items.text: Rabbi Aftoriki's contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Aftoriki's contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Aftoriki raises a contradiction between two verses about the eighth day, and resolves it by distinguishing between sanctification at night and acceptance during the day.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Aftoriki raises a contradiction between the verse 'וְהָיָה שִׁבְעַת יָמִים תַּחַת אִמּוֹ' (it shall be seven days under its mother), which implies the night is fit, and the verse 'מִיּוֹם הַשְּׁמִינִי וָהָלְאָה יֵרָצֶה' (from the eighth day onward it will be accepted), which excludes the night.

Rabbi Aftoriki resolves the contradiction by distinguishing: the night is for sanctification (קדושה) and the day is for acceptance (הרצאה), and cites a supporting verse 'כֵּן תַּעֲשֶׂה לְשֹׁרְךָ לְצֹאנֶךָ' (so shall you do to your ox and your sheep).

items.text: דעת רבי שמעון: אין איסור 'אותו ואת בנו' בקדשים
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna cites Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna reports that Rabbi Shimon holds that the law of "it and its son" does not apply to consecrated animals, because their slaughter is not considered valid slaughter.
items.desc: רב המנונא אומר בשם רבי שמעון שאיסור 'אותו ואת בנו' אינו נוהג בקדשים, משום ששחיטת קדשים אינה שחיטה ראויה עד זריקת הדם.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna reports that Rabbi Shimon holds the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) does not apply to consecrated animals, because their slaughter is not considered valid slaughter.
sub.desc: רב המנונא מביא בשם רבי שמעון שאיסור אותו ואת בנו אינו נוהג בקדשים, משום ששחיטת קדשים אינה שחיטה ראויה.

items.text: Rava's objection from a baraita
items.text_en: Rava's objection from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rava raises an objection from a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says the second animal is only subject to a negative commandment, not karet, which seems to imply the law applies to consecrated animals. The Gemara questions how the second animal could be exempt from karet.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that the second consecrated animal slaughtered outside the Temple is only subject to a negative commandment, not karet, while the Sages disagree.
The Gemara questions how the second animal could be exempt from karet, since the first was already slaughtered outside and the second is fit for inside sacrifice.

items.text: Rava's resolution: the baraita is missing cases
items.text_en: Rava's resolution: the baraita is missing cases
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the baraita is incomplete and actually discusses multiple scenarios: both animals outside, one outside and one inside, and one inside and one outside, with different rulings for the Rabbis and Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by asserting that the baraita is missing cases and actually teaches: both animals outside — for the Rabbis, the first is liable to כרת (extirpation), the second is invalid and exempt from the prohibition of slaughtering outside.
Rava continues: for Rabbi Shimon, both animals are liable to כרת (extirpation).
Rava continues: one outside and one inside — for the Rabbis, the first is liable to כרת (extirpation), the second is invalid and exempt; for Rabbi Shimon, the second is valid.

Rava concludes: one inside and one outside — for the Rabbis, the first is valid and exempt, the second is invalid and exempt; for Rabbi Shimon, the second is subject to a negative prohibition (בל תעשה).

items.text: Gemara's challenge to Rav Hamnuna's view
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge to Rav Hamnuna's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that if the law does not apply to consecrated animals, why is the second animal only subject to a negative commandment and not karet?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Hamnuna's view that the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the mother and its offspring) does not apply to consecrated animals, arguing that if so, the second animal slaughtered outside should be subject to karet (excision), not merely a negative commandment.

items.text: Rava's reinterpretation: lashes, not the law itself
items.text_en: Rava's reinterpretation: lashes, not the law itself
items.desc_en: Rava clarifies that Rav Hamnuna meant that lashes for the law do not apply to consecrated animals, because the warning is a warning of doubt, which is not a valid warning.

sub.desc_en: Rava reinterprets Rav Hamnuna's statement: the prohibition of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the mother and its offspring) does not apply with lashes to consecrated animals.
Rava explains that since the meat is not permitted until the blood is sprinkled, at the time of slaughter it is a warning of doubt (התראת ספק), which is not a valid warning for lashes.

items.text: Rava's consistent principle with hullin and kodashim
items.text_en: Rava's consistent principle with hullin and kodashim
items.desc_en: Rava applies his principle to cases of hullin and kodashim: slaughtering hullin first and then kodashim is exempt, but kodashim first then hullin is liable, and similarly with olah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rava applies his consistent principle: slaughtering hullin first and then kodashim is exempt from the prohibition of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the mother and its offspring).
Rava adds that slaughtering kodashim first and then hullin is liable, and similarly with an olah offering, slaughtering hullin first and then olah is exempt.

items.text: דיון בשחיטת עולה ואיסור אותו ואת בנו
items.text_en: Gemara's initial analysis of slaughter for the altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that even if one slaughters an olah (burnt offering) and then a non-sacred animal, he is exempt from "it and its son" because the first slaughter is not fit for human consumption. Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan argues that consumption by the altar is considered eating, citing a verse about two types of eating.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה במקרה ששחט עולה ואחר כך חולין, ופוטרת משום ששחיטת עולה אינה שחיטה הראויה לאכילה. רבי יוחנן בשם רבי יעקב סובר שאכילת מזבח נחשבת אכילה, ולכן שחיטת עולה ראויה לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that even if one slaughters an olah (burnt offering) and then a non-sacred animal, he is exempt from 'it and its son' because the first slaughter is not fit for human consumption.
sub.desc: הגמרא פוטרת בשחיטת עולה ואחר כך חולין, משום ששחיטת עולה אינה שחיטה הראויה לאכילה.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan argues that consumption by the altar (אכילת מזבח) is considered eating, citing a verse about two types of eating.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן בשם רבי יעקב סובר שאכילת מזבח נחשבת אכילה, ולכן שחיטת עולה ראויה לאכילה.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: מחלוקת רבי שמעון וחכמים
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of slaughter exempt from 'it and its son'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where slaughter is not valid for the prohibition: slaughtering a treifa, for idolatry, the red heifer, a stoned ox, and the heifer whose neck is broken – Rabbi Shimon exempts, the Sages obligate. Additionally, if the animal becomes a neveila, or if one stabs or tears the neck, he is exempt.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת מקרים שבהם השחיטה אינה ראויה לאכילה (טריפה, עבודה זרה, פרה אדומה וכו'), ורבי שמעון פוטר מאיסור אותו ואת בנו, וחכמים מחייבים. במקרים של שחיטה פסולה (ניחור, עיקור) כולם פוטרים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where one slaughters and the animal is found to be a טריפה (torn), or slaughters for idolatry, or slaughters the red heifer, or a stoned ox, or the heifer whose neck is broken — Rabbi Shimon exempts and the Sages obligate.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת: רבי שמעון פוטר וחכמים מחייבים באיסור אותו ואת בנו בשחיטה שאינה ראויה לאכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that one who slaughters and the animal becomes a נבלה (carcass) in his hand, or one who stabs or tears — is exempt from 'it and its son'.
sub.desc: המשנה מוסיפה שבשחיטה פסולה (ניחור, עיקור) כולם פוטרים.

items.text: Reish Lakish's initial ruling on idolatry
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's initial ruling on idolatry
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the Mishnah's dispute applies only when the first animal is slaughtered for idolatry and the second for the table; but if the first is for the table and the second for idolatry, the slaughterer is exempt because he is liable for a greater prohibition (idolatry).

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish limits the Mishnah's dispute to cases where the first animal is slaughtered for idolatry and the second for the table, exempting the slaughterer when the first is for the table and the second for idolatry due to the greater prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and alternative scenario
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection and alternative scenario
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know this, and instead argues that even if the first is for the table and the second for idolatry, he can be liable. This occurs when he was warned for 'it and its son' but not for idolatry. Reish Lakish counters that since if warned he is exempt (due to the greater prohibition), even without warning he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan objects that even schoolchildren know Reish Lakish's ruling, implying it is trivial.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that even in the case where the first is for the table and the second for idolatry, the slaughterer can be liable.
Rabbi Yochanan specifies the scenario: he was warned for 'it and its son' but not for idolatry.
Reish Lakish counters that since if warned he is exempt (due to the greater prohibition), even without warning he is exempt.

items.text: הרחבה למחלוקת בחייבי מיתות שוגגין
items.text_en: General principle: liability for unwarned capital or lashes offenses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that their dispute follows a broader principle: for unwarned capital or lashes offenses combined with another prohibition, Rabbi Yochanan holds liable (since no warning), while Reish Lakish holds exempt (since if warned he would be exempt). The Gemara notes that both cases are necessary to avoid assuming one would concede to the other.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשרת את המחלוקת למחלוקת כללית: בחייבי מיתות שוגגין או חייבי מלקות שוגגין עם דבר אחר (ממון), רבי יוחנן מחייב וריש לקיש פוטר. הצדדים מבהירים את שיטתם, והגמרא מציינת שצריך להשמיע שני המקרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a general principle: Rav Dimi reported that for unwarned capital or lashes offenses combined with another prohibition, Rabbi Yochanan holds liable and Reish Lakish holds exempt.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשרת את המחלוקת למחלוקת כללית שהביא רב דימי: בחייבי מיתות שוגגין או חייבי מלקות שוגגין עם דבר אחר, רבי יוחנן מחייב וריש לקיש פוטר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable because no warning was given for the capital or lashes offense.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה את טעמי המחלוקת: רבי יוחנן מחייב משום שלא התרו בו, וריש לקיש פוטר משום שאם התרו בו היה פטור, ולכן גם כשלא התרו פטור.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish holds exempt because if warned he would be exempt, so without warning he is also exempt.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבהירה את טעמי המחלוקת: רבי יוחנן מחייב משום שלא התרו בו, וריש לקיש פוטר משום שאם התרו בו היה פטור, ולכן גם כשלא התרו פטור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both cases (the 'אותו ואת בנו' dispute and the general principle) are necessary to avoid assuming one sage would concede to the other.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה מדוע יש צורך להשמיע את המחלוקת בשני המקרים: כדי שלא נאמר שבמקרה אחד יודה ריש לקיש לרבי יוחנן או להיפך.

items.text: שאלה על פרה אדומה: האם שחיטתה ראויה לאכילה?
items.text_en: Question about the red heifer's slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether slaughter of the red heifer is considered invalid slaughter, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says the heifer imparts food impurity because it had a time of fitness.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על דברי רבי שמעון במשנה שפטר בפרת חטאת, שהרי ברייתא אומרת שפרה מטמאה טומאת אוכלין משום שהייתה לה שעת הכושר (לאכילה).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the red heifer is a slaughter that is not fit for eating, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon says the heifer imparts food impurity because it had a time of fitness.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי שמעון שפטר בפרת חטאת, שהרי ברייתא אומרת שפרה מטמאה טומאת אוכלין משום שהייתה לה שעת הכושר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that the red heifer imparts food impurity (טוּמְאַת אֳכָלִין) because it had a time of fitness (שְׁעַת הַכּוֹשֶׁר), implying it is considered fit for consumption at some point.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי שמעון שפטר בפרת חטאת, שהרי ברייתא אומרת שפרה מטמאה טומאת אוכלין משום שהייתה לה שעת הכושר.

items.text: דין פרה אדומה לגבי 'אותו ואת בנו'
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's statement about פרה נפדית
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Rabbi Shimon holds that a פרה (red heifer) is redeemed on its pyre. Rabbi Yochanan then says that a פרת חטאת is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו'.
items.desc: רבי שמעון בן לקיש אומר שפרה אדומה נפדית על גבי מערכתה, ולכן יש מצב שהיא ראויה לאכילה. רבי יוחנן חולק וקובע שפרת חטאת אינה משנה, ורבי שמעון מודה שהשוחטה חייב.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that Rabbi Shimon holds that a פרה (red heifer) is redeemed on its pyre.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Shemen bar Abba
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan via Rav Shemen bar Abba
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan asserts that a פרת חטאת (red heifer of purification) is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition of slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day).

items.text: דין עגלה ערופה לגבי 'אותו ואת בנו'
items.text_en: Question about עגלה ערופה and Reish Lakish's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether an עגלה ערופה is considered a valid slaughter (שחיטה ראויה) and thus subject to the prohibition. It cites a Mishnah that if the murderer is found before the עגלה is beheaded, it goes out to pasture. Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai, states that an עגלה ערופה is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו'.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם שחיטת עגלה ערופה אינה שחיטה ראויה? הרי משנה בסוטה אומרת שאם נמצא ההורג לפני עריפה, העגלה יוצאת ורועה בעדר. רבי שמעון בן לקיש בשם רבי ינאי קובע שעגלה ערופה אינה משנה, ורבי שמעון מודה שהשוחטה חייב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether an עגלה ערופה (beheaded heifer) is considered a valid slaughter (שחיטה ראויה) and thus subject to the prohibition, citing a Mishnah that if the murderer is found before the heifer is beheaded, it goes out to pasture.
Reish Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai, answers that an עגלה ערופה is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition against slaughtering an animal and its offspring on the same day).

items.text: קושיה על רבי ינאי מדבריו
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Yannai's other statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yannai himself said he heard a boundary (גבול) regarding the עגלה ערופה but forgot it, and the colleagues say that its descent to the stream (ירידתה לנחל איתן) prohibits it. If so, why not distinguish between before and after the descent?
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם רבי ינאי באמת אמר כך? הרי הוא אמר ששמע גבול בעגלה ערופה ושכחו, והחברים אמרו שירידתה לנחל איתן אוסרתה. אם כן, היה אפשר לתרץ שהמחלוקת היא בין קודם ירידה לאחר ירידה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yannai himself said he heard a boundary (גבול) regarding the עגלה ערופה but forgot it.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yannai's statement is true, why not distinguish between before and after the descent to the stream (ירידתה לנחל איתן)?

items.text: תיקון: רבי שמעון בן לקיש אמר זאת בעצמו
items.text_en: Resolution: Reish Lakish's version and Rav Ashi's question
items.desc_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami says they learn the statement (that עגלה ערופה is not subject to the law) in the name of Reish Lakish. Rav Ashi then questions whether Reish Lakish actually said this, given his position on the birds of the leper.
items.desc: רב פנחס בריה דרב אמי אומר שהמשפט 'עגלה ערופה אינה משנה' נאמר בשם רבי שמעון בן לקיש עצמו, לא בשם רבי ינאי. רב אשי מקשה: האם רבי שמעון בן לקיש באמת אמר כך?

sub.desc_en: Rav Pinchas bar Rav Ami states that they learn the statement (that עגלה ערופה is not subject to the law) in the name of Reish Lakish.
Rav Ashi questions whether Reish Lakish actually said this, given his position on the birds of the leper.

items.text: קושיה ממחלוקת ציפורי מצורע
items.text_en: Contradiction from the birds of the leper
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about when the birds of the leper become forbidden: Rabbi Yochanan says from the time of slaughter, Reish Lakish says from the time of taking. The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish derives this from a גזירה שוה of 'קיחה' from עגלה ערופה, implying that the עגלה is subject to some prohibition from the time of taking.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי נאמר במחלוקת על ציפורי מצורע שרבי שמעון בן לקיש סובר שנאסרות משעת לקיחה, בגזירה שווה מעגלה ערופה. משמע שסובר שעגלה ערופה אסורה מחיים, ולכן שחיטתה אינה ראויה, ופטור מ'אותו ואת בנו'. סותר לכאורה לדבריו הקודמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish about when the birds of the leper become forbidden, and asks for Reish Lakish's reasoning.
The Gemara explains that Reish Lakish derives his position from a גזירה שוה (verbal analogy) of 'קיחה' (taking) from the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer).

items.text: תירוץ: רבי יוחנן אמר זאת
items.text_en: Final resolution: Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that an עגלה ערופה is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו', resolving the contradiction.
items.desc: רבי חייא בר אבא בשם רבי יוחנן אומר שהמשפט 'עגלה ערופה אינה משנה' נאמר על ידי רבי יוחנן, לא על ידי רבי שמעון בן לקיש. כך נפתרת הקושיה.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that an עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken) is not subject to the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition against slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day), thereby resolving the earlier contradiction.

items.text: משנה: שניים שלקחו פרה ובנה
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on two purchasers
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if two people bought a cow and its calf, the one who bought first slaughters first; if the second preceded, he has acquired (the right). Rav Yosef explains that this teaches a halachic principle: the second is called 'zriz' (diligent) and 'niskar' (rewarded) because he did not commit a prohibition and gets to eat meat.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת: שניים שלקחו פרה ובנה, מי שלקח ראשון שוחט ראשון, ואם הקדים השני – זכה. הגמרא מבהירה שזה לעניין דין, אבל אם הקדים השני הרי הוא זריז ונשכר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for two purchasers of a cow and its calf: the first buyer slaughters first, but if the second preceded, he acquires the right.
Rav Yosef explains that the Mishnah teaches a halachic principle: the second buyer is called 'zriz' (diligent) and 'niskar' (rewarded) because he did not commit a prohibition and gets to eat meat.

items.text: משנה: דיני מלקות בשוחט פרה ובניה
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on lashes for violating 'אותו ואת בנו'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details cases of lashes: slaughtering a cow and then its two calves incurs eighty lashes; slaughtering two calves and then the cow incurs forty; slaughtering a cow, its daughter, and its granddaughter incurs eighty; slaughtering a cow, its granddaughter, and then its daughter incurs forty. Sumchos says eighty. The Gemara questions why the last case is not always eighty, and derives from the verse 'לא תשחטו' that one who slaughters the mother and the offspring is liable, but not for the reverse order.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת מקרים של שחיטת פרה ובניה באותו יום, ומספר המלקות. הגמרא דנה מדוע השוחט שני בנים ואחר כך האם לוקה ארבעים, ומסבירה שהפסוק 'אותו ואת בנו' כולל גם בנו ואותו, כפי שנלמד מ'לא תשחטו' בלשון רבים.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases of lashes for violating 'אותו ואת בנו' (the mother and her offspring), with Sumchos citing Rabbi Meir ruling eighty lashes in the last case.
The Gemara questions why the last case is not always eighty, arguing that the verse 'אותו ואת בנו' (it and its son) applies only to the mother then offspring, not the reverse.
The Gemara rejects the objection by citing a baraita that derives from 'לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ' (do not slaughter) that the last two slaughters in any sequence are liable, explaining the Mishnah's rulings.

items.text: דרשת לשון הרבים 'לא תשחטו'
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the plural form of the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah uses the plural 'לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ' instead of the singular 'לֹא תִשְׁחוֹט', and deduces that it teaches two laws: the prohibition applies even to two people, and it also conveys something else.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה מדוע התורה כתבה 'לא תשחטו' בלשון רבים, ומסיקה שזה מלמד שני דברים: האיסור חל גם על שני אנשים השוחטים יחד, וגם על שחיטת האם אחרי הבן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah uses the plural 'לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ' instead of the singular 'לֹא תִשְׁחוֹט', implying it teaches something beyond the basic prohibition.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הפסוק 'לא תשחטו' נצרך לגופו לאיסור עצמו, ואם כן מדוע נכתב בלשון רבים? ומציעה שאם הכוונה רק לאיסור יחיד, היה מספיק לכתוב 'לא תשחוט'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially answers that the plural form teaches that the prohibition applies even to two people, not just one.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: לשון הרבים נצרכת כדי ללמד שגם שני אנשים השוחטים יחד אסורים, שאם נכתב 'לא תשחוט' הייתי אומר שרק יחיד אסור. אך עדיין קשה: היה מספיק לכתוב 'לא ישחטו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the only purpose were to include two people, the Torah could have used the third-person plural 'לֹא יִשְׁחֲטוּ', so the second-person plural must teach something additional.

The Gemara concludes that the plural form 'לֹא תִשְׁחֲטוּ' teaches two laws: the prohibition applies to two people, and it also conveys something else (the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its grandchild).
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה: לשון 'לא תשחטו' מלמדת שני דברים – האיסור חל גם על שני אנשים, וגם על שחיטת האם אחרי הבן.

items.text: בירור שיטת סומכוס: חיוב שתי מלקות על שחיטת 'אותו ואת בנו'
items.text_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef about Sumchus's reasoning
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef what Sumchus's rationale is for holding one liable for two sets of lashes when slaughtering a cow and its granddaughter. Rav Yosef explains that Sumchus holds that eating two olive-sized portions of fat in one lapse of awareness incurs two sin-offerings, and here the bodies are distinct.
items.desc: אביי שואל את רב יוסף מה טעמו של סומכוס המחייב שמונים מלקות. רב יוסף מסביר שסומכוס סובר שאכילת שני זיתי חלב בהעלם אחד מחייבת שתי חטאות, ומכאן שגם כאן חייב שתי מלקות.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef what the reasoning of Sumchos is for holding one liable for eighty lashes.
sub.desc: אביי שואל את רב יוסף מהו טעמו של סומכוס המחייב שמונים מלקות בשחיטת 'אותו ואת בנו'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests that Sumchos holds that eating two olive-bulks of forbidden fat in one lapse of awareness incurs two sin-offerings.
sub.desc: רב יוסף משיב שסומכוס סובר שאכילת שני זיתי חלב בהעלם אחד מחייבת שתי חטאות, ומכאן שגם כאן חייב שתי מלקות.

sub.text: Rav Yosef's explanation of the mishna's choice
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's explanation of the mishna's choice
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the mishna specifically teaches this case to highlight the far-reaching leniency of the Rabbis, who exempt even when the bodies are separate.
Abaye proposes an alternative: perhaps Sumchos holds that eating two olive-bulks of fat in one lapse incurs only one sin-offering, and the double liability here is due to the bodies being separate.
Rav Yosef definitively states that Sumchos holds that eating two olive-bulks of forbidden fat in one lapse of awareness incurs two sin-offerings.

items.text: הוכחה ממשנת כלאיים: זורע כלאיים כלאיים לוקה
items.text_en: Proof from the mishnah on kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a mishnah about one who sows kilayim multiple times, which implies multiple lashes. It clarifies that the case is simultaneous sowing with one warning, and concludes that the Tanna must be Sumchus, but then deflects that it could be the Rabbis teaching that there are two types of kilayim.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא על הזורע כלאיים כלאיים שלוקה שתיים, ומנסה להוכיח שזו שיטת סומכוס. אך דוחה שייתכן שמדובר בשתי התראות נפרדות, והברייתא באה ללמד שיש שני סוגי כלאיים, בניגוד לרבי יאשיה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of Sumchos's opinion, citing a baraita that one who sows diverse kinds twice is flogged, and clarifies that this must mean two sets of lashes.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מניין לרב יוסף שסומכוס סובר כך, ומביאה ברייתא על הזורע כלאיים כלאיים שלוקה שתי מלקיות, ומסיקה שפשוט שמדובר בשתי מלקיות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita, ruling out the case of sequential acts with separate warnings (already known from Nazir), and concludes it must be simultaneous acts with a single warning.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם הברייתא עוסקת בשתי התראות נפרדות, הרי זה פשוט ומפורש במשנת נזיר; על כרחך שהברייתא עוסקת בבת אחת ובהתראה אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the Tanna of the baraita is, arguing that if it were the Rabbis who disagree with Sumchos, they would exempt here a fortiori since they exempt even with separate entities.
