sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: האם הברייתא היא כרבנן החולקים על סומכוס? והרי לדבריהם, במקום שגופין מוחלקין פטרו, כל שכן כאן בכלאיים שאין גופין מוחלקין.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests the baraita is Sumchos, but then deflects: it could be the Rabbis, and the repetition 'diverse kinds, diverse kinds' incidentally teaches that there are two categories of kilayim.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: לא, הברייתא כרבנן, והכפילות באה ללמד שיש שני סוגי כלאיים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the baraita also excludes the opinion of רבי יאשיה (Rabbi Yoshiyah), who requires sowing wheat, barley, and grape seed together; the baraita teaches that even sowing wheat with grape seed or barley with grape seed alone is liable.
sub.desc: הברייתא באה להוציא מדברי רבי יאשיה, הסובר שאין חיוב כלאיים עד שיזרע חיטה ושעורה וחרצן במפולת יד, ומלמדת שגם זריעת חיטה וחרצן ושעורה וחרצן מחייבת.

items.text: הוכחה ממשנת גיד הנשה: אכל מזה כזית ומזה כזית סופג שמונים
items.text_en: Proof from the case of eating two olive-sized portions
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where one who eats an olive-sized portion from each of two animals receives eighty lashes, and Rabbi Yehuda says forty. The Gemara analyzes whether this is simultaneous or sequential, and concludes that the first Tanna is Sumchus, but then deflects that it could be the Rabbis following a different Tanna who holds that a doubtful warning is valid.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה האומרת שאכל משני גידי הנשה סופג שמונים, ורבי יהודה פוטר. מנסה להוכיח שזו שיטת סומכוס, אך דוחה שייתכן שמדובר בזו אחר זו ובשתי התראות, והתנא קמא סובר כאותו תנא שלרבי יהודה התראת ספק שמה התראה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where one who eats an olive-sized portion from each of two animals receives eighty lashes, and Rabbi Yehuda says forty.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה בגיד הנשה: האוכל משני גידים סופג שמונים, ורבי יהודה פוטר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the case is set: if it is sequential with two warnings, why would Rabbi Yehuda exempt him, since he holds that a doubtful warning is invalid.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה בגיד הנשה: האוכל משני גידים סופג שמונים, ורבי יהודה פוטר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that for two simultaneous actions one is liable, but for sequential ones he is exempt, confirming his position on doubtful warnings.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המבארת שרבי יהודה פוטר בזו אחר זו משום התראת ספק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the baraita must be discussing simultaneous eating with a single warning.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיקה שהמשנה עוסקת בבת אחת ובהתראה אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who the first Tanna is: if it is the Rabbis who disagree with Sumchus, they would exempt here too, so it must be Sumchus.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם התנא קמא הוא רבנן, קל וחומר שפטרו כאן; אלא ודאי סומכוס היא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects: it is actually sequential, and the first Tanna follows a different Tanna who holds that a doubtful warning is valid, citing a verse about the Paschal lamb.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: לעולם מדובר בזו אחר זו, והתנא קמא סובר כאותו תנא שלרבי יהודה התראת ספק שמה התראה.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי יהודה ורבי יעקב על לאו שניתק לעשה
items.text_en: Dispute on lashes for the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Torah gave a positive command after a negative command to indicate no lashes. Rabbi Yaakov argues it is because it is a prohibition without an action, for which one is not lashed.
items.desc: רבי יהודה ורבי יעקב נחלקים בטעם הפטור ממלקות באיסור 'לא תותירו': רבי יהודה סובר משום שניתק לעשה, ורבי יעקב סובר משום שאין בו מעשה.

sub.desc_en: רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) states that the verse provides a positive command after a prohibition to indicate that one is not flogged.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מסביר שהכתוב נותן עשה אחר לא תעשה כדי לפטור ממלקות.

sub.desc_en: רבי יעקב (Rabbi Yaakov) argues that the reason for no lashes is not the positive command but because it is a prohibition without an action.
sub.desc: רבי יעקב חולק וטוען שהפטור הוא משום לאו שאין בו מעשה.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the dispute via a baraita
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the dispute via a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about eating two sciatic nerves from two animals, where the first Tanna says eighty lashes and Rabbi Yehuda says forty. It analyzes whether the case is simultaneous or sequential, and identifies the first Tanna as Sumkhos. It concludes that Rabbi Yehuda's view applies when there is less than an olive's bulk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita about eating two sciatic nerves from two animals, where the first Tanna says eighty lashes and Rabbi Yehuda says forty, and analyzes whether the case is simultaneous or sequential.
The Gemara asks who the first Tanna is, and concludes it must be Sumkhos, not the Rabbis.
The Gemara resolves that the case is sequential, and Rabbi Yehuda's view applies when one sciatic nerve lacks an olive's bulk.

items.text: משנת ארבעה פרקים ומכירת בהמה
items.text_en: Mishnah: Four times when a seller must inform
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists four periods when a seller of an animal must inform the buyer if the mother or daughter was already sold for slaughter, to avoid violating the prohibition of slaughtering parent and offspring on the same day. Rabbi Yose HaGelili adds Yom Kippur eve in the Galilee. Rabbi Yehuda qualifies when this applies, and the Mishnah states that during these periods the butcher is compelled to sell even at a loss.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שבארבעה פרקים בשנה המוכר בהמה צריך להודיע אם מכר את האם או הבת לשחיטה. מובאת מחלוקת רבי יהודה ודין כפיית הטבח לשחוט.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists the four periods when a seller must inform the buyer if the mother or daughter was already sold for slaughter.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין ארבעה פרקים בשנה שבהם המוכר בהמה צריך להודיע אם מכר את האם או הבת לשחיטה, ומפרטת את הפרקים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose HaGelili adds Yom Kippur eve in the Galilee to the list.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין ארבעה פרקים בשנה שבהם המוכר בהמה צריך להודיע אם מכר את האם או הבת לשחיטה, ומפרטת את הפרקים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda qualifies that the obligation to inform applies only when the seller has no profit, but if he has profit he need not inform.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מגביל את החיוב להודיע לזמן שאין לו ריווח, ומודה במקרה של חתן וכלה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda concedes that when selling the mother to a groom and the daughter to a bride, the seller must inform, since both will slaughter on the same day.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מגביל את החיוב להודיע לזמן שאין לו ריווח, ומודה במקרה של חתן וכלה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that during these four periods the butcher is compelled to sell even at a loss, and if the animal dies the loss falls on the buyer; during the rest of the year the loss falls on the seller.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת שבארבעה פרקים אלו כופין את הטבח לשחוט, ואם מת הבהמה – מת ללוקח, אבל בשאר ימות השנה – מת למוכר.

items.text: גמרא על המשנה: הולך ושוחט, ודין חתן וכלה
items.text_en: Gemara on the Mishnah's details
items.desc_en: A Tosefta states that if the seller did not inform, the buyer may slaughter without concern. The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the groom and bride is needed, and explains it teaches that the groom's household is busier than the bride's.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא שאם לא הודיעו, הלוקח שוחט ואינו נמנע. ודנה בדין מכירת האם לחתן והבת לכלה, ומסיקה שאורח ארעא שהחתן טורח יותר.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta is cited stating that if the seller did not inform the buyer, the buyer may go ahead and slaughter without concern.
sub.desc: הבאת ברייתא: אם לא הודיעו המוכר, הלוקח שוחט ואינו נמנע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah needed to include Rabbi Yehuda's specific case of the groom and bride.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: למה נקטה המשנה דווקא 'האם לחתן והבת לכלה'?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the Mishnah incidentally teaches a lesson in proper conduct: the groom's household is busier than the bride's.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: למה נקטה המשנה דווקא 'האם לחתן והבת לכלה'?

items.text: קושיית משיכה ותירוץ רב שמואל בר רב יצחק
items.text_en: Gemara on the acquisition mechanism
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the buyer acquires the animal without meshikhah (pulling). Rav Huna says it is when he pulled. Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak explains it is through acquisition by another (zikhui), since during these four periods it is a benefit for the buyer and one can acquire benefit for a person in their absence.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה מדין משיכה, ורב הונא ורב שמואל בר רב יצחק מתרצים: מדובר בזיכוי על ידי אחר, ובארבעה פרקים זכין לו שלא בפניו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the buyer acquires the animal in these four periods without performing meshikhah (pulling).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה: כיצד כופין לשחוט אם לא משך, והרי לא קנה?

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where the buyer did pull the animal.
sub.desc: רב הונא בשם רב מתרץ: מדובר כשמשך, ולכן קנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if pulling occurred, the animal should belong to the buyer even in other seasons, contradicting the Mishnah's ruling.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה: כיצד כופין לשחוט אם לא משך, והרי לא קנה?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves that the Mishnah speaks of acquisition through a third party (zikhui), which is valid in these four periods because it benefits the buyer, but invalid in other seasons because it is a detriment.
sub.desc: רב הונא בשם רב מתרץ: מדובר כשמשך, ולכן קנה.

items.text: תירוץ רבי אלעזר בשם רבי יוחנן: דין תורה מעות קונות
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that during these four periods the Sages upheld their words based on Torah law, because Torah law says money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshikhah to prevent fraud.
items.desc: רבי אלעזר בשם רבי יוחנן מסביר שבארבעה פרקים החזירו חכמים את דין תורה שמעות קונות, כדי שלא ימנע משמחת הרגל.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that during these four periods the Sages upheld their words based on Torah law.
sub.desc: רבי אלעזר בשם רבי יוחנן קובע שבארבעה פרקים אלו החזירו חכמים את דין תורה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that by Torah law money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshikhah (משיכה, pulling) as a גזירה (decree) to prevent the seller from claiming 'your wheat burned in the attic' after receiving payment.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מביא את הטעם שדין תורה מעות קונות, וחכמים תקנו משיכה משום גזירה.

items.text: משנת 'יום אחד' באותו ואת בנו ודרשת בן זומא
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on 'one day' following night
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that 'one day' in the context of 'it and its offspring' follows night, as derived by Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma from Genesis. The Gemara adds a baraita explaining that while in consecrated matters night follows day, here a gezerah shavah teaches that day follows night.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת ש'יום אחד' באיסור אותו ואת בנו הולך אחר הלילה, כדרשת רבי שמעון בן זומא מגזירה שווה ממעשה בראשית. הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המפרשת את הדרשה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the phrase 'one day' in the context of 'it and its offspring' means the day follows the night.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת ש'יום אחד' באיסור אותו ואת בנו הולך אחר הלילה, ומביאה את דרשת רבי שמעון בן זומא בגזירה שווה ממעשה בראשית.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma derives this by a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the phrase 'one day' in the act of Creation, where the day follows the night.

items.text: סיום הפרק הקודם
items.text_en: Closing of previous chapter and transition
items.desc_en: Rabbi's statement about a unique day requiring a proclamation leads to the rule about four times a year a seller must inform the buyer. The chapter concludes with 'הדרן עלך'.
items.desc: רבי אומר ש'יום אחד' בפסוק 'אותו ואת בנו' מתייחס ליום מיוחד הטעון כרוז, ומכאן ארבעה פרקים בשנה שמוכר בהמה צריך להודיע.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi interprets the verse 'one day' to mean a unique day requires a proclamation, establishing that a seller must inform the buyer at four times of the year.
sub.desc: רבי דורש את הפסוק 'יום אחד' כיום מיוחד הטעון הכרזה, ומכאן דין ארבעה פרקים בשנה שמוכר בהמה צריך להודיע.

sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes the chapter with the formula 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you) for the chapter 'אותו ואת בנו'.

items.text: משנת כיסוי הדם
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Covering blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that covering blood applies in the Land and outside, whether the Temple stands or not, to non-sacred animals but not to consecrated ones, to wild animals and birds, to domesticated and undomesticated, and to a hybrid (כוי) due to doubt. It also rules that one may not slaughter a כוי on a Festival, and if slaughtered, its blood is not covered.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שמצוות כיסוי הדם נוהגת בחולין ולא במוקדשין, בחיה ובעוף, בכוי מספק, ואין שוחטים כוי ביו"ט.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that the law of covering the blood (כיסוי הדם) applies in the Land of Israel and outside, with and without the Temple, to non-sacred animals but not to sacred ones, to wild animals and birds, to domesticated and undomesticated animals, and to the hybrid 'כוי' (koy) because it is a doubtful case.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בהלכות כיסוי הדם: נוהג בחולין ולא במוקדשין, בחיה ובעוף, ובכוי מספק, ואין שוחטים כוי ביו"ט.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah adds that one may not slaughter the koy on a festival day, and if one did slaughter it, one does not cover its blood.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: מדוע אין כיסוי במוקדשין?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on consecrated animals and Rabbi Zeira's requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why covering blood does not apply to consecrated animals. It suggests Rabbi Zeira's reason: the slaughterer must place earth below and above the blood, based on the verse 'בעפר'. For consecrated animals, placing earth below is impossible because it would add to the Temple structure, violating the principle that all was given by God, and not placing it would create a separation.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע אין כיסוי במוקדשין? ומציעה טעם מדברי רבי זירא שצריך עפר למטה ולמעלה, ובמזבח אי אפשר. אך דוחה: אפשר לעשות עפר למעלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why covering blood does not apply to consecrated animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע אין כיסוי הדם במוקדשין, ומציעה טעם מדברי רבי זירא שצריך עפר למטה ולמעלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rabbi Zeira's reason: the slaughterer must place earth below and above the blood, derived from the verse 'בְּעָפָר'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע אין כיסוי הדם במוקדשין, ומציעה טעם מדברי רבי זירא שצריך עפר למטה ולמעלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that placing earth below is impossible for consecrated animals because it would add to the Temple structure, violating the principle that all was given by God.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות להניח עפר על המזבח ולבטלו, משום שמוסיף על בניין המזבח.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the alternative of not placing earth below, as it would create a separation (חציצה) between the blood and the ground.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה גם את האפשרות שלא לבטל את העפר, משום שהוא חוצץ בין הדם למזבח.

items.text: Objection: Why not cover only above?
items.text_en: Objection: Why not cover only above?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if placing earth below is impossible, one could still cover the blood from above, fulfilling the requirement partially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: even if placing earth below is impossible, one could still cover the blood from above, fulfilling the requirement partially.

items.text: Answer: Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's ruling and Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.text_en: Answer: Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's ruling and Rabbi Zeira's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers by citing Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef: if one slaughters a wild animal and then a domesticated animal, he is exempt from covering; if domesticated first then wild, he is obligated. This is explained by Rabbi Zeira's principle: anything fit for mixing (ביללה) does not require mixing to be valid, but what is not fit for mixing requires it. Since consecrated blood is not fit for mixing (as it is sprinkled), covering is not applicable.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef rules that slaughtering a wild animal first then a domesticated one exempts from covering the blood, while the reverse obligates covering.

Rabbi Zeira explains that anything fit for mixing (ביללה) does not require mixing to be valid, but what is not fit for mixing requires it; since consecrated blood is not fit for mixing (as it is sprinkled), covering is not applicable.

items.text: תירוץ סופי: קדשי בדק הבית
items.text_en: Further objection and resolution: Consecrated property vs. altar
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not scrape the blood and cover it, as taught that blood on a knife must be covered? It answers: for animals consecrated for the altar, that would be possible, but here we are dealing with animals consecrated for Temple maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), where the blood is not used and covering is not required.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: יגרור את הדם ויכסה? ומתרצת: מדובר בקדשי בדק הבית שאסורים בהנאה, ולכן אין מצוות כיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why not scrape the blood from the knife and cover it, citing the Mishnah that blood on a knife must be covered.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע לא יגרור את הדם מהמזבח ויכסה במקום אחר, כפי שעושים בדם הניתז ועל הסכין?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: for animals consecrated for the altar (קדשי מזבח) that would be possible, but here we are dealing with animals consecrated for Temple maintenance (קדשי בדק הבית), where covering is not required.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: בקדשי מזבח אכן היה צריך לגרור ולכסות, אך כאן מדובר בקדשי בדק הבית שאסורים בהנאה, ולכן אין מצוות כיסוי.

items.text: Question on covering blood for non-sacred animals
items.text_en: Question on covering blood for non-sacred animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the blood of non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard is not covered, given that it is not sacred. It considers two Tannaic views: Rabbi Meir holds that slaughter not fit for consumption is still called slaughter, but requires standing and valuation; Rabbi Shimon holds it is not called slaughter and does not require standing and valuation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the blood of non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard is not covered, noting that such animals require standing and valuation.
The Gemara considers Rabbi Meir's view that slaughter not fit for consumption is still called slaughter, which would require covering the blood.
The Gemara considers Rabbi Shimon's view that slaughter not fit for consumption is not called slaughter, which would exempt the animal from standing and valuation.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi's compromise
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Rabbi's compromise
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who adopts Rabbi Shimon's view on slaughter not fit for consumption and Rabbi Meir's view on standing and valuation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves the contradiction by stating that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who adopts Rabbi Shimon's view on slaughter not fit for consumption and Rabbi Meir's view on standing and valuation.

items.text: Alternative answer: Entirely Rabbi Shimon with a scriptural distinction
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Entirely Rabbi Shimon with a scriptural distinction
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation suggests the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, but here a special verse ("and he shall pour and cover") excludes animals that require additional acts like redemption or dragging. This is extended to include sacred animals of the altar that require dragging.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative answer: the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, but a special verse ("and he shall pour and cover") excludes animals that require additional acts like redemption.
The Gemara extends the exclusion to include sacred animals of the altar that require dragging (גְּרִירָה) in addition to pouring and covering.

items.text: דרשת מר בר רב אשי להוצאת קודשים
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's derivation from 'chaya or bird'
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi derives from the verse 'chaya or bird' that just as a chaya (non-domesticated animal) is never consecrated, so too a bird is never consecrated. The Gemara refines this: just as all chayot are equal regarding covering blood, so too all birds are equal, excluding doves and pigeons which have consecrated species.
items.desc: מר בר רב אשי דורש מהפסוק 'חיה או עוף' שאין חיוב כיסוי דם בעופות המוקדשים, בדומה לחיה שאינה קודש. הגמרא דוחה אפשרות להוציא תורים ובני יונה, ומסיקה שאין לחלק בין מיני עוף.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi derives from the verse 'חיה או עוף' (chaya or bird) that just as a chaya is never consecrated, so too a bird is never consecrated.
sub.desc: מר בר רב אשי דורש מהפסוק 'חיה או עוף' שחיה אינה קודש, כך גם עוף הפטור מכיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the analogy is that a chaya has no consecrated species, then doves and pigeons, which have consecrated species, would be excluded from the obligation of covering blood.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם דנים כחיה, יש להוציא תורים ובני יונה שאינם קודש, אך מינם קודש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara refines the analogy: just as all chayot are equal regarding covering blood, so too all birds are equal, excluding no species.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: כחיה שאין חילוק במיניה, כך בעוף אין לחלק בין מינים.

items.text: דיון על דם בהמה כמים לטבילה
items.text_en: Discussion with Yaakov the heretic: blood of a chaya and immersion
items.desc_en: Yaakov the heretic suggests that since a chaya is included in behemah for signs, behemah should be included in chaya for covering blood. Rava refutes this with a verse comparing blood to water, which does not require covering. The Gemara then discusses whether blood can be used for immersion, concluding with three exclusions in the verse to exclude blood.
items.desc: יעקב המינאה טוען שיש להשוות בהמה לחיה לעניין כיסוי הדם. רבא דוחה זאת מהפסוק 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים'. הגמרא דנה האם דם כשר לטבילה, ודוחה זאת ממיעוטים בפסוק.

sub.desc_en: Yaakov the heretic argues that since a חיה (undomesticated animal) is included in בהמה (domesticated animal) for signs of kashrut, a בהמה should likewise be included in חיה for the mitzva of covering blood.
sub.desc: יעקב המינאה טוען שיש להשוות בהמה לחיה לעניין כיסוי הדם, כשם שחיה בכלל בהמה לסימנים.

sub.desc_en: Rava refutes by citing the verse 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים' (you shall pour it on the ground like water), comparing blood of a domesticated animal to water, which does not require covering.
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את הטענה מהפסוק 'על הארץ תשפכנו כמים', המשווה דם בהמה למים שאינם טעונים כיסוי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if blood is like water, one should be able to immerse impure items in it, and responds with the verse 'אך מעין ובור מקוה מים יהיה טהור' (but a spring and a cistern, a gathering of water, shall be pure), which excludes other substances.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם דם כמים, יטבילו בו? ודוחה ממיעוט 'אך' בפסוק.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the exclusion might only apply to other liquids not called water, but blood is called water (as in the verse), so perhaps immersion in blood is valid.
The Gemara responds that two exclusions are written in the verse: 'מעין מים' (a spring of water) and 'ובור מים' (a cistern of water), implying that blood is excluded.
The Gemara objects that both exclusions might refer to other liquids: one for flowing liquids and one for gathered liquids, not blood.
The Gemara resolves that three exclusions are written: 'מעין מים' (a spring of water), 'ובור מים' (a cistern of water), and 'מקוה מים' (a gathering of water), the third excluding blood.

items.text: ברייתא על 'אשר יצוד' ודרך ארץ
items.text_en: Baraita on 'asher yatzud' – teaching derech eretz
items.desc_en: A baraita expounds the verse 'asher yatzud' (which you hunt) to include even animals that are already caught, like geese and chickens. The phrase 'asher yatzud' teaches derech eretz: one should not eat meat unless it is specifically prepared for this purpose.
items.desc: ברייתא דורשת את הפסוק 'אשר יצוד' ללמד שגם עופות מבויתים חייבים בכיסוי הדם, אך המילה 'יצוד' מלמדת דרך ארץ שלא לאכול בשר אלא בהזמנה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'אֲשֶׁר יָצוּד' (who traps) and asks: from where do we include animals already trapped, like geese and chickens?
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת 'אשר יצוד' ללמד שגם עופות מבויתים חייבים בכיסוי הדם, אך 'יצוד' מלמד דרך ארץ שלא לאכול בשר אלא בהזמנה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita answers: the verse says 'צֵיד' (trapping) to include any case.
The baraita asks: if so, why does the verse specify 'אֲשֶׁר יָצוּד' (who traps)?
The baraita resolves: the Torah teaches derech eretz — a person should not eat meat except with this kind of preparation.

items.text: Baraita on meat consumption and financial prudence
items.text_en: Baraita on meat consumption and financial prudence
items.desc_en: Another baraita teaches that one should eat meat only when there is an appetite, and not buy meat from the market but from one's own flock. It limits consumption to a portion, not all. Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya gives guidelines: one with a maneh buys a litra of vegetables, with ten maneh a litra of fish, with fifty a litra of meat, with a hundred a pot daily, but only from erev Shabbat to erev Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'כי ירחיב ה׳ אלהיך את גבלך' (when the Lord your God expands your border) and teaches that one should not eat meat except when there is an appetite.

The baraita derives from the verse 'וזבחת מבקרך ומצאנך' (and you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your flock) that one should not buy meat from the market but from one's own flock, and should not slaughter all of one's animals but only a portion.

Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya provides financial guidelines: one with a maneh (100 zuz) buys a litra of vegetables, with ten maneh a litra of fish, with fifty a litra of meat, with a hundred a pot daily, but only from ערב שבת (Sabbath eve) to ערב שבת.

items.text: Amoraic statements on financial conduct and further teachings
items.text_en: Amoraic statements on financial conduct and further teachings
items.desc_en: Rav says we must heed the elder's words; Rabbi Yochanan says one with a prutah should spend it on food; Rav Nachman says we borrow and eat. The Gemara then expounds verses from Proverbs about selling a field for goats, not vice versa, and about prioritizing one's own bread over that of one's household. Mar Zutra derives that one should not teach his son meat and wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that we must be concerned with the words of the elder (Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya) regarding financial conduct.
Rabbi Yochanan says that one who has a prutah (small coin) in his pocket should spend it on food, citing his own family background.
Rav Nachman says that people like us borrow and eat, implying reliance on credit for sustenance.
The Gemara expounds verses from Proverbs: one should sell a field to buy goats, not vice versa, and be satisfied with the milk of one's own flock.
Mar Zutra derives from the verse that one's own bread takes precedence over that of his household, and that one should not teach his son to crave meat and wine.

items.text: עצה להתעשרות מבהמה דקה
items.text_en: Opening aggadic statement on wealth through small cattle
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains the verse 'and the wealth of your flock' as meaning that small cattle enrich their owners.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בעצה שעיסוק בבהמה דקה מעשיר, ומסבירה את הפסוק 'ועשתרות צאנך' כמעשירות את בעליהן.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda interprets the verse 'וְעַשְׁתְּרֹת צֹאנְךָ' to mean that small cattle enrich their owners.

items.text: עצות בריאות: שתיית מים פושרים
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on drinking vessels
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan discusses the preference for earthenware cups over metal ones for hot drinks, with exceptions for certain conditions.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן מזהיר מפני שתיית מים פושרים בכלי מתכת ללא תבלינים או רתיחה, אך מתיר בכלי חרס.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states a preference for earthenware cups over metal ones for hot drinks.
The gemara qualifies that the preference applies only to metal vessels, not earthenware ones.
The gemara further qualifies that even for metal vessels, the preference applies only when no splinters are added to the drink.
The gemara adds that even without splinters, the preference applies only when the vessel is not cracked.

items.text: עצה לאיבוד כסף
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on how to waste inherited money
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan advises that one who wishes to waste inherited money should wear fine linen, use glass vessels, and hire workers without supervising them.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן מייעץ כיצד לאבד כסף: ללבוש פשתן רומי, להשתמש בכלי זכוכית לבנים, ולשכור פועלים עם שוורים ללא השגחה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan advises that one who wishes to waste inherited money should wear fine linen, use glass vessels, and hire workers without supervising them.

items.text: הנהגה נכונה בממון ובמשפחה
items.text_en: Rav Avira's teaching on spending priorities
items.desc_en: Rav Avira teaches that one should eat and drink less than one can afford, dress according to one's means, and honor one's wife and children beyond one's means.
items.desc: רב עוירא דורש בשם רבי אמי ורבי אסי: אדם יאכל וישתה פחות ממה שיש לו, יתלבש לפי מה שיש לו, ויכבד אשתו ובניו יותר ממה שיש לו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avira, citing Rabbi Ami or Rabbi Asi, teaches that one should eat and drink less than one can afford, dress according to one's means, and honor one's wife and children beyond one's means.

items.text: Rav Eina's ruling on covering blood for a sick person on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rav Eina's ruling on covering blood for a sick person on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Eina states that one who slaughters for a sick person on Shabbat is obligated to cover the blood. Rabba objects, citing a baraita that a koy slaughtered on Yom Tov does not require covering its blood.

sub.desc_en: Rav Eina rules that one who slaughters for a sick person on Shabbat is obligated to cover the blood.
Rabba objects, expressing astonishment and suggesting that Rav Eina's statement should be removed from him.
Rabba cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that a koy (a hybrid animal) is not slaughtered on Yom Tov, and if one slaughters it, its blood is not covered.

items.text: Kal vachomer from circumcision to covering blood
items.text_en: Kal vachomer from circumcision to covering blood
items.desc_en: A kal vachomer is proposed: if circumcision, whose definite performance overrides Shabbat, has its doubtful case not override Yom Tov, then covering blood, whose definite does not override Shabbat, should certainly not override Yom Tov in a doubtful case.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument): if circumcision, whose definite performance overrides Shabbat, has its doubtful case not override Yom Tov, then covering blood, whose definite does not override Shabbat, should certainly not override Yom Tov in a doubtful case.

items.text: Rebuttal from shofar on borders
items.text_en: Rebuttal from shofar on borders
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: shofar on borders, whose definite does not override Shabbat, yet its doubtful case overrides Yom Tov, disproving the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: An anonymous objection raises the case of shofar on borders, whose definite case does not override Shabbat, yet its doubtful case overrides Yom Tov, disproving the kal vachomer.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's response
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar's response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar responds that circumcision is not practiced on nights of Yom Tov, whereas covering blood is practiced on nights of Yom Tov, so the kal vachomer stands.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar responds that circumcision is not practiced on nights of Yom Tov, whereas covering blood is practiced on nights of Yom Tov, so the kal vachomer stands.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's comment on the response
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's comment on the response
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba notes that this is one of the cases where Rabbi Chiya said he had no answer, yet Rabbi Elazar HaKappar provided one.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba notes that this is one of the cases where Rabbi Chiya said he had no answer, yet Rabbi Elazar HaKappar provided one.

items.text: Clarification of the definite case of covering blood
items.text_en: Clarification of the definite case of covering blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the definite case of covering blood that does not override Shabbat, and suggests it is the case of slaughtering for a sick person on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the definite case of covering blood that does not override Shabbat, and suggests it is the case of slaughtering for a sick person on Shabbat.

items.text: Alternative interpretation: transgressive slaughter
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation: transgressive slaughter
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the definite case might be where one transgressed and slaughtered, not a permitted case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the definite case of covering blood on Shabbat might refer to one who transgressed and slaughtered, not a permitted case.

items.text: Comparison to circumcision: both permitted
items.text_en: Comparison to circumcision: both permitted
items.desc_en: The Gemara argues that just as circumcision is permitted, so too covering blood must be permitted, not transgressive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that just as circumcision is performed לכתחילה (the ideal standard) and is permitted, so too covering the blood is performed לכתחילה and is permitted, not transgressive.

items.text: Repeated objection from shofar
items.text_en: Repeated objection from shofar
items.desc_en: The objection from shofar is repeated: its definite does not override Shabbat, but its doubtful overrides Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Sages repeat the objection from shofar: its definite does not override Shabbat, but its doubtful overrides Yom Tov, challenging the kal vachomer.

items.text: Clarification of the doubtful case of shofar
items.text_en: Clarification of the doubtful case of shofar
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what the doubtful case of shofar is: if it is doubt between weekday and Yom Tov, then certainly a definite Yom Tov overrides Shabbat, so a doubtful case is even more compelling?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the doubtful case of shofar is, arguing that if it is doubt between weekday and Yom Tov, then since definite Yom Tov overrides Shabbat, the doubtful case should certainly override Yom Tov, making the question superfluous.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Rabbi Yose's view and a rebuttal
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous sugya: Rabbi Yose's view and a rebuttal
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the discussion about a person of uncertain gender (tumtum) and the obligation to cover blood. It notes that Rabbi Yose's position aligns with his view that women may blow the shofar. Rabina raises a challenge to the Rabbis' comparison to shofar, and Rabbi Elazar HaKappar offers a counter-argument from circumcision, which Rabbi Abba notes was answered by Rabbi Elazar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a person of uncertain gender (tumtum) regarding the obligation to cover blood.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yose's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yose's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yose's ruling aligns with his view that women may perform the מצוה (commandment) of shofar blowing, citing a baraita about women's optional semikhah.

Rabina raises an objection to the Rabbis' comparison to shofar, arguing that shofar is different because it is performed לכתחילה (the ideal standard) on Shabbat in the Temple, unlike covering blood which has no such dispensation.
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar offers a counter-argument from circumcision, which is not performed at night on festivals, but is performed on other nights, challenging the Rabbis' analogy.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution and Rabbi Abba's comment
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution and Rabbi Abba's comment
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the argument by noting that circumcision is not practiced at night as it is by day, unlike covering blood which applies both day and night; Rabbi Abba then notes that Rabbi Chiyya considered this argument irrefutable, but Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi provided a response.

items.text: Mishnah: Cases exempt from covering blood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases exempt from covering blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where slaughter does not require covering the blood: if the animal is found to be a tereifah, if slaughtered for idolatry, if non-sacred animals are slaughtered inside the Temple or sacred animals outside, and for animals that are stoned. Rabbi Meir obligates covering in these cases, while the Sages exempt. It also states that if the animal becomes neveilah during slaughter, or if one tears or uproots the simanim, one is exempt from covering.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists cases where slaughter does not require covering the blood, including a tereifah, idolatrous slaughter, and Temple-related cases, with Rabbi Meir obligating and the Sages exempting.
The Mishnah adds that if the animal becomes neveilah during slaughter, or if one tears or uproots the simanim, one is exempt from covering the blood.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi's endorsement of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon's views
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi's endorsement of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon's views
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) saw the reasoning of Rabbi Meir regarding 'it and its son' and taught it in the language of the Sages, and similarly saw the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon regarding covering the blood and taught it in the language of the Sages.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports that Rabbi (Yehudah HaNasi) endorsed Rabbi Meir's reasoning on 'it and its son' and Rabbi Shimon's reasoning on covering the blood, teaching each in the language of the Sages.

items.text: Reasoning for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon regarding 'it and its son'
items.text_en: Reasoning for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon regarding 'it and its son'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon's positions on whether slaughter that is not fit (e.g., for idolatry) is considered valid slaughter for the prohibition of 'it and its son'. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says Rabbi Meir learns a gezeirah shavah from 'slaughter' used in the context of slaughtering outside the Temple. Rabbi Mani bar Pattish says Rabbi Shimon learns from the verse 'slaughter slaughter and prepare' that only fit slaughter is considered. The Gemara then discusses why each does not learn from the other's source, and concludes that Rabbi saw Rabbi Meir's reasoning as correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Meir's reasoning regarding the prohibition of 'it and its son'.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that Rabbi Meir derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שחיטה' used in the context of slaughtering outside the Temple.
The Gemara elaborates that just as there, slaughter that is not fit is still called slaughter, so too here, slaughter that is not fit is still called slaughter.
The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Shimon's reasoning.
Rabbi Mani bar Pattish explains that Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'טְבוֹחַ טֶבַח וְהָכֵן' (slaughter and prepare) that only fit slaughter is considered valid slaughter.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir could also learn from the word 'טבוח' (slaughter).
The Gemara rejects the objection, stating that one derives a verbal analogy from the word 'שחיטה' (slaughter) and not from 'טביחה' (slaughtering).
The Gemara digresses to cite a teaching from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that different words can refer to the same concept, but this principle applies only when there is no similar term.
The Gemara resolves that the principle of deriving from similar words applies only when there is no closer parallel, but when there is a closer parallel, one derives from it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon could also learn from the case of slaughtering outside the Temple.
The Gemara rejects the objection, stating that one derives a verbal analogy from non-sacred to non-sacred, but not from non-sacred to sacred.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Meir could argue that the prohibition of 'it and its son' applies even to sacred animals, so the distinction between sacred and non-sacred is not relevant.
The Gemara concludes that this is why Rabbi Chiyya said that Rabbi saw Rabbi Meir's reasoning as correct and taught it in the name of the Sages.

items.text: Reasoning for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon regarding covering blood
items.text_en: Reasoning for Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon regarding covering blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon's positions on whether slaughter that is not fit requires covering the blood. Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says Rabbi Meir learns a gezeirah shavah from 'pouring' used in the context of slaughtering outside the Temple. Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'which may be eaten' that only animals fit for eating require covering. The Gemara notes that Rabbi saw Rabbi Shimon's reasoning as correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Meir's position that slaughter not fit for eating requires covering the blood, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish answers that Rabbi Meir derives a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'שפיכה' (pouring) used in the context of slaughtering outside the Temple.

Rabbi Shimon derives from the verse 'אשר יאכל' (which may be eaten) that only animals fit for eating require covering the blood, and he argues that a טריפה (ritually unfit animal) is also not fit for eating, just like a non-kosher bird.
The Gemara concludes that this is what Rabbi Chiyya meant when he said that Rabbi saw Rabbi Shimon's reasoning as correct and taught it in the language of the Sages.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's statement (fragment)
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's statement (fragment)
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a statement by Rabbi Abba, but the text is cut off, likely continuing on the next amud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a statement by Rabbi Abba, but the text is cut off, likely continuing on the next amud.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that R' Meir and R' Shimon each concede certain aspects of their positions on invalid slaughter: R' Meir agrees it does not permit eating, and R' Shimon agrees it purifies from neveilah.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that R' Meir and R' Shimon each concede certain aspects of their positions on invalid slaughter: R' Meir agrees it does not permit eating, and R' Shimon agrees it purifies from neveilah.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of R' Meir's concession
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of R' Meir's concession
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why R' Meir's concession is needed, as a tereifah cannot be permitted through slaughter. It explains the case involves a live nine-month-old fetus found in a slaughtered tereifah, where one might think the mother's slaughter suffices. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi holds a hybrid view: like R' Meir that invalid slaughter is slaughter, and like the Rabbis that the mother's slaughter purifies the fetus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why R' Meir's concession is needed, since a tereifah cannot be permitted through slaughter.
The Gemara explains the case involves a live nine-month-old fetus found in a slaughtered tereifah, where one might think the mother's slaughter suffices.
The Gemara objects that R' Meir holds a ben peku'a requires slaughter, so the mother's slaughter cannot suffice.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi holds a hybrid view: like R' Meir that invalid slaughter is slaughter, and like the Rabbis that the mother's slaughter purifies the fetus, yet still requires slaughter.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of R' Shimon's concession
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of R' Shimon's concession
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why R' Shimon's concession is needed, citing a source that a tereifah's slaughter purifies from neveilah. It explains the case involves slaughtering a tereifah that is chullin in the Temple courtyard, where one might think since R' Shimon permits benefit, it is not slaughter at all and does not purify. The Gemara teaches that it does purify.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Shimon's concession is needed, since a baraita already teaches that a tereifah's slaughter purifies from neveilah.
The Gemara explains the case involves slaughtering a tereifah that is chullin in the Temple courtyard.

The Gemara resolves that without the teaching, one might think since Rabbi Shimon permits benefit, the slaughter is not considered slaughter at all and does not purify; the teaching shows it does purify.

items.text: Discussion on chullin in the Temple courtyard
items.text_en: Discussion on chullin in the Temple courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether R' Shimon holds that the prohibition of chullin in the Temple courtyard is biblical. Abaye answers yes, citing a baraita where R' Shimon says such animals must be burned, and the Gemara explains that if it were rabbinic, one would not decree a decree for a wild animal.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye whether Rabbi Shimon holds that the prohibition of chullin in the Temple courtyard is biblical (דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא).
Abaye answers yes, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon rules that chullin slaughtered in the courtyard must be burned, and similarly a wild animal.
The Gemara explains that if the prohibition were biblical, the decree extending it to a wild animal makes sense, but if it were rabbinic, one would not decree a decree for a decree.

items.text: Story of Rabbi and the bird in flax
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi and the bird in flax
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya had a bird caught in his flax and came before Rabbi, who told him to slaughter it over water so the blood would attract the bird's mate. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita that one who slaughters and needs the blood must cover it, and suggests alternatives. Rav Dimi and Ravin report that Rabbi said 'go tear' or 'go stab', and the Gemara explains that Rabbi holds that bird slaughter is not biblical, and stabbing is its slaughter, citing a baraita about Moses being commanded on the trachea and esophagus.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya had a bird caught in his flax and came before Rabbi, who told him to slaughter it over water so the blood would attract the bird's mate.

The Gemara questions how Rabbi could instruct slaughtering for blood, citing a baraita that one who slaughters and needs the blood must cover it, and suggests alternatives: either stabbing or tearing.
Rav Dimi and Ravin report that Rabbi actually said 'go tear' or 'go stab' instead of 'slaughter', resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara asks why the version 'go tear' was preferred over 'go stab'.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds that bird slaughter is not biblical, and stabbing is its slaughter, citing a baraita about Moses being commanded on the trachea and esophagus.

items.text: Clarifying the Tanna's statement about 'צֵא נְחוֹר' and 'צֵא טְרוֹף'
items.text_en: Clarifying the Tanna's statement about 'צֵא נְחוֹר' and 'צֵא טְרוֹף'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna's statement 'לא מיבעיא' means that 'צֵא נְחוֹר' is certainly not slaughter at all, but one might think 'צֵא טְרוֹף' is a valid but unfit slaughter requiring covering, so the Tanna teaches otherwise, in accordance with Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Tanna's statement uses 'לא מיבעיא' (not only) to teach that 'צֵא נְחוֹר' (go out and tear) is certainly not slaughter, while 'צֵא טְרוֹף' (go out and tear) might be considered a valid but unfit slaughter requiring covering, so the Tanna teaches otherwise, in accordance with Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba.

items.text: Question for the one who says 'צֵא נְחוֹר'
items.text_en: Question for the one who says 'צֵא נְחוֹר'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says 'צֵא נְחוֹר' does not also say 'צֵא טְרוֹף', and suggests he might hold that an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter, but this is contradicted by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw Rabbi Shimon's view on covering blood and taught it in the language of the Sages.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who says 'צֵא נְחוֹר' does not also say 'צֵא טְרוֹף'.
The Gemara objects that if one holds that an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter, this is contradicted by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw Rabbi Shimon's view on covering blood and taught it in the language of the Sages, implying that an unfit slaughter is considered slaughter.

items.text: Alternative explanation for the Tanna's statement
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for the Tanna's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another interpretation: the Tanna says 'לא מיבעיא' regarding 'צֵא טְרוֹף' because an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter, but regarding 'צֵא נְחוֹר' one might think there is no Torah obligation of slaughter for birds and its tearing is its slaughter, so the Tanna teaches 'כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִיךְ' to indicate a tradition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative interpretation: the Tanna uses 'לא מיבעיא' to prioritize 'צֵא טְרוֹף' because an unfit slaughter is not considered slaughter, but regarding 'צֵא נְחוֹר' one might think there is no Torah obligation of slaughter for birds and its tearing is its slaughter, so the Tanna teaches 'כַּאֲשֶׁר צִוִּיתִיךְ' to indicate a tradition.

items.text: Digression: The merit of Rabbi Chiyya and his sons
items.text_en: Digression: The merit of Rabbi Chiyya and his sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a thorn could fall into Rabbi Chiyya's flax, given that since the return from exile, harmful phenomena ceased and the Sages focused on Rabbi Chiyya and his sons. It answers that their merit protected the world but not themselves, citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav that a heavenly voice declares the world is sustained for Chanina my son, yet he himself subsists on a meager portion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a thorn could fall into Rabbi Chiyya's flax, given that since the return from exile, harmful phenomena ceased and the Sages focused on Rabbi Chiyya and his sons.

The Gemara answers that their merit protected the world but not themselves, citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav that a heavenly voice declares the world is sustained for Chanina my son, yet he himself subsists on a meager portion.

items.text: Mishnah: Deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor slaughtering
items.text_en: Mishnah: Deaf-mute, imbecile, and minor slaughtering
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor slaughter and others see them, one is obligated to cover the blood; if they slaughter alone, one is exempt. Similarly for 'אותו ואת בנו', if others see them, it is forbidden to slaughter after them; if alone, Rabbi Meir permits and the Sages forbid, but they agree that if one slaughtered, he does not receive lashes.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor slaughter and others see them, one is obligated to cover the blood; if they slaughter alone, one is exempt.

The Mishnah adds that for the law of 'אותו ואת בנו' (slaughtering a parent and offspring on the same day), if others see them, it is forbidden to slaughter after them; if alone, Rabbi Meir permits and the Sages forbid, but they agree that one who slaughters does not receive lashes.

items.text: Gemara: Why do the Sages dispute only in the latter clause?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why do the Sages dispute only in the latter clause?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Sages do not dispute in the first clause (covering blood) but do in the second (אותו ואת בנו). It considers possible reasons involving concern that people might eat from their slaughter, but rejects them. It concludes that the Sages dispute the entire matter, but they waited for Rabbi Meir to finish his statement before arguing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Sages do not dispute in the first clause (covering blood) but do dispute in the second clause (אותו ואת בנו).
The Gemara suggests that in the first clause, if we say they are obligated to cover, people might think the slaughter is valid and eat from it.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning should apply in the second clause: if the Sages forbid slaughtering after them, people might think the slaughter is valid and eat from it.
The Gemara answers that in the second clause, people say the meat is not needed, but in the first clause, people say he needs to clean his courtyard.
The Gemara objects that if one slaughters in a garbage dump or if one comes to consult, the previous answer does not apply.
The Gemara counters that the same objection applies to the second clause as well.
The Gemara resolves that the Sages actually dispute the entire matter, but they waited for Rabbi Meir to finish his statement before arguing.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's reasoning and the principle of majority
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's reasoning and the principle of majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir permits slaughter after them. Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Meir would hold them liable for neveila because most of their actions are flawed. Rav Pappa questions why majority is needed, since Rabbi Meir is concerned even for a minority when combined with a chazaka, citing a Mishnah about a child and dough where Rabbi Meir is stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Granted, the Sages are stringent, but what is Rabbi Meir's reasoning for permitting slaughter after them?

Rabbi Yaakov citing Rabbi Yochanan answers that Rabbi Meir would hold them liable for neveila (carcass) because most of their actions are flawed, and Rabbi Ami adds the explanation that the majority of their actions are defective.

sub.text: Rav Pappa to Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa to Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects: Why mention majority? Even a minority should suffice, since Rabbi Meir is concerned for a minority, and when combined with a chazaka (presumption of fitness), it undermines the majority.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a child found near dough with dough in his hand, where Rabbi Meir rules it pure despite a minority of children who handle dough, because the dough stands in a chazaka of purity, demonstrating Rabbi Meir's concern for a minority combined with a chazaka.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on majority vs. doubt
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on majority vs. doubt
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic of using a minority to weaken a presumption against a majority, and asks whether a doubt in ritual impurity can be treated leniently while a doubt in prohibition is treated stringently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the logic of combining a minority with a presumption to weaken a majority, and asks whether a doubt in impurity can be treated leniently while a doubt in prohibition is treated stringently.

items.text: Resolving whether Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Meir or the Sages
items.text_en: Resolving whether Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Meir or the Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a story involving Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Abba to determine which ruling Rabbi adopted later. It concludes from Rabbi Elazar's message that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which of Rabbi's two rulings — like Rabbi Meir or like the Sages — was his final position.

sub.text: Story of Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Abba
sub.text_en: Story of Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Zeira, and Rabbi Abba
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Rabbi Ami rebuked Rabbi Zeira and Rabbi Abba for waiting outside the study hall, and Rabbi Zeira later suggested asking Rabbi Abba's father who heard from Rabbi Yochanan about the final ruling.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion from Rabbi Elazar's message
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion from Rabbi Elazar's message
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the question by citing Rabbi Elazar's message to the diaspora that Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Meir, concluding that this was his final position.

items.text: Mishnah: Covering blood for multiple animals
items.text_en: Mishnah: Covering blood for multiple animals
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters many animals or birds in one place, a single covering of blood suffices for all, but Rabbi Yehuda requires covering the blood of a wild animal before slaughtering a bird.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one covering of blood suffices for many animals or birds slaughtered in one place, but Rabbi Yehuda requires covering the blood of a wild animal before slaughtering a bird.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita supporting the Mishnah, then explains the debate: the Sages derive from 'or' that one covering suffices, while Rabbi Yehuda uses 'or' to divide and derives the covering requirement from 'its blood'.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports the Mishnah's ruling: one covering suffices for multiple animals or birds slaughtered in one place.

Rabbi Yehuda states that one must cover the blood of a חיה (non-domesticated animal) before slaughtering a bird, deriving from the verse 'חיה או עוף' (a non-domesticated animal or a bird) that the covering is separate for each.
The Gemara asks: what are the Sages responding to Rabbi Yehuda when they cite the verse 'כי נפש כל בשר דמו בנפשו הוא' (for the life of all flesh is its blood)?

The Gemara explains that the Sages are saying: the word 'אוֹ' (or) in the verse is needed to divide the categories (i.e., to teach that the covering obligation applies to both חיה and עוף separately, not to require separate coverings for each act).

The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda derives the division from the word 'דָּמוֹ' (its blood) in the verse, while the Sages hold that 'דָּמוֹ' teaches a broader principle about the life-force in blood.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's concession on blessings and a parallel from Rav's students
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's concession on blessings and a parallel from Rav's students
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Yehuda agrees one blessing suffices for covering multiple animals. Ravina questions this, and a story about Rav's students shows that once one engages in covering, a blessing is required.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that Rabbi Yehuda concedes that for the matter of the blessing (ברכה) over covering the blood, one blessing suffices for multiple animals.
Ravina (or Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi) questions: what is the difference between this case and the case of Rav's students?

A story is cited: Rav's students were at a meal, asked for a blessing (ברכה) over wine, then asked to drink; Rav Yeiva Saba ruled in Rav's name that once they said 'give to bless,' they are prohibited from drinking.
The gemara applies the parallel: here too, once one engages in covering (כיסוי), a blessing (ברכה) is required.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about one who slaughters and does not cover, asking how it is possible to slaughter and cover separately if the obligation is immediate.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about one who slaughters and does not cover, asking how it is possible to slaughter and cover separately if the obligation is immediate.

items.text: Mishnah: Obligation to cover blood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Obligation to cover blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughters and does not cover, another person is obligated to cover. If it was covered and then uncovered, one is exempt. If the wind covered it, one is obligated to cover.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one slaughtered and did not cover the blood, and another saw it, the latter is obligated to cover it; if it was covered and then uncovered, the original slaughterer is exempt; if the wind covered it, he is obligated to cover it.

items.text: Baraitot on the source of the obligation
items.text_en: Baraitot on the source of the obligation
items.desc_en: Three baraitot derive from the verse 'And he shall pour and cover' that the one who slaughters must cover, but if another sees it, he is obligated. A story is told where Rabban Gamliel fined someone ten gold coins for covering before the slaughterer.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita derives from the verse 'וְשָׁפַךְ וְכִסָּה' (and he shall pour and cover) that the one who slaughters must cover, and from 'וָאֹמַר לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל' (and I said to the children of Israel) that any Israelite who sees uncovered blood is obligated to cover it.
The second baraita derives from the same verse that the covering must be done with the same substance that was poured, not with the foot, so that מצוות (commandments) are not treated contemptuously.
The third baraita derives that the one who slaughters must cover, and relates a story where Rabban Gamliel fined a person ten gold coins for covering the blood before the slaughterer could do so.

items.text: The reward for the mitzvah: a story with a heretic
items.text_en: The reward for the mitzvah: a story with a heretic
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised whether the ten gold coins were for the mitzvah or for the blessing. A story follows where a heretic challenges Rabbi, and after the heretic dies, Rabbi offers him a choice between a cup of blessing or forty gold coins. A bat kol declares the cup of blessing worth forty gold coins.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: were the ten gold coins given as reward for the mitzvah (מצוה) of covering the blood or for the blessing (ברכה) of Birkat Hamazon, and asks what practical difference this makes.
A heretic challenges Rabbi with a verse that seems to separate the creation of mountains and wind, and Rabbi rebukes him by pointing to the end of the verse.
The heretic asks for three days to prepare a rebuttal, Rabbi fasts, and when about to eat he is told the heretic is at the door, prompting a verse of distress.

The heretic's messenger reports his death, Rabbi invites him to eat, and after the meal offers a choice between a cup of blessing (כוס של ברכה) or forty gold coins; the messenger chooses the cup, and a bat kol declares it worth forty gold coins.
Rabbi Yitzchak notes that this family still exists among the Roman nobility, called the family of Bar Luianus.

items.text: Gemara on 'covered and uncovered'
items.text_en: Gemara on 'covered and uncovered'
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why covering blood differs from returning a lost item, where one must return it even a hundred times. Rav Ashi answers that regarding covering, the verse says 'and cover it' implying a limitation.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi why the case of covering blood that became uncovered is different from the law of returning a lost item, where the Torah commands returning it even a hundred times.
Rav Ashi answers that regarding lost items no limiting term is written, but regarding covering blood the verse writes 'וְכִסָּהוּ' (and cover it) implying a limitation.

items.text: Gemara on 'covered by the wind'
items.text_en: Gemara on 'covered by the wind'
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling applies only if the blood became uncovered again. Rav Papa explains that this shows there is no disqualification for mitzvot. A distinction is made regarding blood absorbed in the ground.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah quotes Rabbi Yochanan that the Mishnah's ruling about blood covered by wind applies only if the blood later became uncovered again; otherwise one is exempt.
The Gemara objects: if the blood was covered and then uncovered, the mitzvah was already fulfilled (דיחוי), so why should one be obligated again?
Rav Papa answers that this case demonstrates the principle that there is no disqualification of דיחוי (a missed opportunity) regarding מצוות (commandments); the obligation renews.
The Gemara objects: why is this different from the case where blood is absorbed into the ground, where one is still obligated to cover it?
The Gemara resolves: there, the ruling applies only when the blood's impression (רישומו) is still recognizable in the ground.

items.text: Mishnah: Blood mixed with other liquids
items.text_en: Mishnah: Blood mixed with other liquids
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blood mixed with water is obligated for covering if it still has the appearance of blood. If mixed with wine, it is viewed as if it were water. If mixed with animal blood, it is viewed as if it were water.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses blood mixed with water, wine, or animal blood, and the conditions for obligation to cover.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Blood mixed with water or other blood
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Blood mixed with water or other blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blood mixed with water is considered as if it were water unless it still has a blood-like appearance. Rabbi Yehuda states that blood cannot nullify blood. It also discusses blood that spurts or is on a knife, requiring covering, with a qualification by Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that blood mixed with water is evaluated as if it were water, and Rabbi Yehuda states that blood cannot nullify blood.
The Mishnah adds that blood that spurts or is on a knife requires covering, with Rabbi Yehuda qualifying that this applies only when there is no other blood present.

items.text: Gemara cites parallel Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara cites parallel Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a parallel Mishnah from another tractate that discusses blood mixed with water, wine, or animal blood, reiterating the principle that blood does not nullify blood according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel Mishnah from another tractate, stating that blood mixed with water, wine, or animal blood is evaluated by appearance, and Rabbi Yehuda rules that blood does not nullify blood.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction and Rav Pappa's application to covering
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's distinction and Rav Pappa's application to covering
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan distinguishes between water falling into blood (not nullified) and blood falling into water (nullified drop by drop). Rav Pappa then applies this to the mitzvah of covering blood, stating that the principle of nullification does not apply to mitzvot.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan, reported by Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, distinguishes between water falling into blood (not nullified) and blood falling into water (nullified drop by drop).
Rav Pappa rules that regarding the mitzvah of covering blood, the nullification principle does not apply — because preconceived rejection (דיחוי) does not apply to mitzvot.

items.text: Shmuel's statement on any reddish appearance and its clarification
items.text_en: Shmuel's statement on any reddish appearance and its clarification
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that any reddish appearance is valid for atonement, qualification, and covering. The Gemara questions what new information this provides, and explains that it is necessary for the case of rainwater that was measured, or that became red on its own.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that any reddish appearance is valid for atonement (הזאה), qualification (הכשר), and covering (כיסוי).
The Gemara asks what new information Shmuel provides, since atonement and covering are already taught in the Mishnah.
The Gemara suggests that Shmuel's statement was needed for the case of qualification (הכשר), but then objects that both blood and water already qualify.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement is needed for the case of rainwater that was measured (i.e., intentionally mixed) with blood.
The Gemara objects that even rainwater, once intentionally measured and poured, is considered significant and should qualify.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel's statement applies to rainwater that became red on its own (without intentional mixing).

items.text: Three opinions on the status of reddish liquid from a corpse
items.text_en: Three opinions on the status of reddish liquid from a corpse
items.desc_en: Three Amoraim give different halakhic consequences for reddish liquid from a corpse: Rabbi Asi says it is like blood for covering, Rabbi Yirmiyah says it incurs karet if there is an olive's bulk, and a baraita teaches it imparts impurity in a tent if there is a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi of Nehardea states that reddish liquid from a corpse is considered like blood for the purpose of covering (כיסוי הדם).
Rabbi Yirmiyah of Difti rules that consuming an olive's bulk of this liquid incurs karet (excision).
A baraita teaches that a quarter-log of this liquid imparts טומאה (ritual impurity) in a tent (אוהל).

items.text: Gemara challenges a Mishnah about liquids of a corpse
items.text_en: Gemara challenges a Mishnah about liquids of a corpse
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that all liquids of a corpse are pure except its blood, and any reddish appearance from it imparts impurity in a tent. It then raises a contradiction from another source about the liquids of a tevul yom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that all liquids of a corpse are pure except its blood, and any reddish appearance from it imparts impurity in a tent.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita about the liquids of a tevul yom (one who immersed that day), which implies that liquids from a corpse should also be impure.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that certain liquids from sources of impurity are considered first-degree impurity, except for liquid that is a father of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that liquids from impure sources are first-degree impurity, except for liquid that is a father of impurity.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of 'light' and 'severe' impurities
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of 'light' and 'severe' impurities
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'light' and 'severe' refer to, and explains that the Sages decreed on the zav because people are not repelled by him, but not on a corpse because people are repelled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'light' and 'severe' impurities refer to, suggesting that 'light' means a sheretz and a zav, and 'severe' means a corpse.
The Gemara rejects the suggestion and clarifies that 'light' means a sheretz and 'severe' means a zav.

items.text: Baraitot on blood that spurts and blood on the knife
items.text_en: Baraitot on blood that spurts and blood on the knife
items.desc_en: Two baraitot teach that blood that spurts and blood on the knife require covering. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel qualify when this applies.

sub.desc_en: The first baraita teaches that blood that spurts and blood on the knife require covering, based on the verse 'וְכִסָּהוּ' (and he shall cover it).
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) qualifies the obligation: it applies only when there is no other blood present; if other blood exists, one is exempt from covering the spurting blood.
A second baraita teaches that the verse 'וְכִסָּהוּ' (and he shall cover it) obligates covering all blood, including blood that spurts and blood on the sides of the animal's throat.

רבן שמעון בן גמליאל (Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel) qualifies the obligation: it applies only if one has not yet covered the blood of the soul; if that blood was already covered, one is exempt from covering the spurting blood.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute among the Tannaim
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute among the Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the differing interpretations of the word 'דמו' (its blood): the Rabbis say all its blood, Rabbi Yehuda says even part of its blood, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the unique blood.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: On what basis do the Tannaim disagree?
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis hold the word 'דמו' (its blood) means all of its blood.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds the word 'דמו' (its blood) means even part of its blood.
The Gemara explains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the word 'דמו' (its blood) means the unique blood, i.e., the blood of the soul.

items.text: Mishnah: Materials for covering blood
items.text_en: Mishnah: Materials for covering blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials that may and may not be used for covering blood, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a general rule: anything that promotes plant growth may be used.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials with which one may or may not cover blood, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel gives a general rule: anything that promotes plant growth may be used.

items.text: Gemara: Definition of fine and coarse sand
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of fine and coarse sand
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan defines fine sand as that which a potter does not need to crush, and coarse sand as that which he does need to crush. The difference between them is sand that crumbles on its own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes fine sand, and Rabba bar bar Chana in the name of Rabbi Yochanan answers: sand that a potter does not need to crush.
The Gemara asks what difference exists between the two definitions, and answers: sand that crumbles on its own is the intermediate case.

items.text: דרשת 'ועפר' לרבות חומרים נוספים
items.text_en: Baraita: Derivation of covering materials from the verse
items.desc_en: A baraita derives from the verse 'וכסהו' that covering must be with earth, and then expands to include fine dung, fine sand, crushed stone, crushed pottery, and fine flax chaff.
items.desc: ברייתא דורשת 'ועפר' למעט אבנים וכלי, ומרבה זבל דק, חול דק, שחיקת אבנים, חרסית ונעורת פשתן דקה.

sub.desc_en: A baraita teaches that the verse 'וְכִסָּהוּ' might imply covering with stones or a vessel, but the verse 'בֶּעָפָר' (in earth) limits it.
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת 'ועפר' למעט אבנים וכלי, ומרבה זבל דק, חול דק, שחיקת אבנים, חרסית ונעורת פשתן דקה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita asks: from where do we include fine dung, fine sand, crushed stone, crushed pottery, and fine flax chaff as valid covering materials?
sub.desc: ברייתא דורשת 'ועפר' למעט אבנים וכלי, ומרבה זבל דק, חול דק, שחיקת אבנים, חרסית ונעורת פשתן דקה.

items.text: Tannaitic baraita on materials for covering blood
items.text_en: Tannaitic baraita on materials for covering blood
items.desc_en: The baraita lists materials that are included (fine sawdust, lime, crushed brick and pot) and excluded (coarse dung, coarse sand, metal filings, uncrushed brick and pot, flour, bran, and coarse meal) based on the verse "ועפר" (and dust). It concludes that only materials that are a type of dust are included.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists materials included and excluded for covering blood, concluding that only dust-like materials are valid.
The baraita explains the inclusion-exclusion rationale: included are those that are a type of dust (מין עפר).

items.text: Gemara's objection and Rav Mari's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and Rav Mari's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as a כלל ופרט (general and specific), which would exclude everything except dust. Rav Mari answers that this is a כלל הצריך לפרט (a general that requires the specific), which is not subject to the rules of כלל ופרט.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse could be interpreted as a כלל ופרט (general and specific), which would exclude everything except dust.
Rav Mari answers that this is a כלל הצריך לפרט (a general that requires the specific), which is not subject to the rules of כלל ופרט.

items.text: דרשת רב נחמן בר רב חסדא וקושיית רבא
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches that covering must be done with something that can be sown and grows. Rava calls this a 'blessing' (i.e., nonsense). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak defends the teaching by citing a baraita: if one is in the desert without ashes, he can grind a gold dinar and cover; if on a ship without earth, he can burn his garment and cover. The Gemara questions the source for gold being considered dust, and Rabbi Zeira cites the verse "ועפרות זהב לו" (and dust of gold).
items.desc: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא דורש שאין מכסים אלא בדבר שזורעים בו ומצמיח. רבא קורא לזה 'בורכא' (שטות). רב נחמן בר יצחק מביא ברייתא המוכיחה שמותר לכסות גם בדבר שאינו מצמיח, כמו אפר או זהב טחון.

sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda teaches that covering blood must be done only with something that can be sown and grows.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא דורש שאין מכסים אלא בדבר שזורעים בו ומצמיח.

sub.desc_en: Rava dismisses the teaching as a 'blessing' (nonsense).
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר רב חסדא דורש שאין מכסים אלא בדבר שזורעים בו ומצמיח.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak defends the ruling by citing a baraita: in the desert one grinds a gold dinar to cover; on a ship one burns his garment to cover.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק שואל את רבא מהי השטות בדרשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the source for considering gold dust as 'עפר' (earth).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אפר נקרא עפר, אבל זהב טחון מניין שמותר?

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira cites the verse 'ועפרות זהב לו' (and dust of gold) to prove that gold dust is called 'עפר'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אפר נקרא עפר, אבל זהב טחון מניין שמותר?

items.text: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Tannaim teach: Beit Shammai says covering is only with dust; Beit Hillel says ash is also called dust, as per the verse "מעפר שרפת" (from the dust of the burning). Beit Shammai responds that it is called 'dust of burning,' not simply 'dust.'

sub.text: Baraita: Bet Shammai and Bet Hillel
sub.text_en: Baraita: Bet Shammai and Bet Hillel
