sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi in the name of Bar Kappara
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in the name of Bar Kappara that all Torah prohibitions are nullified in a ratio of one part forbidden to sixty parts permitted.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אבא פותח בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי משום בר קפרא שכל איסורי התורה בטלים בשישים.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's objection
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak objects, citing Rav Asi that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said in the name of Bar Kappara that all Torah prohibitions are nullified in one hundred, not sixty.
sub.desc: רבי חייא בר אבא פותח בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי משום בר קפרא שכל איסורי התורה בטלים בשישים.

sub.desc_en: The gemara resolves that both positions derive their respective ratios from the verse about the priest's portion of the boiled shoulder (זרוע בשלה), and a supporting baraita is cited.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת ששני החכמים למדו את שיעור הביטול מהפסוק 'זרוע בשלה', ומתחילה להביא את הברייתא הדורשת את המילה 'בשלה'.

items.text: Dispute over the meaning of 'בשלה'
items.text_en: Dispute over the meaning of 'בשלה'
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute between Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and the Sages regarding the interpretation of the word 'בשלה' in the context of the ram of the Nazirite. One opinion holds it means a whole (unslaughtered) ram, while the other holds it means cooked with the ram.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with an anonymous statement that the word 'בשלה' (cooked) in the context of the Nazirite's ram means a whole (unslaughtered) ram.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai argues that 'בשלה' means cooked with the ram, not whole.

items.text: Two explanations for the dispute
items.text_en: Two explanations for the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two alternative explanations (לישנא) for the underlying disagreement. According to the first explanation, all agree the ram is cooked with the meat, but they differ on whether the meat is cut up before cooking. According to the second, all agree the meat is cut up first, but they differ on whether it is cooked with the ram or in a separate pot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes the first explanation: all agree the meat is cooked with the ram, but they differ on whether it is cut up before or after cooking.
The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: all agree the meat is cut up first, but they differ on whether it is cooked with the ram or in a separate pot.
The Gemara clarifies that the first explanation aligns with the view of 'all' (דברי הכל), while the second aligns specifically with Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai.

items.text: מקור המחלוקת בשיעור הביטול
items.text_en: Dispute about the ratio of nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the dispute between those who say the nullification is in sixty (בששים) and those who say it is in one hundred (במאה). The former measures meat and bones together, while the latter measures only the meat.
items.desc: הגמרא מסבירה כיצד המחלוקת בין האומרים 'בשישים' ל'במאה' נובעת מהאופן שבו מעריכים את היחס בין הזרוע האסורה לשאר האיל: אם כוללים עצמות, היחס הוא אחד לשישים; אם רק בשר, היחס הוא אחד למאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says the nullification is in sixty (בששים) measures meat and bones together.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה כיצד המחלוקת בין האומרים 'בשישים' ל'במאה' נובעת מהאופן שבו מעריכים את היחס בין הזרוע האסורה לשאר האיל: אם כוללים עצמות, היחס הוא אחד לשישים; אם רק בשר, היחס הוא אחד למאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the one who says the nullification is in one hundred (במאה) measures only the meat, resulting in a ratio of one in one hundred.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה כיצד המחלוקת בין האומרים 'בשישים' ל'במאה' נובעת מהאופן שבו מעריכים את היחס בין הזרוע האסורה לשאר האיל: אם כוללים עצמות, היחס הוא אחד לשישים; אם רק בשר, היחס הוא אחד למאה.

items.text: Question: Can we derive from this case?
items.text_en: Question: Can we derive from this case?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we can derive a general principle of nullification from the case of the ram, citing a baraita that limits the lesson to this specific case (היתר הבא מכלל איסור).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether we can derive a general principle of nullification from the case of the ram, citing a baraita that limits the lesson to this specific case (היתר הבא מכלל איסור).

items.text: Abaye's answer: For Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: For Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the lesson is needed only for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a substance of its own kind is not nullified (מין במינו לא בטיל). The case of the ram teaches that even for him, nullification applies here.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the lesson from the ram is needed only for Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that a substance of its own kind (מין במינו) is not nullified, but here it is nullified.

items.text: Objection and resolution: A novelty
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: A novelty
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that we could derive the opposite from the verse about the bull and goat (פר ושעיר) which do not nullify each other. It answers that the case of the ram is a novelty (חידוש), and we do not derive from a novelty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that we could derive the opposite rule from the verse about the bull and goat (פר ושעיר), which do not nullify each other.
The Gemara answers that the case of the ram is a novelty (חידוש), and we do not derive halacha from a novelty.

items.text: תירוץ לקושיה על לימוד החומרא
items.text_en: Further objection and resolution: Leniency vs. stringency
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we don't derive a ratio of 160 from the ram. It answers that we derive for stringency (לחומרא), not leniency, since by Torah law nullification is by a simple majority (ברובא בטיל).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם אין ללמוד מכאן, אז גם שיעורי הביטול לא יילמדו מכאן. התשובה היא שאין זה חידוש אלא חומרא, כי מן התורה בטל ברוב, ולכן לומדים מכאן להחמיר בשיעורים גדולים יותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the ram's case is a חידוש (novelty) from which we cannot derive other cases, then why do we derive the ratio of 160 from it?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם אין ללמוד מההיתר של זרוע הנזיר לעניין ביטול, אז גם שיעורי הביטול (שישים או מאה) לא יילמדו ממנו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: we derive only for stringency (לחומרא), not leniency, since by Torah law nullification is by a simple majority (ברובא בטיל).
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שאין זה חידוש אלא חומרא, כי מן התורה בטל ברוב, ולכן לומדים מכאן להחמיר בשיעורים גדולים יותר.

items.text: תירוצו של רבא
items.text_en: Rava's answer: For taste as the essence
items.desc_en: Rava offers an alternative explanation: the lesson is needed for the principle of טעם כעיקר (taste is like the substance), which is prohibited in sacrifices but permitted here.
items.desc: רבא מציע הסבר אחר למיעוט 'זהו': הוא בא למעט את הכלל שטעם כעיקר, שבקדשים אוסר, אבל כאן הטעם מותר.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the lesson is needed for the principle of טעם כעיקר (taste is like the substance), which is prohibited in sacrifices but permitted here.
sub.desc: רבא מציע הסבר אחר למיעוט 'זהו': הוא בא למעט את הכלל שטעם כעיקר, שבקדשים אוסר, אבל כאן הטעם מותר.

items.text: לימוד מחטאת ואי-לימוד מחידוש
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and answer about deriving the nullification rule from chatat
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we don't derive the nullification rule for eiver min hachai from the law of chatat, where contact with its flesh makes other items holy like itself. It answers that chatat is a novel law (chiddush) and we do not derive other laws from a chiddush.
items.desc: הגמרא דנה מדוע אין ללמוד מחטאת שביטול הטעם הוא כמוה, ומשיבה שחטאת היא חידוש ואין למדים מחידוש.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why we do not derive the nullification rule for איבר מן החי (a limb from a living animal) from the law of חטאת (sin-offering), where contact with its flesh makes other items holy like itself.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדוע אין ללמוד מחטאת שביטול הטעם הוא כמוה, ומביאה את הפסוק המלמד שכל הנוגע בבשרה יקדש להיות כמוה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the law of חטאת is a חידוש (novelty) and we do not derive other laws from a חידוש.
sub.desc: הגמרא משיבה שאין ללמוד מחטאת משום שהיא חידוש, ואין למדים מחידוש.

items.text: לימוד לחומרא בלבד
items.text_en: Objection: Why not derive the lenient ratio of one in sixty?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if we cannot derive from chatat because it is a chiddush, then why do we derive the lenient ratio of one in sixty from it? It answers that we are deriving a stringency (chumra), not a leniency, since by Torah law nullification is by majority (rov).
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם אין למדים מחידוש, גם שיעורי הביטול לא ילמדו, ועונה שלומדים לחומרא, שכן מן התורה בטל ברוב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the law of chatat is a חידוש (novelty) from which we cannot derive other cases, then why do we derive the lenient ratio of one in sixty from it?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם אין למדים מחידוש, גם שיעורי הביטול לא ילמדו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: we are not deriving a leniency (קולא) but a stringency (חומרא), since by Torah law nullification is by רוב (majority), and the one-in-sixty rule is stricter.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאם אין למדים מחידוש, גם שיעורי הביטול לא ילמדו.

items.text: פירוש רבנא למקום החתך
items.text_en: Ravina's alternative explanation: the case of the cut place
items.desc_en: Ravina says the law of eiver min hachai was only needed for the place of the cut (mekom chatech), where normally the cut area is forbidden, but here it is permitted because the limb is considered detached.
items.desc: רבנא מסביר שההיתר באיל נזיר נוגע למקום החתך, שבדרך כלל אסור, וכאן הותר.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the law of eiver min hachai was only needed for the place of the cut (mekom chatech), where normally the cut area is forbidden, but here it is permitted because the limb is considered detached.
sub.desc: רבנא מסביר שההיתר באיל נזיר נוגע למקום החתך, שבדרך כלל אסור, וכאן הותר.

items.text: Rav Dimi's statement of the teaching
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's statement of the teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi sits and states this teaching (the previous discussion about nullification).

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi sits and states the teaching about nullification.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: the mishnah about mixtures and the ratio of one in sixty
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: the mishnah about mixtures and the ratio of one in sixty
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi: do all Torah prohibitions require nullification in one hundred? He cites a mishnah about mixtures of leavening, seasoning, and terumah, which states that for a mixture of different species, the nullification is by taste (noten ta'am), not by a fixed ratio. The mishnah's case of lentils and beans shows that if there is no taste, the mixture is permitted even if there is not enough to raise to one hundred and one, implying the ratio is one in sixty.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Dimi: do all Torah prohibitions require nullification in one hundred? He cites a mishnah about mixtures of leavening, seasoning, and terumah, which states that for a mixture of different species, the nullification is by taste (noten ta'am), not by a fixed ratio.
Abaye cites the mishnah's case of lentils and beans: if there is no taste, the mixture is permitted even if there is not enough to raise to one hundred and one, implying the ratio is one in sixty.
Abaye infers that the nullification ratio for mixtures of different species is one in sixty, not one in one hundred.

items.text: Opening question on nullification ratios
items.text_en: Opening question on nullification ratios
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction between the Mishnah's ruling that leaven is nullified in one hundred parts and the later ruling that it requires sixty parts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the apparent contradiction between the Mishnah's ruling that leaven is nullified in one hundred parts and the later ruling that it requires sixty parts.

items.text: Resolution of the Mishnah's two clauses
items.text_en: Resolution of the Mishnah's two clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the first clause of the Mishnah deals with a case where the leaven can leaven, requiring nullification in one hundred and one parts, while the second clause deals with a case where it cannot leaven, requiring only one hundred parts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's first clause (which requires one hundred and one parts) and second clause (which requires sixty) can both be about one hundred.
The Gemara resolves that the first clause requires one hundred and one parts (since the leaven can leaven), while the second clause requires only one hundred parts (since it cannot leaven).

items.text: Further question and silence
items.text_en: Further question and silence
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, if the leaven can leaven, it is not nullified in one hundred and one parts, but the questioner remains silent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, if the leaven has enough potency to leaven, it is not nullified in one hundred and one parts.
The questioner remains silent, indicating no immediate answer was given.

items.text: תירוץ על חומרת השאור והציר
items.text_en: Answer and support from Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: A colleague suggests that leaven is different because its leavening is strong, and then cites Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina who says not all measures are equal, as fish brine requires close to two hundred parts for nullification. The Gemara addresses Rabbi Yehuda's view that a type is not nullified in its own kind, distinguishing brine as mere liquid.
items.desc: אביי מתרץ ששאור שונה כי חימוצו קשה, ורבי יוסי בר חנינא מוסיף שלא כל השיעורים שווים, כדוגמת ציר דג טמא ששיעורו קרוב למאתיים. הגמרא מסבירה שציר נחשב כזיעה ואינו בטל במינו.

sub.desc_en: The colleague suggests that leaven (שאור) is different because its leavening power is strong, so it is not nullified even in a large mixture.
sub.desc: אביי מתרץ את קושייתו הקודמת בכך ששאור שונה משאר איסורים, כי חימוצו חזק ואינו בטל גם במאה ואחת.

sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: The colleague recalls Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's teaching that not all measures are equal, as fish brine requires close to two hundred parts for nullification.
sub.desc: אביי מתרץ את קושייתו הקודמת בכך ששאור שונה משאר איסורים, כי חימוצו חזק ואינו בטל גם במאה ואחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that impure fish brine is forbidden, and Rabbi Yehuda sets its nullification ratio at one quarter in two se'ah (close to 1:200).
sub.desc: אביי מתרץ את קושייתו הקודמת בכך ששאור שונה משאר איסורים, כי חימוצו חזק ואינו בטל גם במאה ואחת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda holds that a type is not nullified in its own kind, so how can he allow brine nullification?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי יהודה, שסובר שמין במינו אינו בטל, ואיך אם כן מתיר ציר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that brine (ציר) is different because it is mere liquid exuded from the fish, not the fish itself, so it is not considered its own kind.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי יהודה, שסובר שמין במינו אינו בטל, ואיך אם כן מתיר ציר.

items.text: כיצד משערים גיד הנשה
items.text_en: How to measure and a dissenting Tanna
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains how to measure the nullification, and the Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow the Tanna who says sinews do not impart flavor.
items.desc: רב הונא אומר שמשערים את הגיד כמו בשר עם ראשי לפתות, והגמרא מציינת שהמשנה אינה כשיטת רבי ישמעאל בנו של רבי יוחנן בן ברוקה שאומר שאין בגידין בנותן טעם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to measure the nullification of forbidden sinews in a mixture.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת כיצד משערים את הגיד, ורב הונא עונה שמשערים אותו כמו בשר עם ראשי לפתות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that the sinews are measured like meat in the heads of the loaves (i.e., they are considered part of the meat for nullification purposes).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת כיצד משערים את הגיד, ורב הונא עונה שמשערים אותו כמו בשר עם ראשי לפתות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow the Tanna who holds that sinews do not impart flavor.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת כיצד משערים את הגיד, ורב הונא עונה שמשערים אותו כמו בשר עם ראשי לפתות.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka who rules that sinews do not impart flavor (and thus are not subject to nullification by taste).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת כיצד משערים את הגיד, ורב הונא עונה שמשערים אותו כמו בשר עם ראשי לפתות.

items.text: סיפור על הוראת רבי חנינא ורבי אמי
items.text_en: Stories about ruling on sinews
items.desc_en: A story is told about a case brought before Rabbi Chanina, where Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina was sitting at the entrance, and later Rabbi Chanina ruled that sinews do not impart flavor. Another story involves Rabbi Ami sending cases to Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chalov, who permitted sinews based on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, though Rabbi Ami did not agree. The halakha is concluded that sinews do not impart flavor.
items.desc: מסופר על אדם שבא לפני רבי חנינא והתיר לו גיד הנשה, ורבי יהודה בר זבינא חלק עליו. רבי חנינא שלח לו שאין בגידין בנותן טעם. רבי אמי היה שולח אנשים לרבי יצחק בן חלוב שהתיר בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי, וההלכה שאין בגידין בנותן טעם.

sub.desc_en: A case came before Rabbi Chanina; Rabbi Yehuda bar Zevina was sitting at the entrance, and after leaving, reported that Rabbi Chanina permitted the sinews.
sub.desc: מסופר על אדם שבא לפני רבי חנינא, ורבי יהודה בר זבינא שישב בפתח שאלו מה הורה לו, והשיב שהתיר לו.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina called the litigant back and declared that sinews do not impart flavor, rebuking the one who had ruled otherwise.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה בר זבינא הורה להחזיר את השאלה לפני רבי חנינא, ורבי חנינא שלח לו תשובה שאין בגידין בנותן טעם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ami sent cases to Rabbi Yitzchak ben Chalov, who permitted sinews based on Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, though Rabbi Ami disagreed; the halakha is concluded that sinews do not impart flavor.
sub.desc: רבי אמי היה שולח את השואלים לרבי יצחק בן חלוב שהתיר בשם רבי יהושע בן לוי, אף שרבי אמי עצמו לא סבר כן, ונפסקה הלכה שאין בגידין בנותן טעם.

items.text: קושיית ביטול ברוב לגיד הנשה
items.text_en: Final question on the sciatic nerve
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the sciatic nerve that was cooked should not be nullified in the majority, introducing a new topic.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה שגיד הנשה שנתבשל עם גידים אחרים ואינו מזוהה, למה לא יתבטל ברוב? זוהי קושיה פתוחה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the sciatic nerve (גיד הנשה) that was cooked should not be nullified in the majority (רוב), challenging the need for a special rule.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על המשנה שגיד הנשה שנתבשל עם גידים אחרים ואינו מזוהה, למה לא יתבטל ברוב?

items.text: תירוץ הגמרא: בריה שאני
items.text_en: Distinction for a creature
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that a limb (gid) is different because it is a 'beriah' (a complete entity) and therefore not nullified.
items.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שגיד הנשה הוא בריה, ולכן אינו בטל בתערובת, בניגוד לחתיכה רגילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that a limb (gid) is different because it is a בְּרִיָּה (a complete entity) and therefore not nullified.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שגיד הנשה הוא בריה, ולכן אינו בטל בתערובת.

items.text: Question about nullification of a piece of neveilah
items.text_en: Question about nullification of a piece of neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a piece of neveilah is not nullified by the majority, and addresses the dispute between those who say 'anything that is normally counted' and those who say 'that which is normally counted'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a piece of neveilah (טריפה) is not nullified by the majority (רוב) of kosher meat.

The Gemara explains that the piece is not nullified because it is 'a thing that is normally counted' (דבר שדרכו לימנות), and even for the opinion that only 'that which is normally counted' (את שדרכו לימנות) is not nullified, the piece is special because it is fit to honor guests (ראויה להתכבד בה לפני האורחים).

items.text: Need for both cases
items.text_en: Need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both the case of the gid (limb) and the case of the piece (chaticha) are necessary to teach, as each alone might lead to a mistaken conclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases are necessary, because if only the case of the gid (limb) were taught, one might mistakenly think the leniency applies only there since it is a distinct entity (בריה), but not to a piece (חתיכה).

The Gemara completes the reasoning: conversely, if only the case of the piece were taught, one might think the leniency applies only there because it is fit to honor guests, but not to the gid; therefore both are necessary.

items.text: דרשת רבה בר בר חנה
items.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah's teaching
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah teaches that a piece of neveilah or non-kosher fish only forbids a mixture if it imparts flavor into the broth, the sauce, and the pieces.
items.desc: רבה בר בר חנה דורש שחתיכת נבלה או דג טמא אינה אוסרת עד שתיתן טעם ברוטב, בקיפה ובחתיכות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah teaches that a piece of neveilah or non-kosher fish only forbids a mixture if it imparts flavor into the broth, the sauce, and the pieces.
sub.desc: רבה בר בר חנה דורש שחתיכת נבלה או דג טמא אינה אוסרת עד שתיתן טעם ברוטב, בקיפה ובחתיכות.

items.text: דרשת רב: חתיכה שנעשתה נבלה
items.text_en: Rav's addition
items.desc_en: Rav adds that once the forbidden piece imparts flavor into another piece, that piece itself becomes neveilah and forbids all other pieces of the same type.
items.desc: רב חולק על רבה בר בר חנה וקובע שחתיכה שקיבלה טעם מהאיסור נהפכת לנבלה ואוסרת את כל החתיכות מאותו המין.

sub.desc_en: Rav adds that once the forbidden piece imparts flavor into another piece, that piece itself becomes neveilah and forbids all other pieces of the same type.
sub.desc: רב מעמיד דרשן ומכריז שחתיכה שקיבלה טעם מהאיסור נהפכת לנבלה ואוסרת את כל החתיכות מאותו המין.

items.text: קושיית רב ספרא ותירוץ אביי
items.text_en: Rav Safra's question to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rav Safra questions Rav's statement, noting that it aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view that a type does not become nullified in its own type, and asks why Rav mentions 'if it imparts flavor' when even without flavor it should be forbidden. Abaye answers that the case is where the forbidden piece was removed beforehand.
items.desc: רב ספרא מקשה על רב: אם הוא כרבי יהודה שמין במינו לא בטל, מדוע צריך נתינת טעם? אביי מתרץ שמדובר במקרה שקדם וסילקו את החתיכה האסורה לפני שהוסיף את האחרות.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra asked Abaye: since Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Yehuda who says a substance of the same type is never nullified, why does Rav require that flavor be imparted — even without flavor it should forbid.
sub.desc: רב ספרא מקשה על רב: אם רב פוסק כרבי יהודה שמין במינו לא בטל, מדוע צריך נתינת טעם? אפילו בלא נתינת טעם היה לאסור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answered that the case is where one removed the forbidden piece before it could forbid the mixture.
sub.desc: רב ספרא מקשה על רב: אם רב פוסק כרבי יהודה שמין במינו לא בטל, מדוע צריך נתינת טעם? אפילו בלא נתינת טעם היה לאסור.

items.text: תירוץ רבא
items.text_en: Rava's statement begins
items.desc_en: Rava begins his own statement on the matter, which will continue in the following segments.
items.desc: רבא מציע תירוץ חלופי לקושיית רב ספרא, אך דבריו נקטעים באמצע.

sub.desc_en: Rava begins his own statement, which continues beyond the provided text.
sub.desc: רבא מתחיל לתרץ את קושיית רב ספרא, אך דבריו נקטעים באמצע.

items.text: המשך דיון בביטול איסור בתערובת
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the earlier sugya
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that even if one did not remove the sciatic nerve first, the mixture is a case of 'its own kind and another kind', and the rule is to remove the kind and nullify it if its own kind is not abundant.
items.desc: הקטע ממשיך את הדיון הקודם בעניין תערובת של איסור והיתר, ומסביר את הכלל של 'מין ומינו ודבר אחר' שבו מבטלים את המין שלו ומצרפים את שאר ההיתר לבטל את האיסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier sugya by ruling that even if one did not first remove the sciatic nerve, the mixture is treated as 'its own kind and another kind', and the rule is to remove the kind and nullify it if its own kind is not abundant.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת את דין התערובת במקרה שלא הסיר את החתיכה האסורה, ומבארת את הכלל של 'מין ומינו ודבר אחר' שבו מבטלים את המין שלו ומצרפים את שאר ההיתר לבטל את האיסור.

items.text: משנת גיד הנשה
items.text_en: Mishnah: The sciatic nerve applies to kosher animals but not to non-kosher ones
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the prohibition of the sciatic nerve applies to kosher animals but not to non-kosher ones. Rabbi Yehuda argues that it applies even to non-kosher animals, citing that it was prohibited to the sons of Jacob when non-kosher animals were still permitted. The Sages respond that the prohibition was given at Sinai, but written in its place.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שאיסור גיד הנשה נוהג בבהמה טהורה ולא בטמאה, ורבי יהודה חולק וסובר שנוהג גם בטמאה, בטענה שנאסר כבר לבני יעקב. חכמים משיבים שהאיסור נאמר בסיני ונכתב במקומו.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that the prohibition of the sciatic nerve applies to kosher animals but not to non-kosher ones.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקובעה שאיסור גיד הנשה נוהג בבהמה טהורה ואינו נוהג בטמאה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that the prohibition applies even to non-kosher animals.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקובעה שאיסור גיד הנשה נוהג בבהמה טהורה ואינו נוהג בטמאה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites that the sciatic nerve was prohibited to the sons of Jacob when non-kosher animals were still permitted to them.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקובעה שאיסור גיד הנשה נוהג בבהמה טהורה ואינו נוהג בטמאה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages respond that the prohibition was given at Sinai but written in its place in the Torah.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בקובעה שאיסור גיד הנשה נוהג בבהמה טהורה ואינו נוהג בטמאה.

items.text: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda holds that a prohibition can take effect where another prohibition already exists, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says that a non-kosher bird does not impart impurity through swallowing because its prohibition is from 'do not eat a non-kosher thing' and not from 'do not eat a carcass'. The Gemara suggests that perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that sinews do not impart flavor, so in a non-kosher animal there is only the prohibition of the sciatic nerve and not the prohibition of impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yehuda holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda rules that a non-kosher bird does not impart impurity through swallowing because its prohibition is from 'do not eat a non-kosher thing' and not from 'do not eat a carcass'.
The Gemara suggests that perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that sinews do not impart flavor, so in a non-kosher animal there is only the prohibition of the sciatic nerve and not the prohibition of impurity.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold that sinews do not impart flavor?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Yehuda hold that sinews do not impart flavor?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the suggestion, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for two prohibitions for eating the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal, implying that sinews do impart flavor. The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds that sinews do impart flavor, and that the prohibition applies to a fetus, so the prohibitions of the sciatic nerve and impurity come simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Yehuda holds sinews do not impart flavor.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda holds one liable for two prohibitions for eating the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal, implying sinews do impart flavor.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yehuda holds sinews do impart flavor, and the prohibitions of the sciatic nerve and impurity come simultaneously for a fetus.

items.text: Objection: Does the sciatic nerve apply to a fetus?
items.text_en: Objection: Does the sciatic nerve apply to a fetus?
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the Mishnah states that the sciatic nerve applies to a fetus, but Rabbi Yehuda says it does not apply to a fetus, and its fat is permitted. The Gemara distinguishes: that is regarding a kosher animal, where the verse says 'all in the animal you may eat', but regarding a non-kosher animal it does apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous answer by citing a Mishnah that states the sciatic nerve applies to a fetus, but Rabbi Yehuda says it does not apply and its fat is permitted.

The Gemara answers that the Mishnah's ruling about the fetus applies only to a kosher animal, where the verse says 'all in the animal you may eat', but regarding a non-kosher animal the sciatic nerve does apply to the fetus.

items.text: Challenge: Do the prohibitions come simultaneously?
items.text_en: Challenge: Do the prohibitions come simultaneously?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the prohibitions come simultaneously, citing a Mishnah about a nazirite shaving for impurity from a fetus whose limbs are not connected by sinews, implying that the impurity prohibition comes first. The Gemara answers that even though the impurity prohibition comes first, the prohibition of the sciatic nerve can take effect because it applies to Noahides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that the prohibitions come simultaneously, citing a Mishnah about a nazirite shaving for impurity from a fetus whose limbs are not connected by sinews, implying that the impurity prohibition comes first.
The Gemara answers that even though the impurity prohibition comes first, the prohibition of the sciatic nerve can take effect because it applies to Noahides.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah and the baraita
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah and the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah itself supports this, as Rabbi Yehuda said the prohibition was given to the sons of Jacob when non-kosher animals were still permitted. The Gemara then cites the baraita about one who eats the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal: Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable for two, and Rabbi Shimon exempts him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's statement of Rabbi Yehuda as proof that the sciatic nerve prohibition was given before the prohibition of non-kosher animals, supporting the idea that the two prohibitions can coexist.
The Gemara cites the baraita about one who eats the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal, where Rabbi Yehuda holds him liable for two transgressions and Rabbi Shimon exempts him.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's exemption and Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's exemption and Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Shimon's ruling that one is exempt from punishment for eating the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal. Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon holds that sinews do not impart flavor, and the verse limits the prohibition to animals whose sinew is forbidden but flesh is permitted, excluding those whose flesh is also forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Shimon exempts one from punishment for eating the sciatic nerve of a non-kosher animal.

The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's position with three logical possibilities: if prohibition applies to prohibition, he should be liable for the nerve; if not, he should be liable for prior impurity; if sinews do not impart flavor, he should still be liable for the nerve.

Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon consistently holds that sinews do not impart flavor, and the verse 'עַל כֵּן לֹא יֹאכְלוּ' (therefore the children of Israel shall not eat) limits the prohibition to animals whose sinew is forbidden but flesh is permitted, excluding this case where both are forbidden.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים בגיד הנשה של נבלה
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir and the Sages on eating the sciatic nerve of a neveilah
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Rav: Rabbi Meir holds one liable for two punishments for eating the sciatic nerve of a neveilah (one for the nerve, one for neveilah), while the Sages say only one. However, the Sages agree with Rabbi Meir regarding the sciatic nerve of an olah or a stoned ox, where two punishments apply.
items.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב מביא מחלוקת: רבי מאיר מחייב שתי מלקות על אכילת גיד הנשה של נבלה, וחכמים מחייבים אחת. חכמים מודים לרבי מאיר בגיד של עולה או שור הנסקל שחייב שתיים, משום שהאיסור חמור יותר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that Rabbi Meir holds one liable for two violations when eating the sciatic nerve of a neveila (carcass), while the Sages say only one.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בשם רב פותח במחלוקת בין רבי מאיר לחכמים לגבי אכילת גיד הנשה של נבלה: רבי מאיר מחייב שתי מלקות, וחכמים מחייבים אחת.

sub.desc_en: The Sages concede to Rabbi Meir that eating the sciatic nerve of an olah (burnt offering) or a stoned ox incurs two violations.
sub.desc: הגמרא מוסיפה שחכמים מודים לרבי מאיר בגיד הנשה של עולה או שור הנסקל שחייב שתי מלקות, משום שהאיסור חמור יותר.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who holds issur kolel but not issur chal al issur
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who holds issur kolel but not issur chal al issur
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Tanna who rejects the principle that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition (issur chal al issur) but accepts the principle of inclusive prohibition (issur kolel) regarding a more severe prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that the principle of איסור חל על איסור (a prohibition taking effect on another prohibition) is rejected, but the principle of איסור כולל (inclusive prohibition) regarding a more severe prohibition is accepted.

items.text: Rava identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
items.text_en: Rava identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGlili
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGlili, based on a mishnah where he distinguishes between a tamei person eating tahor kodashim (liable) and tamei kodashim (exempt). The Rabbis object that even tahor kodashim becomes tamei upon contact.

sub.desc_en: Rava identifies the anonymous Tanna as Rabbi Yosei HaGlili, citing a mishnah where a tamei person who eats kodashim is liable whether the kodashim are tamei or tahor.
Rabbi Yosei HaGlili distinguishes: a tamei person who eats tahor kodashim is liable, but one who eats tamei kodashim is exempt, because he only ate something already tamei.
The Rabbis object that even tahor kodashim becomes tamei upon contact with the tamei person, so the distinction collapses.

items.text: הסבר מחלוקת רבא: טומאת הגוף קודמת או טומאת בשר קודמת
items.text_en: Clarifying the dispute: impurity of the body vs. impurity of the flesh
items.desc_en: Rava explains that all agree one is liable if the body became impure first (issur karet precedes). The dispute is when the flesh became impure first: the Rabbis hold issur kolel (since one is liable for tahor pieces, they are also liable for the tamei one), while Rabbi Yosei HaGlili rejects issur kolel.
items.desc: רבא מבאר שהמחלוקת היא רק כשטומאת הבשר קדמה לטומאת הגוף; חכמים סוברים שיש איסור כולל, ורבי יוסי הגלילי סובר שאין אומרים 'מגו'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Rabbis' objection to Rabbi Yosei HaGlili is valid, and Rava explains that when the body became impure first, all agree one is liable because the issur karet (penalty of karet) precedes.
sub.desc: רבא פותח בביאור המחלוקת: כשטומאת הגוף קדמה, הכל מודים שחייב, משום שאיסור כרת קדם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute is specifically when the flesh became impure first, and only afterward the body became impure.
sub.desc: רבא מבאר שהמחלוקת היא כשטומאת הבשר קדמה; חכמים סוברים שיש איסור כולל, ולכן חייב גם על חתיכה טמאה.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Rabbis hold the principle of איסור כולל (inclusive prohibition), so since one is liable for the pure pieces, they are also liable for the impure one.
sub.desc: רבא מבאר שהמחלוקת היא כשטומאת הבשר קדמה; חכמים סוברים שיש איסור כולל, ולכן חייב גם על חתיכה טמאה.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yosei HaGlili rejects the principle of איסור כולל, so the reasoning of 'since' (מגו) does not apply.
sub.desc: רבא מסיים שרבי יוסי הגלילי אינו מקבל את עקרון האיסור הכולל, ואין אומרים 'מגו'.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על רבי יוסי הגלילי ותירוץ רב אשי
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGlili's view on a severe prohibition overriding a light one, and Rav Ashi's challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that even without issur kolel, Rabbi Yosei HaGlili might hold that a severe prohibition (like tum'at haguf with karet) can take effect on a light one. Rav Ashi challenges this, questioning whether tum'at haguf is indeed more severe than tum'at basar, which has no purification in a mikveh.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה שאף אם אין איסור כולל, איסור חמור (טומאת הגוף) יחול על איסור קל (טומאת בשר). רב אשי מתרץ שאולי טומאת בשר חמורה יותר כי אין לה טהרה במקווה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that even without issur kolel, Rabbi Yosei HaGlili might hold that a severe prohibition (like tum'at haguf with karet) can take effect on a light one.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי יוסי הגלילי: אף שאין איסור כולל, איסור חמור (טומאת הגוף) יחול על איסור קל (טומאת בשר), שהרי טומאת הגוף בכרת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi challenges the assumption that tum'at haguf is more severe, suggesting that tum'at basar might be more severe because it has no purification in a mikveh.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שאין הכרע שטומאת הגוף חמורה, כי ייתכן שטומאת בשר חמורה יותר, שאין לה טהרה במקווה.

items.text: Question about Rabbi Yose HaGlili and איסור כולל
items.text_en: Question about Rabbi Yose HaGlili and איסור כולל
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yose HaGlili rejects the principle of איסור כולל, citing a baraita where he holds one liable separately for Shabbat and Yom Kippur violations, implying he does not accept איסור כולל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yose HaGlili rejects the principle of איסור כולל (a prohibition that encompasses multiple aspects).

items.text: Baraita on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Baraita on Shabbat and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds one liable separately for Shabbat and Yom Kippur, while Rabbi Akiva holds one liable only once, demonstrating their disagreement on איסור כולל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGlili holds one liable separately for Shabbat and Yom Kippur, demonstrating his rejection of איסור כולל.
Rabbi Akiva states that one is liable only once, affirming the principle of איסור כולל.

items.text: שליחת רבין להפוך את השיוך בברייתא
items.text_en: Ravin's message about the Mishnah's presentation
items.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina that the Mishnah's presentation should be reversed, implying a different understanding of the dispute.
items.desc: רבין שולח בשם רבי יוסי בר חנינא שיש להפוך את השיוך בברייתא: הדעה הראשונה היא של רבי עקיבא והשנייה של רבי יוסי הגלילי, כך שרבי יוסי הגלילי סובר שאין איסור כולל.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports in the name of Rabbi Yose bar Rabbi Chanina that the Mishnah's presentation should be reversed, implying a different understanding of the dispute.
sub.desc: רבין שולח בשם רבי יוסי בר חנינא שיש להפוך את השיוך בברייתא, כך שרבי יוסי הגלילי סובר שאין איסור כולל.

items.text: דין שוגג ומזיד בשבת ויום הכיפורים לפי רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's explanation and Rava's resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that according to the reversed version, one is liable if he was negligent on Shabbat but intentional on Yom Kippur, but exempt if the opposite. Abaye explains the reasoning, but Rava objects and offers a historical explanation involving persecution, which is accepted.
items.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר את דעת רבי יוסי הגלילי: אם שגג בשבת והזיד ביום הכיפורים חייב, אבל אם הזיד בשבת ושגג ביום הכיפורים פטור. אביי מסביר ששבת קבועה ויום הכיפורים תלוי בבית דין, ורבא דוחה ומסביר שמדובר בשעת שמדא.

sub.text: רב יצחק בר יעקב בר גיורי משם רבי יוחנן
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that according to the reversed version of Rabbi Yose HaGelili's position, one is liable if negligent on Shabbat and intentional on Yom Kippur, but exempt if the opposite.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מבאר את דעת רבי יוסי הגלילי: שוגג בשבת ומזיד ביום הכיפורים חייב, אבל מזיד בשבת ושוגג ביום הכיפורים פטור.

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks for the reason behind Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.
sub.desc: אביי מסביר: שבת קבועה וקיימת, ואילו יום הכיפורים נקבע על ידי בית דין, ולכן שבת קודמת.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that Shabbat is fixed by nature, while Yom Kippur is fixed by the court, so negligence on Shabbat is more severe.
sub.desc: אביי מסביר: שבת קבועה וקיימת, ואילו יום הכיפורים נקבע על ידי בית דין, ולכן שבת קודמת.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that both Shabbat and Yom Kippur ultimately come together, so Abaye's reasoning is insufficient.
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את דברי אביי: שניהם באים יחד, ולכן אין לומר ששבת קודמת.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves by explaining that there was a period of persecution, and the court declared that Yom Kippur of this year is Shabbat, making the reversed version a historical ruling.
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את דברי אביי: שניהם באים יחד, ולכן אין לומר ששבת קודמת.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the sons of Jacob
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement about the sons of Jacob
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites a verse about the sons of Jacob not eating the sinew, introducing the discussion about the source of the prohibition of the gid hanasheh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda opens by citing the verse about the sons of Jacob not eating the sinew, implying the prohibition began with the patriarchs.

items.text: Response to Rabbi Yehuda: The prohibition was given at Sinai
items.text_en: Response to Rabbi Yehuda: The prohibition was given at Sinai
items.desc_en: The Sages respond to Rabbi Yehuda that the verse says 'sons of Israel,' not 'sons of Jacob,' and they were not called 'sons of Israel' until Sinai, so the prohibition was given at Sinai but written in its place to indicate the reason.

sub.desc_en: The Sages respond to Rabbi Yehuda that the verse says 'בני ישראל' (sons of Israel), not 'בני יעקב' (sons of Jacob), and since they were not called 'בני ישראל' until Sinai, the prohibition was given at Sinai but written in its place to indicate the reason.

items.text: קושיית רבא ותירוץ רב אשי על 'בני ישראל' לפני סיני
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution about the timing of the prohibition
items.desc_en: Rava objects with a verse showing that 'sons of Israel' was used before Sinai. Rav Acha suggests the prohibition began from that time, but Rav Ashi responds that the Torah was not given piecemeal, so it was not yet binding.
items.desc: רבא מקשה מהפסוק 'וישאו בני ישראל את יעקב אביהם' שנאמר לפני מתן תורה, ורב אשי דוחה שאותו זמן לא היה זמן מעשה ולא זמן מתן תורה, ולכן אין ראיה.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects by citing a verse that uses the term 'בני ישראל' (sons of Israel) for events before the giving of the Torah, challenging the claim that the term only applied after Sinai.
sub.desc: רבא מקשה מהפסוק 'וישאו בני ישראל את יעקב אביהם' שנאמר לפני מתן תורה, ומוכיח שהשם 'בני ישראל' היה בשימוש כבר אז.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava suggests that the prohibition of the gid hanasheh (sciatic nerve) might have taken effect from the time of that event (the carrying of Jacob).
sub.desc: רב אחא בריה דרבא שואל את רב אשי: אם כן, יש לאסור את גיד הנשה מאותה שעה שנקראו 'בני ישראל'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rejects the suggestion, arguing that the Torah was not given piecemeal, so that time was neither the time of the event nor the time of the giving of the Torah, and thus the prohibition was not yet binding.
sub.desc: רב אשי דוחה: התורה לא ניתנה פעמים פעמים, ואותה שעה לא הייתה לא זמן מעשה ולא זמן מתן תורה, ולכן אין ראיה.

items.text: מחלוקת תנאים על אבר מן החי
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute on איבר מן החי and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar hold that איבר מן החי applies to all animals, while the Sages limit it to pure animals. Rabbi Yochanan says both derive their views from the same verse.
items.desc: הברייתא מביאה מחלוקת בין רבי יהודה ורבי אלעזר לחכמים: האם איסור אבר מן החי נוהג גם בטמאים או רק בטהורים. רבי יוחנן אומר ששניהם דורשים את אותו פסוק.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar hold that איבר מן החי (a limb from a living animal) applies to all animals, while the Sages limit it to pure animals.
sub.desc: הברייתא מציגה את מחלוקת התנאים: רבי יהודה ורבי אלעזר סוברים שאיסור אבר מן החי נוהג גם בטמאים, וחכמים סוברים שנוהג רק בטהורים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan explains that both sides derive their positions from the same verse, 'רַק חֲזַק לְבִלְתִּי אֲכֹל הַדָּם' (only be strong not to eat the blood).
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מציין ששני הצדדים דורשים את אותו פסוק, ומתחיל להביאו.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda/Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis on the source of eiver min hachai
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda/Rabbi Elazar and the Rabbis on the source of eiver min hachai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar derive the prohibition of a limb from a living animal from the verse 'Do not eat the soul with the flesh,' applying it to any animal whose blood is forbidden, including non-kosher species. The Rabbis argue that the verse only forbids the flesh itself, so the limb prohibition applies only to species whose flesh is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Elazar derive the prohibition of a limb from a living animal (אבר מן החי) from the verse 'Do not eat the soul with the flesh,' applying it to any animal whose blood is forbidden, including non-kosher species.
The Rabbis argue that the verse only forbids the flesh itself, so the limb prohibition applies only to species whose flesh is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's question: Why does Rabbi Yehuda need a verse?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Why does Rabbi Yehuda need a verse?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda needs a verse to derive the prohibition for non-kosher animals, since the prohibition of a limb from a living animal should apply to Noahides as well, and thus could be derived from the Noahide prohibition. It answers that the verse is necessary for Rabbi Elazar's position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda needs a verse to derive the prohibition of a limb from a living animal for non-kosher animals, since the prohibition already applies to Noahides.
The Gemara answers that indeed the verse is necessary for Rabbi Elazar's position, not for Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Elazar and the dispute with the Sages and Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Elazar and the dispute with the Sages and Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Elazar's view that the prohibition applies to both kosher and non-kosher species based on the verse 'Rak chazak levilti achol hadam.' The Sages argue it applies only to kosher species, and Rabbi Meir limits it to kosher domesticated animals alone.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that the prohibition of a limb from a living animal applies to all species, kosher and non-kosher, based on the verse 'Rak chazak levilti achol hadam.'
Rabbi Elazar explains that the verse implies that for any species whose blood is forbidden, its limbs are also forbidden, thus including non-kosher species.
The Sages argue that the prohibition applies only to kosher species, based on the verse 'Lo tochal hanefesh im habasar,' which implies that only animals whose flesh is permitted are included.
Rabbi Meir further restricts the prohibition to only kosher domesticated animals.
The Gemara provides a mnemonic for the names of the Sages in the upcoming discussion.

items.text: Rabba bar Shmuel and others explain Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Rabba bar Shmuel and others explain Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a tradition from Rabba bar Shmuel (or others) in the name of Rav Chisda (or Rav Yosef) explaining Rabbi Meir's reasoning: he derives the limitation from the verse 'And you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your flock.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the reason for Rabbi Meir's opinion.

sub.text: Rabba bar Shmuel / Rav Chisda / Rav Yosef
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Shmuel / Rav Chisda / Rav Yosef
sub.desc_en: The tradition explains that Rabbi Meir derives his limitation from the verse 'And you shall slaughter from your cattle and from your flock.'

items.text: Rav Giddel's distinction between Israelites and Noahides
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's distinction between Israelites and Noahides
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies only to Israelites, but for a Noahide, all agree that the prohibition applies to non-kosher species as well as kosher. A baraita supports this, with a textual variant regarding 'tahorah' vs. 'tehorim.'

sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav states that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages applies only to Israelites, but for a Noahide, all agree that the prohibition applies to non-kosher species as well as kosher.

A baraita supports Rav Giddel's distinction, stating that a Noahide is warned about the limb from a living animal for both impure and pure species, while an Israelite is warned only about pure species.
The gemara notes a textual variant in the baraita: some versions read 'טהורה' (pure, singular) aligning with Rabbi Meir, while others read 'טהורים' (pure, plural) aligning with the Sages.

items.text: Rav Sheizvi's proof from a Mishnah and Rabbi Mani bar Pattish's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheizvi's proof from a Mishnah and Rabbi Mani bar Pattish's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi cites a Mishnah about eating a limb from a living animal from a non-kosher species, which implies it is prohibited for Noahides. The Gemara questions whether it refers to Israelites or Noahides, and Rabbi Mani bar Pattish resolves that the first clause refers to Israelites and the latter to a Noahide.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi cites a Mishnah about eating a limb from a living animal from a non-kosher species, which states that one does not receive lashes and slaughter does not render it permitted, implying it is prohibited for Noahides.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah refers to an Israelite or a Noahide, reasoning that if it were an Israelite, the ruling that slaughter does not render it permitted would be obvious.
Rabbi Mani bar Pattish resolves the contradiction by distinguishing that the first clause of the Mishnah refers to an Israelite and the latter clause to a Noahide.

items.text: Rav's ruling on the minimum measure and the objection from Rav Amram
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on the minimum measure and the objection from Rav Amram
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the prohibition of a limb from a living animal requires a kezayit measure because the Torah uses the term 'eating.' Rav Amram objects from a Mishnah that implies any amount is sufficient, but the Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to a case with a minimal amount of flesh, sinews, and bones, as per Rav Nachman's explanation.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that a limb from a living animal requires a kezayit (olive-sized) measure because the Torah uses the term 'eating' (אכילה) regarding it.

Rav Amram objects from a Mishnah that states one who eats a limb from a living animal does not receive lashes, implying any amount suffices, and if a kezayit were required, the Mishnah should have specified that he ate a kezayit.

The Gemara resolves that just as Rav Nachman explained a similar case involves a minimal amount of flesh, sinews, and bones, here too the Mishnah refers to a minimal amount of flesh, sinews, and bones, not a full kezayit of flesh.
The Gemara introduces another source to further examine Rav's ruling, saying 'Come and hear, as Rav said.'

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that eating a clean bird alive incurs liability for any amount, but dead requires an olive's bulk; an unclean bird always requires any amount. The Gemara applies this to the case of a limb from a living bird.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule that eating a clean bird alive incurs liability for any amount, but dead requires an olive's bulk; an unclean bird always requires any amount, and applies this to the case of a limb from a living bird.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: if one took a bird without an olive's bulk and ate it, Rabbi exempts and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon obligates. Rabbi Elazar argues a fortiori: if one is liable for a limb, certainly for the whole bird. If he strangled it and ate it, all agree it requires an olive's bulk. The dispute is whether a living bird is considered as standing for limbs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: if one took a bird lacking an olive's bulk and ate it, Rabbi exempts and Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon obligates; Rabbi Elazar argues a fortiori from a limb, and if he strangled it, all agree it requires an olive's bulk.
The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether a living bird is considered as standing for limbs (so each limb is a separate entity) or not.

items.text: Rav Nachman's statement and Rav Sherevya's example
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's statement and Rav Sherevya's example
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that the measure for a limb from a living bird is any amount of flesh, sinews, and bones. Rav Sherevya objects: can there be a bird with less than an olive's bulk of flesh yet a limb has an olive's bulk of flesh, sinews, and bones? He answers yes, in the case of a קְלָנִיתָא (a small bird).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that for a limb from a living bird, the measure is any amount of flesh, sinews, and bones.
Rav Sherevya objects: can there be a bird with less than an olive's bulk of flesh yet a limb has an olive's bulk of flesh, sinews, and bones?
Rav Sherevya answers yes, in the case of a קְלָנִיתָא (a small bird).

items.text: Refutation and resolution
items.text_en: Refutation and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita's case of strangling requires an olive's bulk, but a קְלָנִיתָא is an unclean bird, and Rav said an unclean bird requires any amount whether alive or dead. So the example must be a bird similar to a קְלָנִיתָא but clean.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the baraita's case of strangling requires an olive's bulk, but a קְלָנִיתָא is an unclean bird, and Rav said an unclean bird requires any amount whether alive or dead.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita refers to a kosher bird similar to a קְלָנִיתָא, not an actual unclean one.
Rava proposes: if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that thought about food is significant, then one who intended to eat the bird limb by limb and ate it whole is liable.
Abaye questions: can the same act be liable for one person and exempt for another?
Rava answers: each person is judged according to his own thought.

items.text: Rava's first suggestion and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's first suggestion and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that if Rabbi holds that intent regarding food is significant, then if one intended to eat the bird limb by limb and ate it whole, he is liable. Abaye challenges: can it be that if another ate it he is exempt, but this one is liable? Rava answers: each is judged according to his intent.

sub.desc_en: Rava suggests that if Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds that intent regarding food is significant, then if one intended to eat the bird dead and ate it alive, he is exempt.

items.text: Rava's second suggestion and Abaye's challenge
items.text_en: Rava's second suggestion and Abaye's challenge
items.desc_en: Rava suggests that if Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon holds that intent regarding food is significant, then if one intended to eat the bird dead and ate it alive, he is exempt. Abaye challenges similarly, and Rava again answers that each is judged according to his intent.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects: is there a case where if another ate it he would be liable, but if this one ate it he is exempt?
Rava answers: this one is judged according to his intention, and that one according to his intention.
Rava answers that each person is judged according to his own intent (זה לפי מחשבתו וזה לפי מחשבתו).

items.text: Derivation of prohibitions from verses
items.text_en: Derivation of prohibitions from verses
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish derive the prohibitions of ever min hachai and basar min hachai from verses. They dispute which prohibitions are included in each verse, leading to different counts of liability when eating combinations of these items.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse 'לֹא תֹאכַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ עִם הַבָּשָׂר' as referring to אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי (a limb from a living animal) and the verse 'וּבָשָׂר בַּשָּׂדֶה טְרֵפָה לֹא תֹאכֵלוּ' as referring to both בָּשָׂר מִן הַחַי (flesh from a living animal) and בָּשָׂר מִן הַטְּרֵפָה (flesh from a terefah).
Reish Lakish interprets the first verse as referring to both אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי and בָּשָׂר מִן הַחַי, and the second verse as referring only to בָּשָׂר מִן הַטְּרֵפָה.

The Gemara summarizes the practical differences between Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish regarding the number of prohibitions violated when eating various combinations of אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, בָּשָׂר מִן הַחַי, and בָּשָׂר מִן הַטְּרֵפָה.

items.text: Introduction of a contradiction
items.text_en: Introduction of a contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction (to be resolved in the following text).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a contradiction (from another source).

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Yochanan vs. Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that eating a limb from a living tereifah animal incurs two sets of lashes (for the limb and for the tereifah), while Reish Lakish holds only one.

sub.desc_en: The stam presents the dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds that eating a limb from a living tereifah animal incurs two sets of lashes, while Reish Lakish holds only one.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Yosef's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's position is difficult. Rav Yosef resolves the dispute by distinguishing between one animal and two animals: in two animals, both agree two lashes are incurred; the dispute is only about one animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's position is difficult, while Rabbi Yochanan's is straightforward.
Rav Yosef resolves the difficulty by distinguishing between one animal (where they dispute) and two animals (where both agree two lashes are incurred).

items.text: Abaye's explanation: simultaneous vs. sequential prohibitions
items.text_en: Abaye's explanation: simultaneous vs. sequential prohibitions
items.desc_en: Abaye explains the dispute in the case of one animal that became a tereifah at the moment most of it emerged (from the womb). One opinion holds that the animal is considered 'standing for limbs' (each limb is a separate entity), so the prohibitions of limb and tereifah come simultaneously; the other holds it is not, so the limb prohibition cannot take effect on top of the tereifah prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In the case of one animal, on what basis do the two opinions (Mar and Mar) disagree?

Abaye explains the dispute: the animal became a tereifah at the moment most of it emerged; one opinion holds that a living animal is considered 'standing for limbs' (each limb is a separate entity), so the prohibitions of limb and tereifah come simultaneously.
The other opinion holds that a living animal is not considered 'standing for limbs', so the limb prohibition cannot take effect on top of the tereifah prohibition.

items.text: First alternative explanation: both agree animal not for limbs
items.text_en: First alternative explanation: both agree animal not for limbs
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation: both agree the animal is not considered 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is whether the limb prohibition can take effect on top of the tereifah prohibition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: both agree the animal is not considered 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is whether the limb prohibition can take effect on top of the tereifah prohibition.

items.text: Second alternative explanation: both agree animal for limbs, later tereifah
items.text_en: Second alternative explanation: both agree animal for limbs, later tereifah
items.desc_en: Another alternative: both agree the animal is 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is about whether the tereifah prohibition can take effect on top of the limb prohibition when the tereifah occurs later.

sub.desc_en: The gemara proposes a third alternative: both agree the animal is 'standing for limbs' (בהמה בחייה לאברים עומדת), and the dispute is about whether the tereifah prohibition can take effect on top of the limb prohibition when the tereifah occurs later.
The gemara resolves the dispute: one opinion holds that the tereifah prohibition does take effect (אתי וחייל) on the limb prohibition, while the other holds it does not.

items.text: אוקימתת רבא: תלש אבר וטרפה בו
items.text_en: Rava's explanation: plucked limb and tereifah from it
items.desc_en: Rava explains the dispute as a case where one plucked a limb from the animal and then made it a tereifah with that limb. One opinion holds the animal is not 'standing for limbs', so both prohibitions come simultaneously; the other holds it is, so the tereifah prohibition cannot take effect on the limb prohibition.
items.desc: רבא מציע אוקימתה אחרת: מדובר בתולש אבר מהבהמה ובאותו אבר נטרפה. נחלקו אם בהמה עומדת לאברים: רבי יוחנן סובר שאינה עומדת, ולכן שני האיסורים באים יחד; רבי שמעון בן לקיש סובר שעומדת, ולכן איסור אבר קודם ואיסור טריפה אינו חל.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains the case as one where a limb was plucked from the animal and then the animal was made a tereifah with that limb; one opinion holds the animal is not 'standing for limbs', so both prohibitions come simultaneously.
sub.desc: רבא מציע אוקימתה אחרת למחלוקת: מדובר בתולש אבר מהבהמה ובאותו אבר נטרפה.

sub.desc_en: Rava presents the opposing opinion that the animal is 'standing for limbs', so the tereifah prohibition cannot take effect on the limb prohibition.
sub.desc: לדעת רבי יוחנן, בהמה אינה עומדת לאברים, ולכן איסור אבר ואיסור טריפה באים יחד.

items.text: New dispute: eating forbidden fat from a living tereifah
items.text_en: New dispute: eating forbidden fat from a living tereifah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan initially says eating forbidden fat from a living tereifah incurs two lashes, but Rabbi Ammi suggests three. Rabbi Avahu reports that Rabbi Yochanan actually said three.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba reports Rabbi Yochanan's initial ruling that eating forbidden fat (חלב) from a living tereifah incurs two lashes.
Rabbi Ammi objects, suggesting that Rabbi Yochanan should have said three lashes, as Rabbi Ammi himself holds that three are owed.
Rabbi Avahu reports that Rabbi Yochanan actually said three lashes, resolving the dispute in favor of Rabbi Ammi's position.

items.text: Explanation of the fat dispute: simultaneous prohibitions
items.text_en: Explanation of the fat dispute: simultaneous prohibitions
items.desc_en: The dispute is about a case where the animal became a tereifah at the moment most of it emerged. The one who says three holds the animal is 'standing for limbs', so all three prohibitions (fat, limb, tereifah) come simultaneously. The one who says two holds it is not, so only fat and tereifah apply, and the limb prohibition cannot take effect.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the dispute is about, and answers that it concerns a case where the animal became a tereifah at the moment most of it emerged.
The one who says three holds that the animal is 'standing for limbs', so all three prohibitions (fat, limb, tereifah) come simultaneously.
The one who says two holds that the animal is not 'standing for limbs', so only fat and tereifah apply, and the limb prohibition cannot take effect.

items.text: Alternative explanation for fat dispute: limb on fat and tereifah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for fat dispute: limb on fat and tereifah
items.desc_en: An alternative: both agree the animal is not 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is whether the limb prohibition can take effect on top of both the fat and tereifah prohibitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation for the dispute about eating fat from a live tereifah: both agree the animal is not 'standing for limbs', and the debate is whether the limb prohibition can take effect on top of both the fat and tereifah prohibitions.
One opinion holds that the limb prohibition does take effect on top of the fat and tereifah prohibitions.
The other opinion holds that the limb prohibition does not take effect on top of the fat and tereifah prohibitions.

items.text: Final alternative: tereifah on limb, with principle of neveilah on fat
items.text_en: Final alternative: tereifah on limb, with principle of neveilah on fat
items.desc_en: Another alternative: both agree the animal is 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is whether the tereifah prohibition can take effect on the limb prohibition. The one who says it can invokes the principle that the Torah allows the prohibition of neveilah to take effect on the prohibition of fat, and similarly tereifah on fat. The other holds that only fat incurs liability, as it was permitted (in certain contexts).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a final alternative: both agree the animal is 'standing for limbs', and the dispute is whether the tereifah prohibition can take effect on the limb prohibition.

The first opinion holds that the tereifah prohibition can take effect, invoking the principle that the Torah allows the prohibition of neveilah to take effect on the prohibition of fat, and similarly tereifah on fat.
The second opinion holds that only fat incurs liability, as it was permitted (in certain contexts).

items.text: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a limb that was not permitted by the general permission (of eiver min hachai) remains forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that a limb not permitted by the general permission (of eiver min hachai) remains forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on dividing the limb
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on dividing the limb
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish asked Rabbi Yochanan about the law if one divided the limb outside the mouth (patoor) and inside (liable). Ravin reported a dispute: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable because the throat benefited from a kezayit, while Reish Lakish holds patoor because eating requires the stomach.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's question to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish asks Rabbi Yochanan about the law if one divided the limb outside the mouth, and Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is פטור (exempt).
Reish Lakish asks about dividing the limb inside the mouth, and Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is חייב (liable).
Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute the case of dividing inside the mouth: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable, Reish Lakish holds exempt.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rabbi Yochanan holds liable because the throat benefited from a כזית (olive's bulk), while Reish Lakish holds exempt because eating requires the stomach to receive it, which is absent.

items.text: Rav Kahana's resolution for Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's resolution for Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that Reish Lakish would hold liable only in the case of a small piece (gromita ze'irta) that reaches the stomach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Reish Lakish could ever find a case where one is liable for eating a limb from a live animal.
Rav Kahana answers that Reish Lakish would hold liable only in the case of a small piece (גרומיתא זעירתא) that reaches the stomach.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's stricter view
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's stricter view
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar holds that even dividing outside the mouth is liable, because lacking bringing near (mechusar k'rivah) is not like lacking an action.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that even dividing the forbidden limb outside the mouth is liable, because lacking bringing near (מחוסר קריבה) is not like lacking an action (מחוסר מעשה).

items.text: מחלוקת בשיעור כזית בין השיניים
items.text_en: Dispute on kezayit measure: between the teeth vs. between the cheeks
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish says the kezayit excludes what is between the teeth; Rabbi Yochanan includes it. Rav Papa clarifies that all agree on between the teeth; the dispute is about between the cheeks (chanichayim), based on the throat vs. stomach principle.
items.desc: נחלקו רבי יוחנן וריש לקיש אם אוכל התקוע בין השיניים מצטרף לשיעור כזית. רב פפא מבאר שהמחלוקת היא על אוכל שבחניכיים, לא בין השיניים.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish states that the kezayit (olive-sized) measure excludes what is between the teeth.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש פוסק ששיעור כזית נמדד חוץ ממה שתקוע בין השיניים.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan counters that the kezayit includes what is between the teeth.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש פוסק ששיעור כזית נמדד חוץ ממה שתקוע בין השיניים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa resolves that all agree on between the teeth; the dispute is about between the cheeks (חניכיים), based on the principle of throat enjoyment vs. stomach consumption.
sub.desc: רב פפא מבאר שהמחלוקת אינה על מה שבין השיניים אלא על מה שבחניכיים, ושם נחלקו אם מצטרף לשיעור.

items.text: Rabbi Asi's ruling on eating half a kezayit and vomiting
items.text_en: Rabbi Asi's ruling on eating half a kezayit and vomiting
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name that if one ate half a kezayit, vomited it, and ate another half, he is liable because the throat benefited from a kezayit.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that eating half a kezayit, vomiting it, and eating another half makes one liable because the throat benefited from a kezayit.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's question about eating and re-eating the same half-kezayit
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's question about eating and re-eating the same half-kezayit
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Asi about eating half a kezayit, vomiting it, and eating it again: does digestion (ichul) apply? The Gemara explains that Rabbi Elazar sought to derive two principles from Rabbi Asi's statement, but Rabbi Asi was silent until reminded of Rabbi Yochanan's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Rabbi Asi: if one ate half an olive-bulk, vomited it, and ate it again, what is the halakha? The Gemara clarifies that the dilemma is whether the food is considered digested or not.
The Gemara reframes the dilemma: it is about whether we follow the throat or the stomach, and suggests resolving it from Rabbi Asi's earlier statement.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Asi had forgotten his tradition, and Rabbi Elazar was trying to remind him that from the case of eating the same half-olive-bulk one can derive both that it is not considered digested and that the throat derives pleasure from an olive-bulk.

Rabbi Asi was silent, and Rabbi Elazar reminded him that he had previously stated this case before Rabbi Yochanan, who ruled that the person is liable because his throat derives pleasure from a full olive-bulk.

items.text: משנת גיד הנשה וכל הבשר
items.text_en: Transition to new Mishnah on meat and milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous topic and introduces a new Mishnah: all meat is forbidden to cook in milk except fish and locusts, and forbidden to place on the table with cheese except fish and locusts.
items.desc: הגמרא מסיימת את הפרק הקודם בחזרה לגיד הנשה, ומתחילה משנה חדשה האוסרת בישול בשר בחלב למעט דגים וחגבים, ואוסרת העלאת בשר עם גבינה על השולחן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous topic with the formula 'we return to you, the sciatic nerve'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסיימת את הפרק הקודם באמירת 'הדרן עלך' על מסכת גיד הנשה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that all meat is forbidden to cook in milk except fish and locusts, and forbidden to place on the table with cheese except fish and locusts.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת באיסור בישול כל בשר בחלב, למעט דגים וחגבים, ואוסרת העלאת בשר עם גבינה על השולחן.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who vows from meat is permitted fish and locusts, implying that fowl is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who vows from meat is permitted fish and locusts, implying fowl is prohibited.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah implies fowl is biblically prohibited, but Rabbi Akiva holds it is not. It resolves by attributing the first clause to the Rabbis and the second to Rabbi Akiva, based on a baraita about vegetables and gourds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whose opinion the Mishnah follows, since it implies fowl is biblically prohibited, contradicting Rabbi Akiva who holds fowl is not biblically prohibited.
The Gemara objects that the second clause of the Mishnah aligns with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that anything a messenger would distinguish is excluded from the category.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Akiva prohibits gourds for one who vowed from vegetables, and the Sages object that a messenger would say he found only gourds, not vegetables.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the first clause of the Mishnah to the Rabbis and the second clause to Rabbi Akiva, based on the baraita's logic.

items.text: תירוצו של רב יוסף
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: Rabbi's compromise
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef explains that the Mishnah is Rabbi's compromise: in vows he follows Rabbi Akiva, in meat and milk he follows the Rabbis.
items.desc: רב יוסף מתרץ שהמשנה היא כרבי יהודה הנשיא, שפסק כרבי עקיבא בנדרים וכרבנן בבשר בחלב.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef resolves: the Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's, who adopts Rabbi Akiva's view for vows but the Rabbis' view for meat in milk.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מתרץ שהמשנה היא כרבי יהודה הנשיא, שפסק כרבי עקיבא בנדרים וכרבנן בבשר בחלב.

items.text: תירוצו של רב אשי
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: Entirely Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva, interpreting it as distinguishing between biblical and rabbinic prohibitions.
items.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שהמשנה כולה כרבי עקיבא, ופירושה: איסור בשר בחלב כולל חיה ועוף מדרבנן, ודגים וחגבים מותרים לגמרי.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi says: the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Akiva's, and it means that all meat is forbidden to cook in milk, some by Torah law and some by rabbinic law, except fish and locusts.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ שהמשנה כולה כרבי עקיבא, ופירושה: איסור בשר בחלב כולל חיה ועוף מדרבנן, ודגים וחגבים מותרים לגמרי.

items.text: Proof that fowl in milk is biblical
items.text_en: Proof that fowl in milk is biblical
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef infers from the Mishnah's prohibition of raising fowl with milk that fowl in milk is biblically prohibited, otherwise the decree would be a decree upon a decree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef infers from the Mishnah that fowl in milk is prohibited by Torah law, because if it were only rabbinic, we would not decree a further decree of prohibition on bringing it up to the table.
Rav Yosef argues that if fowl in milk were only rabbinic, the Mishnah's decree against raising would be a decree upon a decree, which is not done.

items.text: Support from the principle of no decree upon a decree
items.text_en: Support from the principle of no decree upon a decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about challah outside the land to support that we do not decree a decree upon a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara supports the principle that we do not decree a decree upon a decree, citing a Mishnah about challah outside the land.
The Gemara cites a Mishnah about challah outside the land (חלת חוצה לארץ) as evidence that we do not decree a decree upon a decree.

items.text: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah excerpt
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that chicken may be eaten with a non-priest at the same table and may be given to any priest.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that ḥalla may be eaten with a non-priest at the same table and may be given to any priest.

items.text: Abaye's objection and Rav Sheshet's counter
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and Rav Sheshet's counter
items.desc_en: Abaye argues that allowing chicken and cheese together might lead to eating meat and cheese, a Torah prohibition. Rav Sheshet counters that it's cold with cold, but Abaye fears one might put it in a hot pot. The Gemara further objects that a secondary vessel doesn't cook, so the concern is a primary vessel.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Yosef's inference, arguing that the case of ḥalla from outside Eretz Yisrael brought into Eretz Yisrael would have been a valid proof, but the mishna actually deals with ḥalla remaining outside, so no inference about compound decrees can be drawn.
Abaye explains that the mishna's leniency is because there is no Torah-level prohibition involved, but here permitting chicken and cheese could lead to eating meat and cheese, a Torah prohibition.

Rav Sheshet objects that even if chicken in milk were prohibited by Torah law, it is still a case of cold with cold, which is only rabbinically prohibited; Abaye responds that the decree is lest one place it in a boiling pot.
The Gemara counters that even a boiling pot is only a secondary vessel which does not cook, so the decree must be lest one place it in a primary vessel, which is cooking by Torah law.

items.text: משנת עוף וגבינה על השולחן
items.text_en: Mishnah: Chicken and cheese on the table
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Beit Shammai says chicken may be brought up with cheese but not eaten; Beit Hillel says it may not be brought up nor eaten. Rabbi Yosei calls this a leniency of Beit Shammai and a stringency of Beit Hillel. The Mishnah clarifies that this applies to a table where one eats, not a serving table.
