items.desc: הגמרא מציעה ברייתא כהוכחה לדברי רב שמותר, אך דוחה אותה: ייתכן שהברייתא מלמדת רק על הלב שצריך קריעה לאחר בישול, אבל בכחל לא מועילה קריעה לאחר בישול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to support Rav's first version: for the udder, if not torn, one does not transgress; for the heart, if not torn before cooking, one tears it after and it is permitted, implying the udder does not require tearing.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציעה ברייתא כהוכחה לדברי רב שמותר, ומדייקה ממנה שהכחל אינו צריך קריעה לאחר בישול.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the proof: perhaps the baraita only means that tearing suffices for the heart, but for the udder tearing does not suffice (i.e., it is always forbidden).
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההוכחה: ייתכן שהברייתא מלמדת רק על הלב שקריעה לאחר בישול מועילה, אבל בכחל אינה מועילה.

items.text: גרסה שנייה: רב אוסר בכחל שלא נקרע
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav's statement
items.desc_en: Some say Rav ruled that one does not transgress but it is forbidden. The Gemara challenges this from the Mishnah's language, and deflects similarly to the first version.
items.desc: מובאת גרסה חלופית לדברי רב: אינו עובר על איסור תורה אבל אסור מדרבנן. הגמרא דנה אם המשנה מסייעת לגרסה זו, ומתרצת באותו אופן כמו קודם.

sub.text: איכא דאמרי בשם רבי זירא בשם רב
sub.desc_en: Some say that Rav ruled that one does not violate the Torah prohibition but it is forbidden by rabbinic law, and the Gemara suggests the Mishnah supports this.
sub.desc: מובאת גרסה חלופית לדברי רב: אינו עובר על איסור תורה אבל אסור מדרבנן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the proof, explaining that the Mishnah's language is due to the latter clause about the heart, where there is a rabbinic prohibition, so the first clause uses the same phrasing.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הסיוע: כביכול אין איסור כלל, אבל התנא נקט לשון זו כדי לשמור על סימטריה עם הסיפא לגבי הלב, שם אכן יש איסור מדרבנן.

items.text: הוכחה נוספת לברייתא בגרסה השנייה
items.text_en: Attempted support for the alternative version
items.desc_en: The Gemara again cites the baraita to support the alternative version, but deflects similarly: the baraita may only indicate that tearing suffices for the heart, not that ḥelḥal is permitted without tearing.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה שוב את הברייתא כהוכחה לגרסה השנייה, אך דוחה אותה באותו אופן: ייתכן שהברייתא אינה מוכיחה לגבי כחל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita to support the alternative version of Rav's statement, inferring that only the heart requires tearing after cooking, not the udder.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא כהוכחה לגרסה השנייה: מההבחנה בין לב לכחל משתמע שכחל אינו צריך קריעה לאחר בישול, ולכן מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara deflects the proof, suggesting the baraita may only indicate that tearing suffices for the heart, not that the udder is permitted without tearing.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את ההוכחה: ייתכן שהברייתא אינה מוכיחה לגבי כחל, משום שקריעה לאחר בישול מועילה רק ללב שאינו בולע דם, אך לא לכחל שבולע חלב.

items.text: ברייתא המכריעה: כחל שבישלו בחלבו מותר, קיבה אסורה
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav's first version
items.desc_en: A baraita explicitly states: ḥelḥal cooked in its milk is permitted, but a maw (קֵבָה) cooked in its milk is forbidden. The difference is that the milk in the maw is 'stored' in its intestines (i.e., it is actual milk), while the ḥelḥal's contents are not stored milk.
items.desc: ברייתא נפסקת כתואמת לגרסה הראשונה של רב: כחל שבישלו בחלבו מותר, אבל קיבה שבישלה בחלבה אסורה, וההבדל הוא שכחל אין חלבו נחשב חלב גמור.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited in support of Rav's first version: an udder cooked in its own milk is permitted, while a stomach cooked in its milk is forbidden.
sub.desc: ברייתא מכריעה כגרסה הראשונה של רב: כחל שבישלו בחלבו מותר, קיבה שבישלה בחלבה אסורה, וההבדל הוא שכחל אין חלבו נחשב חלב גמור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the distinction: the stomach's milk is collected in its innards (actual milk), whereas the udder's contents are not collected milk.

items.text: אופן קריעת הכחל
items.text_en: How to tear the ḥelḥal
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda describes the method: tear it crosswise (like warp and woof) and smear it on a wall. Rabbi Elazar instructs his attendant to tear it for him, teaching that such an elaborate method is not required.
items.desc: רב יהודה אומר שקורעים שתי וערב וטחים בכותל, ורבי אלעזר מורה לשמשו לקרוע בלא שתי וערב, ומכאן שאין צורך בשתי וערב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one must tear the udder before cooking.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מורה לקרוע את הכחל שתי וערב ולטחוֹ בכותל כדי להוציא החלב.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda answers that one must tear it crosswise (like warp and woof) and smear it against a wall.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מורה לקרוע את הכחל שתי וערב ולטחוֹ בכותל כדי להוציא החלב.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar instructs his attendant to tear the udder for him, indicating that a simple tear suffices.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מורה לקרוע את הכחל שתי וערב ולטחוֹ בכותל כדי להוציא החלב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what this story adds, since the mishna already requires tearing.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מורה לקרוע את הכחל שתי וערב ולטחוֹ בכותל כדי להוציא החלב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the story teaches that one does not need the elaborate method of tearing crosswise and smearing on a wall; a simple tear suffices.
sub.desc: רב יהודה מורה לקרוע את הכחל שתי וערב ולטחוֹ בכותל כדי להוציא החלב.

items.text: Yalta's request and Rav Nachman's response
items.text_en: Yalta's request and Rav Nachman's response
items.desc_en: Yalta argues that for every prohibition God permitted an analogous item (e.g., blood permitted via liver, forbidden fat via animal fat, etc.), so for meat in milk, ḥelḥal should be permitted. Rav Nachman instructs butchers to give her ḥelḥalim. The Gemara questions this against the Mishnah requiring tearing, and answers that the Mishnah's tearing is only for a pot (i.e., cooking in a pot), but for roasting it is permitted without tearing.

sub.desc_en: Yalta argues that for every prohibition God permitted an analogous item, and therefore she wishes to eat meat cooked in milk.
Rav Nachman instructs his butchers to roast udders for Yalta.
The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's instruction, noting that the Mishnah requires tearing the udder.
The Gemara answers that the requirement to tear applies only to cooking in a pot, not to roasting.
The Gemara questions whether the baraita implies that roasting is only permitted after the fact, not ab initio.
The Gemara answers that roasting is permitted even ab initio, and the baraita's language is due to the latter clause about the stomach.

items.text: פתיחת הסוגיה: דין חלחולה שבושלה בחלבה
items.text_en: Opening statement on cooking meat in its own milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that if one cooked meat in its own milk, it is forbidden even after the fact, and a Tanna taught this as a ruling about the head.
items.desc: הקטע פותח בדיון על חלחולה שבושלה בחלבה, ומבהיר כי האיסור חל גם בדיעבד, תוך השוואה למקרים אחרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that meat cooked in its own milk is forbidden even after the fact, and a Tanna taught this ruling regarding the head.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בקביעה שחלחולה שבושלה בחלבה אסורה אף בדיעבד, ומציינת שהברייתא נקטה לשון דומה ברישא.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry about Rav's teaching on כָּחָל
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry about Rav's teaching on כָּחָל
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar asks Ze'iri about a Tanna who taught Rav regarding כָּחָל, and Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi responds that he never taught Rav about it, and Rav acted independently.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar, upon ascending, asked Ze'iri whether there is a Tanna who taught Rav about the permissibility of כחל (udder meat cooked in its own milk).
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Avudimi responded that he never taught Rav about כחל at all, and Rav found a 'field' (a situation requiring a fence) and built a fence (issued a prohibition).
Rav Yitzchak bar Avudimi explains that Rav independently enacted a stringency, like one who finds an unenclosed field and fences it.

items.text: The incident that led Rav to forbid כָּחָל
items.text_en: The incident that led Rav to forbid כָּחָל
items.desc_en: Rav heard a woman asking how much milk is needed to cook meat, and since he was not well-versed in the laws of meat and milk, he forbade the use of כָּחָל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that Rav visited Tatlefush, heard a woman ask how much milk is needed to cook meat, concluded that people do not know the prohibition of בשר בחלב (meat in milk), and therefore forbade them from eating כחל (udder).

items.text: Two versions of what Rav taught about כָּחָל
items.text_en: Two versions of what Rav taught about כָּחָל
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana teaches the story as above, while Rabbi Yosei bar Abba claims he taught Rav about the כָּחָל of a nursing animal, and through Rav Chiyya's analysis, Rav taught it as a general rule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana taught the version of the story as above (that Rav forbade כחל).
Rabbi Yosei bar Abba taught that he taught Rav about the udder of a nursing animal (כחל של מניקה), and from Rav Chiya's analysis Rav learned it as a general case of כחל.

items.text: מעשה בבית רב פפי: אכילת חלחולה
items.text_en: Ravin and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef's visit to Rav Pappi's house
items.desc_en: Ravin and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef were served a dish of כָּחָל; Rav Yitzchak ate it but Ravin did not. Abaye explains that Ravin was a glutton, but the real reason is that Rav Pappi's wife, being the daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, would not have served it without a reliable tradition.
items.desc: רבין ורב יצחק בר יוסף התארחו אצל רב פפי, ורב יצחק אכל מהתבשיל ואילו רבין נמנע. אביי תמה על רבין, שכן אשת רב פפי הייתה בתו של רבי יצחק נפחא, שהיה מדקדק במצוות, ומכאן שהתבשיל ודאי מותר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Ravin and Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef visited Rav Pappi's house, were served a dish of כחל; Rav Yitzchak ate it, Ravin did not, and Abaye inferred that Ravin was a glutton for not eating, since Rav Pappi's wife, daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak Nafcha (a master of halachic practice), would not have served it without a reliable tradition.
sub.desc: הגמרא מספרת שרבין ורב יצחק בר יוסף התארחו בבית רב פפי, הוגש להם תבשיל חלחולה, רב יצחק אכל ורבין נמנע.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that Ravin's refusal was not due to gluttony but because Rav Pappi's wife, daughter of Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha, would not have served the dish without a reliable tradition permitting it.
sub.desc: הגמרא מספרת שרבין ורב יצחק בר יוסף התארחו בבית רב פפי, הוגש להם תבשיל חלחולה, רב יצחק אכל ורבין נמנע.

items.text: מנהג סורא ופומבדיתא: מעשה רמי בר תמרי
items.text_en: The dispute between Sura and Pumbedita regarding כָּחָל
items.desc_en: In Sura they do not eat כָּחָל, but in Pumbedita they do. Rami bar Tamrei from Pumbedita went to Sura on Yom Kippur eve and ate the כָּחָל that others discarded. He was brought before Rav Chisda, who questioned him about violating the stringencies of the place he left and the place he went to, but Rami claimed he ate outside the techum. Rav Chisda then questioned him about the roasting method and potential issues of yayin nesekh and gezel, to which Rami responded that the wood was from a certain type, the wine was over twelve months old, and the wood was ownerless due to despair.
items.desc: בסורא נמנעו מאכילת חלחולה, ובפומבדיתא אכלו. רמי בר תמרי, שבא מפומבדיתא לסורא בערב יום כיפור, אכל חלחולות בניגוד למנהג המקום. רב חסדא שאלו מדוע לא קיבל עליו חומרי המקום, ורמי השיב שאכל מחוץ לתחום. בהמשך דנו בצלייה בגרעיני ענבים ובשאלת גזל ויאוש.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces the dispute: in Sura they do not eat כָּחָל (udder meat cooked in milk), but in Pumbedita they do.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בתיאור המנהגים השונים: בסורא לא אכלו חלחולות, ובפומבדיתא אכלו; ומספרת שרמי בר תמרי, שבא מפומבדיתא לסורא בערב יום כיפור, אכל חלחולות בניגוד למנהג המקום.

sub.desc_en: The Stam relates that Rami bar Tamrei (also called Rami bar Dikulei) from Pumbedita went to Sura on Yom Kippur eve, and when everyone else discarded their udders, he took and ate them.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בתיאור המנהגים השונים: בסורא לא אכלו חלחולות, ובפומבדיתא אכלו; ומספרת שרמי בר תמרי, שבא מפומבדיתא לסורא בערב יום כיפור, אכל חלחולות בניגוד למנהג המקום.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda brings Rami before him and asks why he acted in this way, violating the stringencies of the place he left.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל את רמי בר תמרי מדוע עשה כך, ורמי משיב שבא ממקומו של רב יהודה שאוכל חלחולות; רב חסדא מקשה עליו מכלל חומרי המקום שיצא ממנו והלך אליו, ורמי משיב שאכל מחוץ לתחום.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei answers that he is from the place of Rav Yehuda, where they eat udder.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל במה צלה את החלחולות, ורמי משיב בגרעיני ענבים; רב חסדא חושש שמא היו מיין נסך, ורמי דוחה שכבר עברו שנים עשר חודש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects that Rami should be subject to the stringencies of both the place he left and the place he went to.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מעלה חשש נוסף שמא הגרעינים היו גזולים, ורמי משיב שהיה יאוש בעלים, שכן צמחו בהם עשבים.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei answers that he ate the udders outside the techum (Sabbath boundary), so he was not subject to the stringencies of Sura.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל את רמי בר תמרי מדוע עשה כך, ורמי משיב שבא ממקומו של רב יהודה שאוכל חלחולות; רב חסדא מקשה עליו מכלל חומרי המקום שיצא ממנו והלך אליו, ורמי משיב שאכל מחוץ לתחום.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rami with what wood he roasted the udders, suspecting a potential issue of יין נסך (wine used for idolatry) from the wood.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל במה צלה את החלחולות, ורמי משיב בגרעיני ענבים; רב חסדא חושש שמא היו מיין נסך, ורמי דוחה שכבר עברו שנים עשר חודש.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei answers that he roasted them with פורצני (a type of wood from a vine that is not used for wine).
sub.desc: רב חסדא מעלה חשש נוסף שמא הגרעינים היו גזולים, ורמי משיב שהיה יאוש בעלים, שכן צמחו בהם עשבים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether the wood might have come from יין נסך (wine used for idolatry), which would render the udders forbidden.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל במה צלה את החלחולות, ורמי משיב בגרעיני ענבים; רב חסדא חושש שמא היו מיין נסך, ורמי דוחה שכבר עברו שנים עשר חודש.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei answers that the wine was over twelve months old, so it is no longer considered יין נסך (wine used for idolatry).
sub.desc: רב חסדא מעלה חשש נוסף שמא הגרעינים היו גזולים, ורמי משיב שהיה יאוש בעלים, שכן צמחו בהם עשבים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks whether the wood might have been stolen, which would make it forbidden due to גזל (theft).
sub.desc: רב חסדא מעלה חשש נוסף שמא הגרעינים היו גזולים, ורמי משיב שהיה יאוש בעלים, שכן צמחו בהם עשבים.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei answers that the wood was ownerless due to יאוש בעלים (despair of the owners), as reeds had grown through it, indicating abandonment.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מעלה חשש נוסף שמא הגרעינים היו גזולים, ורמי משיב שהיה יאוש בעלים, שכן צמחו בהם עשבים.

items.text: שאלות רב חסדא על תפילין וציצית
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's additional questions about tefillin and tzitzit
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda noticed Rami bar Tamrei was not wearing tefillin and asked why; Rami replied he had stomach pain and cited Rav Yehuda that one with stomach pain is exempt. Rav Chisda then asked why he had no tzitzit, and Rami said the tallit was borrowed, citing Rav Yehuda's ruling.
items.desc: רב חסדא הבחין שרמי בר תמרי אינו מניח תפילין ואין לו ציצית. רמי נימק את הפטור מתפילין בשל חולי מעיים, ואת היעדר הציצית בטלית שאולה, בהתאם לדברי רב יהודה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda sees Rami bar Tamrei is not wearing tefillin and asks why.
sub.desc: רב חסדא שואל את רמי בר תמרי מדוע אינו מניח תפילין.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Tamrei explains he has stomach pain and cites Rav Yehuda's ruling that one with stomach pain is exempt from tefillin.
Rav Chisda sees Rami bar Tamrei is not wearing tzitzit and asks why.
Rami bar Tamrei explains the tallit is borrowed and cites Rav Yehuda's ruling that one is exempt from tzitzit on a borrowed garment.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: טלית שאולה פטורה מציצית
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: borrowed garment exempt from tzitzit
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that a borrowed garment is exempt from the obligation of tzitzit for the first thirty days.
items.desc: הקטע הפותח קובע כי טלית שאולה פטורה ממצוות ציצית בשלושים הימים הראשונים של השאילה, שכן אין חובת ציצית על דבר שאינו בבעלותו הקבועה.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that a borrowed garment is exempt from the obligation of tzitzit for the first thirty days.
sub.desc: קובעת שטלית שאולה פטורה ממצוות ציצית בשלושים הימים הראשונים.

items.text: סיפור האדם שלא כיבד את הוריו ופטורו מעונש
items.text_en: Story: a man who did not honor parents is released
items.desc_en: While the Gemara is discussing the mishnah, they bring a man who did not honor his parents and tie him up. The Gemara cites a baraita that for positive commandments whose reward is stated alongside, the earthly court is not commanded to enforce them, and the man is released. A sage praises the speaker's sharpness.
items.desc: הגמרא מספרת על אדם שהובא לדין על אי כיבוד הוריו, ורמי בר תמרי ביקש לשחררו בטענה שמצוות כיבוד הורים היא מצוות עשה ששכרה בצידה, ולכן אין בית דין של מטה מוזהרים להעניש עליה. רב חסדא משבח את חריפותו, ורמי בר תמרי משיב שהיה מפגין חריפות גדולה יותר במקומו של רב יהודה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara narrates that while discussing the mishnah, they brought a man who did not honor his parents and tied him up.
sub.desc: הגמרא מספרת שהביאו אדם שלא כיבד את הוריו וקשרו אותו לעמוד כדי להלקותו.

sub.desc_en: A sage cites a baraita that for positive commandments whose reward is stated alongside, the earthly court is not commanded to enforce them, and orders the man released.
sub.desc: רמי בר תמרי מבקש לשחררו, בטענה שמצוות עשה ששכרה בצידה אין בית דין של מטה מוזהרים עליה.

sub.desc_en: A sage praises the speaker's sharpness, and the speaker responds that if he were in Rabbi Yehuda's place, he would show even greater sharpness.
sub.desc: רמי בר תמרי מבקש לשחררו, בטענה שמצוות עשה ששכרה בצידה אין בית דין של מטה מוזהרים עליה.

items.text: Abaye's question about liver and Rav Zerika's response
items.text_en: Abaye's question about liver and Rav Zerika's response
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Safra to inquire about the status of liver (kaved) when he goes to Eretz Yisrael. Rav Safra finds Rav Zerika, who says he cooked liver for Rabbi Ami and ate it. When Rav Safra reports back, Abaye clarifies that he was not asking about whether the liver itself is permitted, but whether it can prohibit its companion (other meat cooked with it).

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Safra to inquire about the status of liver (כבדא) when he goes to Eretz Yisrael.

sub.text: Rav Zerika's report to Rav Safra
sub.text_en: Rav Zerika's report to Rav Safra
sub.desc_en: Rav Safra finds Rav Zerika, who reports that he cooked liver for Rabbi Ami and ate it.
When Rav Safra returns, Abaye clarifies that he was not asking whether the liver itself is permitted, but whether it can prohibit its companion (other meat cooked with it).

items.text: Gemara's objection: liver does not prohibit its companion
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: liver does not prohibit its companion
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: why would Abaye need to ask about the liver prohibiting its companion? The mishnah states that liver prohibits but is not prohibited, because it emits but does not absorb. Abaye responds that perhaps that mishnah refers to liver of a non-kosher animal (issura).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Abaye does not need to ask about the liver prohibiting itself, citing the mishnah that liver prohibits but is not prohibited because it emits and does not absorb.
Abaye responds that perhaps the mishnah refers to liver of a non-kosher animal (איסורא), which is already prohibited and thus cannot be prohibited further.

items.text: Gemara's question and the story of Rabbi Zerika
items.text_en: Gemara's question and the story of Rabbi Zerika
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement about the reason for the prohibition being 'due to the fatty membrane'. It then recounts a story where Rabbi Zerika and Rabbi Yannai, son of Rabbi Ami, visited the house of Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi and were served a reed (kanya) with its kofeh (a type of fish), and they ate it, implying that such a practice is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the earlier statement that the prohibition is due to the fatty membrane (שַׁמְנוּנִיתָא), asking: if it is due to blood (דְּמָא), what then?

Rabbi Zerika recounts that he and Rabbi Yannai visited Yehuda ben Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi's house, were served a reed (קַנְיָא) with its kofeh (קוֹפֵיהּ, a type of fish), and they ate it, implying that such a practice is permitted.

items.text: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's objection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi (or Rabbi Shmuel from Zerukinya) objects to the story, suggesting that perhaps the reed's mouth was outside the pot, or that it was scalded initially, citing examples of Rav Huna and Rav Nachman who scalded items in vinegar or boiling water.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi objects to the story, suggesting that perhaps the reed's mouth was outside the pot, or that it was scalded initially.

sub.text: Supporting examples from Rav Huna and Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Supporting examples from Rav Huna and Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi supports his objection by citing that Rav Huna scalded items in vinegar and Rav Nachman scalded items in boiling water.

items.text: Rav Pappa's attempted ruling and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's attempted ruling and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa thought to rule before Rava that vinegar is forbidden (for scalding). Rava responded that if vinegar is forbidden, then the item itself is also forbidden, because as it emits, it reabsorbs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa thought to rule before Rava that vinegar (for scalding) is forbidden.
Rava objected that if vinegar is forbidden, then the item itself is also forbidden, because as it emits, it reabsorbs.

items.text: Story of Rav bar Sheva and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Story of Rav bar Sheva and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rav bar Sheva visited Rav Nachman's house, and they brought him cooked liver, but he did not eat. They remarked that a student of the rabbinical academy does not eat, and who is this? Rav bar Sheva. Rav Nachman told them to force him to eat (or: to give him to Shabbat).

sub.desc_en: The story opens: Rav bar Sheva visited Rav Nachman's house, and they brought him cooked liver, but he did not eat.
The household members remark that a student of the rabbinical academy does not eat, and ask who this is, identifying him as Rav bar Sheva.
Rav Nachman tells them to force him to eat (or: to give him to Shabbat).

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about liver
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about liver
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says the liver prohibits (other foods) but is not itself prohibited, because it emits and does not absorb. Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, says: if seasoned, it prohibits and is prohibited; if boiled, it prohibits and is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a Tannaitic dispute: Rabbi Eliezer rules that the liver prohibits other foods but is not itself prohibited, because it emits and does not absorb.
Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, states that if the liver is seasoned it prohibits and is prohibited, and if boiled it prohibits and is prohibited.

items.text: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna and the spleen with a blood clot
items.text_en: Story of Rabbah bar Rav Huna and the spleen with a blood clot
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna visited Rabbah bar Rav Nachman, who brought him three se'ah of spleen. He asked if they knew he was coming, and they cited the verse 'and you shall call the Shabbat a delight'. Meanwhile, he found a spleen that had a blood clot (simpona) of absorbed blood. He told them to cut it crosswise and lengthwise, and to cut underneath.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna visits Rabbah bar Rav Nachman, who brings him three se'ah of spleen; when asked if they knew he was coming, they cite the verse 'and you shall call the Shabbat a delight'.
Rabbah bar Rav Huna finds a spleen with a blood clot (simpona) of absorbed blood and instructs them to cut it crosswise and lengthwise, and to cut underneath.

items.text: Distinction between liver and spleen
items.text_en: Distinction between liver and spleen
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that these rules apply to liver, but spleen is merely fat, as Shmuel was served a dish of spleen on a day he was engaged in work.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rules that the previous restrictions apply only to liver, but spleen is merely fat and not subject to the same laws.
The Gemara cites a precedent that Shmuel was served a dish of spleen on a workday, indicating it is permitted even without special preparation.

items.text: Dispute about liver and spleen above or below meat
items.text_en: Dispute about liver and spleen above or below meat
items.desc_en: It was stated: Liver above meat is permitted, because blood spurts out. Spleen above meat is forbidden, because milk (fat) clings. Rav Dimi from Nehardea taught the opposite: Spleen above meat is permitted (since the fat of a slaughtered animal is rabbinic), liver above meat is forbidden (blood is biblical). Marimar ruled: Both liver and spleen under meat are permitted; above meat, if done, it is permitted, but not initially.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the first position: liver above meat is permitted because blood spurts out, but spleen above meat is forbidden because milk (fat) clings.
Rav Dimi from Nehardea teaches the opposite: spleen above meat is permitted (since the fat of a slaughtered animal is rabbinic), liver above meat is forbidden (blood is biblical).
Marimar rules the halacha: both liver and spleen under meat are permitted; above meat, if done, it is permitted, but not initially (לכתחילה).

items.text: Story of Rav Ashi and the son of Rami bar Abba
items.text_en: Story of Rav Ashi and the son of Rami bar Abba
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi visited the house of Rami bar Abba, his father-in-law, and saw the son of Rami bar Abba doing something (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: The gemara begins a story: Rav Ashi visited the house of his father-in-law Rami bar Abba and saw the son of Rami bar Abba doing something (the text is cut off).

items.text: שפיד כבדא עלוי בשרא
items.text_en: Roasting liver on meat and the status of blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where one roasted liver on top of meat, and a rabbi criticized the action as arrogant. It clarifies that if there is a cavity, meat on top of liver is also forbidden. The difference between meat blood and liver blood is explained: meat blood is fluid, liver blood is congealed.
items.desc: דיון על צליית כבד ובשר יחד: רבא אוסר לכתחילה, ובנוכחות כלי לקבלת שומן הדם האיסור חל גם כשהבשר למעלה מהכבד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the ruling that one who roasted liver on top of meat is called arrogant, asking whether the rabbis' prohibition applies only לכתחילה (a-priori) or also בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara answers that if there is a cavity, meat on top of liver is also forbidden, implying the ruling applies even בדיעבד (after the fact).
The Gemara resolves the distinction: meat blood is fluid (שכין) and flows out, while liver blood is congealed (קפי) and remains absorbed, explaining why liver on meat is more problematic.

items.text: Laws of a knife used for slaughter and a salting bowl
items.text_en: Laws of a knife used for slaughter and a salting bowl
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: a knife used for slaughter may not be used to cut hot food, and for cold food there is a dispute about whether it requires rinsing. Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: a bowl used for salting meat may not be used for hot food, consistent with Shmuel's principle that salted is like hot and pickled is like cooked.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports Shmuel's ruling: a knife used for slaughter may not cut hot food, and for cold food there is a dispute about whether rinsing is required.
Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling: a bowl used for salting meat may not be used for hot food, consistent with Shmuel's principle that salted is like hot and pickled is like cooked.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Shmuel on salted as hot
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Shmuel on salted as hot
items.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan said salted is not like hot and pickled is not like cooked. Abaye challenges this with a story: a bowl used for salting meat in Rabbi Ami's house was broken, implying that Rabbi Ami (a student of Rabbi Yochanan) held that salted is like hot, contradicting the report.

sub.desc_en: Ravin reports that Rabbi Yochanan rules that salted is not like hot and pickled is not like cooked.
Abaye rejects Ravin's report, citing a bowl in Rabbi Ami's house that was broken after salting meat, implying Rabbi Ami held salted is like hot.
Abaye asks why Rabbi Ami, a student of Rabbi Yochanan, would break the bowl unless he heard from Rabbi Yochanan that salted is like hot.
Abaye concludes that Rabbi Ami's action proves Rabbi Yochanan actually held that salted is like hot, contradicting Ravin's report.

items.text: Distinction between a salting bowl and a knife cut radish
items.text_en: Distinction between a salting bowl and a knife cut radish
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana states: a bowl used for salting meat is forbidden for hot food, but a radish cut with a knife is permitted with kutaḥ (a dairy dip). Abaye explains: the bowl absorbed forbidden taste (meat), the knife absorbed permitted taste (raw meat). Rava objects: even permitted taste becomes forbidden when eaten with dairy. Rava instead distinguishes: the radish can be tasted to check for meat flavor, but the bowl cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana states that a bowl used for salting meat is forbidden for hot food, but a radish cut with a knife is permitted with kutaḥ (a dairy dip).
Abaye explains that the bowl absorbed forbidden taste (meat), while the knife absorbed permitted taste (raw meat).
Rava objects that even permitted taste becomes forbidden when eaten with dairy, so Abaye's distinction fails.
Rava instead distinguishes: the radish can be tasted to check for meat flavor, but the bowl cannot.

items.text: Objection: using a non-Jew to taste
items.text_en: Objection: using a non-Jew to taste
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava: why not have a non-Jew taste the radish? The Gemara cites a precedent: for meat and milk, a non-Jew tastes. Rava responds: his statement applies when no non-Jew is available.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava: why not have a non-Jew (קפילא ארמאה) taste the radish, citing the precedent of a pot that cooked meat and milk where a non-Jew tastes.
Rava responds that his statement applies only when no non-Jew (קפילא) is available, as the Gemara itself resolved the meat-and-milk case similarly.

items.text: דגים שעלו בקערה – מחלוקת רב ושמואל
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on fish in a meat bowl
items.desc_en: It was stated: fish that were cooked in a meat bowl – Rav forbids eating them with kutaḥ (dairy), Shmuel permits. Rav says it is a direct taste transfer; Shmuel says it is a secondary taste transfer (נותן טעם בר נותן טעם). The Gemara notes that Rav's ruling was inferred from an incident where he tasted a dish and detected a flavor, though that case is distinguished because the bile was abundant.
items.desc: רב אוסר דגים חמים שעלו בקערה של בשר לאכלם בכותח, שמואל מתיר; מחלוקתם תלויה בהגדרה 'נותן טעם בר נותן טעם'; הגמרא מצטטת סיפור על רב הממחיש טעם משני.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a dispute: fish cooked in a meat bowl – Rav forbids eating them with kutaḥ (dairy), Shmuel permits.
The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rav considers it a direct taste transfer (נותן טעם), Shmuel considers it a secondary taste transfer (נותן טעם בר נותן טעם).
The Gemara notes that Rav's ruling was inferred from an incident where he tasted a dish and detected a flavor, but distinguishes that case because the bile was abundant.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's test of Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's test of Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar was before Mar Shmuel, who ate fish from a meat bowl with kutaḥ. Shmuel offered some to Rabbi Elazar, who refused. Rabbi Elazar then went to Rav and asked if Shmuel retracted. Rav replied that Shmuel would not give him something he didn't agree with.

sub.text: Narrative: Rabbi Elazar before Mar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rabbi Elazar before Mar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar was standing before Mar Shmuel, who ate fish from a meat bowl with kutaḥ and offered some to Rabbi Elazar, who refused.

sub.text: Mar Shmuel's question to Rabbi Elazar
sub.text_en: Mar Shmuel's question to Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Mar Shmuel asked Rabbi Elazar why he refused, noting that his teacher Rav had accepted such food from Shmuel.

sub.text: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry and Rav's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's inquiry and Rav's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar went to Rav and asked if Shmuel had retracted his ruling; Rav replied that Shmuel would never give him something he did not agree with.

items.text: Final ruling and distinction between fish and radish
items.text_en: Final ruling and distinction between fish and radish
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi act according to their respective traditions: one eats fish from a meat bowl with kutaḥ (following Shmuel), the other eats fruit without a blessing (following Rabbi Chiyya). Chizkiya states the halakha in the name of Abaye: fish from a meat bowl are permitted with kutaḥ, but a radish cut with a meat knife is forbidden with kutaḥ, and this applies only to a radish (sharp and absorbs easily).

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes a scene where Rav Huna and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi sit on opposite sides of a bridge, and each is served food according to his own tradition: one eats fish from a meat bowl with kutaḥ, the other eats fruit without a blessing.

sub.text: Each rabbi's challenge to the other
sub.text_en: Each rabbi's challenge to the other
sub.desc_en: Each rabbi calls the other an orphan for acting contrary to his own tradition, and each explains his reasoning: one follows Shmuel regarding fish, the other follows Rabbi Chiyya's teaching that bread exempts all foods and wine exempts all drinks.
Chizkiya states the halakha in the name of Abaye: fish that came up in a meat bowl are permitted with kutaḥ, but a radish cut with a meat knife is forbidden with kutaḥ.
The gemara adds that this ruling applies only to a radish, which is sharp and absorbs easily.

items.text: Opening distinction between sharp and non-sharp foods
items.text_en: Opening distinction between sharp and non-sharp foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between sharp items (like horseradish) that absorb flavor due to their sharpness, and non-sharp items (like leeks) that do not, unless cut with a sharp knife.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes between sharp items (like horseradish) that absorb flavor due to their sharpness, and non-sharp items (like leeks) that do not, unless cut with a sharp knife.

items.text: Rav Dimi's question about salt and brine jars
items.text_en: Rav Dimi's question about salt and brine jars
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi asks Rav Nachman whether one may place a jar of salt next to a jar of brine (kutach). Rav Nachman forbids it because salt is sharp, but permits placing a jar of vinegar next to brine, as vinegar is not sharp.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi asks Rav Nachman whether one may place a jar of salt next to a jar of brine (kutach).
Rav Nachman forbids placing salt next to brine, but permits placing vinegar next to brine.
The gemara asks what is the difference between salt and vinegar that explains the different rulings.
The gemara explains that salt retains its forbidden status (as a sharpener) in its own right, while vinegar does not.

items.text: Case of a chick falling into brine
items.text_en: Case of a chick falling into brine
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rava from Pashrunya permitted a chick that fell into a brine jar, reasoning that Shmuel's principle 'salt is like boiling' applies only when the salt renders the food inedible, but brine is edible due to its salt.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case where a chick fell into a brine jar, and Rav Chinana bar Rava from Pashrunya permitted it.
Rava asks rhetorically who but Rav Chinana bar Rava would be wise enough to permit such a case.
Rav Chinana bar Rava reasoned that Shmuel's principle 'salt is like boiling' applies only when the salt renders the food inedible, but this brine is edible due to its salt.

items.text: Distinction between raw and roasted
items.text_en: Distinction between raw and roasted
items.desc_en: The Gemara adds that the leniency applies only to raw meat; roasted meat requires peeling, and if it has cracks, the entire piece is forbidden. If seasoned with spices, the whole is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the leniency of not requiring peeling applies only to raw meat, but roasted meat requires peeling.
The Gemara adds that if the roasted meat has cracks, the entire piece is forbidden.
The Gemara rules that if the meat is seasoned with spices, the entire piece is forbidden.

items.text: Loaf used to cut meat
items.text_en: Loaf used to cut meat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that a loaf on which meat was cut is forbidden to eat, but only if the loaf was firm and the meat was cut with pressure. Shmuel threw such a loaf to his dog, while Rav Huna gave it to his servant due to his sensitive disposition, and Rava ate it, calling it 'meat wine'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that a loaf on which meat was cut is forbidden to eat, but only if the loaf was firm, the meat was cut with pressure, and the loaf was firm; a soft loaf is not a concern.
The gemara reports that Shmuel threw such a loaf to his dog, Rav Huna gave it to his servant due to his sensitive disposition, and Rava ate it, calling it 'meat wine'.

items.text: Placing a vessel under meat to catch blood
items.text_en: Placing a vessel under meat to catch blood
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that one may not place a vessel under meat until all redness has drained. Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa says this is when the steam rises. Rav Ashi objects that the lower part may have finished while the upper part hasn't, and concludes that the only remedy is to put two lumps of salt in the vessel.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that one may not place a vessel under meat until all redness has drained.

sub.text: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa answers that the sign is when the steam rises.
Rav Ashi objects that the lower part may have finished draining while the upper part hasn't.
Rav Ashi concludes that the only remedy is to put two lumps of salt in the vessel.

items.text: Gemara's question about Shmuel's ruling on a loaf cut with meat
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Shmuel's ruling on a loaf cut with meat
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika challenges Rav Ashi's earlier statement that Shmuel permits eating a loaf cut with meat, citing Shmuel's own ruling that such a loaf is forbidden. The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the case: there, the pressure of the knife causes the meat to exude its flavor into the bread.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's challenge
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika's challenge
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rav Ika challenges Rav Ashi by citing Shmuel's own ruling that a loaf cut with meat is forbidden, contradicting the earlier claim that Shmuel permits it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing the case: there, the pressure of the knife causes the meat to exude its flavor into the bread.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on fish and fowl salted together
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on fish and fowl salted together
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that fish and fowl salted together are forbidden. The Gemara questions this: if in a perforated vessel, even fish and fowl should be permitted; if in an unperforated vessel, even fowl with fowl would be forbidden. The Gemara explains that in a perforated vessel, fish exude first due to their soft skin, then fowl exude later, and then reabsorb from each other, causing prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that fish and fowl salted together are forbidden.
The Gemara questions the ruling: if in a perforated vessel, even fish and fowl should be permitted; if in an unperforated vessel, even fowl with fowl would be forbidden.
The Gemara explains that in a perforated vessel, fish exude first due to their soft skin, then fowl exude later, and then reabsorb from each other, causing prohibition.

items.text: Rav Mari bar Rachel's case of salted kosher and treifa meat
items.text_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel's case of salted kosher and treifa meat
items.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel salted kosher meat together with treifa meat and came before Rava. Rava rules that the verse 'the unclean' (Vayikra 11:34) teaches that the brine, gravy, and scum of forbidden meat are also forbidden, thus the kosher meat is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari bar Rachel salted kosher meat together with treifa meat and came before Rava for a ruling.
Rava rules that the verse 'the unclean' (Vayikra 11:34) teaches that the brine, gravy, and scum of forbidden meat are also forbidden, thus the kosher meat is prohibited.

items.text: דחיית דברי שמואל לטובת דרשת רבה
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Shmuel's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not derive the law from Shmuel's statement that salted food is like hot and pickled is like cooked. It answers that without the explicit teaching, one might have thought this applies only to blood but not to brine or gravy.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע רבה לא הסתמך על דברי שמואל ש'מליח הרי הוא כרותח', ומתרצת שאילו היה עושה כן, היה מקום לטעות שהדין חל רק על דם ולא על ציר ורוטב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not derive the law from Shmuel's principle that salted food is like boiling and pickled like cooked.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע רבה לא הביא ראיה מדברי שמואל, שאומר שמליח דינו כרותח וכבוש כמבושל, כדי לבסס את דינו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that without the explicit teaching one might have thought the principle applies only to blood, not to brine and gravy, so the teaching is needed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת: אילו הביא רבה משמואל, הייתי אומר שהדין אמור רק על דם, אבל ציר ורוטב – לא; לכן השמיענו רבה דרשה מפסוק ללמד שגם ציר ורוטב אסורים.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about salted fish
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about salted fish
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a clean fish salted with an unclean fish. It analyzes whether both were salted or one was salted and the other unsalted, concluding that the baraita's structure implies both salted are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita about a kosher fish salted with a non-kosher fish, questioning whether both were salted, and answers that the kosher fish was salted and the non-kosher unsalted.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's latter clause implies the first clause deals with both salted, and then explains that the latter clause clarifies the first.
The Gemara argues that it is reasonable that the first clause refers to both salted, as otherwise the latter clause would be redundant.
The Gemara rejects the reasoning, explaining that the latter clause was taught to clarify that the first clause permits even both salted.
The Gemara brings a third clause of the baraita, inferring that both salted are permitted.
The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting the third clause uses parallel language to the second clause and does not address both salted.

items.text: Siman (mnemonic)
items.text_en: Siman (mnemonic)
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is provided for the following teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic for remembering the three halakhot stated by Shmuel below.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on salting meat
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on salting meat
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that meat does not release its blood unless salted well and rinsed well. The Gemara notes a dispute between Rav Huna and a baraita about the order of salting and rinsing, and resolves it based on whether the meat was cut by a butcher.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel rules that meat is not rid of its blood unless salted and rinsed thoroughly.
The Gemara notes that Rav Huna holds one salts and then rinses, while a baraita teaches one rinses, salts, and rinses again.
The Gemara resolves that the two rulings do not disagree: one case refers to meat already rinsed by the butcher, the other to meat not yet rinsed.
The Gemara adds that Rav Dimi of Neharde'a would salt meat with coarse salt and then shake it off.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's ruling on blood in intestines
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's ruling on blood in intestines
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya says that blood is not considered retained in the intestines, and this is applied to the karkesha, intestines, and the spleen's membrane.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya rules that no blood is presumed to be retained in the intestines, and this is applied to the karkesha, intestines, and the membrane of the spleen.
The Gemara explains that Rav Mesharshiya's ruling was interpreted to apply specifically to the karkesha (rumen), intestines, and the spleen's membrane.

items.text: הצורך בכלי מנוקב ומליחת חתיכות בודדות
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on placing salted meat
items.desc_en: Shmuel says salted meat must be placed only on a perforated vessel. Rav Sheshet salted each bone separately, and the Gemara questions why not two together, concluding there is no difference.
items.desc: שמואל קובע שאין להניח בשר מלוח אלא על כלי מנוקב. רב ששת מלח חתיכה אחת בכל פעם, והגמרא דנה האם הדבר הכרחי.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that salted meat may only be placed on a perforated vessel to let blood drain.
sub.desc: שמואל קובע שיש להניח בשר מלוח רק על כלי מנוקב כדי שהדם יצא.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet salted meat one piece at a time.
sub.desc: מסופר שרב ששת נהג למלוח חתיכה אחת בכל פעם, והגמרא תוהה על הסיבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav Sheshet did not salt two pieces together, suspecting cross-absorption.
sub.desc: מסופר שרב ששת נהג למלוח חתיכה אחת בכל פעם, והגמרא תוהה על הסיבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even one piece could reabsorb blood from one side to another.
sub.desc: מסופר שרב ששת נהג למלוח חתיכה אחת בכל פעם, והגמרא תוהה על הסיבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that there is no difference between one piece and two; all are permitted.
sub.desc: מסופר שרב ששת נהג למלוח חתיכה אחת בכל פעם, והגמרא תוהה על הסיבה.

items.text: איסור שבירת מפרקת קודם יציאת נפש
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling in the name of Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: Shmuel says in Rabbi Chiyya's name that breaking an animal's neck before death makes the meat heavy, robs people, and causes blood to be absorbed. The Gemara questions whether this prohibition applies only to others or also to the one who does it, and leaves it unresolved.
items.desc: רבי חייא בשם שמואל אוסר שבירת מפרקת הבהמה קודם שתצא נפשה, משום שמכביד את הבשר, גוזל את הבריות ומבליע דם. הגמרא מתלבטת האם האיסור הוא רק גזל או גם איסור אכילה למשתמש עצמו.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel says in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that breaking an animal's spinal column before its soul departs makes the meat heavy, robs people, and causes blood to be absorbed in the limbs.
sub.desc: שמואל בשם רבי חייא פוסק שהשובר מפרקת הבהמה קודם יציאת הנפש מכביד את הבשר, גוזל את הבריות ומבליע דם באיברים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Shmuel mean the prohibition applies only because it robs people, implying it is permissible for oneself, or is it also forbidden for oneself because of blood absorption?
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק האם הכוונה היא שהאיסור הוא רק משום גזל (אך למשתמש לעצמו מותר) או שגם למשתמש לעצמו הבשר אסור משום דם.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the dilemma unresolved (תיקו).
sub.desc: הגמרא מעלה ספק האם הכוונה היא שהאיסור הוא רק משום גזל (אך למשתמש לעצמו מותר) או שגם למשתמש לעצמו הבשר אסור משום דם.

items.text: דין עוף עם גבינה על השולחן
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on bird and cheese
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bringing a bird and cheese to the table does not violate a prohibition. The Gemara infers that eating them does violate a prohibition, suggesting bird meat in milk is Torah law, but reinterprets the Mishnah to mean one does not come to violate a prohibition.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שהעלאת עוף עם גבינה על השולחן אינה עוברת בלא תעשה. הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות שהמשנה מלמדת שעוף בחלב אסור מהתורה, ומפרשת שהכוונה שלא יבוא לידי איסור.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that placing bird meat with cheese on the table does not violate a negative commandment.
sub.desc: המשנה קובעת שהעלאת עוף וגבינה על שולחן אחד אינה עוברת בלא תעשה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that eating bird meat with cheese would violate a Torah prohibition, suggesting that bird meat in milk is Torah law.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah to mean that one who places bird meat with cheese will not come to violate a Torah prohibition (since the prohibition is rabbinic).

items.text: Mishnah on meat and milk combinations
items.text_en: Mishnah on meat and milk combinations
items.desc_en: The Mishnah details which meat and milk combinations are forbidden or permitted for cooking and benefit. Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGlili offer different derivations from the verse 'You shall not cook a kid in its mother's milk' to exclude certain animals.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rules: kosher animal meat in kosher animal milk is forbidden; non-kosher combinations are permitted.
Rabbi Akiva expounds the three mentions of 'גדי' (kid) to exclude undomesticated animal, bird, and non-kosher animal from the Torah prohibition.

Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from the juxtaposition of neveila (unslaughtered carcass) and the kid-in-milk verse that only meat subject to neveila is forbidden, excluding bird which has no mother's milk.

items.text: Gemara's source for the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's source for the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to derive the source for these laws, citing Rabbi Elazar who quotes the verse 'And Yehuda sent the kid of the goats'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?
Rabbi Elazar answers by citing a verse: 'And Yehuda sent the kid of the goats'.

items.text: Derivation that 'גדי' includes all kosher animals
items.text_en: Derivation that 'גדי' includes all kosher animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive from the verse 'גדי עזים' that any unqualified 'גדי' includes even a cow or ewe. It then tries to derive the same from 'גדיי העזים', but concludes that these are two verses that come as one and thus cannot teach a general principle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the specification 'גדי עזים' (kid of goats) implies that an unqualified 'גדי' (kid) includes all kosher domesticated animals like a cow or ewe.
The Gemara questions the previous inference, suggesting that from 'גדיי העזים' (kids of the goats) one might derive the opposite — that 'גדי' always means a goat specifically.
The Gemara rejects the objection, stating that the two verses are two written statements that come as one (שני כתובים הבאים כאחד) and therefore do not teach a general principle.

items.text: Resolution for those who hold verses teach
items.text_en: Resolution for those who hold verses teach
items.desc_en: For those who hold that two verses can teach a principle, the Gemara notes that there are two exclusions: 'עזים' and 'העזים', which limit the scope.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous resolution works for the opinion that two verses that come as one do not teach a principle, but asks what can be said for the opinion that they do teach.
The Gemara answers that even for that opinion, there are two exclusions written — 'עִזִּים' and 'הָעִזִּים' — which indicate that the specification is only in those verses.

items.text: דרישות שמואל על שלושת ה'גדי'
items.text_en: Shmuel's drashot on 'גדי' and 'בחלב אמו'
items.desc_en: Shmuel expounds the three occurrences of 'גדי' to include forbidden fat, a dead animal, and a fetus, and to exclude blood, the afterbirth, and a non-kosher animal. He also expounds 'בחלב אמו' to exclude milk of a male, a slaughtered animal, and a non-kosher animal.
items.desc: שמואל דורש את שלושת הופעות המילה 'גדי': לרבות חלב, מתה ושליל, ולהוציא דם, שליה וטמאה. כמו כן הוא דורש את שלושת הפעמים 'בחלב אמו': להוציא זכר, שחוטה וטמאה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel introduces the drashah, stating that the first three instances of 'גדי' include forbidden fat, a dead animal, and a fetus.
sub.desc: שמואל פותח בדרישת שלושת הפעמים 'גדי' לרבות חלב, מתה ושליל.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel continues, stating that the next three instances of 'גדי' exclude blood, the afterbirth, and a non-kosher animal.
sub.desc: שמואל ממשיך ודורש את שלושת הפעמים 'גדי' להוציא דם, שליה וטמאה.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel expounds the three occurrences of 'בחלב אמו' to exclude milk of a male, a slaughtered animal, and a non-kosher animal.
sub.desc: שמואל דורש את שלושת הפעמים 'בחלב אמו' להוציא זכר, שחוטה וטמאה.

items.text: Reconciliation of Shmuel's six drashot with three 'גדי' verses
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Shmuel's six drashot with three 'גדי' verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that only three 'גדי' are written, yet Shmuel derives six laws. It explains that Shmuel holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, so the prohibition of forbidden fat and a dead animal come from one verse. Blood and the afterbirth are not 'גדי', leaving two verses: one to include a fetus and one to exclude a non-kosher animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a discrepancy: only three occurrences of 'גדי' are written, yet Shmuel derived six halakhot from them.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, so the prohibitions of חלב (forbidden fat) and נבלה (carcass) derive from a single verse.
The Gemara explains that blood and the afterbirth (שליה) do not require their own verses: blood is not a 'גדי' and the afterbirth is merely a secretion.
Thus, only two verses remain: one to include a fetus (שליל) and one to exclude a non-kosher animal (בהמה טמאה).

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Shmuel's view on איסור חל על איסור
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Shmuel's view on איסור חל על איסור
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Shmuel elsewhere holds that a prohibition does not take effect on another prohibition, based on a verse. Three answers are given: either Shmuel generally holds it does take effect and the other case is an exception, or he generally holds it does not and the case of 'גדי' is an exception, or the two statements are from different periods of his life.

sub.desc_en: Raises a contradiction: Does Shmuel really maintain that a prohibition takes effect where another already exists, given his own statement (in the name of Rabbi Elazar) that an impure priest who eats impure terumah (תרומה) is exempt from the death penalty? This suggests the opposite view.

If you wish, say that in general a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, but in the terumah (תרומה) case the verse explicitly excludes impure terumah with the phrase 'and die therein if they desecrate it'.

If you wish, say that in general Shmuel holds that a prohibition does not take effect on another, but the case of 'גדי' (kid) is an exception because the Torah itself includes it by repeating the word 'kid'.
If you wish, say that the statement about 'גדי' (kid) is Shmuel's own opinion, while the statement about terumah (תרומה) is his teacher's opinion.

items.text: גדי שלא הניקה
items.text_en: Inquiry about a kid that never nursed
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami asks Rav whether cooking a kid that never nursed in milk is prohibited. Rav answers that since Shmuel needed to exclude male milk, which never comes from a mother, this kid, which could become a mother, is prohibited.
items.desc: רב אחדבוי בר אמי שאל את רב לגבי בישול בחלב גדי שלא הניקה. רב השיב: מכך ששמואל נזקק להוציא חלב זכר, משמע שגדי שבא לכלל אֵם – אסור, אף שלא הניקה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami asks Rav whether one who cooks meat in the milk of a goat that has never nursed is liable.
sub.desc: רב אחדבוי בר אמי שאל את רב: מה דין מבשל בחלב גדי שעדיין לא הניק?

sub.desc_en: Rav answers that since Shmuel excluded only male milk, which never comes from a mother, milk from a goat that will become a mother is prohibited.
sub.desc: רב אחדבוי בר אמי שאל את רב: מה דין מבשל בחלב גדי שעדיין לא הניק?

items.text: מחלוקת בבישול חלב בחלב
items.text_en: Dispute about cooking forbidden fat in milk
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi disagree on whether one is liable for cooking forbidden fat in milk. The Gemara initially suggests the dispute is about whether a prohibition can take effect on another, but concludes that all agree on eating there is no liability; the dispute is about cooking, with one holding it is a single prohibition and the other that the Torah expressed eating in terms of cooking.
items.desc: רבי אמי ורבי אסי נחלקו במבשל חלב בחלב: אחד אמר לוקה, ואחד אמר אינו לוקה. הגמרא דוחה שהיא מחלוקת על איסור חל על איסור; כולם מודים שאין על אכילה. המחלוקת היא על הבישול עצמו, ומי שאומר לוקה סובר שהוא איסור אחד (בישול בשר בחלב), ומי שאומר אינו לוקה סובר שהתורה הוציאה אכילה בלשון בישול.

sub.desc_en: Stam reports a dispute between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi about whether one who cooks forbidden fat in milk is flogged.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רבי אמי לרבי אסי לגבי המבשל חלב בחלב – האם לוקה או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute hinges on whether a prohibition can take effect where another prohibition already exists.
sub.desc: פותח במחלוקת בין רבי אמי לרבי אסי לגבי המבשל חלב בחלב – האם לוקה או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects that suggestion, stating that all agree a prohibition does not take effect on another, so regarding eating there is no liability for all.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: כולם מודים שאיסור אינו חל על איסור לגבי אכילה, ואין בכך מחלוקת.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the dispute is about cooking: one holds it is a single prohibition, and the other holds that the Torah expressed eating in terms of cooking to teach a lesson.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: כולם מודים שאיסור אינו חל על איסור לגבי אכילה, ואין בכך מחלוקת.

items.text: Dispute on liability for cooking and eating meat in milk
items.text_en: Dispute on liability for cooking and eating meat in milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a dispute: one holds that one is not liable for cooking or eating, while another holds that all agree one is liable for cooking, and the dispute is only about eating, with the second version explaining that the Torah used cooking language for eating to indicate liability. A third resolution states that the two opinions are not in conflict.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the first version of the dispute: since one is not flogged for eating, one is also not flogged for cooking.
The Gemara presents the second version: all agree one is flogged for cooking, and the dispute is only about eating, with the Torah using cooking language for eating to indicate liability.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the two versions are not in conflict but each states a different case.

items.text: Baraita on cooking various items in milk and support for Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Baraita on cooking various items in milk and support for Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: A baraita lists cases where cooking in milk-water is exempt, but cooking piggul, notar, or tamei in milk is liable, indicating the tanna holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition. The exemption for milk-water supports Reish Lakish's view that milk-water is not considered milk for the prohibition of cooking meat in milk.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing cases where cooking in milk-water, blood, bones, etc. in milk is exempt from liability.
The baraita continues that cooking piggul, notar, or tamei in milk is liable, indicating a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition.
The Gemara infers that this tanna holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition.
The Gemara notes that the exemption for cooking in milk-water supports Reish Lakish's view that milk-water is not considered milk for the prohibition of cooking meat in milk.

items.text: Derivation of cow and ewe milk from 'its mother's milk'
items.text_en: Derivation of cow and ewe milk from 'its mother's milk'
items.desc_en: A baraita attempts to derive cow and ewe milk from 'its mother's milk' via a kal vachomer, but the Gemara objects that the derivation is flawed because the mother is unique in being permitted for slaughter with the offspring. Rav Ashi explains that the verse 'its mother's milk' is needed to counter this objection.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that from 'in its mother's milk' only the mother's milk is derived, and asks about the source for cow and ewe milk.
The baraita proposes a קל וחומר (a fortiori inference) to include cow and ewe, but concludes that a verse is needed.
The Gemara objects: why is a verse needed if the inference already derives it?
Rav Ashi explains that the verse is needed because the inference is flawed: the mother is unique in being prohibited for slaughter with the offspring, so the verse must include cow and ewe.

items.text: Derivation of older sister's milk from 'its mother's milk'
items.text_en: Derivation of older sister's milk from 'its mother's milk'
items.desc_en: Another baraita attempts to derive older sister's milk via a kal vachomer from the mother, but the Gemara objects that the mother is unique in being permitted for slaughter with the offspring. Rav Ashi again explains that the verse is needed to counter this objection.

sub.desc_en: A baraita states that from 'in its mother's milk' only the mother's milk is included, and asks where the older sister's milk is derived.
The baraita proposes a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference) from the mother to the older sister, concluding that a verse is needed to include the older sister.
The Gemara questions why a verse is needed if the kal vachomer already derives the older sister.
Rav Ashi explains that the verse is needed because the kal vachomer can be refuted: the mother is unique in being prohibited for slaughter with the offspring, unlike the older sister.

items.text: Derivation of younger sister's milk through a binyan av and resolution
items.text_en: Derivation of younger sister's milk through a binyan av and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara derives younger sister's milk from a common principle (binyan av) between mother and older sister, but questions why older sister cannot also be derived this way. It answers that it can, and the verse 'its mother's milk' is needed for the earlier baraita's derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: we have found a source for the older sister; from where do we derive the younger sister? It answers: it comes from between them (a binyan av).

The Gemara objects: from which case should it be derived? If from the mother, one can refute with the stringency of slaughter prohibition; if from the older sister, one can refute with the stringency of not entering the pen for tithe.
The Gemara resolves: the inference reverts to a common denominator — both are meat and prohibited to cook in milk — so the younger sister is also included.
The Gemara questions: if so, the older sister should also be derivable from the common denominator.
The Gemara answers: yes, indeed it can; rather, the verse 'its mother's milk' is needed for the earlier baraita's derivation.

items.text: Initial kal vachomer for cooking meat in milk
items.text_en: Initial kal vachomer for cooking meat in milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: from where do we derive that the meat itself is prohibited when cooked in its mother's milk? It proposes a kal vachomer: if in slaughter, where fruit (the young) with fruit (the mother) is not prohibited, yet fruit with the mother is prohibited, then in cooking, where fruit with fruit is prohibited, it is logical that fruit with the mother should be prohibited. The verse 'in its mother's milk' teaches otherwise.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where the mother's meat being cooked in its own milk is prohibited.
The Gemara proposes a kal vachomer to derive the prohibition.
The verse 'in its mother's milk' teaches that the kal vachomer is rejected.

items.text: First refutation: mule analogy
items.text_en: First refutation: mule analogy
items.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami explains that the kal vachomer is not automatic because one could argue: a horse born of a horse (fruit with fruit) is prohibited, but a horse born of a mule (fruit with mother) is permitted, as shown by the case of a mule.

sub.desc_en: Rav Achadvoi bar Ami explains why the verse is needed: the kal vachomer can be refuted by the case of a horse that is brother of a mule, where fruit-with-fruit is forbidden but fruit-with-mother is permitted.

items.text: Counter-refutation: paternal lineage
items.text_en: Counter-refutation: paternal lineage
items.desc_en: The Gemara counters: there, the father's seed causes the prohibition, as a mule born of a horse (fruit with fruit) is permitted, but a mule born of a mule (fruit with mother) is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the refutation by asserting that the prohibition is caused by the father's seed, not the maternal relationship.

The Gemara provides supporting evidence: a mule born of a horse and mare (male offspring) is permitted to mate with a female mule (fruit with fruit), but prohibited to mate with its mother (fruit with mother), demonstrating the prohibition depends on paternal lineage.

items.text: Second refutation: slave analogy
items.text_en: Second refutation: slave analogy
items.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina proposes another refutation: a slave born of a maidservant (fruit with fruit) is prohibited, but a slave born of a freedwoman (fruit with mother) is permitted. The Gemara counters that the manumission document causes the prohibition, as a slave born of a freedwoman (fruit with fruit) is permitted, but a slave born of a maidservant (fruit with mother) is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Ravina objects that the a fortiori inference is invalid, as shown by a slave (עבד) son of a maidservant who is brother of a freedwoman: fruit with fruit is prohibited but fruit with mother is permitted.

The Gemara rejects the objection, explaining that the manumission document (גט שיחרור) causes the prohibition, as shown by the case of a slave son of a freedwoman and brother of a maidservant: fruit with fruit is permitted but fruit with mother is prohibited.

items.text: Third refutation: kil'ei zera'im
items.text_en: Third refutation: kil'ei zera'im
items.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin offers another refutation: kil'ei zera'im (mixed seeds) prove that fruit with fruit is prohibited, but fruit with mother is permitted, since wheat and barley are not prohibited when in separate pots.

sub.desc_en: Rav Idi bar Avin proposes a third refutation: the law of כלאי זרעים (mixed seeds) shows that fruit with fruit is prohibited while fruit with mother is permitted, as wheat and barley in a jar are not prohibited.

items.text: Final resolution: two bodies vs. one body
items.text_en: Final resolution: two bodies vs. one body
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi concludes: the kal vachomer fails because one could argue that fruit with fruit involves two separate bodies, whereas fruit with mother is one body, so a verse is necessary.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi rejects the previous attempts and explains that the a fortiori inference is invalid because fruit-with-fruit involves two separate bodies, unlike fruit-with-mother which is one body, so a verse is necessary.

items.text: איסור אכילה והנאה מבשר בחלב
items.text_en: Prohibition of eating and benefiting from meat in milk
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi derives the prohibition of eating meat in milk from the verse 'Do not eat any abomination', and Rabbi Avahu's principle extends this to benefit, unless the Torah specifies otherwise, as with neveilah.
items.desc: רב אשי דורש מהפסוק 'לא תאכל כל תועבה' שאיסור בישול בשר בחלב כולל איסור אכילה, ומוסיף על פי רבי אבהו שאיסור 'לא יאכל' כולל גם איסור הנאה, אלא אם פירש הכתוב אחרת כמו בנבלה.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asks from where the prohibition of eating meat in milk is derived, and answers from the verse 'לא תאכל כל תועבה' (anything abominable to you is forbidden to eat).
sub.desc: רב אשי דורש מהפסוק 'לא תאכל כל תועבה' שאיסור בישול בשר בחלב כולל גם איסור אכילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where the prohibition of deriving benefit from meat in milk is derived, since only the prohibition of eating was mentioned.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהיכן נלמד שאיסור הנאה קיים, בנוסף לאיסור אכילה?

sub.text_en: Rav Ashi citing Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Elazar
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers in accordance with Rabbi Abbahu citing Rabbi Elazar, who established the principle that any scriptural formulation 'לא יאכל', 'לא תאכל', or 'לא תאכלו' implies both a prohibition of eating and of deriving benefit, unless the Torah explicitly permits benefit as it did with neveilah (animal carcass).
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מהיכן נלמד שאיסור הנאה קיים, בנוסף לאיסור אכילה?

items.text: מחלוקת רבי מאיר ורבי יהודה במכירת נבלה
items.text_en: Baraita on neveilah and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses the verse about neveilah: Rabbi Meir derives that both giving and selling are permitted to both a ger and a gentile, while Rabbi Yehuda limits it to giving to a ger and selling to a gentile. The Gemara explains their reasoning, including the use of the word 'or' and a logical distinction.
items.desc: ברייתא מביאה מחלוקת האם מותר למכור נבלה לגר ולגוי בכל דרך (רבי מאיר) או רק ככתוב: לגר בנתינה ולגוי במכירה (רבי יהודה). הגמרא מבארת את טעמי המחלוקת, כולל משמעות המילה 'או' להקדמה או ללימוד כפשוטו.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites the verse permitting a unslaughtered animal carcass (נבלה) to be given to a ger (resident alien) or sold to a gentile, with Rabbi Meir deriving that both giving and selling to either is permitted, while Rabbi Yehuda limits it to giving to a ger and selling to a gentile.
sub.desc: ברייתא מצטטת את המקרא ומביאה את דעת רבי מאיר שמותר לתת או למכור נבלה גם לגר וגם לגוי, ואת דעת רבי יהודה המצמצם: לגר רק בנתינה ולגוי רק במכירה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for his limited interpretation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את טעמו של רבי יהודה: ה'או' בפסוק מורה על חלוקה דווקא, ולא על היתר כללי.

sub.desc_en: Answer: If Rabbi Meir were correct, the verse would have written without the word 'or'; the presence of 'or' shows each option is specific to its recipient.
sub.desc: הגמרא מבארת את טעמו של רבי יהודה: ה'או' בפסוק מורה על חלוקה דווקא, ולא על היתר כללי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir's position: the word 'or' comes to prioritize giving to a ger over selling to a gentile.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר מסביר שה'או' בא להקדים נתינה לגר על מכירה לגוי, אבל אינו מחלק ביניהם; רבי יהודה חולק וסובר שהקדמה זו סברא היא, ואין צורך בפסוק.

sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's counterargument
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda counters that the priority of giving to a ger over selling to a gentile does not need a verse, as it is logical: one is commanded to sustain a ger but not a gentile.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר מסביר שה'או' בא להקדים נתינה לגר על מכירה לגוי, אבל אינו מחלק ביניהם; רבי יהודה חולק וסובר שהקדמה זו סברא היא, ואין צורך בפסוק.

items.text: סימן לחטיבות הבאות
items.text_en: Transition to next topic
items.desc_en: A mnemonic is given for the next set of topics, and the Gemara begins a new discussion with 'Rather, from now...'.
items.desc: הגמרא נותנת סימן ('שַׁבָּת, חוֹרֵשׁ, וְכִלְאֵי זְרָעִים, אוֹתוֹ וְאֶת בְּנוֹ, וְשִׁילּוּחַ הַקֵּן') לנושאים שיידונו בהמשך, ומתחילה בקושיה על דברי רב אשי הקודמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara provides a mnemonic device for the upcoming set of topics.
sub.desc: הגמרא נותנת סימן לנושאים שיידונו בהמשך ומתחילה בקושיה על דברי רב אשי הקודמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new discussion with 'אלא מעתה (rather, from now...)'.

items.text: Sabbath labor and benefit
items.text_en: Sabbath labor and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether products of Sabbath labor should be forbidden for benefit, as they are 'done for you.' It answers with a verse: 'For it is holy to you' – the day is holy, not its products. It then compares to plowing with diverse animals and muzzling, concluding that if Sabbath labor permits benefit, these certainly do.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether products of Sabbath labor should be forbidden for benefit, since it is a practice God made abominable.
The answer cites the verse 'כִּי קֹדֶשׁ הִיא לָכֶם' (for it is holy to you), deriving that the day is holy but its products are not.
The Gemara objects: plowing with diverse animals and muzzling during threshing should also forbid the produce for benefit.
The Gemara resolves with an a fortiori argument: if even the severe case of Shabbat permits benefit, these lighter cases certainly permit it.

items.text: Kil'ei zera'im and benefit
items.text_en: Kil'ei zera'im and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether kil'ei zera'im (mixed seeds) should be forbidden for benefit. It deduces from the verse about kil'ei hakerem (vineyard mixtures) that only those are forbidden, implying kil'ei zera'im are permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether kil'ei zera'im (mixed seeds) should also be forbidden for benefit under the same abomination principle.
The Gemara deduces from the verse about kil'ei hakerem (vineyard mixtures) that only those are forbidden for benefit, implying kil'ei zera'im are permitted.

items.text: Distinction between kil'ei hakerem and kil'ei zera'im
items.text_en: Distinction between kil'ei hakerem and kil'ei zera'im
items.desc_en: A potential distinction is raised: kil'ei hakerem are forbidden both for eating and benefit, while kil'ei zera'im might be forbidden only for eating but permitted for benefit. The Gemara rejects this by linking kil'ei zera'im to kil'ei behemah (mixed breeding), where the offspring is permitted, so too the produce of mixed seeds is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a possible distinction: kil'ei hakerem are forbidden both for eating and benefit, while kil'ei zera'im might be forbidden only for eating but permitted for benefit.

The Gemara rejects the distinction by citing a scriptural juxtaposition (איתוקש) between kil'ei zera'im and kil'ei behemah (mixed breeding), teaching that just as the offspring of mixed animal species is permitted, so too the produce of mixed seeds is entirely permitted.

items.text: Kil'ei behemah and benefit
items.text_en: Kil'ei behemah and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how we know that kil'ei behemah (mixed breeding) is permitted for benefit. It answers: since the Torah forbids it for the altar (for God), it implies it is permitted for common use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where do we derive that the offspring of diverse kinds of animals is permitted for benefit.
The Gemara answers that since the Torah forbids it for the altar, it implies permission for common use.

items.text: Oto v'et b'no and benefit
items.text_en: Oto v'et b'no and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day (oto v'et b'no) should forbid benefit. It answers: since the Torah forbids a time-deficient animal for the altar, it implies it is permitted for common use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: the prohibition of slaughtering an animal and its young on the same day (אותו ואת בנו) should forbid benefit from the offspring.
The Gemara answers: from the fact that the Merciful One prohibits a time-deficient animal for the altar, learn by inference that it is permitted for ordinary people.

items.text: Shilu'ach haken and benefit
items.text_en: Shilu'ach haken and benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mother bird sent away (shilu'ach haken) should be forbidden for benefit. It answers: the Torah did not command 'send' for a stumbling block (i.e., to cause loss).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mother bird sent away in violation of shilu'ach haken should be forbidden for benefit.
The Gemara answers that the Torah did not command 'send' to create a stumbling block (i.e., to cause loss), so the bird remains permitted.

items.text: Resh Lakish's derivation for basar b'chalav
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's derivation for basar b'chalav
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish derives that meat cooked in milk is forbidden from the verse 'Do not eat from it raw or cooked thoroughly,' interpreting the extra word 'cooked thoroughly' to indicate another cooking that is like this one – that is, meat in milk. Rabbi Yochanan responds (but the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish asks: From where is it derived that meat cooked in milk is forbidden? He cites the verse 'Do not eat from it raw or cooked thoroughly.'
Resh Lakish explains that the extra word 'cooked thoroughly' teaches there is another cooking like this one – namely, meat in milk, thereby proving the prohibition.
Rabbi Yochanan begins a response to Resh Lakish (the text cuts off here).

items.text: Opening question: What does 'lo tochelenu' refer to?
items.text_en: Opening question: What does 'lo tochelenu' refer to?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about Rabbi's teaching that the verse 'lo tochelenu' speaks of meat in milk. It considers whether it might refer to any other prohibition and concludes from context that it deals with two species.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi's teaching that the verse 'לֹא תֹּאכְלֶנּוּ' refers to meat in milk.
The Gemara resolves by applying the principle of 'דבר הלמד מעניינו' (contextual interpretation), concluding the verse deals with two species.

items.text: Clarification: The verse teaches about benefit as well
items.text_en: Clarification: The verse teaches about benefit as well
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without this verse, one might have thought the prohibition applies only to eating but not to benefit; therefore the verse teaches that benefit is also prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that without this verse, one might have thought the prohibition applies only to eating but not to benefit; therefore the verse teaches that benefit is also prohibited.

items.text: Rabbi's source for prohibition of benefit
items.text_en: Rabbi's source for prohibition of benefit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi derives the prohibition of benefit from a gezeirah shavah between 'ki am kadosh' and 'velo yihyeh kadesh', linking it to a context of benefit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derive that meat cooked in milk is prohibited for benefit?
