The Gemara answers: He derives it from a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) between the phrase 'כִּי עַם קָדוֹשׁ' here and the phrase 'וְלֹא יִהְיֶה קָדֵשׁ' below, where the latter is in a context of benefit, so here too benefit is prohibited.

items.text: דרשות בית רבי אליעזר ורבי ישמעאל
items.text_en: Tannaitic derivations from the school of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer derives from 'lo tochal kol neveilah' that one may not cook and sell neveilah. The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the three occurrences of 'lo tevashel gedi bachalev imo' that eating, benefit, and cooking are all prohibited.
items.desc: בית רבי אליעזר דורש מפסוק נבלה שאסור לבשל בשר בחלב ולמכור. בית רבי ישמעאל דורש משלוש פעמים 'לא תבשל גדי' לאיסורי אכילה, הנאה ובישול.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Eliezer derives from the verse 'לֹא תֹאכְלוּ כׇל נְבֵלָה' a prohibition against cooking and selling a neveilah.
sub.desc: דבי רבי אליעזר דורש מפסוק הנבלה שאסור לבשל בשר בחלב ולמכרו, כלומר איסור הנאה.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the three occurrences of 'לֹא תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ' that eating, benefit, and cooking are all prohibited.
sub.desc: דבי רבי ישמעאל דורש משלוש פעמים 'לא תבשל גדי' לאיסורי אכילה, הנאה ובישול.

items.text: Isi ben Yehudah's derivation
items.text_en: Isi ben Yehudah's derivation
items.desc_en: Isi ben Yehudah derives the prohibition of meat in milk from a gezeirah shavah between 'ki am kadosh' and 've'anshei kodesh tihyun li', linking it to the prohibition of eating tereifah.

sub.desc_en: Isi ben Yehudah asks the source for the prohibition of meat in milk and answers via a verbal analogy (גזירה שווה) between 'כִּי עַם קָדוֹשׁ' and 'וְאַנְשֵׁי קֹדֶשׁ', concluding that just as tereifah is forbidden, so too meat in milk is forbidden.

items.text: Kal vachomer for benefit from orlah, with refutations
items.text_en: Kal vachomer for benefit from orlah, with refutations
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to derive the prohibition of benefit from a kal vachomer from orlah, but is refuted because orlah never had a time of permissibility. It then tries from chametz on Pesach, but is refuted because chametz carries karet. It then tries from kil'ei hakerem, which has no karet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is the prohibition of benefit from meat in milk derived, and proposes a kal vachomer from ערלה (orlah).
The Gemara rejects the kal vachomer because ערלה (orlah) is unique in that it never had a time of permissibility.
The Gemara suggests that חמץ בפסח (leaven on Passover) proves the point, as it had a time of permissibility but is prohibited for benefit.
The Gemara rejects this because חמץ בפסח (leaven on Passover) is unique in being punishable by כרת (karet).
The Gemara suggests that כלאי הכרם (diverse kinds in a vineyard) prove the point, as they have no כרת (karet) yet are prohibited for benefit.

items.text: Attempt to derive both eating and benefit from orlah via mah hatzad, with refutations
items.text_en: Attempt to derive both eating and benefit from orlah via mah hatzad, with refutations
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a mah hatzad from orlah to derive both eating and benefit, but is refuted by the example of plowing with an ox and donkey or muzzling an ox. It then tries to use kil'ei hakerem as the second side, but Rav Ashi objects that neveilah could refute the argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a verbal analogy is needed, and proposes deriving both eating and benefit from orlah via a kal vachomer.
The Gemara objects that plowing with an ox and donkey or muzzling an ox proves that a sin can be committed yet benefit is permitted, refuting the kal vachomer.
The Gemara asks why it needs to say 'kil'ei hakerem will prove', suggesting instead that orlah alone should prove and then a mah hatzad should be constructed.
Rav Ashi objects that neveilah could refute the mah hatzad, as it is prohibited for eating but permitted for benefit.

items.text: Rav Mordechai's report of Resh Lakish's rules for mah hatzad
items.text_en: Rav Mordechai's report of Resh Lakish's rules for mah hatzad
items.desc_en: Rav Mordechai tells Rav Ashi that Resh Lakish said: for a mah hatzad we refute from within the sides, not from outside. He then explains that a mah hatzad can be refuted with any commonality, but a kal vachomer cannot. The Gemara questions why the commonality of 'gidulei karka' does not refute the mah hatzad, and Rav Mordechai repeats Resh Lakish's principle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mordechai reports in the name of Resh Lakish that for a 'מה הצד' (common element analogy) we refute from within the sides themselves, not from an external case.

The Gemara asks: If so, why not derive the halakha via a 'מה הצד' (common element analogy)? It answers that the analogy can be refuted because the common element of the two sources is that they are 'גידולי קרקע' (produce of the ground).
The Gemara objects: If so, even now that the Gemara invokes diverse kinds in a vineyard, the same refutation of 'גידולי קרקע' (produce of the ground) applies.

Rav Mordechai reports in the name of Resh Lakish that for a 'מה הצד' (common element analogy) we refute with any commonality, but for a 'קל וחומר' (a fortiori inference) from one case to another, we do not refute with just any commonality.
The Gemara asks: But let us refute from all of them (orla, leavened bread, and diverse kinds) that they are all 'גידולי קרקע' (produce of the ground).
Rav Mordechai begins to report a further principle from Resh Lakish, but the text cuts off, leaving the resolution implied.

items.text: כללי ההיקש והבניין אב
items.text_en: Principles of kal vachomer derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara sets forth general rules for deriving leniencies and stringencies from one case to another. It distinguishes between deriving from one case to another (where only leniencies and stringencies are derived, not minor details) and from one case to two (where even minor details are derived).
items.desc: הגמרא דנה בכללי ההיקש: בהיקש מיחיד ליחיד פרכינן קולא וחומרא, אך לא פרכינן כל דהו. בהיקש מאחד לשניים פרכינן אפילו כל דהו. בהיקש מאחד לשלושה, אם הדין חוזר פרכינן כל דהו, ואם לאו פרכינן רק קולא וחומרא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule for a kal vachomer from one source to another: one can refute by invoking a unique leniency and stringency, but not by any unique aspect.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בכללי ההיקש: בהיקש מיחיד ליחיד פרכינן קולא וחומרא, אבל לא פרכינן כל דהו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds the rule for deriving from one source to two: even any unique aspect can refute; for three sources, it depends on whether the inference reverts.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בכללי ההיקש: בהיקש מיחיד ליחיד פרכינן קולא וחומרא, אבל לא פרכינן כל דהו.

items.text: Challenge from kil'ei hakerem
items.text_en: Challenge from kil'ei hakerem
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: why not derive a leniency from kil'ei hakerem (diverse kinds in a vineyard) to meat and milk? Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that kil'ei hakerem had a time of permissibility before rooting, so the derivation does not apply.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge: why not derive a leniency from the prohibition of כלאי הכרם (diverse kinds in a vineyard) to meat and milk, since the former had no time of permissibility?

Rav Adda bar Ahavah answers that the roots of כלאי הכרם (diverse kinds in a vineyard) are prohibited from the start, yet they had a time of permissibility before taking root, so the derivation does not apply.

items.text: Support from a baraita and resolution
items.text_en: Support from a baraita and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Shemayah bar Ze'eira cites a baraita about a perforated pot in a vineyard, which seems to contradict Rav Adda. Abaye resolves the contradiction by citing two verses: one indicates that planting from the start is prohibited at rooting, while the other indicates that if it grew on its own, it is prohibited only if it adds 1/200.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shemayah bar Ze'eira raises an objection from a mishna about a perforated pot in a vineyard, which implies that only the growth is prohibited, not the original plant, contradicting Rav Adda bar Ahava's claim that the roots are prohibited from the start.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by citing two verses: one indicates prohibition upon growth, the other upon planting, showing two distinct scenarios.
Abaye explains the reconciliation: if planted from the start in the vineyard, it is prohibited at rooting; if brought in already grown, it is prohibited only if it adds 1/200.

items.text: מחלוקת על איסור הנאה מבשר בחלב
items.text_en: Mishnah and baraita on meat and milk
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah does not align with a baraita where Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda says in the name of Rabbi Shimon that meat and milk are prohibited for eating but permitted for benefit, based on a gezerah shavah from the verse about holy people.
items.desc: הגמרא מציינת שהמשנה האוסרת הנאה מבשר בחלב אינה כתנא אחר, שכן רבי שמעון בן יהודה בשם רבי שמעון מתיר הנאה, על סמך היקש לטריפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the mishnah does not align with a baraita attributed to Rabbi Shimon ben Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת שהמשנה האוסרת הנאה אינה כתנא אחר, ומביאה ברייתא בשם רבי שמעון בן יהודה בשם רבי שמעון המתיר הנאה על סמך היקש לטריפה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that meat cooked in milk is prohibited for eating but permitted for benefit, citing a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the verse about holy people.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציינת שהמשנה האוסרת הנאה אינה כתנא אחר, ומביאה ברייתא בשם רבי שמעון בן יהודה בשם רבי שמעון המתיר הנאה על סמך היקש לטריפה.

sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes the גזירה שווה (verbal analogy): just as a טריפה (ritually unfit animal) is prohibited for eating but permitted for benefit, so too meat and milk is prohibited for eating but permitted for benefit.

items.text: שיטת רבי עקיבא: חיה ועוף אינם מן התורה
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva's opinion on non-kosher animals and fowl
items.desc_en: Rabbi Akiva holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition, so the verses about chelev and neveilah are unnecessary for a kosher animal; they come to exclude non-kosher animals, fowl, and non-kosher domesticated animals from the prohibition of meat and milk.
items.desc: רבי עקיבא דורש את שלושת הפעמים 'גדי' להוציא חיה, עוף ובהמה טמאה. הגמרא מסבירה שהוא סובר שאיסור חל על איסור, ולכן חלב ומותה אינם צריכים קרא, ושליל הוא גדי מעליא.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Akiva's opinion that the verses about chelev and neveilah exclude non-kosher animals, fowl, and non-kosher domesticated animals from the prohibition of meat and milk.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שיטת רבי עקיבא, שהרי שלושת הפעמים 'גדי' כבר הופקו לדרשת שמואל, ולא נותרו להוצאת חיה ועוף.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether these excluded categories are already covered by Shmuel's principle that non-kosher animals are not subject to the meat-and-milk prohibition.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על שיטת רבי עקיבא, שהרי שלושת הפעמים 'גדי' כבר הופקו לדרשת שמואל, ולא נותרו להוצאת חיה ועוף.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Akiva holds that a prohibition can take effect on another prohibition (איסור חל על איסור), so the verses for chelev and neveilah are unnecessary for kosher animals and come only to exclude non-kosher categories.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שרבי עקיבא סובר איסור חל על איסור, ולכן חלב ומותה אינם צריכים קרא, ושליל הוא גדי מעליא, ושלושת הפעמים 'גדי' נשארו להוצאת חיה, עוף ובהמה טמאה.

items.text: הבדל בין רבי יוסי הגלילי לרבי עקיבא
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the difference between Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Rabbi Akiva: one opinion holds that non-kosher animals are prohibited by Torah law, while the other holds they are rabbinic. Alternatively, the dispute is about fowl: Rabbi Akiva says fowl is rabbinically prohibited, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili says it is permitted even rabbinically.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת את ההבדל בין רבי יוסי הגלילי לרבי עקיבא: יש אומרים שהבדל בחיה (רבי יוסי אוסר מן התורה, רבי עקיבא מדרבנן), ויש אומרים שהבדל בעוף (רבי עקיבא אוסר מדרבנן, רבי יוסי מתיר לגמרי).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili cites the verse 'לֹא תֹאכְלוּ' (you shall not eat) as his proof, and the Gemara asks what difference exists between his position and Rabbi Akiva's.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה ההבדל המעשי בין שיטת רבי יוסי הגלילי לשיטת רבי עקיבא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the difference concerns non-domesticated kosher animals (חיה): Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds their prohibition is from the Torah (דאורייתא), while Rabbi Akiva holds it is rabbinic (דרבנן).
sub.desc: תירוץ ראשון: ההבדל הוא בחיה – רבי יוסי אוסר חיה בחלב מן התורה, ורבי עקיבא אוסר רק מדרבנן.

sub.desc_en: Alternatively, the difference concerns fowl (עוף): Rabbi Akiva holds fowl is rabbinically prohibited, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds it is not even rabbinically prohibited.
sub.desc: תירוץ חלופי: ההבדל הוא בעוף – רבי עקיבא אוסר עוף בחלב מדרבנן, ורבי יוסי הגלילי מתיר לגמרי.

items.text: מעשה בעוף בחלב ומנהג המקומות
items.text_en: Practical evidence and story with Levi
items.desc_en: A baraita supports the dispute: in Rabbi Eliezer's place they cut trees for charcoal, while in Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's place they ate fowl with milk. Levi visited Yosef Rishba and was served a peacock head in milk but said nothing; Rabbi questioned why he didn't excommunicate them, and Levi explained that the place followed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
items.desc: ברייתא מתארת שבמקום רבי אליעזר כרתו עצים לשם מילה, ובמקום רבי יוסי הגלילי אכלו עוף בחלב. מעשה בלוי שאכל ראש טווס בחלב בבית יוסף רישבא, ורבי לא שמתינהו משום שהיה מקום רבי יהודה בן בתירא שנהגו כרבי יוסי הגלילי.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports the dispute by describing the practices in the places of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
sub.desc: ברייתא מביאה ראיה ממנהג המקומות: במקום רבי אליעזר כרתו עצים לשם מילה, ובמקום רבי יוסי הגלילי אכלו עוף בחלב.

sub.desc_en: Levi visited Yosef Rishba and was served a peacock head in milk but said nothing.
sub.desc: מסופר שלוי אכל ראש טווס בחלב בבית יוסף רישבא, ורבי שאלו מדוע לא שימתם אותם.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi asked Levi why he did not excommunicate them for serving fowl with milk.
sub.desc: מסופר שלוי אכל ראש טווס בחלב בבית יוסף רישבא, ורבי שאלו מדוע לא שימתם אותם.

sub.desc_en: Levi explained that the place followed Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who permits fowl with milk.
sub.desc: לוי משיב לרבי שהמקום הוא של רבי יהודה בן בתירא, ושם נהגו כרבי יוסי הגלילי שפטר עוף מאיסור בשר בחלב.

items.text: משנה: קיבת גוי ונבילה
items.text_en: Mishnah on rennet of a gentile or neveilah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that the rennet (keivah) of a gentile or of a neveilah is prohibited, but if one curdles milk with the skin of a kosher rennet, it is permitted.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שקיבת גוי וקיבת נבילה אסורות, אך המעמיד גבינה בעור קיבה כשרה מותר.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah rules that the rennet of a gentile or of a neveilah is prohibited, but curdling milk with the skin of a kosher rennet is permitted.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין קיבת גוי ונבילה האסורה, ובהמשך דנה במעמיד גבינה בעור קיבה כשרה.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: דיני קיבת גוי, נבלה, כשירה שינקה מטריפה וטריפה שינקה מכשירה
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a non-Jew's rennet and that of a neveilah are prohibited if they impart flavor. It then distinguishes between a kosher animal that nursed from a tereifah (its rennet is prohibited) and a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal (its rennet is permitted, because the milk in its stomach is merely a secretion).
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שקיבת גוי וקיבת נבלה אסורות, קיבת כשירה שינקה מטריפה אסורה, וקיבת טריפה שינקה מכשירה מותרת, מפני שהחלב המכונס בה אינו חלק מגופה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that rennet from a non-Jew or a neveilah is prohibited if it imparts flavor, then distinguishes between a kosher animal that nursed from a tereifah (rennet prohibited) and a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal (rennet permitted, because the milk is merely a secretion).
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדיני קיבת גוי ונבלה, כשירה שינקה מטריפה וטריפה שינקה מכשירה, וקובעת את ההבדלים ביניהם.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא על קיבת גוי ותירוצי רב הונא
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is a non-Jew's rennet not neveilah? Rav Huna explains that we are dealing with a kid purchased from a non-Jew, and we suspect it may have nursed from a tereifah. The Gemara objects that we do not suspect such nursing regarding eggs, so it amends to suspect nursing from a non-kosher animal. It then explains why we suspect a non-kosher animal (common) but not a tereifah (uncommon), and why this concern applies only to non-Jews, not Jews.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: הרי קיבת גוי היא נבלה? רב הונא מתרץ שמדובר בלוקח גדי מן הגוי, וחוששים שמא ינק מטמאה. הגמרא דנה מדוע לא חוששים לטריפה (שאינה שכיחה) ומסבירה את ההבדל בין יהודים לגויים בהרחקת בהמותיהם מטמאות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Is the rennet of a non-Jew's animal not considered neveilah (carcass)?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המשנה מבדילה בין קיבת גוי לקיבת נבלה, הרי קיבת גוי עצמה נבלה?

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that the mishna deals with a Jew who purchased a kid from a non-Jew, and we suspect it may have nursed from a tereifah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדוע המשנה מבדילה בין קיבת גוי לקיבת נבלה, הרי קיבת גוי עצמה נבלה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Are we concerned about nursing from a tereifah? A baraita permits buying eggs from non-Jews without such concern.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא שקונים ביצים מן הגויים ואין חוששים לא משום נבלה ולא משום טרפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara amends: Rather, we suspect it may have nursed from a non-kosher animal, not a tereifah.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מברייתא שקונים ביצים מן הגויים ואין חוששים לא משום נבלה ולא משום טרפה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the difference between a tereifah (not suspected) and a non-kosher animal (suspected)?
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה ההבדל בין טרפה לטמאה, מדוע חוששים לטמאה ולא לטרפה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: A tereifah is uncommon, while a non-kosher animal is common.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת: מה ההבדל בין טרפה לטמאה, מדוע חוששים לטמאה ולא לטרפה?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If it is common, we should also be concerned for our own animals.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם טמאה שכיחה, נחשוש גם אצלינו (ישראל)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: Jews separate from non-kosher animals and distance them, so the Sages did not decree; non-Jews do not separate, so the Sages decreed.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם טמאה שכיחה, נחשוש גם אצלינו (ישראל)?

items.text: שיטת שמואל: קיבת שחיטת גוי נבלה
items.text_en: Shmuel's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the Mishnah teaches one law: the rennet of a non-Jew's slaughter is neveilah. The Gemara questions this from Shmuel's own statement that non-Jewish cheese is prohibited only because they use the skin of a neveilah's rennet, implying the rennet itself is permitted. The resolution is that the statements are from before and after Shmuel's retraction.
items.desc: שמואל מפרש שהמשנה עוסקת בקיבת שחיטת גוי עצמה, והיא נבלה. הגמרא מקשה מדברי שמואל עצמו שהתיר קיבה לעומת עור קיבה, ומתרצת שמדובר לפני חזרה ולאחר חזרה של רבי יהושע.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the Mishnah teaches only one law: the rennet of an animal slaughtered by a gentile is considered neveilah (carcass).
sub.desc: שמואל מפרש שהמשנה עוסקת בקיבת שחיטת גוי עצמה, והיא נבלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's position by citing his own statement that gentile cheese is prohibited only because they use the skin of a neveilah's rennet, implying the rennet itself is permitted.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מדברי שמואל עצמו שהתיר קיבה לעומת עור קיבה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishnah's ruling is from before Shmuel's retraction, while his statement about cheese is from after his retraction.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שמדובר לפני חזרה ולאחר חזרה של רבי יהושע.

items.text: קושיית הסתירה בין קיבת נבלה לקיבת טריפה ותירוץ רבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Contradiction in the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the first clause says a non-Jew's rennet is prohibited, but the second clause permits the rennet of a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal. Rav Chisda distinguishes that the first case appears like eating neveilot, while here there is slaughter. Rava objects that if neveilah (disgusting) is prohibited, a slaughtered tereifah (more tempting) should certainly be prohibited. Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the statements are from before and after the retraction, and the Mishnah remains unchanged.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מדברי המשנה נראה שקיבת נבלה אסורה וקיבת טריפה מותרת, והרי זה סותר? רב חסדא מתרץ משום מראית עין, ורבא דוחה אותו. רבי יוחנן מתרץ שמדובר לפני חזרה ולאחר חזרה, והמשנה לא זזה ממקומה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: the first clause of the Mishnah prohibits the rennet of a non-Jew's animal and a neveilah, but the second clause permits the rennet of a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה סתירה בין רישא למציעתא: מדוע קיבת נבלה אסורה ואילו קיבת טריפה מותרת?

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda answers that the first clause prohibits the rennet because it appears like eating neveilot, while here there is slaughter, so it is less problematic.
sub.desc: רב חסדא מתרץ: רישא אסורה משום מראית עין, אבל בטריפה יש שחיטה ואין חשש מראית עין.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects with a kal vachomer argument: if neveilah (disgusting) is prohibited, a slaughtered tereifah (more tempting) should certainly be prohibited.
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את תירוץ רב חסדא בקל וחומר: אם בנבלה המאוסה אסרו, כל שכן בטריפה שאינה מאוסה שיש לחשוש שיבוא לאכול מבשרה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan resolves that the first clause was taught before the retraction and the second clause after, and the Mishnah remains unchanged.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן מיישב: רישא נשנית קודם חזרת רבי יהושע, מציעתא לאחר חזרתו, והמשנה לא זזה ממקומה.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on using rennet for cheese
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on using rennet for cheese
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan initially says one may use rennet from a neveilah but not from a non-Jew's slaughter, aligning with Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Shimon bar Abba asks whom this follows, and Rabbi Yochanan confirms it follows Rabbi Eliezer. Later, Rabbi Yochanan retracts and permits both, disregarding Rabbi Eliezer's view.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that one may curdle milk with rennet from a neveilah (carcass) but not from an animal slaughtered by a gentile.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba asks Rabbi Chiya bar Abba whose opinion this ruling follows.
Rabbi Shimon bar Abba answers his own question, identifying the ruling as following Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that a gentile's presumed intention in slaughter is for idol worship.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba confirms that the ruling indeed follows Rabbi Eliezer, implying no other opinion could explain it.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan retracts his earlier position and now permits rennet from both a neveilah and a gentile's slaughter, disregarding Rabbi Eliezer's view.

items.text: Final halachic ruling
items.text_en: Final halachic ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the halacha: one may not use the skin of a neveilah's rennet, but may use the rennet itself from a neveilah, from a non-Jew's slaughter, from a kosher animal that nursed from a tereifah, and certainly from a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal, because the milk in it is merely a secretion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara issues the final halachic ruling: one may not use the skin of a neveilah's rennet, but may use the rennet itself from a neveilah, from a non-Jew's slaughter, from a kosher animal that nursed from a tereifah, and certainly from a tereifah that nursed from a kosher animal, because the milk in it is merely a secretion.

items.text: משנה חדשה: חומרות בחלב ובדם
items.text_en: Beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a comparison between the stringencies of chelev (forbidden fat) and blood, stating that chelev has a stringency over blood, and blood has a stringency over chelev.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת בהשוואה בין חומרות איסור חלב לאיסור דם, ומתחילה למנות את החומרות שבחלב.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that there is a stringency in the prohibition of חֵלֶב (forbidden fat) over that of blood, and vice versa, beginning with the stringency of חֵלֶב.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בהשוואה בין חומרות איסור חלב לאיסור דם, ומתחילה למנות את החומרות שבחלב.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: חומרי חלב ודם
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Distinction between חלב and blood
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that חלב of lesser holy offerings is subject to מעילה, piggul, nosar, and tum'ah, unlike blood. It also notes that blood applies to all animals (including non-kosher) while חלב applies only to kosher domesticated animals.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שבחלב קדשים יש מעילה וחיוב על פיגול, נותר וטומאה, מה שאין כן בדם. לעומת זאת, בדם יש חומרא שהוא נוהג בכל בהמה חיה ועוף, טמאים וטהורים, ואילו חלב נוהג רק בבהמה טהורה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that חלב (forbidden fat) of lesser holy offerings is subject to מעילה (misuse), piggul, notar, and tum'ah, unlike blood, and notes that blood applies to all animals while חלב applies only to kosher domesticated animals.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בהצגת ההבדלים בין חלב קדשים לדם: בחלב יש מעילה וחיובי פיגול, נותר וטומאה, ואילו בדם אין חיובים אלו, אך חומרת הדם שהיא נוהגת בכל בעלי החיים.

items.text: Gemara's first question and Rabbi Yannai's derivation
items.text_en: Gemara's first question and Rabbi Yannai's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the law that חלב of lesser holy offerings has מעילה. Rabbi Yannai derives it from the verse 'כאשר יורם משור זבח השלמים', comparing the ram of the peace-offering to the bull of the anointed priest, teaching that just as the bull has מעילה, so too the peace-offering's fats have מעילה. Rabbi Chanina objects, suggesting a simpler derivation from the verse 'כל חלב לה׳'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source of the law that חלב (forbidden fat) of offerings of lesser sanctity is subject to מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).

Rabbi Yannai derives the law from the verse 'כאשר יורם משור זבח השלמים' (as it is taken off from the bull of the peace offering), comparing the peace-offering bull to the bull of the anointed priest, teaching that just as the latter has מעילה (misuse), so too the former has מעילה.

Rabbi Chanina objects, suggesting that a simpler derivation exists: the verse 'כל חלב לה׳' (all fat is the Lord's) already includes the sacrificial portions of offerings of lesser sanctity in the prohibition of מעילה (misuse).

items.text: Abaye's resolution: both verses needed
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: both verses needed
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that both verses are necessary. If only 'חלב' were written, one might exclude the diaphragm and two kidneys. If only 'כאשר יורם' were written, one might exclude the fat tail (אליה) which is not in the ox. Therefore both verses are needed.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that if only 'חלב' were written, one might exclude the diaphragm and two kidneys, so the verse 'כאשר יורם' is needed.
Abaye continues that if only 'כאשר יורם' were written, one might exclude the fat tail (אליה) which is not in the ox, so the verse 'כל חלב' is needed.

items.text: Discussion on the fat tail (אליה) and its status
items.text_en: Discussion on the fat tail (אליה) and its status
items.desc_en: Rav Mari asks Rav Zevid: if the fat tail is called 'חלב', why is it not prohibited in eating? Rav Zevid answers that the verse says 'כל חלב שור וכשב ועז' – something common to ox, sheep, and goat (the fat tail is only in sheep). Rav Ashi adds that the fat tail is called 'חלבו האליה' but not 'חלב' alone; nevertheless, one might think it is not subject to מעילה, but the answer of Rav Zevid is correct.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mari asks Rav Zevid: if the fat tail is called 'חלב' (forbidden fat), why is it not prohibited for consumption?
Rav Zevid answers that the verse 'כל חלב שור וכשב ועז' (all fat of ox, sheep, and goat) refers only to something common to all three, excluding the fat tail which is unique to sheep.
Rav Ashi offers an alternative explanation: the fat tail is called 'חלבו האליה' (its fat, the tail) but not 'חלב' (fat) by itself.
The Gemara objects: if so, one might think the fat tail is not subject to מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).
The Gemara concludes that the correct explanation is that of Rav Zevid, not Rav Ashi's.

items.text: Source that blood has no מעילה
items.text_en: Source that blood has no מעילה
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source that blood is exempt from מעילה. Ulla says the verse 'לכם' indicates it is for you (permitted). The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches from 'לכפר' – it is given for atonement, not for מעילה. Rabbi Yochanan says the verse 'הוא' teaches that blood before atonement is like after atonement: just as after atonement there is no מעילה, so before atonement there is no מעילה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the source that blood is exempt from מעילה (misuse of consecrated property).
Ulla derives from the verse 'לכם' (to you) that blood is given for your benefit, not for מעילה.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches from 'לכפר' (to atone) that blood is given for atonement, not for מעילה.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from 'הוא' (it is) that blood before atonement is like after atonement, so there is no מעילה before atonement either.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding blood after atonement
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding blood after atonement
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the comparison should be reversed – after atonement should have מעילה like before? The answer: there is no item that has fulfilled its mitzvah and still has מעילה. The Gemara then challenges with the example of תרומת הדשן (removal of ashes) which has מעילה even after its mitzvah. The Gemara answers that תרומת הדשן and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and two such verses do not teach a general rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the comparison could be reversed: after atonement should have מעילה (misuse) like before atonement.
The Gemara answers that there is no item whose mitzvah has been performed and still has מעילה (misuse).
The Gemara objects with the example of תרומת הדשן (removal of ashes), which has מעילה (misuse) even after its mitzvah is performed.
The Gemara resolves that תרומת הדשן (removal of ashes) and priestly garments are two verses that come as one, and such verses do not teach a general rule.

items.text: Alternative resolution and dispute about two verses
items.text_en: Alternative resolution and dispute about two verses
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who say the ashes require burial, but for Rabbi Dosa who says they may not be used for the next Yom Kippur, what can be said? The Gemara offers another pair: תרומת הדשן and עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken) are two verses that come as one. This works for those who say two such verses do not teach, but for those who say they do teach, the Gemara leaves the issue unresolved (תרי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the previous answer works for the Rabbis who say the ashes require burial, but for Rabbi Dosa who says they may not be used for the next Yom Kippur, what can be said?

The Gemara answers that rather, the cases of תרומת הדשן (removal of the ashes) and עגלה ערופה (the heifer whose neck is broken) are two verses that come as one, and any two verses that come as one do not teach their common element to apply to other cases.
The Gemara objects that this works for the one who says two verses that come as one do not teach, but for the one who says they do teach, what can be said?
The Gemara leaves the issue unresolved with the word 'תרי' (two), indicating the dispute remains.

items.text: דין דם קרבנות: מיעוטים מנותר, מעילה וטומאה
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter: three verses for blood
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that three verses are needed to exclude blood from the laws of notar, me'ilah, and tum'ah, but piggul requires no verse because blood itself is a matir.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת מדוע נצרכו שלושה פסוקים בדם, ומשיבה: אחד למעט מנותר, אחד למעט ממעילה, ואחד למעט מטומאה. פיגול אינו צריך מיעוט כי הדם עצמו מתיר ואינו מתפגל.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that exclusions are written in the two cases of the removal of ashes and the heifer whose neck is broken.
sub.desc: הסברת מיעוטים הכתובים בפרשות שונות המלמדים שההלכה אינה נוהגת אלא באותן פרשות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why three verses are needed with regard to blood.
sub.desc: שאלה: מדוע נצרכו שלושה פסוקים בדם לעניין מיעוטים?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that one verse excludes blood from notar, one from me'ilah, and one from tum'ah.
sub.desc: תשובה: שלושת הפסוקים ממעטים את הדם מנותר, ממעילה ומטומאה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that no verse is needed for piggul because blood itself is a matir, as taught in a mishna.
sub.desc: הבהרה: פיגול אינו צריך מיעוט, שהרי הדם עצמו מתיר ואינו מתפגל, כמבואר במשנה.

items.text: סיום הפרק
items.text_en: Closing formula of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The standard closing phrase 'Hadran alach' marks the end of the previous chapter.
items.desc: מילת 'הדרן' מסמנת סיום הפרק הקודם ומעבר למשנה הבאה.

sub.desc_en: The standard closing formula 'Hadran alach' marks the end of the previous chapter.
sub.desc: סיום פרק 'כל הבשר' וסימן מעבר לפרק הבא.

items.text: משנה: צירוף עור, רוטב, קיפה, אלל וכו' לטומאת אוכלין
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: items that combine for food impurity
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists skin, gravy, spices, alal, bones, sinews, horns, and hooves as combining for food impurity but not for carcass impurity. It adds a case of slaughtering a non-kosher animal for a gentile, and Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on alal.
items.desc: המשנה מפרטת דברים המצטרפים לבשר להשלים כביצה לטומאת אוכלין, אך אינם מצטרפים לטומאת נבלות. כמו כן, שוחט בהמה טמאה לנכרי ומפרכסת מטמאה טומאת אוכלין אך לא נבלות עד שתמות או שיתיז ראשה. רבי יהודה מוסיף שאלל המכונס במקום אחד מצטרף לכזית.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists items (skin, gravy, spices, alal, bones, sinews, horns, hooves) that combine for food impurity but not for carcass impurity.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת ברשימת דברים המצטרפים לבשר להשלים כביצה לטומאת אוכלין, אך אינם מצטרפים לטומאת נבלות.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds a parallel case: slaughtering a non-kosher animal for a gentile while it twitches imparts food impurity but not carcass impurity until death or decapitation.
sub.desc: המשנה מביאה דוגמה נוספת: שוחט בהמה טמאה לנכרי ומפרכסת מטמאה טומאת אוכלין אך לא נבלות עד שתמות או שיתיז ראשה, ומסכמת שהתורה ריבתה לטמא טומאת אוכלין יותר מטומאת נבלות.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that collected alal (meat residue) in one place, if it has an olive-bulk, imparts carcass impurity.
sub.desc: רבי יהודה מוסיף שאלל המכונס במקום אחד מצטרף לכזית ומטמא טומאת נבלות.

items.text: גמרא: מקור ששומרים מצטרפים לטומאה קלה אך לא לחמורה
items.text_en: Gemara: shomrim for light impurity but not for severe impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that protective layers (shomrim) convey light food impurity but not severe carcass impurity, deriving the former from the verse 'al kol zera zaru'a' and the latter from 'be'nivlatah'.
items.desc: הגמרא מבארת שהמשנה עולה בקנה אחד עם ברייתא: שומרים מצטרפים לטומאת אוכלין (קלה) אך לא לטומאת נבלות (חמורה). מקור לטומאה קלה מדרשת 'על כל זרע זרוע' שהזרע בקליפתו נחשב אוכל. מקור לטומאה חמורה מדרשת 'בנבלתה' – ולא בעור שאין עליו כזית בשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that protective layers (shomrim) join for light impurity but not for severe impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בהצגת ברייתא המבחינה בין טומאה קלה לחמורה לעניין צירוף שומרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that protective layers join for light impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה מקור הדין ששומרים מצטרפים לטומאה קלה.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the rule from the verse 'על כל זרע זרוע' (upon any sowing seed), which includes seeds in their protective shells.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה מקור הדין ששומרים מצטרפים לטומאה קלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the source for the rule that protective layers do not join for severe impurity.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה מקור הדין ששומרים אינם מצטרפים לטומאה חמורה.

sub.desc_en: The Sages derive the rule from the verse 'בנבלתה' (in its carcass), which excludes hide without an olive-bulk of flesh.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מה מקור הדין ששומרים אינם מצטרפים לטומאה חמורה.

items.text: דין נוגע בעור כנגד בשר הנבלה
items.text_en: Opening derivation about touching neveilah from behind
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by questioning a baraita that seems to imply that touching neveilah from behind does not impart impurity. Rava explains that the baraita is actually missing a clause: it first states that the verse 'be-nivlatah' excludes a hide without an olive's bulk of flesh, and then considers whether a hide with an olive's bulk of flesh, when touched from behind, might not be impure, concluding with the verse 'yitma' to include it.
items.desc: הבריאה דנה באדם הנוגע בעור הנבלה מאחוריו, וקובעת שלמרות שהעור אינו מצטרף לבשר להשלים כזית, הוא נחשב כיד ומטמא במגע. הגמרא מבהירה שהבריאה חסרה ומשלימה את החסר.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by considering whether one who touches the hide from behind the flesh might not become impure, and concludes with the verse 'יִטְמָא' (shall be impure) to include it.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדין הנוגע בעור הנבלה מאחוריו, ומסיקה שכיוון שנאמר 'יטמא' – הוא טמא אף בלי נגיעה ישירה בבשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the baraita is saying, noting that it seems contradictory.

Rava explains that the baraita is incomplete: it first teaches that the verse 'בְּנִבְלָתָהּ (its carcass excludes a hide without an olive's bulk of flesh, and the hide does not join to complete the measure.
The baraita then considers whether one might exclude even a hide with an olive's bulk of flesh when touched from behind, and that it would not even serve as a handle.
The baraita concludes with the verse 'יִטְמָא' (shall be impure) to include that the hide with an olive's bulk of flesh does impart impurity when touched from behind.

items.text: כלל במשנת עוקצין: יד, שומר, ולא יד ולא שומר
items.text_en: Mishnah about hands and guards
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that distinguishes between a hand (yad) and a guard (shomer): a hand that is not a guard is impure and conveys impurity but does not combine; a guard, even if not a hand, is impure, conveys impurity, and combines; something that is neither hand nor guard is not impure and does not convey impurity.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה משנה המגדירה שלושה סוגי עוקצים: יד בלבד (מטמא אך לא מצטרף), שומר (מטמא ומצטרף), ולא יד ולא שומר (לא מטמא ולא מצטרף).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a hand (yad) that is not a guard (shomer): it is impure and conveys impurity but does not combine.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה את משנת עוקצין המגדירה את דיני יד, שומר ושאינם, כתשתית לדיון הבא.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for a guard (shomer): it is impure, conveys impurity, and combines; something that is neither hand nor guard is not impure and does not convey impurity.

items.text: Scriptural sources for hands and guards
items.text_en: Scriptural sources for hands and guards
items.desc_en: The Gemara seeks the biblical source for hands (yadot) and guards (shomer). It derives hands from the word 'lakhem' in the verses about seeds and neveilah. For guards, it argues that a kal vachomer from hands would suffice to include them for conveying impurity, so the explicit mention of shomer in the Torah must be to teach that it combines (mitztaref).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the halakha of handles (ידות) is written and answers with the verses from seeds and neveilah, showing that 'לכם' includes handles for importing and exporting impurity.
The Gemara argues that a kal vachomer (a fortiori inference) from the law of handles suffices to teach that guards also import and export impurity, so no separate verse is needed for that.
The Gemara resolves that since the Torah explicitly mentions guards (שומר), the verse must be there to teach that guards combine (מצטרף) with the food to form the requisite measure for impurity.

items.text: Refining the functions of hands and guards
items.text_en: Refining the functions of hands and guards
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers alternative possibilities: perhaps a hand only brings in impurity but does not take it out, and a guard both brings in and takes out but does not combine. It rejects the first possibility with a logical argument: if a hand can bring in, certainly it can take out. It then considers that a hand might only take out but not bring in, but rejects this because an extra 'yad' is written in the verse about the oven.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a possibility: perhaps a hand (appendage that serves as a handle) only brings in impurity but does not take it out, while a guard both brings in and takes out but does not join together with the food.
The Gemara rejects the first possibility with a logical argument: if a hand can bring impurity into the food, it certainly can take it out, so the proposed limitation is untenable.
The Gemara raises an alternative possibility: perhaps a hand only takes out impurity but does not bring it in, while a guard both takes out and brings in but does not join together with the food.
The Gemara rejects this alternative by citing that an extra verse about a hand is written concerning an oven, indicating that a hand both brings in and takes out impurity.

items.text: Determining which verse is extra
items.text_en: Determining which verse is extra
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies that the word 'lakhem' appears in three contexts: seeds, oven, and neveilah. It asks which one is extra, since one could derive hands from the others. It considers each source: seeds have abundant impurity, oven imparts impurity through its air, neveilah imparts impurity to people and through carrying. None alone can serve as a source for the others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses the question of which of the three verses mentioning 'lakhem' (for you) is superfluous, as all teach the inclusion of handles.
The Gemara asks which of the three contexts (seeds, oven, or neveilah) provides the extra verse.
The Gemara rejects deriving handles from seeds alone because seeds have the stringency of abundant impurity, which others lack.
The Gemara rejects deriving handles from an oven alone because it has the stringency of imparting impurity through its airspace.
The Gemara rejects deriving handles from neveilah alone because it has stringencies: imparting impurity to people, through carrying, and impurity emanating from itself.

items.text: Attempting to derive one from two and resolving with a different application
items.text_en: Attempting to derive one from two and resolving with a different application
items.desc_en: The Gemara tries to derive one source from the other two, but each attempt fails due to unique characteristics. It then suggests that the hand of neveilah is not needed for neveilah itself, but can be applied to hands in general (yad de'alma), teaching that a hand brings in and takes out, and a guard combines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one cannot derive one case from another, so let one come from two.
The Gemara asks which case can be derived, and proposes not writing the hand for seeds, but rejects it because seeds require prior wetting.
Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua objects that un-wetted produce is like an unfinished oven, so the distinction is not valid.
The Gemara refutes differently: those cases become impure without contact, unlike seeds.
The Gemara asks about not writing the hand for an oven, but rejects it because the other cases are food.
The Gemara resolves that the hand of neveilah is not needed for neveilah itself, so apply it to hands in general.
The Gemara concludes that a hand brings in and takes out, and a guard combines.

items.text: Final resolution: hand of neveilah is needed, guard of neveilah is extra
items.text_en: Final resolution: hand of neveilah is needed, guard of neveilah is extra
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the hand of neveilah is actually necessary, because without it one might argue 'dayo lavo min hadin lihiyot kanidon' – that neveilah would not impart impurity to a person. Therefore, the extra verse is the guard of neveilah, which is not needed for neveilah itself; it is applied to teach that a hand brings in and takes out, and a guard combines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse for the hand of neveilah is still necessary, because without it one would apply the principle 'דיו לבא מן הדין להיות כנדון' (it is sufficient for a conclusion derived from an a fortiori inference to be like its source) and conclude that neveilah does not transmit impurity to a person.

The Gemara resolves that the hand of neveilah is indeed necessary, but the guard of neveilah is not needed; the verse about the guard is superfluous for neveilah itself, since it neither combines (to form the requisite measure) nor is needed for exporting impurity (which is derived a fortiori from the hand).

The Gemara concludes: since the guard of neveilah is not needed for its own context, apply it to the hand of neveilah; and if the hand of neveilah is also not needed, apply it to the hand in general, teaching that a hand exports impurity, a hand imports impurity, and a guard combines to form the requisite measure.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on shomer of neveilah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on shomer of neveilah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote a separate verse for the shomer of neveilah, suggesting it could be derived from a kal vachomer from yad, but then rejects this because yad itself is only for insertion, not for joining.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Torah wrote a separate verse for the shomer of neveilah, suggesting it could be derived from a kal vachomer from yad, but then rejects this because yad itself is only for insertion, not for joining.

items.text: Answer: Yad was written for insertion
items.text_en: Answer: Yad was written for insertion
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse about yad was originally written for the concept of insertion (hachnasah), not for joining.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the verse about yad was originally written for the concept of insertion (hachnasah), not for joining.

items.text: Gemara's challenge: Why is shomer of neveilah needed?
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge: Why is shomer of neveilah needed?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the shomer of neveilah is needed at all, since it cannot be used for joining and its other function (insertion and removal) could be derived via kal vachomer from yad. The Gemara responds that the Torah sometimes writes a kal vachomer explicitly, and where there is a possibility to expound, we expound.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the shomer of neveilah is needed at all, since it cannot be used for joining and its other function could be derived via kal vachomer.
The Gemara explains that the shomer of neveilah is needed for its own sake, and the Torah sometimes writes a kal vachomer explicitly.
The Gemara objects that if so, the shomer of other foods could also be derived by kal vachomer, yet the Torah wrote it explicitly.
The Gemara resolves that where there is a possibility to expound, we expound, so the shomer of neveilah is needed for its own sake while the shomer of other foods is derived by exposition.

items.text: דעת רב חבביא: שומר דנבלה נדון כיד
items.text_en: Rav Chaviva's distinction
items.desc_en: Rav Chaviva explains that the shomer of neveilah is different because it is a product of human action (ma'aseh yad), so it is classified as a yad.
items.desc: רב חבביא מסביר כי שומר דנבלה, מאחר שתפקידו כשל יד (הכנסה והוצאה), מיישמים את החידוש שלו לידות ולא לשומרים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva distinguishes the shomer of neveilah, explaining that since it is a product of human action (מעשה יד), it is classified as a yad.
sub.desc: רב חביבא עונה ששומר דנבלה נדון כיד מכיוון שתפקידו דומה ליד (הכנסה והוצאה), ולכן החידוש מוחל על ידות ולא על שומרים.

items.text: התקפת רב יהודה בר ישמעאל ומקור לצירוף שומרים
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael objects based on a mishnah about the pith of a pomegranate, and then raises another question about the source for the joining of skin, gravy, and sediment. The Gemara resolves by citing three verses: one for guards of seeds, one for guards of trees, and one for guards of meat, eggs, and fish.
items.desc: רב יהודה בר ישמעאל מקשה על דין צירוף שומר שבא מ'על כל זרע זרוע', שהרי כמה שומרים (פיטמא של רמון, עור ורוטב) אינם נזרעים. הגמרא עונה: שלושה כתובים – לרעים, לאילנות, לבשר ביצים ודגים.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael objects by citing a mishnah that the pith of a pomegranate joins to convey טומאה (ritual impurity) but its blossom does not, challenging the rule about guards.
sub.desc: רב יהודה בר ישמעאל מקשה מברייתא על הפיטמא של רמון שמצטרפת, למרות שאינה נזרעת, ובכך מערער על הדרשה מ'על כל זרע זרוע'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael asks why the pith joins but the blossom does not, given that the verse 'עַל כׇּל זֶרַע זֵרוּעַ' (on all seed that is sown) is available to include both.

sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael's further question
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael raises another question: from where do we derive that skin, gravy, and sediment join to convey טומאת אוכלים (impurity of foods)?
sub.desc: רב יהודה בר ישמעאל מקשה קושיה נוספת מברייתא על עור ורוטב שמצטרפים לטומאת אוכלים, אף שאינם נזרעים, ושואל מה מקור דין זה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves by citing three verses: one for guards of seeds, one for guards of trees, and one for guards of meat, eggs, and fish.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת ששלושה כתובים שונים מלמדים על שומר לזרעים, לאילנות ולבשר ביצים ודגים, ואין צורך שהדבר יהא נזרע דווקא.

items.text: מחלוקת רב ורבי יוחנן: יש יד להכשר?
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on yad for hechsher
items.desc_en: Rav states that there is a yad for impurity but not for hechsher, while Rabbi Yochanan says there is a yad for both. The Gemara explains their dispute: either based on whether a verse is expounded before or before its predecessor, or based on whether hechsher is considered the beginning of impurity.
items.desc: רב פוסק שאין יד להכשר, ורבי יוחנן פוסק שיש יד להכשר. הגמרא מביאה שני הסברים למחלוקת: אחד בדרש הפסוק (לפניו ולפני פניו) ואחד בסברא (הכשר כתחילת טומאה).

sub.text: רב חייא בר אשי משם רב
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav states that there is a yad (handle) for impurity but not for hechsher (making food susceptible to impurity).
sub.desc: רב פוסק שיש דין יד לטומאה אבל לא להכשר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan disagrees and states that there is a yad for both impurity and hechsher.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן חולק ופוסק שיש יד אף להכשר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what underlies their dispute and offers two possible explanations: a logical reason or a scriptural derivation.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת במה נחלקו רב ורבי יוחנן ומציעה שני הסברים אפשריים: סברא או דרשת הפסוק.

sub.desc_en: One explanation: Rav holds that a verse is expounded only to its immediate predecessor, not to the one before that, limiting the scope of the yad verse.
sub.desc: הסבר ראשון: רב סובר שדורשים מקרא שלפניו בלבד ולא לפני פניו, ולכן יד להכשר לא נלמד.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan holds that a verse is expounded both to its immediate predecessor and to the one before that, thus including hechsher.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן סובר שדורשים גם לפני פניו, ולכן יד להכשר נלמד.

sub.desc_en: Alternatively, the dispute is logical: Rabbi Yochanan considers hechsher the beginning of impurity, so it has a yad, while Rav does not.
sub.desc: הסבר שני: רבי יוחנן סובר שהכשר הוא תחילת טומאה ולכן יש בו דין יד, ורב סובר שאין הכשר תחילת טומאה.

items.text: ברייתא כרבי יוחנן
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view: just as there is a yad for impurity, so too there is a yad for hechsher, and both require detachment.
items.desc: תניא כוותיה דרבי יוחנן: כשם שיש יד לטומאה, כך יש יד להכשר, ואין מקבלים טומאה והכשר אלא כשהן תלושים.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rabbi Yochanan's view: just as there is a yad for impurity, so too there is a yad for hechsher, and both require detachment.
sub.desc: ברייתא תומכת בדעת רבי יוחנן: כשם שיש יד לטומאה, כך יש יד להכשר, ושניהם אינם חלים אלא כשהפירות תלושים.

items.text: מחלוקת על שיעור מינימום ליד ושומר
items.text_en: Dispute on minimum size for yad and shomer
items.desc_en: Rav says there is no yad for less than an olive's bulk and no shomer for less than a bean's bulk, while Rabbi Yochanan says there is. An objection is raised from a mishnah about two bones with half-olives that combine to make the house impure, and Yehuda ben Nakosa questions how two bones combine for an olive's bulk.
items.desc: רב ורבי יוחנן נחלקים: רב אומר אין יד לפחות מכזית ואין שומר לפחות מכפול, רבי יוחנן אומר שיש. מובאת ברייתא הנראית כקושיה לשתי הדעות, ויהודה בן נקוסא מקשה על צירוף פחות מכזית.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that there is no yad (handle) for less than an olive's bulk and no shomer (protective covering) for less than a bean's bulk.
sub.desc: רב קובע כי אין דין יד בפחות מכזית ואין דין שומר בפחות מכפול.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan disputes Rav, asserting that there is a yad for less than an olive's bulk and a shomer for less than a bean's bulk.
sub.desc: רבי יוחנן חולק וטוען שיש דין יד ושומר אף בפחות מהשיעורים האמורים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a mishnah about two bones each with half an olive's bulk of flesh that, when inserted into a house, render the house impure, implying that half-olive amounts can combine.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא המקשה על דברי רב ורבי יוחנן, שבה שני חצאי זיתים מטמאים את הבית אף על פי שאין בכל אחת מהם כזית שלם.

sub.text: יהודה בן נקוסא משום רבי יעקב
sub.text_en: Yehuda ben Nakosa in the name of Rabbi Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Yehuda ben Nakosa, citing Rabbi Yaakov, questions how two separate bones can combine to form an olive's bulk, challenging the assumption that half-olive amounts are significant.
sub.desc: יהודה בן נקוסא מקשה בשם רבי יעקב: כיצד שני עצמות מצטרפים לכזית, הרי על כל אחד מהם פחות מכזית בשר?

items.text: דחיית שיטת רב בברייתא של פתח הבית
items.text_en: Rav's and Rabbi Yochanan's interpretations of the first baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rav can reconcile the baraita about a kulis with either a yad or shomer interpretation. Two answers are proposed: either Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa (yad) or like the Tanna Kamma (shomer). Rabbi Yochanan holds the entire baraita is about yad and follows the Tanna Kamma.
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב כיצד מיישב את הברייתא על פתח הבית. מוצעות שתי אפשרויות: או שהברייתא עוסקת ביד והוא כרבי יהודה בן נקוסא, או שהיא עוסקת בשומר והוא כתנא קמא. רבי יוחנן מיישב את הברייתא כולה ביד ותנא קמא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how Rav can interpret the baraita if it is about a yad (handle), since the first clause would be difficult.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רב כיצד מיישב את הברייתא על פתח הבית, ומפרטת את הקושיה: אם הברייתא ביד – קשה רישא; אם בשומר – קשה סיפא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara adds that if the baraita is about a shomer (protection), the last clause would be difficult.
The Gemara offers two possible resolutions: either the baraita is about shomer or about yad.
sub.desc: הסתמא מציעה שתי אפשרויות ליישוב שיטת רב: או שהברייתא עוסקת בשומר, או שהיא עוסקת ביד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara specifies that if the baraita is about yad, Rav follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Nakosa; if about shomer, Rav follows the Tanna Kamma.
sub.desc: הסתמא מבארת: אם הברייתא ביד – רב כרבי יהודה בן נקוסא; אם בשומר – רב כתנא קמא.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the entire baraita is about yad and he follows the Tanna Kamma.

items.text: Second baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Acheirim on kulis
items.text_en: Second baraita: Rabbi Yehuda and Acheirim on kulis
items.desc_en: A new baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says a kulis with a kezayit of meat drags the whole bone to impurity; Acheirim say even a kefol suffices. The Gemara again questions Rav's position, and offers two resolutions: Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda (yad) or like Acheirim (shomer). Rabbi Yochanan holds the entire baraita is about shomer and follows Acheirim.

sub.desc_en: A new baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says a kulis with a kezayit of meat drags the whole bone to impurity; Acheirim say even a kefol suffices.
The Gemara questions how Rav interprets this baraita, noting that if it is about a handle (yad) the end is difficult, and if about protection (shomer) the beginning is difficult.
The Gemara offers two resolutions: Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda (yad) or like Acheirim (shomer).
Rabbi Yochanan holds the entire baraita is about shomer and follows Acheirim.

items.text: Clarification of Acheirim's statement
items.text_en: Clarification of Acheirim's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Acheirim mention a kefol, implying a measure. It explains that since the Tanna Kamma stated a measure (kezayit), Acheirim also stated a measure (kefol).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Acheirim can be said to state a measure, since they use the term 'kefol' (a bean), which is not a standard measure.
The Gemara answers that since the Tanna Kamma stated a measure (kezayit), Acheirim also stated a measure (kefol), using a bean as their unit.

items.text: Rava's proof that the baraita deals with shomer
items.text_en: Rava's proof that the baraita deals with shomer
items.desc_en: Rava argues that the term 'kulis' (a bone with marrow) indicates the baraita deals with shomer, as marrow is a shomer for the bone.

sub.desc_en: Rava argues that the term 'קולית' (a bone with marrow) indicates the baraita deals with shomer, as marrow is a shomer for the bone.

items.text: מחלוקת על שיעור 'כפול' של אחרים
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan on the measure
items.desc_en: It is stated: Rabbi Chanina says this (kefol) is a measure, Rabbi Yochanan says it is not a measure. The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan can say it is not a measure when the baraita says 'kefol'. The answer is that Acheirim were merely stating a measure in response to the Tanna Kamma.
items.desc: רבי חנינא ורבי יוחנן נחלקו: האם 'כפול' של אחרים הוא שיעור מדויק או לא. רבי יוחנן סובר שאחרים מטמאים אפילו בפחות משיעור זה, והביאור הוא שמאחר שתנא קמא נקב בשיעור, גם אחרים נקבו בשיעור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Chanina says 'kefol' is a measure, while Rabbi Yochanan says it is not a measure.
sub.desc: רבי חנינא ורבי יוחנן חלוקים אם 'כפול' הוא שיעור מדויק או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yochanan can say 'kefol' is not a measure when the baraita explicitly uses the term 'kefol'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי יוחנן: הרי הברייתא מפורשת 'כפול' כבית-שעור? ומתרצת שאין זו קושיא, שכן מאחר שתנא קמא נקב שיעור, גם אחרים נקבו שיעור אף על פי שסוברים פחות מכך.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Acheirim were merely stating a measure in response to the Tanna Kamma, not that 'kefol' itself is a fixed measure.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה על רבי יוחנן: הרי הברייתא מפורשת 'כפול' כבית-שעור? ומתרצת שאין זו קושיא, שכן מאחר שתנא קמא נקב שיעור, גם אחרים נקבו שיעור אף על פי שסוברים פחות מכך.

items.text: מחלוקת רב אליעזר בן עזריה: טומאה בתרמילי קטניות
items.text_en: Baraita of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah on pods
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah declares pure a pod of beans but impure a pod of lentils because one wants their handling. The Gemara explains, like Rav Acha bar Rava said regarding a stalk, it is due to being a yad. Here too it is a stalk and due to being a yad, and 'handling' means 'use'.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא של רבי אלעזר בן עזריה המטהר בתרמילי פול ומטמא בתרמילי קטנית משום שרוצה במשמושן. הגמרא דוחה שזה מדין 'יד' בקולחא, ולא שומר, ומיישבת את הסוגיה עם דעת רב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah declares pure a pod of beans but impure a pod of lentils because one wants their handling.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא כראיה נגד דעת רב ורבי חנינא, לפיה תרמילי קטניות נחשבים שומר אף בפחות מכזית.

sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation via Rav Acha bar Rava
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains, like Rav Acha bar Rava said regarding a stalk, it is due to being a yad (handle).
sub.desc: הגמרא מקבילה לדברי רב אחא בריה דרבא, ומסבירה שהברייתא עוסקת בקולחא (עוקץ) ודין יד, לא שומר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: here too it is a stalk and due to being a yad, and 'handling' means 'use'.
sub.desc: הגמרא מיישבת: גם כאן מדובר בקולחא ומשום יד, ומבארת כי 'במשמושן' הכוונה לתשמישן – שימוש ביד לאחיזה.

items.text: קושיית בית רבי ישמעאל על שיעור שומר
items.text_en: Baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael on seeds in their husks
items.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael derives from the verse 'all seed that is sown' that seeds are sown in their husks (e.g., wheat, barley, lentils). The Gemara notes that a 'beriah' (a complete entity) is different.
items.desc: הגמרא מביא לימוד מבית רבי ישמעאל שזרע דגן יוצא בקליפתו, והרי גרגירי חיטה ושעורה פחותים מכשיעור. נדחה שדין בריה שאני, ובלשון אחרת: גרגיר נחשב 'בריה' ואין צורך בשיעור.

sub.text_en: Supporting baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael cites the verse 'all seed that is sown' to teach that seeds are sown in their husks, listing wheat, barley, and lentils as examples.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ברייתא מבית רבי ישמעאל המלמדת שדגנים יוצאים לזריעה בקליפתם, ומכאן שגם שומר הפחות משיעור פול מטמא, בניגוד לשיטת רבי חנינא ורב.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes that a 'beriah' (a complete entity) is different from ordinary seeds, implying a special halachic status.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה את הראיה מפני שגרגיר דגן נחשב 'בריה' בפני עצמה, ולכן דינו שונה משומר רגיל.

items.text: בקשת רב אושעיא, תחילת דיון חדש
items.text_en: Rav Oshaya's question
items.desc_en: Rav Oshaya raises a question, which is left unresolved.
items.desc: הגמרא מתחילה בעיה חדשה: 'בעי רב אושעיא', המהווה פתח לדיון הבא שאינו מפורש בהמשך הקטעים שניתנו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Oshaya raises a question, which is left unresolved.
sub.desc: רב אושעיא מעלה בעיה תלמודית חדשה, המהווה פתיחה לדיון הבא.

items.text: בעיית שני שומרין והצטרפותם
items.text_en: Question on combining two protectors
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether two separate protective layers can combine to convey impurity. It considers a case where one protector lies atop another, and questions whether such a configuration exists. The discussion introduces a distinction between layers that protect each other versus those that protect only themselves.
items.desc: הגמרא שואלת האם שני שומרים (כגון קליפות) יכולים להצטרף יחד עם האוכל לשיעור כביצה לטומאה. ר' אושעיא מברר זאת בשומר שחולק, אם הוא מצטרף או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether two protective layers (שומרין) can combine to convey impurity, and questions whether a configuration of one protector atop another exists.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda discusses three onion peels, showing that only the innermost peel combines, implying that protectors on top of protectors do not combine.
Rav Oshaya raises a different question: whether a protector of food that has been divided (into separate pieces) can still serve as a protector.
The Gemara suggests that since each piece does not protect the other, they do not combine to form a valid protector.
Alternatively, since each piece protects itself, they might combine to form a valid protector.

items.text: תשובה ממשנת ר' אלעזר בן עזריה
items.text_en: First attempted proof from Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya declares bean pods pure but legume pods impure because one wants their handling. Rav Acha bar Rava explains this refers to the stalk, which serves as a handle (יד).
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה ממשנת ר' אלעזר בן עזריה המטהר בתרמילי פול ומטמא בקטנית, שרומזת שהשומרים מצטרפים, אך רב אחא בריה דרבא דוחה שהכוונה ליד (לקלח) ולא לשומר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah where Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya declares bean pods pure but legume pods impure because one wants their handling, as a potential proof for the question of whether two guards combine.
Rav Acha bar Rava explains that the mishnah refers to the stalk, which serves as a handle (יד), not as a guard, and the phrase 'because one wants their handling' means 'because one wants their use'.

items.text: Second attempted proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Second attempted proof from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that seeds are sown in their husks, indicating the husk is a protector. Rav Acha bar Rava again explains this as a handle. The Gemara analogizes this to the spine, which serves as a protector.

sub.text: Gemara's citation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation from the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that seeds are sown in their husks, indicating the husk is a protector.
Rav Acha bar Rava explains that the husk is considered a handle (יד), not a protector (שומר).
The Gemara analogizes the spine to a protector (שומר), not a handle, resolving the proof attempt.

items.text: Objection regarding the need for upper and lower layers
items.text_en: Objection regarding the need for upper and lower layers
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why a lower layer would need an upper one, and suggests it might be in a single row. It then objects that there wouldn't be an egg's bulk of food in a single row of wheat from Shimon ben Shataḥ's time, and concludes that even a single grain would be enormous.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the lower layer would need the upper layer, and suggests the grains are in a single row.
The Gemara objects that there wouldn't be an egg's bulk of food in a single row, except with the large wheat of Shimon ben Shataḥ.
The Gemara concludes that even a single grain of that enormous wheat would suffice.

items.text: Discussion of two bones and a hair as a handle
items.text_en: Discussion of two bones and a hair as a handle
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah about two bones with half-olive portions of flesh that combine when their ends enter a tent. Yehuda ben Nakosa questions how bones combine. Resh Lakish says this applies only to bone, which is a handle, but hair is not. Rabbi Yochanan argues that even hair is a handle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Tosefta: two bones each with half an olive-bulk of flesh, whose ends enter a tent, render the tent impure.

sub.text: Yehuda ben Nakosa in the name of Rabbi Yaakov
sub.text_en: Yehuda ben Nakosa in the name of Rabbi Yaakov
sub.desc_en: Yehuda ben Nakosa questions how two bones can combine to form an olive-bulk.
Resh Lakish rules that the halakha applies only to a bone, which is a handle, but a hair is not a handle.
Rabbi Yochanan argues that even a hair constitutes a handle.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's objection to Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita where touching a hair opposite an olive's bulk of flesh on skin conveys impurity. He argues this is because the hair is a handle. The Gemara deflects, saying it is a protector, and questions whether there can be a protector atop a protector, answering that it is hollowed out.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan cites a baraita about touching a hair opposite an olive's bulk of flesh on skin conveying impurity, and argues that this is because the hair is a handle (יד).
The Gemara deflects, saying the hair is a protector (שומר), not a handle.
The Gemara questions whether there can be a protector atop a protector.
The Gemara answers that the hair is hollowed out (מחלחל), so it is not a protector atop a protector.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that if hair is a handle, tefillin could not be written properly due to gaps. The Gemara resolves by citing a Western tradition that a hole through which ink passes is not a hole. Alternatively, it explains that the hair is between hairs, like the space between rows of grain, which serves as a handle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yaakov objects that if hair penetrates the hide, then tefillin could not be written with perfect writing due to holes.
The Gemara answers that Rav Acha bar Yaakov overlooked the Western tradition that any hole over which ink passes is not considered a hole.
Alternatively, the Gemara explains that the entire mishna is about a handle, and the hair is among many hairs, like the awn among awns, which serves as a handle.
The Gemara cites where Rabbi Ila'i's statement was originally said: regarding an awn among awns that serves as a handle.

items.text: Alternative version and conclusion
items.text_en: Alternative version and conclusion
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the discussion is presented, concluding that hair is a protector, not a handle, because a single hair is useless. The Gemara again cites Rabbi Ila'i about the space between rows, and notes that some teach the discussion differently.

sub.desc_en: Introduces an alternative version of the preceding discussion.
Argues that it is reasonable to conclude the impurity is due to protection, not a handle, because a single hair has no function as a handle.
Answers that the mishna refers to a hair among many hairs, analogous to Rabbi Ila'i's ruling about an awn among many awns, where it can serve as a handle.
Cites the source of Rabbi Ila'i's statement about an awn among many awns, which can become impure and impart impurity but does not join together.
Notes that some teach the entire discussion in a different version.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that skin, gravy, and sediment combine to convey food impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that skin, gravy, and sediment combine to convey food impurity.

items.text: Dispute about a single hair as a shomer
items.text_en: Dispute about a single hair as a shomer
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan argue whether a single hair is considered a 'shomer' (guard) for impurity purposes. Reish Lakish limits the Mishnah to a bone, while Rabbi Yochanan includes even a hair. Rav Acha challenges Reish Lakish with the case of tefillin, and the Gemara resolves it with a principle from the West.

sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish limits the Mishnah's ruling to a bone, asserting that a single hair does not qualify as a shomer (guard) for impurity.
Rabbi Yochanan counters that even a single hair is considered a shomer.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's objection to Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish objects that there cannot be a shomer upon a shomer, as the hair would merely be a loose covering.
Rav Acha challenges Reish Lakish: if a hair is not a shomer, how can tefillin be written, since a hair would block complete writing?
The Gemara resolves the challenge by citing the Western principle that any hole through which ink passes is not considered a hole, so the hair does not impede writing.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about skin with meat
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about skin with meat
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan challenges Reish Lakish with a baraita: touching a hair opposite a piece of meat on skin conveys impurity. Reish Lakish deflects, saying it is due to being a 'yad' (handle), not a shomer. The Gemara explains the hair's function using Rabbi Ila'a's principle about the space between hairs.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) objects to ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) by citing a ברייתא (baraita): touching a hair opposite an olive-bulk of flesh on hide conveys impurity; he suggests this is because the hair is a שומר (protective layer), but ריש לקיש (Reish Lakish) deflects, saying it is due to being a יד (handle).

The גמרא (Gemara) asks: For what function is a single hair fit as a handle? It answers using רבי אילעא (Rabbi Ila'a)'s principle: the case involves a hair among many hairs, like an awn among many awns.
The גמרא (Gemara) cites the source of רבי אילעא (Rabbi Ila'a)'s statement: a משנה (mishna) about an awn on stalks, where he explains it refers to an awn among many awns.

items.text: Definition of 'rotav' (gravy)
items.text_en: Definition of 'rotav' (gravy)
items.desc_en: Rava defines 'rotav' as fat. Abaye objects that fat itself is food and should be impure, so the Gemara redefines it as congealed fat. The Gemara then discusses whether non-congealed fat combines, citing Reish Lakish's principle about brine on vegetables for Yom Kippur, distinguishing between 'yatovei da'ata' and 'itztrifei'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'rotav' (gravy) refers to, and Rava answers that it means fat.
Abaye objects that fat itself is food and should be impure, so the Gemara redefines 'rotav' as congealed fat.
The Gemara questions why the mishna specifies congealed fat, citing Reish Lakish's principle that brine on vegetables combines for Yom Kippur.
The Gemara distinguishes that regarding Yom Kippur, the reason is 'yatovei da'ata' (settling the mind), so any amount suffices.
The Gemara resolves that regarding impurity, the issue is 'itztrifei' (combining), so only congealed fat combines, not liquid.

items.text: Definition of 'keifa' (sediment)
items.text_en: Definition of 'keifa' (sediment)
items.desc_en: Rabba defines 'keifa' as 'firma' (crumbs). Abaye objects that it is itself food, so Rav Pappa redefines it as spices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'keifa' (sediment) means in the Mishnah.
Rabba defines 'keifa' as 'firma' (crumbs).
Abaye objects that crumbs are themselves food and would already be susceptible to טומאת אוכלין (food impurity), so they cannot be a separate category.
Rav Pappa redefines 'keifa' as spices (תבלין), which are not themselves food but serve as a flavoring agent.

items.text: Derivation of drinking from eating via 'nefesh'
items.text_en: Derivation of drinking from eating via 'nefesh'
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about congealing blood or melting fat, and questions how drinking is considered eating. Reish Lakish derives from the word 'nefesh' that drinking is included. This is applied to three cases: chelev, chametz, and neveilah of a kosher bird, with a distinction for neveilah heated by the sun.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how drinking melted chelev can be considered eating, since the Torah requires eating.
Reish Lakish answers that the word 'נפש' (soul) in the verse includes drinking as a form of eating.
A baraita is cited applying the same rule to chametz, and the Gemara questions how drinking melted chametz incurs karet.
Reish Lakish again answers that the word 'נפש' includes drinking.

sub.text: Supporting baraita about neveilah of a kosher bird
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita about neveilah of a kosher bird
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited applying the same rule to neveilah of a kosher bird, and the Gemara questions how drinking melted neveilah imparts impurity.
Reish Lakish answers that the word 'נפש' includes drinking, but the Gemara notes a distinction: neveilah heated by the sun is not included because it is putrid.

items.text: Why all three cases are necessary
items.text_en: Why all three cases are necessary
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Torah needed to write the derivation for chelev, chametz, and neveilah separately, as each has a unique characteristic that prevents learning from the others. It then analyzes possible combinations and addresses an objection about chelev of a wild animal being permitted for common use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by explaining why all three cases (chelev, chametz, neveilah) are necessary, as each has a unique characteristic that prevents deriving the others from it.
The Gemara asks why one case cannot be derived from the other two, and systematically rejects each possible combination due to shared features.

The Gemara objects that if chelev of a domesticated animal is permitted for the altar, neveilah is also permitted for the altar via bird sin-offering, and if chelev of a wild animal is permitted for common use, neveilah is also permitted for priests via bird sin-offering.
The Gemara answers that the objection is resolved because priests receive their portion from the altar, not as common property.

items.text: Why the Torah needed to forbid their brine, gravy, and sediment
items.text_en: Why the Torah needed to forbid their brine, gravy, and sediment
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah explicitly forbids the brine, gravy, and sediment of impure things, since it could be derived from the previous cases. It answers that without the explicit verse, one might apply the principle 'dayo lavo min hadin' and require a kezayit, so the verse teaches that any amount combines.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah needed to explicitly forbid the brine, gravy, and sediment of impure things, since these could be derived from the previous cases of forbidden fat, leaven, and neveila.

The Gemara answers that without the explicit verse, one might apply the principle of דיו לבא מן הדין (the derived case is limited to the source case) and require a kezayit, so the verse teaches that any amount combines.

items.text: Initial objection to deriving from sheratzim
items.text_en: Initial objection to deriving from sheratzim
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah didn't write the law for sheratzim, and then derive other cases from them. It answers that sheratzim are unique because their impurity is in a minimal quantity (mashehu), so they cannot serve as a source.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Torah didn't write the law for sheratzim and derive other cases from them.
The Gemara answers that sheratzim are unique because their impurity is in a minimal quantity (משהו), so they cannot serve as a source.

items.text: Derivation for tevel, new grain, etc.
items.text_en: Derivation for tevel, new grain, etc.
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing items (tevel, new grain, hekdesh, shevi'it, kilayim) whose liquids are like themselves. It asks where this is derived from, and rejects deriving from the previous cases because those involve prohibitions that come automatically (issur ha'ba me'elav).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing items (tevel, new grain, hekdesh, shevi'it, kilayim) whose liquids are like themselves, and asks for the derivation.
The Gemara objects that one cannot derive from the previous cases (sheratzim) because those involve prohibitions that come automatically (איסור הבא מאליו).
The Gemara asks: for cases where the prohibition does not come automatically, from where do we derive this rule?

items.text: Derivation from bikurim and its refutation
