It distinguishes Reishit HaGez from the gifts of the foreleg, jaw, and maw, noting that Reishit HaGez applies only to sheep and only in a large quantity. The Mishnah then defines a large quantity (Beit Shammai: two; Beit Hillel: five), discusses the amount to be given (five selas in Judea, ten in Galilee, clean and sufficient for a small garment), and addresses cases of dyeing, buying wool from a gentile or another Jew, and multiple types.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that Reishit HaGez applies in and outside the Land, with and without the Temple, to non-sacred animals but not to consecrated ones.
The Mishnah distinguishes Reishit HaGez from the gifts of the foreleg, jaw, and maw, noting that Reishit HaGez applies only to sheep and only in a large quantity.

sub.text: Mishnah — Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Mishnah — Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah defines a large quantity: Beit Shammai says two sheep, citing a verse; Beit Hillel says five, citing a different verse.

sub.text: Mishnah — Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas and Sages
sub.text_en: Mishnah — Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas and Sages
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah records a dispute: Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas requires five sheep each shearing a maneh and a half, while the Sages say five sheep shearing any amount suffice.
The Mishnah specifies the amount to give: five selas in Judea, ten in Galilee, clean and sufficient for a small garment, based on the verse 'תִּתֵּן לוֹ'.
The Mishnah rules that if one dyed the wool before giving it, he is exempt; if he whitened it without dyeing, he remains liable.
The Mishnah addresses cases of buying wool from a gentile or another Jew, and multiple types, concluding that each gives for himself.

items.text: Gemara's First Question: Why Not for Consecrated Animals?
items.text_en: Gemara's First Question: Why Not for Consecrated Animals?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Reishit HaGez does not apply to consecrated animals, and answers with a scriptural derivation: the verse says 'your flock' (צֹאנְךָ), excluding consecrated flock.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the law of Reishit HaGez does not apply to consecrated animals.
The Gemara answers with a scriptural derivation: the verse says 'your flock' (צֹאנְךָ), excluding consecrated flock.

items.text: Clarification: Temple Sacrifices vs. Temple Funds
items.text_en: Clarification: Temple Sacrifices vs. Temple Funds
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that even without the verse, consecrated animals would be exempt because they cannot be sheared (as per the verse 'do not shear your firstborn'). It resolves that this applies only to sacrifices for the altar, but here we are dealing with animals consecrated for Temple maintenance (Bedek HaBayit), which are permitted in shearing by Torah law.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: The reason is that the Merciful One wrote 'your sheep' — excluding consecrated animals. But what about Temple sacrifices? They are also excluded. However, the Gemara clarifies that this applies only to animals consecrated for the altar (which cannot be sheared), but here we are dealing with animals consecrated for Bedek HaBayit (Temple maintenance), which are permitted in shearing by Torah law.

items.text: Objection and Resolution: Rabbi Elazar's Statement and Rabbi Mani bar Pattish's Answer
items.text_en: Objection and Resolution: Rabbi Elazar's Statement and Rabbi Mani bar Pattish's Answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar said animals consecrated for Bedek HaBayit are forbidden in shearing by rabbinic law. The Gemara initially suggests that one might think to shear and give, but then notes the animal is consecrated. It proposes redeeming it, but that requires evaluation and appraisal. Rabbi Mani bar Pattish resolves that the case is where one consecrated his animal for Bedek HaBayit except for its shearings, so the verse 'your flock' excludes consecrated property.

items.text: Further Objection: Why Not Also for Altar Sacrifices?
items.text_en: Further Objection: Why Not Also for Altar Sacrifices?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the same reasoning (consecrating except for shearings) would not apply to altar sacrifices. It answers that the animal would become emaciated. For Bedek HaBayit, one can stipulate except for shearing and emaciation, but for altar sacrifices, even if one stipulates, the sanctity spreads to the whole animal, as per Rabbi Yossi's principle that dedicating a limb on which life depends consecrates the entire animal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the same reasoning applies, why not also exempt altar sacrifices (קדשי מזבח) from the gift?
The Gemara answers: for Bedek HaBayit (קדשי בדק הבית) the animal would also become emaciated (כחשי), so one can stipulate exemption from shearing and emaciation.
The Gemara objects: for altar sacrifices (קדשי מזבח) one could also stipulate exemption from shearing and emaciation.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution via Rabbi Yossi and Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: even with such a stipulation, the sanctity spreads to the entire animal, as per Rabbi Yossi's principle that dedicating a limb on which life depends consecrates the whole animal, and even Rabbi Meir agrees when the limb is life-dependent.

items.text: Rava's Alternative Resolution: Consecrating the Shearings Themselves
items.text_en: Rava's Alternative Resolution: Consecrating the Shearings Themselves
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different resolution: the case is where one consecrated the shearings themselves. One might think to shear, redeem, and give, but the verse 'the shearing of your flock you shall give to him' implies one who lacks only shearing and giving, excluding this case which requires shearing, redemption, and giving.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the difficulty by positing the case involves consecrating the shearings themselves, which requires shearing, redemption, and giving, thus excluded by the verse 'גֵּז צֹאנְךָ תִּתֶּן לוֹ' (the shearing of your flock you shall give to him).

items.text: Alternative Use of 'Your Flock': Excluding Partnership Animals
items.text_en: Alternative Use of 'Your Flock': Excluding Partnership Animals
items.desc_en: The Gemara now explains that the verse 'your flock' (צֹאנְךָ) is actually needed to exclude partnership animals, as taught in a baraita: Rabbi Il'ai exempts partners, while the Sages obligate them. The Sages use 'your flock' to exclude partnership with a gentile, while Rabbi Il'ai derives that from 'first of your grain' (רֵאשִׁית דְּגָנְךָ). The Sages argue that 'first' (רֵאשִׁית) interrupts the context, but Rabbi Il'ai says the vav connects it back.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the verse 'צֹאנְךָ' (your flock) comes to exclude, since it was already used to exclude consecrated animals.
The Gemara cites a baraita: partnership animals are obligated in ראשית הגז (first shearing), but Rabbi Il'ai exempts them.
The Gemara explains Rabbi Il'ai's reasoning: the verse 'צֹאנְךָ' excludes partnership animals.
The Gemara explains that the Sages use 'צֹאנְךָ' to exclude partnership with a gentile, and asks how Rabbi Il'ai derives that exclusion.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Il'ai's alternative derivation
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Il'ai's alternative derivation
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Il'ai derives the exclusion of partnership with a gentile from 'רֵאשִׁית דְּגָנְךָ' (first of your grain), and that the Sages argue that 'רֵאשִׁית' interrupts the context, while Rabbi Il'ai holds that the vav reconnects it.

items.text: Rabbis' position on the absence of vav and reishit
items.text_en: Rabbis' position on the absence of vav and reishit
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that the Torah did not write the vav or the word 'reishit' in the relevant verse, implying that partnership with a gentile is not exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Rabbis assert that the Torah did not write the vav or the word 'reishit' in the verse, implying that partnership with a gentile is not exempt from the gifts.

items.text: Rabbi Il'ai's distinction between sanctity of money and body
items.text_en: Rabbi Il'ai's distinction between sanctity of money and body
items.desc_en: Rabbi Il'ai explains that the two verses (one with vav and one with reishit) are separated because one deals with sanctity of money and the other with sanctity of the body, and then they are combined.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Il'ai explains that one verse (דגנך) refers to sanctity of money (תרומה) and the other (ראשית) to sanctity of the body (ראשית הגז), so the Torah separates them in the verses and then combines them with the conjunction vav.

items.text: Alternative explanation: partnership with a gentile in terumah
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: partnership with a gentile in terumah
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: the Rabbis actually obligate terumah in a partnership with a gentile, citing a baraita where Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute about a field partnership, but both agree that a gentile partnership is liable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation: the Rabbis actually obligate terumah in a partnership with a gentile.
A baraita is cited: Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dispute about a field partnership between an Israelite and a gentile regarding tithes.
The Gemara explains that the dispute is only about the principle of ברירה (retroactive clarification), but both agree that a gentile partnership is liable for terumah.

items.text: Another alternative: both derive from 'tzoncha'
items.text_en: Another alternative: both derive from 'tzoncha'
items.desc_en: Another explanation suggests that both Rabbi Il'ai and the Rabbis derive their positions from the word 'tzoncha' (your flock), but they differ on whether a gentile partnership is considered designated to the Jew.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative explanation that both Rabbi Il'ai and the Rabbis derive their positions from the word 'צֹּאנְךָ' (your flock).
The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning regarding a partnership with a gentile?
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Il'ai exempts a partnership with a gentile because the animal is not designated to the Jew, and similarly the Jew's portion is not designated to him.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis obligate the Jew in a partnership with a gentile because the gentile is not subject to the obligation, but the Jew is subject to the obligation.

items.text: Rava's statement: Rabbi Il'ai admits regarding terumah
items.text_en: Rava's statement: Rabbi Il'ai admits regarding terumah
items.desc_en: Rava states that Rabbi Il'ai concedes regarding terumah that partnership with a gentile is exempt, because the verse 'degancha' (your grain) excludes partnership, and the word 'terumoteichem' (your terumot) is written to include something else.

sub.desc_en: Rava opens by stating that Rabbi Il'ai concedes regarding terumah that partnership with a gentile is exempt, based on the verse 'דגנך' (your grain).
Rava explains that the Torah wrote 'תרומתיכם' (your terumot) to include something else, and 'דגנך' (your grain) serves to exclude partnership with a gentile.

items.text: Challah: derivation from 'reishit' and 'arisoteichem'
items.text_en: Challah: derivation from 'reishit' and 'arisoteichem'
items.desc_en: For challah, although the word 'reishit' appears and one might learn from 'reishit hagez' that partnership is exempt, the Torah writes 'arisoteichem' (your doughs) to teach that it applies to each individual's dough, not partnership. The Gemara questions why not learn from terumah instead, and concludes that 'arisoteichem' means 'your doughs' (each individually).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of challah: although the word 'reishit' appears and one might learn from 'reishit hagez' that partnership is exempt, the Torah writes 'arisoteichem' to teach that it applies individually.
The Gemara objects: if not for 'arisoteichem', one would learn from 'reishit hagez', but instead one should learn from terumah that partnership is exempt.
The Gemara resolves: indeed, one would learn from terumah, but 'arisoteichem' teaches that challah is given from each individual's dough, not partnership.

items.text: Pe'ah: derivation from 'sadecha' and 'kutzrechem'
items.text_en: Pe'ah: derivation from 'sadecha' and 'kutzrechem'
items.desc_en: For pe'ah, although the verse says 'sadecha' (your field) excluding partnership, the Torah writes 'uvkutzrechem et ketzir artzec'hem' (when you reap the harvest of your land) to include partnership, and 'sadecha' comes to exclude a gentile partnership.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that for pe'ah, although the verse says 'sadecha' (your field) excluding partnership, the Torah writes 'uvkutzrechem et ketzir artzec'hem' (when you reap the harvest of your land) to include partnership.
The Gemara resolves that 'sadecha' comes to exclude a gentile partnership.

items.text: Bekhorah: derivation from 'bekorcha' and 'uvchorot bekarc'hem'
items.text_en: Bekhorah: derivation from 'bekorcha' and 'uvchorot bekarc'hem'
items.desc_en: For bekhorah (firstborn animal), although the verse says 'bekorcha' (your firstborn) excluding partnership, the Torah writes 'uvchorot bekarc'hem' (and the firstborn of your cattle) to include partnership, and 'bekorcha' comes to exclude a gentile partnership.

sub.desc_en: The gemara notes that regarding bekhorah (firstborn animal), although the verse 'כל הבכור אשר יולד בבקרך ובצאנך' (every firstborn that is born in your cattle and your flock) implies only yours, not partnership, the Torah writes 'ובכורת בקרכם וצאנכם' (and the firstborn of your cattle and your flock) to include partnership.
The gemara resolves that the verse 'ובכורת בקרכם וצאנכם' includes partnership, while 'בקרך וצאנך' comes to exclude a gentile partnership.

items.text: Mezuzah: derivation from 'beitecha' and 'lema'an yirbu yemeichem'
items.text_en: Mezuzah: derivation from 'beitecha' and 'lema'an yirbu yemeichem'
items.desc_en: For mezuzah, although the verse says 'beitecha' (your house) excluding partnership, the Torah writes 'lema'an yirbu yemeichem' (that your days may be multiplied) to include partnership, and 'beitecha' comes to teach the law of Rabbah.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that for mezuzah, although the verse says 'בֵּיתֶךָ' (your house) excluding partnership, the Torah wrote 'לְמַעַן יִרְבּוּ יְמֵיכֶם' (that your days may be multiplied) to include partnership.
The gemara asks what then is the purpose of the word 'בֵּיתֶךָ' (your house) if it does not exclude partnership.
The gemara answers that 'בֵּיתֶךָ' comes to teach the law of Rabbah, as Rabbah said.

items.text: Opening rule: Ma'aser exempts partnership
items.text_en: Opening rule: Ma'aser exempts partnership
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that ma'aser (tithe) is exempt for partnership property, deriving this from the plural form 'ma'asroteichem' despite the singular 'ma'asar degancha' which excludes a gentile partner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that ma'aser (tithe) is exempt for partnership property, deriving this from the plural form 'ma'asroteichem' despite the singular 'ma'asar degancha' which excludes a gentile partner.

items.text: Matnot: Derivation and Rava's ruling
items.text_en: Matnot: Derivation and Rava's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests learning matnot (priestly gifts) from reishit hagez via a gezerah shavah of 'netinah', but then notes the verse 'me'et zovchei hazavach' teaches a different law, as Rava says the butcher has the right to the gifts.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of priestly gifts (מתנות), noting that the Torah wrote 'ונתן' (and he shall give), implying individual ownership.
The Gemara proposes learning from reishit hagez (ראשית הגז) via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) of 'נתינה' (giving), that partnership exempts from gifts.
The Gemara objects that the verse 'מאת זובחי הזבח' (from the slaughterers of the sacrifice) teaches a different law, undermining the analogy.
The Gemara explains that without the verse, one might have learned from reishit hagez, but instead we should learn from תרומה (terumah).
Rava resolves that the verse 'מאת זובחי הזבח' teaches that the butcher has the right to the gifts, not the owner.

items.text: Bikkurim: Excluding partnership and outside Israel
items.text_en: Bikkurim: Excluding partnership and outside Israel
items.desc_en: Bikkurim (first fruits) are exempt for partnership, derived from 'bikkurei chol asher be'artzam', while 'artzecha' excludes produce from outside the Land of Israel.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that regarding ביכורים (first fruits), even though the verse says 'your land', it excludes partnership produce.
The gemara explains that the verse 'ביכורי כל אשר בארצם' teaches partnership inclusion, while 'ארצך' comes to exclude produce from outside the Land of Israel.

items.text: Tzitzit: Exempting borrowed garments
items.text_en: Tzitzit: Exempting borrowed garments
items.desc_en: Tzitzit is exempt for partnership, but 'kesutcha' teaches that a borrowed tallit is exempt for thirty days, as per Rav Yehudah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that regarding tzitzit, although the verse says 'your garment' (כְּסוּתְךָ), implying only your own garment is obligated, partnership garments are exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the word 'your garment' (כְּסוּתְךָ) is needed for Rav Yehudah's ruling that a borrowed tallit is exempt from tzitzit for thirty days.

items.text: Ma'akeh: Exempting synagogues and study halls
items.text_en: Ma'akeh: Exempting synagogues and study halls
items.desc_en: Ma'akeh (parapet) is exempt for partnership, but 'gagecha' excludes synagogues and study halls from the obligation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that regarding ma'akeh (parapet), although the verse says 'לגגך' (your roof), implying only your own roof, partnership property is excluded.

The Gemara resolves that the verse 'כי יפול הנופל ממנו' (for the fallen may fall from it) includes partnership property, while 'גגך' (your roof) excludes synagogues and study halls from the obligation.

items.text: Rav Beivai and Rav Chanina: Challenging the rules with bekhorah and matnot
items.text_en: Rav Beivai and Rav Chanina: Challenging the rules with bekhorah and matnot
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye cites a beraita where partnership animals are liable for bekhorah, but Rabbi Il'ai exempts them. Rav Chanina from Sura cites a similar dispute for matnot, where Rabbi Il'ai exempts via gezerah shavah from reishit hagez.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye challenges the general rules by citing a beraita where partnership animals are liable for bekhorah (firstborn), but Rabbi Il'ai exempts them.

The gemara asks for Rabbi Il'ai's reasoning, and explains that he derives from the verse 'בקרך וצאנך' (your ox and your sheep) that the obligation applies only to an individual's animal, not a partnership, despite the plural form 'בקרכם וצאנכם' (your oxen and your sheep) referring to all Israel.

Rav Chanina from Sura similarly challenges the rules by citing a beraita where partnership animals are liable for matnot (priestly gifts), but Rabbi Il'ai exempts them via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from reishit hagez (first shearing).

items.text: Deriving matnot from terumah: Rabbi Il'ai's position and limitations
items.text_en: Deriving matnot from terumah: Rabbi Il'ai's position and limitations
items.desc_en: The Gemara deduces that Rabbi Il'ai exempts matnot from partnership, learning from terumah via gezerah shavah. This leads to a discussion of whether matnot applies only in Israel, with Rabbi Yosei from Neharde'a confirming this. Abaye questions whether reishit hagez shares other terumah laws (tovel, death/extra fifth, order of separation, new on old), and the Gemara resolves each with scriptural derivations, noting a dispute between Rabbi Il'ai and the Rabbis regarding accumulation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rabbi Il'ai would need a separate derivation for matnot from reishit hagez if he already holds that partnership is liable for terumah, since a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from terumah would suffice.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Il'ai must also exempt partnership from terumah, resolving the contradiction.
The Gemara asks whether matnot, like terumah, applies only in Israel and not outside the land.
Rabbi Yosei from Neharde'a confirms that Rabbi Il'ai indeed limits matnot and reishit hagez to the land of Israel, citing a baraita.
Rava explains that Rabbi Il'ai derives the territorial limitation of reishit hagez from terumah via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'נתינה' (giving).
Abaye questions whether reishit hagez, like terumah, renders the remaining produce forbidden (טובלת) until separated.

Rava answers that the verse 'וראשית גז צאנך תתן לו' (and the first of the shearings of your flock you shall give to him) indicates that only the first portion is given, not that it renders the rest forbidden.
Abaye asks whether reishit hagez, like terumah, carries the penalties of death (for a non-priest who eats it intentionally) and an extra fifth (for unintentional consumption).
The Gemara answers that the verses 'ומתו בו' (and they shall die in it) and 'ויסף עליו' (and he shall add a fifth to it) apply only to terumah, not to reishit hagez.
Abaye asks whether reishit hagez, like terumah, must be separated first, with maaser rishon and maaser sheni following after it.
The Gemara answers that the word 'ראשית' (first) in the verse indicates that only the first portion is given, not that it precedes other tithes.
Abaye asks whether reishit hagez, like terumah, cannot be separated from new wool to exempt old wool.
The Gemara answers affirmatively that the same rule applies to reishit hagez.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that wool from two or three years does not combine to reach the minimum for reishit hagez, implying that accumulation is not permitted.
The Gemara cites another baraita that explicitly states that wool from different years does not combine, contradicting the idea that accumulation is permitted.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita that permits accumulation to Rabbi Il'ai and the one that prohibits it to the Rabbis.

items.text: גדל בחיוב וגדל בפטור בראשית הגז
items.text_en: Growing in obligation vs. exemption: Reishit hagez and terumah parallel
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares reishit hagez to terumah regarding growth in obligation: if grown in a liable state, it is liable; if in an exempt state, exempt. This is supported by a beraita about a field in Syria, and a mishnah about buying a gentile's flock.
items.desc: אביי מקשה: כמו בתרומה, שגידול תחת גוי פוטר, כך בראשית הגז צאן גוי פטורה. רבה משיב מהמשנה: הלוקח גז צאן גוי פטור, אבל צאנו לגזוז חייב, כלומר אם קנה את הצאן עצמה לפני הגיזה, חייב. המשנה סותרת את דברי אביי.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes a parallel: just as with תרומה (priestly portion), growth in a liable state makes it liable and in an exempt state exempt, so too with ראשית הגז (first shearing).
sub.desc: אביי מקשה: כמו בתרומה שגידול תחת גוי פוטר, כך בראשית הגז צאן גוי פטורה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about an Israelite who buys a field in Syria from a gentile, where Rabbi Akiva and the Sages dispute liability for תרומה based on when the field was acquired relative to its growth stage.
sub.desc: מביא ברייתא המוכיחה שבתרומה גידול תחת גוי פוטר, ומראה את מחלוקת רבי עקיבא וחכמים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the parallel by citing a mishnah: one who buys the shearing of a gentile's flock is exempt from ראשית הגז, but if the flock is his own to shear, he is liable — confirming the principle of growth in obligation.
sub.desc: רבא דוחה את הקושיה מהמשנה: הלוקח גז צאן גוי פטור, אבל צאנו לגזוז חייב, כלומר קניית הצאן עצמה מחייבת.

items.text: Rejection of Rabbi Il'ai's view
items.text_en: Rejection of Rabbi Il'ai's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Il'ai, who holds that ראשית הגז is like תרומה in all respects.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Il'ai.

items.text: Comparison to תרומה: giving from one type to another
items.text_en: Comparison to תרומה: giving from one type to another
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether, like תרומה, one may not give ראשית הגז from one type to another. It cites a baraita about two types of figs and wheat where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree about תרומה, and applies it to ראשית הגז.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, just as with תרומה (priestly portion) one may not separate from one type for another, so too with ראשית הגז (first sheared wool) one may not separate from one type of sheep for another.
The Gemara cites a baraita about two types of figs and wheat, where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree regarding תרומה, and applies the principle to ראשית הגז.

items.text: דיון במשנת 'שני מינים' ועצה טובה
items.text_en: Resolution: good advice, not a law
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the comparison, explaining that the Mishnah's case of two types (black and white) is merely good advice to give from both, not a legal requirement. The same applies to the case of males and females.
items.desc: רבא מאשר את הדין ומביא ראיה מהמשנה על שני מיני צאן. הגמרא מקשה מסיפא של המשנה על זכרים ונקבות, ומתרצת שהמשנה נותנת עצה טובה להפריש משני המינים כדי לתת לכהן מהרך ומהקשה.

sub.desc_en: Rava affirms the halakha and cites the Mishnah's case of two types (gray and white) as support that one may not separate from one type on behalf of another.
sub.desc: רבא מאשר את הדין ומביא ראיה מהמשנה על שני מיני צאן (שחופות ולבנות) שכל אחד נותן לעצמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the latter clause (males vs. females) cannot be explained as two types, so the same reasoning should apply to the first clause.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מסיפא של המשנה על זכרים ונקבות, שגם שם נאמר 'זה נותן לעצמו וזה נותן לעצמו', והרי אין שם שני מינים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that both cases in the Mishnah are merely good advice to give from both types, not a legal requirement.
sub.desc: הגמרא מתרצת שהמשנה נותנת עצה טובה להפריש משני המינים כדי לתת לכהן מהרך ומהקשה.

items.text: Reiteration of Rabbi Il'ai's exclusion
items.text_en: Reiteration of Rabbi Il'ai's exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara reaffirms that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Il'ai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reaffirms that the Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Il'ai.

items.text: Comparison to תרומה: requirement of recognizable remainder
items.text_en: Comparison to תרומה: requirement of recognizable remainder
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether, like תרומה, ראשית הגז requires that the remainder be recognizable. It cites a contradiction between two baraitot about dedicating all one's wool, and resolves that one follows Rabbi Il'ai and the other follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, like תרומה (priestly portion), ראשית הגז (first shearing) requires that the remainder be recognizable.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita: one who dedicates all his grain as תרומה or all his dough as חלה says nothing, but one who says 'all my shearing is ראשית' his words stand.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the two baraitot by attributing one to Rabbi Il'ai and the other to the Rabbis.

items.text: מנהג העולם כשלושה זקנים
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: the world follows three elders
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that the current practice follows three elders: Rabbi Il'ai regarding ראשית הגז (only in the Land), Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira regarding words of Torah (not susceptible to impurity), and Rabbi Yoshiya regarding כלאים (requires a handful of seed).
items.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק קובע שהמנהג המקובל הוא להקל כדעת שלושה זקנים: רבי אלעאי בראשית הגז (נוהג רק בארץ), רבי יהודה בן בתירא בדברי תורה (אינם מקבלים טומאה), ורבי יאשיה בכלאיים (חיוב רק בזריעה משולשת בבת אחת).

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak opens by stating that the world follows three elders, beginning with Rabbi Il'ai regarding ראשית הגז (the first shearing).
sub.desc: רב נחמן בר יצחק פותח ואומר שהמנהג המקובל הוא כדעת שלושה זקנים, ומתחיל בדעת רבי אלעאי בראשית הגז.

sub.text_en: Supporting baraita for Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira rules that words of Torah are not susceptible to impurity.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את דעת רבי יהודה בן בתירא שאין דברי תורה מקבלים טומאה, כחלק מהמנהג המקובל.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak cites a baraita where Rabbi Yoshiya rules that one is liable for כלאים (mixed seeds) only when sowing wheat, barley, and a grape seed with a single hand-throw.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה את דעת רבי יאשיה בכלאיים, שאין חיוב אלא בזריעה משולשת בבת אחת, כחלק מהמנהג המקובל.

items.text: Question: why not list חומר in ראשית הגז regarding טריפה?
items.text_en: Question: why not list חומר in ראשית הגז regarding טריפה?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not list a stringency of ראשית הגז over the other gifts, namely that it applies to טריפה. Ravina answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who exempts טריפה from ראשית הגז via a גזירה שוה of 'נתינה' from מתנות.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah did not list a stringency of ראשית הגז over the other gifts, namely that it applies to טריפה, unlike the other gifts.
Ravina answers that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Shimon, who exempts טריפה from ראשית הגז via a גזירה שוה of 'נתינה' from מתנות.

items.text: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.text_en: Analysis of Rabbi Shimon's derivation
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's גזירה שוה from מתנות, suggesting it should be from תרומה (only in the Land). It then proposes a different derivation from מעשר via 'צאן' 'צאן', and defends it against a possible derivation from בכור. The discussion includes various arguments about which comparison is more fitting.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Shimon learns a גזירה שוה from מתנות, he should instead learn from תרומה, which would limit the law to the Land of Israel, contradicting the Mishnah.
The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Shimon actually learns a גזירה שוה from מעשר via 'צאן' 'צאן', which excludes טריפה.
The Gemara cites the verse that excludes a טריפה from מעשר because it cannot pass under the rod.
The Gemara objects that one could instead learn from בכור, which includes even a טריפה.
The Gemara defends the derivation from מעשר because it shares the features of males and being subject to impurity.
The Gemara adds that מעשר applies to multiple animals from the womb, unlike בכור.
The Gemara adds that מעשר applies to humans, is simple (non-sacred), and was given before the giving of the Torah.
The Gemara counters that one could instead learn from בכור, which shares the features of being an orphan and being purchased.
The Gemara lists additional features of בכור (partnership, giving, before a priest) without resolving the comparison.

items.text: Transition from previous topic
items.text_en: Transition from previous topic
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a discrepancy in the number of cases between the laws of first-shearing and the previous topic, and explains that a simple case is preferred over a complex one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the previous topic listed fewer cases than the laws of first-shearing, noting that the former had more cases.
The Gemara answers that a simple case is preferred over a complex one, so the Mishnah chose the simpler example.

items.text: Derivation that first-shearing applies only to sheep
items.text_en: Derivation that first-shearing applies only to sheep
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda derives from a verbal analogy (גיזה גיזה) between the verse for first-shearing and the verse about Jacob's sheep that it applies only to sheep (כבשים).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that first-shearing applies only to sheep and asks for the scriptural source.
Rav Chisda derives from a verbal analogy (גיזה גיזה) between the verse for first-shearing and the verse about Jacob's sheep that it applies only to sheep (כבשים).

items.text: Rejection of alternative derivation from firstborn
items.text_en: Rejection of alternative derivation from firstborn
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers deriving the law from the firstborn animal, but rejects it because the verse there teaches a different lesson about not working or shearing the firstborn.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes deriving the law of first shearing from the firstborn animal via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) on the word 'גיזה'.
The Gemara rejects the derivation because the verse about the firstborn teaches a different lesson: that the prohibitions of working and shearing apply to both ox and sheep interchangeably.

items.text: Exclusion of wool used for sackcloth and goat hair
items.text_en: Exclusion of wool used for sackcloth and goat hair
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verse 'תתן לו' excludes wool given for sackcloth, and then addresses whether goat hair is obligated, concluding that it is not because it is not normal shearing, citing Rabbi Yose's principle and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's derivation.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara derives from the verse 'תתן לו' that the gift of ראשית הגז excludes wool given for sackcloth.
The Gemara asks whether goat hair (נוצה של עיזים) should be obligated in ראשית הגז.
The Gemara answers that goat hair is not obligated because it is not considered normal shearing (גיזה).
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yose, who holds that only normal practice is considered, would still obligate goat hair because it is a normal practice for goats.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi resolves that goat hair is exempt because, like the requirement for a servant to be fit for service, the wool must be fit for normal service (שירות), which goat hair is not.

items.text: Purpose of the verbal analogy
items.text_en: Purpose of the verbal analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the verbal analogy (גיזה גיזה) is used to exclude sheep with hard wool, as taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose the verbal analogy (גיזה גיזה) serves, given that the exclusion of goats is already derived from the requirement of serviceability.
The Gemara answers that the verbal analogy comes to exclude sheep with hard wool from the obligation of ראשית הגז (first shearing), as taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.text: Contradiction in baraitot about shearing and washing
items.text_en: Contradiction in baraitot about shearing and washing
items.desc_en: Two baraitot appear to contradict each other regarding whether washing sheep after shearing obligates first-shearing; the Gemara resolves that one follows the Rabbis and the other follows Rabbi Yose, and clarifies Rabbi Yose's position on gleaning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a contradiction between two baraitot: one exempts from first-shearing when shearing goats and washing sheep, while the other exempts for goats but obligates for washing sheep.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita follows the Rabbis and the other follows Rabbi Yose, who holds that only actions directly analogous to harvesting obligate.

A baraita is cited showing that Rabbi Yose limits gleaning (לקט) to what comes from harvesting, not from plucking, establishing his principle that only actions resembling the primary process obligate.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yose's position seems identical to the Tanna Kamma's, questioning the redundancy.
The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabbi Yose's, and the Tanna Kamma's statement is actually a continuation of Rabbi Yose's own teaching, clarifying his principle.

items.text: Rabbi Yose's principle about normal practice
items.text_en: Rabbi Yose's principle about normal practice
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava and Ravina bring proofs that Rabbi Yose agrees that normal practice (אורחיה) is considered, citing examples from gleaning and pe'ah.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi whether Rabbi Yose agrees that normal practice (אורחיה) is considered, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yose derives gleaning laws from the root 'קציר' (harvest).
The baraita continues, showing Rabbi Yose's method of expanding the gleaning law to include uprooting and plucking by using the extended forms of the root 'קצר'.
Ravina adds a second proof from a Mishnah about onion beds, where Rabbi Yose requires pe'ah from each bed separately (since each is a normal planting), while the Sages allow one pe'ah for all.

items.text: Discussion on the number of sheep required for first-shearing
items.text_en: Discussion on the number of sheep required for first-shearing
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the minimum number of sheep for first-shearing, citing various opinions including Rav Kahana, Rav Ashi, and the school of Rabbi Yishmael, and concludes with a statement about the authority of Rabbi's teachings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how many sheep constitute a 'large number' for first-shearing, noting that for Beit Shammai two sheep suffice, but questions the reasoning of Beit Hillel.
Rav Kahana answers that the verse uses 'עֲשׂוּיוֹת' (made) to indicate sheep that perform two commandments: first-shearing and priestly gifts.
The Gemara objects that one could equally say the two commandments are firstborn and gifts.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that a firstborn animal is already obligated in one commandment, so it cannot count as a second.
Rav Ashi explains that 'עֲשׂוּיוֹת' means the sheep make their owners arise to perform the commandment.

sub.text: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Baraita of the school of Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael in the name of Rabbi Yosei states that the minimum is four sheep, citing the verse 'וְאַרְבַּע צֹאן תַּחַת הַשֶּׂה' (and four sheep for the lamb).
Rabbi declares that even if the words of the Sages were Torah and his own words were tradition, one would still follow his words, and certainly when their words are tradition and his are Torah.
The Gemara objects by citing Mar's principle that a third decisive opinion does not resolve a dispute.

items.text: Opening dispute on the measure of 'any amount'
items.text_en: Opening dispute on the measure of 'any amount'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the law is based on tradition from Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The Mishnah cites Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas, and the Gemara asks how much 'any amount' is. Rav says a maneh and a half, provided they are five selas; Shmuel says sixty and gives one sela to the priest. Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan as saying six, five for the priest and one for himself; Ulla cites Rabbi Elazar as saying 'any amount' was taught.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that the law is based on a tradition from Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi.
The Gemara asks how much 'any amount' is in the Mishnah's ruling of Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas.
Rav says the amount is a maneh and a half (five selas), provided they are five selas; Shmuel says sixty and gives one sela to the priest.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah cites Rabbi Yochanan as saying the amount is six selas, five for the priest and one for himself.
Ulla cites Rabbi Elazar as saying that 'any amount' was taught, implying no fixed measure.

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah with the opinions
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah with the opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah states the priest receives five selas, which is consistent with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan but difficult for Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar. It then challenges that even for Rav it is difficult, since Rav and Shmuel both said first shearing is in sixty. The Gemara resolves that they were discussing a case where a Jew has many fleeces and wants to give them to a priest, and we tell him not to reduce each one from five selas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah states the priest receives five selas, which is consistent with Rav and Rabbi Yochanan but difficult for Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar.
The Gemara objects that even for Rav it is difficult, since Rav and Shmuel both said first shearing is in sixty.
The Gemara resolves that Rav and Shmuel were discussing a case where a Jew has many fleeces and wants to give them to a priest, and we tell him not to reduce each one from five selas.

items.text: The general rule of sixty for terumah and peah
items.text_en: The general rule of sixty for terumah and peah
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel both state that first shearing, terumah, and peah are each in sixty. The Gemara questions this regarding terumah, since the Mishnah says a generous eye gives one in forty. It distinguishes between biblical and rabbinic measures: biblically it is sixty, rabbinically forty. For peah, the Mishnah says it has no measure, but the Gemara explains that biblically it has no measure, rabbinically it is sixty. It further clarifies that the rabbinic measure of sixty for peah applies only outside the Land of Israel.

sub.text: Stam (Gemara's citation of Rav and Shmuel)
sub.text_en: Stam (Gemara's citation of Rav and Shmuel)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement that Rav and Shmuel both rule that first shearing, terumah, and peah are each given in a ratio of one in sixty.
The Gemara questions the ruling for terumah, citing the Mishnah that a generous eye gives one in forty.
The Gemara distinguishes: biblically the measure is sixty, rabbinically it is forty.
The Gemara objects that Shmuel himself said a single grain of wheat exempts an entire heap, implying a biblical measure of one in many, not sixty.
The Gemara resolves: biblically the measure follows Shmuel's lenient view, rabbinically for biblical terumah it is one in forty, and rabbinically for rabbinic terumah it is one in sixty.
The Gemara questions the ruling for peah, citing the Mishnah that peah has no fixed measure.
The Gemara answers: biblically peah has no measure, rabbinically it is one in sixty.
The Gemara asks what new information is conveyed, since the Mishnah already states that peah has no measure and one may not reduce it below sixty.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah's rule applies in the Land of Israel, while Rav and Shmuel's statement applies outside the Land of Israel.

items.text: Anecdote about Isi bar Hini and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Anecdote about Isi bar Hini and Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: When Isi bar Hini came up from Babylonia, he found Rabbi Yochanan teaching his son the word 'רחלים' (ewes) and corrected him to 'רחלות'. Rabbi Yochanan defended it as biblical language. Isi then asked who is the head of the academy in Babylonia, and Rabbi Yochanan said 'Abba Arikha'. Isi rebuked him for calling Rav by that name, recalling how Rav sat before Rabbi and sparks flew between them.

sub.desc_en: When Isi bar Hini came up from Babylonia, he found Rabbi Yochanan teaching his son the word 'רחלים' (ewes) and corrected him to 'רחלות'; Rabbi Yochanan defended it as biblical language, and Isi distinguished between biblical and rabbinic language.

Isi asked who is the head of the academy in Babylonia; Rabbi Yochanan answered 'Abba Arikha', and Isi rebuked him for calling Rav by that name, recalling how Rav sat before Rabbi with sparks flying between them.

items.text: Final resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Final resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: Isi asked Rabbi Yochanan about the measure for first shearing, and Rabbi Yochanan said sixty. Isi objected that we learned 'any amount'. Rabbi Yochanan replied that then what difference is there between him and Isi? When Rav Dimi came, he reported that Rav said sixty and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yannai said six. Abaye noted that Rav Dimi gave one and took one. The Gemara reconciles Rabbi Yochanan's statements as his own vs. his teacher's, and Rav's statements as referring to a maneh of forty selas.

sub.desc_en: Isi bar Hini asks Rabbi Yochanan what the measure for first shearing (ראשית הגז) is.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the measure is sixty (one part in sixty).
Isi objects that the Mishnah teaches 'any amount' (כל שהן), implying no fixed measure.
Rabbi Yochanan retorts that if there is no fixed measure, then what difference is there between him and Isi (i.e., why ask at all)?
When Rav Dimi came from Eretz Yisrael, he reported that Rav said sixty and Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yannai said six.
Abaye objects to Rav Dimi that his report gives one resolution (for Rav) but creates a new difficulty (for Rabbi Yochanan's inconsistency).
The Gemara resolves Rabbi Yochanan's apparent inconsistency: his own opinion is sixty (as he told Isi), while his statement of six is from his teacher Rabbi Yannai.
The Gemara objects that Rav's own statements are inconsistent: here he says sixty, but earlier (seg 1) he said a maneh and a half (מנה ופרס).

The Gemara resolves Rav's inconsistency by explaining that the 'maneh' he mentioned refers to a maneh of forty selas (i.e., a smaller maneh), so the total is sixty selas, consistent with his other statement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference and measurement of the belt
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference and measurement of the belt
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing a baraita about the measurement of a new wineskin and the belt (avnet) of the priest, linking it to the Mishnah's discussion of the priestly garments. It establishes the standard of a maneh of forty selas.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that establishes a maneh (מנה) of forty selas (סלעים) as the standard measurement for a new wineskin (חמת) that is still pure.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on the belt measurement
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion on the belt measurement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov gives a specific measurement for the belt: one-fourth of a maneh of forty selas, comparing it to the width of a loom's shuttle.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov gives a specific measurement for the belt: one-fourth of a maneh of forty selas, comparing it to the width of a loom's shuttle.

items.text: Clarification of the priest's whitening process
items.text_en: Clarification of the priest's whitening process
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the priest does not give the fleece to the owner whitened; rather, the priest whitens it and it stands at five selas.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna clarifies that the priest does not give the fleece whitened to the owner; rather, the priest whitens it and it stands at five selas.

items.text: Derivation of the belt from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the belt from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi derives from the verse 'to stand to serve' that the garment must be suitable for service, identifying it as the avnet (belt). The Gemara rejects the possibility of the me'il (robe) because one cannot grasp the larger option when a smaller one suffices.

items.text: Rejection of the wool cap and requirement of equality for Aaron and his sons
items.text_en: Rejection of the wool cap and requirement of equality for Aaron and his sons
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the wool cap (kipah shel tzemer) but rejects it because the verse requires a garment common to Aaron and his sons, and the cap was only for the High Priest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the garment in question might be the wool cap (כִּיפָּה שֶׁל צֶמֶר) worn by the High Priest, citing a baraita that describes it.
The Gemara rejects the proposal, citing the verse 'הוּא וּבָנָיו' (he and his sons), which requires a garment common to both Aaron and his sons, whereas the wool cap was exclusive to the High Priest.

items.text: Debate about the identity of the High Priest's belt
items.text_en: Debate about the identity of the High Priest's belt
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether the belt of the High Priest is the same as that of an ordinary priest. For the opinion that they are different, the derivation works; for the opinion that they are the same, the belt is still considered a common garment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the belt (אבנט) is not common to both priests, and for the opinion that the High Priest's belt is different from the ordinary priest's belt, the derivation works well.

The Gemara objects: for the opinion that the High Priest's belt is the same as the ordinary priest's belt, what can be said? The belt is still called a belt in the world (i.e., it is a common garment).

items.text: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya on shearing and selling
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Chisda and Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya on shearing and selling
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda holds that if one shears and sells the first shearing, he is liable for reishit ha-gez; Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya holds he is exempt because at the time of shearing, the animal was not yet his flock.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase 'he did not manage to give it' as the starting point for the dispute.
The gemara introduces a dispute: if one shears and sells the first shearing, Rav Chisda holds he is liable for reishit ha-gez, while Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya holds he is exempt.
Rav Chisda explains his position: the shearer is liable because he performed the shearing.
Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya explains his position: at the time the shearing reaches the required quantity, the animal is no longer 'your flock' because it was sold, so the obligation does not apply.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya from a Mishnah that obligates one who buys a gentile's fleece, implying liability follows the shearer. Rav Chisda explains that the case is where the gentile transferred ownership for thirty days.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya from a Mishnah that obligates one who buys a gentile's fleece, implying liability follows the shearer, not the owner at shearing time.
Rav Chisda explains the Mishnah in accordance with Rabbi Natan bar Hoshaya: the case is where the gentile transferred ownership of the fleece to the buyer for thirty days before shearing.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna who follows the seller when there is a remainder
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna who follows the seller when there is a remainder
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna that holds that when there is a remainder with the seller, we follow the seller. Rav Chisda identifies it as Rabbi Yehuda, citing a Mishnah about pe'ah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is the Tanna who holds that when there is a remainder with the seller, we follow the seller.
Rav Chisda identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda, citing a Mishnah about selling stalks of trees in a field.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that if the field owner left a remainder, he gives pe'ah for the entire field, showing that the seller is followed when there is a remainder.

items.text: Rava's objection and distinction between pe'ah and reishit ha-gez
items.text_en: Rava's objection and distinction between pe'ah and reishit ha-gez
items.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Yehuda's ruling applies only when the owner began to harvest, but in shearing, beginning to shear does not obligate the entire flock. Thus, the analogy fails.

sub.desc_en: Rava objects that Rabbi Yehuda himself requires the owner to have begun harvesting for the rule to apply.
Rava rejects the analogy: in pe'ah, beginning to harvest obligates the entire field, but in shearing, beginning to shear does not obligate the entire flock.

items.text: Rava's alternative identification of the Tanna
items.text_en: Rava's alternative identification of the Tanna
items.desc_en: Rava identifies the Tanna as the one from the Mishnah about selling the innards of a cow, where the priestly gifts are given to the priest and not deducted from the price, unless sold by weight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yehuda says: when? When the field owner did not leave, but if the field owner left — he gives peah on the whole.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's Gemara on מתנות כהונה
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous Mishnah's Gemara on מתנות כהונה
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if the seller retained some animals, he is liable for the priestly gifts because the buyer can claim the gift is still with him; if the seller did not retain any, the buyer is liable because the seller can claim he did not sell the gift.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that priestly gifts are not sold, so the seller is liable if he retained animals, and the buyer is liable if he did not.

items.text: Return to the Mishnah: הדרן עלך ראשית הגז
items.text_en: Return to the Mishnah: הדרן עלך ראשית הגז
items.desc_en: The standard formula הדרן עלך marks the end of the chapter on ראשית הגז (first shearing) and the transition to the next chapter on שילוח הקן.

sub.desc_en: The standard formula הדרן עלך marks the end of the chapter on ראשית הגז (first shearing) and the transition to the next chapter on שילוח הקן.

items.text: Mishnah: שילוח הקן and its scope
items.text_en: Mishnah: שילוח הקן and its scope
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that שילוח הקן applies in the Land and outside, whether the Temple stands or not, to non-sacred birds but not to sacred ones. It compares the stringency of כיסוי הדם, which applies to both wild and domestic animals and birds, and to both prepared and unprepared nests. It then defines 'unprepared' as birds like geese and chickens that nested in an orchard, but if they nested in a house, or in the case of doves of the Herodion, one is exempt. A non-kosher bird is exempt; a non-kosher bird sitting on kosher eggs or vice versa is exempt; and Rabbi Eliezer obligates sending away a male קורא (a type of bird), while the Sages exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that שילוח הקן (sending away the mother bird) applies universally, in the Land and outside, whether the Temple stands or not, to non-sacred birds but not to sacred ones, and compares it to כיסוי הדם (covering the blood).
The Mishnah defines 'unprepared' nests, lists exemptions for non-kosher birds and mixed eggs, and records the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a male קורא (a type of bird).

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's phrasing
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah's phrasing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Meisha disagree: one says that wherever the Mishnah says 'in the Land and outside the Land' it is unnecessary, except for ראשית הגז, to exclude Rabbi Ilai who said it applies only in the Land. The other says that wherever it says 'whether the Temple stands or not' it is unnecessary, except for 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition of slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day), because one might have thought it only applies when the Temple stands. Both agree that wherever it says 'in non-sacred and sacred' it is necessary, except for גיד הנשה (the sciatic nerve), which is obvious because sanctification removes its prohibition. The Gemara questions this, noting that it was established regarding the offspring of sacred animals, and explains that the Tanna included unnecessary clauses alongside necessary ones.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Meisha (first opinion)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Meisha (first opinion)
sub.desc_en: One of the two sages states that wherever the Mishnah says 'in the Land and outside the Land' it is unnecessary, except for ראשית הגז (the first shearing), to exclude Rabbi Ilai who held it applies only in the Land.

sub.text: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Meisha (second opinion)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Meisha (second opinion)
sub.desc_en: The other sage states that wherever it says 'whether the Temple stands or not' it is unnecessary, except for 'אותו ואת בנו' (the prohibition of slaughtering a parent and its offspring on the same day), because one might have thought it only applies when the Temple stands.
Both agree that wherever it says 'in non-sacred and sacred' it is necessary, except for גיד הנשה (the sciatic nerve), which is obvious because sanctification removes its prohibition.
The Gemara objects: was it not established that the case of גיד הנשה (the sciatic nerve) in sacred animals is about the offspring of sacred animals, which is not obvious?
The Gemara resolves: the Tanna included unnecessary clauses alongside necessary ones, so the inclusion of גיד הנשה (the sciatic nerve) is not a problem.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation that sacred birds are exempt from שילוח
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation that sacred birds are exempt from שילוח
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah says 'in non-sacred but not in sacred': the verse 'שלח תשלח את האם' implies one is commanded to send away the mother, but for a sacred bird one is commanded to bring it to the Temple treasury. Ravina then derives that a kosher bird that killed a person is exempt from שילוח, because one is commanded to bring it to court, not to send it away. The Gemara begins to clarify the case, asking if the bird's trial has concluded.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah exempts sacred birds from שילוח (sending away the mother bird).
The Gemara answers that the verse 'שלח תשלח את האם' implies one is commanded to send away the mother, but for a sacred bird one is commanded to bring it to the Temple treasury.
Ravina derives that a kosher bird that killed a person is exempt from שילוח, because one is commanded to bring it to court, not to send it away.
The Gemara begins to clarify the case, asking if the bird's trial has concluded.

items.text: Introduction: The case of a condemned person who hasn't been judged
items.text_en: Introduction: The case of a condemned person who hasn't been judged
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement refers to a person who is liable for death but whose trial is incomplete, and who is brought to court to fulfill the verse 'you shall purge the evil from your midst.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the condemned person is liable for death but his trial is incomplete, and he is brought to court to fulfill the verse 'you shall purge the evil from your midst.'

items.text: Analyzing the case of consecrated birds
items.text_en: Analyzing the case of consecrated birds
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines possible scenarios for consecrated birds in a nest. It rejects a bird's nest in one's house (since it's 'prepared'), and a random nest (since one cannot consecrate what isn't his). It then considers taking the chicks and consecrating them (but the owner is exempt from shiluach if he returns them). Finally, it settles on the case where one took the mother bird, consecrated her, and she returned, citing a baraita that one is liable for shiluach if the consecration occurred after the obligation arose.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the case of consecrated birds is, and rejects the possibility of a nest in one's house because the verse 'when a bird's nest happens before you' excludes a prepared (מזומן) nest.
The Gemara rejects the possibility of consecrating a random nest, since one cannot consecrate what is not in his domain, as derived from the verse 'when a man consecrates his house'.

The Gemara rejects the case where one took the chicks, consecrated them, and returned them, because even with non-consecrated birds one is exempt from shiluach (sending away) if the mother returns to the chicks.

The Gemara resolves that the case is where one took the mother bird, consecrated her, and she returned, citing a baraita of Rabbi Yochanan ben Yosef that one is liable for covering the blood if the consecration occurred after the obligation arose.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute
items.desc_en: Rav says the case involves consecrating the produce of one's dovecote or beehive, while Shmuel says it involves consecrating one's chicken for Temple maintenance (bedek habayit).

sub.desc_en: Rav states that the case involves consecrating the produce of one's dovecote or beehive, which then rebelled (flew away).
Shmuel states that the case involves consecrating one's chicken for Temple maintenance (בדק הבית), which then rebelled.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav doesn't accept Shmuel's view. Rav explains that his case involves items consecrated for the altar (kodshei mizbe'ach), whose sanctity is inherent and cannot be voided, so they are exempt from shiluach. But consecrating a chicken for bedek habayit (temple maintenance) has only monetary sanctity, which can be voided if the chicken rebels, making it liable for shiluach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav does not accept Shmuel's view, given that Shmuel's explanation is understandable.

Rav explains that his case involves items consecrated for the altar (קדשי מזבח), whose inherent sanctity cannot be voided, so they are exempt from shiluach; but consecrating a chicken for bedek habayit has only monetary sanctity, which can be voided if the chicken rebels, making it liable for shiluach.

items.text: Shmuel's reasoning and the dispute with Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Shmuel's reasoning and the dispute with Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: Shmuel argues that even a consecrated chicken remains in God's treasury, citing 'the earth is the Lord's'. Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel, but Reish Lakish objects that once it rebels, its sanctity is voided. Rabbi Yochanan responds with the same verse.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel argues that even a consecrated chicken that rebelled remains in God's treasury, citing the verse 'the earth is the Lord's and its fullness'.
Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Shmuel regarding a consecrated chicken that rebelled.
Reish Lakish objects that once the chicken rebels, its sanctity is voided.
Rabbi Yochanan responds that even after rebellion, the chicken remains in God's treasury, citing the same verse.

items.text: Contradictions in Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's views
items.text_en: Contradictions in Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's views
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes apparent contradictions in both Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish's positions regarding liability for lost consecrated items. It resolves Reish Lakish's contradiction by distinguishing between before and after hearing from his teacher. Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between saying 'upon me' (obligation) and 'this is' (designation).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises contradictions between Rabbi Yochanan's statements and between Reish Lakish's statements.
The Gemara cites a dispute where Rabbi Yochanan holds one is liable for lost consecrated money until it reaches the treasurer, while Reish Lakish holds it is always in God's treasury.
The Gemara resolves Reish Lakish's contradiction by distinguishing between before and after he heard from his teacher Rabbi Yochanan.
The Gemara resolves Rabbi Yochanan's contradiction by distinguishing between saying 'עָלַי' (upon me, creating a personal obligation) and 'הֲרֵי זוֹ' (this is, mere designation).

items.text: Reish Lakish's position on 'upon me' for bedek habayit
items.text_en: Reish Lakish's position on 'upon me' for bedek habayit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Reish Lakish holds that even saying 'upon me' for bedek habayit does not impose liability. It cites a baraita distinguishing between neder (obligation) and nedavah (donation) for altar sacrifices. Reish Lakish distinguishes between kodshei mizbe'ach (requiring offering) and kodshei bedek habayit (not requiring offering). A mishnah about a house or ox is reconciled by noting that liability only applies when the item is lost, but if it exists, it is considered in God's treasury.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the previous discussion that Reish Lakish holds that even saying 'עלי' (upon me) for bedek habayit does not impose liability.
The Gemara cites a baraita that distinguishes between neder (obligation) and nedavah (donation) for altar sacrifices, where neder imposes liability for loss but nedavah does not.

Reish Lakish distinguishes between קדשי מזבח (altar sanctity), which require offering and thus impose liability for loss, and קדשי בדק הבית (Temple treasury sanctity), which do not require offering and thus do not impose liability even with 'עלי'.
The Gemara objects by citing a mishnah that explicitly states that saying 'בית זה עלי קרבן' (this house upon me as a korban) imposes liability for loss, contradicting Reish Lakish's position.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the mishnah's liability applies only when the item is lost (dead or fallen), but if it still exists, it is considered to be in God's treasury and the person is not liable.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna's statement on valuations and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna's statement on valuations and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that all agree regarding valuations (arachin) that even saying 'upon me' does not impose liability, because the phrase 'upon me' is not used in the Torah for valuations. Rava objects, noting that one could say 'I am hereby for my valuation' or 'for the valuation of so-and-so'. A baraita from Rabbi Natan is cited to support that consecrated items and tithes can be redeemed and are not subject to liability if lost.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that all agree regarding valuations (ערכין) that even saying 'עלי' (upon me) does not impose liability, because the Torah does not use the phrase 'עלי' for valuations.

The Gemara questions how one could phrase a valuation vow without using 'עלי', asking: if one says 'ערכי' (my valuation), to whom does it refer? If one says 'ערך פלוני' (the valuation of so-and-so), to whom does it refer?
Rava objects, arguing that one could say 'הריני בערכי' (I am hereby for my valuation) or 'הריני בערך פלוני' (I am hereby for the valuation of so-and-so), thus using 'עלי' is not necessary.

A baraita from Rabbi Natan is cited, deriving from the verse 'ונתן את הערכך ביום ההוא קדש לה׳' that consecrated items and tithes, which can be redeemed, are not subject to liability if lost, supporting that valuations without 'עלי' do not impose liability.

items.text: Clarification of Rav Hamnuna's statement on valuations
items.text_en: Clarification of Rav Hamnuna's statement on valuations
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies a previous statement about valuations (arakhin). Rav Hamnuna says that everyone agrees that for valuations, even if one did not say 'upon me,' he is obligated, as the verse says 'and he shall give your valuation' – the animals are unconsecrated until they come into the hands of the treasurer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by raising the possibility that with regard to valuations, the consecrator might not bear financial responsibility, and then rejects it by citing the verse 'וְנָתַן אֶת הָעֶרְכְּךָ' (and he shall give your valuation), indicating the money is non-sacred until it enters the treasurer's possession.

Rav Hamnuna (רַב הַמְנוּנָא) clarifies that everyone agrees on valuations: even without saying 'עָלַי' (upon me), one is obligated, as the verse 'וְנָתַן אֶת הָעֶרְכְּךָ' (and he shall give your valuation) teaches that the animals are unconsecrated until they come into the treasurer's hands.

items.text: Derivation of the laws of shiluach haken from the verse
items.text_en: Derivation of the laws of shiluach haken from the verse
items.desc_en: The Tanna Kamma expounds the verse 'If a bird's nest chances before you' to derive various laws: it must be a chance find (not prepared), a kosher bird (not non-kosher), in private or public domain, in trees or on the ground. The verse 'before you in the way' teaches that it must be where the nest is not in your possession, excluding doves that nest in dovecotes or attics.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by citing the verse 'כי יקרא קן צפור לפניך' (If a bird's nest chances before you) and asks what additional teaching it comes to convey.

The baraita explains that since the verse says 'שלח תשלח' (you shall surely send), one might think one must search mountains and hills for a nest; therefore 'כי יקרא' teaches that the mitzvah applies only when the nest chances before you.

The baraita derives from each word of the verse: 'קן' (nest) applies in any case, 'צפור' (bird) means a kosher bird, 'לפניך' (before you) refers to private property, 'בדרך' (on the way) to public domain, and 'בכל עץ' (in any tree) and 'או על הארץ' (or on the ground) include trees and pits, ditches, and caves.

The baraita explains that 'לפניך בדרך' (before you on the way) teaches that the mitzvah applies only when the nest is not in your possession, excluding doves that nest in dovecotes or attics and domesticated pigeons, which are exempt from shiluach haken.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the derivation and Rav Yehuda's teaching
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the derivation and Rav Yehuda's teaching
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the phrase 'before you in the way' since 'chances' already excludes a prepared nest. It explains that 'before you' includes birds that were before you and fled, and 'in the way' is used for Rav Yehuda's teaching that a nest found in the sea is obligated, as the verse says 'who gives a way in the sea.' The Gemara rejects extending this to a nest in the sky.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the need for the word 'דרך' (way) in the verse, since the exclusion of a prepared nest is already derived from 'כי יקרא' (when it chances), and also questions the purpose of 'לפניך' (before you).

The Gemara explains that 'לפניך' includes birds that were before you and fled, and 'בדרך' is used for Rav Yehuda's teaching that a nest found in the sea is obligated, as the verse says 'who gives a way in the sea.'
The Gemara rejects extending the teaching to a nest found in the sky, since the verse 'דרך נשר' (way of an eagle) is a specific phrase, not the general term 'דרך' (way).

items.text: Aggadic allusions to biblical figures in the Torah
items.text_en: Aggadic allusions to biblical figures in the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a series of aggadic questions: finding a nest on a person's head, and allusions to Moses, Haman, Esther, and Mordechai in the Torah. Each is answered with a verse or wordplay.

sub.desc_en: The Papunai ask Rav Mattana whether a nest found on a person's head is subject to the mitzvah of shiluach haken.
Rav Mattana answers by citing the verse 'וַאֲדָמָה עַל רֹאשׁוֹ' (and earth upon his head), implying that a person's head is considered like earth, so the nest is subject to the mitzvah.
The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah is there an allusion to Moses?
The Gemara answers that the word 'בְּשַׁגַּם' (beshagam) in the verse 'בְּשַׁגַּם הוּא בָּשָׂר' alludes to Moses, as the numerical value of 'בשגם' equals that of 'משה'.
The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah is there an allusion to Haman?
The Gemara answers that the word 'הֲמִן' (hamin) in the verse 'הֲמִן הָעֵץ' alludes to Haman.
The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah is there an allusion to Esther?
The Gemara answers that the word 'אַסְתִּיר' (astir) in the verse 'וְאָנֹכִי הַסְתֵּר אַסְתִּיר' alludes to Esther.
The Gemara asks: from where in the Torah is there an allusion to Mordechai?
The Gemara answers that the phrase 'מׇר דְּרוֹר' (mor dror) in the Torah alludes to Mordechai, as the Targum translates it as 'מֵירָא דַּכְיָא' (pure myrrh).

items.text: Dispute about the name 'Hordasiyot' and a story of doves
items.text_en: Dispute about the name 'Hordasiyot' and a story of doves
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon about the correct name for a type of dove: 'Hardasiyot' (named after Herod) or 'Hadrasiyot' (named after their place). Rav Kahana tells a story about seeing such doves that would say 'kiri kiri,' and one that couldn't, leading to its slaughter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon about the name of a type of dove: one teaches 'Hadrasiyot' (named after Herod) and the other 'Hardasiyot' (named after their place).
Rav Kahana recounts seeing such doves that would say 'kiri kiri,' and one that could not, leading to its slaughter.
Rav Ashi reports that Rabbi Chanina said the doves spoke in words (מילין), and corrects the phrasing to 'in words' (במילין).

items.text: Proof that non-kosher birds are exempt from shiluach haken
items.text_en: Proof that non-kosher birds are exempt from shiluach haken
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak derives from the verse that only a kosher bird (called 'tzipor') is obligated, not a non-kosher one. The Gemara brings several attempted proofs from other verses that 'tzipor' includes non-kosher birds, but each is refuted by distinguishing between 'tzipor' (kosher) and 'kanaf' (non-kosher and locusts).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where is it derived that a non-kosher bird is exempt from the mitzva of sending away the mother bird?

רבי יצחק (Rabbi Yitzchak) answers: The verse says 'קן צפור' (a bird's nest), not 'קן עוף'; the word 'עוף' would include both kosher and non-kosher, but 'צפור' is only found for kosher birds, not for non-kosher ones.
The Gemara objects: Come and hear from the verse 'תבנית כל צפור כנף' (the likeness of any winged bird), where 'צפור' apparently includes both kosher and non-kosher, and 'כנף' adds locusts.
The Gemara rejects the objection: No, 'צפור' refers only to kosher birds, while 'כנף' refers to non-kosher birds and locusts.

The Gemara objects again: Come and hear from the verse 'החיה וכל בהמה רמש וצפור כנף' (the beast and all cattle, creeping things, and winged bird), where 'צפור' apparently includes both kosher and non-kosher, and 'כנף' adds locusts.
The Gemara rejects again: No, 'צפור' refers only to kosher birds, while 'כנף' refers to non-kosher birds and locusts.
The Gemara objects: Come and hear from the verse 'כל צפור כל כנף' (every bird of every wing), asking whether it is not as we previously challenged.
The Gemara rejects: No, it is as we resolved, distinguishing 'צפור' as kosher and 'כנף' as non-kosher and locusts.
The Gemara objects: Come and hear from the verse 'ואתה בן אדם אמור לצפור כל כנף' (And you, son of man, say to every bird of every wing), asking whether it is not as we challenged.
The Gemara rejects: No, it is as we resolved, distinguishing 'צפור' as kosher and 'כנף' as non-kosher and locusts.
The Gemara introduces another attempted proof, but the text breaks off.

items.text: Opening question on the term 'birds'
items.text_en: Opening question on the term 'birds'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the term 'birds' in Daniel 4:9 refers specifically to 'birds of the sky' or just 'birds' in general, implying a distinction between kosher and non-kosher birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the term 'birds' in Daniel 4:9 refers specifically to 'birds of the sky' or just 'birds' in general, implying a distinction between kosher and non-kosher birds.

items.text: Analysis of 'every clean bird'
items.text_en: Analysis of 'every clean bird'
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the verse 'every clean bird' to determine if it implies the existence of non-kosher birds, and discusses whether the exclusion refers to treifa or the slaughter of a leper, concluding that the context of slaughter applies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse 'every clean bird' and asks whether it implies the existence of unclean birds, concluding it implies forbidden birds.
The Gemara objects that the forbidden bird cannot be a treifa (טריפה) since that is explicitly written, nor the slaughter of a leper since that is derived from the end of the verse.

The Gemara resolves that the forbidden bird is indeed the slaughter of a leper, serving to impose both a positive and negative commandment, and rejects the alternative of treifa because the context is about slaughter.

items.text: Interpretation of 'live birds' in the metzora ritual
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'live birds' in the metzora ritual
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'live birds' in the context of the metzora, suggesting it implies some birds are not 'live in your mouth', and then considers whether 'clean' implies non-kosher or treifa birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the phrase 'live birds' (שתי צפרים חיות) implies that some birds are not 'live in your mouth' (i.e., not fit for the ritual).
The Gemara answers that 'live' means their limbs' heads are alive (i.e., not severed), not that they are alive in your mouth.
The Gemara asks from the end of the verse 'clean birds' whether it implies there are unclean birds.
The Gemara answers that 'clean' implies there are טריפות (ritually unfit birds), not unclean ones.

items.text: Debate on treifa and the derivation from Rabbi Yishmael's school
items.text_en: Debate on treifa and the derivation from Rabbi Yishmael's school
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that treifa birds are excluded from 'live', but this depends on whether a treifa is considered alive. It then cites a baraisa from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that draws an analogy between inner and outer sacrificial birds to equate the qualifying and atoning birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how treifot are excluded from 'חַיּוֹת' (live birds), noting that this works only for one who holds a treifa is alive, but asks what can be said for one who holds it is not alive.
The Gemara cites a baraisa from the school of Rabbi Yishmael that draws an analogy between the qualifying (מכשיר) and atoning (מכפר) birds in the inner and outer sacrificial contexts.

The baraisa concludes that just as in the inner service the qualifying bird is equated to the atoning bird, so too in the outer service the qualifying bird is equated to the atoning bird, thereby excluding treifot.

items.text: Four Amoraim's exclusions for the metzora's birds
items.text_en: Four Amoraim's exclusions for the metzora's birds
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, Rava, Rav Pappa, and Ravina each propose different exclusions from the metzora's birds: birds of an apostate city, pairing another bird before sending, birds exchanged for idolatry, and a bird that killed a person before verdict.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proposes that the word 'kosher' excludes birds of an apostate city, and clarifies that this disqualification applies to slaughter, not sending.
Rava says the word 'kosher' excludes pairing another bird with it before its sending, and specifies that this applies to sending, not slaughter.
Ravina says the word 'kosher' excludes a bird that killed a person before its verdict, and clarifies that this disqualifies it for slaughter, not sending.

items.text: Application of 'take for yourself' to shiluach hakan
items.text_en: Application of 'take for yourself' to shiluach hakan
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of a non-kosher bird sitting on kosher eggs, and applies Rav Kahana's principle that 'take for yourself' excludes taking for your dogs, extending this to treifa birds and their chicks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah exempts one from shiluach hakan when a kosher bird sits on non-kosher eggs, since the bird itself is a kosher צפור (bird).
