The Gemara answers by applying Rav Kahana's principle that the verse 'תקח לך' (you may take for yourself) excludes taking for your dogs, so non-kosher eggs are not fit for taking.
The Gemara asks where Rav Kahana's statement was originally said, and cites a ברייתא (baraita) about a טריפה (terefa) mother and chicks, with Rav Kahana's derivation from the verse.
The Gemara objects by suggesting a קל וחומר (a fortiori) argument: if טריפה (terefa) chicks exempt one from shiluach, then a טריפה (terefa) mother should also be exempt.

items.text: Clarification of the verse regarding a terefah mother
items.text_en: Clarification of the verse regarding a terefah mother
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the verse needs to exclude a non-kosher bird if it already excludes a terefah mother. Abaye explains that the case is actually about a chick whose mother is terefah, which is still obligated in sending away.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the verse needs the word 'צפור' (bird) to exclude a non-kosher bird, if a terefah mother is already excluded.
Abaye answers that the case is about a chick whose mother is terefah, which is still obligated in sending away, so the verse excludes a non-kosher bird.

items.text: Rav Hoshaya's query about slaughtering part of the simanim
items.text_en: Rav Hoshaya's query about slaughtering part of the simanim
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether reaching into the nest and slaughtering only a minority of the simanim (signs of kosher slaughter) obligates sending away the mother, since the bird is still alive. The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether reaching into the nest and slaughtering only a minority of the simanim (signs of kosher slaughter) obligates sending away the mother, since the bird is still alive.

The Gemara presents two possible interpretations: either the bird is considered already designated for dogs (פטור) or, since the slaughter can be completed, it is still considered taken for oneself (חייב).
The Gemara leaves the question unresolved (תיקו).

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's queries about various partitions and egg arrangements
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's queries about various partitions and egg arrangements
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a cloth, wings, spoiled eggs, two rows of eggs, or a male on top of eggs with a female on top of the male constitute a valid nest for the obligation of sending away. All questions remain unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a cloth or wings interposed between the mother and the eggs invalidates the nest for the obligation of sending away.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether spoiled eggs, two rows of eggs, or a male on top of eggs with a female on top of the male constitute a valid nest; all questions remain unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's query about a dove on partridge eggs and vice versa
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's query about a dove on partridge eggs and vice versa
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about the obligation when a dove sits on partridge eggs or a partridge on dove eggs. Abaye brings a baraita that a non-kosher bird on kosher eggs or kosher on non-kosher eggs is exempt, implying that kosher on kosher is obligated, but the Gemara deflects that the case might involve a partridge.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about the obligation of shiluach (sending away the mother) when a dove sits on partridge eggs or a partridge on dove eggs.
Abaye cites a baraita that a non-kosher bird on kosher eggs or kosher on non-kosher eggs is exempt from shiluach, implying that kosher on kosher eggs is obligated.
The Gemara deflects that the baraita might refer to a partridge (קורא), not a dove, leaving the query unresolved.

items.text: Dispute about a male partridge (korei zachar)
items.text_en: Dispute about a male partridge (korei zachar)
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a male partridge (korei zachar). Rabbi Eliezer obligates sending away, while the Sages exempt. Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning via a gezerah shavah. Rabbi Elazar clarifies that the dispute is only about a male partridge, but a female partridge is obligated by all, and a regular male bird is exempt by all. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer obligates sending away a male partridge, while the Sages exempt.
Rabbi Avahu explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning via a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) from the word 'דְּגִירָה' (brooding) used in two verses.
Rabbi Elazar clarifies that the dispute is only about a male partridge, but a female partridge is obligated by all, and the Mishnah's wording 'male' is to show Rabbi Eliezer's stringency.
Rabbi Elazar further clarifies that a regular male bird is exempt by all, and the Mishnah's mention of 'male partridge' is to show the Sages' leniency.
A baraita supports Rabbi Elazar's distinction: a regular male bird is exempt, a male partridge is disputed between Rabbi Eliezer (obligates) and the Sages (exempt).

items.text: Mishnah: Cases of a hovering mother and non-viable eggs/chicks
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cases of a hovering mother and non-viable eggs/chicks
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if the mother is hovering but her wings touch the nest, one is obligated to send her away; if not, exempt. If there is only one chick or egg, one is obligated. If the chicks can fly or the eggs are spoiled, one is exempt, based on the verse requiring viable eggs and chicks that need their mother.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the first case: if the mother is hovering with wings touching the nest, one is obligated to send her away; if only one chick or egg is present, one is obligated because the verse says 'קן' (nest) in any case.
The Mishnah states the second case: if the chicks can fly or the eggs are spoiled, one is exempt, based on the verse requiring viable eggs and chicks that need their mother.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the case of a hovering mother and the dispute with Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the case of a hovering mother and the dispute with Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that 'rovetzes' excludes a hovering mother, but if her wings touch the nest, she is considered rovetzes. Rav Yehuda says that if the mother sits between two branches, we see if she would fall on them when shaken. A challenge is raised from a baraita, and the Gemara resolves it by distinguishing between touching from the side and touching from above. Rabbi Yirmeya explains that the Mishnah's case is when the wings touch from the side.

sub.desc_en: The baraita teaches that 'רובצת' (hovering) excludes a hovering mother, and deduces from the word 'רובצת' rather than 'יושבת' that even if wings touch the nest, she is still considered hovering.

Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if the mother sits between two branches, we see whether she would fall on the eggs when shaken; if so, she is considered רובצת and obligated in shiluach, otherwise exempt.

The Gemara raises a challenge from a baraita that distinguishes between sitting between them (exempt) and on top of them (obligated), implying that sitting between branches is exempt, contradicting Rav Yehuda.

The Gemara initially interprets the baraita: just as 'between them' means touching them, so too 'on top of them' means touching them, but sitting on branches (רובדי אילן) is exempt, challenging Rav Yehuda.

The Gemara resolves: the baraita means that 'on top of them' is like 'between them' in that she does not touch them, and this is precisely the case of sitting on branches (רובדי אילן), supporting Rav Yehuda.
The Gemara argues logically: if sitting on branches were exempt, the baraita should have mentioned that case first, as it is more obvious than a hovering mother.
The Gemara counters that the case of a hovering mother was necessary to teach that even if her wings touch the nest, she is exempt, which is not obvious from the branch case.
The Gemara objects that our Mishnah explicitly states that when the mother's wings touch the nest, she is obligated in shiluach, contradicting the baraita's ruling.

Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah's case where wings touch the nest refers to touching from the side, not from above, so the baraita's ruling about hovering from above is consistent.

items.text: Alternative version of the dispute about the baraita
items.text_en: Alternative version of the dispute about the baraita
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the Gemara presents the same baraita as supporting Rav Yehuda's position, but the Gemara rejects this by reinterpreting the baraita's cases, concluding that sitting between branches is exempt.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version proposes that the baraita supports Rav Yehuda's position.
The Gemara asks whether the baraita's case of sitting above them is analogous to sitting between them, where the bird is not touching from above, thus supporting Rav Yehuda's ruling about branches.
The Gemara rejects the analogy, explaining that sitting above them requires touching, and sitting between branches is exempt, as shown by the baraita's emphasis on hovering.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's wording
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'rovedei ilan' (birds that perch on trees) separately from 'me'ofefet' (a hovering bird), since the latter is a subset of the former. Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah refers to a case where the wings touch the nest from the side.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah lists 'rovedei ilan' (birds that perch on trees) separately from 'me'ofefet' (a hovering bird), since the latter is a subset of the former, and suggests that even if the wings touch the nest, one is exempt from sending the mother.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah elsewhere teaches that if the wings touch the nest, one is obligated to send the mother, contradicting the previous suggestion.
Rav Yehuda answers that the Mishnah's case is where the wings touch the nest from the side, not from above, resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Derivation from the verse about eggs and chicks
items.text_en: Derivation from the verse about eggs and chicks
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi suggests to Rava that if there is only one chick or one egg, one is exempt from sending the mother, requiring 'chicks or eggs' in plural. The Gemara then derives from the verse that chicks and eggs are analogous to each other.

sub.text: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi proposes to Rava that the Mishnah should be reversed: if there is only one chick or one egg, one is exempt from sending the mother, because the verse requires 'chicks or eggs' in the plural.
The Gemara states that if there are fledgling chicks or spoiled eggs, one is obligated to send the mother, because the term 'קן' (nest) applies in any case.
The Gemara resolves that the verse's extra wording 'על האפרוחים או על הביצים' serves to equate chicks and eggs for the law of sending the mother.

items.text: Mishnah: Repeated sending and taking the mother
items.text_en: Mishnah: Repeated sending and taking the mother
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sends the mother and she returns, even multiple times, one is obligated to send her again. If one says 'I will take the mother and send the children,' he is obligated. If he took the children and returned them to the nest, and the mother returned, he is exempt.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one sends the mother and she returns, even multiple times, one is obligated to send her again, based on the verse 'שַׁלֵּחַ תְּשַׁלַּח'.
The Mishnah adds that if one says 'I will take the mother and send the children,' he is obligated to send the mother, again based on the same verse.
The Mishnah concludes that if one takes the children and returns them to the nest, and then the mother returns to them, he is exempt from sending the mother.

items.text: Gemara: Derivation from double verb
items.text_en: Gemara: Derivation from double verb
items.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the double verb 'shale'ach teshale'ach' is needed. Rava explains that 'shale'ach' implies even a hundred times, and 'teshale'ach' teaches that even for a mitzvah one must send the mother.

sub.text: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.text_en: A certain rabbi's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: A certain rabbi asks Rava why the Mishnah requires sending the mother multiple times, suggesting that 'שַׁלֵּחַ' means once and 'תְּשַׁלַּח' means twice.
Rava answers that 'שַׁלֵּחַ' implies even a hundred times, and 'תְּשַׁלַּח' teaches that the obligation applies even for a mitzvah matter, not just a discretionary one.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's question and resolution
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Yosef bar Rava asks Rav Kahana that without the extra word, one might think a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment. The Gemara answers that the case is where one already took the mother, violating the negative commandment, and the positive commandment of sending comes to override the positive commandment of not taking.

sub.text: Rabbi Abba's objection to Rav Kahana
sub.text_en: Rabbi Abba's objection to Rav Kahana
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba objects that without the extra word 'תְּשַׁלַּח', one might think that a positive commandment does not override a negative commandment combined with a positive one, but here the positive commandment of sending the mother would not override the prohibition of taking the mother.

The Gemara answers that the verse is needed for a case where one already took the mother, violating only a positive commandment, and teaches that the positive commandment of sending the mother overrides the positive commandment of not taking her.

items.text: Objections based on different Tannaitic views
items.text_en: Objections based on different Tannaitic views
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises objections: according to the one who says 'kiyemo v'lo kiyemo' (fulfilled and not fulfilled), the case is different. According to Rabbi Yehuda who says 'shale'ach' from the beginning implies, there is no positive commandment at all.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous resolution works only for the Tanna who holds the principle of 'קִיְּימוֹ וְלֹא קִיְּימוֹ' (fulfilled and not fulfilled), but for the one who holds 'בִּטְּלוֹ וְלֹא בִּטְּלוֹ' (nullified and not nullified), as long as one does not slaughter the mother, one does not violate the negative commandment.
The Gemara further objects that according to Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that 'שַׁלֵּחַ' (send) from the beginning implies the obligation, there is no positive commandment at all in this case.

items.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's resolution and analogy
items.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's resolution and analogy
items.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi explains the case as one who took the mother with intent to send her, so there is no violation of the negative commandment, only a positive commandment. The Gemara then discusses why this positive commandment overrides another positive commandment, using the example of a metzora (leper) who is forbidden from marital relations.

sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi resolves the difficulty by positing a case where one took the mother bird with intent to send her, so there is no violation of the negative commandment, only a positive commandment, and the positive commandment of sending should override the positive commandment of taking.
The Gemara questions why the positive commandment of sending the mother should override the positive commandment of taking, asking what is the strength of this positive commandment over that one.

The Gemara explains that one might think the positive commandment of marital peace (שלום בית) is greater, since the Torah allows God's holy name to be erased for the sake of peace between a husband and wife.

The Gemara concludes that the case of a metzora (leper) who is forbidden from marital relations until purification teaches that the positive commandment of sending the mother overrides the positive commandment of taking, despite the leper's prohibition.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one takes the mother with the children, Rabbi Yehuda says he is lashed and does not send, while the Sages say he sends and is not lashed. The general rule is that for any negative commandment that has a positive commandment to rectify it, one is not lashed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one who takes the mother with the children is flogged and does not send her, while the Sages say he sends her and is not flogged, with the general rule that for a negative commandment that includes a positive commandment, one is not flogged.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's inquiry and proof
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Abba bar Memel's inquiry and proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel questions whether Rabbi Yehuda's opinion is because he holds that one is lashed for a 'lav hanitak l'aseh' (negative commandment that is rectified by a positive commandment), or because he holds 'shale'ach' from the beginning implies. A proof is brought from a Mishnah about a thief and robber, showing Rabbi Yehuda holds one is lashed for such a lav hanitak l'aseh.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba bar Memel raises a dilemma: is Rabbi Yehuda's ruling because he holds that one is flogged for a לאו שניתק לעשה (prohibition that is rectified by a positive command)?
Or perhaps Rabbi Yehuda generally holds that one is not flogged for such a prohibition, but here the reason is because he interprets 'שַׁלֵּחַ' (send) as applying from the outset.

The Gemara brings a proof from a baraita about a thief and robber, where Rabbi Yehuda holds they are flogged despite the prohibition being a לאו שניתק לעשה (prohibition rectified by a positive command), concluding that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that one is flogged for such a prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's comment on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's comment on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira says that he told them that any Mishnah that is not taught in the study hall... (the text is cut off).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira begins a statement, saying that he told them that any Mishnah that is not taught in the study hall...

items.text: Rejection of a previous proof
items.text_en: Rejection of a previous proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and the school of Rabbi Oshaya dismiss a previously cited baraita as a corrupted text, warning not to use it as a proof in the study hall, because it may have been taught in the context of the general category of lashes.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya and the school of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya and the school of Rabbi Oshaya
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya and the school of Rabbi Oshaya dismiss a baraita as a corrupted text, warning not to use it as a proof in the study hall, because it may have been taught in the context of the general category of lashes.

items.text: Proof from Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
items.text_en: Proof from Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita taught by Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya stating that Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who violates 'do not return' or 'do not destroy' is liable to lashes. The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that a לאו שניתק לעשה is punishable by lashes, but it is rejected with the alternative explanation that Rabbi Yehuda interprets 'you shall surely let go' as referring to the initial act.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita taught by Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Chiyya stating that Rabbi Yehuda holds one who violates 'do not return' or 'do not destroy' is liable to lashes.
The Gemara infers that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that a לאו שניתק לעשה (a prohibition coupled with a positive commandment) is punishable by lashes.

The Gemara rejects the inference, suggesting that Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning there is that the verse 'you shall surely let go' refers to the initial act, not that a לאו שניתק לעשה is punishable by lashes.

items.text: Proof from the Paschal lamb
items.text_en: Proof from the Paschal lamb
items.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof to Rav Ashi from the verse regarding the Paschal lamb, where Rabbi Yehuda says that the positive commandment after the negative indicates no lashes. The Gemara concludes that this proves Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that 'send' refers to the initial act.

sub.desc_en: Ravina brings a proof to Rav Ashi from the Paschal lamb verse, where Rabbi Yehuda says the positive commandment after the negative indicates no lashes.

The Gemara concludes that this proves Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning is that 'שַׁלֵּחַ' (send) refers to the initial act, not that the negative is a לאו שניתק לעשה (a prohibition that can be rectified by a positive command).

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Idi brings a proof to Rav Ashi from the Mishnah, where Rabbi Yehuda says 'he is lashed and does not send'. If Rabbi Yehuda held that a לאו שניתק לעשה is punishable by lashes, he should have said 'he is lashed and sends'. The Gemara deflects by suggesting the Mishnah means he is not exempt until he is lashed.

sub.text: Rav Idi's proof to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Idi's proof to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Idi argues from the Mishnah that if Rabbi Yehuda held a לאו שניתק לעשה (a prohibition coupled with a positive commandment) is punishable by lashes, the Mishnah should have said 'he is lashed and sends', not 'he is lashed and does not send'.
The Gemara deflects by suggesting the Mishnah means he is not exempt from sending until he is lashed, not that he is exempt from sending entirely.

items.text: How to send the mother bird
items.text_en: How to send the mother bird
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the distance and manner of sending the mother bird. Rav Yehuda says she must go out from under his hand, and there is a dispute between Rav Huna (by its feet) and Rav Yehuda (by its wings), each citing a verse.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks up to what distance one must send the mother bird, and Rav Yehuda answers that she must go out from under his hand.
The Gemara asks by which part of the bird one sends her, and Rav Huna answers by her feet, citing a verse.
Rav Yehuda argues that one sends the bird by its wings, since they are its wings.

items.text: Case of clipping wings and sending
items.text_en: Case of clipping wings and sending
items.desc_en: A man clipped the mother bird's wings, sent her, and then took her again. Rav Yehuda had him flogged and told him to go grow her wings and send her. The Gemara questions this: according to Rabbi Yehuda he is lashed and does not send, according to the Rabbis he sends and is not lashed. The answer is that it was according to the Rabbis, and the lashes were rabbinic lashes of rebellion.

sub.desc_en: A man clipped the mother bird's wings, sent her, and then took her again.
Rav Yehuda had the man flogged and told him to go grow her wings and send her.
The Gemara questions how Rav Yehuda could both flog and require sending, since according to Rabbi Yehuda one is flogged and does not send, and according to the Rabbis one sends and is not flogged.
The Gemara resolves that the ruling follows the Rabbis, and the flogging was a rabbinic lashes of rebellion (מכת מרדות).

items.text: Case of a single egg and Rava's action
items.text_en: Case of a single egg and Rava's action
items.desc_en: A man came before Rava asking about a single egg. Rava initially thought he didn't know the law, but the man clarified he knew. Rava cited the Mishnah that one is obligated to send even for one egg. The man sent it, and Rava gave him a document and took the egg. The Gemara notes there is no concern for suspicion since it was after the fact.

sub.desc_en: A man came before Rava asking about a single egg; Rava initially thought the man didn't know the basic law of sending away the mother bird.
The man clarified that he knew the law but was asking about a single egg, and Rava confirmed he understood.
Rava cited the Mishnah that one is obligated to send away even a single egg or chick.

sub.text: Narrative: man sends, Rava gives document and takes egg
sub.text_en: Narrative: man sends, Rava gives document and takes egg
sub.desc_en: The man sent the egg, and Rava gave him a document and took the egg.
The Gemara notes there is no concern for suspicion since it was after the fact (כִּלְאַחַר יָד).

items.text: Doves of a dovecote and the principle of acquisition
items.text_en: Doves of a dovecote and the principle of acquisition
items.desc_en: The Rabbis taught that doves of a dovecote are obligated in sending but forbidden due to theft because of the ways of peace. The Gemara questions this based on Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle that one's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge. Rabba answers that the obligation applies before the egg falls into the courtyard. The Gemara then discusses the reason for the prohibition of theft, and concludes with an explanation involving a minor and his father's obligation to return due to the ways of peace.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that doves of a dovecote or attic are obligated in sending away the mother, but are forbidden due to robbery because of the ways of peace.

The Gemara objects: If Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina's principle that one's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge applies, then the verse 'כי יקרה' (if it happens) excludes readily available items, contradicting the baraita.
Rabba answers: The obligation to send away applies when the majority of the egg has emerged, but acquisition by the courtyard only occurs when it falls; the baraita refers to before it falls.
The Gemara asks: If so, why are they forbidden due to robbery? It answers: The prohibition refers to the mother, or alternatively, once the majority emerges, the owner's mind is on the egg.
Rav Yehuda citing Rav adds: It is prohibited to acquire eggs the mother is resting on, and the courtyard cannot acquire what the owner cannot acquire himself.
The Gemara asks: If so, why are they only forbidden due to the ways of peace? If one sent away the mother, it is full robbery; if not, he must send her away.
The Gemara answers: The case involves a minor; the father of the minor is obligated to return the eggs due to the ways of peace.

items.text: Acquisition of dovecote fruits by Levi bar Simon
items.text_en: Acquisition of dovecote fruits by Levi bar Simon
items.desc_en: Levi bar Simon transferred the fruits of his dovecote to Rav Yehuda. He came before Shmuel, who told him to go shake the nest so the birds would fly up and be acquired. The Gemara questions why this was necessary, suggesting a sudar acquisition or a Yom Tov issue.

sub.desc_en: Levi bar Simon transferred ownership of the produce of his dovecote to Rav Yehuda.
Shmuel instructed Rav Yehuda to go bang on the nest so the birds would rise up and be acquired.
The Gemara questions why this action was necessary, suggesting acquisition by means of a cloth (סודר) would suffice.
The Gemara raises an alternative possibility that the incident occurred on a festival day (יום טוב), which would explain the need for a different procedure.

items.text: Conclusion of previous sugya on acquisition
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous sugya on acquisition
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a previous issue about acquiring fruit by explaining that Levi bar Simon did not yet own them, and instructed the agent to first acquire them for himself and then transfer them via a sudar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the previous sugya by explaining that Levi bar Simon did not yet own the fruit, so he instructed the agent to first acquire them for himself and then transfer them via a sudar (kerchief).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Prohibition of taking mother with young
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Prohibition of taking mother with young
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not take a mother bird with its young, even for purifying a leper, and derives a kal vachomer that if a light commandment like shiluach haken promises long life, certainly heavy commandments do.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the prohibition of taking a mother bird with its young, even for purifying a leper, and derives a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) that reward for light commandments implies greater reward for heavy ones.

items.text: Rabbi Yaakov's teaching: Reward is in the World to Come
items.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov's teaching: Reward is in the World to Come
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov teaches that every mitzvah's reward is stated alongside it, but it refers to the World to Come. He illustrates with a story of a son who fulfilled both honoring parents and shiluach haken, yet died immediately, showing the reward is not in this world.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov teaches that every mitzvah's reward is stated alongside it, but it refers to the World to Come, citing the examples of honoring parents and shiluach haken.
Rabbi Yaakov illustrates with a story of a son who fulfilled both honoring parents and shiluach haken, yet died immediately, showing the reward is not in this world.
Rabbi Yaakov concludes that the reward of 'long days' and 'goodness' refers to the World to Come, not this world.

items.text: Gemara's challenges and defense of the story
items.text_en: Gemara's challenges and defense of the story
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the story: perhaps it didn't happen, or the son was sinning. It defends Rabbi Yaakov by saying he saw it happen, and bad thoughts are not joined to action. It then suggests that if reward existed in this world, it would protect from such thoughts, concluding there is no reward in this world. It addresses a contradiction with Rabbi Elazar's statement that messengers of mitzvot are not harmed, distinguishing return journeys.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the story actually happened.
The Gemara answers that Rabbi Yaakov himself witnessed the event.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the son was sinning by having bad thoughts, and answers that bad thoughts are not joined to action by God.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the son was thinking about idolatry, citing a verse and Rav Acha bar Yaakov's statement that such thoughts are considered idolatry.
The Gemara resolves that if reward existed in this world, it would protect from such thoughts, concluding there is no reward in this world.
The Gemara objects with Rabbi Elazar's statement that messengers of a מצוה (commandment) are not harmed, and answers that the return journey is different.
The Gemara objects further that Rabbi Elazar said messengers are not harmed even on the return, and answers that a rickety ladder is a place of fixed danger, citing Samuel's fear of Saul.

items.text: Further challenge and resolution regarding messengers of mitzvot
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution regarding messengers of mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Elazar that messengers of mitzvot are not harmed even on return, but resolves that the ladder was rickety, a place of fixed danger, as per Samuel's concern about being killed by Saul.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the conclusion that there is no reward for mitzvot in this world by citing Rabbi Elazar's principle that messengers of mitzvot are not harmed.
The Gemara initially distinguishes that the protection applies only on the outward journey, not on the return.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar explicitly stated the protection applies both on the outward journey and on the return.

The Gemara resolves that the ladder was rickety, a place of fixed danger, which is different, citing Samuel's fear of being killed by Saul as a precedent for avoiding a place of fixed danger even for a mitzvah.

items.text: Elisha ben Avuya's fall and the lesson of reward
items.text_en: Elisha ben Avuya's fall and the lesson of reward
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says that if Elisha ben Avuya (Acher) had interpreted the verse like Rabbi Yaakov, he would not have sinned. The Gemara recounts what he saw: either a similar tragic event or the tongue of Rabbi Chutzpit the translator lying in the garbage, leading him to doubt reward, not knowing the reward is in the World to Come.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef comments that if Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) had interpreted this verse like Rabbi Yaakov his grandson, he would not have sinned; he either saw a similar incident or the tongue of Rabbi Chutzpit the Meturgeman in the trash, not knowing the reward is in the world-to-come.
The Gemara asks what Acher saw that led him to sin.
The Gemara offers two accounts: either Acher saw a similar tragic event, or he saw the tongue of Rabbi Chutzpit the translator lying in the garbage and despaired.
The Gemara explains that Acher did not know that the reward for these commandments is in the World to Come, which is entirely good and long.
